plantar branches decompressed inadequately Tarsal tunnel syndrome results from compression of the tibial nerve within the fibro-osseous tunnel behind the medial malleolus, deep to the flexor retinaculum. Raised pressure within this confined space may arise from space-occupying lesions, hindfoot valgus or other deformity, post-traumatic scarring, tenosynovitis or venous engorgement. Sustained compression impairs axonal transport and causes local demyelination, producing sensory disturbance in the plantar distribution and, in advanced cases, weakness and wasting of the intrinsic foot muscles. Outcomes are good when a discrete compressive cause such as a ganglion is identified and released, whereas idiopathic cases are less predictable and may have incomplete relief of symptoms.

and acute kidney injury risk during strenuous activity Tarui disease is caused by deficiency of the muscle subunit of phosphofructokinase, which catalyses the conversion of fructose-6-phosphate to fructose-1,6-bisphosphate, a committed and rate-limiting step of glycolysis. The block prevents muscle from using both stored glycogen and blood glucose for anaerobic energy production, so exercise capacity is limited and lactate fails to rise with exertion. Because ingested glucose cannot be utilised and instead suppresses the alternative free-fatty-acid fuel supply, a carbohydrate meal can paradoxically worsen exercise tolerance. The muscle-type PFK subunit is also expressed in erythrocytes, so its deficiency reduces red-cell glycolysis and causes a compensated haemolysis, with increased purine turnover contributing to hyperuricaemia. Most patients have a normal life expectancy with lifestyle adaptation, though exercise capacity is limited; recurrent rhabdomyolysis, complications of haemolysis, and gout are the main long-term concerns, and rare infantile-onset forms carry a poorer prognosis.

embouchure dystonia and the sporting yips are others The same muscles function normally during other activities, which is the defining feature Symptoms often begin as loss of fine control or cramping and progress to overt posturing as the task continues A sensory trick may temporarily relieve the dystonia in some patients It typically affects adults engaged in repetitive precision tasks and can be occupationally disabling Over time the dystonia may spread to related tasks, with loss of the original task specificity Dystonia at rest or spreading beyond the specific task, suggesting a secondary or generalising process Sensory loss, weakness or wasting suggesting a compressive or neuropathic lesion Young onset with additional neurological features suggesting an inherited dystonia Features of Wilson's disease in a younger patient Dismissing early symptoms as overuse injury or anxiety Not observing the patient performing the actual triggering task Neglecting the occupational and psychological impact Assuming permanent task specificity, when the dystonia can spread to related tasks Task-specific focal dystonia is thought to arise from maladaptive plasticity within the sensorimotor system, with reduced inhibition at cortical, subcortical and spinal levels and abnormal integration of sensory feedback with motor output. Extensive repetitive practice of a skilled task appears to drive aberrant cortical reorganisation that blurs the normally distinct representations of individual digits or muscles, so that performing the specific over-learned movement triggers involuntary co-contraction and abnormal posturing. Task-specific dystonia is generally chronic and spontaneous remission is uncommon, though severity can fluctuate. It is not life-threatening but may curtail or end a career dependent on the affected skill. Botulinum toxin injection targeted to the overactive muscles is a mainstay of treatment, and some patients benefit from retraining, ergonomic modification or a change of technique, with results that vary between individuals.

Tatton-Brown-Rahman syndrome — TBRS, DNMT3A overgrowth syndrome, DNMT3A-related overgrowth and intellectual disability Sotos syndrome (NSD1-related) Weaver syndrome (EZH2-related) Malan syndrome (NFIX-related) Cohen syndrome and other obesity-associated intellectual disability syndromes Fragile X syndrome Other chromatin- or methylation-related overgrowth disorders Exome or genome sequencing, or a targeted overgrowth/intellectual disability gene panel Chromosomal microarray to exclude copy number abnormalities Developmental, behavioural, and psychiatric assessment Full blood count and clinical review with a low threshold for haematology referral given malignancy risk Echocardiography if a congenital heart anomaly is suspected Spinal assessment for scoliosis This is an overgrowth-with-intellectual-disability syndrome featuring tall stature, macrocephaly, and a recognisable facial appearance with heavy, straight eyebrows and narrow palpebral fissures It is caused by heterozygous variants in DNMT3A, which encodes a DNA methyltransferase central to establishing DNA methylation patterns during development Intellectual disability is usually mild to moderate, and behavioural features including autistic traits and psychiatric symptoms are frequently reported Obesity and a tendency to a heavier build are common, and some individuals have joint hypermobility, scoliosis, or congenital heart anomalies Because somatic DNMT3A variants are recurrent drivers in haematological malignancy, there is a recognised predisposition to acute myeloid leukaemia and other blood cancers, warranting clinical vigilance Diagnosis is molecular, typically via exome or genome sequencing or an overgrowth/intellectual disability panel, after considering Sotos and Weaver syndromes There is no disease-specific therapy; management is anticipatory and multidisciplinary with developmental support and awareness of the haematological risk Unexplained cytopenias, easy bruising, recurrent infection, or constitutional symptoms suggesting haematological malignancy Rapid neurological change or regression prompting re-evaluation Progressive scoliosis with respiratory or neurological compromise Symptoms of a significant congenital cardiac lesion Diagnosing Sotos syndrome clinically and failing to test DNMT3A Overlooking the haematological malignancy predisposition when investigating cytopenias or constitutional symptoms Attributing obesity and behavioural difficulties to unrelated causes rather than the underlying syndrome Neglecting genetic counselling regarding the autosomal dominant, usually de novo, inheritance Tatton-Brown-Rahman syndrome is a chromatin-related overgrowth disorder caused by germline heterozygous variants in DNMT3A. This gene encodes a DNA methyltransferase responsible for de novo methylation of DNA, an epigenetic process that governs gene expression programmes during growth and neurodevelopment. Impaired DNMT3A function disturbs these methylation patterns, producing generalised overgrowth, macrocephaly, and neurodevelopmental features. Because the same gene is a recurrently mutated driver in myeloid malignancy at the somatic level, constitutional variants confer an increased lifetime risk of haematological cancers. Inheritance is autosomal dominant, and the majority of cases are de novo. Many individuals have a relatively stable course determined mainly by their level of intellectual disability and associated features. The recognised predisposition to haematological malignancy is an important long-term consideration and should prompt prompt evaluation of suggestive symptoms, though most patients do not develop cancer.

involves visceral storage Not offering carrier screening to at-risk populations before conception Attributing the exaggerated startle to a benign cause and delaying evaluation Tay-Sachs disease results from biallelic pathogenic variants in HEXA, which encodes the alpha subunit of the enzyme beta-hexosaminidase A. Deficient enzyme activity prevents degradation of GM2 ganglioside, which accumulates progressively within neuronal lysosomes of the central nervous system. Neuronal engorgement and dysfunction drive relentless neurodegeneration. Because storage is largely confined to neurons, visceral organomegaly is typically absent, distinguishing it from disorders such as Sandhoff disease, in which both hexosaminidase A and B are deficient. The infantile form is progressive and fatal, typically within the first few years of life. Juvenile-onset disease progresses more slowly with death in later childhood or adolescence, while late-onset forms have a more variable and protracted course. Management remains supportive.

The nervous system is especially vulnerable, producing profound hypotonia, developmental impairment, white matter disease and, in severe cases, progressive neurodegeneration, while the severity varies with the specific genotype including the severe founder variant. Outcome varies widely with genotype: milder cases have static severe developmental impairment, whereas the severe form, including the founder variant, is often progressive with neurodegeneration, respiratory compromise and shortened survival; care is supportive, centring on feeding, respiratory management, seizure control and developmental support.

As in other mastocytosis, clonal mast cells (often KIT-associated) release mediators, though the weal-and-flare response is frequently muted. Because it presents in adults, it is regarded, like other adult cutaneous mastocytosis, as potentially reflecting underlying systemic mast cell disease. The cutaneous lesions are persistent but benign; prognosis is influenced by any associated systemic mastocytosis, which should be sought given the adult onset.

precipitant Reassurance about the reversible nature is central, and treating any identified underlying cause such as iron repletion or thyroid correction is the mainstay rather than specific hair the presumed trigger Associated systemic symptoms pointing to occult illness or malignancy Patchy rather than diffuse loss suggesting alopecia areata or tinea capitis Attributing all diffuse shedding to effluvium and overlooking early androgenetic alopecia or diffuse alopecia areata Looking back only to when shedding began rather than two to three months earlier for the true trigger Missing a treatable systemic cause such as iron deficiency or thyroid disease Reassuring a patient without excluding a scarring process on close scalp examination Telogen effluvium results from a disturbance of the normal hair cycle in which an abnormally large proportion of follicles are prematurely shifted from the growing (anagen) phase into the resting (telogen) phase. After a latency of roughly two to three months these synchronised telogen hairs are shed as new anagen hairs emerge beneath them. Recognised triggers include physiological stress such as childbirth, febrile illness and major surgery, rapid weight loss, iron and other nutritional deficiency, thyroid disturbance, and numerous drugs. Because the follicles themselves are not destroyed and the ostia remain intact, the process is non-scarring and reverses once the precipitant resolves. Acute telogen effluvium is self-limiting and typically resolves with full regrowth over several months once the trigger has passed; chronic telogen effluvium may fluctuate over years but does not itself cause permanent baldness, although it can unmask underlying androgenetic thinning.

Giant cell (temporal) arteritis — ESR / CRP (markedly raised) Temporal artery biopsy Start high-dose steroids if suspected Visual loss is an emergency — do not delay steroids Migraine - common in the elderly (more prevalent than GCA) and may improve with prednisone, so a steroid response does not by itself confirm GCA (Harrison 22e p.115). Nonarteritic anterior ischemic optic neuropathy - associated with a crowded 'disc-at-risk' / small optic cup, in which glucocorticoids should NOT be prescribed, contrasting with the arteritic form (Harrison 22e p.227). Isolated polymyalgia rheumatica without arteritis (Harrison 22e p.2903). Other inflammatory causes of secondary headache such as sarcoidosis and Behcet's syndrome (Harrison 22e p.115). Temporal artery biopsy: yield improved by harvesting a long segment (3-5 cm) with serial sectioning because involvement is segmental/patchy; biopsy may still show vasculitis even after about 14 days of glucocorticoids, but prolonged treatment can mask findings (Harrison 22e p.227, p.2903). Temporal artery ultrasonography (alone or with axillary arteries) showing a noncompressible 'halo' sign supports the diagnosis (Harrison 22e p.2903). Large-vessel imaging by MR or CT angiography to confirm large-vessel disease suggested by diminished pulses or bruits; PET is increasingly studied but its diagnostic/monitoring role remains unclear (Harrison 22e p.2903). Note: in patients treated with an IL-6 inhibitor, CRP and ESR normalize and can no longer be used to monitor disease activity or assess for infection (Harrison 22e p.2902). Seronegative rheumatoid arthritis or other inflammatory arthropathy mimicking the peripheral arthritis of PMR (Harrison 22e p.2903). Occurs almost exclusively in people over 50; mean age of onset around 70, with women making up roughly two-thirds of cases. Rare in Black patients; higher incidence in Scandinavian populations (Harrison 22e p.115, p.2902). Four phenotypic patterns can occur together, in isolation, or at different times: cranial arteritis, polymyalgia rheumatica, large-vessel disease, and systemic inflammation (Harrison 22e p.2902). Headache is the dominant cranial symptom; it is usually dull/boring rather than throbbing, may be unilateral or bilateral, is temporally located in only about half of patients, often worse at night, and aggravated by cold (Harrison 22e p.115). Scalp tenderness can be marked - brushing hair or resting the head on a pillow may be intolerable; the temporal (or less often occipital) artery may be tender, thickened, nodular, reddened or have overlying red skin streaks (Harrison 22e p.115). The temporal artery may pulsate early in disease but can become occluded later (Harrison 22e p.2902). Jaw and tongue claudication and scalp pain are recognized cranial-ischemic features; rarer cranial ischemic events include stroke and scalp or tongue infarction (Harrison 22e p.115, p.2902). ESR and/or CRP are elevated in most patients, but a normal ESR does NOT exclude giant cell arteritis (Harrison 22e p.115). Other supportive labs: normochromic or slightly hypochromic anemia, raised alkaline phosphatase (liver function abnormalities common), and increased IgG and complement (Harrison 22e p.2902). Most patients report head or eye complaints before any visual loss, so attention to early cranial symptoms with prompt therapy reduces the risk of blindness (Harrison 22e p.2902). Polymyalgia rheumatica overlaps strongly: PMR is seen in 40-50% of GCA patients, and 10-20% who present with isolated PMR later develop GCA - GCA and PMR are regarded as a spectrum of one disease process (Harrison 22e p.2902). In PMR, creatine kinase is not elevated and rheumatoid factor / anti-CCP should be negative; a worsening peripheral arthritis pattern should prompt reconsideration of seronegative RA or other inflammatory arthropathy (Harrison 22e p.2903). Ischemic optic neuropathy is the dreaded complication; about half of untreated patients develop blindness from ophthalmic-artery involvement, and arteritic AION is the leading cause of rapidly developing bilateral blindness in patients over 60 (Harrison 22e p.115). In suspected arteritic AION / visual loss, start glucocorticoids IMMEDIATELY without waiting for biopsy to protect vision in the fellow eye - a sight-saving principle; do not delay therapy pending diagnostic studies (Harrison 22e p.227, p.2903). Sudden visual loss / blindness can be the presenting or emergent feature (Harrison 22e p.2902). Aortic aneurysm: GCA patients are 18 times more likely than the general population to develop thoracic aortic aneurysms, carrying risk of rupture or dissection (Harrison 22e p.2903). Subclavian stenosis presenting as arm claudication signals large-vessel involvement (Harrison 22e p.2902). A normal ESR does not rule out GCA (Harrison 22e p.115). A single negative temporal artery biopsy does not exclude the disease because lesions are segmental/patchy - take a long segment and serial sections (Harrison 22e p.2903). Improvement of headache on prednisone is non-specific (migraine also responds), so do not use the steroid response alone to confirm GCA (Harrison 22e p.115). Once an IL-6 inhibitor is started, ESR/CRP can no longer track activity or flag infection (Harrison 22e p.2902). Minor ESR/CRP rises during tapering may reflect other causes (including infection) rather than a true flare, especially in a symptom-free patient (Harrison 22e p.2903). Glucocorticoids should not be given for the nonarteritic form of AION - distinguishing arteritic from nonarteritic AION matters (Harrison 22e p.227). A panarteritis of medium- and large-sized arteries, classically branches of the carotid (especially the temporal artery) but systemically involving the aorta and its branches. Histology shows mononuclear inflammatory infiltrate within the vessel wall with frequent giant cell formation, intimal proliferation, and fragmentation of the internal elastic lamina; organ damage results from ischemia of involved vessels. It is considered an antigen-driven process: CD4+ T cells enter via the adventitial vasa vasorum, become activated, and drive macrophage differentiation, with restricted clonal T-cell expansion suggesting an arterial-wall antigen. Lesional T cells produce mainly IL-2 and IFN-gamma; both IFN-gamma-producing TH1 and IL-17-producing TH17 lineages contribute and may differ in glucocorticoid responsiveness. Associated with HLA-DR4 and HLA-DRB1*04 variants. (Harrison 22e p.2902) Acute mortality directly from GCA is uncommon; when fatal it is usually due to cerebrovascular events or myocardial infarction. The main late mortality risk is rupture or dissection of an aortic aneurysm (18-fold increased thoracic aortic aneurysm risk). Disease is highly glucocorticoid-responsive but relapsing: symptom recurrence during steroid tapering occurs in 60-85% of patients, most require at least 2 years of treatment, and glucocorticoid toxicity affects 35-65% and is a major source of morbidity. (Harrison 22e p.2903)

than a CSF1-driven neoplasm Diffuse-type tenosynovial giant cell tumour is a locally aggressive neoplasm of synovial-lined structures underpinned by a translocation involving the CSF1 gene, most Overexpression of colony-stimulating factor 1 recruits large numbers of non-neoplastic macrophages that bear the CSF1 receptor, so the bulk of the lesion is a reactive inflammatory infiltrate driven by a minority neoplastic population, the so-called landscape effect. The tumour is benign but locally aggressive, and while the localised form is usually cured by excision, the diffuse form recurs frequently and can cause substantial joint damage. Malignant transformation is rare, and CSF1R-directed therapy has improved outcomes in advanced diffuse disease.

Tension-type headache — Clinical diagnosis Atypical features warrant imaging Migraine (the main differential, defined by migrainous accompaniments TTH lacks) (Harrison 22e p.3514) Migraine-TTH overlap / mixed phenotype with intercurrent migraine attacks (Harrison 22e p.3514) TTH is a clinical diagnosis; neuroimaging is not routine but CT or MRI of the brain is indicated when the examination is abnormal or the headache is recent-onset, with CT and MRI being comparably sensitive as initial screens (Harrison 22e p.157). Lumbar puncture may be required when a serious secondary cause is suspected and a benign etiology cannot otherwise be established (Harrison 22e p.157). General evaluation of acute headache may add palpation of cranial arteries, cervical spine assessment, blood pressure and urine for cardiovascular/renal status, and ocular examination including funduscopy and intraocular pressure (Harrison 22e p.157). Chronic migraine within the chronic daily headache spectrum (Harrison 22e p.158, Table 17-3) Medication-overuse headache (refractory daily/near-daily headache from analgesic overuse) (Harrison 22e p.158-159) Other secondary causes of chronic daily headache: post-traumatic, inflammatory (e.g., giant cell arteritis, sarcoidosis, Behcet syndrome), and chronic CNS infection (Harrison 22e p.158, Table 17-3) TTH is recognized as bilateral, tight, band-like discomfort that builds gradually, fluctuates in intensity, and can persist near-continuously for days (Harrison 22e p.3514). The most reliable bedside approach is to reserve the TTH label for headaches entirely lacking accompanying features such as nausea, vomiting, photophobia, phonophobia, osmophobia, throbbing quality, or worsening with movement (Harrison 22e p.3514). Migraine is the principal differential of TTH; the presence of any migrainous accompaniment points away from TTH and toward migraine (Harrison 22e p.3514). Patients who fit the TTH phenotype but also have migraine at other times, a family history of migraine, childhood migrainous syndromes, or typical migraine triggers may be biologically distinct from those with pure featureless TTH (Harrison 22e p.3514). Diagnostic boundaries are genuinely blurred: the International Headache Society main definition permits some nausea, photophobia, or phonophobia, whereas the stricter appendix definition does not, and Harrison favors the appendix (feature-free) definition to separate TTH from migraine (Harrison 22e p.3514). Among primary-care patients with headache lasting 3 months or more and no neurologic symptoms or signs, fewer than 10% actually have TTH and more than 90% have migraine, so a confident TTH label in this setting is uncommon (Harrison 22e p.3514). TTH is the most prevalent primary headache type overall, accounting for roughly 69% of primary headaches in a population series (Harrison 22e p.156, Table 17-1). Sudden-onset or first severe headache, or the 'worst headache ever' (Harrison 22e p.156-157, Table 17-2) Vomiting preceding the headache (Harrison 22e p.156, Table 17-2) Subacute worsening over days or weeks (Harrison 22e p.156, Table 17-2) Pain provoked by bending, lifting, or coughing (Harrison 22e p.156, Table 17-2) Pain that disturbs sleep or is present immediately on awakening (Harrison 22e p.156, Table 17-2) Onset after age 55 (Harrison 22e p.156, Table 17-2) Fever or unexplained systemic signs, or a known systemic illness (Harrison 22e p.156, Table 17-2) Abnormal neurologic examination (Harrison 22e p.156, Table 17-2) Local tenderness, e.g., over the temporal artery region (Harrison 22e p.156, Table 17-2) Serious secondary causes to consider with new severe headache include meningitis, subarachnoid hemorrhage, epidural/subdural hematoma, glaucoma, tumor, and purulent sinusitis (Harrison 22e p.157) Over-applying the TTH label: in chronic headache without neurologic signs, more than 90% of patients actually have migraine, so TTH is frequently overdiagnosed (Harrison 22e p.3514). Assuming muscle contraction confirms TTH; it does NOT distinguish TTH from migraine (Harrison 22e p.3514). Overlooking medication overuse, which can convert episodic headache into refractory daily/near-daily headache and blunt the effect of preventive treatment (Harrison 22e p.158-159). Mistaking a serious secondary headache for benign primary headache when an underlying cause has activated or worsened the primary syndrome (Harrison 22e p.158). The mechanism of TTH is incompletely understood. Harrison favors a primary disorder of central nervous system pain modulation alone, contrasting it with migraine, which involves more generalized disturbance of sensory modulation. Despite the name, there is no clear evidence that nervous tension is causative; importantly, muscle contraction does NOT reliably distinguish TTH from migraine, as no difference in contraction is seen between the two headache types. A genetic contribution has been suggested but is unreliable, since current diagnostic criteria likely contaminated those studies with migraine patients (Harrison 22e p.3514). TTH is classified as episodic when infrequent and chronic when occurring on 15 or more days per month; the pain fluctuates and may persist near-continuously for many days. Chronic TTH falls within the chronic daily headache group, which carries considerable disability, and may be complicated by medication overuse (Harrison 22e p.3514, p.158). Pain is characteristically mild to moderate, bilateral, tight and band-like, and non-throbbing. By frequency the IHS scheme distinguishes infrequent episodic, frequent episodic, chronic (>=15 days/month), and probable TTH; Harrison emphasizes the episodic-versus-chronic distinction (Harrison 22e p.3514, p.155 IHS classification).

As the joint displaces, the radial head is driven against the capitellum and fractures, the coronoid process fractures as the trochlea rides over it, and the lateral collateral ligament complex avulses from the lateral epicondyle. Historically a difficult injury with poor results, but a systematic surgical protocol restoring the bony and ligamentous stabilisers has improved outcomes; stiffness, recurrent instability and post-traumatic arthritis remain recognised risks.

inflammatory variant Terrien marginal degeneration is a non-inflammatory (in its usual form) peripheral corneal thinning of uncertain cause, in which the peripheral stroma progressively degenerates and thins while the overlying epithelium stays intact. Lipid is deposited at the leading edge and superficial vessels grow into the gutter. The thinning typically starts superiorly and gradually extends circumferentially, producing a shallow peripheral trough. Progressive structural weakening flattens the peripheral cornea and steepens the meridian at right angles, generating high against-the-rule or oblique astigmatism, and severe thinning predisposes to perforation. The degeneration is usually slowly progressive with vision limited mainly by astigmatism, which can often be managed optically. Advanced thinning carries a risk of perforation and may require tectonic surgery, but the condition rarely leads to central corneal opacification.

Terry nails — Terry's nails, White nails of Terry Half-and-half (Lindsay) nails Muehrcke lines True leukonychia Anaemia-related nail pallor Normal ageing nail changes Neapolitan nails of the elderly Liver function tests and assessment for chronic liver disease Fasting glucose or HbA1c for diabetes Cardiac assessment where heart failure is suspected Full blood count to exclude anaemia Clinical examination of all nails and lunulae Review of age and comorbidities to gauge significance Terry nails show a ground-glass white opacification of most of the nail bed with a preserved narrow distal band of normal pink to brown, usually only a couple of millimetres wide. The whitening obscures the lunula and typically affects all nails uniformly, being best appreciated on the fingernails. It is an apparent leukonychia of nail bed origin, so the white area does not migrate distally with nail growth. Classic associations include cirrhosis and chronic liver disease, but Terry nails are also seen in congestive cardiac failure, type 2 diabetes and with advancing age. The finding is asymptomatic and matters chiefly as a pointer to underlying systemic disease. It is distinguished from half-and-half nails by the position and width of the distal coloured band and the absence of the sharp demarcation seen in renal disease. Terry nails can occur in otherwise healthy older people, so context and additional signs guide the extent of investigation. Bedside recognition can prompt earlier detection of occult hepatic or cardiac disease. New Terry nails with stigmata of chronic liver disease or decompensation Accompanying breathlessness or oedema suggesting cardiac failure Rapid onset in a previously well younger patient Coexisting features suggesting the sharp demarcation of half-and-half nails and renal disease Confusing Terry nails with half-and-half nails and misdirecting the systemic workup Overlooking the sign in older patients where it may still indicate occult disease Assuming the change is a primary nail disorder rather than a systemic marker Attempting to treat the nail rather than the underlying condition Terry nails represent an apparent leukonychia in which the nail plate is normal but the nail bed is altered. The favoured explanation is a combination of reduced nail bed vascularity and an increase in connective tissue within the bed, which together diminish the normal pink translucency and produce a uniform white, ground-glass appearance. A narrow distal zone retains its normal vascular pattern, giving the characteristic band of preserved colour at the free margin. The changes are thought to reflect systemic alterations in the microvasculature and are commonly encountered where there is impaired hepatic function, cardiac failure or the vascular changes of diabetes and ageing. Because the abnormality lies in the bed rather than the plate, the pattern remains fixed as the nail grows. Terry nails are benign in themselves and require no treatment, but they can be an early clue to significant hepatic, cardiac or metabolic disease whose prognosis they reflect. In healthy older individuals they carry no adverse significance.

In chronic kidney disease, persistent hyperphosphataemia, reduced active vitamin D, and hypocalcaemia drive secondary hyperparathyroidism with diffuse then nodular parathyroid hyperplasia. Torsion of one of these pedunculated appendages, most often the appendix testis (hydatid of Morgagni), causes ischaemia and infarction of the remnant with local inflammation and pain. Because the testicular blood supply is unaffected, the testis remains viable, and the process settles as the infarcted appendage necroses and resolves. The main clinical importance is distinguishing it from true testicular torsion, which is a surgical emergency. The condition is benign and self-limiting, resolving over days with conservative management and analgesia, with no long-term testicular consequences.

preservation, hormone replacement where hypogonadism is confirmed, and counselling A discrete mass within an atrophic testis suggesting a tumour Rapid or progressive bilateral atrophy without an obvious cause Features of hypogonadism such as loss of libido, fatigue, or reduced secondary sexual characteristics History suggesting an untreated or missed testicular torsion Overlooking a tumour within a small or previously undescended testis Attributing atrophy to a single cause without a systematic endocrine and genetic assessment Missing anabolic steroid use as a reversible contributor Failing to discuss and arrange fertility preservation before it is too late Testicular atrophy results from injury to or loss of the germinal epithelium and, in some cases, the Leydig cells, leading to shrinkage of testicular volume. Ischaemic insults such as torsion or vascular injury, inflammatory damage from orchitis, the raised scrotal temperature and venous stasis of a varicocele, obstruction or heat effects, direct trauma, and gonadotoxic drugs or radiation all damage the seminiferous tubules. Endocrine causes act by removing the gonadotropin drive needed to maintain the testis, as in hypogonadotropic hypogonadism or suppression by exogenous androgens, while genetic conditions such as Klinefelter syndrome cause progressive tubular sclerosis. The common endpoint is a small, firm-to-soft testis with reduced or absent spermatogenesis. Prognosis depends on the cause and its reversibility: atrophy from established ischaemic, inflammatory, or genetic damage is usually permanent with impaired fertility, whereas atrophy from reversible factors such as varicocele or suppressive drugs may improve when the cause is addressed; hormone replacement can manage hypogonadism.

Testicular Cancer — Testicular germ cell tumor, Testicular GCT, Germ cell tumor of the testis Epididymitis Orchitis Testicular atrophy Hereditary persistence of AFP or hepatic disease (false AFP elevation) Non-germ-cell testicular tumors Epididymitis (a trial of antibacterials may be considered, but failure to respond should prompt scrotal ultrasound) Orchitis Scrotal ultrasound of both testicles (GCT typically hypoechoic, possibly multifocal) Serum AFP, hCG, and LDH before and after orchiectomy CT scan of abdomen and pelvis for staging Chest x-ray, with chest CT if retroperitoneal disease or lung nodules are present Pathologic review of the entire orchiectomy specimen by an experienced pathologist Serum microRNA miR-371a-3p (a promising investigational biomarker undergoing validation) Testicular atrophy Hereditary persistence of AFP (mildly elevated baseline AFP) Hepatic disease causing false AFP elevation False hCG elevation from hypogonadism, marijuana use, or assay interference Germ cell tumors (GCTs) account for about 95% of all testicular neoplasms; non-GCTs of the testis are much less common, and roughly 5% of GCTs arise in extragonadal sites such as the mediastinum, retroperitoneum, and pineal gland. Testicular cancer is regarded as a model curable neoplasm: about 95% of newly diagnosed patients are cured, and treatment is dictated by pathology (seminoma vs nonseminoma) and stage. It is the most common malignancy in adolescent and young adult males (age 15-39), most often diagnosed in Caucasians and much less common in African Americans; incidence in those over 50 is rising. Strongest risk factors are a prior history of GCT, cryptorchidism, and germ cell neoplasia in situ; a prior GCT carries a 1-2% risk of a contralateral tumor (usually metachronous), and cryptorchidism raises risk roughly four- to sixfold. Orchidopexy before puberty reduces but does not eliminate the cryptorchidism-associated risk, and the contralateral normally descended testis also remains at risk. A solid mass on scrotal ultrasound (typically hypoechoic, sometimes multifocal) must be considered malignant until proven otherwise; transscrotal aspiration or biopsy must never be performed because it risks seeding the scrotum or inguinal nodes. Tumor marker biology is key: seminomas never secrete AFP, so a histologic seminoma with elevated AFP is managed as a nonseminomatous GCT; hCG can be elevated in both seminoma and nonseminoma, and choriocarcinoma may produce markedly high hCG. Serum tumor markers (AFP, hCG, LDH) should be measured before and after orchiectomy; AFP is elevated in roughly 60-70% of nonseminomatous GCTs, while most seminomas and up to a third of nonseminomas have no marker elevation. Lymphatic spread follows a predictable pattern: left-sided tumors drain first to left paraaortic nodes below the left renal vessels, right-sided tumors to aortocaval nodes below the right renal vessels, then to retrocrural, mediastinal, and supraclavicular nodes; the lung is the most common hematogenous site. Genetically, most GCTs show excess copies of isochromosome 12p (i[12p]); the strongest heritable-risk locus identified is KITLG (KIT ligand) on chromosome 12, and overall heritability is nearly 50%. Teratoma is chemotherapy-resistant and must be managed surgically; the other nonseminomatous subtypes (embryonal carcinoma, yolk sac tumor, choriocarcinoma) and seminomas are chemosensitive. Sperm banking should be offered before chemotherapy: about 30% of newly diagnosed patients already have severe oligospermia or azoospermia, and treatment-related sterility is common (though ~80% recover spermatogenesis over years). Painless testicular mass (pathognomonic of GCT) or testicular swelling, firmness, or discomfort Back or flank pain suggesting retroperitoneal metastases Cough, dyspnea, or hemoptysis indicating lung metastases Gynecomastia in the setting of elevated hCG Suspected epididymitis/orchitis that fails to respond to antibiotics Rapidly progressive disease with life-threatening symptoms (e.g., hemoptysis) warranting emergent treatment even without tissue diagnosis Performing transscrotal biopsy or aspiration of a testicular mass, which can seed the scrotum or inguinal nodes and should never be done. Misclassifying a histologic seminoma with elevated AFP as a true seminoma, when it must be approached as a nonseminomatous GCT. Over-relying on tumor markers for diagnosis, since most seminomas and up to a third of nonseminomas have no marker elevation. Diagnostic delay (not uncommon) leading to more advanced stage at presentation, including mislabeling a GCT as epididymitis/orchitis. Assuming residual postchemotherapy masses are benign: imaging cannot distinguish necrosis/fibrosis from teratoma or viable tumor, and enlarging cystic retroperitoneal masses with normalized markers may represent growing teratoma syndrome. Forgetting that LDH is a nonspecific marker whose main role is risk classification in metastatic disease, not diagnosis. GCTs originate from the primordial germ cell, and most malignant GCTs arise from germ cell neoplasia in situ; the precise molecular steps driving progression from in situ neoplasia to invasive tumor are not fully defined. Genetic analysis shows excess copy number of isochromosome 12p in most cases, and genome-wide studies implicate several loci, most strongly KITLG on chromosome 12. Tumors are classified as seminoma (must be 100% seminoma; any mixed tumor is treated as nonseminomatous) or nonseminoma. Seminomas may contain syncytiotrophoblastic cells that secrete hCG but never secrete AFP. Nonseminomatous subtypes include embryonal carcinoma (the most undifferentiated, able to differentiate into the others, and may secrete AFP and/or hCG), yolk sac tumor (often AFP-secreting), choriocarcinoma (aggressive, often very high hCG), and teratoma (mature, immature, or malignant somatic tissue derived from two or more germ layers). Outcomes are excellent overall, with about 95% of newly diagnosed patients cured. Nearly all stage I patients (seminoma and nonseminoma) achieve cure. In metastatic (stage III) disease classified by the International Germ Cell Consensus Classification, most patients have good-risk disease with >90% cure; intermediate- and poor-risk groups have approximately 80% and 50% five-year survival, respectively. About 20-30% of patients with metastatic GCT treated with cisplatin-based chemotherapy do not achieve durable control, with most relapses occurring within 2 years of completing treatment. Three main AJCC TNM-based stages: Stage I limited to the testis; Stage II involving retroperitoneal lymph nodes (subgrouped IIA/IIB/IIC by node size: <=2 cm, >2-5 cm, >5 cm); Stage III with lymph node involvement beyond the retroperitoneum and/or distant metastases. Stage III is further stratified into good-, intermediate-, and poor-risk groups by the International Germ Cell Consensus Classification using histology, primary site, presence of nonpulmonary visceral metastases, and postorchiectomy marker levels (e.g., for NSGCT good-risk: AFP <1000 ng/mL, hCG <5000 mIU/mL, LDH <1.5x ULN; poor-risk: AFP >10,000 ng/mL, hCG >50,000 mIU/mL, LDH >10x ULN, mediastinal primary, or nonpulmonary visceral metastases). Marker half-lives: AFP 5-7 days, hCG 24-36 hours.

Progression yields either seminoma, which resembles undifferentiated germ cells, or non-seminomatous tumours that recapitulate embryonic and extra-embryonic differentiation (embryonal carcinoma, yolk sac tumour, choriocarcinoma, teratoma), often as mixed tumours. Spread is typically lymphatic to the retroperitoneal nodes following gonadal drainage, with later haematogenous dissemination to lung and other viscera; choriocarcinoma has a particular tendency to early blood-borne spread. Testicular germ cell tumour is among the most curable solid malignancies; the great majority of patients, including many with metastatic disease, achieve long-term cure with stage-appropriate surgery, surveillance, cisplatin-based chemotherapy, or radiotherapy, though prognosis worsens with high-risk marker elevation and non-pulmonary visceral metastases.

infiltrates the interstitium between seminiferous tubules, often with vascular invasion. The testis behaves as an immune-privileged sanctuary site, which is thought to contribute to the characteristic pattern of relapse in other sanctuary sites such as the contralateral testis and the central nervous system even after apparent local control. Disease may be confined to the testis at presentation or reflect systemic nodal or extranodal lymphoma. Primary testicular lymphoma tends to behave aggressively with a significant risk of relapse in the central nervous system and contralateral testis; outcomes have improved with combined immunochemotherapy plus CNS prophylaxis and contralateral radiotherapy, but late relapses mean prolonged follow-up is required.

Testicular microlithiasis — TML, testicular microliths, microlithiasis of the testis Large-cell calcifying Sertoli cell tumour Calcification from prior granulomatous orchitis Burnt-out (regressed) germ-cell tumour Tunica albuginea calcification Testicular scarring or old infarct Calcified intratesticular haematoma Scrotal ultrasound to characterise and quantify the foci and assess for any associated mass Testicular tumour markers (AFP, beta-hCG, LDH) if a discrete lesion is seen Semen analysis in subfertile men Clinical examination with teaching of testicular self-examination Interval ultrasound surveillance in higher-risk patients An incidental ultrasound finding of multiple tiny, usually sub-millimetre to a few millimetres, non-shadowing echogenic foci scattered through the testicular parenchyma Classically described as a 'starry sky' appearance, with classic or diffuse microlithiasis defined as five or more microliths per ultrasound field Usually asymptomatic and discovered during scrotal imaging performed for another reason such as pain, subfertility, or a lump The association with testicular germ-cell tumour is real, but its clinical significance and the need for surveillance are debated, since most men with microlithiasis never develop cancer Risk is considered higher when microlithiasis coexists with other factors - subfertility, testicular atrophy, cryptorchidism or prior undescended testis, a personal or family history of germ-cell tumour, or a contralateral tumour In the absence of additional risk factors most guidance advises teaching testicular self-examination rather than routine repeat ultrasound, reserving surveillance imaging for higher-risk men Microlithiasis is not itself a premalignant lesion and needs no treatment; the emphasis is on appropriate risk stratification A discrete focal testicular mass on ultrasound Elevated testicular tumour markers A rapidly changing testicular size or a new hard lump Coexisting cryptorchidism or a prior germ-cell tumour Testicular atrophy accompanying the microlithiasis Over-investigating low-risk men with repeated ultrasounds and provoking unnecessary anxiety Conversely, failing to arrange surveillance in men who have microlithiasis together with significant risk factors Assuming microlithiasis is itself premalignant and requires treatment Not teaching and documenting testicular self-examination as the key safety-net Testicular microlithiasis represents calcified concretions within the lumen of the seminiferous tubules. Cells that degenerate within a tubule fail to be cleared and act as a nidus for laminated calcium deposition surrounded by a glycoprotein matrix, producing the characteristic tiny echogenic foci seen on ultrasound. The same disordered tubular environment that favours these calcifications is thought to be shared with abnormalities of the germinal epithelium, which may explain the statistical association with germ-cell neoplasia and with subfertility, even though the microliths themselves are not a precursor lesion. In isolation the prognosis is excellent and the great majority of men remain free of malignancy; the outlook is chiefly determined by the presence or absence of additional germ-cell-tumour risk factors.

Testicular torsion — torsion of the testis, spermatic cord torsion, testis torsion Epididymo-orchitis Torsion of a testicular or epididymal appendage (appendix testis) Incarcerated or strangulated inguinal hernia Idiopathic scrotal oedema Testicular trauma or haematoma Testicular tumour with haemorrhage Henoch-Schonlein purpura involving the scrotum Urgent surgical exploration when clinical suspicion is high (imaging must not delay this) Colour Doppler ultrasound to assess intratesticular blood flow when the diagnosis is uncertain and readily available Urinalysis, which is typically normal and helps distinguish from infection Assessment of the contralateral testis given the frequently bilateral anatomical predisposition Classic presentation is sudden, severe unilateral scrotal pain of rapid onset, often with nausea and vomiting, most commonly in adolescents and young men but also seen in neonates Examination typically shows a swollen, exquisitely tender, high-riding testis that may lie transversely (horizontal lie) with an absent cremasteric reflex It is a time-critical surgical emergency: testicular salvage is high if detorsion occurs within about six hours and falls sharply thereafter The bell-clapper anomaly, in which the tunica vaginalis invests the testis abnormally, predisposes to intravaginal torsion and is often bilateral Diagnosis is fundamentally clinical; imaging should never delay surgery when torsion is strongly suspected Colour Doppler ultrasound showing absent or reduced intratesticular blood flow supports the diagnosis, but a normal study does not reliably exclude it Definitive treatment is emergency scrotal exploration with detorsion and orchidopexy of the affected testis, plus fixation of the contralateral testis because the predisposing anomaly is usually bilateral Manual detorsion may be attempted as a temporising measure but does not replace surgical exploration and fixation Testicular torsion is a urological emergency; salvage depends on detorsion within roughly six hours, so exploration must not be delayed for investigations Sudden severe scrotal pain with a high-riding testis and absent cremasteric reflex until proven otherwise Neonatal torsion, which may present with a firm, discoloured, painless scrotal swelling Progressive testicular ischaemia leading to non-viable testis and need for orchidectomy Attributing acute scrotal pain to epididymo-orchitis and delaying surgical exploration Waiting for or relying on ultrasound when clinical suspicion is high Assuming a normal Doppler study excludes torsion, especially in intermittent or partial torsion Failing to fix the contralateral testis, leaving it at risk of subsequent torsion Dismissing intermittent testicular pain that may represent recurrent torsion-detorsion Testicular torsion is twisting of the spermatic cord that obstructs venous drainage first and then arterial inflow, producing ischaemia and, if unrelieved, haemorrhagic infarction of the testis. The intravaginal form, most common in adolescents, is facilitated by the bell-clapper deformity where the tunica vaginalis surrounds the testis and epididymis completely, allowing the testis to rotate freely within it. Extravaginal torsion occurs in neonates when the entire tunica and its contents twist above the level of attachment. The degree of twisting and the duration of ischaemia determine the likelihood of viability. Testicular viability depends critically on time to detorsion, with excellent salvage within a few hours and progressively poorer outcomes beyond six to twelve hours; a non-viable testis requires orchidectomy, and infarction may later affect fertility.

Tetanus — lockjaw Strychnine poisoning Dystonic reactions to antidopaminergic (antidopaminergic drug) agents Stiff person syndrome Somatic symptom disorder Hypocalcemia (in neonatal tetanus) Meningoencephalitis (in neonatal tetanus) Oropharyngeal, peritonsillar, or submaxillary infection / lymphadenitis and cranial nerve disease (mimics of cephalic tetanus / trismus) Intracranial hemorrhage Peritonitis or acute abdominal emergency (versus continuous abdominal rigidity of tetanus) Oropharyngeal infection Peritonsillar infection Submaxillary lymphadenitis Meningoencephalitis Diagnosis is clinical; confirmatory laboratory testing is limited. Wound culture of C. tetani cannot confirm the diagnosis (a positive culture is non-confirmatory). Serum antitetanus IgG measured before antitoxin/immunoglobulin administration: levels >0.1 IU/mL (standard ELISA) are deemed protective and argue against tetanus. Serum tetanus toxin bioassay may help if antibody is below the protective threshold, but a negative result does not exclude tetanus and the assay is not generally performed. PCR and recombinase polymerase amplification to detect the tetanus neurotoxin gene are promising but emerging techniques. Strychnine poisoning Neuroleptic malignant syndrome Dystonic reaction to antidopaminergic drugs Stiff person syndrome Somatic symptom disorder Hypocalcemia Intracranial hemorrhage Trismus (lockjaw) is typically the earliest symptom, progressing to neck and trunk rigidity, dysphagia, and pharyngeal/laryngeal spasm; risus sardonicus and opisthotonos reflect the characteristic sustained muscle rigidity. Generalized tetanus is the most common form, characterized by muscle rigidity with generalized spasms; localized tetanus affects only isolated muscle groups but can progress to the generalized form. Cephalic tetanus is a localized form involving the cranial nerves, which can cause pharyngeal or laryngeal spasm leading to aspiration, airway obstruction, or respiratory failure. Neonatal tetanus classically presents with loss of the ability to suck and cry (a newborn normal in the first 2 days who deteriorates between days 3 and 28), poor feeding, rigidity, and generalized spasms. Laryngeal spasm causing apnea or respiratory failure is a life-threatening event and, without immediate respiratory support, is the most common cause of death. Autonomic nervous system disturbance characteristically emerges in the second week of severe disease, with fluctuating heart rate and blood pressure, sweating, gastrointestinal stasis, and increased tracheal secretions; cardiovascular events then become the major threat. Disease severity is graded with the Ablett classification (Grades I-IV), where Grade IV is Grade III plus autonomic dysfunction. Abdominal rigidity in tetanus is characteristically continuous, distinguishing it from the rigidity of peritonitis or an acute abdomen. Roughly 20-30% of cases have no identifiable entry wound; superficial limb abrasions are the most common portal of entry in adults, while deeper injuries (open fractures, drug injection) are linked to more severe disease. Natural infection does not confer protective immunity because tetanus toxin is poorly immunogenic, so survivors still require a full primary immunization course. Laryngeal spasm with apnea or respiratory failure - life-threatening and the most common cause of death. Autonomic nervous system disturbance (labile heart rate and blood pressure, sweating, GI stasis, increased tracheal secretions), typically in the second week, marking high cardiovascular mortality risk. Short incubation period (wound to first symptom) and short period of onset (first symptom to first generalized/pharyngeal/laryngeal spasm) - rapid progression predicts worse outcome. Dysphagia with laryngeal hyperactivity, which makes airway management difficult and raises aspiration risk. Diagnosis is clinical - waiting for laboratory confirmation is misguided; a positive wound culture does not confirm and a protective antitetanus IgG (>0.1 IU/mL) argues against the diagnosis. Treatment should not be delayed once tetanus is clinically diagnosed. Assuming natural infection confers immunity: tetanus toxin is poorly immunogenic, so survivors still require a full primary immunization course. Overlooking absence of a wound: about 20-30% of cases have no identifiable entry site, so a negative wound history does not exclude tetanus. Failure to identify and debride the entry wound (to remove anaerobic foci) can lead to recurrent or prolonged disease. Long-term ICU care with deep sedation predisposes to hospital-acquired infections (ventilator-associated pneumonia, bloodstream and urinary tract infection, sepsis), venous thromboembolism, and other complications - prognosis depends on controlling these. Tetanus is caused by tetanus toxin (tetanospasmin) produced by Clostridium tetani, an anaerobic, gram-positive, spore-forming rod whose resilient environmental spores enter through wounds, abrasions, or the umbilical stump and germinate in anaerobic tissue. Only toxin-producing organisms cause disease. The toxin is a 150-kDa protein cleaved into a heavy (100-kDa) and light (50-kDa) chain joined by a disulfide bond; the heavy-chain carboxy terminal binds presynaptic motor nerve terminals, leading to internalization and retrograde intra-axonal transport to motor nuclei of cranial nerves and spinal cord ventral horns. The toxin then crosses the synapse into GABA-ergic presynaptic inhibitory interneurons, where the light chain (a zinc-dependent endopeptidase) cleaves VAMP2 (synaptobrevin), blocking inhibitory neurotransmitter release. Loss of inhibition produces unregulated motor activity (muscle rigidity and spasms), and similar disinhibition in the autonomic system produces autonomic instability; elevated circulating catecholamines in severe disease drive cardiovascular complications. Tetanus has a high survival rate when complications are controlled and interventions are prompt, though recovery is prolonged, typically taking about 4-6 weeks. Rapid onset predicts more severe disease: the shorter the incubation period (wound to first symptom) and the period of onset (first symptom to first generalized or pharyngeal/laryngeal spasm), the worse the prognosis. The Tetanus Severity Score (TSS) outperforms the Dakar and Philips scores for predicting severity and outcome (sensitivity ~66%, specificity ~91%; a cutoff score of >=8 predicts death). Surviving adults, especially the elderly, may have reduced long-term functional outcomes, while affected children and neonates have a higher incidence of neurologic sequelae (neonates may face increased risk of learning disabilities, behavioral problems, cerebral palsy, and deafness). Ablett classification of tetanus severity: Grade I (mild) - mild trismus, general spasticity, no respiratory compromise, no spasms, no dysphagia; Grade II (moderate) - moderate trismus and rigidity, short spasms, mild dysphagia, moderate respiratory involvement, respiratory rate >30/min; Grade III (severe) - severe trismus, generalized rigidity, prolonged spasms, severe dysphagia, apneic spells, pulse >120/min, respiratory rate >40/min; Grade IV (very severe) - Grade III features plus autonomic dysfunction. Prognostic scoring is provided by the Tetanus Severity Score (TSS), which is superior to the Dakar and Philips scores.

aims to halt progression, and because established deficits may not fully reverse the timing of surgery is important Progressive neurological deterioration such as weakness, sensory loss, or worsening gait New or worsening bladder or bowel dysfunction Rapidly progressive scoliosis or foot deformity in a child with cutaneous stigmata Dismissing lumbosacral cutaneous stigmata that signal occult dysraphism Delaying imaging in a child with unexplained gait, foot, or bladder problems Expecting full reversal of long-standing deficits after detethering Tethered cord syndrome results from abnormal caudal fixation of the spinal cord so that it is placed under longitudinal traction. Normally the conus ascends to around the L1/2 level; when it is anchored, whether by a short, thick, or fatty filum terminale, a dysraphic lesion such as a lipoma, a dermal sinus tract, or a split-cord malformation, normal movement is restricted and the cord is stretched, particularly with growth and flexion. The resulting mechanical strain impairs neuronal metabolism and blood flow in the conus, producing progressive neurological, urological, and orthopaedic dysfunction, and overlying cutaneous stigmata reflect the associated dysraphism. Detethering usually arrests progression and often relieves pain; motor and sensory recovery is variable and bladder dysfunction may only stabilise rather than reverse, so outcomes are best when surgery is performed before significant fixed deficits develop. Re-tethering can occur and require further surgery.

Tetralogy of Fallot — TOF, ToF Transposition of the great arteries Tricuspid atresia Pulmonary atresia with ventricular septal defect Truncus arteriosus Severe isolated pulmonary stenosis Double-outlet right ventricle Echocardiography to define the outflow tract, septal defect, aortic override, and pulmonary artery anatomy Chest radiograph looking for a boot-shaped heart and pulmonary vascularity Electrocardiogram showing right axis deviation and right ventricular hypertrophy Pulse oximetry and, in spells, assessment of acidosis Cardiac catheterisation or CT/MR angiography when coronary or pulmonary artery anatomy is unclear Genetic evaluation for 22q11.2 deletion when associated features are present The most common cyanotic congenital heart lesion beyond infancy, comprising four features: a large ventricular septal defect, an overriding aorta, right ventricular outflow tract obstruction, and right ventricular hypertrophy. The degree of cyanosis reflects the severity of right ventricular outflow obstruction; some infants are minimally cyanotic (so-called pink Fallot) while others present with marked desaturation. A harsh systolic ejection murmur at the left upper sternal border arises from the outflow obstruction, not from the septal defect itself; the murmur softens during a hypercyanotic spell as flow across the outflow tract falls. Hypercyanotic (tet) spells are episodes of sudden, worsening cyanosis with agitation and deep breathing, often on waking or after feeding or crying, and can be life-threatening. Calming manoeuvres for a spell aim to increase systemic vascular resistance and outflow through the lungs: comforting the child, bringing the knees to the chest, and giving oxygen, with pharmacological support as needed. The chest radiograph classically shows a boot-shaped heart with a concave main pulmonary artery segment and normal or reduced pulmonary vascularity. Echocardiography confirms the anatomy and defines the outflow tract, pulmonary arteries, and coronary artery course before surgery. Older, unrepaired children may adopt squatting to relieve exertional cyanosis by transiently raising systemic resistance and pulmonary blood flow. Complete surgical repair, involving closure of the septal defect and relief of outflow obstruction, is the definitive treatment and is usually performed in infancy. Hypercyanotic (tet) spell with deepening cyanosis, agitation, and a disappearing murmur Loss of consciousness, seizures, or limpness during a spell Duct-dependent presentation with severe outflow obstruction and cardiovascular collapse as the ductus closes Profound or worsening hypoxaemia unresponsive to calming measures Metabolic acidosis indicating inadequate pulmonary blood flow Interpreting a softening or absent murmur reassuringly when it actually signals a severe hypercyanotic spell Aggressively sedating or agitating an infant in a spell rather than using calming, resistance-raising manoeuvres Overlooking a duct-dependent lesion in a neonate whose cyanosis worsens as the ductus arteriosus closes Attributing exertional symptoms or squatting in an older child to behaviour rather than underlying cyanotic heart disease Failing to screen for associated 22q11.2 deletion and other anomalies Anterior and cephalad deviation of the infundibular septum during development produces right ventricular outflow tract obstruction, a malaligned ventricular septal defect, and an aorta that overrides the defect. Obstruction to pulmonary outflow, combined with the large communication between the ventricles, allows deoxygenated right ventricular blood to shunt right-to-left into the aorta, producing systemic desaturation. The volume of pulmonary blood flow and the resulting cyanosis depend dynamically on the balance between the fixed and dynamic outflow obstruction and systemic vascular resistance; a fall in systemic resistance or a spasm of the infundibulum increases right-to-left shunting and precipitates a hypercyanotic spell. With timely complete surgical repair the long-term outlook is generally good, though survivors need lifelong cardiology follow-up for pulmonary regurgitation, residual outflow obstruction, arrhythmia, and possible need for pulmonary valve replacement. Untreated disease carries high morbidity and mortality from progressive cyanosis, spells, and complications.

Tetrasomy 18p — isochromosome 18p, i(18p) syndrome, tetrasomy 18p syndrome Other supernumerary marker chromosome syndromes 18p deletion syndrome, which reflects the opposite dosage change Cerebral palsy, given the tone abnormalities Non-specific syndromic intellectual disability Other causes of neonatal hypotonia Karyotype to identify the marker chromosome FISH or microarray to confirm the marker is derived from 18p Chromosomal microarray to characterise copy number MRI of the brain if seizures or a movement disorder are present Developmental and speech and language assessment Feeding and swallow evaluation in infancy Caused by a supernumerary isochromosome made up of two short arms of chromosome 18, giving four copies of 18p Presents with developmental delay or intellectual disability, usually moderate, with frequent speech delay Neonatal feeding difficulties and hypotonia, sometimes later evolving into spasticity, are common Microcephaly and characteristic facial features such as a narrow or oval face, strabismus, and a high nasal bridge are typical Behavioural difficulties and, in some, a movement disorder or seizures may occur Growth restriction and low birth weight are frequent The isochromosome usually arises de novo, most often from a maternal meiotic error, so recurrence risk is low but not zero Severe neonatal feeding difficulty with failure to thrive Seizures Progressive spasticity affecting mobility Reporting a marker chromosome without identifying its origin, which requires FISH or microarray Misattributing tone abnormalities to cerebral palsy without cytogenetic testing Overlooking spasticity that evolves after initial hypotonia Assuming a high recurrence risk when most cases are de novo Tetrasomy 18p results from a supernumerary marker chromosome that is an isochromosome of the short arm of chromosome 18, so that four copies of 18p are present, comprising the two normal chromosome 18s plus the two arms of the isochromosome. The extra dosage of genes on 18p disturbs neurodevelopment and growth, producing the characteristic pattern of intellectual disability, hypotonia evolving to spasticity, and dysmorphism. It generally occurs sporadically through a meiotic or post-meiotic error, commonly of maternal origin. Life expectancy is generally not markedly reduced; most individuals have moderate intellectual disability with ongoing motor and speech difficulties, and outcome depends on the severity of neurological involvement.

Tetrodotoxin (pufferfish) poisoning — pufferfish poisoning, fugu poisoning, TTX poisoning, tetraodon poisoning Paralytic shellfish (saxitoxin) poisoning Blue-ringed octopus envenomation Guillain-Barre syndrome or botulism Ciguatera poisoning (overlapping paraesthesiae) Myasthenic crisis Other cause of acute neuromuscular respiratory failure Clinical diagnosis based on ingestion history and characteristic progression Continuous respiratory monitoring and serial forced vital capacity Pulse oximetry and arterial blood gases for ventilatory failure Electrocardiography and cardiac monitoring for bradyarrhythmia Electrolytes and baseline bloods to exclude alternative causes Toxin detection in food or biological samples where laboratory capability exists Follows ingestion of pufferfish (fugu) or other tetrodotoxin-containing seafood, especially when improperly prepared Symptoms begin within minutes to a few hours with perioral and lingual paraesthesiae, then spread to the face and extremities Progresses to nausea, vomiting, ascending flaccid paralysis, bulbar weakness and respiratory failure in severe cases Consciousness is usually preserved even in advanced paralysis, as the toxin has limited central effect There is no antidote; management is supportive with airway protection and mechanical ventilation until the toxin clears Early gastrointestinal decontamination may be considered soon after ingestion, and cardiovascular support given for hypotension and bradyarrhythmia Severity grading based on progression of paraesthesiae, weakness and cardiorespiratory signs helps guide monitoring and disposition Spreading paraesthesiae with progressive limb and bulbar weakness Declining respiratory effort or oxygen saturation Hypotension or significant bradycardia Rapid symptom onset after ingestion (suggesting a large dose) Preserved awareness with advancing paralysis heralding respiratory arrest Underestimating the speed of progression from paraesthesiae to respiratory failure Assuming immobility reflects unconsciousness, when awareness is usually retained Waiting for an antidote instead of instituting supportive ventilation Failing to recognise the diagnosis in the absence of a clear pufferfish history Tetrodotoxin is a potent, heat-stable toxin concentrated in the liver, gonads, skin and viscera of pufferfish and produced by symbiotic bacteria. It binds with high affinity to voltage-gated sodium channels on nerve and skeletal muscle membranes, blocking sodium influx and preventing action potential generation and propagation. The result is a rapidly progressive sensory disturbance and flaccid paralysis, including of the respiratory muscles, with respiratory failure the main cause of death. Autonomic effects can cause hypotension and bradycardia, while relative sparing of the central nervous system leaves consciousness intact. Outcome depends on timely airway and ventilatory support; patients who survive the first hours with adequate ventilation generally recover fully within days, whereas untreated respiratory failure is rapidly fatal.

Thallium poisoning — thallium toxicity, thallotoxicosis, thallium salt poisoning, rodenticide thallium poisoning Guillain-Barre syndrome or other acute polyneuropathy Arsenic or other heavy-metal poisoning Vasculitic or paraneoplastic neuropathy Vitamin deficiency neuropathy (e.g. thiamine) Porphyria Other causes of alopecia such as chemotherapy or autoimmune disease Twenty-four-hour urinary thallium concentration and blood thallium level Nerve conduction studies demonstrating axonal sensorimotor neuropathy Full blood count, renal and liver function and electrolytes Electrocardiogram for conduction disturbance and repolarisation changes Abdominal radiograph, as some thallium salts are radio-opaque Examination of nails and hair for Mees' lines and follicular changes The classic triad is gastrointestinal upset, a painful ascending sensory-predominant peripheral neuropathy and, later, alopecia Alopecia is a hallmark but is delayed by one to several weeks, so early diagnosis rests on the painful neuropathy and gastrointestinal symptoms Consider deliberate poisoning, as thallium is odourless and tasteless and has been used for homicidal and suicidal intent Autonomic features, tachycardia, hypertension and constipation, together with painful acral dysaesthesiae, are useful early clues Mees' lines (transverse white bands) may appear on the nails weeks after exposure Diagnosis is confirmed by elevated urine (and blood) thallium concentrations, ideally with a 24-hour urine collection Prussian blue is the specific therapy, binding thallium in the gut to interrupt enterohepatic and enteroenteric recirculation and enhance faecal elimination, alongside supportive care Multi-dose oral binding, generous bowel regimen and, in severe cases, extracorporeal removal are considered under poisons-centre guidance Rapidly progressive peripheral neuropathy or ascending weakness Respiratory muscle involvement or bulbar dysfunction Seizures, encephalopathy or coma Cardiac arrhythmia or autonomic instability Evidence of deliberate poisoning requiring safeguarding and forensic involvement Missing the diagnosis before alopecia develops and mislabelling it as Guillain-Barre syndrome Failing to consider intentional poisoning and to involve safeguarding or forensic services Not sending appropriate urine and blood specimens for heavy-metal analysis Overlooking enterohepatic recirculation and stopping binding therapy prematurely Attributing painful paraesthesiae to a psychiatric or functional cause Thallium is a heavy metal whose monovalent ion mimics potassium, allowing it to enter cells through potassium transport pathways and disrupt potassium-dependent processes. It interferes with mitochondrial oxidative phosphorylation, binds sulfhydryl groups on enzymes and structural proteins, and disrupts ribonucleic acid and protein synthesis. High metabolic demand tissues, including neurons and the actively dividing cells of hair follicles, are especially vulnerable, explaining the prominent peripheral neuropathy and characteristic delayed alopecia. Thallium undergoes enterohepatic recirculation, which sustains systemic exposure. Prognosis depends on dose and timeliness of chelation; mild cases may recover fully, but severe poisoning can leave permanent neurological deficits or be fatal, and hair usually regrows in survivors over subsequent months.
