indicating a likely lethal dysplasia Cloverleaf skull with signs of raised intracranial pressure Feeding and airway compromise requiring urgent palliative planning Confusing it with severe achondroplasia or homozygous achondroplasia without molecular confirmation Underestimating the lethality and delaying appropriate counselling and palliative planning Missing the distinction between type I and type II femoral and skull morphology Failing to offer autopsy and genetic counselling to inform recurrence risk Thanatophoric dysplasia is caused by strongly activating variants in FGFR3. The resulting profound constitutive receptor signalling severely disrupts growth-plate chondrocyte proliferation and endochondral ossification, producing extreme limb shortening and a markedly hypoplastic thoracic cage. The small thorax restricts lung development, and the consequent pulmonary hypoplasia is the usual cause of neonatal death. The same signalling excess also affects cortical brain development in some cases, contributing to the cloverleaf skull and neurological abnormalities seen particularly in type II. Thanatophoric dysplasia is almost universally lethal in the perinatal period, with most affected infants dying shortly after birth from respiratory failure. Rare survivors with intensive respiratory support have severe disability and profound growth restriction.

The Bradyarrhythmias: Disorders of the Atrioventricular Node — AV block, Atrioventricular block, AV conduction block, Heart block, Bradyarrhythmia due to AV node disease Sinus node dysfunction / sinus bradycardia (sick sinus syndrome) as a competing cause of symptomatic bradycardia Drug effect (beta blockers, verapamil, diltiazem, digoxin) producing reversible AV conduction slowing Heightened vagal tone (sleep, well-conditioned athletes, carotid sinus hypersensitivity, vasovagal/cough/micturition syncope) Acute myocardial ischemia/infarction-related conduction block Infiltrative cardiomyopathy (sarcoidosis, amyloidosis, hemochromatosis) Congenital complete heart block (e.g., maternal lupus) Lyme carditis (Borrelia burgdorferi) - a common infectious cause of AV block, typically AV-nodal with narrow junctional escape >40 beats/min, usually improving within about a week of antibiotic therapy Infective endocarditis with perivalvular abscess - AV block here should prompt urgent surgical consultation Viral myocarditis Chagas disease Toxoplasmosis 12-lead ECG to classify the degree and pattern of block and assess QRS width/escape rhythm Transthoracic echocardiography to assess for structural/valvular disease, ejection fraction, and wall motion Advanced imaging (cardiac MRI, CT, FDG-PET, technetium pyrophosphate scanning) for infiltrative disease, especially when block develops at age <=60 years Ambulatory/continuous ECG monitoring to correlate symptoms with bradyarrhythmia Provocative testing - vagal maneuvers, carotid sinus massage, exercise, atropine, isoproterenol - to localize the level of block Invasive electrophysiologic study with His bundle electrogram (AH and HV interval measurement) in syncope with suspected high-grade or infranodal block Evaluation for ischemia when clinical suspicion is present Senile degenerative fibrosis/calcification of the conduction system (Lev disease) Lenegre disease (sclerodegenerative distal bundle branch disease in younger patients) Aortic (and less commonly mitral) valve annular calcification encroaching on the conduction system Cardiac sarcoidosis and amyloidosis Autoimmune/rheumatologic disease (SLE, rheumatoid arthritis, mixed connective tissue disease, scleroderma) Neuromuscular disease (myotonic dystrophy, Kearns-Sayre syndrome, muscular dystrophies) Iatrogenic injury (valve/cardiac surgery, TAVR, septal myectomy/alcohol septal ablation, catheter ablation) Hereditary progressive familial heart block (e.g., SCN5A mutations) and lamin A/C cardiomyopathy The AV node is specialized for slow conduction, creating a delay between atrial and ventricular activation and acting as the electrical gatekeeper to the ventricle; its intrinsic backup pacemaker (escape) rate is roughly 20-60 beats/min, normally overridden by the faster sinus node (60-100 beats/min). First-degree AV block means every atrial impulse still conducts but with an abnormally prolonged PR interval (>200 ms); the term block is a misnomer since conduction is delayed, not interrupted. Mobitz I (Wenckebach) second-degree block shows progressive PR lengthening before a dropped beat with grouped beating and progressive RR shortening; it is typically within the AV node, hemodynamically stable, and usually does not warrant pacing when asymptomatic. Mobitz II second-degree block shows a fixed PR interval before a dropped beat, is usually infranodal with a wider QRS, carries a risk of sudden death from an unreliable escape rhythm, and warrants permanent pacing even without symptoms. In 2:1 AV block the ECG cannot reliably distinguish type I from type II; a PR <160 ms with a wide QRS before the conducted beat favors infranodal (type II) block. QRS width of the escape rhythm localizes the block: a narrow QRS escape implies block in the AV node or proximal His with a faster, more stable junctional rhythm, whereas a wide QRS escape (without preexisting bundle branch block) implies distal His or bundle branch block and a slower, less reliable rhythm. Vagal maneuvers and carotid sinus massage slow AV nodal conduction but may paradoxically improve infranodal conduction, while atropine, isoproterenol, and exercise improve AV nodal conduction but may worsen infranodal conduction - useful for localizing the level of block. On the His bundle electrogram, the AH interval (AV nodal conduction) is normally <130 ms and the HV interval (His-Purkinje conduction) is normally <=55 ms; a markedly prolonged HV interval predicts progression to higher-grade block. Functional causes of AV block (autonomic, metabolic/endocrine, drug-related) tend to be reversible, whereas most structural causes producing fibrosis are permanent. Congenital complete heart block with a narrow QRS typically increases heart rate with exercise, whereas acquired complete heart block (especially wide QRS) does not respond to exercise. Acquired persistent AV conduction failure is rare in healthy adults (estimated incidence about 1 per 5000 per year in the U.S.), but becomes much more common with ischemia, aging/fibrosis, or infiltrative disease. Idiopathic progressive fibrosis/sclerosis of the conduction system is the most common acquired cause, accounting for roughly 50% of AV block; it often begins in the fourth decade and is accelerated by atherosclerosis, hypertension, and diabetes. Wide-complex escape rhythm at a slow rate (e.g., ~30 beats/min) implying infranodal block and an unreliable escape Mobitz II second-degree or complete (third-degree) heart block Syncope or presyncope attributable to bradycardia Markedly prolonged HV interval (>100 ms carries an annual incidence of complete AV block approaching 10%) High-grade AV block complicating anterior MI (distal block, wide unstable escape, high mortality) New AV block with infective endocarditis suggesting perivalvular abscess Alternating bundle branch block or bifascicular/trifascicular block with intermittent third-degree block Mislabeling 2:1 AV block as type I when it may be infranodal type II - the surface ECG cannot reliably distinguish them Assuming all AV block is benign vagal phenomenon and missing serious infranodal disease that warrants pacing despite absent symptoms Overlooking reversible/treatable causes (offending drugs, electrolyte derangement, ischemia, hypothyroidism, sleep apnea, Lyme carditis) before committing to permanent therapy Failing to pursue advanced imaging for infiltrative disease (e.g., sarcoidosis) when AV block presents at a younger age (<=60 years) Misinterpreting Mobitz I at very short paced cycle lengths as pathologic - it can be a normal physiologic response; it is abnormal at cycle lengths >500 ms (<120 beats/min) without high vagal tone Not recognizing that a new perivalvular abscess in endocarditis can present as AV block requiring urgent surgery AV nodal myocytes sit at a relatively high resting membrane potential (~-60 mV), exhibit slow phase-0 upstrokes mediated by L-type calcium current (with a relative lack of fast sodium current), and show spontaneous phase-4 depolarization, conferring backup automaticity. Weak electrical coupling from sparse gap junctions (predominantly connexin-40) plus increased extracellular volume slows conduction and protects the ventricle. The AV junction comprises a transitional (atrionodal) cell zone showing decremental conduction, the compact node, and the penetrating His bundle; conduction continues through the His, right and left bundle branches, and the fast-conducting Purkinje network (1-3 m/s). Bradycardia and block arise when conduction across this axis is compromised by fibrosis/sclerosis, calcification (Lev, Lenegre disease), ischemia/infarction, infiltrative or inflammatory disease, drugs, heightened vagal tone, or congenital/genetic abnormalities; consequences range from fatigue and syncope to asystolic death if no reliable escape emerges. Functional (autonomic/metabolic/drug) causes are often reversible while structural fibrosis is typically permanent. Prognosis depends heavily on the level of block. AV-nodal (proximal) block - including Mobitz I and most inferior-MI-related block - tends to have a faster, stable narrow-complex escape and is often reversible with a favorable outcome. Infranodal (distal His-Purkinje) block, Mobitz II, and high-grade block in anterior MI carry unstable wide-complex escape rhythms, higher mortality, and a risk of sudden asystolic death, so pacing is indicated even when asymptomatic. Functional/reversible causes generally resolve; structural fibrotic disease is usually permanent and progressive. Electrocardiographic grading: First-degree AV block - all atrial impulses conduct but PR is prolonged (>200 ms), delay usually within the AV node. Second-degree AV block - intermittent failure of AV conduction; Type I/Mobitz I/Wenckebach (progressive PR prolongation until a dropped beat, usually AV-nodal) and Type II/Mobitz II (fixed PR before a dropped beat, usually infranodal, often with wide QRS). Third-degree (complete) AV block - complete AV dissociation with a ventricular (escape) rate slower than the atrial rate.

The Hyperbilirubinemias — Gilbert syndrome, Crigler-Najjar syndrome, Dubin-Johnson syndrome, Rotor syndrome, unconjugated hyperbilirubinemia, conjugated hyperbilirubinemia, inherited hyperbilirubinemias Hemolytic anemias (hereditary spherocytosis, G6PD deficiency, beta-thalassemia) causing unconjugated hyperbilirubinemia Ineffective erythropoiesis (thalassemia major, megaloblastic anemia, congenital dyserythropoietic anemias, lead poisoning) Drug-induced unconjugated hyperbilirubinemia (rifampin, novobiocin, atazanavir, indinavir, chloramphenicol, gentamicin) Physiologic, breast-milk, and Lucey-Driscoll neonatal jaundice Acquired hepatocellular or cholestatic liver disease (acute viral hepatitis, common bile duct stone) with mixed hyperbilirubinemia Benign recurrent intrahepatic cholestasis (BRIC) and progressive familial intrahepatic cholestasis (PFIC types 1-3) Acute viral hepatitis, which the first cholestatic episodes of benign recurrent intrahepatic cholestasis may mimic Fractionation of serum bilirubin into conjugated (direct) and unconjugated (indirect) components Urinalysis for bilirubinuria (present in conjugated, absent in unconjugated hyperbilirubinemia) Standard liver biochemistries (aminotransferases, alkaline phosphatase, albumin, prothrombin time) and hemolysis workup (reticulocytes, haptoglobin) Urinary coproporphyrin isomer analysis to distinguish Dubin-Johnson (>=80% isomer I, normal total) from Rotor (markedly increased total, isomer I usually <70%) Phenobarbital challenge to separate Crigler-Najjar type II (>25% fall) from type I (no response) UGT1A1 genotyping (e.g., A[TA]7TAA promoter for Gilbert syndrome); oral cholecystography (gallbladder non-visualized in Dubin-Johnson, visualized in Rotor) Extrahepatic biliary obstruction (e.g., choledocholithiasis) presenting with conjugated hyperbilirubinemia Intrahepatic cholestatic injury Resorbing large hematoma or massive tissue infarction causing transient unconjugated hyperbilirubinemia Bilirubin is the terminal product of heme catabolism, with roughly 70-90% derived from breakdown of hemoglobin in senescent red cells; hepatic handling involves four linked steps: carrier-mediated uptake, intracellular binding to glutathione-S-transferases (ligandins), conjugation by UGT1A1, and canalicular excretion (Harrison 22e p.2637-2638). Conjugation by UGT1A1 adds one or two glucuronic acid moieties, disrupting internal hydrogen bonding so the resulting glucuronides become water-soluble; conjugation is obligatory for biliary excretion (Harrison 22e p.2638). Unconjugated bilirubin is too tightly albumin-bound to be filtered and does not appear in urine, whereas conjugated (water-soluble) bilirubin is readily filtered, so bilirubinuria indicates a conjugated (direct) hyperbilirubinemia; the kidney acts as an overflow valve so renal failure can amplify jaundice in conjugated hyperbilirubinemia (Harrison 22e p.2638). Isolated hemolysis in an otherwise healthy person produces a purely unconjugated hyperbilirubinemia with direct fraction <=15% of total; because marrow erythropoiesis can rise only about eightfold, hemolysis alone rarely sustains a bilirubin above ~68 micromol/L (4 mg/dL), so higher values imply concomitant hepatic dysfunction (Harrison 22e p.2638-2639). Gilbert syndrome is a common, benign cause of mild unconjugated hyperbilirubinemia (usually <51 micromol/L, <3 mg/dL) with normal liver tests and histology; levels rise with fasting, stress, fatigue, alcohol, and intercurrent illness and fall with caloric intake or enzyme inducers (Harrison 22e p.2640). Crigler-Najjar type I shows extreme lifelong unconjugated hyperbilirubinemia (~340-765 micromol/L, 20-45 mg/dL) with essentially absent UGT1A1 activity, no response to phenobarbital, and high kernicterus risk; type II has lower levels, detectable enzyme, pigmented bile, and a >25% bilirubin fall with phenobarbital (Harrison 22e p.2639-2640). Dubin-Johnson syndrome is a benign, autosomal recessive predominantly conjugated hyperbilirubinemia (typically 34-85 micromol/L) caused by mutation of the canalicular transporter MRP2 (ABCC2); the liver is grossly black from lysosomal pigment and urinary coproporphyrin is >=80% isomer I despite a normal total (Harrison 22e p.2640-2641). Rotor syndrome resembles Dubin-Johnson clinically (conjugated hyperbilirubinemia, bilirubinuria) but the liver is normal in color, the gallbladder is visualized on oral cholecystography, and total urinary coproporphyrin is markedly increased with isomer I usually <70%; it results from combined deficiency of OATP1B1 and OATP1B3 (Harrison 22e p.2641-2642). Most neonates develop mild physiologic unconjugated hyperbilirubinemia between days 2 and 5 (peak typically <85-170 micromol/L, 5-10 mg/dL) due to low UGT1A1 and enterohepatic recycling, resolving within about 2 weeks (Harrison 22e p.2639). A rapidly rising neonatal unconjugated bilirubin, or absolute levels above ~340 micromol/L (20 mg/dL), risks bilirubin encephalopathy (kernicterus) as pigment crosses an immature blood-brain barrier and deposits in the basal ganglia (Harrison 22e p.2639). Acquired liver disease (acute hepatitis, common bile duct stone) generally produces a mixed conjugated and unconjugated hyperbilirubinemia, and serum levels or fractions cannot reliably distinguish intrahepatic from extrahepatic obstruction (Harrison 22e p.2640). Gilbert syndrome impairs glucuronidation of the irinotecan (CPT-11) active metabolite SN-38, predisposing to severe diarrhea and myelosuppression; the HIV protease inhibitors indinavir and atazanavir inhibit UGT1A1 and worsen hyperbilirubinemia, most markedly in preexisting Gilbert syndrome (Harrison 22e p.2640). Rapidly rising neonatal unconjugated bilirubin or absolute level above ~340 micromol/L (20 mg/dL) signaling risk of kernicterus Sustained unconjugated hyperbilirubinemia above ~68 micromol/L (4 mg/dL) attributed to hemolysis, implying additional hepatic dysfunction Conjugated hyperbilirubinemia with bilirubinuria, prompting evaluation for hepatocellular or obstructive disease Intercurrent febrile illness in Crigler-Najjar that can precipitate late-onset bilirubin encephalopathy Prolonged, debilitating cholestatic attacks in BRIC and progression of PFIC to end-stage liver disease Assuming hemolysis alone explains a markedly elevated bilirubin; sustained levels above ~68 micromol/L (4 mg/dL) imply coexisting hepatic dysfunction Using serum bilirubin levels or conjugated/unconjugated proportions to differentiate intrahepatic from extrahepatic causes of jaundice, which is not reliable Overdiagnosing Gilbert syndrome from a single value, since levels fluctuate widely and at least 25% of patients show transiently normal bilirubin on follow-up Male predominance in Gilbert syndrome may be artifactual, reflecting use of male-derived reference ranges Mistaking the first episodes of benign recurrent intrahepatic cholestasis for acute viral hepatitis Prescribing drugs cleared by glucuronidation (notably irinotecan) without caution in Gilbert syndrome given risk of severe toxicity Bilirubin, the end product of heme degradation (chiefly from senescent erythrocyte hemoglobin), circulates tightly bound to albumin and is processed by hepatocytes in four steps: carrier-mediated uptake, intracellular binding to glutathione-S-transferases, conjugation with glucuronic acid by UGT1A1 (the physiologically critical isoform encoded by exon A1 plus shared exons 2-5 of the UGT1 gene complex on chromosome 2), and ATP-dependent canalicular excretion of mono- and diglucuronides via MRP2. A portion of glucuronides is also exported into the portal circulation by MRP3 and recaptured by sinusoidal OATP1B1/OATP1B3. Unconjugated hyperbilirubinemia arises from overproduction (hemolysis, ineffective erythropoiesis, resorption of large hematomas/infarcts), decreased hepatic uptake (drugs such as rifampin, novobiocin; contributory in Gilbert syndrome), or impaired conjugation (neonatal immaturity, breast-milk jaundice, drug inhibition of UGT1A1, and hereditary UGT1A1 defects of Crigler-Najjar I/II and Gilbert syndrome). Gilbert syndrome most often reflects a homozygous extra TA insertion (A[TA]7TAA rather than A[TA]6TAA) in the UGT1A1 promoter reducing enzyme expression; Crigler-Najjar reflects coding/structural UGT1 mutations causing absent (type I) or markedly reduced (type II) activity. Predominantly conjugated familial hyperbilirubinemias result from defective canalicular excretion: Dubin-Johnson from MRP2 (ABCC2) mutation and Rotor from combined OATP1B1/OATP1B3 deficiency impairing reuptake of refluxed conjugated bilirubin. Gilbert, Dubin-Johnson, and Rotor syndromes are benign with normal life expectancy and no progression to chronic liver disease. Crigler-Najjar type I carries a grave prognosis: before phototherapy most patients died of kernicterus in infancy or early childhood, and even survivors developed bilirubin-induced neurologic dysfunction, with early liver transplantation the best means to prevent brain injury and death. Crigler-Najjar type II is far less often complicated by kernicterus and is generally compatible with normal life, though intercurrent illness, fasting, or low albumin can precipitate dangerous bilirubin elevations. BRIC is benign and does not cause cirrhosis, whereas PFIC progresses to end-stage liver disease in childhood. Inherited unconjugated hyperbilirubinemia forms a severity continuum by residual UGT1A1 activity: Crigler-Najjar type I (activity absent; bilirubin ~340-765 micromol/L, 20-45 mg/dL; no phenobarbital response; usual kernicterus), Crigler-Najjar type II (reduced activity, typically <=10% of normal; bilirubin ~100-430 micromol/L, 6-25 mg/dL; >25% phenobarbital response; rare kernicterus), and Gilbert syndrome (activity ~10-35% of normal; bilirubin usually <=70 micromol/L, 4 mg/dL absent fasting/hemolysis; normal histology). Familial conjugated hyperbilirubinemias of canalicular function (Dubin-Johnson, Rotor) are benign, distinguished from the progressive cholestatic disorders BRIC (episodic, non-progressive) and PFIC (progressive to end-stage liver disease).

The Metabolic Syndrome — Syndrome X, Insulin resistance syndrome, MetS Type 2 diabetes mellitus / impaired glucose tolerance Genetic lipodystrophies (e.g., Berardinelli-Seip congenital, Dunnigan familial partial lipodystrophy) Acquired lipodystrophy (e.g., HIV-related and antiretroviral-associated) Polycystic ovary syndrome Cushing's syndrome / other endocrine causes of central obesity and hypertension Primary dyslipidemias Fasting lipid panel (triglycerides, HDL cholesterol) and fasting glucose are required for diagnosis Waist circumference measurement and blood pressure Optional insulin-resistance biomarkers individualized to the patient: apoB, hsCRP, fibrinogen, uric acid, urinary albumin/creatinine ratio, liver function tests Sleep study if symptoms of obstructive sleep apnea are present If PCOS suspected (clinical features and anovulation): testosterone, luteinizing hormone, follicle-stimulating hormone MAFLD assessment via FIB-4 fibrosis score or elastography DEXA, CT, or MRI if discrimination of visceral versus subcutaneous fat is needed Lipodystrophy syndromes (severe insulin resistance with many overlapping components) Cushing's syndrome (central adiposity, hypertension, hyperglycemia) Polycystic ovary syndrome with insulin resistance Metabolic syndrome is a clustering of metabolic abnormalities (central obesity, hypertriglyceridemia, low HDL cholesterol, hyperglycemia, and hypertension) that together raise the risk of cardiovascular disease and diabetes. Diagnosis under NCEP:ATPIII (2001) requires three or more of: waist circumference >102 cm in men or >88 cm in women; triglycerides >=150 mg/dL; HDL <40 mg/dL (men) or <50 mg/dL (women); BP >=130/85 mmHg; fasting glucose >=100 mg/dL (or specific medication for, or prior diagnosis of, the relevant condition). The Harmonizing definition uses ethnicity-specific waist circumference cutoffs (e.g., for South Asian and Chinese men >=90 cm, Europid men >=94 cm, Japanese men >=85 cm), reflecting that risk at a given waist circumference differs between populations. Visceral (intra-abdominal) adipose tissue is more strongly linked to insulin resistance, diabetes, and CVD than subcutaneous fat, but waist circumference alone cannot reliably distinguish the two depots; DEXA, CT, or MRI is needed for that distinction. Normal-weight individuals can still be insulin-resistant and meet criteria for metabolic syndrome, a phenotype that is particularly evident in populations from India, Southeast Asia, and Central America. The syndrome is typically asymptomatic; physical examination often shows only elevated waist circumference and blood pressure, which should trigger a search for the other biochemical components. Lipoatrophy and acanthosis nigricans, when present, signal severe insulin resistance, though they are far less common than the standard components. Hypertriglyceridemia is an excellent marker of the insulin-resistant state; fasting triglycerides above roughly 180 mg/dL (~2.0 mM) are typically accompanied by a predominance of small, dense, more atherogenic LDL particles. Most patients (~75%) with type 2 diabetes or impaired glucose tolerance have metabolic syndrome, and its presence in these groups marks a higher CVD burden than in those without the syndrome. Conditions strongly associated with insulin resistance and the syndrome include metabolic-associated fatty liver disease (MAFLD/MASH), polycystic ovary syndrome, and obstructive sleep apnea, which should be screened for during evaluation. Obstructive sleep apnea can predict metabolic syndrome even without excess adiposity, and insulin resistance tends to be more severe in apnea patients than in weight-matched controls. Hyperuricemia reflects insulin-resistance-related defects in renal tubular handling of uric acid and may itself contribute to hypertension via effects on endothelial nitric oxide synthase and activation of the renin-angiotensin-aldosterone system. Acanthosis nigricans or lipoatrophy indicating severe insulin resistance Established type 2 diabetes or impaired glucose tolerance (markedly elevated diabetes and CVD risk) Coexisting metabolic syndrome and elevated hsCRP (associated with increased all-cause mortality) Features suggesting MASH/advanced liver fibrosis (precursor of cirrhosis and hepatocellular carcinoma) Symptoms of obstructive sleep apnea Waist circumference does not reliably separate subcutaneous from visceral fat, so it can misestimate true metabolic risk without imaging. A single ethnicity-blind waist cutoff under- or over-estimates risk across populations; ethnicity-specific thresholds are needed. Normal body weight does not exclude the syndrome, so insulin resistance can be missed in lean individuals. Whether metabolic syndrome adds CVD or diabetes risk beyond the simple sum of its individual components remains debated, so it should not be over-interpreted as an independent diagnosis. Fasting insulin levels or HOMA capture only part of insulin resistance, so they inadequately quantify the contribution of resistance to hypertension. Obstructive sleep apnea and PCOS are commonly overlooked associated conditions if not actively screened for. Insulin resistance is the most widely accepted unifying mechanism. Early insulin resistance manifests as postprandial then fasting hyperinsulinemia, eventually progressing to hyperglycemia as compensatory beta-cell secretion fails. An overabundance of circulating free fatty acids (FFAs), released from expanded adipose tissue and from lipoprotein-lipase-mediated lipolysis, drives the process: FFAs impair insulin-mediated glucose uptake in muscle, promote intramuscular and cardiac triglyceride accumulation, and increase hepatic glucose and triglyceride production with VLDL secretion. Insulin normally suppresses lipolysis (its most sensitive action), so resistance amplifies FFA release in a self-perpetuating loop. Increased VLDL/apoB and elevated apoC-III inhibit lipoprotein lipase, raising triglyceride-rich remnants; HDL becomes small, dense, and cleared faster, lowering HDL cholesterol. Loss of insulin-mediated vasodilation (nitric oxide) with preserved renal sodium reabsorption and sympathetic activation, plus adipose angiotensinogen expression, contributes to hypertension. Contributing/associated mechanisms include leptin resistance, reduced anti-inflammatory adiponectin, increased proinflammatory cytokines (IL-1, IL-6, IL-18, TNF-alpha, resistin) from adipose-derived macrophages, a prothrombotic state (fibrinogen, PAI-1), oxidative stress with mitochondrial dysfunction, and alterations in the gut microbiome (increased Firmicutes/Bacteroidetes ratio). Metabolic syndrome roughly doubles the risk of cardiovascular death and confers about a threefold higher risk of acute myocardial infarction or stroke; the risk for type 2 diabetes is increased three- to fivefold (fasting glucose explaining most of this). In the REGARDS cohort, metabolic syndrome carried a relative risk of about 1.34 for all-cause mortality, with the relationship to hsCRP and mortality stronger in white than in black participants. Prevalence among patients with coronary heart disease may reach up to 60% in those over 75. Risk and prevalence are modifiable: cardiac rehabilitation and lifestyle change (improved nutrition, physical activity, weight reduction) can reduce the prevalence of the syndrome. There is no graded severity scale; the syndrome is defined categorically by meeting three or more of the five diagnostic components (NCEP:ATPIII 2001 or the ethnicity-adjusted Harmonizing definition, Table 420-1). Risk rises with the number of components present and with associated markers such as elevated hsCRP.

symptomatic skin nodules, painful testes, or nerve/muscle for PAN) ANCA testing (anti-PR3 / cANCA and anti-MPO / pANCA) with awareness of variable predictive value by presentation Catheter-directed (dye) arteriography for suspected PAN; serum creatinine Hepatitis B and C serologies/RNA (PAN, cryoglobulinemic vasculitis) Serum cryoglobulins, rheumatoid factor, and complement levels for cryoglobulinemic vasculitis Skin biopsy with immunofluorescence (IgA and C3 deposition in IgA vasculitis; leukocytoclastic vasculitis in cutaneous vasculitis) Echocardiography at diagnosis in EGPA given cardiac mortality risk Consider DADA2 (adenosine deaminase type 2 deficiency) evaluation in early-onset PAN-like vasculitis Antiphospholipid syndrome Thrombotic thrombocytopenic purpura / thrombotic microangiopathies Atrial myxoma Lymphoma and carcinomatosis Drug toxicity (cocaine, levamisole-adulterated cocaine, amphetamines, ergot alkaloids, methysergide, arsenic) Sarcoidosis Atheroembolic disease Amyloidosis Migraine Fibromuscular dysplasia Heritable connective tissue disorders Segmental arterial mediolysis Reversible cerebral vasoconstriction syndrome Vasculitis is inflammation of and damage to blood vessel walls that typically narrows the lumen and produces downstream tissue ischemia; it may be the sole disease, may be secondary to another disease, and may be single-organ or multisystem. Suspect vasculitis in any unexplained systemic illness; clinical clues include palpable purpura, pulmonary infiltrates with microscopic hematuria, chronic sinusitis, mononeuritis multiplex, unexplained ischemic events, and glomerulonephritis with multisystem disease. Definitive diagnosis usually rests on biopsy of clinically involved tissue; 'blind' biopsy of organs without subjective or objective involvement has very low yield and should be avoided. Catheter-directed arteriography is used when PAN, Takayasu, or primary CNS vasculitis is suspected. ANCA subtypes: cANCA targets proteinase-3 (>90% positive in active granulomatosis with polyangiitis); pANCA most relevantly targets myeloperoxidase (variably positive in microscopic polyangiitis, EGPA, and isolated necrotizing crescentic glomerulonephritis). Only anti-MPO and anti-PR3 are convincingly vasculitis-associated. Granulomatosis with polyangiitis classically combines granulomatous vasculitis of the upper and lower respiratory tracts with glomerulonephritis; upper airway involvement occurs in ~95% and renal disease (~77% over course) dominates prognosis. Renal lesion is pauci-immune (no immune-complex deposition). Microscopic polyangiitis resembles GPA but lacks granulomatous inflammation; it favors small vessels (capillaries, venules, arterioles), with glomerulonephritis in at least 79% and alveolar hemorrhage in ~12%. Upper airway disease and lung nodules are atypical and, if present, point instead to GPA. ANCA (usually anti-MPO) in ~75%. EGPA (Churg-Strauss) is defined by asthma, blood and tissue eosinophilia, and vasculitis; eosinophilia exceeds 1000 cells/uL in >80% and ANCA (usually anti-MPO) is present in ~48%. Cardiac involvement is the leading cause of death, so echocardiography is advised at diagnosis. Polyarteritis nodosa is a necrotizing vasculitis of small- and medium-sized muscular arteries that spares pulmonary arteries and does NOT cause glomerulonephritis, granuloma, or significant eosinophilia; renal involvement is arteritis (microaneurysms, hypertension), not glomerular. ANCA are rarely found; screen all patients for hepatitis B and C. Giant cell arteritis occurs almost exclusively after age 50, presents with fever, anemia, high ESR/CRP, and headache; ischemic optic neuropathy with sudden blindness is the dreaded complication, and patients carry an ~18-fold increased risk of thoracic aortic aneurysm. Treatment should not be delayed for biopsy. Polymyalgia rheumatica (aching/stiffness of neck, shoulder and hip girdles with raised ESR/CRP) coexists with GCA in 40-50% of GCA patients; creatine kinase is normal and RF/anti-CCP should be negative. ~10-20% with isolated PMR later develop GCA. Takayasu arteritis is a large-vessel panarteritis with strong predilection for the aortic arch and its branches, classically in adolescent girls and young women; suspect it in a young woman with diminished or absent pulses, an interarm blood-pressure discrepancy, or arterial bruits. IgA vasculitis (Henoch-Schonlein) is a small-vessel, immune-complex (IgA) vasculitis most common in children 4-7 years, with palpable purpura over buttocks/lower limbs, arthralgias, colicky GI symptoms (intussusception risk), and usually mild self-limited glomerulonephritis; serum complement is normal and IgA is elevated in about half. Cryoglobulinemic vasculitis is most often associated with hepatitis C (estimated in ~5% of chronic HCV); rheumatoid factor is almost always present, hypocomplementemia occurs in ~90%, and membranoproliferative glomerulonephritis accounts for ~80% of renal lesions. Temporal artery biopsy yield improves with a 3-5 cm segment and serial sectioning because involvement is segmental; biopsy may still show arteritis after about 14 days of glucocorticoid therapy, so starting treatment promptly does not preclude later diagnosis. Rapidly progressive glomerulonephritis or rising creatinine (GPA, microscopic polyangiitis, cryoglobulinemic vasculitis) Hemoptysis / diffuse alveolar hemorrhage (microscopic polyangiitis, GPA) New or worsening headache, jaw or tongue claudication, scalp tenderness, or any visual symptom in a patient over 50 (impending GCA-related blindness) Subglottic stenosis or progressive airway obstruction in GPA Mononeuritis multiplex Abdominal pain with GI bleeding suggesting bowel infarction/perforation (PAN, EGPA, IgA vasculitis with intussusception) Cardiac involvement (myocarditis/coronary vasculitis) in EGPA or PAN Interarm blood-pressure discrepancy, absent pulses, or aortic aneurysm/dissection in large-vessel disease Concurrent anti-GBM antibody positivity in ANCA-associated vasculitis Do NOT treat a rise in ANCA titer alone as evidence of relapse; only ~43% of patients relapsed within a year of an ANCA rise, and many remain ANCA-positive for years in remission. ANCA predictive value falls sharply when renal disease is absent (~30-60% with sinus/lung-only disease vs ~90% with active glomerulonephritis), so biopsy is needed to exclude infection or malignancy that can cause false-positive ANCA. Upper airway lesions in GPA should NEVER be irradiated; midline destructive disease mimics include NK/T-cell lymphoma and cocaine/levamisole injury (anti-neutrophil-elastase ANCA, granulocytopenia point to levamisole). Eosinophilia is rare in PAN; when markedly elevated it should redirect toward EGPA. In PAN, MR and CT arteriography lack the resolution to visualize the small/medium aneurysms, so catheter-directed dye arteriography is required. When tocilizumab or other IL-6 blockade is used in GCA, ESR and CRP normalize and can no longer be used to gauge disease activity or detect infection. TMP-SMX should never be used alone to treat active GPA involving organs beyond the sinonasal tissue. Failure to exclude infection (especially endocarditis) before starting empirical immunosuppression in a rapidly deteriorating patient can be catastrophic. Glucocorticoids do not reliably benefit the skin or renal disease of IgA vasculitis and do not shorten its course or reduce recurrence. Most vasculitic syndromes are thought to be at least partly immune-mediated responses to antigenic stimuli, with the precise mechanism varying by disease. Three principal hypothesized mechanisms are recognized. (1) Pathogenic immune-complex formation/deposition (e.g., IgA vasculitis, lupus vasculitis, serum-sickness/cutaneous syndromes, HCV-associated cryoglobulinemic vasculitis, HBV-associated vasculitis): antigen-antibody complexes formed in antigen excess deposit in vessel walls whose permeability has been raised by vasoactive amines, activate complement (notably chemotactic C5a), recruit neutrophils that phagocytose complexes and release intracytoplasmic enzymes damaging the wall, with later mononuclear infiltration and luminal compromise. (2) ANCA production (GPA, microscopic polyangiitis, EGPA): when neutrophils/monocytes are primed by TNF-alpha or IL-1 or alternative-complement activation, PR3 and MPO translocate to the cell membrane where ANCA can engage them, triggering degranulation, reactive oxygen species, endothelial injury, and release of IL-1/IL-8; however, some patients have active GPA without ANCA and titers correlate poorly with activity, so a primary pathogenic role remains debated. (3) Pathogenic T-lymphocyte responses and granuloma formation (giant cell arteritis, Takayasu arteritis, GPA, EGPA): cytokine-activated endothelium expresses HLA class II and secretes IL-1, enabling CD4+ T-cell interactions; IL-1 and TNF-alpha upregulate ELAM-1 and VCAM-1 to enhance leukocyte adhesion. In GCA the disease is antigen-driven, with clonally restricted T cells suggesting an arterial-wall antigen, and both TH1 (IFN-gamma) and TH17 (IL-17) CD4 lineages contribute. The size, type, and location of affected vessels, host genetic predisposition, environmental exposures, reticuloendothelial clearance of complexes, hemodynamic factors, and endothelial integrity all influence the ultimate phenotype. Outcome varies markedly by syndrome and by treatment. Untreated granulomatosis with polyangiitis was once uniformly fatal within months; modern cyclophosphamide- or rituximab-based regimens with glucocorticoids achieve improvement in >90% and remission in ~75%, with 5-year survival >80%, though 50-70% of remissions are followed by relapse and many patients accrue irreversible damage (renal insufficiency, hearing loss, subglottic stenosis, saddle-nose deformity). Treated microscopic polyangiitis has ~74% 5-year survival with relapse in at least 34%, mortality from alveolar hemorrhage or GI/cardiac/renal disease. Untreated EGPA has a ~25% 5-year survival; with treatment about 72% survive at 78 months, and myocardial involvement causes ~39% of deaths. Untreated PAN carries a 10-20% 5-year survival (death from bowel infarction/perforation and cardiovascular causes); combination immunosuppression markedly improves survival, with relapse in ~10-20%. GCA seldom causes acute death but carries late risk of aortic aneurysm rupture/dissection; PMR generally responds well. Takayasu is usually chronic and relapsing with widely variable reported survival. IgA vasculitis prognosis is excellent (mortality exceedingly rare; 1-5% of children reach end-stage renal disease, possibly higher in adults; recurrences in 10-40%). In cryoglobulinemic vasculitis, glomerulonephritis is a poor prognostic sign (~15% progress to end-stage renal disease, 40% of whom later die of cardiovascular disease, infection, or liver failure). For ANCA-associated vasculitis (GPA/microscopic polyangiitis), Harrison frames management by severe vs nonsevere disease. Severe disease involves life- or organ-threatening manifestations and is judged by both extent and the specific organ affected: pulmonary disease may be nonsevere (nodules without respiratory compromise) or severe (alveolar hemorrhage), whereas active glomerulonephritis is ALWAYS considered severe even when renal function is normal. Treatment is conceptually divided into a remission-induction phase followed by a maintenance phase, with regimen choice stratified by this severity assessment along with relapse history and comorbidities.

Excessive circulating beta-hCG, or heightened ovarian sensitivity to normal levels, over-stimulates the theca interna cells lining the ovarian follicles. This drives exaggerated luteinisation and the formation of multiple fluid-filled cysts, usually affecting both ovaries and producing considerable ovarian enlargement. Because the process is hormonally driven, the cysts involute as the beta-hCG concentration declines, for example after evacuation of a molar pregnancy or delivery. The outlook is excellent, as theca lutein cysts almost always resolve spontaneously once the underlying hCG stimulus subsides, without the need for surgery.

theca lutein cysts — theca-lutein cysts, hCG-associated luteinised ovarian cysts Hyperreactio luteinalis (florid theca-lutein cysts in pregnancy without trophoblastic disease) Ovarian hyperstimulation syndrome Bilateral cystic ovarian neoplasm (mucinous or serous cystadenoma, borderline tumour) Polycystic ovaries Bilateral haemorrhagic corpus luteum cysts or endometriomas Ovarian torsion Simple follicular cysts Quantitative serum hCG and its trend Pelvic ultrasound with Doppler to assess cyst morphology, ovarian perfusion and possible torsion Uterine evaluation for hydatidiform mole or retained trophoblastic tissue Thyroid function tests if clinically hyperthyroid Serum androgens if virilisation is present Chest imaging where choriocarcinoma or metastatic trophoblastic disease is suspected Interval imaging to document regression Theca-lutein cysts are the largest of the functional ovarian cysts and are characteristically bilateral and multilocular, arising from excessive or prolonged stimulation of ovarian theca cells by human chorionic gonadotrophin. They are the classic ovarian finding of gestational trophoblastic disease (complete hydatidiform mole and choriocarcinoma) and also accompany multiple gestation, fetal hydrops, ovarian hyperstimulation syndrome, and exogenous gonadotrophin or clomifene therapy. On ultrasound the enlarged ovaries show numerous thin-walled locules in a 'spoke-wheel' pattern, usually without solid components. Most are asymptomatic and found incidentally, but large cysts may cause pelvic pressure, and complications include torsion, rupture, intraperitoneal haemorrhage and occasionally ascites. Because they are hCG-dependent, they regress once the stimulus is removed (after evacuation of a mole, delivery, or resolution of the underlying cause), although regression may lag behind the fall in hCG by weeks to months. Management is conservative and expectant; surgery is reserved for acute complications such as torsion or haemorrhage, ideally with ovarian conservation. In gestational trophoblastic disease, persistent or re-enlarging theca-lutein cysts should prompt reassessment for persistent trophoblastic activity. Maternal virilisation and clinical hyperthyroidism (from the weak thyrotrophic activity of hCG) are occasionally seen when hCG concentrations are very high. Acute severe pelvic pain with peritonism suggesting torsion, rupture or haemorrhage Haemodynamic instability from intraperitoneal bleeding Plateauing or rising hCG after molar evacuation indicating persistent gestational trophoblastic neoplasia Solid or papillary components, or failure to regress, raising suspicion of neoplasm Resecting hormone-dependent cysts that would regress spontaneously, sacrificing ovarian tissue Failing to investigate for gestational trophoblastic disease when bilateral theca-lutein cysts are found Misinterpreting the multicystic ovaries as malignancy Attributing all pelvic pain to the cysts and missing a coexisting torsion Expecting immediate regression and re-intervening before the natural lag after hCG decline Theca-lutein cysts develop when ovarian theca-interna cells are excessively stimulated by human chorionic gonadotrophin, which acts on the luteinising-hormone receptor to drive luteinisation, follicular over-recruitment and cystic dilatation. Markedly raised hCG, as in complete molar pregnancy, choriocarcinoma or multiple gestation, is the usual driver, although heightened ovarian sensitivity can produce them at more modest levels. The affected ovaries enlarge and become studded with multiple thin-walled, fluid-filled cysts lined by luteinised theca and granulosa cells, frequently bilateral and symmetrical. The luteinised cells may secrete androgens, and the high hCG can exert weak thyroid-stimulating activity. Because the cysts are functional and hormone-dependent, removal or decline of the hCG source allows involution. The cysts are benign and self-limiting and almost always involute spontaneously once the hCG source resolves. The outlook is excellent provided complications such as torsion or haemorrhage are managed and any underlying trophoblastic disease is treated.

Missing secondary corneal involvement Thelaziasis results from the deposition of infective Thelazia larvae onto the conjunctiva by drosophilid flies that feed on lacrimal secretions. The larvae mature into adult worms within the conjunctival sac and adnexal structures, where their movement and cuticular surface mechanically irritate the ocular surface. This provokes reflex tearing, conjunctival inflammation and a foreign-body reaction; persistent presence of worms can lead to keratitis and corneal ulceration. Because the parasite remains largely superficial in the eye, disease is usually localised rather than systemic. Prognosis is excellent once the worms are removed, with rapid symptomatic relief and full recovery unless corneal damage has already occurred.

features are vomiting, tremor, agitation, tachycardia and, in severe cases, seizures and arrhythmias Hypokalaemia, hypomagnesaemia, hyperglycaemia and a metabolic (lactic) acidosis reflect intense recurrent or refractory Ventricular or unstable supraventricular arrhythmia Very high serum concentration, especially after modified-release ingestion Severe hypokalaemia, acidosis or haemodynamic instability Chronic toxicity in an older or comorbid patient even at moderate levels Relying on a single level and missing continued absorption from slow-release tablets Underestimating chronic toxicity because the concentration seems only modestly raised Neglecting to correct hypokalaemia and hypomagnesaemia driving arrhythmia Delaying extracorporeal removal in severe or very high-level poisoning Using unopposed agents that worsen catecholamine-driven cardiovascular effects Theophylline is a methylxanthine that inhibits phosphodiesterase, raising intracellular cyclic adenosine monophosphate, and antagonises adenosine receptors. It also releases endogenous catecholamines, producing a state of intense beta-adrenergic stimulation. The result is central nervous system excitation with tremor, agitation and seizures, cardiovascular effects including tachycardia and dysrhythmias, and metabolic disturbances such as hypokalaemia from intracellular potassium shift, hyperglycaemia and lactic acidosis. Adenosine antagonism lowers the seizure threshold. In chronic toxicity, accumulation from impaired clearance produces serious effects at lower measured concentrations than in acute single overdose. Mild toxicity generally resolves with supportive care and gastrointestinal decontamination, but severe poisoning with seizures or arrhythmias, and chronic toxicity in vulnerable patients, carries significant mortality; prompt enhanced elimination improves outcome in severe cases.

zone of coagulation surrounded by zones of stasis and hyperaemia that can progress to necrosis if perfusion falls. Loss of the skin barrier and a systemic inflammatory response increase capillary permeability, causing large fluid shifts, intravascular volume depletion, and burn shock in extensive injuries. Inhalational injury combines direct thermal damage to the upper airway, chemical injury to the lower airways from combustion products, and systemic asphyxiants such as carbon monoxide and cyanide. Later, the denuded surface predisposes to infection and hypermetabolism. Prognosis depends on burn size and depth, age, inhalational injury, and comorbidity. Small partial-thickness burns heal well, whereas large or full-thickness burns and inhalational injury carry higher mortality and long-term morbidity, including scarring and functional loss.

Thiamine-responsive megaloblastic anaemia — Rogers syndrome, TRMA, SLC19A2, thiamine transporter 1 deficiency Vitamin B12 or folate deficiency megaloblastic anaemia Congenital sideroblastic anaemias Myelodysplastic syndrome in childhood Pearson marrow-pancreas syndrome and other mitochondrial disorders Wolfram syndrome (DIDMOAD) given diabetes with deafness Neonatal or MODY-type diabetes syndromes SLC19A2 molecular genetic testing Full blood count and blood film showing macrocytic anaemia Bone marrow examination for megaloblastic change and ringed sideroblasts Fasting glucose and glycated haemoglobin for diabetes Audiometry for sensorineural hearing loss Ophthalmological and echocardiographic assessment for associated anomalies Recognise the classic triad: megaloblastic anaemia, diabetes mellitus and progressive sensorineural deafness, all presenting in infancy or early childhood Autosomal recessive disorder caused by biallelic pathogenic variants in SLC19A2, encoding high-affinity thiamine transporter 1 (THTR1) The megaloblastic anaemia does not respond to vitamin B12 or folate, but does respond to pharmacological thiamine supplementation Thiamine treatment can correct the anaemia and improve glycaemic control, though it usually does not reverse the sensorineural hearing loss The bone marrow shows megaloblastic changes and often ringed sideroblasts Diabetes is typically non-autoimmune and may become insulin-dependent over time Additional features can include optic atrophy, retinal changes, cardiac defects and short stature Lifelong thiamine supplementation is required; interruption can allow anaemia and hyperglycaemia to recur Severe symptomatic anaemia requiring transfusion in an infant Uncontrolled hyperglycaemia or diabetic ketoacidosis Rapidly progressive hearing loss Cardiac decompensation from associated structural defects Treating the anaemia with B12 or folate and concluding the marrow is unresponsive Failing to link the anaemia, diabetes and deafness as one syndrome Stopping thiamine once counts normalise, allowing relapse Missing the diagnosis in a child labelled as having early-onset diabetes alone Rogers syndrome results from loss of function of the high-affinity thiamine transporter THTR1 encoded by SLC19A2. Cells that depend heavily on this transporter for thiamine uptake, notably haematopoietic precursors, pancreatic beta cells and cochlear cells, become thiamine deficient at the intracellular level despite normal systemic thiamine. Impaired thiamine-dependent enzyme activity (including transketolase and the pyruvate and alpha-ketoglutarate dehydrogenase complexes) disrupts nucleic acid ribose synthesis and energy metabolism, producing megaloblastic dyserythropoiesis, beta-cell failure with diabetes, and cochlear degeneration with deafness. Supraphysiological thiamine can drive residual low-affinity transport and restore intracellular thiamine, correcting the haematological and metabolic features. Thiamine supplementation typically corrects the anaemia and improves diabetes control, but sensorineural deafness is usually irreversible and lifelong treatment with monitoring is needed to maintain remission.

Thiel-Behnke corneal dystrophy — corneal dystrophy of Bowman layer type 2, honeycomb corneal dystrophy Reis-Bucklers corneal dystrophy Granular and lattice corneal dystrophies Map-dot-fingerprint dystrophy Recurrent erosion from other cause Anterior corneal scarring Slit-lamp examination of the honeycomb subepithelial opacities TGFBI genetic testing to confirm and distinguish from Reis-Bucklers Anterior segment imaging and topography Assessment of erosion frequency and visual impact Family history and examination of relatives An autosomal dominant Bowman layer dystrophy, generally associated with the TGFBI gene Produces a characteristic honeycomb pattern of subepithelial opacities Presents in childhood or adolescence with recurrent corneal erosions It runs a more slowly progressive and generally milder course than Reis-Bucklers dystrophy Distinguishing it from Reis-Bucklers can require correlation of clinical, imaging, histological and genetic findings Recurrent erosions are managed conservatively, with superficial ablation for visually significant opacity Progressive visual loss from opacification Infective keratitis complicating an erosion Recurrence within a graft Frequent disabling erosions Failing to distinguish it from Reis-Bucklers, which affects prognosis and surgical planning Choosing penetrating keratoplasty when a superficial approach suffices Missing infective keratitis during erosions Overlooking the family history Thiel-Behnke corneal dystrophy is a Bowman layer dystrophy, in most families linked to mutations in the TGFBI gene (distinct in phenotype from Reis-Bucklers). Abnormal protein deposition disrupts the Bowman layer, producing a honeycomb pattern of subepithelial opacities and impairing epithelial adhesion, which leads to recurrent corneal erosions from childhood. Opacification progresses slowly, gradually affecting vision, and, as with other anterior TGFBI dystrophies, the abnormality can recur after superficial treatment or grafting. The course is slowly progressive and milder than Reis-Bucklers; vision is often preserved for longer, and superficial ablation can help, though recurrence is possible.

Thiemann disease — Thiemann epiphyseal osteochondrosis, osteochondrosis of the phalangeal epiphyses Juvenile idiopathic arthritis Other osteochondroses Erosive or inflammatory arthritis Skeletal dysplasia with epiphyseal involvement Frostbite epiphyseal injury Radiographs of the hands showing epiphyseal changes Inflammatory markers and autoantibodies (normal, to exclude arthritis) Family history and, where relevant, assessment for a hereditary pattern Clinical assessment of the interphalangeal joints Exclusion of skeletal dysplasia if widespread A rare osteochondrosis affecting the epiphyses of the phalanges of the hands (and sometimes toes) It typically presents in adolescence with painless or mildly painful swelling of the interphalangeal joints There may be a familial (autosomal dominant) pattern in some cases Radiographs show irregularity, fragmentation and flattening of the phalangeal epiphyses It can be mistaken for juvenile inflammatory arthritis, but inflammatory markers are normal and there is no true synovitis The course is usually benign, though residual joint deformity or early osteoarthritis may occur Features suggesting true inflammatory arthritis Widespread epiphyseal disease suggesting a dysplasia Significant functional impairment or deformity Atypical distribution Misdiagnosing it as juvenile idiopathic arthritis and giving unnecessary treatment Overlooking a hereditary pattern Confusing it with skeletal dysplasia Attributing normal-marker joint swelling to inflammation Thiemann disease is an osteochondrosis in which the epiphyses of the phalanges undergo avascular change with disturbed endochondral ossification during growth. The affected epiphyses become fragmented and flattened before reconstituting, and the process is thought to reflect ischaemia of the growing epiphysis, sometimes with a hereditary predisposition. The result is enlargement and deformity of the interphalangeal joints, which can lead to residual deformity or secondary degenerative change. The condition is generally benign and self-limiting with skeletal maturity, although some patients are left with digital deformity or early interphalangeal osteoarthritis.

features that would reclassify the patient as having Alport syndrome Thin basement membrane nephropathy is a disorder of the type IV collagen network that forms the glomerular basement membrane. Heterozygous variants in COL4A3 or COL4A4, which encode alpha chains of type IV collagen, produce a structurally thinner but largely functional basement membrane. The attenuated membrane is more permeable to red cells, giving rise to persistent glomerular (dysmorphic) microscopic haematuria, but in most people the filtration barrier otherwise functions normally so proteinuria, hypertension and renal impairment are absent or minimal. Because the same genes, when affected biallelically or with certain variants, cause autosomal recessive or dominant Alport syndrome, the condition represents the mild end of a continuous type IV collagen disease spectrum, and a minority of carriers show slow progression over decades. The great majority of individuals maintain normal renal function lifelong with isolated haematuria, but because COL4A3/COL4A4 carriers occasionally progress, ongoing surveillance for proteinuria, hypertension and renal decline is warranted.

drug withdrawal, supportive care, and treatment of neutropenic sepsis or bleeding Severe neutropenia with fever or sepsis Profound thrombocytopenia with bleeding Pancytopenia developing after starting or dose-escalating a thiopurine Concurrent allopurinol without appropriate dose reduction Rapidly falling counts on routine monitoring Starting standard doses without checking TPMT (and where relevant NUDT15) status Co-prescribing allopurinol without reducing the thiopurine dose Assuming normal enzyme activity removes the need for blood count monitoring Attributing cytopenias to disease activity rather than drug toxicity Thiopurines are prodrugs metabolised along competing pathways. One route, via hypoxanthine-guanine phosphoribosyltransferase, generates cytotoxic thioguanine nucleotides that are incorporated into DNA and mediate both the therapeutic immunosuppressive effect and marrow toxicity. Two enzymes divert drug away from this cytotoxic route: thiopurine methyltransferase (TPMT), which methylates the drug, and xanthine oxidase, which oxidises it. Individuals with genetically low TPMT activity shunt more drug into thioguanine nucleotide production, causing accumulation and severe myelosuppression at standard doses. NUDT15 normally dephosphorylates active thioguanine metabolites, and loss-of-function variants similarly increase active drug and marrow toxicity. Inhibition of xanthine oxidase by allopurinol removes another escape route, greatly amplifying toxicity unless the thiopurine dose is reduced. Marrow toxicity usually recovers after withdrawal and supportive care, but severe neutropenic sepsis can be fatal. Identifying at-risk genotypes and monitoring counts allows most patients to be treated safely.

repair) approaches are selected according to aneurysm location, anatomy, and patient fitness Sudden severe chest or back pain suggesting acute dissection or impending or actual rupture, a surgical emergency Haemodynamic instability or syncope indicating rupture or tamponade New hoarseness, stridor, or dysphagia from rapid enlargement Rapid interval growth or diameter exceeding operative thresholds Dismissing incidental thoracic aortic dilatation without arranging appropriate surveillance Applying general size thresholds to patients with connective tissue disease who warrant earlier repair Attributing acute chest and back pain solely to cardiac causes and missing dissection Neglecting family screening in heritable aortopathies Thoracic aortic aneurysm is a permanent localised dilatation of the thoracic aorta resulting from weakening of the aortic wall. Degeneration of medial elastin and smooth muscle, driven by genetic connective tissue disorders, bicuspid valve-associated aortopathy, atherosclerosis, or ageing, reduces wall integrity. According to the law of Laplace, increasing diameter raises wall tension, promoting further expansion in a self-perpetuating cycle. As the wall weakens it becomes vulnerable to acute dissection, in which an intimal tear allows blood to track within the media, and ultimately to rupture. Prognosis depends on aneurysm size, growth rate, and aetiology; small aneurysms often remain stable under surveillance, whereas large or rapidly expanding lesions carry a high risk of dissection or rupture. Elective repair markedly improves survival compared with the very high mortality of rupture, though operative risk varies with aneurysm extent and comorbidity.

can mimic intra-abdominal or intrathoracic (cardiac or pulmonary) disease when pain is referred anteriorly MRI is the investigation of choice, and CT helps characterise disc calcification Asymptomatic or purely painful herniations are managed conservatively, whereas progressive myelopathy warrants surgical decompression, often by an anterior or lateral approach to avoid cord retraction Signs of myelopathy such as lower-limb weakness or spasticity, gait disturbance, a sensory level, or sphincter dysfunction Rapidly progressive neurological deficit Constitutional symptoms suggesting malignancy or infection Wrong-level surgery due to difficulty counting thoracic levels Underestimating the risk of cord injury with posterior approaches that require cord retraction Misattributing referred thoracic or abdominal pain to visceral disease and missing the spinal cause Thoracic disc herniation occurs when nucleus pulposus displaces beyond the annulus in the thoracic spine. The rigid rib cage and the orientation of the facets make this region relatively stable, so herniations are less frequent than in the cervical or lumbar spine, and the lower thoracic levels, where mobility increases towards the thoracolumbar junction, are most often involved. A narrow thoracic canal and the tenuous, watershed vascular supply of the thoracic cord mean that central herniations readily compress the cord and compromise its perfusion, producing myelopathy. A substantial proportion of thoracic herniations calcify and may adhere to or erode through the dura. Most thoracic disc herniations are asymptomatic or cause pain that settles with conservative care; when myelopathy is present, timely decompression can halt progression and often improves function, although established cord damage may not fully recover.

cervical rib or elongated C7 transverse process MRI of the brachial plexus and thoracic outlet to identify fibrous bands, a mass or a Pancoast tumour Vascular studies if concurrent arterial or venous compression is suspected Cervical spine MRI if radiculopathy is a competing diagnosis True neurogenic thoracic outlet syndrome is a rare lower-trunk (C8-T1) brachial plexopathy caused by chronic compression, classically by a cervical rib with a taut fibrous band inserting on the first rib The characteristic Gilliatt-Sumner hand shows thenar wasting that is most marked over abductor pollicis brevis, with lesser hypothenar and interosseous wasting, reflecting predominant T1 and C8 involvement Sensory symptoms and any sensory loss follow a medial forearm and medial hand (medial antebrachial and ulnar) distribution, and aching pain is common along the medial arm It occurs most often in young to middle-aged women, is usually unilateral, and should be sharply distinguished from the far commoner disputed or non-specific thoracic outlet syndrome, which lacks objective neurological or electrophysiological signs The classic electrophysiological signature is a reduced median motor response (thenar wasting) with a reduced ulnar sensory response, plus a relatively preserved median sensory and reduced ulnar motor response, indicating a lower-trunk lesion Provocative manoeuvres such as the elevated arm stress test and Adson test are suggestive but non-specific and cannot confirm the diagnosis alone Imaging looks for a cervical rib, an elongated C7 transverse process or a fibrous band; surgical decompression by band and rib resection is indicated for confirmed true neurogenic disease with objective deficits A supraclavicular or apical mass, or Horner syndrome, raising concern for a Pancoast tumour Rapidly progressive weakness or widespread wasting suggesting motor neurone disease Signs of acute limb ischaemia, distal emboli or subclavian vein thrombosis indicating vascular thoracic outlet compromise Constitutional symptoms or weight loss suggesting malignancy Diagnosing true neurogenic disease on positional symptoms and provocative tests alone, without objective wasting or electrophysiological confirmation Overlooking a Pancoast tumour as a cause of lower-plexus signs Confusing thenar wasting with carpal tunnel syndrome by not recognising the accompanying medial hand sensory loss Mislabelling early motor neurone disease as thoracic outlet syndrome Operating on patients with the disputed, non-specific form who lack objective neurological deficits The brachial plexus and subclavian vessels traverse the thoracic outlet through the interscalene triangle, the costoclavicular space and the retropectoralis minor space. In true neurogenic thoracic outlet syndrome, a congenital cervical rib or elongated C7 transverse process gives rise to a fibrous band that stretches to the first rib and angulates the lowest components of the plexus, chiefly the T1 fibres and to a lesser extent C8, which form the lower trunk. Chronic traction and compression at this point cause progressive axonal loss preferentially affecting the T1-derived median motor fibres to the thenar muscles, together with C8-T1 sensory fibres, producing the characteristic pattern of thenar-predominant wasting and medial hand sensory loss. This structural, fixed compression contrasts with the intermittent, positional and often purely subjective symptoms of non-specific thoracic outlet syndrome. Surgical resection of the responsible cervical rib and fibrous band typically halts progression and relieves pain, but established thenar wasting and axonal sensory loss often recover only partially. The much commoner non-specific form has a variable outcome and does not carry the same structural prognosis.

causing arm and hand pain, paraesthesiae, and weakness, often with wasting of the thenar or intrinsic hand muscles in advanced true neurogenic cases Venous disease (Paget-Schroetter or effort dangerous, causing hand ischaemia, digital emboli, or a subclavian aneurysm, and is strongly associated with a cervical rib or bony anomaly Predisposing factors include a cervical rib, anomalous first rib, fibrous bands, and hypertrophied scalene muscles, often with a history of repetitive overhead activity or trauma Provocative manoeuvres and posture-dependent symptoms aid clinical assessment, but imaging and nerve studies are needed to confirm the subtype Management ranges from physiotherapy and postural correction in neurogenic disease to anticoagulation with venous decompression in effort thrombosis and prompt surgical decompression and arterial repair in the arterial form Hand or digital ischaemia, or a subclavian aneurysm, indicating arterial thoracic outlet syndrome Acute painful arm swelling and cyanosis suggesting subclavian vein thrombosis Progressive muscle wasting and weakness in true neurogenic disease Distal embolic events threatening the hand or fingers Overdiagnosing neurogenic disease without objective imaging or neurophysiological support Missing arterial thoracic outlet syndrome as a source of unexplained hand or digital ischaemia Failing to identify a cervical rib or bony anomaly driving vascular compression Treating effort thrombosis with anticoagulation alone without considering decompression Confusing the syndrome with cervical radiculopathy or distal nerve entrapment Thoracic outlet syndrome arises from compression of the brachial plexus, subclavian vein, or subclavian artery as they pass through the confined space bounded by the scalene muscles, the first rib, and the clavicle. Congenital factors such as a cervical rib, an anomalous first rib, or fibrous bands narrow this space, while acquired factors including scalene muscle hypertrophy, poor posture, and post-traumatic scarring can further reduce it. Neurogenic compression of the lower brachial plexus produces sensory and motor symptoms in the arm and hand. Venous compression, aggravated by repetitive arm effort, promotes turbulence, intimal injury, and thrombosis of the subclavian vein, the basis of Paget-Schroetter effort thrombosis. Arterial compression, usually against a bony anomaly, damages the subclavian artery wall and can lead to post-stenotic aneurysm, mural thrombus, and distal embolisation causing hand ischaemia. Neurogenic thoracic outlet syndrome often improves with conservative physiotherapy and postural measures, with surgery reserved for refractory or true neurogenic cases. Venous effort thrombosis generally does well with anticoagulation and decompression, while arterial disease requires prompt surgical treatment and, once complicated by embolisation or aneurysm, carries the greatest risk to the limb.

autosomal recessive inheritance and its recurrence risk 3M syndrome is caused by loss of function of components of a protein complex (CUL7, OBSL1 and CCDC8) that regulates cell growth, cytoskeletal thromboangiitis obliterans — Buerger disease, Buerger's disease Atherosclerotic peripheral arterial disease Thromboembolic arterial occlusion Systemic vasculitides such as polyarteritis nodosa or ANCA-associated vasculitis Connective tissue disease vasculopathy (systemic sclerosis, systemic lupus erythematosus) Antiphospholipid syndrome and hypercoagulable states Popliteal artery entrapment or adventitial cystic disease Ergotism, cocaine or cannabis-associated arteritis Echocardiography and proximal arterial imaging to exclude an embolic source Autoimmune and vasculitis serology (antinuclear antibodies, ANCA, complement, rheumatoid factor) Antiphospholipid antibodies and a thrombophilia screen Catheter or CT/MR arteriography of both upper and lower limbs seeking corkscrew collaterals Urine and serum toxicology for cocaine and cannabis Screening for diabetes and hyperlipidaemia to exclude atherosclerotic disease A non-atherosclerotic, segmental inflammatory occlusive disease affecting the small and medium arteries and veins of the extremities. Occurs almost exclusively in tobacco users, characteristically young men, though incidence in women is rising with changing smoking patterns. Presents with distal extremity ischaemia — digital ischaemia, foot or instep claudication, rest pain, ulceration and gangrene. Superficial migratory thrombophlebitis and Raynaud phenomenon are common accompanying features. Both upper and lower limbs are typically involved, and the Allen test is frequently abnormal, so the hands must always be examined. Angiography classically shows segmental occlusions with 'corkscrew' collaterals and normal, smooth proximal vessels free of atheroma. Complete and permanent tobacco cessation, including smokeless products and nicotine replacement, is the only proven measure that halts progression and prevents amputation. Diagnosis is essentially one of exclusion, guided by criteria such as those of Olin and Shionoya. Ischaemic rest pain or tissue loss with digital ulceration or gangrene Ascending infection or spreading cellulitis of an ischaemic digit Continued tobacco use despite established disease Rapidly progressive multi-limb ischaemia Misattributing distal ischaemia in a young smoker to premature atherosclerosis. Underestimating ongoing nicotine exposure from smokeless tobacco or nicotine replacement as a driver of progression. Failing to consider the diagnosis in young women. Examining only the lower limbs and missing upper-limb and Allen test involvement. Thromboangiitis obliterans is characterised by a highly cellular, inflammatory occlusive thrombus within small and medium arteries and veins, with relative preservation of the vessel wall and internal elastic lamina, distinguishing it from both atherosclerosis and classic necrotising vasculitis. Tobacco exposure is central: constituents of tobacco are thought to provoke endothelial dysfunction and an immune-mediated inflammatory response, possibly involving hypersensitivity to tobacco antigens and impaired endothelium-dependent vasodilatation. The result is segmental thrombotic occlusion of distal vessels with sparing of proximal arteries. Limb prognosis is excellent with complete tobacco abstinence, whereas continued smoking leads to recurrent ischaemia and a high risk of amputation; overall life expectancy is close to normal as the disease spares the coronary and cerebral circulations.

the neonatal assessment TAR syndrome is a disorder of megakaryopoiesis and limb development linked to reduced function of RBM8A, a gene encoding a core component of the exon junction complex that regulates messenger RNA processing. Affected individuals typically inherit a rare loss-of-function allele on one chromosome and a common low-expressing regulatory variant on the other, so the gene product is insufficient in the tissues that depend most on it. The resulting deficiency impairs megakaryocyte production and maturation, producing a hypomegakaryocytic thrombocytopenia, while parallel effects on limb morphogenesis cause bilateral radial aplasia with sparing of the thumbs. Unlike the classic inherited bone-marrow failure syndromes, the thrombocytopenia is usually isolated and tends to remit over the first years of life rather than progressing to pancytopenia. The thrombocytopenia is typically most dangerous in infancy and generally improves toward near-normal platelet counts in later childhood, so with careful support through the early high-risk period the long-term haematological outlook is good.

transplantation is the definitive treatment for evolving marrow failure Diagnosis integrates the skeletal anomaly, marrow findings, and genetic testing of MECOM and HOXA11 Progression from isolated thrombocytopenia to pancytopenia indicating evolving marrow failure Severe bleeding from profound thrombocytopenia Emergence of clonal cytogenetic abnormalities or dysplasia Signs of an associated anomaly such as significant cardiac or renal dysfunction Attributing the thrombocytopenia to immune causes and overlooking the skeletal clue of limited forearm rotation Failing to anticipate and monitor for progression to full marrow failure Not screening for associated cardiac, renal, and hearing abnormalities Missing the diagnosis when radioulnar synostosis is subtle or not actively sought MECOM (EVI1) and HOXA11 encode transcriptional regulators critical for haematopoietic stem-cell maintenance and megakaryocyte development, and MECOM also has roles in limb patterning. Pathogenic mutations impair the transcriptional programme that sustains stem-cell self-renewal and megakaryopoiesis, producing amegakaryocytic thrombocytopenia that may extend to trilineage marrow failure. The overlapping developmental role in the upper limb explains the associated proximal radioulnar synostosis, linking the haematological and skeletal manifestations to disruption of shared regulatory pathways. Outlook is determined by progression to marrow failure; with vigilant monitoring and timely allogeneic stem-cell transplantation, outcomes can be good, whereas untreated evolving aplasia carries substantial risk.

Thrombophilia — hypercoagulable state, inherited thrombophilia, prothrombotic state Antiphospholipid syndrome Occult malignancy Myeloproliferative neoplasm including JAK2-associated disease Paroxysmal nocturnal haemoglobinuria Provoked thrombosis from surgery, immobility, or hormonal therapy Genetic testing for factor V Leiden and prothrombin G20210A Functional antithrombin, protein C, and protein S assays timed away from acute events and anticoagulation Antiphospholipid antibody panel including lupus anticoagulant, anticardiolipin, and anti-beta-2-glycoprotein I Full blood count and JAK2 testing where a myeloproliferative disorder is suspected Age-appropriate malignancy evaluation in unprovoked events Thrombophilia denotes an inherited or acquired tendency to venous, and less often arterial, thrombosis Common inherited causes include factor V Leiden and the prothrombin G20210A variant; deficiencies of antithrombin, protein C, and protein S are rarer but more strongly prothrombotic Acquired causes include the antiphospholipid syndrome, malignancy, pregnancy, oestrogen therapy, nephrotic syndrome, and immobility Clinical features that suggest an underlying thrombophilia include venous thromboembolism at a young age, recurrent events, unusual sites such as cerebral or splanchnic veins, a strong family history, and warfarin-induced skin necrosis Testing rarely changes acute management and is confounded by the acute event, anticoagulation, and pregnancy, so it should be timed carefully and directed by whether the result will alter decisions Antithrombin, protein C, and protein S levels are unreliable during acute thrombosis and while on anticoagulation, whereas genetic tests for factor V Leiden and prothrombin variants are unaffected Management centres on anticoagulation for events and on risk assessment for prophylaxis during high-risk periods rather than on the laboratory label itself Extensive or life-threatening thrombosis such as massive pulmonary embolism or cerebral venous thrombosis Thrombosis at unusual sites suggesting an underlying myeloproliferative disorder or malignancy Skin necrosis after starting a vitamin K antagonist, suggesting protein C or S deficiency Recurrent pregnancy loss or arterial events raising concern for antiphospholipid syndrome Testing during the acute event or while on anticoagulation, producing misleading levels Allowing a positive result to prolong anticoagulation unnecessarily when clinical risk is low Overlooking acquired causes such as malignancy or antiphospholipid syndrome by focusing only on inherited defects Testing asymptomatic relatives without clear benefit or counselling Thrombosis arises when the balance of Virchow's triad shifts toward clot formation through hypercoagulability, stasis, or endothelial injury. Inherited thrombophilias tilt this balance by either increasing procoagulant activity or reducing natural anticoagulant function: factor V Leiden and prothrombin variants enhance clotting, while deficiencies of antithrombin, protein C, and protein S remove restraints on thrombin generation. Acquired states add further procoagulant stimuli, such as antiphospholipid antibodies, tumour-derived tissue factor, or oestrogen effects. Most thrombotic events reflect the interaction of one or more of these predispositions with a transient provoking factor. Prognosis depends on the specific defect and on whether events are provoked; many people with common low-risk variants never have a thrombosis, whereas antithrombin deficiency and antiphospholipid syndrome carry higher recurrence risk and may warrant extended anticoagulation.
