recommended in atypical APLS or scleroderma renal involvement without hypertension) Urinalysis and urine albumin-to-creatinine ratio (screening in sickle cell nephropathy) LDH-to-AST ratio (about 13:1 in HELLP/preeclampsia vs about 29:1 without preeclampsia), antithrombin III (decreased in HELLP not TTP), D-dimer (elevated in HELLP not TTP) Malignant hypertension (histologically indistinguishable from scleroderma renal crisis) Preeclampsia/HELLP syndrome Cancer-associated TMA (tumor microvascular obstruction) Drug-induced TMA Acute tubular necrosis (contributes to renal failure in HELLP) Thrombotic microangiopathy (TMA) is a pathologic lesion of endothelial injury in terminal arterioles and capillaries, with platelet and hyaline thrombi causing partial or complete occlusion; it is usually but not always accompanied by microangiopathic hemolytic anemia (MAHA) featuring thrombocytopenia and schistocytes. Renal histology of TMA shows swollen endocapillary cells (endotheliosis), fibrin thrombi, platelet plugs, arterial intimal fibrosis, and a membranoproliferative glomerular pattern; fibrin thrombi may extend into the arteriolar pole producing glomerular collapse and at times cortical necrosis, and recovered kidneys may develop secondary focal segmental glomerulosclerosis. The classic TTP pentad (MAHA, thrombocytopenia, neurologic symptoms, fever, renal failure) is rare: fewer than 5% of immune-mediated TTP cases show the full pentad, so do not wait for all five to act. TTP is defined as MAHA associated with ADAMTS13 activity below 5-10%; ultra-large von Willebrand factor multimers accumulate, form clots, and shear erythrocytes, but loss of ADAMTS13 alone may need an additional trigger (infection, surgery, pancreatitis, pregnancy) to provoke clinical disease. Atypical (complement-mediated) HUS reflects alternative complement pathway dysregulation; affected patients often have low C3 with normal C4, and factor H deficiency is the most common defect, with more than 70 factor H gene mutations described. Shiga toxin-producing E. coli (STEC) HUS, classically D+ (diarrhea-associated) HUS, mostly affects children under 5 but can affect adults; bloody diarrhea precedes MAHA within one week in over 80% of cases, fever is typically absent, and neurologic involvement is common, especially in adults. Scleroderma renal crisis presents with acute kidney injury, abrupt-onset hypertension, and a normal urine sediment (though none is strictly required); it occurs in about 12% of diffuse but only ~2% of limited systemic sclerosis, and its renal histology of 'onion-skinning' arcuate artery intimal/medial proliferation is indistinguishable from malignant hypertension. Antiphospholipid syndrome produces a predisposition to arterial and venous thrombosis and recurrent fetal loss; 'triple positivity' (lupus anticoagulant, anti-beta-2 glycoprotein I, and anticardiolipin antibodies) carries the highest thrombosis risk, and APLS is the leading cause of stroke in patients under 45. HELLP syndrome (hemolysis, elevated liver enzymes, low platelets) is a microvascular pregnancy complication; the defining organ is the liver (subcapsular hematoma with potential rupture), renal failure occurs in about half of patients, and proteinuria is present in 86-100%. Renal vein thrombosis can present with flank pain, tenderness, hematuria, rapid renal decline, and proteinuria, or be silent and discovered during a pulmonary embolism workup; the left renal vein is more commonly involved and two-thirds of cases are bilateral. Sickle cell nephropathy arises from occlusion of the vasa recta in the renal medulla, where low oxygen tension and high osmolarity favor hemoglobin S polymerization and sickling; sequelae include hyposthenuria, hematuria, and papillary necrosis (which can also occur in sickle trait). Drug-induced TMA occurs via two mechanisms: dose-dependent toxic/endothelial damage (chemotherapeutics such as proteasome inhibitors, mitomycin C, gemcitabine; immunosuppressives such as calcineurin inhibitors, interferon, sirolimus) or non-dose-dependent drug-induced autoantibodies (e.g., quinine, which can react even after a single re-exposure). Neurologic deterioration (seizures, encephalopathy, cerebral infarction) in HUS/TTP, especially in adults Untreated immune-mediated TTP carries a mortality exceeding 90%, and 20% die within the first month even with modern therapy Catastrophic antiphospholipid syndrome: rapid onset, multiorgan failure, and severe thrombotic events Scleroderma renal crisis with cardiac involvement (myocarditis, pericarditis, arrhythmias) indicating an especially poor prognosis, or with pulmonary edema HELLP syndrome with subcapsular hepatic hematoma/spontaneous liver rupture, cerebral infarction/hemorrhage/edema, or placental abruption HSCT-associated TMA, which carries a 75% mortality within 3 months Bilateral renal vein thrombosis with rapid decline in renal function or life-threatening complications Waiting for the full TTP pentad before acting is a mistake, since fewer than 5% of immune-mediated TTP cases display all five features. Assuming TMA always shows MAHA can mislead: TMA is usually but not always accompanied by microangiopathic hemolysis, and in antiphospholipid syndrome renal TMA is common while signs of MAHA and platelet consumption are usually absent. Scleroderma renal crisis is histologically indistinguishable from malignant hypertension and the two can coexist, so renal biopsy is recommended for atypical renal involvement, especially when hypertension is absent. ADAMTS13 reduction in HELLP (30-60%) is milder than in TTP (below ~10%), so interpreting modest reductions as diagnostic of TTP can mislead during pregnancy when aHUS and TTP can also be triggered. Thrombocytopenia in HIV-related TMA may prohibit renal biopsy, yet biopsy is required for diagnosis because other HIV-associated renal diseases mimic it; ADAMTS13 activity is not reduced in HIV-related TMA. In drug-induced autoantibody TMA (e.g., quinine), disease can recur after even a single re-exposure in a previously sensitized patient, so it is not strictly dose-dependent. Distinguishing HSCT-associated TMA is difficult because thrombocytopenia, anemia, and renal insufficiency are common after transplantation for other reasons. Thrombotic renovascular disorders share endothelial injury of the renal microvasculature (terminal arterioles and capillaries) leading to platelet/hyaline thrombi and microangiopathic hemolysis. In TTP, deficient ADAMTS13 activity (below ~5-10%, from congenital mutation in cTTP/Upshaw-Schulman syndrome or acquired autoantibody in iTTP) allows ultra-large von Willebrand factor multimers to accumulate, forming platelet-rich thrombi that shear red cells; an inflammatory trigger is often required to manifest disease. In atypical HUS, dysregulation of the alternative complement pathway (commonly factor H deficiency, or defects in factor I, factor B, CD46/membrane cofactor protein, C3, CFHR1/3/5, thrombomodulin, or autoantibody to factor H in DEAP HUS) causes complement-mediated endothelial damage. STEC HUS results from Shiga toxins (Stx1/Stx2, verotoxins) binding the glycolipid receptor Gb3 on renal microvascular cells, inducing inflammatory cytokines (IL-8, MCP-1, SDF-1) and chemokine receptors (CXCR4/CXCR7) with platelet aggregation; Streptococcus pneumoniae neuraminidase can expose the cryptic Thomsen-Friedenreich antigen so preformed IgM triggers MAHA. Scleroderma renal crisis features arcuate artery intimal/medial proliferation with onion-skinning, fibrinoid necrosis, and thrombosis. Antiphospholipid syndrome causes intralobular fibrous intimal hyperplasia and arterial/arteriolar occlusion. Renal vein thrombosis results from endothelial damage, venous stasis, or hypercoagulability (notably nephrotic syndrome, especially membranous nephropathy). Prognosis varies by subtype. Untreated immune-mediated TTP has a mortality exceeding 90%, and even with modern therapy about 20% die within the first month from microvascular thrombosis. HSCT-associated TMA is highly lethal, with roughly 75% mortality within 3 months. Scleroderma renal crisis historically had over 90% mortality at 1 month, reduced to about 30% at 3 years with renin-angiotensin system blockade; nearly two-thirds of patients may require dialysis, with renal recovery in about half (median ~1 year). HELLP syndrome carries a mortality of about 7.4-34% and usually resolves spontaneously after delivery. POEMS syndrome rarely progresses to end-stage renal disease. Renal injury in aHUS can be severe and progress to end-stage renal disease, with recurrence risk after transplant depending on the complement-regulatory protein involved. Chronic kidney disease develops in roughly 25-33% of sickle cell nephropathy patients, and nephrotic-range proteinuria predicts progression to renal failure. No single unified severity scale; classification is by etiologic subtype and laboratory criteria. TTP is defined as MAHA with ADAMTS13 activity below 5-10% and subdivided into congenital (cTTP/Upshaw-Schulman) and immune (iTTP) forms. HUS variants include STEC/D+ HUS, pneumococcal neuraminidase-associated HUS, atypical complement-mediated HUS (aHUS), and DEAP HUS. HSCT-associated TMA has formal diagnostic criteria (Harrison Table 329-1): the International Working Group requires schistocytes (over 4% in one set, or RBC fragmentation with at least 2 schistocytes per high-power field), de novo/progressive thrombocytopenia, rising LDH, falling hemoglobin or increased transfusion need, negative Coombs, falling haptoglobin, and concurrent renal/neurologic dysfunction without other explanation. Antiphospholipid syndrome severity is stratified by antibody profile, with 'triple positivity' conferring the highest thrombosis risk and a catastrophic variant defined by rapid multiorgan failure.

thrombotic thrombocytopenic purpura — TTP, Moschcowitz syndrome haemolytic uraemic syndrome (including Shiga toxin-associated and complement-mediated forms) disseminated intravascular coagulation HELLP syndrome and severe pre-eclampsia malignant hypertension catastrophic antiphospholipid syndrome drug-induced thrombotic microangiopathy disseminated malignancy with microangiopathy blood film and reticulocyte count lactate dehydrogenase, haptoglobin and unconjugated bilirubin direct antiglobulin test ADAMTS13 activity with anti-ADAMTS13 antibody or inhibitor assay coagulation screen (characteristically normal or near-normal) renal function and urinalysis troponin and electrocardiogram to detect cardiac involvement TTP results from a severe deficiency of the von Willebrand factor-cleaving protease ADAMTS13, either acquired through an autoantibody or, rarely, congenital (Upshaw-Schulman syndrome). The classic pentad of fever, microangiopathic haemolytic anaemia, thrombocytopenia, renal impairment and fluctuating neurological signs is seldom complete; unexplained microangiopathic haemolysis with thrombocytopenia is sufficient to act. The blood film is central to diagnosis, showing prominent schistocytes, thrombocytopenia and polychromasia, with a raised lactate dehydrogenase, raised unconjugated bilirubin, low haptoglobin and a negative direct antiglobulin test. Neurological features characteristically fluctuate and range from headache and confusion to seizures, focal deficits and coma, and may be transient. TTP is a haematological emergency: plasma exchange should be started urgently on clinical suspicion, without waiting for the ADAMTS13 result to return. Platelet transfusion is generally avoided unless there is life-threatening haemorrhage, as it may aggravate microvascular thrombosis. Standard adjuncts to plasma exchange in acquired TTP include corticosteroids, rituximab and the anti-von Willebrand factor agent caplacizumab. The PLASMIC score aids estimation of the likelihood of severe ADAMTS13 deficiency while the confirmatory assay is awaited, and congenital TTP is managed with plasma infusion rather than exchange. any new or fluctuating neurological deficit, seizure or reduced consciousness chest pain, arrhythmia or other evidence of cardiac involvement severe thrombocytopenia with active bleeding a rapidly rising lactate dehydrogenase indicating ongoing microangiopathy haemodynamic instability or evolving multi-organ dysfunction giving prophylactic platelet transfusions, which may worsen microthrombosis delaying plasma exchange while awaiting the ADAMTS13 result confusing TTP with DIC, forgetting that the coagulation screen is usually normal in TTP overlooking subtle or transient neurological signs and clinically silent cardiac involvement attributing the picture to sepsis or malignancy and missing a treatable thrombotic microangiopathy Deficient activity of ADAMTS13, the metalloprotease that cleaves ultra-large von Willebrand factor multimers as they are released from endothelium, allows these hyperadhesive multimers to persist in the circulation. They spontaneously bind and aggregate platelets under high shear, generating platelet-rich microthrombi in the arterioles and capillaries of multiple organs, especially the brain, heart and kidneys. Passage of red cells across these partially occluded, fibrin- and platelet-laden vessels causes mechanical fragmentation and a microangiopathic haemolytic anaemia, while platelet consumption produces thrombocytopenia. In acquired disease an IgG autoantibody inhibits or clears ADAMTS13, whereas the congenital form is due to biallelic mutations in the ADAMTS13 gene. Unlike DIC, the coagulation cascade is not primarily activated, so the clotting screen is typically normal. Untreated TTP carries a very high mortality, but prompt plasma exchange with immunosuppression allows most patients to survive the acute episode. Acquired TTP is prone to relapse and warrants long-term monitoring of ADAMTS13 activity.

Understaging by omitting PET-CT and missing metastatic disease Proceeding to incomplete resection without considering neoadjuvant therapy for locally advanced tumours Thymic carcinoma arises from the epithelial cells of the thymus but, unlike thymoma, shows overtly malignant cytological features, loss of the organotypic thymic architecture, and an infiltrative, destructive growth pattern. The tumour cells lose the immature T-lymphocyte-rich background characteristic of thymoma, which underlies both the different immunohistochemical profile and the rarity of associated autoimmune syndromes. It invades local mediastinal structures including the pericardium, great vessels, and lung, and disseminates via lymphatics and the bloodstream, so a substantial proportion present with advanced or metastatic disease. Thymic carcinoma carries a markedly poorer prognosis than thymoma, driven by frequent local invasion and metastasis; completely resected, early-stage disease has the best outcome, while advanced disease has limited survival despite multimodality treatment.

Thymoma — thymic epithelial tumour, thymic carcinoma, thymoma Lymphoma involving the anterior mediastinum Germ cell tumour of the mediastinum Retrosternal or ectopic thyroid mass Thymic cyst or thymic hyperplasia Metastatic disease to the mediastinum Parathyroid adenoma or other mediastinal masses Contrast-enhanced CT of the chest to characterise the anterior mediastinal mass and local invasion MRI to clarify cystic versus solid components and vascular involvement Testing for anti-acetylcholine receptor antibodies and evaluation for myasthenia gravis Full blood count and immunoglobulin levels to detect associated red cell aplasia or hypogammaglobulinaemia Biopsy when the diagnosis is uncertain or the tumour appears unresectable, and PET-CT for suspected thymic carcinoma Thymomas are the most common tumours of the anterior mediastinum in adults and are frequently discovered incidentally on chest imaging There is a strong association with myasthenia gravis, and a proportion of patients present first with neuromuscular symptoms; other paraneoplastic syndromes include pure red cell aplasia and hypogammaglobulinaemia Local symptoms, when present, arise from mass effect and include chest pain, cough, dyspnoea, and features of superior vena cava obstruction Thymic carcinoma is a distinct and more aggressive entity than thymoma, with greater invasiveness, higher metastatic potential, and worse prognosis Staging emphasises the degree of local invasion beyond the capsule and into surrounding structures, which is the main determinant of behaviour and treatment Complete surgical resection is the cornerstone of treatment for resectable disease, and completeness of resection strongly influences outcome Radiotherapy is used adjuvantly for invasive or incompletely resected tumours, and chemotherapy, often platinum-based, is used for advanced or unresectable disease Patients with associated myasthenia gravis require optimisation of neuromuscular status before surgery to reduce perioperative respiratory risk Superior vena cava obstruction with facial swelling and distended neck veins Respiratory compromise or myasthenic crisis in a patient with a mediastinal mass Rapidly enlarging or invasive anterior mediastinal mass suggesting thymic carcinoma New pleural or pericardial effusion indicating advanced spread Overlooking underlying myasthenia gravis and precipitating perioperative respiratory failure Failing to distinguish aggressive thymic carcinoma from indolent thymoma Biopsying a potentially resectable encapsulated tumour when upfront resection is preferable Missing associated paraneoplastic cytopenias or immunodeficiency Thymomas are neoplasms of the thymic epithelial cells, typically accompanied by variable numbers of non-neoplastic immature T lymphocytes. They are classified histologically by epithelial morphology and lymphocyte content, while thymic carcinoma shows overt cytological malignancy and loss of organotypic features. The abnormal thymic microenvironment can disrupt immune tolerance, accounting for the frequent paraneoplastic autoimmune phenomena, most notably myasthenia gravis mediated by anti-acetylcholine receptor antibodies. Tumours may remain encapsulated or invade the capsule, mediastinal fat, pleura, pericardium, and adjacent great vessels. Encapsulated, completely resected thymomas have an excellent long-term prognosis, whereas invasive tumours and especially thymic carcinoma carry higher recurrence and mortality; degree of invasion and completeness of resection are the key prognostic factors.

recurrence A thyroglossal duct cyst is a remnant of the embryological tract along which the thyroid descends from the foramen caecum of the tongue to its cervical position, and it may retain ectopic thyroid follicular tissue. Malignant transformation of this tissue, most often into papillary carcinoma, gives rise to thyroglossal duct carcinoma. Because the epithelium is of thyroid follicular type, the tumour behaves like a well-differentiated thyroid cancer and can, in a minority of cases, coexist with a primary carcinoma in the orthotopic gland, raising the question of whether disease is truly primary within the cyst or represents metastatic spread. Outcome is generally excellent given the predominantly papillary, well-differentiated histology, with adverse features being invasive disease, nodal or distant spread, and a coexisting higher-risk primary thyroid cancer.

thyroglossal cyst During development the thyroid gland descends from the foramen caecum at the tongue base to its final pretracheal position, leaving behind the thyroglossal duct, which normally Persistence of epithelial remnants along this tract allows a fluid-filled cyst to form anywhere from the tongue base to the thyroid, but most commonly at or near the hyoid bone. Its intimate relationship with the hyoid explains the movement with swallowing and tongue protrusion, and retained secretions or infection cause enlargement and inflammation. Following a properly performed Sistrunk procedure the outlook is excellent with low recurrence. Recurrence is more likely after inadequate surgery or when a preceding infection has distorted the tissue planes, and malignant change within the cyst is rare.

associated lymphadenopathy Acute infection with abscess formation and airway or swallowing compromise Imaging showing the cyst may contain the only functioning thyroid tissue Proceeding to surgery without confirming a normal thyroid gland and inadvertently removing the only functioning thyroid tissue Performing simple excision rather than removing the central hyoid and tract, leading to recurrence Repeated incision and drainage of an infected cyst instead of definitive excision once settled Overlooking malignant transformation in a cyst with solid components During embryogenesis the thyroid gland descends from the foramen caecum at the tongue base to its final pretracheal position, leaving behind the thyroglossal duct, which normally involutes. Persistence of epithelial remnants of this duct allows a cyst to form anywhere along the tract, most often at or just below the hyoid bone in the midline. Because the tract passes intimately through the body of the hyoid, the cyst elevates with swallowing and tongue protrusion. Retained secretions expand the cyst, and communication with the oral cavity predisposes to infection. Excision by the Sistrunk procedure gives a low recurrence rate, whereas simple cystectomy that leaves the tract or hyoid segment recurs more often. Carcinoma within a thyroglossal duct cyst is rare and, when confined, generally has a favourable outlook.

Thyroid Nodular Disease and Cancer — thyroid nodule, thyroid carcinoma, papillary thyroid cancer, medullary thyroid cancer Benign hyperplastic (colloid) nodule Follicular adenoma Oncocytic (Hurthle cell) adenoma Thyroid cyst (colloid cyst) Multinodular goiter (nodule within an MNG) Toxic adenoma / hyperfunctioning ('hot') nodule Noninvasive follicular thyroid neoplasm with papillary-like nuclear features (NIFTP) - no longer considered malignant Thyroglossal duct cyst / developmental abnormality Thyroid lymphoma Metastasis to the thyroid from another primary Serum TSH (first test in nodule evaluation) Radionuclide (I-123) scan if TSH suppressed, to identify hyperfunctioning 'hot' nodule Thyroid and cervical lymph node ultrasound with risk-stratification (ACR TI-RADS / ATA / EU-TIRADS) Ultrasound-guided fine-needle aspiration (FNA) with Bethesda System cytology reporting Molecular testing of indeterminate FNA samples (next-generation sequencing, microRNA, gene-expression panels) Serum thyroglobulin (Tg) for surveillance of differentiated cancer after thyroidectomy/ablation Serum calcitonin (and RET mutation testing) for medullary thyroid carcinoma Whole-body radioiodine scan (WBS) for iodine-avid metastases or elevated Tg with negative imaging Neck/chest cross-sectional imaging (CT/MRI) and PET-CT (18FDG or Ga-68 Dotatate avidity raises malignancy suspicion) Hashimoto's thyroiditis (background for thyroid lymphoma; may produce a goitrous, nodular-feeling gland) Subclinical thyrotoxicosis from autonomous nodule (mimics need for cancer workup but reflects functioning, benign nodule) Hoarseness from gastroesophageal reflux rather than laryngeal nerve invasion by tumor Thyroid nodules are common: ~3-7% of adults by palpation, but up to 50% have nodules on ultrasound, with the majority <1 cm. The vast majority of nodules are benign (Harrison 22e p.3040, p.3044, p.3048). Initial workup of a nodule begins with a TSH level. If TSH is suppressed, a radionuclide scan is done; a hyperfunctioning ('hot') nodule is almost never malignant, so FNA is unnecessary. Otherwise proceed to thyroid ultrasound (Harrison 22e p.3048). Thyroid ultrasound with a validated risk-stratification system (e.g., ACR TI-RADS, TR1-TR5) is used to decide which nodules need fine-needle aspiration (FNA), combining sonographic pattern with nodule size; more suspicious patterns warrant FNA at lower size cutoffs (Harrison 22e p.3042, p.3048). FNA, ideally ultrasound-guided, is the diagnostic procedure of choice for nodules. Cytology is reported with the six-tier Bethesda System (version 3): benign ~4% malignancy risk, AUS ~22%, follicular neoplasm ~30%, suspicious for malignancy ~74%, malignant ~97% (Harrison 22e p.3044, p.3049). Papillary thyroid cancer (PTC) is the most common type (80-85% of well-differentiated cancers); classic and follicular variants are usually indolent, spread mainly via lymphatics, and have an excellent prognosis (>95% present at stage I or II) (Harrison 22e p.3046). Follicular thyroid cancer (FTC) accounts for ~5% of US thyroid cancers and cannot be distinguished from benign follicular lesions by FNA cytology alone; diagnosis requires histologic evidence of capsular and/or vascular invasion (Harrison 22e p.3046-3047, p.3048). Medullary thyroid carcinoma (MTC) arises from calcitonin-producing C cells, accounts for ~5% of thyroid cancers, and can be sporadic or familial (MEN 2A, MEN 2B, familial MTC); elevated serum calcitonin is a marker of residual/recurrent disease (Harrison 22e p.3048). All patients with MTC should be tested for RET mutations so that genetic counseling and family testing can be offered; pheochromocytoma must be excluded before surgery in any patient with a RET mutation (Harrison 22e p.3048). Anaplastic thyroid cancer (ATC) is poorly differentiated and aggressive with a bleak prognosis; most patients die within 6 months of diagnosis (Harrison 22e p.3040, p.3048). Serum thyroglobulin (Tg) is a sensitive marker of residual/recurrent disease for PTC, FTC, and oncocytic carcinoma after total thyroidectomy and radioablation, while calcitonin serves this role for MTC (Harrison 22e p.3045, p.3047). Molecular diagnostic panels (next-generation sequencing, microRNA, gene expression) are increasingly used on FNA samples with indeterminate cytology (AUS, follicular neoplasm) to distinguish benign from malignant lesions and reduce unnecessary diagnostic surgery; current validated tests have negative predictive values >95% (Harrison 22e p.3046, p.3050). Nodule fixed to adjacent structures (firm/hard, immobile) Vocal cord paralysis or hoarse voice (suggests recurrent laryngeal nerve involvement) Lateral cervical lymphadenopathy ipsilateral to the nodule Rapidly enlarging neck mass Prior head/neck irradiation before age 18 (e.g., mantle radiation for Hodgkin's, cranial radiation for childhood leukemia) Childhood/adolescent exposure to ionizing radiation from fallout Age <20 or >65 years Male gender Family history of PTC in two or more first-degree relatives, MEN 2, or syndromes (Cowden's, familial adenomatous polyposis, Carney complex, PTEN hamartoma) 18FDG or Ga-68 Dotatate PET avidity of the nodule Thyroid cancer is being overdiagnosed: rising incidence is driven by small T1 papillary tumors while disease-specific mortality has not changed in 40 years; routine FNA is not recommended for nodules <1 cm unless metastatic cervical nodes are present. A hyperfunctioning ('hot') nodule on radionuclide scan is almost never malignant; FNA is unnecessary and should not be performed for these. FNA cytology cannot reliably distinguish benign follicular adenoma from follicular carcinoma because nuclear features do not differ; the distinction requires histologic evidence of capsular/vascular invasion. LT4 (TSH-suppression) therapy does NOT shrink nodules in iodine-replete (iodine-sufficient) populations and should not be used for that purpose; if it has not reduced nodule size after 6-12 months it should be stopped. Spongiform nodules (TR1) have <3% cancer risk and warrant observation rather than FNA. Iodine-containing contrast agents should be avoided in nodular goiter due to the risk of the Jod-Basedow effect (iodine-induced thyrotoxicosis from autonomous nodules). NIFTP can only be diagnosed on surgical pathology, so it is still included within Bethesda malignancy risk estimates. Hoarseness more commonly reflects benign causes (e.g., reflux) than malignancy, but new vocal cord paralysis is a genuine red flag. In MTC, surgery should not proceed until pheochromocytoma has been excluded in any patient with a RET mutation. For thyroid lymphoma, initial surgical resection should be avoided because it may spread otherwise localized disease. Thyroid nodular disease reflects disordered growth of thyroid cells that may be hyperplastic or neoplastic. Thyroid neoplasms can arise from follicular cells (papillary, follicular, oncocytic, poorly differentiated, anaplastic carcinomas), calcitonin-producing C cells (medullary carcinoma), lymphocytes (lymphoma), or stromal/vascular elements. Cancers are monoclonal, arising from mutations conferring a growth advantage or resistance to cell death. Activation of the RET-RAS-BRAF (MAPK) signaling pathway is seen in up to 70% of PTCs; BRAF V600E mutations occur in up to 60% of PTC, RET rearrangements in ~15% (more frequent after Chernobyl fallout), and RAS mutations in ~15%. FTCs harbor BRAF/RAS mutations plus PAX8-PPARgamma rearrangements (~70% have a mutation/rearrangement). Anaplastic cancers accumulate additional TERT promoter, BRAF, CTNNB1 (beta-catenin), and TP53 mutations driving dedifferentiation and genetic instability. MEN 2-associated MTC carries inherited activating RET point mutations and is preceded by C-cell hyperplasia. External and fallout radiation predispose to chromosomal breaks and increase risk of benign and malignant nodules, especially in children. Most differentiated cancers retain TSH receptor expression and respond to TSH, the basis for both LT4 suppression and radioiodine uptake. Prognosis spans a wide range by histologic type. Differentiated cancers (PTC and FTC) are often curable with good prognosis in early-stage disease; the 20-year disease-specific mortality for low-risk thyroid cancer is ~1%, and most PTC present at stage I/II with survival similar to expected. Mortality rises markedly in stage IV disease, especially with distant metastases (stage IVB, ~1% of patients). FTC, particularly angioinvasive, carries less favorable outcomes than PTC partly due to more stage IV presentation; poor features include distant metastases, age >55, tumor >4 cm, and marked vascular invasion. MTC is more aggressive in MEN 2B than MEN 2A, and familial MTC more aggressive than sporadic. Anaplastic thyroid cancer is aggressive with a bleak prognosis, most patients dying within 6 months. Older age (>65) and male gender are associated with worse outcomes overall. Histologic classification (WHO/Table 397-1): follicular cell-derived (benign follicular/oncocytic adenoma; low-risk neoplasms including NIFTP; malignant - papillary, follicular, oncocytic, differentiated/poorly differentiated high-grade, anaplastic), C-cell-derived medullary carcinoma, mixed medullary-follicular, lymphoma, and others. Staging uses the AJCC/UICC 8th-edition TNM system (tumor size and extrathyroidal invasion, regional nodal metastases, distant metastases) for differentiated and anaplastic cancers. Sonographic risk stratification uses ACR TI-RADS levels TR1 (benign) to TR5 (highly suspicious). FNA cytology uses the six-tier Bethesda System v3 (I nondiagnostic ~13%, II benign ~4%, III AUS ~22%, IV follicular neoplasm ~30%, V suspicious for malignancy ~74%, VI malignant ~97% malignancy risk). MTC risk in MEN 2 is further stratified by specific RET mutation.

Under-dosing replacement and allowing persistent goitre or hypothyroidism Thyroid dyshormonogenesis is caused by inherited defects in the enzymatic machinery the thyroid uses to synthesise hormone. Depending on the gene involved, iodide may not be trapped or organified, thyroglobulin may be abnormal, or the hydrogen peroxide needed for organification may be deficient. Impaired hormone output lowers circulating thyroid hormone and, through loss of negative feedback, raises thyroid-stimulating hormone. The resulting chronic stimulation causes the gland to enlarge into a goitre, while the hormone deficiency itself threatens growth and, critically in infancy, neurodevelopment. When congenital hypothyroidism is detected by screening and treated promptly with adequate replacement, growth and neurodevelopment are usually normal; delayed treatment risks permanent cognitive impairment, and the goitre generally regresses once hormone levels are restored.

Thyroid eye disease — thyroid-associated orbitopathy, Graves ophthalmopathy, thyroid orbitopathy, TED, TAO Orbital cellulitis Orbital inflammatory syndrome (orbital pseudotumour) Orbital tumour or lymphoma Carotid-cavernous fistula IgG4-related orbital disease Myasthenia gravis (as a cause of diplopia and lid signs, and a recognised association) Thyroid function tests and thyroid autoantibodies including TSH-receptor antibodies Assessment of clinical activity score and disease severity grading Exophthalmometry to quantify proptosis Orbital CT or MRI to assess muscle enlargement and apical crowding Visual acuity, colour vision, visual fields, and pupillary assessment to detect optic neuropathy Ocular motility and diplopia assessment An autoimmune orbitopathy most often associated with Graves disease, though patients may be hyperthyroid, euthyroid, or hypothyroid at presentation Cardinal features include eyelid retraction, lid lag on downgaze, proptosis, restrictive strabismus with diplopia, and ocular surface exposure It follows an active inflammatory phase lasting months to a couple of years, followed by a quiescent fibrotic phase; treatment strategy depends on which phase the patient is in Smoking strongly worsens the disease and its response to treatment, so cessation is a key intervention Disease activity and severity are assessed separately, for example using a clinical activity score and grading of soft tissue, proptosis, motility, corneal, and optic nerve findings Active moderate-to-severe disease is managed with immunosuppression and orbital measures, while stable disease may require rehabilitative surgery in the sequence of orbital decompression, then squint, then eyelid surgery The most feared complication is dysthyroid optic neuropathy from apical crowding, which threatens sight and needs urgent treatment Dysthyroid optic neuropathy with reduced acuity, impaired colour vision, a relative afferent pupillary defect, or disc swelling requiring urgent treatment Corneal exposure or ulceration from severe proptosis and lagophthalmos Rapidly progressive proptosis or globe subluxation Marked orbital congestion with raised intraocular pressure Assuming euthyroid patients cannot have thyroid eye disease and delaying diagnosis Missing early optic neuropathy because central acuity can be preserved while colour vision and fields deteriorate Performing rehabilitative surgery during the active inflammatory phase Neglecting smoking cessation and ocular surface protection Thyroid eye disease is an autoimmune inflammatory disorder of the orbit linked to Graves disease. Autoantibodies against the thyroid-stimulating hormone receptor, expressed on orbital fibroblasts, drive activation and differentiation of these cells. The resulting inflammation causes accumulation of glycosaminoglycans, oedema, and enlargement of the extraocular muscles and orbital fat. The expanded orbital contents within a fixed bony cavity produce proptosis, restrictive myopathy, and, when the crowded orbital apex compresses the optic nerve, dysthyroid optic neuropathy. Over time inflammation gives way to fibrosis, leaving fixed muscle restriction and lid changes. Many patients have mild, self-limiting disease, but moderate-to-severe cases can leave lasting proptosis, diplopia, and disfigurement; optic neuropathy risks permanent visual loss if not treated promptly, and smoking cessation improves the overall outlook.

free T3 when TSH is suppressed but free T4 is normal (to detect T3 toxicosis) Anti-TPO (and anti-thyroglobulin) antibodies for autoimmune thyroid disease TRAb / thyroid-stimulating immunoglobulin assay for Graves' disease and to predict fetal/neonatal thyrotoxicosis Serum thyroglobulin for thyroiditis and post-thyroidectomy cancer surveillance Radioiodine (123I/131I) uptake and thyroid scan, or 99mTc pertechnetate imaging, to define etiology of thyrotoxicosis Thyroid ultrasound (10-12 MHz) with risk-stratification systems (TI-RADS) and ultrasound-guided fine-needle aspiration for nodules TBG excess from estrogen (pregnancy, oral contraceptives, tamoxifen) raising total T4/T3 while free hormone stays normal TBG deficiency (X-linked) lowering total T4/T3 with normal free levels and euthyroid state Biotin supplement interference falsely lowering TSH and falsely raising T4/T3 in biotinylated assays Drugs displacing hormone from binding proteins (salicylates, salsalate) or impairing T4-to-T3 conversion (propranolol, amiodarone, glucocorticoids, propylthiouracil, oral contrast agents) TSH is the single most useful physiologic marker of thyroid hormone action; because of its long plasma half-life (~50 min) a single measurement reliably reflects circulating levels (p.3021). A normal TSH essentially excludes a primary thyroid abnormality, so the logical first step in evaluation is to determine whether TSH is suppressed, normal, or elevated (p.3026). Primary hyperthyroidism produces a low/suppressed TSH and primary hypothyroidism produces an elevated TSH because thyroid hormone exerts dominant negative feedback on TSH gene expression (p.3021, p.3026). TSH is a glycoprotein with an alpha subunit shared with LH, FSH, and hCG and a unique beta subunit; the structurally similar hCG weakly stimulates the TSH-R, lowering TSH in the first trimester of pregnancy (p.3021, p.3024). T4 is secreted in roughly 15-fold excess over T3 and acts largely as a prohormone, being converted peripherally to the more potent T3 by deiodinases (p.3023-3024). Nuclear thyroid hormone receptors silence target genes when unliganded by binding co-repressors, so hormone deficiency causes both loss of stimulation and active gene repression, giving deficiency a more profound effect than receptor gene deletion (p.3025). About 5-15% of euthyroid women and up to 2% of euthyroid men carry thyroid (anti-TPO) antibodies and are at increased risk of future thyroid dysfunction; nearly all autoimmune hypothyroid patients and up to 80% of Graves' patients have TPO antibodies (p.3026). Functioning (hot) thyroid nodules are almost never malignant and do not require fine-needle aspiration, whereas non-functioning (cold) nodules carry a ~5-10% malignancy risk (p.3026-3027). Serum thyroglobulin is elevated in all forms of thyrotoxicosis except factitious thyrotoxicosis (exogenous hormone), and its principal clinical use is surveillance after thyroidectomy/radioablation for thyroid cancer (p.3026). After total thyroidectomy and radioablation for thyroid cancer, thyroglobulin should be <0.2 ng/mL in the absence of anti-Tg antibodies; a measurable level suggests incomplete ablation or recurrence (p.3026). Retrosternal goiter causing venous distention and dyspnea on raising the arms (Pemberton's sign) Suspicious sonographic nodule features (hypoechoic solid nodule, irregular margins, punctate echogenic microcalcifications) with >90% cancer risk Cervical or supraclavicular lymphadenopathy on thyroid examination suggesting malignancy High maternal TRAb/TSI (>3x upper limit of normal) in the third trimester predicting fetal/neonatal thyrotoxicosis Untreated maternal/neonatal hypothyroidism in iodine-deficient regions risking cretinism (intellectual disability, growth retardation) Treating low total T4 in TBG deficiency: attempts to normalize total T4 cause thyrotoxicosis and are futile due to rapid clearance. Relying on TSH alone in suspected hypothalamic-pituitary (secondary) hypothyroidism, where TSH is inappropriately low-to-normal for a low T4; free T4 must also be measured. Failing to stop biotin supplements >=2 days before testing, leading to falsely low TSH and falsely high T4/T3. Missing T3 toxicosis (2-5% of cases) if only free T4 is checked when TSH is suppressed. Misinterpreting transiently low TSH (0.01-0.1 mIU/L) of early pregnancy, recent hyperthyroidism treatment, or glucocorticoid/dopamine therapy as true thyrotoxicosis. Performing fine-needle aspiration on a hot/functioning nodule, which is almost never malignant; scintigraphy should precede biopsy when TSH is subnormal. Confusing thyroid hormone resistance or a TSH-secreting adenoma with simple primary hyperthyroidism because of elevated hormones with non-suppressed TSH. The hypothalamic-pituitary-thyroid axis is a classic endocrine feedback loop. Hypothalamic TRH stimulates pituitary thyrotrope production of TSH, which binds the TSH-R (a Gs-coupled seven-transmembrane GPCR) on the basolateral surface of thyroid follicular cells, activating adenylyl cyclase/cAMP and phospholipase C to drive gland growth and hormone synthesis. Iodide is actively trapped by the sodium-iodide symporter (NIS), transported apically via pendrin, and oxidized/organified onto tyrosyl residues of thyroglobulin by thyroid peroxidase using DUOX-generated hydrogen peroxide; iodotyrosines are coupled to form T4 and T3, which are released after lysosomal proteolysis of reabsorbed thyroglobulin. Circulating hormone is largely protein-bound (TBG, transthyretin, albumin) with only the small unbound fraction biologically available; deiodinases (types I, II, III) regulate peripheral conversion of T4 to active T3 or inactivating reverse T3. T3 acts mainly through nuclear receptors TRalpha and TRbeta, which heterodimerize with RXR on thyroid response elements, exchanging co-repressors for co-activators upon ligand binding. Thyroid hormones feed back, predominantly via TRbeta2 in hypothalamus and pituitary, to suppress TRH and TSH, establishing the axis set point. Most physiologic and binding-protein variants (TBG abnormalities, familial dysalbuminemic hyperthyroxinemia, classic TRbeta resistance) are benign and require no treatment once recognized, the main goal being avoidance of inappropriate therapy. Early thyroid hormone replacement in congenital hypothyroidism prevents severe developmental abnormality, whereas untreated iodine deficiency in early life causes irreversible cretinism and even mild deficiency can subtly reduce IQ. Not applicable as a discrete disease; thyroid status is categorized biochemically by TSH and free hormone levels into euthyroid, subclinical hypo-/hyperthyroidism (abnormal TSH with normal free hormones), and overt hypo-/hyperthyroidism (abnormal TSH with abnormal free hormones), with trimester-specific reference ranges applied in pregnancy.

to thrive with a hypermetabolic state despite apparent hypothyroid features Progressive spasticity and loss of developmental milestones Recurrent aspiration or feeding difficulty from severe hypotonia Misdiagnosis leading to inappropriate high-dose thyroxine that worsens thyrotoxic effects Mistaking the raised triiodothyronine for ordinary thyrotoxicosis and treating with antithyroid drugs Giving standard levothyroxine and expecting neurological improvement Overlooking the diagnosis in a boy labelled as cerebral palsy Failing to recognise and manage the peripheral hypermetabolic state MCT8, encoded by SLC16A2 on the X chromosome, is a transmembrane transporter that moves thyroid hormone into cells, and it is critical for delivering hormone across the blood-brain barrier and into neurones. When it is defective, thyroid hormone cannot reach the developing brain, producing a state of cerebral hypothyroidism and severe neurodevelopmental impairment. At the same time excess hormone circulates and enters tissues that rely on other transporters, and increased peripheral conversion generates high triiodothyronine, giving a thyrotoxic effect on tissues such as muscle and driving the paradoxical thyroid function tests. The neurodevelopmental impairment is severe and largely irreversible, and most affected boys have profound disability; management is supportive, and experimental thyroid hormone analogues aim mainly to reduce the peripheral thyrotoxic burden rather than restore neurological function.

thyroidectomy for a disease that is treated medically Overlooking an underlying Hashimoto thyroiditis that provides the diagnostic context Primary thyroid lymphoma is a non-Hodgkin B-cell malignancy arising within the thyroid, almost invariably against a background of chronic lymphocytic (Hashimoto) thyroiditis. Persistent autoimmune stimulation recruits and expands intrathyroidal lymphoid tissue, and acquired genetic changes in this population can give rise to a clonal marginal-zone (MALT) lymphoma or transform into an aggressive diffuse large B-cell lymphoma. The proliferating lymphoid cells rapidly efface and expand the gland, producing a fast-growing mass and compressive symptoms, but the disease responds to lymphoma-directed chemotherapy and radiotherapy rather than to thyroidectomy. Prognosis is generally good and far better than for anaplastic carcinoma, particularly for localised MALT lymphoma; aggressive diffuse large B-cell histology, advanced stage, and extrathyroidal spread reduce response and survival.

Thyroid nodule — thyroid lump, solitary thyroid nodule, thyroid mass, nodular goitre Benign colloid or hyperplastic nodule Follicular adenoma Differentiated thyroid carcinoma (papillary or follicular) Medullary or anaplastic thyroid carcinoma Thyroid cyst or focal thyroiditis Parathyroid or other neck mass mimicking a thyroid nodule Serum TSH as the first-line test Thyroid ultrasound to characterise the nodule and assess cervical lymph nodes Radionuclide thyroid scan when TSH is suppressed Ultrasound-guided fine-needle aspiration cytology Molecular marker testing for indeterminate cytology Serum calcitonin when medullary carcinoma is suspected Thyroid nodules are common and usually benign, but the central task is to identify the minority that are malignant Initial evaluation begins with a serum TSH; a suppressed value points towards an autonomously functioning (usually benign) nodule and warrants a radionuclide scan Ultrasound characterises nodules and stratifies malignancy risk, with features such as marked hypoechogenicity, microcalcifications, irregular margins, and a taller-than-wide shape raising concern Fine-needle aspiration is the key diagnostic test, with results reported using standardised cytology categories that guide management Hot (functioning) nodules on scanning rarely harbour malignancy, so aspiration is generally directed at non-functioning nodules History of childhood neck irradiation, family history of thyroid cancer, rapid growth, hoarseness, or fixed hard nodules increase suspicion of cancer Molecular testing of indeterminate cytology samples can refine the risk of malignancy and help avoid unnecessary surgery Rapidly enlarging, hard, or fixed nodule New hoarseness or vocal cord palsy suggesting recurrent laryngeal nerve involvement Cervical lymphadenopathy History of head and neck irradiation or family history of thyroid cancer or MEN syndromes Compressive symptoms such as dysphagia or stridor Proceeding to biopsy before checking TSH and missing an autonomous nodule that does not need aspiration Relying on nodule size alone rather than sonographic risk features to decide on aspiration Falsely reassuring the patient after a non-diagnostic aspirate without repeating sampling Overlooking calcitonin measurement when clinical features suggest medullary carcinoma Thyroid nodules arise from focal proliferation of follicular cells and may be colloid nodules, adenomas, cysts, areas of thyroiditis, or carcinomas. Autonomously functioning nodules develop constitutive activation of thyroid hormone production, often through activating mutations of the TSH-receptor or G-protein signalling pathway, suppressing TSH and appearing 'hot' on scanning. Malignant nodules result from oncogenic alterations (for example in the MAPK pathway) driving unregulated growth, and their behaviour ranges from indolent differentiated cancers to aggressive anaplastic disease. Most nodules are benign and can be followed conservatively, and even most malignant nodules are differentiated cancers with an excellent prognosis after treatment, though anaplastic and some medullary cancers carry a poor outlook.

include eyelid retraction, lid lag, proptosis (exophthalmos), and restrictive myopathy causing diplopia The enlarged extraocular muscles typically spare their tendinous insertions on orbital imaging, a feature that helps distinguish it from orbital myositis Disease runs an active inflammatory phase followed by a quiescent fibrotic phase, and treatment strategy depends on which phase and how severe the disease is Smoking is a major modifiable risk factor that worsens severity and reduces treatment response The sight-threatening complications are dysthyroid optic neuropathy from apical crowding and corneal exposure from severe proptosis and lid retraction Management includes restoring and stabilising thyroid status, ocular surface lubrication, and, in active moderate-to-severe disease, immunosuppression with corticosteroids and, where appropriate, orbital radiotherapy Orbital decompression relieves optic-nerve compression or disfiguring proptosis, with squint and lid surgery reserved for the stable phase Reduced acuity, dyschromatopsia, or a relative afferent pupillary defect indicating dysthyroid optic neuropathy Severe corneal exposure with breakdown from marked proptosis and lid retraction Rapidly progressive proptosis or congestion in the active phase Choroidal folds or disc swelling suggesting posterior compression Assuming normal thyroid function excludes the diagnosis, since patients can be euthyroid Missing early dysthyroid optic neuropathy because proptosis and external signs may be modest Not counselling about smoking as a key modifiable risk factor Operating on lids or muscles before the disease has become inactive Confusing tendon-sparing muscle enlargement with orbital myositis, which involves the tendons Thyroid eye disease is an autoimmune process in which autoantibodies, particularly against the thyrotropin receptor, activate orbital fibroblasts that share antigens with the thyroid gland. Activated fibroblasts proliferate, secrete glycosaminoglycans that draw water into the tissues, and can differentiate into fat cells, causing the extraocular muscles and orbital fat to swell within the bony orbit. This expansion produces proptosis, congestion, and restrictive myopathy, while the muscle bellies enlarge with relative sparing of their tendons. Crowding at the orbital apex can compress the optic nerve, and proptosis with lid retraction exposes the cornea. After the active inflammatory phase the enlarged muscles may fibrose, leaving fixed restriction and deformity. Many patients stabilise after the active phase with good outcomes, especially with smoking cessation and prompt treatment, but a minority develop sight-threatening optic neuropathy or corneal breakdown, and residual proptosis, lid malposition, and diplopia often require surgical rehabilitation in the stable phase.

Thyroid storm — TFTs (TSH↓, free T4/T3↑) ECG Burch-Wartofsky score Life-threatening — beta-blockade, antithyroid drugs Other causes of thyrotoxicosis besides Graves' disease must be considered (e.g. toxic adenoma, toxic multinodular goitre, destructive thyroiditis, ectopic thyroid tissue, factitious thyrotoxicosis); radionuclide scan/uptake or color-flow Doppler ultrasonography helps distinguish hyperthyroidism from destructive thyroiditis (Harrison 22e p.3078). Suppressed TSH with elevated total and unbound (free) T4 and T3 (Harrison 22e p.3078). T3 toxicosis (only T3 raised) in 2-5% of patients, more in areas of borderline iodine intake; T4 toxicosis (raised T4, normal T3) is occasionally seen when hyperthyroidism is iodine-induced (Harrison 22e p.3078). TRAb (TSH receptor antibody) measurement to support a diagnosis of Graves' disease (Harrison 22e p.3078). Watch for confounding biochemistry: elevated bilirubin, liver enzymes and ferritin, plus microcytic anaemia and thrombocytopenia, may accompany thyrotoxicosis (Harrison 22e p.3078). Thyrotoxic crisis (thyroid storm) is a rare, life-threatening exacerbation of hyperthyroidism (Harrison 22e p.3080). Characteristic features include fever, delirium, seizures, coma, vomiting, diarrhoea and jaundice (Harrison 22e p.3080). Often precipitated by an acute intercurrent illness (e.g. stroke, infection, trauma, diabetic ketoacidosis), by surgery (especially thyroid surgery), or by radioiodine treatment given to a patient whose hyperthyroidism is only partially treated or untreated (Harrison 22e p.3080). Apathetic thyrotoxicosis: in the elderly, features may be subtle or masked, presenting mainly with fatigue and weight loss, and can be mistaken for depression (Harrison 22e p.3076). Thyrotoxicosis may be complicated by a form of hypokalaemic periodic paralysis, particularly common in Asian males (Harrison 22e p.3076). Treatment of the thyrotoxic state alone restores sinus rhythm in up to 75% of patients with thyrotoxicosis-associated atrial fibrillation who have no underlying cardiac disease (Harrison 22e p.3077). Fever, delirium, seizures or coma in a thyrotoxic patient indicate thyroid storm (Harrison 22e p.3080). Death is most often due to cardiac failure, arrhythmia or hyperthermia (Harrison 22e p.3080). Radioiodine therapy in a patient with partially treated or untreated hyperthyroidism can itself precipitate thyrotoxic crisis (Harrison 22e p.3080). In the elderly, thyrotoxicosis may be masked (apathetic thyrotoxicosis), delaying recognition (Harrison 22e p.3076). Thyroid storm represents a severe, decompensated form of thyroid hormone excess (thyrotoxicosis), typically arising when an acute stressor is superimposed on partially treated or untreated hyperthyroidism. Excess circulating thyroid hormone drives a hypermetabolic, hyperadrenergic state; high cardiac output produces a bounding pulse, widened pulse pressure and may precipitate or worsen heart failure or angina, particularly in the elderly or those with pre-existing heart disease (Harrison 22e p.3077, p.3080). Mortality remains high (4-17%) even with treatment, usually from cardiac failure, arrhythmia or hyperthermia (Harrison 22e p.3080).

thyrotoxicosis can be responsible Attacks are commonly triggered by a high-carbohydrate meal, strenuous exercise followed by rest, or stress, typically overnight or in the early morning The hypokalaemia reflects an intracellular shift of potassium rather than true depletion, driven by thyroid-hormone-enhanced sodium-potassium-ATPase activity Thyrotoxic symptoms may be subtle, so thyroid function should be checked in any young man with hypokalaemic paralysis Acute treatment uses cautious potassium and beta-blockade for thyrotoxic periodic paralysis, with close monitoring to avoid rebound hyperkalaemia Definitive prevention depends on rendering the patient euthyroid, after which attacks cease Respiratory muscle involvement or bulbar weakness compromising ventilation Severe hypokalaemia with cardiac arrhythmia Rebound hyperkalaemia during potassium replacement Coexisting features of thyroid storm Overzealous potassium replacement causing dangerous rebound hyperkalaemia as potassium redistributes Missing subtle thyrotoxicosis in a young man presenting with paralysis Confusing the condition with familial periodic paralysis and overlooking the thyroid cause Failing to treat the underlying thyrotoxicosis, leaving the patient prone to further attacks Neglecting cardiac monitoring during acute hypokalaemia Thyrotoxic periodic paralysis arises when excess thyroid hormone increases the activity of the sodium-potassium-ATPase pump in skeletal muscle, driving potassium into cells. This intracellular shift is amplified by insulin and adrenergic stimulation, explaining the triggering by carbohydrate loads, exercise and stress. The resulting acute hypokalaemia hyperpolarises and then paradoxically renders muscle membranes inexcitable, producing flaccid weakness. Because potassium is redistributed rather than lost, total body potassium is normal, which underlies the risk of rebound hyperkalaemia if too much potassium is administered. A genetic predisposition affecting muscle ion channels is thought to contribute in susceptible individuals. The prognosis is excellent once euthyroidism is achieved, as attacks resolve completely; recurrence is the rule while thyrotoxicosis persists.

thyroxine with non-suppressed TSH as an assay error and ignoring it Treating the thyroid (with ablation or thyroidectomy) instead of addressing the pituitary source Confusing a thyrotropinoma with resistance to thyroid hormone and missing the tumour Overlooking co-secretion of growth hormone or prolactin from the same adenoma A thyrotropinoma is a benign monoclonal tumour of pituitary thyrotroph cells that secretes biologically active TSH in an unregulated manner, escaping the normal negative feedback of thyroid hormones. The persistent TSH drive stimulates the thyroid gland to enlarge and to overproduce thyroxine and triiodothyronine, producing central (secondary) hyperthyroidism with a goitre. Because the tumour often retains the capacity to release the glycoprotein hormone alpha-subunit disproportionately, the alpha-subunit to TSH ratio is typically increased. Larger tumours also exert local mass effect and may co-secrete other anterior pituitary hormones. With complete surgical removal many patients achieve biochemical cure and resolution of hyperthyroidism, but large or invasive tumours may leave residual disease requiring medical therapy or radiotherapy, and lifelong follow-up is needed to detect recurrence.

Transient ischaemic attack — Urgent CT/MRI + carotid imaging ECG (AF) ABCD² risk; start antiplatelet/statin High early stroke risk — urgent TIA clinic / admission Seizure (esp. ongoing focal seizure without convulsive activity) — positive symptoms and a marching spread over seconds favour seizure (p.3378, p.3428) Migraine, including acephalgic migraine even in older first-time patients — slower march over minutes with headache, nausea or scintillating visual symptoms (p.3428) Intracranial tumour presenting acutely via haemorrhage, seizure or hydrocephalus (p.3428) Metabolic encephalopathy — fluctuating mental status without focal findings (p.3428) Stroke recrudescence — fever/sepsis unmasking a prior deficit that clears as infection is treated (p.3428) CT- or MRI-based angiography of neck and intracranial vessels to assess large-vessel stenosis/occlusion (MRA is highly sensitive for extracranial carotid stenosis but tends to overestimate severity) (p.3445, p.3430) Echocardiography (transthoracic or transoesophageal), with bubble-contrast/agitated-saline study to detect right-to-left shunt (PFO/ASD) for suspected paradoxical embolism (p.3445) Cardiac telemetry following the initial ECG; ambulatory/prolonged ECG monitoring to detect intermittent atrial fibrillation if none is found in hospital (p.3445) Retinal/funduscopic exam for cholesterol (Hollenhorst) plaques and examination of cervical/peripheral vessels and heart (p.3445) Baseline labs: CBC, ESR, electrolytes, glucose, lipid profile, creatinine/BUN, PT/PTT, urinalysis, chest x-ray (p.3445) Seizure (focal, may mimic transient deficit) (p.3378, p.3428) Migraine / acephalgic migraine with transient aura (p.3428) Syncope from systemic hypotension (cardiac arrhythmia, sepsis, haemorrhagic shock) (p.3428) Metabolic encephalopathy (p.3428) TIA classically produces 'negative' symptoms (transient loss of function); positive sensory symptoms or involuntary movements point instead to seizure (p.3378). Most TIAs last under 1 hour, well within the historical 24-hour window (p.3448). About 25% of symptomatic internal carotid disease is heralded by recurrent transient monocular blindness (amaurosis fugax), typically described as a horizontal shade sweeping down or up across one eye, lasting a few minutes (p.3430). A high-pitched carotid bruit fading into diastole suggests a tight stenosis; paradoxically the bruit may fade or vanish as occlusion becomes imminent and flow drops (p.3430). Causes of TIA and ischaemic stroke are identical, so the diagnostic evaluation of a TIA should parallel that of a completed stroke (p.3448). Most strokes after a TIA occur within the first 2 days — the early window is the highest-risk period and warrants urgent (not deferred) workup (p.3448) Stuttering or crescendo course of small-vessel TIAs heralding lacunar infarct can progress to severe permanent disability (p.3447) Amaurosis fugax indicates a symptomatic internal carotid source needing prompt carotid evaluation (p.3430) A TIA is a clinical diagnosis: a normal brain imaging study does NOT rule it out (p.3448). If a relevant infarction is seen on imaging, the event is reclassified as a stroke regardless of how briefly symptoms lasted — the modern definition is tissue-based, not purely time-based (p.3428, p.3448). Patients with carotid/vertebrobasilar TIA may report symptoms 'in one eye' when the deficit is actually a homonymous hemifield loss affecting both eyes (p.3430-equivalent / cortical visual TIA). Acephalgic migraine can mimic TIA even with no prior migraine history and even after age 65 (p.3428). A TIA results from transient focal cerebral ischaemia when blood flow falls for longer than several seconds; neurons lack glycogen so deficits appear within seconds, but because the occluded vessel reopens and flow is restored before infarction occurs, symptoms resolve completely. Mechanisms mirror ischaemic stroke: emboli to the brain (cardiac or proximal arterial source) or in-situ thrombosis of an intracranial vessel. Small-vessel (lacunar) TIAs may recur several times a day and last only minutes (Harrison 22e p.3428, 3448, 3447). Stroke risk after a TIA is approximately 10-15% within the first 3 months, with most events occurring in the first 2 days; this early risk is well predicted by the ABCD2 score, so urgent evaluation and treatment are justified (Harrison 22e p.3448). ABCD2 score (Harrison 22e p.3448) stratifies early stroke risk after TIA: 1 point each for Age >=60, BP (SBP >140 or DBP >90 mmHg), and Diabetes; for Clinical features 2 points for unilateral weakness or 1 for speech disturbance without weakness; for Duration 2 points for >=60 min or 1 for 10-59 min. The 3-month stroke rate rises with the total: ~0% at score 0-1, ~3% at 2-3, ~8% at 4, ~12% at 5, ~17% at 6, and ~22% at 7.

producing in-toeing at the level of the foot Residual clubfoot deformity External tibial torsion or femoral retroversion causing out-toeing Neuromuscular gait abnormality such as cerebral palsy Blount disease or other tibial deformity mimicking torsional malalignment Full rotational profile assessment including thigh-foot angle and transmalleolar axis Foot progression angle observed during gait Assessment of hip rotation to exclude a coexisting femoral cause Examination of the feet for metatarsus adductus or other deformity Standing lower-limb radiographs only when angular deformity or a pathological cause is suspected Computed tomography rotational study reserved for surgical planning in severe cases Internal tibial torsion is the commonest cause of in-toeing in toddlers and typically becomes apparent when the child begins to walk The deformity is assessed on the rotational profile by the thigh-foot angle and the transmalleolar axis, with the child prone and the knee flexed Tibial torsion normally shifts outward with growth, so mild internal torsion in infancy corrects to a modest external value by later childhood The condition is usually physiological, frequently bilateral or asymmetrical, and resolves spontaneously without treatment in the great majority Reassurance and observation are the mainstays, and passive stretching, special shoes, braces, and night splints have not been shown to alter the natural history External tibial torsion is less common, tends to worsen with growth, and may contribute to patellofemoral maladjustment or an out-toeing gait Surgical derotation osteotomy is reserved for the rare severe, persistent, and functionally significant deformity in an older child Progressive worsening rather than the expected spontaneous improvement Marked asymmetry between the two limbs Associated pain, limp, or functional limitation Short stature, disproportion, or other features suggesting a skeletal dysplasia or metabolic bone disease Neurological signs indicating an underlying neuromuscular disorder Prescribing braces, special shoes, or night splints that do not change the natural course and burden the family Failing to complete a full rotational profile and thereby missing a coexisting femoral cause Reassuring without follow-up when the deformity is progressive or asymmetrical Attributing a pathological angular deformity such as Blount disease to simple torsion Recommending surgery before the natural resolution that occurs with skeletal growth has been allowed Tibial torsion describes the normal axial rotation of the tibia between the knee and ankle, which in fetal life is internally rotated and gradually rotates externally through infancy and childhood as part of normal skeletal development. Persistence of the immature internally rotated pattern produces internal tibial torsion and an in-toeing gait, while excessive external rotation produces external torsion and out-toeing. It represents a variation of normal maturation influenced by intrauterine positioning and sleeping or sitting postures rather than a structural disease, and the growing bone remodels along the physiological path in the overwhelming majority of children. The natural history is overwhelmingly benign, with internal tibial torsion resolving spontaneously in almost all children as the tibia derotates with growth, and lasting functional or arthritic consequences are not expected.

Tick-borne encephalitis — TBE, tick-borne encephalitis virus infection, TBEV infection, Central European encephalitis, Russian spring-summer encephalitis Herpes simplex virus and other viral encephalitides Bacterial meningitis or meningoencephalitis Lyme neuroborreliosis (also Ixodes-transmitted) Enteroviral meningitis West Nile virus and other flaviviral neuroinvasive disease Guillain-Barre syndrome when flaccid paralysis predominates Serum and cerebrospinal fluid IgM and IgG serology for tick-borne encephalitis virus Cerebrospinal fluid analysis showing lymphocytic pleocytosis and raised protein Magnetic resonance imaging of the brain and spinal cord for thalamic, cerebellar, brainstem, or anterior-horn involvement RT-PCR on blood during the early viraemic phase, recognising it is often negative by the neurological phase Testing for co-transmitted Lyme borreliosis given shared Ixodes vectors Electrophysiology when myelitis or peripheral involvement is suspected A flavivirus transmitted by Ixodes ticks across endemic parts of Europe and Asia, with European, Siberian, and Far Eastern subtypes of differing severity The illness is classically biphasic: an initial viraemic flu-like phase, a symptom-free interval of about a week, then a second neurological phase with meningitis, encephalitis, or myelitis An important additional route is consumption of unpasteurised milk or dairy products from infected goats, sheep, or cattle (alimentary transmission) The Far Eastern subtype tends to cause more severe monophasic disease with higher mortality and sequelae, while the European subtype more often shows the classic biphasic pattern Neurological sequelae such as cognitive impairment, ataxia, and flaccid paralysis (especially of the shoulder girdle) can be long-lasting There is no specific antiviral; management is supportive, and an effective inactivated vaccine is the mainstay of prevention for residents and travellers to endemic areas Diagnosis is usually serological (IgM and IgG in serum and cerebrospinal fluid), as viraemia and detectable RNA have often cleared by the neurological phase Declining consciousness or brainstem signs indicating severe encephalitis Flaccid limb or respiratory-muscle weakness from myelitis Seizures or status epilepticus Rapidly progressive monophasic course suggesting a more severe viral subtype Signs of raised intracranial pressure Discharging a patient during the afebrile interval and missing the second neurological phase Relying on RT-PCR in the neurological phase, when serology is the appropriate test Overlooking alimentary transmission from unpasteurised dairy products Failing to consider co-infection with Lyme borreliosis from the same tick exposure Not offering vaccination to at-risk residents and travellers as prevention Tick-borne encephalitis virus is inoculated during the bite of an infected Ixodes tick, or ingested in unpasteurised dairy products. It first replicates locally and in regional lymph nodes, producing the initial viraemic phase with nonspecific febrile symptoms. In a proportion of patients the virus subsequently crosses the blood-brain barrier and infects neurons, particularly in the brainstem, cerebellum, and anterior horns of the spinal cord, provoking an inflammatory meningoencephalitis or myelitis. By the time neurological disease appears, viraemia has typically resolved and the host antibody response is detectable, which is why diagnosis is largely serological. Many patients recover fully, but a substantial minority, especially with the Siberian or Far Eastern subtypes or with encephalitic or myelitic involvement, are left with persistent neurological sequelae, and mortality is highest with the Far Eastern subtype.

Typhoid fever Rickettsial infections Dengue and other arboviral fevers Brucellosis Thick and thin peripheral blood films taken during fever to demonstrate spirochaetes PCR of blood for Borrelia puncture if central nervous system involvement is suspected Caused by several Borrelia species (such as Borrelia hermsii in North America and Borrelia duttonii in Africa) and transmitted by the bite of soft (argasid) Ornithodoros ticks, whose bites are brief and painless and often not recalled Exposure is classically linked to sleeping in rustic cabins or dwellings harbouring rodent-associated ticks, so a careful environmental history is important After an incubation of about a week there is abrupt high fever, rigors, headache, myalgia and arthralgia lasting a few days, followed by an afebrile interval and then one or more relapses The relapsing pattern reflects successive waves of spirochaetaemia as the organism undergoes antigenic variation to evade the developing antibody response Diagnosis is often made by seeing spirochaetes on a peripheral blood film (thick and thin films, ideally taken during a febrile spike) using Giemsa or Wright staining Tetracyclines such as doxycycline are the mainstay of treatment, with beta-lactams as alternatives, and treatment is usually given empirically once the diagnosis is suspected A Jarisch-Herxheimer reaction is common on starting treatment, so patients should be observed and supported through it Neurological features such as meningism, cranial nerve palsies or altered consciousness Myocarditis with heart failure or arrhythmia Marked haemorrhagic tendency or profound thrombocytopenia Severe Jarisch-Herxheimer reaction with hypotension after the first antibiotic dose Pregnancy, in which disease and vertical transmission carry added risk Not examining blood films during a febrile spike, when spirochaetaemia is highest Failing to warn about and manage the Jarisch-Herxheimer reaction Missing the diagnosis because the painless soft-tick bite is not recalled Attributing recurrent fevers to a relapsing viral illness or malaria without a film Overlooking central nervous system or cardiac complications in severe cases Relapsing fever borreliae are spirochaetes inoculated during the brief feeding of soft ticks. They multiply in the bloodstream to produce high-grade spirochaetaemia, which drives the febrile episodes. As host antibodies clear the dominant serotype, the organism switches its surface antigens through programmed antigenic variation, allowing an antigenically distinct population to expand and cause a further febrile relapse; this cycle repeats, producing the characteristic relapsing pattern. High spirochaetal loads can involve the spleen, liver, central nervous system and heart, and the sudden release of bacterial products on antibiotic-induced lysis provokes the Jarisch-Herxheimer reaction. With appropriate antibiotics tick-borne relapsing fever generally has a good prognosis and low mortality, though the Jarisch-Herxheimer reaction can be severe; untreated or complicated disease, particularly with cardiac or neurological involvement, carries higher risk.

diagnostic step) Serial forced vital capacity and respiratory monitoring Nerve conduction studies to help differentiate from Guillain-Barre syndrome Cerebrospinal fluid analysis to exclude inflammatory neuropathy Electrolytes including potassium and calcium Pulse oximetry and arterial blood gases if respiratory involvement Presents with an ascending, symmetrical flaccid paralysis that the Australian form (Ixodes holocyclus), paralysis may worsen after tick removal, and specific measures differ Sensation is typically preserved and reflexes are reduced or absent, helping distinguish it from other causes The principal danger is progression to bulbar and respiratory muscle weakness requiring ventilatory support Bulbar weakness with impaired swallowing or airway protection Declining respiratory function or vital capacity Rapidly ascending or worsening paralysis Deterioration after tick removal (notably with Ixodes holocyclus) Very young child with progressive weakness Missing the attached tick, especially in the scalp, and misdiagnosing Guillain-Barre syndrome Assuming immediate improvement in all cases, when Ixodes holocyclus paralysis can worsen after removal Crushing or incompletely removing the tick, potentially leaving mouthparts or expressing more saliva Underestimating the speed of respiratory decline in a young child During prolonged attachment and feeding, certain ticks secrete a salivary neurotoxin that impairs neuromuscular transmission, principally by interfering with presynaptic release of acetylcholine and with nerve conduction. The result is a progressive, ascending, symmetrical flaccid paralysis with hyporeflexia but preserved sensation. Toxin production relates to the duration of feeding and the engorgement of the tick, and the clinical course after tick removal differs between the North American species, where recovery is usually prompt, and Ixodes holocyclus, in which deterioration can continue for a period after removal. Prognosis is excellent once the tick is found and removed, with most patients (particularly the North American form) recovering fully over days; the main risk is respiratory failure before diagnosis, and the Australian form may deteriorate transiently after removal.

producing painful, non-suppurative swelling of the upper costal cartilages, most often the second or third The presence of visible and palpable localised swelling distinguishes Tietze syndrome from costochondritis, which causes tenderness without swelling Usually affects a single site and tends to occur in younger adults, in contrast to the more diffuse, multi-level costochondritis Pain is
