and other serious causes of chest pain Imaging is used chiefly to exclude other pathology, though MRI or CT may show cartilage enlargement and oedema Management is reassurance, activity modification, NSAIDs, and local corticosteroid injection for resistant cases Chest pain with cardiac features (exertional, radiating, associated with breathlessness or diaphoresis) Constitutional symptoms or a hard fixed mass suggesting malignancy Fever and progressive swelling raising concern for infection Pain unresponsive to conservative measures with atypical features Anchoring on a musculoskeletal cause and missing cardiac or pulmonary disease Confusing it with costochondritis by overlooking the characteristic localised swelling Ordering unnecessary invasive investigation for a benign self-limiting condition Failing to consider SAPHO syndrome or malignancy when swelling is atypical or persistent Tietze syndrome is a localised, benign inflammation of the costochondral, costosternal or sternoclavicular cartilage of unknown precise cause. Repetitive minor trauma, coughing or physical strain is thought to trigger a self-limiting inflammatory and possibly reparative response within the costal cartilage, producing cartilage enlargement with surrounding soft-tissue oedema. Unlike infective or destructive processes there is no suppuration or bony erosion; the visible fusiform swelling reflects benign cartilage and perichondrial thickening rather than joint destruction, and the condition resolves once the inflammation settles although the swelling may persist for some time. Tietze syndrome is benign and usually self-limiting, with pain settling over weeks to months, although the palpable swelling can persist for a prolonged period; recurrence is possible but serious sequelae do not occur.

tilted disc syndrome — Fuchs coloboma, congenital tilted disc Chiasmal compression from pituitary adenoma or craniopharyngioma Optic nerve coloboma Peripapillary staphyloma Myopic degeneration with peripapillary atrophy Optic disc hypoplasia Glaucomatous optic neuropathy Retinoschisis producing field loss Automated static perimetry with refractive correction in place Optical coherence tomography of the optic nerve head and peripapillary retinal nerve fibre layer Cycloplegic refraction to characterise myopic astigmatism Fundus photography documenting situs inversus and inferonasal crescent Fundus autofluorescence to delineate peripapillary RPE changes Neuroimaging (MRI of the sella/chiasm) when field defect respects the vertical midline or is progressive Congenital anomaly caused by oblique insertion of the optic nerve into the globe, producing an ovoid disc with a raised superotemporal and depressed inferonasal margin. Almost always bilateral though frequently asymmetric; the disc long axis is typically directed inferonasally. Situs inversus of the retinal vessels is a characteristic sign, with vessels emerging in an anomalous nasal direction before doubling back. An inferonasal fundus ectasia (staphylomatous crescent) and thinning of the retinal pigment epithelium and choroid accompany the tilt. Refractive error is usually myopic astigmatism with the astigmatic axis oriented obliquely along the ectasia. Superotemporal visual field defects that characteristically do NOT respect the vertical midline help distinguish it from chiasmal compression. Refracting the patient and repeating perimetry after correcting the induced myopic defocus can abolish the pseudo-bitemporal field loss. Considered a mild form of the optic disc dysplasia/coloboma spectrum and is usually a benign, non-progressive finding. Visual field defect that strictly respects the vertical midline, suggesting a chiasmal lesion rather than the disc anomaly Progressive field loss or new dyschromatopsia on follow-up Development of a serous macular detachment or subretinal fluid Choroidal neovascular membrane presenting with sudden central distortion Misinterpreting the pseudo-bitemporal field defect as chiasmal compression and initiating unnecessary neuroimaging without first correcting refraction and repeating perimetry. Overlooking associated inferonasal serous retinal detachment or choroidal neovascularisation as the cause of new symptoms. Attributing the ovoid disc appearance to glaucoma and treating for raised intraocular pressure inappropriately. Failing to recognise associated systemic or midline associations in syndromic cases. Tilted disc syndrome arises from incomplete or abnormal closure of the embryonic fetal fissure and an oblique entry of the optic nerve through the scleral canal during development. The result is an obliquely inserted, ovoid optic disc with the superotemporal portion elevated and the inferonasal portion recessed, accompanied by an inferonasal ectasia in which the retinal pigment epithelium, choroid and sclera are attenuated. This localised ectasia distorts the regional refractive geometry, producing myopic astigmatism, and the associated retinal thinning creates relative field depression corresponding to the ectatic zone. Because the anomaly straddles but does not strictly honour the vertical raphe, field defects mimic but do not truly respect the vertical meridian. Vision is generally stable and good once refractive error is corrected, and the anomaly itself is non-progressive. Rarely, associated maculopathy such as serous detachment or choroidal neovascularisation may threaten central acuity.

Timothy syndrome — CACNA1C-related disorder, long QT syndrome type 8, LQT8, Timothy syndrome type 1 Other genetic long QT syndrome subtypes Acquired QT prolongation from drugs or electrolyte CACNA1C variants Developmental and neurological assessment Evaluation of immune function, glucose homeostasis and dental health as indicated A rare multisystem disorder caused by gain-of-function variants in the L-type calcium channel gene CACNA1C, classified as long QT syndrome type 8 Marked QT prolongation predisposes to life-threatening ventricular arrhythmia and sudden death, often in infancy or early childhood Extracardiac features commonly include cutaneous syndactyly of the fingers and toes, facial dysmorphism, and neurodevelopmental problems such as autism spectrum features Congenital heart defects, immune dysfunction, hypoglycaemia and dental abnormalities can also occur The classic form usually arises from de novo variants, so a negative family history does not exclude it Management focuses on preventing arrhythmia with beta-blockers, careful avoidance of QT-prolonging drugs and an implantable cardioverter defibrillator in high-risk children Functional 2:1 atrioventricular block can occur because the very long ventricular repolarisation leaves the ventricle refractory to alternate atrial beats Care is multidisciplinary given the cardiac, developmental and systemic involvement Marked QT prolongation with syncope or documented ventricular arrhythmia Functional 2:1 atrioventricular block in an infant Aborted cardiac arrest Syndactyly with cardiac and neurodevelopmental features prompting urgent cardiac evaluation Assuming a negative family history excludes the diagnosis, when most cases are de novo Attributing an infant's QT prolongation to reversible causes and missing the genetic syndrome Focusing on the cardiac problem and overlooking the syndactyly and developmental clues Using QT-prolonging medications that can precipitate torsades Underestimating the systemic and immune complications Timothy syndrome is caused by gain-of-function variants in CACNA1C, which encodes the pore-forming subunit of the L-type calcium channel (CaV1.2). The variants impair voltage-dependent inactivation of the channel, so calcium entry into cells is prolonged. In cardiomyocytes this lengthens the action potential and markedly prolongs the QT interval, promoting early afterdepolarisations and torsades-de-pointes ventricular arrhythmia. Because CaV1.2 is expressed widely, the same channel dysfunction disrupts development and function of other tissues, producing the syndactyly, neurodevelopmental, immune and other systemic features that distinguish the syndrome from isolated long QT syndrome. Timothy syndrome carries a high risk of early sudden death from malignant ventricular arrhythmia, and survivors face substantial neurodevelopmental and systemic morbidity; multidisciplinary care and arrhythmia prevention improve but do not eliminate the risk.

Tinea Versicolor — pityriasis versicolor, PV, Malassezia infection Vitiligo (complete depigmentation without scale) Pityriasis alba Post-inflammatory hypo- or hyperpigmentation Seborrhoeic dermatitis Tinea corporis due to a true dermatophyte Erythrasma or, when hypopigmented patches are extensive, early indeterminate leprosy in endemic areas Usually clinical, confirmed by microscopy of skin scrapings showing hyphae and spores Wood's lamp examination for characteristic fluorescence Culture is generally unnecessary because the organism is a normal commensal Consideration of underlying immunosuppression or endocrine factors in extensive or recalcitrant disease Presents as multiple well-defined oval macules and patches on the upper trunk, shoulders, and neck, which coalesce and carry a fine, powdery scale revealed by gently stretching or scratching the skin Lesions vary in colour, appearing hypopigmented on tanned or darker skin and pink-brown on paler skin, which explains the name versicolor It is caused by an overgrowth of commensal Malassezia yeast rather than a true dermatophyte, so despite the name it is not classic ringworm Warmth, humidity, sweating, oily skin, and immunosuppression favour the shift from yeast to the pathogenic filamentous form Microscopy of scale shows the typical spaghetti-and-meatballs pattern of short hyphae and spores, confirming the diagnosis Treatment relies on topical antifungal or keratolytic agents, with systemic antifungals reserved for extensive or recurrent disease; recurrence is common and prophylactic regimens may be needed Warn patients that pigmentary changes can persist for weeks to months after successful treatment, as this does not indicate treatment failure A Wood's lamp may show a coppery-orange or pale fluorescence, aiding assessment Widespread or unusually treatment-resistant disease prompting evaluation for immunosuppression Persistent hypopigmented patches that lack scale and could represent another disorder such as vitiligo or, in endemic settings, leprosy Signs of deeper Malassezia infection such as folliculitis with pustules in an immunocompromised patient Interpreting residual hypopigmentation after treatment as treatment failure Confusing hypopigmented patches with vitiligo and omitting to examine for scale Failing to counsel about the high recurrence rate and the role of maintenance therapy Overlooking predisposing factors such as heat, humidity, or immunosuppression that drive relapse Tinea versicolor results from overgrowth of lipophilic Malassezia yeasts that are normal residents of sebum-rich skin. Under predisposing conditions such as heat, humidity, occlusion, and increased sebum, the yeast converts to its hyphal, pathogenic form and proliferates within the stratum corneum. The organism produces dicarboxylic acids, notably azelaic acid, that inhibit melanocyte tyrosinase and cause the hypopigmented patches, while an associated low-grade inflammatory and hyperkeratotic response produces the scale and, in some, hyperpigmentation. Because the yeast is part of the normal flora, the condition is more a disturbance of host-commensal balance than a transmissible infection, and it readily recurs. The condition is benign and responds well to antifungal therapy, but recurrence is frequent because the causative yeast is part of the normal skin flora and predisposing conditions persist; residual pigmentary change resolves gradually over weeks to months once treated.

anaemia, thyroid dysfunction or vascular risk factors where clinically indicated Tinnitus is the perception of sound in the absence of an external source and is a symptom rather than a disease in itself It is usefully divided into subjective tinnitus, heard only by the patient, and the much rarer objective tinnitus, which can also be detected by the examiner Most subjective tinnitus accompanies sensorineural hearing loss from noise exposure, presbycusis, ototoxic drugs or Meniere disease Pulsatile tinnitus that is synchronous with the heartbeat suggests a vascular cause such as a ototoxic and other implicated medications, caffeine, stress and poor sleep should be reviewed Because there is often no curative treatment, management centres on treating any underlying cause, hearing aids or sound therapy for masking, and cognitive and habituation-based approaches such as tinnitus retraining therapy Unilateral tinnitus with asymmetrical hearing loss suggesting a retrocochlear tumour Pulsatile tinnitus requiring vascular imaging to exclude a treatable vascular lesion Associated neurological signs, facial numbness or weakness Sudden hearing loss accompanying the tinnitus, which is an emergency Tinnitus with severe distress, depression or suicidal ideation needing urgent mental health support Missing an acoustic neuroma behind unilateral tinnitus Failing to image pulsatile tinnitus for a vascular source Dismissing the symptom without exploring its psychological impact and sleep disturbance Overlooking ototoxic medication or reversible contributors Promising a cure rather than framing management around control and habituation Subjective tinnitus is thought to arise from aberrant neural activity generated when the cochlea or auditory nerve is damaged; loss of input leads to maladaptive changes and increased spontaneous firing and reorganisation in the central auditory pathways, so the brain perceives sound that is not present. Emotional and attentional networks amplify and sustain the perception, which explains why distress and the loudness of tinnitus are only loosely related. Objective tinnitus, in contrast, has a genuine internal acoustic source: turbulent or pulsatile blood flow in vascular lesions, or repetitive contraction of palatal, tensor tympani or stapedius muscles, generates a real sound transmitted to the ear. Many patients habituate over time and cope well with reassurance, sound enrichment and psychological approaches, and tinnitus linked to a treatable cause may improve when that cause is addressed; however, some individuals have persistent, distressing tinnitus that requires ongoing support.

TMEM165-CDG (CDG-IIk) — TMEM165, congenital disorder of glycosylation type IIk, CDG-IIk, Golgi manganese/calcium transporter defect Other type II CDG subtypes (e.g. MGAT2-CDG, B4GALT1-CDG, COG-complex CDG, SLC35A2-CDG) Primary skeletal dysplasias and spondylo-epi-metaphyseal dysplasias Mucopolysaccharidoses and other storage disorders with bone involvement Type I CDGs when the transferrin pattern is ambiguous Syndromic short stature Hepatic involvement from other metabolic causes Transferrin isoelectric focusing or mass spectrometry showing a type II pattern TMEM165 molecular genetic testing Skeletal survey for spondylo-epi-metaphyseal dysplasia Liver function tests and imaging Growth and endocrine assessment Biochemical monitoring during a galactose supplementation trial A type II CDG caused by defects in TMEM165, a Golgi transporter involved in manganese and calcium homeostasis required for glycosyltransferase activity Distinguished by a prominent skeletal phenotype with spondylo-epi-metaphyseal dysplasia, short stature and skeletal dysplasia in addition to developmental delay Hepatic involvement, growth failure and variable dysmorphism accompany the skeletal features Transferrin analysis shows a type II pattern reflecting defective galactosylation of complex glycan antennae Because the defect involves Golgi manganese handling, in vitro and some clinical data suggest galactose or manganese supplementation can improve glycosylation markers Management is supportive and multidisciplinary; galactose supplementation may be trialled with biochemical monitoring Diagnosis is confirmed by TMEM165 molecular genetic testing Progressive skeletal deformity or severe short stature Significant hepatic dysfunction Developmental regression Failure to thrive with multisystem involvement Investigating the skeletal dysplasia in isolation without considering a glycosylation disorder Not distinguishing type I from type II defects on transferrin analysis Overlooking a potential galactose or manganese-responsive component Interpreting biochemical response as proven clinical cure TMEM165 is a Golgi membrane protein that regulates manganese and calcium homeostasis in the secretory pathway. Many Golgi glycosyltransferases, particularly galactosyltransferases, depend on manganese as a cofactor, so loss of TMEM165 function impairs terminal galactosylation of complex N-glycans, producing a type II processing defect on transferrin analysis. The manganese dependence explains why supplying galactose or manganese can partially restore glycosylation. Hypoglycosylation of bone matrix and other proteins is thought to drive the characteristic skeletal dysplasia. Prognosis is variable; the skeletal dysplasia and growth failure are often prominent, and biochemical improvement with galactose supplementation has been reported, although its long-term clinical benefit is still being defined. Neurodevelopmental outcome depends on disease severity.

Temporomandibular joint disorder — TMD, temporomandibular disorder, TMJ dysfunction, myofascial pain dysfunction Odontogenic pain from pulpal or periapical disease Otitis or other ear pathology Trigeminal neuralgia or other neuropathic facial pain Giant cell (temporal) arteritis in older patients Salivary gland disease Referred pain from cervical spine or headache disorders Clinical assessment of jaw movement, joint sounds, and muscle tenderness Evaluation of occlusion and parafunctional habits MRI for suspected internal derangement when symptoms persist CT or cone-beam imaging for bony or degenerative joint changes Inflammatory markers if temporal arteritis is a concern in older patients Temporomandibular disorders are a group of musculoskeletal conditions affecting the jaw joints, the muscles of mastication, or both Typical features are jaw pain, joint sounds such as clicking or crepitus, limited or deviated mouth opening, and pain on chewing Pain is often localised to the preauricular region and may radiate to the temple, ear, or face, and can mimic ear or dental pathology Most cases are muscular (myofascial) rather than intra-articular, and parafunctional habits like clenching and grinding are common contributors Disc displacement with reduction typically produces reciprocal clicking, whereas displacement without reduction causes locking and restricted opening It is largely a clinical diagnosis; imaging is reserved for atypical, persistent, or red-flag presentations Initial management is conservative, including reassurance, jaw rest, soft diet, physiotherapy, occlusal splints, and stress and habit control Psychological factors, stress, and chronic pain behaviours strongly influence symptoms and treatment response New onset facial pain with headache, scalp tenderness, or visual symptoms in an older patient suggesting giant cell arteritis Progressive limitation of opening, a hard end-feel, or a mass suggesting joint ankylosis or neoplasia Unilateral worsening symptoms with cranial nerve signs pointing to a sinister cause Recent significant trauma raising the possibility of condylar fracture Proceeding to irreversible occlusal or surgical treatment before trying conservative care Missing giant cell arteritis in an older patient with jaw and temporal symptoms Attributing all facial pain to the joint and overlooking dental or neuropathic causes Neglecting parafunctional habits and psychosocial factors that drive symptoms Temporomandibular disorders arise from a multifactorial interplay of biomechanical overload, parafunctional habits, trauma, and psychosocial stress acting on the masticatory system. Sustained muscle hyperactivity from clenching or grinding produces myofascial pain and fatigue, while abnormal loading and internal derangement of the joint can disturb the normal disc-condyle relationship, causing clicking, locking, or degenerative change. Central sensitisation and psychological factors can amplify and perpetuate pain. The result is a spectrum ranging from purely muscular pain to intra-articular disc displacement and degenerative joint disease. Most patients improve with conservative, reversible measures and the condition often follows a self-limiting or fluctuating course, though a minority develop chronic pain or progressive degenerative joint change.

TNF-receptor-associated periodic syndrome (TRAPS) — TRAPS, TNFRSF1A, familial Hibernian fever, TNF receptor 1-associated periodic syndrome, autosomal dominant periodic fever Familial Mediterranean of TNFRSF1A Full blood count showing neutrophilia during attacks Urinalysis for proteinuria as an early marker of AA amyloidosis Serum immunoglobulins including IgD to help distinguish related receptor Fever episodes are characteristically prolonged, often lasting one to three weeks, distinguishing it from the shorter attacks of other periodic fever syndromes A migratory, tender erythematous rash overlying underlying myalgia, typically moving distally along a limb, is a suggestive feature Periorbital oedema with conjunctivitis or periorbital pain is a classic ocular manifestation Attacks commonly include serositis (abdominal and chest pain), arthralgia and monocytic fasciitis AA (secondary) amyloidosis is the major long-term complication, driven by chronic inflammation, and warrants surveillance Therapy is directed at the interleukin-1 axis and, in some cases, interleukin-6 blockade, whereas continuous tumour necrosis factor inhibition has been less reliably effective New or increasing proteinuria suggesting evolving AA amyloidosis Persistently elevated inflammatory markers between attacks indicating uncontrolled subclinical inflammation Severe serositis mimicking an acute surgical abdomen Progressive renal impairment Expecting brief attacks and dismissing TRAPS because fevers are unusually prolonged Failing to monitor for proteinuria and missing early amyloidosis Assuming tumour necrosis factor blockade is always effective, when interleukin-1 targeting is often preferred Repeated surgery for recurrent serositis mistaken for a surgical abdomen TRAPS is an autosomal dominant autoinflammatory syndrome caused by mutations in TNFRSF1A, the gene for the 55-kDa tumour necrosis factor receptor 1. Rather than a simple loss of receptor shedding, the mutant receptor misfolds and is retained within the endoplasmic reticulum, provoking a cellular stress response, enhanced production of reactive oxygen species, and ligand-independent, exaggerated pro-inflammatory signalling. This drives excess innate cytokine output, particularly along the interleukin-1 pathway, producing recurrent systemic inflammation. Persistent elevation of acute phase proteins over years predisposes to deposition of serum amyloid A protein in tissues and the development of AA amyloidosis. With effective anti-inflammatory therapy attacks can be controlled and quality of life preserved, but untreated or poorly controlled disease carries a meaningful risk of AA amyloidosis and consequent renal failure, which is the principal determinant of long-term outcome.

Toddler's diarrhoea (chronic nonspecific diarrhoea) — chronic nonspecific diarrhoea of childhood, toddler's diarrhoea, functional diarrhoea Coeliac disease Cow's milk protein allergy Chronic giardiasis or other gut infection Carbohydrate malabsorption such as lactose intolerance or excess fructose or sorbitol intake Inflammatory bowel disease in the older child Cystic fibrosis or other pancreatic insufficiency when there is failure to thrive Overflow diarrhoea complicating constipation Careful growth monitoring and a detailed dietary history, which are the mainstay Coeliac serology if there are any concerns about growth or symptoms Stool microscopy, culture, and parasite testing if infection is suspected Faecal elastase if pancreatic insufficiency is a concern Full blood count and inflammatory markers if organic disease is suspected Faecal calprotectin where inflammatory bowel disease is considered Assessment of fluid and fruit-juice intake A common cause of chronic loose stools in an otherwise well, thriving pre-school child, typically between about one and five years of age Stools are frequent and loose and may contain recognisable undigested food, giving the classic peas-and-carrots appearance By definition the child grows well, is not dehydrated, and has no blood in the stool or systemic symptoms It is often linked to dietary factors summarised as the four Fs: excessive fluid, fruit juice, low fat, and high fibre It reflects rapid intestinal transit rather than malabsorption or infection Diagnosis is clinical in a thriving child with a normal examination, and extensive investigation is unnecessary in the absence of red flags Management is reassurance and dietary adjustment, normalising fluid intake, reducing fruit juice and sorbitol-containing drinks, ensuring adequate dietary fat, and avoiding excessive fibre The condition is self-limiting and typically resolves by school age Faltering growth or weight loss Blood or mucus in the stool Nocturnal diarrhoea or systemic symptoms such as fever or vomiting Signs of dehydration or malnutrition Onset in early infancy or persistence beyond the expected age Subjecting a thriving child to unnecessary invasive investigation Over-restricting the diet and causing nutritional harm, particularly inappropriate fat or calorie restriction Missing coeliac disease or another organic cause when growth is faltering Reflexly excluding milk without supporting evidence Failing to address excessive fruit juice and sugary-drink intake Toddler's diarrhoea is a functional disorder of accelerated gastrointestinal transit rather than a disease of the gut mucosa. Excessive intake of fluids and of fructose- or sorbitol-containing drinks, together with a relatively low-fat diet, speeds transit and reduces the time available for water and nutrient reabsorption. The result is frequent loose stools containing undigested food residue, occurring in a child who is otherwise thriving with no evidence of malabsorption, inflammation, or infection. The outlook is excellent: this is a benign, self-limiting condition that resolves spontaneously, usually by around school age, without long-term consequences.

Toddler's diarrhoea — Chronic nonspecific diarrhoea of childhood, Functional diarrhoea, Peas-and-carrots diarrhoea Coeliac disease Cow's milk or other food protein allergy Giardiasis and other chronic enteric infections Carbohydrate malabsorption (lactose intolerance, congenital sucrase-isomaltase deficiency) Cystic fibrosis and other causes of exocrine pancreatic insufficiency Inflammatory bowel disease Constipation with overflow soiling masquerading as diarrhoea Plotting and review of the growth chart (central to the diagnosis) Coeliac serology (tissue transglutaminase IgA with total IgA) Stool microscopy, culture and Giardia antigen testing Faecal calprotectin if inflammatory bowel disease is suspected Faecal elastase or sweat test if pancreatic insufficiency or cystic fibrosis is suspected Full blood count, inflammatory markers and ferritin Dietary diary review of fluid, juice, fat and fibre intake The most common cause of chronic diarrhoea in a well, thriving preschool child, broadly between six months and five years of age. Passage of several loose stools daily, often containing recognisable undigested food such as vegetable fragments (the 'peas and carrots' sign). Classic diurnal pattern: the first stool of the day is larger and more formed, with subsequent stools becoming progressively looser, and no diarrhoea overnight. Normal growth and the absence of nocturnal symptoms are the cardinal reassuring features and are central to the diagnosis. Strongly linked to excessive intake of fruit juice and squash rich in fructose and sorbitol, overhydration and paradoxically low-fat, high-fibre 'toddler' diets. It is a functional disorder of rapid intestinal transit; there is no malabsorption and nutrient absorption is preserved. Management is dietary through the 'four Fs': ensure adequate Fat, reduce excess Fluid, limit Fruit juice, and provide appropriate rather than excessive Fibre. Investigations are usually unnecessary when the history is classic and the growth trajectory is normal. Faltering growth or weight loss Nocturnal diarrhoea waking the child Blood or mucus in the stool Bilious or persistent vomiting, significant abdominal pain or distension Steatorrhoea with bulky, pale, greasy, offensive stools Undertaking extensive investigations or imposing restrictive diets in a thriving child with a classic history. Over-restricting dietary fat, which can worsen symptoms and compromise energy intake. Assuming a functional cause without checking growth and thereby missing coeliac disease or giardiasis. Overlooking constipation with overflow soiling presenting as apparent diarrhoea. Escalating fibre inappropriately in the belief that it will firm the stools. Toddler's diarrhoea is a functional disorder attributed to dysregulated intestinal motility with rapid small- and large-bowel transit, in the absence of mucosal, infective or malabsorptive disease. Excessive ingestion of fluids, particularly fruit juices and squashes rich in poorly absorbed carbohydrates such as fructose and sorbitol, delivers an osmotic carbohydrate load to the colon that exceeds absorptive and fermentative capacity, drawing water into the lumen and accelerating transit. Diets low in fat, which would normally slow gastric emptying and transit, and disproportionately high in fibre further shorten transit time. The net effect is frequent loose stools containing undigested food, without impaired nutrient absorption, so growth and development are preserved. A benign, self-limiting condition that resolves spontaneously by school age, typically around four to five years, as bowel habit matures and continence is established; growth and development are unaffected.

as confirmation, since some tumours and lymphoma also respond transiently Missing orbital apex extension threatening vision Overlooking invasive fungal infection in an immunocompromised or diabetic patient Tolosa-Hunt syndrome is a non-specific granulomatous inflammation involving the cavernous sinus, superior orbital fissure, or orbital apex. The inflammatory tissue compresses and irritates the ocular motor nerves and the trigeminal fibres passing through this compartment, producing painful ophthalmoplegia. The cause is unknown and the histology resembles that of idiopathic orbital inflammation. Because the same anatomical region can be affected by tumour, aneurysm, infection, and systemic granulomatous disease, the syndrome remains a diagnosis of exclusion supported by imaging and steroid responsiveness. The syndrome usually responds well to corticosteroids with resolution of pain and gradual recovery of ophthalmoplegia, but recurrences are common and some patients retain residual nerve deficits.

recanalisation Fluctuating or declining consciousness signalling active basilar apex occlusion Progressive brainstem signs indicating evolving basilar thrombosis needing urgent intervention Bilateral thalamic involvement causing profound hypersomnolence Cortical blindness with denial of deficit that may mask serious infarction Attributing somnolence and confusion to a metabolic cause and missing basilar occlusion Focusing on limb power and overlooking the diagnostic eye movement and visual signs Delaying vascular imaging in a patient without obvious hemiparesis Mistaking peduncular hallucinosis for a primary psychiatric disturbance Top-of-the-basilar syndrome follows occlusion, typically embolic, of the distal basilar artery and its terminal branches, which supply the midbrain, thalamus, and the medial temporal and occipital lobes through the posterior cerebral and thalamoperforating arteries. Ischaemia of the rostral midbrain and pretectum disrupts vertical gaze, convergence, and pupillary control, while bilateral paramedian thalamic and reticular infarction impairs arousal and produces somnolence and behavioural change. Involvement of the occipitotemporal cortex causes cortical visual loss, visual hallucinations, and amnesia. The clustering of eye movement, arousal, visual, and memory deficits with relatively preserved strength reflects this rostral posterior-circulation territory. Outcome hinges on the extent of infarction and speed of recanalisation; timely reperfusion can yield good recovery, but extensive rostral brainstem and bilateral thalamic infarction carries high morbidity and mortality.

Chronic tophaceous gout — tophaceous gout, chronic gout, gouty tophi, chronic gouty arthropathy Rheumatoid arthritis with nodules Calcium pyrophosphate crystal arthropathy Osteoarthritis with Heberden and Bouchard nodes Chronic infection or osteomyelitis Xanthomas or other soft-tissue nodules Basic calcium phosphate periarticular deposition Aspiration or biopsy of a tophus or joint with polarised microscopy for negatively birefringent urate crystals Serum urate to guide and monitor treat-to-target therapy Radiographs for punched-out erosions with overhanging edges Dual-energy CT to quantify and map urate deposits Ultrasound for tophi and the double-contour sign Renal function and assessment of cardiovascular and metabolic comorbidity Swab or culture if an ulcerated tophus raises suspicion of secondary infection Chronic tophaceous gout is the advanced stage in which longstanding, poorly controlled hyperuricaemia leads to visible or palpable deposits of monosodium urate (tophi) in and around joints and soft tissues Tophi commonly form over the first metatarsophalangeal joint, the fingers, the olecranon bursa, the Achilles tendon, and the helix of the ear, and may ulcerate to discharge chalky white material The condition reflects a large total-body urate burden and usually indicates years of untreated or undertreated gout Tophi cause joint-destroying erosions, deformity, chronic pain, and reduced function, and can restrict movement or entrap nerves Radiographs show characteristic well-defined 'punched-out' erosions with sclerotic margins and overhanging edges, with joint space relatively preserved until late Aspiration or biopsy of a tophus reveals abundant needle-shaped, negatively birefringent monosodium urate crystals The cornerstone of management is long-term urate-lowering therapy to a low target (treat-to-target), which over time dissolves tophi and prevents further damage; it is not started or stopped during an acute flare and is continued through flares An ulcerated or discharging tophus with possible secondary infection Nerve compression caused by a tophaceous mass Coexistent septic arthritis in a chronically damaged joint Significant renal impairment influencing the choice of therapy Failing to commit to long-term treat-to-target urate-lowering therapy Stopping urate-lowering therapy once tophi shrink, allowing recurrence Starting or stopping urate-lowering therapy during an acute flare Missing secondary infection of an ulcerated tophus Attributing the deformity to another arthropathy without confirming urate crystals Prolonged hyperuricaemia produces a large body burden of monosodium urate that precipitates as aggregated crystal masses (tophi) surrounded by a chronic granulomatous, foreign-body inflammatory reaction. Tophi within and around joints erode bone and cartilage, generating the characteristic punched-out erosions and progressive structural damage, while in soft tissues they form firm nodules that may ulcerate and discharge. Sustained lowering of the serum urate below the saturation point reverses the process by allowing the crystals to dissolve gradually. With sustained urate-lowering therapy to target, tophi gradually resolve, attacks stop, and further joint damage is prevented; established erosions and deformity may nonetheless be permanent, and poor adherence leads to ongoing destruction and disability.

high, rather than exploring Over-diagnosing epididymo-orchitis and giving unnecessary antibiotics Failing to reassess a boy whose pain worsens or fails to settle The appendix testis is a small pedunculated Mullerian duct remnant at the upper pole of the testis. Its narrow stalk predisposes it to twisting, which cuts off its blood supply and causes ischaemia and infarction of the appendage. The resulting inflammation produces localised pain and tenderness, and the infarcted appendage may be visible as a bluish nodule beneath the scrotal skin. Because the testis itself is not compromised, the process is self-limiting and resolves as the appendage necroses and is reabsorbed. Torsion of the appendix testis is benign and self-limiting; symptoms typically resolve within one to two weeks with conservative care and there is no threat to testicular viability or future fertility.

a hard midline palatal swelling with normal mucosa needs no biopsy No treatment is required unless prosthetic needs, recurrent trauma, or patient concern warrant surgical removal Ulceration that fails to heal or shows induration, raising suspicion of neoplasia Rapid growth, which is atypical for a torus A soft or fluctuant rather than bony-hard swelling suggesting another lesion Signs of infection or abscess formation Mistaking a torus for a neoplasm or abscess and over-investigating Missing a genuine palatal tumour by assuming any midline swelling is a torus Traumatising the thin overlying mucosa during denture fitting Recommending surgery when observation would suffice A torus palatinus is a developmental, benign exostosis composed of dense cortical bone with a variable amount of trabecular bone, arising along the midline palatal suture. Its growth is slow and it typically becomes apparent from adolescence or early adulthood; both genetic predisposition and functional or masticatory factors have been proposed as contributors. The lesion is not neoplastic and has no malignant potential, and the thin mucosa stretched over the bony prominence is easily traumatised, which accounts for the occasional ulceration seen clinically. The prognosis is excellent as the torus is entirely benign; although it continues to grow slowly it causes no harm, and surgical removal, when indicated, is generally curative with uncommon recurrence.

Overlooking a restrictive atrial septum that critically limits systemic output Failing to monitor for recurrent pulmonary vein stenosis after repair In total anomalous pulmonary venous return the pulmonary veins fail to connect to the left atrium and instead drain into the systemic venous system, so oxygenated and deoxygenated blood mix within the right atrium. Survival depends on an obligatory right-to-left shunt through a patent foramen ovale or atrial septal defect to fill the left heart and systemic circulation. When the anomalous pathway is obstructed, as often occurs when an infracardiac vein passes through the diaphragm, pulmonary venous pressure rises steeply, causing pulmonary oedema, pulmonary hypertension and profound cyanosis. Unobstructed connections instead deliver a large volume of recirculated blood to the lungs, producing pulmonary overcirculation, right heart volume loading and congestive failure. With timely surgical repair the outlook is good, but obstructed neonatal presentations carry significant early risk, and postoperative pulmonary vein stenosis is a serious complication that can recur and worsen prognosis.

medication is reserved for troublesome tics Pharmacological options for severe tics include agents acting on dopaminergic transmission and certain alpha-adrenergic agents, chosen by symptom burden and comorbidity Psychoeducation, school liaison, and treating comorbid conditions usually improve function more than suppressing the tics themselves Self-injurious tics causing physical harm Abrupt, explosive onset or neurological signs suggesting a secondary or acquired cause Severe comorbid depression with suicidal ideation Marked functional deterioration from comorbid ADHD or obsessive-compulsive symptoms Focusing on tic suppression while neglecting more impairing comorbid ADHD or obsessive-compulsive disorder Assuming coprolalia is required for diagnosis when it is uncommon Overmedicating mild tics that do not warrant pharmacotherapy Misinterpreting suppressible tics as voluntary or attention-seeking Missing an atypical presentation that points to a secondary movement disorder Tourette syndrome is a neurodevelopmental disorder involving dysfunction of cortico-striato-thalamo-cortical circuits, with abnormalities in dopaminergic neurotransmission within the basal ganglia thought to underlie the generation of tics. It is highly heritable with a complex polygenic basis, and environmental and possibly immune-mediated factors may modulate expression, while overlapping circuitry accounts for the frequent association with obsessive-compulsive and attentional symptoms. Tics typically emerge in childhood, peak in severity in early adolescence, and then decline in many patients, with a substantial proportion experiencing marked improvement or near-resolution by adulthood. Prognosis for overall function depends heavily on comorbid conditions, which often persist and drive impairment, so their recognition and treatment strongly influence outcome.

The truncated protein is thought to act in a dominant-negative fashion in addition to reducing normal gene dosage, disturbing the developmental programmes SALL1 controls. Toxic and Drug-Induced Hepatitis — Drug-induced liver injury, DILI, Hepatotoxicity, Toxic hepatitis Acute viral hepatitis (A, B, C) - idiosyncratic hepatocellular DILI can be clinically and histologically indistinguishable Autoimmune hepatitis (especially with nitrofurantoin, minocycline, hydralazine, methyldopa) Alcoholic hepatitis (amiodarone produces a pseudoalcoholic picture) Ischemic hepatitis / shock liver Biliary obstruction and primary sclerosing cholangitis (DILI can mimic sclerosing cholangitis after floxuridine or long-term ketamine) Cholestasis of pregnancy (shares genetic canalicular transporter defects with estrogen-induced cholestasis) Acute viral hepatitis A, B, and C Serial ALT, AST, alkaline phosphatase and bilirubin to define pattern and compute the R value (ALT/ALP as multiples of upper limit of normal) Serum acetaminophen level timed 4-8 h after ingestion, interpreted against the treatment nomogram (levels above 300 mcg/mL at 4 h predict severe injury; below 150 mcg/mL injury unlikely) Acetaminophen-protein (acetaminophen-Cys) adduct measurement by HPLC as an investigational diagnostic marker Arterial blood lactate in acute liver failure (above 3.5 mmol/L suggests likely need for transplantation) Autoantibodies (ANA, anti-smooth muscle, anti-LKM2, anti-mitochondrial) when an autoimmune-pattern or checkpoint-inhibitor injury is suspected Liver biopsy when the pattern is uncertain (may show centrilobular necrosis, microvesicular steatosis, granulomas, phospholipid-laden lamellar bodies in amiodarone, or vanishing bile ducts) Exclusion of viral, autoimmune and biliary causes; structured causality assessment (DILIN expert opinion, RUCAM, or newer RECAM) Autoimmune hepatitis Alcoholic / nonalcoholic steatohepatitis Ischemic hepatopathy Mechanical biliary obstruction Drug-induced liver injury (DILI) is the single most common cause of acute liver failure, and hepatotoxicity signals are the leading reason candidate compounds fail to gain approval during drug development; a meticulous history covering prescription, over-the-counter, herbal, dietary, occupational and household chemical exposures is essential (Harrison 22e p.2665). Two broad categories are recognized: direct (intrinsic) toxic injury, which is predictable, dose-dependent and has a short latency (often hours), and idiosyncratic injury, which is infrequent (roughly 1 in 1,000 to 1 in 100,000 exposures), less clearly dose-related and typically appears 5-90 days after starting the drug (Harrison 22e p.2665-2666). The R value, the ratio of ALT to alkaline phosphatase (each as a multiple of the upper limit of normal), classifies the injury pattern: R greater than 5 indicates hepatocellular injury, R less than 2 indicates cholestatic injury, and R of 2-5 indicates a mixed pattern (Harrison 22e p.2667). Hy's Law, named for Hyman Zimmerman, holds that drug-induced jaundice during a trial predicts serious liver injury, with roughly a 10-to-1 ratio of jaundiced cases to cases of acute liver failure; such cases often portend failure of drug approval (Harrison 22e p.2667). Acetaminophen is the prototypic direct hepatotoxin and the most prevalent cause of acute liver failure in the Western world; it produces dose-related centrilobular necrosis, and aminotransferases can exceed 10,000 IU/L, far above levels seen in viral hepatitis, often with a relatively low bilirubin in this hyperacute injury (Harrison 22e p.2668). A characteristic biochemical clue to acetaminophen toxicity is the combination of extremely high aminotransferases with low bilirubin; clinical suspicion should prompt empiric N-acetylcysteine even before history is confirmed, since denial or altered mentation can obscure the diagnosis (Harrison 22e p.2668). Isoniazid causes transient mild aminotransferase elevation in about 10% of recipients early in therapy (an 'adaptive' response that usually resolves despite continued use); clinically significant hepatocellular injury can appear over a latency of up to 6 months and rises sharply with age, being highest in those over 50 and lowest in those under 20 (Harrison 22e p.2670). Amoxicillin-clavulanate is the most commonly implicated single agent in DILI in the United States and Europe, producing a fairly specific mixed or predominantly cholestatic injury that may begin after the drug has already been stopped owing to a long latency (Harrison 22e p.2667, 2670-2671). Complementary and alternative medicines, including herbal and dietary weight-loss and body-building products, now account for more than 20% of DILI cases in the United States; implicated agents include green tea extract (Camellia sinensis), kava, germander, chaparral, comfrey (pyrrolizidine alkaloids), Hydroxycut and OxyElite Pro (Harrison 22e p.2671). Certain drugs produce an autoimmune-hepatitis-like phenotype with positive antinuclear antibodies, classically nitrofurantoin, minocycline, hydralazine and alpha-methyldopa (Harrison 22e p.2667, 2670-2671). Immune checkpoint inhibitors (anti-CTLA-4 ipilimumab; anti-PD-1 pembrolizumab and nivolumab) cause an immune-mediated hepatitis within weeks, often ANA-positive, mediated predominantly by CD8+ lymphocytes and responsive to glucocorticoids; concurrent immune injury to thyroid, muscle and colon may occur (Harrison 22e p.2671-2672). Withdrawal of the suspected agent at the first sign of an adverse reaction, or when aminotransferases reach five times the upper limit of normal, is critical, because continued use despite symptoms and signs is associated with lethal outcomes (Harrison 22e p.2668). Jaundice arising during drug exposure (Hy's Law) predicts serious injury and possible liver failure Coagulopathy and hepatic encephalopathy - markers of acute liver failure, which develops in about 10% of DILI cases Aminotransferases above 10,000 IU/L with a low bilirubin - hyperacute acetaminophen pattern Continued ingestion despite nausea, fatigue or jaundice (common scenario in fatal isoniazid and acetaminophen toxicity) Acetaminophen ingestion of 25 g or more, or high timed plasma levels on the nomogram Arterial lactate above 3.5 mmol/L in acetaminophen acute liver failure Concurrent renal failure or myocardial injury in acetaminophen overdose DILI is nearly always a diagnosis of exclusion; causality is hard to prove and many disorders produce an identical clinicopathologic picture Mild transient aminotransferase elevations that resolve during continued therapy ('adaptation,' seen with isoniazid, valproate, phenytoin and statins) can be mistaken for significant toxicity Long latency drugs (notably amoxicillin-clavulanate and nitrofurantoin) may cause injury that manifests only after the drug has been stopped Idiosyncratic reactions occurring in under 1 in 10,000 recipients are missed by clinical trials and only detected through postmarketing surveillance (e.g., troglitazone) In chronic alcohol users, glutathione depletion and CYP2E1 induction can make the toxic acetaminophen dose as low as 2 g Activated charcoal or cholestyramine are ineffective if given more than 30 minutes after acetaminophen ingestion Routine liver test monitoring during statin therapy is not recommended, and asymptomatic isolated aminotransferase elevations need not prompt discontinuation Herbal/dietary supplements may contain undeclared pharmaceuticals (e.g., diclofenac in antirheumatic 'herbs'), so the history must specifically probe alternative-medicine use Hepatotoxicity arises from direct hepatocyte injury (free radicals or reactive metabolites causing membrane lipid peroxidation) or from drug/metabolite activation of innate or adaptive immune pathways, apoptotic signaling, and disruption of bile excretory transport. Interference with canalicular pumps allows injurious endogenous bile acids to accumulate, producing cholestasis; other mechanisms inhibit protein synthesis or impair mitochondrial fatty-acid oxidation, leading to lactic acidosis and microvesicular steatosis. Most drugs are metabolized via phase I cytochrome P450 (oxidation) followed by phase II conjugation (glucuronidation, sulfation) or glutathione inactivation; most toxicity reflects formation of a reactive phase I metabolite, with glutathione depletion removing a protective pathway. For acetaminophen, phase II conjugation yields harmless metabolites, but a fraction is converted by CYP2E1 to the toxic intermediate NAPQI, normally detoxified by glutathione; when glutathione is overwhelmed or depleted, NAPQI binds covalently to hepatocyte macromolecules forming protein adducts that drive necrosis. Susceptibility to idiosyncratic injury is influenced by HLA haplotypes (e.g., amoxicillin-clavulanate, flucloxacillin), polymorphisms in metabolizing pathways and protective cytokines, and activation of nuclear receptors such as CAR and PXR. Factors potentiating acetaminophen injury include enzyme induction (alcohol via CYP2E1, phenobarbital, isoniazid), fasting/starvation and other states that lower hepatic glutathione (Harrison 22e p.2665-2666, 2668-2670). Most DILI is self-limited and resolves after withdrawal of the offending agent. Acute liver failure develops in about 10% of DILI cases; once that threshold (coagulopathy plus encephalopathy) is reached, spontaneous recovery occurs in fewer than 30%, and over 40% of those patients undergo liver transplantation. Survivors of acetaminophen overdose rarely have lasting liver injury, though the associated acute kidney injury (seen in nearly 75% of severe cases) is almost always self-limited. Anabolic steroid cholestasis typically resolves over weeks to months with prolonged jaundice. Some agents cause chronic injury: methotrexate, tamoxifen and amiodarone can lead to cirrhosis, and several drugs cause chronic autoimmune-like hepatitis (Harrison 22e p.2668-2670). Injury pattern is graded by the R value (ALT/ALP as multiples of ULN): hepatocellular (R > 5), cholestatic (R < 2), or mixed (R 2-5). Severity is judged clinically by progression to acute liver failure (coagulopathy plus encephalopathy). Causality likelihood is assessed by structured tools including the DILIN expert-opinion scale (definite, highly likely, probable, possible, unlikely), RUCAM, and the newer RECAM. Hy's Law identifies high-risk hepatocellular injury when jaundice accompanies hepatocellular enzyme elevation (Harrison 22e p.2667-2668).

Drug hepatotoxicity is generally not more frequent in those with pre-existing chronic liver disease, although the severity of outcome may be greater; statins specifically can be used safely in chronic hepatitis C and steatosis (p.2668, p.2671-2672). Liver injury can follow ingestion of essentially any xenobiotic (industrial toxins, drugs, herbal/dietary supplements). Most drugs are lipophilic and undergo phase I oxidation/methylation by cytochrome P450 enzymes followed by phase II conjugation (glucuronidation, sulfation) or glutathione inactivation to a water-soluble form for renal/biliary excretion; most hepatotoxicity arises from a reactive phase I metabolite, and glutathione depletion compounds the injury. Damage occurs through several overlapping routes: direct hepatocyte injury via free radicals/reactive intermediates causing membrane lipid peroxidation; activation of innate or adaptive immune responses (HLA-haplotype-dependent hapten binding, cytotoxic lymphocytes, antibody-mediated cytotoxicity); triggering of apoptosis via TNF-alpha/Fas pathways; disruption of bile canalicular transport pumps (e.g., MRP3) leading to toxic bile-acid accumulation and cholestasis; and inhibition of mitochondrial beta-oxidation/respiration producing lactic acidosis and microvesicular steatosis. Nuclear receptors such as CAR and PXR can also induce hepatotoxicity. For acetaminophen specifically, a minor fraction is converted by CYP2E1 to the reactive metabolite NAPQI, normally detoxified by conjugation with hepatoprotective glutathione; when NAPQI overwhelms or glutathione is depleted, NAPQI binds covalently to hepatocyte macromolecules forming protein adducts that drive centrilobular necrosis. Most DILI is self-limited and resolves after the offending agent is withdrawn. However, acute liver failure develops in about 10% of DILI cases; once that threshold (coagulopathy plus hepatic encephalopathy) is reached, spontaneous recovery occurs in fewer than 30%, and liver transplantation is undertaken in more than 40% of these patients (p.2668). For acetaminophen, up to 72% of poisoned patients in some Scandinavian series progress to encephalopathy and coagulopathy (lower in the UK/US); a single dose of 10-15 g can cause clinical injury and fulminant fatal disease is usually associated with >=25 g; the N-acetylcysteine antidote markedly reduces severity and is most effective given early (within ~8-12 h), though it retains some benefit up to 24-36 h. Survivors of acetaminophen overdose rarely have ongoing liver injury (p.2668, p.2670). Several agents cause chronic injury or progression to cirrhosis (methotrexate, tamoxifen, amiodarone), and the autoimmune-pattern agents (nitrofurantoin, minocycline, hydralazine, methyldopa) can lead to cirrhosis if not recognised early (p.2668-2670). Injury pattern is classified by the R value (ALT/ALP as multiples of ULN): R >5.0 hepatocellular, R <2.0 cholestatic, R 2.0-5.0 mixed (p.2667). Hy's Law serves as a severity/prognostic marker: jaundice (significant bilirubin rise) accompanying hepatocellular DILI predicts a markedly higher risk of acute liver failure (about a 10:1 jaundice-to-failure ratio) (p.2667). The aminotransferase threshold of >5x ULN (or >3x ULN with symptoms) marks the point at which the offending agent should be withdrawn (p.2668). Causality (not severity) is graded on a five-point likelihood scale by DILIN (definite, highly likely, probable, possible, unlikely) (p.2668). The clinical endpoint of severity is acute liver failure, defined by coagulopathy plus hepatic encephalopathy (p.2668).

long-standing multinodular goitre acquires foci of autonomous function. Over time, subpopulations of follicular cells accumulate somatic activating mutations, particularly of the TSH receptor, so that individual nodules secrete thyroid hormone independently of TSH. As autonomous mass increases, circulating thyroid hormone rises and suppresses pituitary TSH, silencing the internodular parenchyma and producing the characteristic patchy scintigraphic pattern. Because the autonomous tissue avidly traps iodine, exposure to iodinated contrast or iodine-rich drugs such as amiodarone can abruptly increase hormone synthesis and precipitate thyrotoxicosis. With definitive treatment by radioactive iodine or surgery the outlook is good; untreated disease, especially in the elderly, carries substantial cardiovascular and bone morbidity, and large goitres may cause progressive compression.

toxic optic neuropathy — toxic optic neuritis, drug-induced optic neuropathy Nutritional optic neuropathy Leber hereditary optic neuropathy Compressive or chiasmal lesion Demyelinating optic neuritis Maculopathy Functional (non-organic) visual loss Detailed medication, occupational and toxin exposure history Colour vision testing and automated perimetry Optical coherence tomography of the retinal nerve fibre layer Magnetic resonance imaging to exclude a compressive lesion Serum or urine toxicology and heavy-metal levels where indicated Arterial blood gas and osmolar gap in suspected methanol poisoning Vitamin B12 and folate to exclude a coexisting nutritional cause Typically bilateral, symmetric, painless and progressive visual loss with a centrocaecal scotoma and dyschromatopsia, closely overlapping the nutritional form. Frequent offenders include ethambutol, methanol, amiodarone, prolonged linezolid, isoniazid, disulfiram, tobacco and heavy metals such as lead and thallium. Ethambutol toxicity is dose- and duration-dependent, is often reversible if detected early, and mandates baseline and periodic monitoring of acuity and colour vision. Methanol poisoning causes acute severe loss with disc oedema and a high anion-gap metabolic acidosis and may be permanent or fatal. The papillomacular bundle is preferentially affected, producing temporal disc pallor as atrophy develops. A meticulous drug, occupational and social history is essential, and removal of the offending agent is the mainstay of management. Pupillary responses are relatively spared and a relative afferent pupillary defect is minimal when the process is symmetric. Coexisting nutritional deficiency frequently aggravates toxic injury and should be sought and corrected. Acute severe visual loss with metabolic acidosis indicating a methanol emergency Rapidly progressive loss or systemic signs of toxicity No recovery despite withdrawal of the suspected agent Asymmetry or focal neurological signs suggesting an alternative diagnosis Continuing the offending drug because of inadequate monitoring, as with ethambutol Failing to recognise methanol toxicity as a treatable emergency Ignoring a concurrent nutritional deficiency that worsens the injury Omitting baseline visual assessment before commencing a known optic-toxic agent Most toxins injure the optic nerve by impairing mitochondrial oxidative phosphorylation and generating oxidative stress within the metabolically demanding papillomacular bundle. Ethambutol chelates copper and iron and interferes with metal-dependent respiratory chain enzymes, while the methanol metabolite formic acid directly inhibits cytochrome c oxidase. The energy failure preferentially damages small central fibres, accounting for the characteristic central and centrocaecal field defects and eventual temporal atrophy. Many cases, particularly ethambutol-related, improve after early withdrawal of the offending agent, whereas methanol poisoning frequently causes permanent, severe loss. Chronic unrecognised exposure results in irreversible optic atrophy.

desquamation can occur late Management combines aggressive fluid resuscitation, prompt source control, and antibiotic principles pairing a beta-lactam with a protein-synthesis inhibitor such as clindamycin to switch off toxin production Intravenous immunoglobulin is considered as an adjunct to neutralise circulating superantigens in severe disease Mortality is high, so early recognition, critical-care support, and surgical debridement of any necrotising focus are decisive Pain disproportionate to examination findings suggesting underlying necrotising infection requiring urgent debridement Rapidly progressing hypotension and organ failure indicating established septic shock Skin crepitus, bullae, dusky discolouration or rapidly advancing erythema pointing to deep tissue necrosis Falling urine output and rising creatinine signalling early multi-organ dysfunction Attributing severe limb pain to a minor injury and missing early necrotising infection Relying on antibiotics alone without urgent surgical source control Omitting a protein-synthesis inhibitor such as clindamycin, forgoing its anti-toxin effect Underestimating fluid requirements and delaying critical-care escalation Invasive strains of Streptococcus pyogenes release pyrogenic exotoxins and other superantigens that bind directly to MHC class II molecules and T-cell receptors outside the normal antigen groove. This triggers polyclonal T-cell activation and an overwhelming release of pro-inflammatory cytokines (a cytokine storm), producing capillary leak, vasodilatation, hypotension, and multi-organ failure. Bacteraemia and deep tissue invasion, often within necrotising soft-tissue infection, amplify the toxin load and accelerate the shock state. Even with intensive treatment, mortality remains substantial and is highest when there is an associated necrotising soft-tissue infection or delayed source control; survival depends on early recognition, rapid surgery, and organ support.

Toxoplasmosis — Toxoplasma gondii infection Mononucleosis-like syndrome from acute toxoplasmic lymphadenopathy: EBV infection, CMV infection, HIV infection, Bartonella (cat-scratch disease), and lymphoma (Harrison 22e p.1800-1801). CNS mass lesions in an AIDS patient: primary CNS lymphoma, metastatic tumor, brain abscess, progressive multifocal leukoencephalopathy (JC virus), fungal infection, and mycobacterial infection (Harrison 22e p.1801). Chorioretinitis in an immunocompetent individual: tuberculosis, syphilis, and histoplasmosis (Harrison 22e p.1801). Chorioretinitis in an AIDS patient: CMV, syphilis, HSV, VZV, and fungal infection (Harrison 22e p.1801). Cerebral toxoplasmosis must also be differentiated from herpes simplex encephalitis, cryptococcal meningitis, and HIV-associated neurocognitive disorder (HAND) (Harrison 22e p.1800). Congenital infection: CMV, HSV, rubella, syphilis, and listeriosis (Harrison 22e p.1801). Primary CNS lymphoma (EBV-associated) presenting as ring-enhancing brain lesion(s) in AIDS Cytomegalovirus infection Epstein-Barr virus infection (infectious mononucleosis) Bartonella henselae (cat-scratch disease) Progressive multifocal leukoencephalopathy (JC virus) Cryptococcal meningitis Herpes simplex encephalitis Tuberculous, fungal, or bacterial brain abscess Pneumocystis pneumonia (Toxoplasma pneumonia can be confused with it) Serology: combined IgG and IgM antibody to Toxoplasma; circulating IgA favors acute infection; Sabin-Feldman dye test, indirect fluorescent antibody test, and ELISA measure IgG; double-sandwich IgM-ELISA or IgM-ISAGA preferred for IgM (Harrison 22e p.1801). IgG avidity testing to help time infection, particularly useful in pregnancy (Harrison 22e p.1801). PCR amplification of T. gondii DNA from blood, CSF, ocular fluid, bronchoalveolar lavage, or amniotic fluid; PCR is the mainstay for detecting organisms but a negative PCR does not rule out toxoplasmosis (Harrison 22e p.1801). Double-dose contrast CT and contrast MRI of the brain (standard imaging for Toxoplasma encephalitis); MRI is more sensitive for monitoring response (Harrison 22e p.1802). CSF analysis in suspected CNS disease (modest pleocytosis and protein elevation without glucose change; CSF PCR specific but not sensitive) (Harrison 22e p.1800-1801). Lymph node biopsy / histology showing follicular hyperplasia and clusters of epithelioid macrophages; demonstration of tachyzoites establishes acute infection (Harrison 22e p.1799, p.1801). Dilated ophthalmologic examination for chorioretinitis; ocular fluid PCR, Western blot, or Goldmann-Witmer coefficient for ocular disease (Harrison 22e p.1801-1802). In HIV-infected persons, screening for IgG antibody to Toxoplasma at the time of HIV diagnosis to identify latent infection (Harrison 22e p.1801). Weekly blood PCR screening after allogeneic HSCT in patients seropositive before transplant; pre-transplant donor and recipient serologies (Harrison 22e p.1800). Next-generation sequencing (metagenomics) of blood or body fluids, especially in immunocompromised individuals (Harrison 22e p.1801). Primary CNS lymphoma Metastatic brain tumor / other CNS malignancy Lymphoma (as a cause of lymphadenopathy) Caused by the obligate intracellular parasite Toxoplasma gondii; up to a third of the world's population is latently infected (Harrison 22e p.1797). Two transmissible stages reach humans: tissue cysts containing bradyzoites in undercooked meat (e.g., lamb, pork, venison, ground beef), and sporulated oocysts shed in cat feces that contaminate soil, food, or water; sporulated oocysts are environmentally hardy and highly infectious (Harrison 22e p.1797). In the immunocompetent host, acute infection is usually asymptomatic and self-limited, going unrecognized in 80-90% of acquired infections (Harrison 22e p.1799). The most common manifestation of symptomatic acute toxoplasmosis in immunocompetent patients is cervical lymphadenopathy; nodes are usually nontender and discrete, with associated headache, malaise, fatigue, and low-grade fever (temperature usually <40 degrees C) (Harrison 22e p.1799). The classic severe presentation is reactivation encephalitis in immunocompromised hosts (especially HIV-positive individuals or transplant recipients) in whom latent infection has reactivated (Harrison 22e p.1797). In AIDS, >95% of Toxoplasma encephalitis cases are due to recrudescent infection, typically developing when the CD4+ T-cell count falls below 100/microL; encephalitis is the predominant manifestation while meningeal involvement is uncommon (Harrison 22e p.1800). On MRI/CT, Toxoplasma encephalitis classically produces multiple ring-enhancing lesions, most often in the basal ganglia and corticomedullary junction; a single lesion increases the likelihood of primary CNS lymphoma (Harrison 22e p.1801-1802). T. gondii is the most common cause of posterior uveitis in immunocompetent individuals and is estimated to cause about 35% of all chorioretinitis cases in the US and Europe (Harrison 22e p.1799, p.1801). Congenital toxoplasmosis results from transplacental passage during primary maternal infection; infants may be asymptomatic at birth but later manifest chorioretinitis, strabismus, epilepsy, hydrocephalus, microcephaly, intellectual disability, and psychomotor retardation (Harrison 22e p.1797, p.1799). Antibody titers are NOT useful for establishing reactivation or following infection activity in immunocompromised patients; however, an absence of positive serology suggests an alternative diagnosis (Harrison 22e p.1800). Diagnosis rests on serology (combined IgG and IgM, with circulating IgA favoring acute infection) and PCR; PCR of body fluids is specific but its sensitivity may be low (Harrison 22e p.1801). A therapeutic trial of anti-Toxoplasma medications is frequently used in AIDS patients with CNS mass lesions: >50% improve by day 3 and >90% by day 7, whereas worsening by day 7 (or lymphoma) prompts brain biopsy (Harrison 22e p.1802). Focal neurologic deficits, seizures, altered mental status, or ring-enhancing CNS mass lesion(s) in an HIV/AIDS patient (especially CD4+ <100/microL) - reactivation Toxoplasma encephalitis, which is rapidly fatal if untreated (Harrison 22e p.1800). A solitary ring-enhancing CNS lesion - increases the likelihood of primary CNS lymphoma over toxoplasmosis (Harrison 22e p.1802). Failure to improve clinically by day 7 of empiric anti-Toxoplasma therapy - prompts brain biopsy and consideration of lymphoma or alternative diagnosis (Harrison 22e p.1802). Fulminant sepsis, fever of unknown origin, or pneumonia in an immunocompetent person with travel to or residence in South/Central America - virulent atypical genotypes (Harrison 22e p.1797-1799). Toxoplasma pneumonia / disseminated disease in immunocompromised hosts may progress to acute respiratory failure with hemoptysis, metabolic acidosis, hypotension, and disseminated intravascular coagulation (Harrison 22e p.1800). Acute maternal infection in pregnancy (risk of transplacental transmission; severity highest with first-trimester infection) (Harrison 22e p.1798). Acute toxoplasmosis is asymptomatic and self-limited in 80-90% of immunocompetent adults and children, so the diagnosis is easily missed (in one epidemic, toxoplasmosis was correctly diagnosed in only 3 of 25 patients who sought care) (Harrison 22e p.1799). Antibody titers do not establish reactivation or track infection activity in immunocompromised patients; do not rely on serial titers to gauge active disease (Harrison 22e p.1800). A negative PCR does not rule out toxoplasmosis - PCR is specific but may be of low sensitivity depending on the body fluid (Harrison 22e p.1801). Isolation/demonstration of tissue cysts (bradyzoites) from biopsied tissue indicates only the presence of cysts and should NOT be misinterpreted as evidence of acute toxoplasmosis; only demonstration of tachyzoites (e.g., in lymph nodes) establishes acute infection (Harrison 22e p.1801). IgM can persist for >1 year, so a positive IgM with positive IgG should not necessarily be interpreted as acute disease; a negative IgM with positive IgG indicates distant infection (Harrison 22e p.1801). MRI/CT findings are not pathognomonic - 40% of CNS lymphomas are multifocal and 50% are ring-enhancing, and the false-negative rate for both MRI and CT is ~10% (Harrison 22e p.1802). In AIDS patients with TE, IgM is usually undetectable and titers may be borderline/low (or transplant patients on B-cell-targeted immunosuppression may become seronegative); fewer than 3% have no demonstrable antibody at diagnosis (Harrison 22e p.1800, p.1801). Up to 25% of congenitally infected newborns may be seronegative with normal routine physical examinations, so eye, brain, CSF, and radiologic assessment are needed (Harrison 22e p.1802). Toxoplasma pneumonia can be confused with Pneumocystis pneumonia, and organisms may also be found in healthy tissue, complicating interpretation (Harrison 22e p.1800). If a patient is seronegative for T. gondii, the likelihood that a CNS mass lesion is due to toxoplasmosis is <10%, favoring earlier biopsy (Harrison 22e p.1802). T. gondii is an intracellular coccidian. Ingested tissue cysts (bradyzoites) or oocysts (sporozoites) release organisms that invade gut epithelium and transform into rapidly dividing tachyzoites, which can infect and replicate in all nucleated mammalian cells via a parasitophorous vacuole, causing cell death and focal necrosis with an acute mononuclear inflammatory response. Parasites disseminate as free tachyzoites or within phagocytic 'Trojan horse' cells through blood and lymphatics to lymphatic tissue, skeletal muscle, myocardium, retina, placenta, and CNS. In the immunocompetent host, humoral and cell-mediated immunity (parasiticidal antibody, macrophage activation, IFN-gamma, IL-12-driven TH1 response, CD8+ cytotoxic T lymphocytes) controls infection; tissue cysts containing bradyzoites then form 7-10 days after systemic infection and persist principally in the CNS and muscle, completing the asexual cycle and establishing lifelong chronic infection. Subclinical cycles of cyst rupture and reformation are the probable source of recrudescent infection. Immunocompromised or fetal hosts lack the immune factors (notably CD8+ T cells; reactivating T cells fail to secrete IFN-gamma and IL-2) needed to contain tachyzoite spread, allowing progressive focal destruction (necrotizing encephalitis, pneumonia, myocarditis). The sexual stage occurs only in the cat (definitive host), producing oocysts shed in feces (Harrison 22e p.1797-1800). In immunocompetent individuals, acute infection is usually asymptomatic and self-limited, resolving within several weeks though lymphadenopathy may persist for months; chronic infection persists lifelong with little consequence. Ocular disease can be self-limited but episodic chorioretinitis flares progressively destroy retinal tissue and may lead to glaucoma. In immunocompromised hosts, disease may be rapidly fatal if untreated, mandating prompt diagnosis and therapy; with treatment of Toxoplasma encephalitis, >50% improve by day 3 and >90% by day 7, but relapses are common and maintenance/secondary prophylaxis is needed while CD4+ counts remain low. For congenital toxoplasmosis, factors associated with severe disability include delayed diagnosis/treatment, neonatal hypoxia and hypoglycemia, profound visual impairment, uncorrected hydrocephalus, and raised intracranial pressure; with appropriate treatment upward of 70% of children have normal developmental, neurologic, and ophthalmologic findings at follow-up. Infected infants normal at birth may still have higher rates of learning disabilities and chronic neurologic sequelae (Harrison 22e p.1797-1801). Harrison does not provide a formal severity grading system for toxoplasmosis. Clinical stratification is by host immune status and syndrome: (1) immunocompetent acute infection - usually asymptomatic/self-limited (most commonly cervical lymphadenopathy); (2) ocular toxoplasmosis (chorioretinitis); (3) reactivation disease in the immunocompromised host - most importantly Toxoplasma encephalitis in AIDS (typically CD4+ <100/microL), which is rapidly fatal if untreated, plus pneumonitis, myocarditis, and disseminated disease; and (4) congenital toxoplasmosis, with severity inversely related to gestational age at maternal infection (earliest infection = lowest transmission but most severe fetal disease) (Harrison 22e p.1797-1800).

tracheal stenosis — tracheal narrowing, post-intubation tracheal stenosis asthma or chronic obstructive pulmonary disease tracheomalacia or excessive dynamic airway collapse extrinsic compression by goitre, mediastinal mass or vascular anomaly primary or secondary tracheal tumour granulomatosis with polyangiitis with subglottic stenosis relapsing polychondritis tracheobronchial amyloidosis or tracheobronchopathia osteochondroplastica flexible and rigid bronchoscopy to map length, calibre and maturity of the stricture multidetector CT of the neck and chest with multiplanar and virtual bronchoscopic reconstruction pulmonary function testing with inspiratory and expiratory flow-volume loops anti-neutrophil cytoplasmic antibody testing where vasculitis is suspected mucosal biopsy for amyloid, granulomatous or neoplastic disease serum inflammatory markers and autoimmune serology as indicated laryngoscopic assessment of glottic and subglottic involvement A fixed narrowing of the tracheal lumen; the commonest acquired cause is post-intubation or post-tracheostomy injury, followed by inflammatory, infiltrative and neoplastic disease. Post-intubation stenosis typically develops at the level of the cuff or the stoma, where mucosal ischaemia from pressure leads to ulceration, cartilage damage and circumferential fibrotic scarring. Symptoms often appear weeks to months after extubation, with progressive exertional dyspnoea, stridor and a sensation of difficulty moving air; wheeze frequently prompts misdiagnosis as asthma. Biphasic stridor suggests a fixed lesion at the thoracic inlet; stridor usually becomes audible once the lumen is critically narrowed, so its absence does not exclude significant stenosis. The flow-volume loop classically shows flattening of both inspiratory and expiratory limbs, the pattern of a fixed extrathoracic or intrathoracic upper-airway obstruction. Consider granulomatosis with polyangiitis (subglottic involvement), amyloidosis, sarcoidosis, relapsing polychondritis and tracheobronchopathia osteochondroplastica among non-iatrogenic causes. Bronchoscopy defines the length, calibre, maturity and location of the stricture and distinguishes simple web-like from complex cartilaginous stenoses, guiding whether endoscopic dilation or resection is appropriate. Idiopathic subglottic stenosis characteristically affects women in mid-adult life and tends to recur after endoscopic treatment. stridor at rest or use of accessory muscles indicating critical airway narrowing rapidly progressive dyspnoea or inability to lie flat hypoxaemia, exhaustion or altered consciousness suggesting impending airway failure haemoptysis or systemic features raising concern for malignancy or active vasculitis recent extubation with worsening breathlessness suggesting evolving high-grade stenosis Attributing fixed wheeze and dyspnoea to asthma and delaying airway imaging or bronchoscopy. Underestimating severity because symptoms are minimal until the lumen is critically reduced. Performing repeated dilations of a lesion that has a treatable systemic inflammatory cause without addressing the underlying disease. Overlooking concurrent malacia, which limits the durability of dilation alone. Inserting a stent in benign disease without strong indication, given the risk of granulation, migration and secondary infection. Acquired tracheal stenosis most often follows mucosal injury from an endotracheal or tracheostomy tube. Sustained cuff or tube pressure exceeding mucosal perfusion causes ischaemic ulceration; the exposed cartilage undergoes chondritis and may soften or fragment, and subsequent healing produces circumferential granulation and mature fibrous scar that contracts the lumen. Depending on the site and mechanism, stenosis may be a thin fibrous web, a longer cartilaginous 'A-frame' collapse, or a complex segment with associated malacia. Inflammatory causes (granulomatosis with polyangiitis, relapsing polychondritis, sarcoidosis) narrow the airway through mucosal and cartilaginous inflammation and fibrosis, while infiltrative diseases such as amyloidosis and tracheobronchopathia osteochondroplastica deposit material within the submucosa. Regardless of cause, the reduced cross-sectional area sharply increases airflow resistance; because resistance rises steeply as the radius falls, patients may be nearly asymptomatic until the lumen is severely compromised, after which small further reductions cause marked dyspnoea and stridor. Short, mature, web-like stenoses often respond durably to endoscopic dilation, whereas complex, long or cartilaginous strictures usually require segmental tracheal resection with reconstruction, which achieves good long-term results in experienced centres; inflammatory and idiopathic subglottic disease is prone to recurrence and needs ongoing surveillance.
