failure or life-threatening episodes of near-complete airway collapse Severe secretion retention with recurrent pneumonia Rapidly worsening symptoms suggesting an evolving compressive lesion Syncope or exercise-limiting obstruction from severe dynamic collapse Relying on static inspiratory imaging and missing the dynamic collapse Mislabelling the disease as refractory asthma or COPD and escalating ineffective therapy Overlooking a treatable underlying cause such as extrinsic compression Proceeding to airway stenting without a trial confirming benefit, given stent-related complications Tracheobronchomalacia results from structural weakness of the central airway wall, either from deficient or softened cartilaginous support or from laxity and redundancy of the posterior membranous wall. During expiration and coughing, when intrathoracic pressure rises above intraluminal pressure, the weakened airway collapses excessively, obstructing airflow and impairing the shear forces needed to clear secretions. Congenital forms reflect immature or deficient cartilage, while acquired forms follow injury from prolonged intubation or tracheostomy, chronic inflammation, recurrent infection, emphysema, trauma, or chronic compression by adjacent structures. The dynamic nature of the collapse explains why symptoms are provoked by exertion and cough and why static imaging can underestimate severity. Prognosis depends on severity and cause; mild disease is often managed conservatively with good quality of life, while severe symptomatic malacia can be disabling but may improve substantially with positive-pressure support, stenting, or tracheobronchoplasty.

tracheobronchomegaly — Mounier-Kuhn syndrome, tracheobronchial dilatation bronchiectasis from other causes (cystic fibrosis, post-infective, immunodeficiency) tracheomalacia or excessive dynamic airway collapse without dilatation chronic obstructive pulmonary disease with recurrent infection saber-sheath trachea tracheobronchial diverticula from other causes connective-tissue disease with airway involvement acquired tracheal dilatation adjacent to fibrotic lung disease (traction) chest CT with measurement of tracheal and main bronchial diameters dynamic expiratory CT to demonstrate excessive airway collapse flexible bronchoscopy to assess wall flaccidity, diverticula and collapse pulmonary function testing including flow-volume loop analysis sputum culture and assessment of bronchiectasis-related infection evaluation for associated connective-tissue or cartilage disorder assessment of immune function where recurrent infection is prominent Tracheobronchomegaly (Mounier-Kuhn syndrome) is marked abnormal dilatation of the trachea and main bronchi due to atrophy or deficiency of the elastic and smooth muscle of the airway wall. The dilated airway is abnormally compliant, so it collapses on expiration and cough, impairing clearance and predisposing to recurrent infection and bronchiectasis. Corrugation of the airway wall between the cartilage rings produces mucosal outpouchings (tracheal diverticulosis), classically giving a scalloped contour on imaging. It usually presents in adult men with chronic productive cough, recurrent lower respiratory infection, breathlessness and, in some, a loud ineffective cough. Diagnosis rests on measuring the tracheal and main bronchial diameters on CT, which exceed defined upper limits of normal. Dynamic imaging or bronchoscopy demonstrates the excessive expiratory collapse that accompanies the fixed dilatation. Associations include connective-tissue and cartilage disorders (such as Ehlers-Danlos and cutis laxa) and, in children, certain congenital syndromes. Management is largely supportive — airway clearance, prompt treatment of infection and immunisation — as no therapy reverses the structural abnormality; positive-pressure support may aid selected patients. recurrent or severe lower respiratory infections with clinical deterioration progressive respiratory failure from ineffective cough and secretion retention haemoptysis complicating established bronchiectasis acute large-airway obstruction from retained secretions or mucus plugging features of a systemic connective-tissue disorder requiring broader assessment Overlooking the diagnosis by not measuring airway calibre on CT in a patient with recurrent infection and bronchiectasis. Attributing the ineffective cough and recurrent infection solely to bronchiectasis without recognising the underlying megatrachea. Relying on static imaging and missing the dynamic expiratory collapse. Inserting airway stents without strong indication, given the poor structural support and complication risk. Failing to screen for an associated heritable connective-tissue disorder. Tracheobronchomegaly results from deficiency or atrophy of the elastic fibres and smooth muscle within the membranous and cartilaginous portions of the tracheal and main bronchial walls. The weakened wall dilates progressively under normal transmural pressures, and the redundant, poorly supported tissue between cartilage rings herniates outward to form the characteristic corrugations and diverticula. The enlarged, flaccid airway loses its structural rigidity and collapses during expiration and coughing; because cough depends on generating high linear airflow velocities in a stable airway, the dynamic collapse renders cough ineffective and severely impairs mucus clearance. Retained secretions and recurrent infection damage the distal airways, producing bronchiectasis and further inflammation in a self-perpetuating cycle. The condition may be idiopathic, familial, or associated with heritable connective-tissue disorders in which generalised deficiency of elastic tissue affects the airway as one of several sites. The course is variable: some patients remain stable with mild symptoms for years, whereas those with extensive bronchiectasis and recurrent infection may progress to chronic respiratory impairment; management is supportive, as the structural airway abnormality is not reversible.

Tracheobronchopathia osteochondroplastica — TPO, TBO, tracheopathia osteoplastica, osteochondroplastic tracheobronchopathy Amyloidosis of the airway Tracheobronchial calcification from other causes Endobronchial tuberculosis Papillomatosis or other endobronchial tumours Granulomatosis with polyangiitis affecting the airway Relapsing polychondritis Bronchoscopy revealing the cobblestone nodular appearance and sparing of the posterior wall CT of the airways showing calcified submucosal nodules Biopsy demonstrating cartilage and bone within nodules Pulmonary function tests including flow-volume loops for fixed obstruction Assessment for recurrent infection and secretion retention Exclusion of amyloidosis and other infiltrative airway diseases A rare benign condition characterised by multiple submucosal cartilaginous and bony nodules projecting into the lumen of the trachea and large bronchi Characteristically spares the posterior membranous wall of the trachea because the nodules arise from cartilage, which is absent posteriorly Often asymptomatic and found incidentally; when symptomatic it causes chronic cough, wheeze, haemoptysis, hoarseness, and recurrent infections Bronchoscopy shows a distinctive cobblestone or rock-garden appearance with hard nodules that can make instrumentation difficult CT demonstrates calcified nodules along the anterolateral tracheal walls with sparing of the posterior membrane Usually a disease of older adults and generally follows a slow, benign course Diagnosis is typically made bronchoscopically or on imaging, with biopsy confirming cartilage and bone within the nodules Significant central airway obstruction causing stridor or exertional breathlessness Recurrent or severe lower respiratory infections from impaired clearance Haemoptysis requiring exclusion of other airway pathology Difficult airway during intubation or bronchoscopy due to rigid nodules Mistaking the nodular airway appearance for malignancy or amyloidosis without biopsy Failing to recognise the diagnostic clue of posterior membrane sparing Underestimating the risk of a difficult airway during instrumentation Attributing chronic cough or recurrent infection to more common causes and overlooking the diagnosis Tracheobronchopathia osteochondroplastica is defined by the formation of multiple submucosal nodules composed of cartilage and heterotopic bone, sometimes with marrow, that bulge into the airway lumen. These nodules are thought to arise from the perichondrium and cartilaginous rings, which explains their anterolateral distribution and the characteristic sparing of the posterior membranous wall that lacks cartilage. The cause is unknown, with proposed contributions from chronic inflammation, metabolic and degenerative processes, and abnormal bone morphogenetic signalling within airway connective tissue. Over time the nodules can narrow and stiffen the airway, causing airflow obstruction, impaired secretion clearance, and recurrent infection. The condition is usually benign and slowly progressive; most patients have a good prognosis with symptomatic management, and significant airway compromise requiring intervention is uncommon.

Tracheoesophageal Fistula — TEF, TOF/TEF, esophageal atresia with tracheoesophageal fistula, EA/TEF Isolated oesophageal atresia without fistula Laryngeal cleft Choanal atresia Severe gastro-oesophageal reflux with aspiration Vascular ring causing feeding difficulty Swallowing dysfunction of neurological origin Attempted passage of a nasogastric tube with radiograph showing tube coiling in the upper pouch Chest and abdominal radiograph to assess the pouch and bowel gas pattern Echocardiography to identify cardiac anomalies and aortic arch side before surgery Renal ultrasound and spinal and limb assessment for VACTERL anomalies Bronchoscopy or contrast study to define an H-type fistula when suspected An abnormal congenital communication between the trachea and oesophagus, most often occurring together with oesophageal atresia; the commonest anatomical type is proximal oesophageal atresia with a distal tracheoesophageal fistula. Typical newborn features include excessive drooling and frothy secretions, choking, coughing, and cyanosis with feeds, and inability to pass a nasogastric tube into the stomach. A characteristic radiographic clue is a feeding tube coiling in the upper oesophageal pouch; gas in the stomach and bowel indicates a distal fistula, while a gasless abdomen suggests atresia without a distal fistula. Aspiration of saliva and, via the fistula, gastric contents into the airway causes respiratory compromise and pneumonitis. An isolated H-type fistula without atresia may present later with recurrent coughing during feeds, cyanotic spells, and recurrent respiratory infections. Initial management protects the airway and lungs: keep the infant nil by mouth, apply continuous suction to the upper pouch, and position to reduce aspiration and reflux through the fistula. It is frequently part of the VACTERL association, so evaluation for vertebral, anorectal, cardiac, renal, and limb anomalies is important. Definitive treatment is surgical division of the fistula and repair of the oesophageal atresia, timed according to the infant's stability and anatomy. Long-term issues can include anastomotic stricture, gastro-oesophageal reflux, tracheomalacia, and dysphagia requiring ongoing follow-up. Choking, cyanosis, and respiratory distress with attempted feeding Aspiration pneumonitis from overflow of secretions or reflux through the fistula Progressive gastric and bowel distension impairing ventilation via a large distal fistula Recurrent respiratory infections and cyanotic spells suggesting a missed H-type fistula Associated critical cardiac or other major anomalies within the VACTERL spectrum Feeding a newborn with excessive drooling before excluding oesophageal atresia, precipitating aspiration Missing a delayed-presenting H-type fistula in a child with recurrent feeding-related respiratory symptoms Failing to search for associated VACTERL anomalies, especially cardiac lesions, before surgery Overlooking that a gasless abdomen indicates atresia without a distal fistula Underestimating long-term reflux, stricture, and tracheomalacia complications requiring follow-up Abnormal separation of the primitive foregut into trachea and oesophagus during embryogenesis leaves an abnormal connection between the two and, commonly, a discontinuous oesophagus (atresia). In the common configuration, the upper oesophagus ends in a blind pouch while the lower oesophagus connects to the trachea. Swallowed secretions collect in and overflow from the upper pouch into the airway, and the distal fistula allows gastric contents to reflux into the trachea and air to distend the stomach. These mechanisms produce aspiration, chemical pneumonitis, and, with a large distal fistula, gaseous abdominal distension that further impairs ventilation. With early diagnosis and surgical repair the outlook is generally favourable, and prognosis is influenced strongly by prematurity, birth weight, and associated anomalies, particularly cardiac lesions. Many children require management of later complications such as strictures, reflux, and tracheomalacia but achieve good long-term function.

tracheomalacia — tracheobronchomalacia, expiratory central airway collapse asthma with poorly reversible airflow obstruction chronic obstructive pulmonary disease fixed tracheal stenosis vocal cord dysfunction / inducible laryngeal obstruction extrinsic tracheal compression by mediastinal mass or vascular ring excessive dynamic airway collapse from an over-compliant membranous wall relapsing polychondritis affecting the airway dynamic inspiratory-expiratory (cine) CT of the central airways awake flexible bronchoscopy during spontaneous and forced breathing pulmonary function testing with flow-volume loop analysis trial of continuous positive airway pressure as a diagnostic-therapeutic stent echocardiography or CT angiography where vascular ring or compression is suspected evaluation for relapsing polychondritis where cartilage inflammation is suspected contrast oesophagram if tracheo-oesophageal fistula or vascular ring is possible Characterised by excessive expiratory collapse of the trachea (and often main bronchi) due to weakness of the cartilaginous rings, the posterior membranous wall, or both, producing a crescentic or 'frown-shaped' lumen on dynamic imaging. Congenital forms associate with prematurity, tracheo-oesophageal fistula/oesophageal atresia, vascular rings and cartilage disorders; acquired forms follow prolonged intubation, tracheostomy, chronic inflammation (relapsing polychondritis), COPD or extrinsic compression. The cardinal symptom is a harsh, barking or 'seal-like' cough, often with expiratory wheeze, exertional dyspnoea and difficulty clearing secretions leading to recurrent lower respiratory infection. Symptoms characteristically worsen with any manoeuvre that raises intrathoracic pressure — coughing, forced expiration, crying in infants, or supine posture. Dynamic (inspiratory-expiratory or cine) CT and awake flexible bronchoscopy with the patient breathing spontaneously are the reference investigations; static end-inspiratory imaging alone frequently misses the diagnosis. Flow-volume loops may show expiratory flow oscillations or a characteristic notch, but normal spirometry does not exclude the condition. Distinguish primary cartilage/membranous weakness (tracheomalacia) from dynamic excessive collapse driven by an over-compliant posterior membrane (excessive dynamic airway collapse), as management emphasis differs. Continuous positive airway pressure can act as a pneumatic stent, relieving symptoms and guiding suitability for surgical stabilisation such as posterior tracheobronchopexy. recurrent 'dying spells', cyanotic or apparent life-threatening events in an infant acute respiratory distress with inability to clear secretions recurrent or non-resolving lower respiratory tract infection syncope or near-syncope precipitated by cough (cough syncope) rapidly progressive dyspnoea suggesting associated systemic cartilage disease Relying on static end-inspiratory imaging or a single bronchoscopic snapshot, which can miss dynamic expiratory collapse. Misdiagnosing the barking cough and wheeze as refractory asthma and escalating bronchodilators or steroids without benefit. Overlooking a treatable underlying cause such as a vascular ring, mediastinal mass or relapsing polychondritis. Placing airway stents indiscriminately, as they carry substantial complications including granulation, migration and infection. Failing to recognise associated gastro-oesophageal reflux or aspiration that perpetuates airway inflammation. Tracheomalacia results from structural weakness of the tracheal wall so that it cannot maintain patency against the transmural pressure swings of respiration. Weakness may lie in deficient or soft cartilaginous rings (reducing the normal cartilage-to-membrane ratio) or in an excessively lax, redundant posterior membranous wall. During expiration and cough, positive intrathoracic pressure exceeds the airway's structural resistance, so the intrathoracic trachea collapses inward, dynamically narrowing the lumen; the extrathoracic trachea, by contrast, tends to collapse on inspiration. This flow limitation impairs secretion clearance, promotes air trapping and turbulent flow, and predisposes to mucus retention and recurrent infection. Congenital disease reflects intrinsic cartilage immaturity or maldevelopment (often with associated foregut or vascular anomalies), whereas acquired disease reflects cartilage destruction or degeneration from pressure necrosis, chronic inflammation, or long-standing extrinsic compression. Congenital tracheomalacia frequently improves as the airway cartilage matures over the first one to two years of life, whereas acquired and syndromic forms tend to be persistent and may progress; severe or diffuse disease carries appreciable morbidity but can respond well to positive-pressure support or surgical stabilisation in selected patients.

Trachyonychia (twenty-nail dystrophy) — twenty-nail dystrophy, rough nails, sandpaper nails Nail lichen planus (with risk of scarring and pterygium in severe cases) Nail psoriasis Alopecia areata-associated nail changes Chronic eczema affecting the nail matrix Idiopathic twenty-nail dystrophy of childhood Nail changes of lichen striatus Clinical examination of all twenty nails and the hair and skin for associated disease Onychoscopy to characterise pitting, ridging, and surface changes Assessment for alopecia areata, lichen planus, and psoriasis elsewhere Nail matrix biopsy reserved for atypical, scarring, or diagnostically uncertain cases Mycology if fungal infection needs to be excluded Longitudinal review to monitor spontaneous improvement, especially in children Trachyonychia produces rough, brittle, longitudinally ridged nails with a sandpaper-like surface, often with a loss of lustre It may affect several or all twenty nails, hence the older term twenty-nail dystrophy, and is more common in children It is a reaction pattern of the nail matrix rather than a single disease, and is associated with alopecia areata, lichen planus, and psoriasis Two clinical forms are recognised: an opaque, rough sandpaper type and a shinier variety with numerous small superficial pits It is usually a benign, cosmetic problem that does not scar the nail, particularly in the idiopathic childhood form Diagnosis is generally clinical, and matrix biopsy is reserved for atypical cases because the appearance rarely predicts the underlying association Management is largely supportive with reassurance and nail protection, as many childhood cases improve spontaneously over years Features suggesting nail lichen planus with scarring, such as pterygium formation, which needs prompt attention Rapidly progressive or destructive nail change inconsistent with benign trachyonychia Associated systemic or extensive cutaneous disease requiring specific treatment Single-nail atypical change that does not fit the diffuse pattern and warrants biopsy Over-investigating a benign, self-limiting childhood presentation Missing scarring lichen planus of the nail, which requires earlier intervention Assuming a fungal cause and treating with antifungals without confirmation Promising rapid resolution when recovery is typically slow over months to years Trachyonychia reflects inflammation of the nail matrix that disturbs the orderly production of the nail plate, so that the emerging nail is irregular, rough, and ridged. The matrix inflammation is a shared final pathway for several conditions, including alopecia areata, lichen planus, psoriasis, and eczema, which is why the clinical appearance alone seldom identifies the cause. Because the inflammation usually affects the matrix without destroying it, the process is generally non-scarring and the nail can recover, although the widespread involvement of many nails reflects a diffuse matrix response. Trachyonychia is generally benign and non-scarring, and the idiopathic childhood form often resolves spontaneously over several years, although nails associated with lichen planus can occasionally scar and warrant closer follow-up.

Traction alopecia — marginal alopecia, hairstyle-induced hair loss, traumatic marginal alopecia Frontal fibrosing alopecia, with band-like frontotemporal recession, scarring and eyebrow loss Androgenetic alopecia Alopecia areata in an ophiasis pattern Trichotillomania Telogen effluvium Detailed hairstyling and cultural or occupational history Trichoscopy to assess hair casts, density and follicular ostia Recognition of marginal loss with a retained fringe sign Scalp biopsy where scarring or an alternative diagnosis such as frontal fibrosing alopecia is suspected Photographic documentation to monitor progression Hair loss caused by prolonged or repetitive tension on the hair from tight hairstyles such as braids, weaves, ponytails and buns, and from the use of extensions Classically affects the frontotemporal and marginal (hairline) scalp, producing a band of thinning with retention of a rim of fine hairs at the very margin, the useful fringe sign Early disease is non-scarring and reversible, but persistent traction eventually destroys follicles and leads to permanent scarring alopecia Hair casts, which are cylindrical concretions encircling the shaft, together with perifollicular erythema or pustules, indicate ongoing traction damage It is more common where cultural or occupational styling imposes chronic tension, and is also seen with tight religious head coverings and turbans Diagnosis is clinical from the pattern and history, and trichoscopy shows hair casts and reduced density with early preservation of ostia The key intervention is to release the tension and change styling early, before follicular loss becomes permanent Loss of follicular ostia indicating conversion to permanent scarring alopecia Perifollicular erythema and scaling suggesting a coexisting lymphocytic scarring alopecia such as frontal fibrosing alopecia Rapidly progressive marginal loss despite change of hairstyle Assuming marginal recession is always traction and missing frontal fibrosing alopecia, which also affects the hairline and eyebrows Failing to advise a change of hairstyle early, allowing reversible loss to become permanent Overlooking the fringe sign, a helpful clue to the diagnosis Not recognising that pustules may reflect secondary folliculitis rather than a primary infection Traction alopecia results from sustained mechanical tension transmitted to the hair follicle by tight hairstyling. Repeated pulling first produces perifollicular inflammation and extrusion of hairs, then, if traction continues over months to years, progressive follicular miniaturisation, atrophy and eventual fibrous replacement. Loss predominates at the margins where tension is greatest, and the process converts from a reversible non-scarring phase to an irreversible scarring one as follicular ostia are lost. If tension is relieved during the early inflammatory phase hair usually regrows, but longstanding traction causes irreversible scarring alopecia, so prevention through early modification of hairstyling is essential.

Transfusion-related acute lung injury — TRALI, transfusion-related acute lung injury Transfusion-associated circulatory overload (TACO) Acute respiratory distress syndrome from other causes Anaphylactic transfusion reaction Cardiogenic pulmonary oedema Bacterial contamination of a component with sepsis Chest radiograph or CT showing bilateral infiltrates Arterial blood gas or pulse oximetry to quantify hypoxaemia Natriuretic peptide levels and echocardiography to help exclude circulatory overload Investigation of implicated donors for anti-HLA and anti-neutrophil antibodies via the transfusion service Exclusion of infective and cardiac causes Presents as acute hypoxaemia and non-cardiogenic pulmonary oedema developing during or within about six hours of transfusion Bilateral pulmonary infiltrates appear on chest imaging without evidence of left atrial hypertension or fluid overload A key distinction from TACO is the absence of features of circulatory overload; jugular venous pressure and natriuretic peptides are typically not elevated Often mediated by donor anti-leukocyte (anti-HLA or anti-neutrophil) antibodies, so plasma-rich components from multiparous or previously transfused donors carry higher risk Historically a leading cause of transfusion-related mortality, which fell substantially after mitigation strategies such as using predominantly male-donor plasma Management is supportive with oxygen and lung-protective ventilation as needed; diuretics are unhelpful and the picture is one of capillary leak rather than volume excess Most patients improve within one to three days, distinguishing it from other causes of ARDS Acute severe hypoxaemia and respiratory distress during or shortly after transfusion requiring urgent oxygen and possible ventilatory support Rapid clinical deterioration necessitating critical care Diagnostic uncertainty with concurrent features of overload or sepsis Recurrence on re-exposure to a component from an implicated donor Misattributing the picture to fluid overload and giving diuretics, delaying appropriate supportive care Failing to stop the transfusion and report the reaction to the transfusion service Not investigating and deferring implicated donors, risking further cases Overlooking TRALI in ventilated critically ill patients where hypoxaemia is attributed solely to underlying illness TRALI reflects acute injury to the pulmonary capillary endothelium leading to increased permeability and protein-rich alveolar oedema. A widely used two-hit model proposes that a predisposing condition (such as sepsis, surgery, or inflammation) primes and sequesters neutrophils in the lung; a second hit from transfused antibodies against recipient leukocyte antigens, or from biologically active lipids and cytokines accumulated in stored components, then activates these neutrophils. The resulting release of reactive oxygen species and proteases damages the endothelium and produces non-cardiogenic pulmonary oedema. Most cases resolve within one to three days with supportive care and hypoxaemia improves, but severe episodes can be fatal; identification and deferral of implicated donors prevents further cases.

body-fluid sugar analysis for sedoheptulose and seven-carbon sugar derivatives Liver function tests, coagulation profile and full blood count Abdominal imaging to assess hepatosplenomegaly and hepatic architecture Renal and cardiac assessment for associated anomalies TALDO1 molecular genetic testing to confirm the diagnosis Autosomal recessive defect of transaldolase (TALDO1 gene) in the non-oxidative branch of the pentose phosphate pathway, leading to accumulation of polyols and seven-carbon sugars Often presents in the neonatal or antenatal period with hepatosplenomegaly, liver dysfunction, coagulopathy and thrombocytopenia, sometimes with hydrops A multisystem disorder that can include dysmorphic features, cutis laxa or skin changes, cardiac and renal anomalies, and anaemia Urine polyol analysis shows elevated erythritol, arabitol and ribitol, and characteristic seven-carbon sugars such as sedoheptulose and its derivatives Progressive liver disease with fibrosis or cirrhosis is a major feature, and hepatocellular carcinoma has been reported There is no specific enzyme-replacement therapy, so management is supportive with monitoring of hepatic, renal, haematological and cardiac function, and antioxidant approaches have been explored Diagnosis relies on the urinary polyol/sugar pattern with confirmatory TALDO1 molecular testing Neonatal liver failure with coagulopathy or bleeding Hydrops fetalis or severe antenatal hepatosplenomegaly Progressive hepatic fibrosis or signs suggesting hepatocellular carcinoma Multisystem deterioration with cardiac or renal failure Overlooking transaldolase deficiency in neonatal liver failure by not requesting urinary polyol analysis Attributing hepatosplenomegaly and cytopenias solely to congenital infection Failing to monitor for evolving hepatic fibrosis and hepatocellular carcinoma over time Missing associated renal, cardiac or dysmorphic features that point to a multisystem metabolic disorder Transaldolase catalyses a reversible step in the non-oxidative branch of the pentose phosphate pathway that interconverts sugar phosphates and links the pathway with glycolysis. Its deficiency disrupts the balance of pentose phosphate intermediates, causing accumulation of polyols (such as erythritol, arabitol and ribitol) and seven-carbon sugars (including sedoheptulose). The disturbed pathway is thought to increase oxidative stress and impair regeneration of reducing equivalents, contributing to progressive injury of the liver, kidneys, heart and blood cells. The result is a multisystem disorder dominated by hepatosplenomegaly, hepatic fibrosis, coagulopathy and cytopenias, often evident from birth. The disorder is variable but often serious, with progressive liver disease, coagulopathy and multisystem involvement; some individuals survive into later childhood or adulthood while others succumb to neonatal liver failure or complications such as hepatocellular carcinoma.

deficiency and other causes of B12 malabsorption Inherited disorders of intracellular cobalamin metabolism (cblC, cblE, cblG and related) Imerslund-Grasbeck syndrome Folate metabolism disorders infancy with failure to thrive, vomiting, weakness, pancytopenia or megaloblastic anaemia and an evolving encephalopathy Autosomal recessive disorder caused by biallelic pathogenic variants in TCN2, B12 (usually hydroxocobalamin or cyanocobalamin) to overcome the transport defect and maintain intracellular cobalamin Untreated or late-treated disease leads to irreversible neurological injury and immune dysfunction with recurrent infection Absolute transcobalamin level or its saturation, and molecular testing, confirm the diagnosis Distinguish from inherited intracellular cobalamin metabolism severe infections from immune dysfunction Failure to thrive with persistent vomiting Excluding B12 deficiency because total serum B12 is normal Under-dosing or spacing parenteral B12 too widely to keep intracellular cobalamin adequate Confusing it with intracellular cobalamin metabolism disorders that need additional therapy Missing associated immunodeficiency and its infection risk Transcobalamin is the transport protein that binds newly absorbed vitamin B12 and delivers it to cells via receptor-mediated endocytosis. In transcobalamin deficiency, biallelic TCN2 variants abolish functional transcobalamin, so although B12 is absorbed and present in plasma bound to haptocorrin, it cannot enter tissues. The resulting intracellular cobalamin deficiency impairs the two B12-dependent reactions, methionine synthase and methylmalonyl-CoA mutase, causing accumulation of homocysteine and methylmalonic acid. This disrupts DNA synthesis in rapidly dividing cells (producing megaloblastic anaemia and immune deficiency) and impairs myelin and neuronal metabolism, giving a progressive neurological picture. High-dose parenteral B12 raises free cobalamin sufficiently to enter cells by alternative means and reverse the deficiency. With early diagnosis and adequate parenteral B12 the haematological and immune features resolve and neurological outcome is good, but delayed treatment risks permanent neurodevelopmental damage.

from decompensated heart failure Acute respiratory distress syndrome Anaphylactic transfusion reaction Pulmonary embolism Pneumonia or aspiration Chest imaging showing pulmonary oedema, cardiomegaly and upper-lobe blood diversion Natriuretic peptide levels, typically raised, to support a cardiogenic mechanism Assessment of fluid balance and jugular venous pressure Echocardiography to evaluate ventricular function and filling pressures Arterial blood gas or oximetry to quantify hypoxaemia Renal function to gauge fluid-handling capacity Presents as acute dyspnoea, hypoxaemia, hypertension and features of cardiogenic pulmonary oedema during or shortly after transfusion It is essentially hydrostatic pulmonary oedema caused by an inability to accommodate the transfused volume Raised jugular venous pressure and a positive fluid balance help distinguish it from lung injury Natriuretic peptide levels are typically elevated, reflecting cardiac strain, in contrast to acute lung injury Risk is greatest in the elderly, in small patients, and in those with cardiac or renal impairment Management is to stop or slow the transfusion, sit the patient upright, give oxygen and administer diuretics It responds to diuresis, which is the key clinical distinction from transfusion-related acute lung injury Prevention rests on slow transfusion rates, single-unit prescribing and consideration of prophylactic diuretics in at-risk patients Acute breathlessness with hypertension and raised jugular venous pressure during transfusion Rapidly progressive hypoxaemia in an elderly or fluid-overloaded patient Frank pulmonary oedema requiring urgent oxygen and diuresis Failure to improve with diuretics, prompting reconsideration of lung injury Confusing it with transfusion-related acute lung injury and withholding the diuretics that would help Transfusing at excessive rates or in multiple units where a single unit would suffice Overlooking the elderly and small patients who are most vulnerable to volume overload Ignoring a raised natriuretic peptide and pre-existing cardiac history when assessing dyspnoea Transfusion-associated circulatory overload results from the intravascular volume of a transfusion exceeding what the circulation can accommodate. In patients with limited cardiac reserve or impaired renal handling of fluid, the added volume raises left atrial and pulmonary capillary hydrostatic pressure, forcing fluid across an intact alveolar-capillary membrane into the alveoli. The oedema is therefore hydrostatic and cardiogenic in nature, accompanied by raised filling pressures and cardiac strain that elevate natriuretic peptides. Rapid infusion rates, large volumes and pre-existing cardiac or renal disease are the principal contributors, and because the mechanism is volume-related the process reverses with diuresis and reduction of the circulating load. Recognised promptly and treated with diuresis and respiratory support, most patients recover quickly, but it is a common and under-recognised cause of transfusion-related morbidity and death, particularly in frail patients with cardiac disease.

Transfusion-associated graft-versus-host disease — TA-GvHD, Transfusion-associated GvHD Drug reaction with eosinophilia and systemic symptoms or other drug eruption Viral infection such as cytomegalovirus with marrow suppression Sepsis with multi-organ dysfunction Chemotherapy or radiotherapy toxicity Graft-versus-host disease after haematopoietic stem-cell transplantation Autoimmune or paraneoplastic marrow failure Skin biopsy showing basal vacuolar change, dyskeratosis and lymphocytic infiltrate Bone marrow examination demonstrating hypoplasia or aplasia HLA typing and chimerism studies to detect donor lymphocytes in recipient blood or tissue Full blood count tracking progressive pancytopenia Liver function tests documenting cholestatic derangement Review of transfusion history for non-irradiated cellular components in an at-risk recipient A rare but almost uniformly fatal complication caused by viable donor T lymphocytes engrafting and attacking recipient tissues. Occurs when the recipient cannot reject donor lymphocytes, either through immunosuppression or when the donor is homozygous for an HLA haplotype the recipient carries, as in directed donations from relatives. Typically presents one to six weeks after transfusion with fever, a maculopapular rash, diarrhoea, deranged liver function and progressive pancytopenia. The defining and lethal feature is marrow aplasia, distinguishing it from graft-versus-host disease after stem-cell transplantation where the graft marrow is spared. Gamma or X-ray irradiation of cellular components to inactivate donor lymphocytes is the mainstay of prevention; leucoreduction alone is insufficient. At-risk groups include recipients of directed donations from first-degree relatives, HLA-matched platelets, intrauterine or neonatal exchange transfusions, and the severely immunocompromised. Diagnosis is supported by skin biopsy and by demonstrating donor-derived lymphocytes or chimerism in the recipient. Established disease responds poorly to immunosuppression, underscoring that prevention is essential. Progressive pancytopenia developing one to six weeks after transfusion Fever with rash, diarrhoea and deranged liver function in an at-risk recipient Transfusion of non-irradiated components to a severely immunocompromised patient Receipt of a directed donation from a blood relative Marrow aplasia without an alternative explanation Assuming leucoreduction alone prevents the disease when irradiation is required. Failing to identify at-risk recipients who require irradiated components. Overlooking the danger of directed donations from first-degree relatives. Attributing the rash, diarrhoea and cytopenia to drugs or infection and delaying diagnosis. Expecting immunosuppressive treatment to reverse established disease. Transfusion-associated graft-versus-host disease results from immunocompetent donor T lymphocytes that are transfused within a cellular blood component and are not eliminated by the recipient's immune system. These viable donor lymphocytes recognise recipient HLA antigens as foreign, proliferate and mount a cytotoxic attack against host tissues bearing those antigens, principally skin, gut, liver and, critically, the bone marrow. Engraftment is favoured either by profound recipient immunosuppression or by a one-way HLA match, in which the donor is homozygous for an HLA haplotype shared with the recipient so that the recipient does not perceive the donor cells as foreign while the donor cells still attack the recipient. The consequent immune destruction of the marrow produces intractable aplasia and overwhelming infection. The condition is almost always fatal, usually within weeks, from marrow failure with overwhelming infection and bleeding, because established disease responds poorly to treatment. This dismal outlook makes irradiation of at-risk cellular components the essential intervention.

leukoreduction alone is insufficient Diagnosis is supported by skin biopsy and by demonstrating donor-derived lymphocytes or chimerism in the recipient Established disease responds poorly to immunosuppression, so prevention through irradiation of at-risk transfusions is paramount Fever, rash, diarrhoea, and falling blood counts within weeks of transfusion in an at-risk patient Progressive pancytopenia signalling marrow aplasia Any cellular transfusion given without irradiation to a severely immunocompromised recipient or from a first-degree relative Rapid multi-organ deterioration requiring urgent haematology involvement Failing to irradiate cellular components for immunocompromised recipients or directed family donations Assuming leukoreduction alone prevents the disease Attributing the rash, diarrhoea, and cytopenias to drugs or infection and delaying recognition Not flagging patients who require lifelong irradiated components in their transfusion records TA-GVHD occurs when immunologically competent donor T lymphocytes contained in a cellular blood component are not eliminated by the recipient's immune system and instead engraft, proliferate, and mount an immune attack against host tissues bearing foreign HLA antigens. This happens when the recipient is profoundly immunosuppressed or when the donor is homozygous for an HLA haplotype shared with the recipient, so the recipient fails to recognise the donor cells as foreign. The activated donor lymphocytes target skin, gut, liver, and bone marrow, with marrow involvement producing the aplasia that drives the high mortality. The prognosis is extremely poor once established, with mortality generally exceeding ninety per cent largely from marrow aplasia and infection; the emphasis therefore lies entirely on prevention by irradiating cellular components for at-risk patients.

Transfusion-associated hyperkalaemia — Transfusion hyperkalaemia, Hyperkalaemic cardiac arrest of transfusion Hyperkalaemia from renal failure Hyperkalaemia from tissue injury, rhabdomyolysis or tumour lysis Citrate toxicity causing hypocalcaemic arrhythmia Acute haemolytic transfusion reaction releasing intracellular potassium Acidosis-driven potassium shift Drug-induced hyperkalaemia Serum or point-of-care potassium during rapid or large-volume transfusion Electrocardiogram for peaked T waves and QRS widening Ionised calcium given the interplay with citrate Arterial blood gas for acidosis and potassium Renal function tests Review of red-cell storage age and irradiation status in at-risk recipients Potassium leaks from stored red cells into the supernatant over time, so older units carry a higher extracellular potassium load. Clinically important hyperkalaemia is most likely with rapid, large-volume transfusion through central lines, and in neonatal and paediatric large-volume or exchange transfusion. Irradiation of red cells accelerates potassium leakage, so irradiated units are best transfused promptly and within a shortened shelf life. The feared outcome is transfusion-associated hyperkalaemic cardiac arrest, particularly in small infants during rapid infusion. Risk is compounded by renal impairment, acidosis, hypocalcaemia and hypothermia which impair potassium handling and cardiac stability. Electrocardiographic changes progress from peaked T waves to widened QRS and sine-wave patterns before arrest. Preventive measures include using fresher or washed red cells for at-risk recipients and controlling infusion rate and line position. Emergency management follows standard hyperkalaemia treatment with cardiac membrane stabilisation and measures to shift and remove potassium. Peaked T waves or widening QRS during transfusion Bradycardia or cardiac arrest during rapid transfusion in an infant Rapid central infusion of old or irradiated red cells Hyperkalaemia in a recipient with renal impairment or acidosis Large-volume or exchange transfusion in a neonate Using the oldest or freshly irradiated units for rapid large-volume paediatric transfusion. Assuming a normal baseline potassium removes the risk during rapid infusion. Overlooking the additive risks of acidosis, hypocalcaemia and hypothermia. Failing to monitor the electrocardiogram and potassium during high-risk transfusion. Confusing hyperkalaemic changes with citrate-induced hypocalcaemic arrhythmia. During refrigerated storage, red cells progressively lose intracellular potassium because the energy-dependent sodium-potassium membrane pump is inactive at cold temperatures, so potassium accumulates in the unit's supernatant, increasing with storage age and after irradiation, which damages the membrane. When such units are transfused slowly the load is trivial, but rapid infusion of large volumes, especially directly into the central circulation, can deliver a potassium bolus faster than it can be redistributed or excreted. Neonates and infants are especially vulnerable because of their small blood volume and the relatively large transfused volumes used in exchange and massive transfusion. Superimposed renal impairment, acidosis, hypocalcaemia and hypothermia reduce potassium tolerance and myocardial stability, and the resulting acute hyperkalaemia can cause conduction disturbance and cardiac arrest. When anticipated and prevented by choice of fresher or washed cells and controlled infusion, the risk is low; however, transfusion-associated hyperkalaemic cardiac arrest, though rare, has a high mortality, particularly in infants. Prompt recognition and standard hyperkalaemia management are life-saving.

alloantibody screen and crossmatch Bacterial culture of the component and recipient before starting broad-spectrum antibiotics when bacterial contamination suspected Chest x-ray (bilateral interstitial infiltrates in TRALI; predominantly alveolar infiltrates in TACO) and brain natriuretic peptide (elevated in TACO) Serum ferritin, MRI and liver biopsy to assess iron overload in frequently transfused patients Test for IgA deficiency in patients with anaphylactic or repeated allergic reactions TRALI may be difficult to distinguish from other causes of hypoxia, particularly circulatory overload (TACO) G6PD/enzymatic RBC defects and underlying haemolytic conditions exacerbated by transfusion can mimic immune-mediated haemolytic transfusion reaction Hyperhaemolysis in sickle cell disease can mimic and be exacerbated by transfusion Acute immune-mediated haemolytic reactions occur when recipient preformed antibodies lyse transfused donor RBCs, during or up to 24 h after transfusion; anti-A/anti-B antibodies cause most of the most severe (potentially fatal) reactions, though alloantibodies against Rh, Kell, and Duffy antigens can also cause severe haemolysis (Harrison 22e p.906). The most dramatic acute haemolytic reactions are usually caused by a failure in product or patient identification, erroneous blood grouping, or unidentified recipient anti-RBC alloimmunisation - i.e. a clerical/identification error (Harrison 22e p.906). Acute haemolytic reactions may present with hypotension, tachypnoea, tachycardia, fever (rise of 1-2 degrees C), chills, chest and back/flank pain, haemoglobinuria, and haemoglobinemia; in the most severe cases DIC, acute renal failure, shock, and death may occur (Harrison 22e p.906). RED FLAG: when an adverse reaction is suspected the transfusion must be STOPPED, the recipient's clinical status assessed, and supportive care initiated; a thorough clerical check is crucial to prevent a possible second misidentified transfusion (Harrison 22e p.908). Management of acute immune haemolytic reaction is mainly supportive: prompt interruption of transfusion, biological workup, vigorous isotonic saline hydration with diuretics to maintain urine output; may require forced alkaline diuresis, electrolyte correction, and pressor support, and in DIC with bleeding, platelet/plasma/cryoprecipitate or fibrinogen (Harrison 22e p.908). Diagnosis of transfusion-associated haemolysis relies on persistent/worsening anaemia, depleted haptoglobin, haemoglobinemia and haemoglobinuria, and elevated LDH and unconjugated bilirubin; the direct antiglobulin test (DAT/direct Coombs) is most often positive, as is the indirect antiglobulin test (IAT) (Harrison 22e p.908). Delayed haemolytic reactions present with icterus and persisting or worsening anaemia and result from an anamnestic response in previously sensitised patients who had a negative alloantibody screen at transfusion (low antibody levels); the alloantibody becomes detectable 1-2 weeks after transfusion (Harrison 22e p.906). FNHTR (febrile non-haemolytic transfusion reaction) is the most frequent reaction to cellular components (up to 300 per 100,000), characterised by chills, rigors and a rise of at least 1 degree C, caused by proinflammatory cytokines in the component or recipient antibodies against donor antigens; it is a diagnosis of exclusion once infection and haemolysis are ruled out (Harrison 22e p.911). Leukocyte reduction (especially prestorage) can prevent FNHTR; premedication with antipyretics has generally proven ineffective and may mask relevant clinical symptoms (Harrison 22e p.911). Most allergic transfusion reactions are mild (rash, pruritus, urticaria, localised oedema) and relate to plasma proteins; rarely they are severe/anaphylactic with bronchospasm, respiratory distress, hypotension, nausea, vomiting and shock - anaphylaxis can occur after only a few millilitres of component (Harrison 22e p.911). TRALI is characterised by occurrence or worsening of hypoxia and NONcardiogenic pulmonary oedema with bilateral interstitial infiltrates on chest x-ray during or within 6 h of transfusion (delayed cases up to 72 h); it is among the most common causes of transfusion-related fatalities and treatment is supportive only (Harrison 22e p.911). TRALI usually results from donor plasma containing high-titre anti-HLA class II antibodies binding recipient cognate antigen (anti-HLA class I and anti-HNA antibodies may also be involved); a cytokine/chemokine-mediated mechanism without HLA interaction can also occur (Harrison 22e p.911). TACO (transfusion-associated circulatory overload) is common and underrecognised and is now the main cause of transfusion-related death since TRALI risk was mitigated; it presents with dyspnoea, hypoxia, bilateral and predominantly ALVEOLAR infiltrates on chest x-ray, frequent systolic hypertension, and elevated BNP (fever may also occur) (Harrison 22e p.912). TRALI vs TACO distinction: TRALI gives noncardiogenic oedema with predominantly interstitial infiltrates within 6 h, whereas TACO is volume overload with predominantly alveolar infiltrates (within 12 h), systolic hypertension and elevated BNP; TACO risk factors include older age, renal failure, preexisting fluid overload, cardiac dysfunction, large transfusion volume and excessive transfusion rate (Harrison 22e p.911-912). Transfusion-related GVHD is extremely rare but fatal in over 90% of cases; mediated by engrafted donor T lymphocytes in a recipient unable to reject them, it presents 5-10 days post-transfusion with cytopenia, fever, characteristic skin rash, diarrhoea and liver function abnormalities, and is prevented by irradiation (minimum 25 Gy) of cellular components in at-risk patients (Harrison 22e p.911). Transfusion-transmitted bacterial infection remains a significant concern, notably with platelet concentrates stored at room temperature; some gram-negatives such as Yersinia grow at 4 degrees C and can contaminate RBC units - recipients may develop abrupt fever and chills deteriorating to septic shock, DIC and death, and after culture sampling broad-spectrum antibiotics should be started promptly (Harrison 22e p.913). Iron overload: each RBC concentrate contains 200-250 mg of iron; in frequently transfused recipients untreated accumulation impairs endocrine, hepatic and cardiac function (death may occur from cardiac failure or arrhythmia), assessed by serum ferritin, MRI and liver biopsy, and prevented/treated by monitoring and iron chelation (Harrison 22e p.912). Acute hypotensive transfusion reactions are an abrupt drop in systolic blood pressure of more than 30 mmHg early after starting transfusion that resolves once transfusion is stopped; they are more likely in patients taking ACE inhibitors (impaired bradykinin metabolism) and the same product should NOT be restarted (Harrison 22e p.912). STOP the transfusion immediately when any adverse reaction is suspected Fever, flank/back pain and haemoglobinuria suggesting acute haemolytic (ABO-incompatible) reaction - perform an urgent clerical/identification check to prevent a second misidentified transfusion Hypotension (systolic drop of at least 30 mmHg) - haemolytic, anaphylactic or septic shock Dyspnoea within 6 h (TRALI) or within 12 h (TACO) of transfusion Temperature rise over 2 degrees C - favours transfusion-transmitted bacterial infection or haemolysis Rash over two-thirds of body within 5 minutes with dyspnoea and shock - anaphylaxis Development of DIC, acute renal failure or shock during/after transfusion Premedication with antipyretics for FNHTR is generally ineffective and may mask relevant clinical warning symptoms FNHTR must not be diagnosed until infection and haemolysis are excluded Failing to perform a clerical/identification check risks a second misidentified (incompatible) transfusion TRALI and TACO are easily confused; both cause hypoxia and bilateral infiltrates - TACO is now the leading cause of transfusion death and is underrecognised In acute hypotensive reactions the same blood product should not be restarted; consider switching ACE inhibitor for patients needing further transfusion Delayed haemolytic reactions occur despite a negative pretransfusion alloantibody screen (low antibody levels) - icterus and worsening anaemia 1-2 weeks later Iron overload is frequently underreported in chronically transfused patients Further RBC transfusion in hyperhaemolytic reaction (sickle cell disease) typically exacerbates ongoing haemolysis Adverse reactions to blood components arise via immune or nonimmune mechanisms. Immune-mediated acute haemolysis occurs when recipient preformed antibodies (anti-A/anti-B IgM/IgG, or alloantibodies to Rh, Kell, Duffy) lyse transfused donor RBCs, with complement activation; ABO incompatibility classically results from clerical/identification error. Delayed haemolysis reflects an anamnestic alloantibody response (neoformed allogeneic IgG, C3b-mediated opsonisation and ADCC-mediated phagocytosis) detectable 1-2 weeks later. FNHTR is driven by proinflammatory cytokines accumulated in the component or recipient antibodies against donor leukocyte antigens. Allergic/anaphylactic reactions relate to plasma proteins and soluble mediators triggering histamine/serotonin release (IgA-deficient recipients may react to IgA). TRALI results from donor anti-HLA (class II, also class I) or anti-HNA antibodies binding recipient antigen, or cytokine/chemokine priming, causing neutrophil aggregation in pulmonary vasculature and release of inflammatory mediators producing noncardiogenic pulmonary oedema. TACO is hydrostatic circulatory overload from excessive volume/rate relative to cardiac/renal reserve. Transfusion-associated GVHD is mediated by engrafted donor T lymphocytes attacking host HLA antigens. (Harrison 22e p.906-912) Most adverse reactions are non-life-threatening, though serious reactions can present with mild symptoms. An average of ~37 transfusion-associated fatalities (possible-to-definite imputability) were reported yearly to the FDA between 2017-2021 among ~15 million transfused components, with leading causes of death being TACO (32%), TRALI (21%), haemolysis (21%) and microbial contamination (13%). Acute haemolysis is often self-limiting but can be fatal (DIC, acute renal failure, shock). Transfusion-associated GVHD is fatal in over 90% of cases and highly resistant to treatment. (Harrison 22e p.906-911) Warning-sign based recognition of transfusion adverse reactions (Harrison Table 118-5): fever of at least 38 degrees C (rise of 1-2 degrees C within 4 h favours FNHTR or TRALI; rise over 2 degrees C favours bacterial infection/haemolysis); hypotension (systolic drop of at least 30 mmHg) suggesting haemolytic, anaphylactic or septic shock; dyspnoea (TRALI within 6 h, TACO within 12 h, severe allergy within 4 h); haemoglobinuria (intravascular haemolysis); rash (minor allergy if under two-thirds body, severe if over two-thirds, anaphylaxis if with dyspnoea/shock within 5 min); icterus (delayed haemolysis); rash/diarrhoea/fever 2 days-6 weeks (GVHD); gum bleeding/purpura 5-12 days (posttransfusion purpura). Reactions are also categorised as immune-mediated vs nonimmunologic, and by timing (acute vs delayed). (Harrison 22e p.908)

circulatory overload and treating with diuretics that do not help Attributing the hypoxaemia solely to the underlying illness and missing the transfusion trigger Failing to report the reaction, so implicated donors are not investigated Assuming a normal natriuretic peptide excludes any transfusion reaction Transfusion-related acute lung injury is an acute inflammatory injury of the pulmonary capillary endothelium. In the antibody-mediated form, donor anti-leucocyte antibodies bind recipient neutrophil or human leucocyte antigens, activating neutrophils that are already sequestered in the pulmonary microvasculature. A widely used two-hit model holds that an initial insult such as sepsis or surgery primes and sequesters neutrophils, after which the transfused antibody or accumulated biological response modifiers provides the second hit. The resulting neutrophil activation damages the endothelium, increasing permeability so that protein-rich fluid floods the alveoli. Because the mechanism is inflammatory rather than hydrostatic, cardiac filling pressures remain normal. Most patients improve within a few days with supportive respiratory care and the pulmonary infiltrates resolve, but severe cases requiring mechanical ventilation carry appreciable mortality and it remains a leading cause of transfusion-related death.

Transfusion-related immunomodulation — TRIM, Transfusion-associated immunomodulation Postoperative infection from surgical or patient-related factors Immunosuppression from underlying malignancy or its treatment Confounding by indication where sicker patients receive more blood Nutritional or metabolic causes of impaired immunity Hospital-acquired infection unrelated to transfusion Cancer recurrence driven by tumour biology rather than transfusion Review of transfusion exposure including number of units and leucoreduction status Assessment of cytokine and lymphocyte-subset changes in research settings Natural-killer-cell activity assays in study contexts Audit of postoperative infection rates against transfusion exposure Correlation with red-cell storage age where data are available Multivariable analysis to adjust for confounding by indication Refers to the immunosuppressive and pro-inflammatory effects of allogeneic transfusion rather than an acute clinical reaction. First recognised through improved renal allograft survival in patients transfused before transplantation, an observation that led to the concept. Proposed adverse associations include increased postoperative infection and possibly cancer recurrence, though causation remains debated and confounded by the reasons for transfusion. Donor leucocytes and their soluble products are considered central mediators, providing the rationale for universal leucoreduction. Effects are thought to involve shifts in the balance of regulatory and effector T cells, altered cytokine profiles and suppression of natural-killer-cell and macrophage function. Older or non-leucoreduced red cells and the storage lesion may amplify the immunomodulatory effect. The strongest practical implication is support for restrictive transfusion thresholds and blood conservation strategies. It is a chronic, epidemiological phenomenon and should not be confused with acute transfusion reactions. Rising postoperative infection rates linked to liberal transfusion practice Use of non-leucoreduced components where leucoreduction is standard Unnecessary transfusion above evidence-based thresholds Failure to apply blood conservation in surgery with high transfusion demand Repeated allogeneic exposure in patients with malignancy where recurrence is a concern Treating transfusion-related immunomodulation as an acute reaction with immediate symptoms. Overstating causation given substantial confounding by indication. Ignoring the case for restrictive transfusion thresholds and blood conservation. Assuming leucoreduction abolishes all immunomodulatory effects. Neglecting other explanations for postoperative infection or cancer recurrence. Transfusion-related immunomodulation describes durable alterations in recipient immunity following exposure to allogeneic blood. Several mechanisms are proposed and probably act together. Transfused donor leucocytes present alloantigen and, in the absence of appropriate costimulation, may induce clonal deletion or anergy and expand regulatory T-cell populations, biasing the recipient toward tolerance and immunosuppression. Soluble mediators accumulating during storage, including cytokines, soluble HLA molecules and bioactive lipids, further modulate antigen-presenting-cell and natural-killer-cell function and shift the cytokine balance away from a T-helper-1 pattern. The net effect is downregulation of cell-mediated immunity, which may explain both the beneficial tolerance seen in transplantation and the postulated harms of increased infection and tumour recurrence. As a chronic epidemiological effect rather than an acute event, the clinical impact varies and remains contested; the pragmatic response is to minimise unnecessary allogeneic exposure through restrictive thresholds and leucoreduction. Definitive causal attribution of individual outcomes is generally not possible.
