monitoring is central to surveillance New heart failure or arrhythmia suggesting cardiac iron loading Rising ferritin despite chelation indicating inadequate iron control Deranged liver function or signs of cirrhosis Emerging diabetes or hypogonadism from endocrine iron deposition Delaying chelation until organ damage is already established Relying on ferritin alone without imaging to assess cardiac and hepatic iron Underestimating cardiac risk, which is the principal cause of mortality Poor adherence to chelation going unrecognised during follow-up Each unit of transfused red cells delivers a substantial quantity of iron, and because humans lack a regulated pathway for iron excretion, repeated transfusion inexorably expands total body iron. Once transferrin becomes saturated, non-transferrin-bound iron appears in plasma and is taken up by parenchymal cells, where it catalyses the generation of reactive oxygen species. This oxidative injury damages the myocardium, hepatocytes and endocrine tissue, leading over time to cardiomyopathy and arrhythmia, hepatic fibrosis and cirrhosis, and endocrine failure including diabetes and hypogonadism. Coexisting ineffective erythropoiesis in some underlying disorders suppresses hepcidin and further increases dietary iron absorption, compounding the transfusional load. With effective chelation and monitoring, organ damage can be prevented or partly reversed and survival is greatly improved, but poor adherence or late intervention leads to progressive cardiac and hepatic disease and premature death.

transient neonatal pustular melanosis — transient neonatal pustulosis, TNPM erythema toxicum neonatorum neonatal herpes simplex infection bullous impetigo or staphylococcal pustulosis congenital or neonatal candidiasis infantile acropustulosis miliaria incontinentia pigmenti (vesicular stage) Wright or Giemsa stain of pustule contents showing predominant neutrophils Gram stain and bacterial culture to exclude staphylococcal infection viral swabs and PCR for herpes simplex if vesicular and clinically suspected potassium hydroxide preparation to exclude candidal pustulosis septic screen if the neonate is systemically unwell skin biopsy only in atypical or uncertain cases clinical follow-up to confirm expected fading of pigmented macules A benign self-limiting neonatal eruption that, unlike erythema toxicum, is typically present at birth and lacks a surrounding erythematous flare. It evolves through three overlapping stages: fragile superficial pustules, then a collarette of fine scale, then residual hyperpigmented macules. The pigmented macules can persist for weeks to months and are frequently the only finding by the time the infant is examined. Unlike erythema toxicum, it commonly involves the palms, soles, chin, forehead, neck and lower back, and shows no age or maturity predilection. It is disproportionately common in infants with darker, more heavily pigmented skin. Pustule cytology shows a predominance of neutrophils, in contrast to the eosinophil-rich smear of erythema toxicum neonatorum. Diagnosis is clinical in a well infant; the pustules are sterile and no treatment is required beyond parental reassurance. The residual hyperpigmentation represents postinflammatory change and fades completely without intervention. an unwell, febrile or poorly feeding neonate, which is incompatible with this benign diagnosis grouped vesicles suggesting neonatal herpes simplex infection positive Gram stain or bacterial culture of pustule contents linear or blaschkoid vesicular lesions suggesting incontinentia pigmenti progressive or atypical eruption not following the expected pustule-scale-macule sequence confusing residual hyperpigmented macules with a pathological pigmentary disorder or bruising mislabelling the sterile pustules as bacterial infection and treating unnecessarily failing to distinguish it from erythema toxicum, which is not usually present at birth and is eosinophil-predominant overlooking neonatal herpes simplex in a vesicular eruption over-investigating a well infant with classic features Transient neonatal pustular melanosis is a benign, idiopathic neonatal pustular dermatosis. The early pustule is a sterile, subcorneal or intracorneal collection of neutrophils, occasionally with a few eosinophils, without evidence of infection or follicular targeting in the way erythema toxicum shows. As the fragile pustule ruptures, a fine collarette of scale remains, and localised postinflammatory increase in epidermal melanin produces the characteristic hyperpigmented macule. The cause of the initial sterile neutrophilic pustulation is unknown, and it is regarded as a transient reactive phenomenon of newborn skin. The prominence of residual pigmentation in more darkly pigmented infants reflects their greater melanocyte activity and readiness to develop postinflammatory hyperpigmentation. The prognosis is excellent; the pustular and scaling phases resolve within days and the residual hyperpigmented macules fade completely over several weeks to a few months without treatment or scarring.

Transient osteoporosis of the hip — transient osteoporosis, transient bone marrow oedema of the hip Avascular necrosis of the femoral head Septic arthritis or osteomyelitis Subchondral insufficiency fracture Inflammatory arthritis Complex regional pain syndrome MRI showing bone marrow oedema without necrosis Radiographs (osteopenia appears later) Inflammatory markers to exclude infection Assessment for pregnancy and osteoporosis risk factors Follow-up imaging to confirm resolution A self-limiting cause of hip pain characterised by transient bone marrow oedema and reversible osteopenia Classically affects middle-aged men and women in the third trimester of pregnancy Presents with progressive hip pain and limp without preceding trauma Radiographs show osteopenia of the femoral head after some weeks, while MRI shows marrow oedema without the necrosis of avascular necrosis It is considered part of the bone marrow oedema syndrome spectrum and is a key differential of early avascular necrosis It resolves spontaneously over months with protected weight bearing and analgesia Features suggesting septic arthritis or osteomyelitis Imaging evidence of established avascular necrosis or subchondral collapse A subchondral fracture line Failure to resolve as expected Mistaking it for avascular necrosis and intervening unnecessarily Missing a subchondral insufficiency fracture Overlooking infection when there are systemic features Failing to protect the hip, risking fracture during the osteopenic phase Transient osteoporosis of the hip is characterised by self-limiting bone marrow oedema of the femoral head and neck with associated localised, reversible bone loss. The cause is uncertain; proposed mechanisms include transient ischaemia, altered local blood flow or a neurovascular response, and in pregnancy mechanical and hormonal factors may contribute. Unlike avascular necrosis, there is no established osteonecrosis, and the oedema and osteopenia resolve completely, distinguishing it on MRI and by its benign natural history. The condition is benign and self-limiting, typically resolving over six to twelve months with conservative management and no long-term sequelae.

transient synovitis hip — Irritable hip, Toxic synovitis Septic arthritis of the hip Osteomyelitis of the proximal femur or pelvis Legg-Calve-Perthes disease Slipped capital femoral epiphysis, particularly in older or heavier children Juvenile idiopathic arthritis Reactive or post-streptococcal arthritis and acute rheumatic fever Occult trauma or malignancy such as leukaemia presenting with bone or joint pain Hip ultrasound to detect and quantify effusion and to guide aspiration where needed CRP, ESR and full blood count Blood cultures where infection is suspected Plain radiographs of the pelvis and hips, including anteroposterior and frog-lateral views, to exclude Perthes, slipped epiphysis and fracture Joint aspiration with Gram stain, culture and cell count when septic arthritis cannot be excluded MRI where osteomyelitis, Perthes disease or occult pathology is considered Peripheral blood film and further haematological work-up if atypical or systemic features are present Transient synovitis is the commonest cause of acute atraumatic hip pain and limp in young children, typically affecting the pre-school and early school-age group, and is more common in boys. A preceding or concurrent viral upper respiratory tract illness is frequently reported, supporting a post-infectious reactive aetiology. Affected children are usually well or only mildly unwell, afebrile or with low-grade temperature, and tend to limp or remain weight-bearing rather than refuse to move the limb entirely. The hip is characteristically held flexed, abducted and externally rotated, with pain and guarding most marked at the extremes of internal rotation. The central clinical task is to distinguish it from septic arthritis; validated prediction rules combining weight-bearing status, fever and inflammatory markers help stratify risk. Inflammatory markers and the white cell count are normal or only mildly raised, in contrast to the marked elevation typical of septic arthritis. Ultrasound commonly demonstrates a hip joint effusion but cannot reliably differentiate a sterile from an infected collection. It remains a diagnosis of exclusion; management is supportive with rest and simple analgesia or anti-inflammatory agents, with planned review to confirm resolution. Inability to bear weight combined with fever and markedly raised inflammatory markers, suggesting septic arthritis Systemic toxicity, rigors or a rapidly deteriorating child Night pain, weight loss, bruising or pallor suggesting malignancy Symptoms failing to settle within the expected short timeframe Migratory or multi-joint involvement Misdiagnosing early septic arthritis as transient synovitis and delaying intervention Relying on ultrasound to differentiate a sterile from a septic effusion Missing Perthes disease or a slipped epiphysis on inadequate radiographs that omit frog-lateral views Failing to safety-net and arrange review for non-resolving symptoms Overlooking leukaemia presenting as bone or joint pain Transient synovitis is a self-limiting, non-pyogenic inflammation of the hip synovium that produces a sterile reactive effusion and consequent joint irritability. It is widely regarded as a post-infectious or reactive phenomenon, frequently following a viral illness, in which transient immune-mediated synovial inflammation and effusion raise intra-articular pressure and provoke pain, guarding and a characteristic protective posture. The synovial reaction resolves spontaneously without cartilage destruction, distinguishing it fundamentally from the pyogenic, cartilage-damaging process of septic arthritis with which it is most often confused. The prognosis is excellent and the condition is self-limiting, with most children recovering fully within one to two weeks; a minority experience recurrent episodes. Rarely, a small proportion of children initially labelled as having transient synovitis are subsequently diagnosed with Perthes disease.

Transient Tachypnea of the Newborn — TTN, transient tachypnoea of the newborn, wet lung, retained fetal lung fluid Neonatal respiratory distress syndrome Early-onset neonatal pneumonia or sepsis Meconium aspiration syndrome Persistent pulmonary hypertension of the newborn Congenital heart disease Air-leak syndromes Chest radiograph showing wet-lung features Pulse oximetry and monitoring of oxygen requirement Blood gas if distress is significant Sepsis screen and consideration of antibiotics when infection cannot be excluded Blood glucose monitoring A common, benign, self-limited cause of respiratory distress in term and late-preterm newborns caused by delayed clearance of fetal lung fluid. It typically presents soon after birth with tachypnoea, mild grunting, nasal flaring, and mild recession, usually without severe distress. Delivery by caesarean section (especially without labour), maternal diabetes, and rapid or precipitous delivery are recognised risk factors. The chest radiograph classically shows prominent perihilar vascular markings, fluid in the interlobar fissures, hyperinflation, and sometimes small pleural effusions. It is largely a diagnosis of exclusion, and sepsis and pneumonia should be considered, particularly if distress is marked or prolonged. Management is supportive with oxygen as required and attention to feeding; the condition usually resolves within the first day or two of life. Oxygen requirement is generally modest, and the need for high oxygen or escalating support should prompt reconsideration of the diagnosis. Distress persisting well beyond 2-3 days argues against transient tachypnoea and warrants further evaluation. High or rising oxygen requirement Distress persisting beyond the first few days of life Marked recession, grunting, or signs of respiratory failure Features suggesting sepsis or pneumonia Differential pre- and post-ductal saturations suggesting pulmonary hypertension or cardiac disease Anchoring on transient tachypnoea and missing early sepsis or pneumonia Overlooking congenital heart disease presenting with tachypnoea Failing to reconsider the diagnosis when oxygen needs are high or distress is prolonged Unnecessarily delaying feeding or investigation in a stable infant Attributing every caesarean-born tachypnoeic infant to TTN without appropriate observation During fetal life the lungs are filled with fluid that is normally cleared around birth by labour-associated catecholamine and hormonal surges that switch alveolar epithelial cells from fluid secretion to sodium-driven absorption, aided by mechanical squeeze during vaginal delivery. When this clearance is delayed or incomplete, residual fluid remains in the interstitium and air spaces, reducing lung compliance and causing tachypnoea and mild hypoxaemia until the fluid is reabsorbed. The condition is benign and self-limited, resolving within hours to a few days with supportive care and no long-term respiratory sequelae in the great majority of infants.

Transient tachypnoea of the newborn — TTN, wet lung, retained fetal lung fluid Neonatal respiratory distress syndrome Early-onset neonatal sepsis or pneumonia Meconium aspiration syndrome Persistent pulmonary hypertension of the newborn Congenital heart disease Pneumothorax Clinical assessment of respiratory rate, effort and oxygenation Chest radiograph showing perihilar streaking and fissural fluid Sepsis screen where infection cannot be excluded Blood gas to assess gas exchange Pre- and post-ductal saturations if pulmonary hypertension or cardiac disease is considered A common, self-limiting cause of neonatal respiratory distress from delayed clearance of fetal lung fluid Typically presents soon after birth with tachypnoea, mild recession and grunting in a near-term or term baby Elective caesarean birth without labour is a major risk factor, as is late prematurity and maternal diabetes It is largely a diagnosis of exclusion, with infection and other causes of distress ruled out Chest radiography classically shows prominent perihilar streaking and fluid in the horizontal fissure Management is supportive with oxygen and respiratory support as needed, and it usually resolves within a day or two Worsening or persistent distress beyond the expected short course Hypoxaemia out of proportion suggesting pulmonary hypertension or cardiac disease Features suggesting sepsis or pneumonia Sudden deterioration suggesting pneumothorax Attributing distress to TTN and missing early sepsis or pneumonia Overlooking a cardiac cause of persistent hypoxaemia Assuming resolution without reassessing worsening distress Failing to recognise persistent pulmonary hypertension Transient tachypnoea of the newborn results from delayed absorption of the fluid that normally fills the fetal lungs. During labour and vaginal birth, hormonal changes and thoracic compression promote clearance of this fluid via epithelial sodium channels and the lymphatics; when this process is incomplete, as after caesarean birth without labour, residual fluid in the airspaces and interstitium impairs gas exchange and reduces compliance, producing tachypnoea and mild distress. As the fluid is reabsorbed over hours to a couple of days, the symptoms resolve. The condition is benign and self-limiting, resolving within one to three days with supportive care and no long-term respiratory sequelae.

Transposition of the Great Arteries — TGA, d-TGA, transposition of great vessels Tetralogy of Fallot Total anomalous pulmonary venous return Tricuspid atresia Truncus arteriosus Persistent pulmonary hypertension of the newborn Severe respiratory disease causing cyanosis Echocardiography to confirm ventriculoarterial discordance, mixing sites, and coronary anatomy Hyperoxia test showing little rise in oxygenation with supplemental oxygen (suggesting a cardiac cause) Chest radiograph looking for an egg-on-a-string silhouette Blood gas to assess hypoxaemia and acidosis Pulse oximetry, including pre- and post-ductal comparison In d-transposition the aorta arises from the right ventricle and the pulmonary artery from the left ventricle, so the systemic and pulmonary circulations run in parallel rather than in series. It is a leading cause of cyanosis presenting in the newborn period, often in an otherwise well-grown, term infant. Survival depends on mixing between the two parallel circuits through a patent foramen ovale, atrial or ventricular septal defect, or the ductus arteriosus. Cyanosis is typically profound and, unlike many respiratory causes, does not improve substantially with supplemental oxygen. A prostaglandin infusion is started to maintain ductal patency and improve intercirculatory mixing while the infant is stabilised. Balloon atrial septostomy may be performed to enlarge the atrial communication and improve mixing when cyanosis is severe. Chest radiograph may show an egg-on-a-string cardiac silhouette with a narrow mediastinum, though this is not always present. Echocardiography confirms the discordant great-artery connections, defines associated defects, and maps the coronary arteries before surgery. The arterial switch operation, restoring normal ventriculoarterial connections, is the definitive repair and is performed in the neonatal period. Severe cyanosis in a newborn that fails to improve with supplemental oxygen Rapid deterioration and acidosis as the ductus arteriosus and foramen ovale close, restricting mixing Duct-dependent collapse before prostaglandin is established Worsening metabolic acidosis indicating inadequate systemic oxygen delivery Inadequate intercirculatory mixing requiring urgent septostomy Attributing severe neonatal cyanosis to lung disease and delaying cardiac evaluation because oxygen does not help Failing to start prostaglandin promptly, allowing the ductus to close and mixing to fail Overlooking the need to enhance mixing (septostomy) in a critically hypoxaemic infant Assuming a normal chest radiograph excludes the diagnosis Not mapping coronary anatomy before surgical planning Abnormal division of the truncus arteriosus results in the aorta connecting to the right ventricle and the pulmonary artery to the left ventricle. As a consequence, deoxygenated systemic venous blood is pumped back to the body and oxygenated pulmonary venous blood is returned to the lungs, forming two separate parallel circuits. Life is only possible if oxygenated and deoxygenated blood mix through a communication at the atrial, ventricular, or ductal level. Inadequate mixing produces severe systemic hypoxaemia and progressive metabolic acidosis, which worsens as the ductus arteriosus and foramen ovale close after birth. With prompt stabilisation and an arterial switch operation in the neonatal period, most children do well with good long-term function, though follow-up is required for coronary, valve, and great-artery complications. Without intervention the condition is rapidly fatal.

It may follow infection or vaccination as a para- or post-infectious immune response, arise from autoimmune demyelinating disease such as multiple sclerosis, NMOSD, or MOG antibody disease, or occur with systemic autoimmune conditions. Breakdown of the blood-cord barrier and inflammatory cell infiltration produce cord swelling and dysfunction. Outcome is variable and depends on cause, severity, and rapidity of onset. Some patients recover substantially, while others are left with significant residual deficits. Recurrent disease and poorer recovery are more typical of NMOSD and longitudinally extensive lesions, underscoring the importance of accurate aetiological diagnosis and timely immunotherapy.

to distinguish quiescent trapped lung from active entrapment that needs treatment of ongoing disease Following a resolved pleural inflammatory process, a mature, relatively acellular fibrous membrane forms over the visceral pleura. This inelastic peel mechanically restrains the lung so that it cannot expand to fill the hemithorax. Trapped lung itself is a stable, benign mechanical problem; symptomatic cases can improve after decortication if the underlying lung is healthy, whereas the outlook is dominated by any underlying malignant or infective cause when present.

traps syndrome — TNF receptor-associated periodic syndrome, familial Hibernian fever, TNFRSF1A-associated periodic syndrome Familial Mediterranean fever Mevalonate kinase deficiency (hyper-IgD syndrome) Cryopyrin-associated periodic syndrome spectrum Systemic juvenile idiopathic arthritis and adult-onset Still's disease PFAPA syndrome Cyclic neutropenia Occult infection or lymphoma causing prolonged fever TNFRSF1A gene sequencing, interpreting low-penetrance variants with caution Serial acute-phase reactants (C-reactive protein, serum amyloid A) during and between episodes Serum soluble TNF receptor 1 concentration between attacks Magnetic resonance imaging of affected muscle groups to demonstrate fasciitis rather than myositis Urinalysis for proteinuria and, if positive, tissue biopsy with Congo red staining for amyloid Ophthalmological assessment when periorbital oedema and conjunctivitis are prominent Autosomal dominant disorder caused by variants in TNFRSF1A encoding the p55 tumour necrosis factor receptor 1; originally described in families of northern European (Irish and Scottish) ancestry as familial Hibernian fever. Attacks are notably prolonged compared with other periodic fevers, frequently lasting a week or more and sometimes several weeks, which can lead to repeated investigation for infection or malignancy. Migratory myalgia with a warm, tender overlying erythematous patch that moves centrifugally down a limb is highly characteristic and reflects a monocytic fasciitis rather than true myositis. Periorbital oedema, often with conjunctivitis and periorbital pain, is a distinctive sign that is uncommon in the other hereditary periodic fevers. Serositis with abdominal pain, pleuritic chest pain and arthralgia is common, and reactive AA amyloidosis is an important long-term complication, particularly with cysteine-residue variants. Interleukin-1 blockade is the most reliably effective treatment; corticosteroids attenuate attacks but with escalating requirements, and anti-TNF responses are inconsistent with some agents paradoxically worsening disease. Low-penetrance variants such as R92Q and P46L are common in the general population and may produce milder, atypical or incompletely penetrant phenotypes. Reduced shedding of soluble TNF receptor 1 between attacks can support the diagnosis but is neither fully sensitive nor specific. Emergence of proteinuria indicating renal AA amyloidosis Escalating corticosteroid dependence to control increasingly frequent or prolonged attacks A prolonged febrile episode where serious infection or malignancy has not been adequately excluded Clinical deterioration after starting certain anti-TNF agents Misattributing prolonged febrile attacks to recurrent infection and administering repeated antibiotic courses Reporting a low-penetrance variant such as R92Q as definitively diagnostic without correlating with phenotype Mistaking periorbital oedema for allergy or angio-oedema Interpreting migratory limb erythema and myalgia as cellulitis or thrombophlebitis Variants in TNFRSF1A, especially those affecting conserved cysteine residues in the extracellular domain, cause misfolding of the mutant receptor with intracellular retention and aggregation in the endoplasmic reticulum rather than defective receptor shedding alone. The retained receptor provokes endoplasmic reticulum stress, augmented mitochondrial reactive oxygen species and ligand-independent pro-inflammatory signalling that enhances responsiveness to inflammatory stimuli. The net effect is exaggerated innate immune activation with prominent interleukin-1 beta-driven inflammation, accounting for both the prolonged inflammatory attacks and the responsiveness to interleukin-1 blockade, while sustained serum amyloid A elevation underlies the risk of AA amyloidosis. Interleukin-1 blockade controls attacks and inflammation in most patients, allowing corticosteroid sparing and reducing the risk of amyloidosis. Untreated disease, especially with high-penetrance cysteine variants, carries a meaningful risk of AA amyloidosis and progressive renal impairment.

and a trend in the score matters more than any single reading The overriding aim is to prevent secondary brain injury by avoiding hypoxia and hypotension, which independently worsen outcome Maintain hypercarbia Falling GCS or a drop of two or more points indicating deterioration Unequal, dilated, or unreactive pupil suggesting uncal herniation from a mass lesion needing urgent decompression immediately to limit secondary injury Attributing hypotension to the brain injury and overlooking extracranial haemorrhage Allowing hypoxia, hypercarbia, or hypotension that aggravate secondary injury Missing an expanding haematoma by not repeating imaging after clinical deterioration Over-sedating so that neurological reassessment becomes impossible Failing to reverse anticoagulation promptly in a bleeding head injury The primary injury is the mechanical damage sustained at impact, which cannot be reversed. Secondary injury develops over hours to days from hypoxia, hypotension, oedema, haematoma expansion, seizures, and disturbed autoregulation. Because the skull is a fixed compartment, expanding blood or oedema raises intracranial pressure; once compensatory mechanisms are exhausted, small volume increases cause steep pressure rises. Rising intracranial pressure reduces cerebral perfusion pressure and drives ischaemia, and pressure gradients can force brain tissue across dural folds or the foramen magnum, producing herniation and brainstem compression. Outcome ranges from full recovery in mild injury to death or severe disability in severe injury. Prevention of secondary insults, timely evacuation of surgical lesions, and control of intracranial pressure improve results, whereas sustained raised pressure and low cerebral perfusion predict poor recovery.

traumatic optic neuropathy — TON, post-traumatic optic neuropathy Orbital compartment syndrome from retrobulbar haemorrhage Globe rupture or severe anterior segment injury Commotio retinae or traumatic maculopathy Retinal detachment Occipital or cortical visual injury Functional (non-organic) visual loss Computed tomography of the head and orbits with dedicated fine optic canal views Assessment of visual acuity and pupils for a relative afferent pupillary defect Colour vision testing and visual fields when the patient is able to cooperate Measurement of intraocular pressure and assessment for proptosis and a tense orbit Magnetic resonance imaging when a sheath haematoma or soft-tissue injury is suspected Optical coherence tomography of the retinal nerve fibre layer at follow-up Follows blunt or penetrating head and orbital trauma, classically frontal or brow impact that transmits force to the tightly tethered intracanalicular optic nerve. Distinguish direct injury, such as nerve laceration, avulsion, bony fragment or sheath haematoma, from indirect injury from deceleration and shearing forces. There is acute visual loss with a relative afferent pupillary defect, while the disc is often normal at onset and becomes pale after several weeks. It is commonly associated with maxillofacial and orbital fractures and closed head injury and may be masked in an unconscious patient. Computed tomography of the orbits and optic canal with fine cuts is central to assessment, identifying fractures, haematoma and nerve impingement. Management is controversial and includes observation, high-dose corticosteroids or optic canal decompression, with no proven benefit from routine steroids. High-dose corticosteroids are potentially harmful in the setting of significant head injury, as shown in major head-injury trials. An orbital compartment syndrome from retrobulbar haemorrhage is a treatable emergency requiring urgent lateral canthotomy and cantholysis. Proptosis with raised intraocular pressure and a tense orbit indicating a compartment syndrome needing emergency canthotomy An expanding orbital haematoma Bilateral visual loss or no perception of light Associated significant intracranial injury Missing the diagnosis in an unconscious or multiply injured patient Administering high-dose corticosteroids in significant head injury despite evidence of harm Overlooking a treatable retrobulbar haemorrhage requiring urgent orbital decompression Delaying surgical decompression when a clear compressive lesion is present Traumatic optic neuropathy involves both primary and secondary mechanisms. Primary injury results from direct disruption of axons or from mechanical force transmitted to the firmly anchored intracanalicular segment, where the nerve is least able to dissipate energy. Secondary injury then evolves within the confined bony optic canal through oedema, ischaemia, oxidative stress and apoptotic cell death, causing progressive axonal loss. A retrobulbar haemorrhage can additionally compress the nerve and its blood supply, producing a compartment-type ischaemic insult. Outcome is variable; poor prognostic features include no perception of light at presentation, an optic canal fracture, older age and loss of consciousness. Some patients recover useful vision spontaneously.

traumatic panniculitis — mobile encapsulated lipoma, post-traumatic fat necrosis erythema nodosum breast carcinoma (for breast lesions) infective panniculitis pancreatic panniculitis lupus panniculitis factitial panniculitis subcutaneous sarcoidosis deep incisional or excisional biopsy including subcutaneous fat for histopathology ultrasound or mammography for breast lesions (oil cyst, rim calcification) tissue cultures to exclude infection when clinically indicated MRI for deep or diagnostically uncertain lesions core biopsy of suspicious breast masses to exclude malignancy review of medication and occupational or activity history for repetitive trauma An inflammation of subcutaneous fat provoked by mechanical injury, blunt trauma, pressure or repetitive friction, producing tender nodules or plaques at the site of insult. Common sites reflect exposure to trauma: the breasts, thighs, buttocks and shins; a history of a precipitating event is often but not always elicited. Cold-related and pressure-related forms overlap clinically; the breast is a classic site where post-traumatic fat necrosis can mimic carcinoma. Lesions evolve from firm tender nodules to indurated, sometimes fibrotic or calcified masses, and may become mobile and encapsulated over time. Histology shows a mostly lobular panniculitis with fat necrosis, lipophages (foamy macrophages), lipomembranous (membranocystic) change and later fibrosis. Imaging of breast lesions may reveal an oil cyst with rim calcification, a helpful clue to a benign traumatic aetiology. Diagnosis rests on correlating a clear mechanical history with compatible histology after excluding infective and systemic panniculitides. Most lesions are self-limiting and resolve with conservative care; the main clinical imperative is to avoid mistaking them for malignancy. a firm, fixed or enlarging breast mass that cannot be confidently distinguished from carcinoma systemic features (fever, weight loss) suggesting infection or an alternative systemic panniculitis ulceration or discharge raising concern for infection or factitial disease absence of any plausible traumatic history prompting a search for another cause Misinterpreting a post-traumatic breast mass as carcinoma, or vice versa, without appropriate imaging and biopsy. Accepting a trivial or coincidental trauma history and overlooking a systemic panniculitis. Sampling too superficially and missing the lobular fat pathology. Assuming all fat necrosis is traumatic and failing to consider pancreatic or infective causes. Attributing recurrent lesions to trauma when factitial disease is responsible. Mechanical trauma, sustained pressure or repetitive friction disrupts adipocytes and their vascular supply, releasing intracellular lipid into the interstitium. Free triglycerides are hydrolysed by tissue lipases into free fatty acids, which incite a lobular inflammatory response dominated by lipophagic macrophages that engulf the liberated lipid. Ischaemia from injured vessels contributes to fat necrosis. Over time the infiltrate gives way to foreign-body granulomas, lipomembranous change and fibrosis, with occasional dystrophic calcification and oil-cyst formation. In the breast this reparative fibrosis can produce a firm, spiculated mass that clinically and radiologically simulates carcinoma. The condition is benign and usually self-limiting, resolving over weeks to months, though residual fibrosis, calcification or an encapsulated fatty nodule may persist.

colobomata threatening the cornea Progressive obstructive sleep apnoea with growth or cardiorespiratory consequences Difficult airway anticipated during any anaesthetic Assuming intellectual disability and thereby underestimating the child's potential Failing to anticipate a difficult airway before sedation or surgery Overlooking recessively inherited forms when TCOF1 testing is negative Neglecting corneal protection in the presence of eyelid colobomata Delaying hearing rehabilitation, harming speech and language outcomes The condition results principally from haploinsufficiency of the treacle protein encoded by TCOF1, which participates in ribosomal RNA transcription and processing within the nucleolus. Reduced ribosome biogenesis is thought to trigger nucleolar stress and stabilisation of p53, leading to excessive apoptosis of cranial neural crest cells during early development. Because these neural crest cells populate the first and second branchial arches that form the midface, mandible, and external and middle ear, their depletion produces the symmetrical hypoplasia of the malar bones, mandible, and ear structures. With multidisciplinary craniofacial care, airway and hearing support, and staged reconstruction, most individuals achieve good function and normal cognition, though repeated surgery over childhood and adolescence is often required.

be mistaken for a functional bowel disorder Dehydration during acute diarrhoeal episodes, particularly in young children Weight loss or failure to thrive suggesting a broader malabsorptive process disorder without taking a focused dietary history Overlooking trehalose as a hidden ingredient in some processed foods Failing to include trehalase in the disaccharidase assay panel Assuming symptoms Trehalase, encoded by TREH, hydrolyses the disaccharide trehalose into two glucose molecules for absorption. When trehalase activity is deficient, ingested trehalose, present mainly in mushrooms and certain processed foods, is not digested and remains in the lumen. The unabsorbed sugar draws water osmotically into the bowel and is fermented by colonic bacteria into gas and short-chain acids, producing diarrhoea, bloating and flatulence after trehalose-containing meals. Because exposure is intermittent and food-specific, symptoms occur only after relevant ingestions. Prognosis is excellent, as symptoms are entirely controlled by avoiding trehalose-rich foods and there are no systemic consequences. Recognition prevents unnecessary investigation for functional disorders.

by the human body louse, with organisms shed in louse faeces and inoculated through scratched skin Historically a major cause of illness among soldiers in the trenches of the First World War, it persists today among homeless people, heavy drinkers and others exposed to body lice, hence the term urban trench fever After an incubation of around 1-2 weeks patients develop fever, severe headache, from mild self-limiting illness to prolonged or relapsing bacteraemia, and Bartonella quintana is an important cause of culture-negative endocarditis The same organism causes bacillary angiomatosis in immunocompromised hosts, so the clinical spectrum depends heavily on host immunity Diagnosis relies on serology, PCR and prolonged-incubation blood cultures, and treatment uses prolonged antimicrobial courses, with delousing essential to prevent reinfection and spread New murmur, heart failure or embolic events suggesting endocarditis Prolonged or relapsing bacteraemia despite treatment Profound immunosuppression predisposing to bacillary angiomatosis Occurrence in a homeless or crowded population signalling wider transmission risk Severe or persistent constitutional symptoms with weight loss Not considering the diagnosis in homeless or louse-infested patients with fever Relying on routine short-incubation blood cultures, which are typically negative Failing to investigate for endocarditis in persistent bacteraemia Overlooking delousing and social measures, leading to reinfection Confining the differential to typhus and missing this treatable Bartonella infection Bartonella quintana is a fastidious Gram-negative bacterium maintained in humans and transmitted by the body louse. Following inoculation through louse-faeces contamination of broken skin, the organism enters the bloodstream and characteristically infects erythrocytes and vascular endothelial cells, establishing a persistent or relapsing intraerythrocytic bacteraemia that accounts for the recurrent febrile episodes. In immunocompetent hosts this produces the self-limiting or relapsing febrile illness of trench fever, whereas the ability to adhere to cardiac valves underlies its role in chronic culture-negative endocarditis. Acute trench fever is generally self-limiting with a good outcome, but Bartonella quintana bacteraemia and endocarditis are serious, may require valve surgery, and mandate prolonged antibiotic therapy; reinfection is likely if louse infestation is not addressed.

Trench foot (non-freezing cold injury) — non-freezing cold injury, NFCI, cold immersion foot Frostbite (a true freezing injury) Immersion foot from warm-water exposure Chilblains (pernio) Cellulitis or other soft tissue infection Peripheral vascular disease with critical ischaemia Compartment syndrome after prolonged immobility Clinical diagnosis from history of prolonged cold, wet exposure and characteristic foot findings Assessment of peripheral pulses, capillary refill, and neurological (sensory) function Skin and soft tissue examination for blistering, necrosis, or secondary infection Inflammatory markers and wound swabs if secondary infection is suspected Vascular imaging where an alternative ischaemic cause is considered A non-freezing cold injury caused by prolonged exposure of the feet to cold, wet conditions, classically described in soldiers standing in cold water-filled trenches Develops at temperatures above freezing, so tissue does not freeze; the injury is from sustained cold and damp rather than ice crystal formation Early on the foot is cold, numb, pale, and often swollen; on rewarming it becomes hyperaemic, red, painful, and may blister A characteristic biphasic course of initial anaesthesia followed by a painful hyperaemic phase is typical Management is gradual rewarming, keeping the foot dry, elevation, meticulous foot care, and analgesia for the painful phase Prevention centres on keeping feet dry and warm, regularly changing wet socks, and avoiding constrictive footwear Severe or repeated injury can leave long-term cold sensitivity, chronic pain, and sensory disturbance Tissue necrosis, deep blistering, or evidence of secondary infection Features suggesting a true freezing injury (frostbite) requiring different management Signs of systemic infection or sepsis from an infected wound Severe, persistent pain or sensory loss suggesting significant nerve injury Confusing trench foot with frostbite and mismanaging the rewarming approach Applying rapid or excessive direct heat, worsening reperfusion injury Underestimating the painful hyperaemic phase and providing inadequate analgesia Neglecting preventive foot care, allowing recurrence Trench foot follows prolonged exposure of tissue to cold, wet conditions without freezing. Sustained cold-induced vasoconstriction reduces perfusion, and the combination of hypoxia, endothelial injury, and alternating vasoconstriction and reperfusion damages nerves, small vessels, and soft tissue. Because temperatures remain above freezing there is no ice crystal formation, distinguishing it from frostbite; instead the injury is a microvascular and neural insult that, when severe, can progress to tissue necrosis and leaves the characteristic biphasic clinical course of numb ischaemia followed by a painful hyperaemic reperfusion phase. Mild cases recover over days to weeks with rewarming and foot care, but moderate to severe non-freezing cold injury may leave prolonged cold hypersensitivity, chronic neuropathic pain, and sensory deficits that can persist for months or longer.

Triangular fibrocartilage complex injury — TFCC injury, TFCC tear Ulnar impaction syndrome Distal radioulnar joint instability of other cause Extensor carpi ulnaris tendon pathology Lunotriquetral ligament injury Hook of hamate fracture or pisotriquetral pathology Clinical examination including the fovea sign and distal radioulnar joint stability testing Radiographs assessing ulnar variance MRI, ideally with arthrography, to image the tear Wrist arthroscopy as the definitive diagnostic and often therapeutic tool Comparison with the contralateral wrist for instability The triangular fibrocartilage complex stabilises the distal radioulnar joint and cushions the ulnar wrist, and its injury causes ulnar-sided wrist pain Symptoms include ulnar wrist pain worse with rotation and gripping, clicking and sometimes distal radioulnar joint instability Injuries are broadly traumatic or degenerative, the latter associated with positive ulnar variance and ulnar impaction The fovea sign, with tenderness in the soft spot between the ulnar styloid and flexor carpi ulnaris, supports the diagnosis MRI, and definitively wrist arthroscopy, characterise the tear and its location Peripheral traumatic tears in the vascular zone can heal or be repaired, whereas central and degenerative tears are managed differently Distal radioulnar joint instability Associated fracture Progressive pain and weakness despite conservative care Features suggesting an alternative structural injury Attributing ulnar wrist pain to a simple sprain and missing the diagnosis Overlooking distal radioulnar joint instability Not recognising ulnar impaction as the driver of a degenerative tear Expecting central avascular tears to heal like peripheral ones The triangular fibrocartilage complex comprises the articular disc, ligaments and sheath that support the distal radioulnar joint and transmit load across the ulnar wrist. Acute injury from a fall onto the extended wrist or forceful rotation tears the complex, while chronic degenerative tears develop where excess ulnar length increases load on the disc (ulnar impaction). The peripheral portion is vascular and can heal, whereas the central avascular disc does not, which determines whether repair or debridement is appropriate. Loss of complex integrity may destabilise the distal radioulnar joint. Many injuries respond to a period of immobilisation and rehabilitation; peripheral repairs and procedures to address ulnar impaction generally do well, whereas untreated instability can lead to chronic pain and arthritis.

Trichiasis — misdirected eyelashes Entropion Epiblepharon Distichiasis Cicatricial conjunctival disease (for example trachoma, ocular mucous membrane pemphigoid) Chronic blepharitis Slit-lamp examination of lash direction, lid margin and cornea Fluorescein staining to assess corneal involvement Assessment for underlying cicatricial or infective cause Eversion of the lid to exclude entropion and scarring Consideration of biopsy where a cicatrising immunobullous disease is suspected Posterior misdirection of eyelashes from a normally positioned lid margin, so lashes rub against the ocular surface Causes foreign-body sensation, watering, redness and, if chronic, corneal abrasion and scarring It differs from entropion, in which the whole lid margin turns inward Common causes include chronic blepharitis, cicatrising conditions and, globally, trachoma Trachomatous trichiasis is a leading infective cause of blindness worldwide and a target of elimination programmes Management ranges from epilation and cryotherapy or electrolysis to lid surgery for cicatricial disease Corneal ulceration or scarring threatening vision Features of a progressive cicatrising conjunctival disease Extensive or recurrent disease Signs suggesting ocular mucous membrane pemphigoid Confusing trichiasis with entropion, which needs different surgery Missing an underlying cicatrising disease such as mucous membrane pemphigoid Neglecting corneal protection in chronic cases Relying on simple epilation alone, which is often followed by recurrence Trichiasis arises when eyelash follicles or the lid margin are distorted so that lashes grow toward the globe despite a normally positioned lid. Chronic inflammation, scarring or cicatrisation of the lid margin, as in trachoma, chronic blepharitis or other cicatrising conjunctival diseases, redirects the lashes posteriorly. The abrasive lashes irritate the cornea and conjunctiva, and persistent rubbing can cause epithelial breakdown, corneal scarring and visual loss. Isolated trichiasis is readily treated by lash removal or ablation, though recurrence is common; cicatricial disease requires treating the underlying cause and may need lid surgery to protect the cornea.

Trichinellosis — trichinosis, Trichinella spiralis infection, trichiniasis Dermatomyositis or polymyositis Other causes of eosinophilia with myalgia (eosinophilia-myalgia syndrome, hypereosinophilic syndrome) Influenza or other viral myositis Leptospirosis Angioedema or allergic reaction (periorbital swelling) Other tissue-invasive helminth infections Systemic vasculitis Full blood count and blood film for eosinophilia Serum creatine kinase and other muscle enzymes Trichinella serology (antibody testing) Detailed dietary history for raw or undercooked pork or game Muscle biopsy for encysted larvae in uncertain cases ECG and cardiac assessment, and neurological evaluation, when complications are suspected A zoonotic tissue nematode infection acquired by eating raw or undercooked meat containing Trichinella larvae, classically pork but also wild game such as bear and boar The early intestinal phase causes diarrhoea, abdominal pain and nausea within days of ingestion The later muscle-invasion phase produces fever, myalgia, weakness and the characteristic periorbital and facial oedema Marked peripheral eosinophilia and raised muscle enzymes (creatine kinase) are typical laboratory findings Splinter haemorrhages, conjunctival and subungual haemorrhages, and a rash may be seen Serology becomes positive over the first weeks; muscle biopsy showing encysted larvae is diagnostic when needed Treatment combines anthelmintics such as albendazole or mebendazole with corticosteroids to control the inflammatory reaction in severe disease Serious complications include myocarditis, encephalitis and respiratory muscle involvement, which are the main causes of death Chest pain, arrhythmia or heart failure suggesting myocarditis Headache, confusion or focal deficits suggesting encephalitis Breathlessness from respiratory muscle involvement Severe systemic illness with very high eosinophilia and muscle enzyme elevation Missing the dietary history of undercooked pork or wild game Mistaking the myositis and periorbital oedema for dermatomyositis or an allergic reaction Relying on early serology, which may be negative in the first days of illness Failing to give anthelmintics early, before larvae encyst in muscle, when the diagnosis is suspected Overlooking cardiac or neurological complications that determine prognosis Trichinellosis begins when a person eats raw or undercooked meat containing encysted Trichinella larvae. Gastric digestion frees the larvae, which mature into adult worms in the small intestine; the females release newborn larvae that penetrate the mucosa and disseminate through the bloodstream and lymphatics. These larvae preferentially invade striated skeletal muscle, where they encyst within modified muscle cells (nurse cells), provoking an intense eosinophilic and inflammatory response. This muscle invasion accounts for the myositis, myalgia and periorbital oedema, while migration through other tissues can inflame the myocardium, central nervous system and respiratory muscles, explaining the potentially fatal complications. Most cases are mild and self-limiting with a good outcome, but heavy infections with myocardial, neurological or respiratory involvement can be life-threatening; prompt treatment shortens illness and reduces complications.

Trichinellosis and Other Tissue Nematode Infections — Trichinosis, Trichinella infection, Tissue nematode infections, Visceral larva migrans, Ocular larva migrans, Toxocariasis, Cutaneous larva migrans, Creeping eruption, Cerebral angiostrongyliasis, Rat lungworm disease, Gnathostomiasis Polymyositis / dermatomyositis (myalgia, weakness, elevated muscle enzymes) - note T. pseudospiralis can mimic a prolonged polymyositis-like illness Periorbital edema from other causes (allergic, nephrotic, angioedema) Acute myocarditis of other etiology Eosinophilic meningitis from other parasites (see infectionMimics) Retinoblastoma (mimicked by ocular toxocariasis retinal granuloma) Other hypereosinophilic syndromes Other causes of eosinophilic meningitis in endemic areas: gnathostomiasis, paragonimiasis, schistosomiasis, neurocysticercosis, and coccidioidomycosis Other eosinophilia-associated helminthiases (e.g., strongyloidiasis, filariasis) Pleurodynia (coxsackievirus B) and bacterial myositis as causes of myalgia overlapping with trichinellosis Peripheral blood eosinophilia (develops in >90% of symptomatic trichinellosis, may peak at >50% at 2-4 weeks) Serum muscle enzymes including creatine phosphokinase (elevated in most symptomatic trichinellosis) Trichinella parasite-specific serology (titer rise usually only after the third week of infection) Muscle biopsy (>=1 g, near tendon insertions in symptomatic muscle) with fresh tissue compressed between glass slides and examined microscopically, since routine histology may miss larvae ELISA for toxocaral antibodies (may be negative in ocular larva migrans); leukocytosis and hypergammaglobulinemia in visceral larva migrans; chest x-ray for transient pulmonary infiltrates CSF examination for angiostrongyliasis (opening pressure, cell count, eosinophilic pleocytosis, protein, glucose); A. cantonensis PCR on CSF/tissue (available via CDC and Hawaii Dept of Public Health) Idiopathic inflammatory myopathies (polymyositis, dermatomyositis) Retinoblastoma (versus ocular larva migrans) Allergic/angioedematous periorbital swelling Idiopathic hypereosinophilic syndrome Trichinellosis follows ingestion of meat (classically pork, but increasingly wild game such as bear and walrus) containing encysted Trichinella larvae; most infections are mild or asymptomatic, but heavy burdens can be life-threatening (Harrison 22e p.1810). Disease severity tracks larval burden: light infections (<10 larvae/g muscle) tend to be asymptomatic, whereas heavy infections (>50 larvae/g muscle) can be life-threatening (Harrison 22e p.1811). Clinical course is biphasic: an early enteric phase (diarrhea, abdominal pain, constipation, nausea) in the first weeks, followed in the second week by larval-migration symptoms (fever, periorbital/facial edema, eosinophilia) and then a myositis phase as larvae encyst (Harrison 22e p.1811). Periorbital and facial edema with subconjunctival, retinal, and nail-bed (splinter) hemorrhages are characteristic of the migratory phase of trichinellosis (Harrison 22e p.1811). Most deaths in trichinellosis result from myocarditis (with tachyarrhythmias or heart failure) and, less commonly, encephalitis or pneumonitis (Harrison 22e p.1811). Muscle involvement preferentially affects the extraocular muscles, biceps, and the jaw, neck, lower back, and diaphragm muscles, with symptoms peaking around 3 weeks (Harrison 22e p.1811). Visceral larva migrans (most often Toxocara canis) chiefly affects preschool children who ingest soil contaminated with embryonated eggs, producing fever, hepatosplenomegaly, wheezing, and extraordinary eosinophilia that can approach 90% (Harrison 22e p.1812). Ocular larva migrans typically occurs in older children/young adults without pica and usually lacks eosinophilia or visceral signs; the retinal granuloma can mimic retinoblastoma and lead to unnecessary enucleation if misdiagnosed (Harrison 22e p.1812). Cutaneous larva migrans ('creeping eruption'), usually from the dog/cat hookworm Ancylostoma braziliense, produces an intensely pruritic serpiginous track that advances several centimeters per day; the larvae cannot mature in humans and self-resolve over weeks to a couple of months (Harrison 22e p.1812). Angiostrongylus cantonensis (rat lungworm) is the most common cause of human eosinophilic meningitis; CSF shows elevated opening pressure, pleocytosis (150-2000 cells/uL) with eosinophilic pleocytosis >20%, elevated protein, and normal glucose (Harrison 22e p.1813). Gnathostomiasis is acquired from raw fish/poultry (e.g., som fak, sashimi) and causes migratory, recurrent pruritic cutaneous swellings; CNS invasion produces eosinophilic myeloencephalitis with agonizing radicular pain followed by paraplegia, and cerebral involvement is often fatal (Harrison 22e p.1813). Stool examination is worthless in toxocariasis because the larvae never develop into egg-producing adults in the human host (Harrison 22e p.1812). Myocarditis with tachyarrhythmias or heart failure (leading cause of death in trichinellosis) Encephalitis or pneumonitis in trichinellosis Dysphagia, dyspnea, or diaphragmatic muscle involvement Severe neurologic, pneumonic, or myocardial involvement in visceral larva migrans (rare deaths) Ascending radicular pain and paresthesias followed by paraplegia in gnathostomiasis (myeloencephalitis) Cerebral involvement with focal hemorrhages in gnathostomiasis (often fatal) Permanent neurologic sequelae from heavy CNS angiostrongyliasis Most mild trichinellosis cases remain undiagnosed; a high index of suspicion and a careful dietary/exposure history are needed. Trichinella serology is typically negative until after the third week, so a presumptive clinical diagnosis (fever, eosinophilia, periorbital edema, myalgia after a suspect meal) may be required early. Stool examination is useless in toxocariasis because larvae do not mature into egg-producing adults in humans. Ocular toxocariasis can be mistaken for retinoblastoma, risking unnecessary enucleation; it often lacks eosinophilia and visceral signs. In angiostrongyliasis, A. cantonensis larvae are only rarely seen in CSF and serologic tests are unstandardized and may be negative at symptom onset. Arctic T. nativa larvae in walrus or bear meat are relatively freeze-resistant and may remain viable despite freezing, so usual freezing prevention may fail. Gnathostomiasis may present with ocular or CNS involvement without antecedent cutaneous swellings. These are zoonotic tissue-dwelling nematode infections arising from incidental human exposure; symptoms derive largely from invasive larval stages that (except for Trichinella) do not mature in humans. In trichinellosis, ingested encysted larvae are freed by gastric acid and proteases, invade small-bowel mucosa, mature to adults, and after about one week females release newborn larvae that migrate via the circulation to striated muscle, where most species encyst by radically transforming muscle-cell architecture into a 'nurse cell'; host immune responses help expel adult intestinal worms but have little effect on muscle larvae. Migrating larvae provoke a marked local and systemic hypersensitivity reaction with eosinophilia. In visceral larva migrans, ingested Toxocara eggs hatch, penetrate the gut, and disseminate to liver, lungs, CNS, and other tissues, eliciting intense eosinophilic granulomatous inflammation. In cutaneous larva migrans, animal hookworm larvae penetrate skin and burrow along the dermal-epidermal junction. In angiostrongyliasis, ingested infective larvae migrate to the brain and die there, inciting eosinophilic inflammation, hemorrhage, necrosis, and granuloma formation. In gnathostomiasis, aberrant migration of a single larva into cutaneous, visceral, neural, or ocular tissue causes local inflammation, including ascending migration along nerve tracts producing myeloencephalitis (Harrison 22e p.1810-1813). Most lightly infected trichinellosis patients recover uneventfully, with symptoms peaking near 3 weeks and subsiding gradually over a prolonged convalescence; heavy infections can be life-threatening, with death usually due to myocarditis. Most visceral larva migrans infections are self-limited (rare deaths from severe organ involvement). Cutaneous larva migrans self-resolves over weeks to a couple of months as the larvae die. Cerebral angiostrongyliasis is usually self-limited with complete recovery, though heavy infections can leave permanent neurologic sequelae or cause death. Gnathostomiasis cutaneous swellings can recur intermittently over years; CNS gnathostomiasis is a serious complication and cerebral involvement is often fatal (Harrison 22e p.1811-1813). Trichinellosis severity correlates with muscle larval burden: light/asymptomatic infection <10 larvae per gram of muscle; heavy, potentially life-threatening infection >50 larvae per gram of muscle. Clinically graded as mild, moderate, and severe (severe = significant myositis/myocarditis) per Harrison's tissue nematode framework (Harrison 22e p.1811-1812).

Trichodysplasia spinulosa (polyomavirus) — trichodysplasia spinulosa polyomavirus infection, TSPyV infection, viral-associated trichodysplasia, pilomatrix dysplasia Lichen spinulosus and keratosis pilaris Multiple trichoepitheliomas or other adnexal tumours Follicular mycosis fungoides Phrynoderma (vitamin A deficiency) and other follicular hyperkeratoses Sarcoidosis or other granulomatous facial dermatoses Drug-induced follicular eruptions in transplant recipients Skin biopsy with histopathology of dystrophic follicles and abnormal inner root sheath proliferation Electron microscopy demonstrating intranuclear polyomavirus particles PCR for trichodysplasia spinulosa polyomavirus DNA from skin or spines Review of the immunosuppressive regimen and degree of net immunosuppression Assessment of underlying transplant or haematological condition Dermatological examination to map the extent of facial and hair involvement A rare skin disorder caused by the trichodysplasia spinulosa polyomavirus, which infects the inner root sheath cells of hair follicles It occurs almost exclusively in immunocompromised patients, particularly solid-organ transplant recipients and those on intensive immunosuppression for haematological disease The characteristic finding is numerous folliculocentric papules bearing keratinous spines, concentrated on the central face, especially the nose, eyebrows, and ears Progressive involvement produces a thickened, spiny (leonine) facial appearance with loss of eyebrow and eyelash hair (madarosis) and alopecia Histology shows dystrophic, enlarged hair follicles with abnormally proliferating inner root sheath cells containing trichohyaline granules and viral inclusions Diagnosis is supported by skin biopsy, electron microscopy showing polyomavirus particles, and PCR detection of the trichodysplasia spinulosa polyomavirus Management centres on reducing immunosuppression where possible, with topical antiviral or retinoid therapy reported to help; it can regress as immune function recovers Rapidly progressive facial disfigurement and hair loss Extensive disease indicating heavy net immunosuppression Diagnostic uncertainty raising concern for a follicular malignancy Secondary bacterial infection of affected skin Mistaking the facial papules for keratosis pilaris or a benign follicular disorder and missing the diagnosis Failing to link the eruption to the patient's immunosuppression Not obtaining a biopsy or molecular testing to confirm the polyomavirus Overlooking the potential for regression on reducing immunosuppression and pursuing unnecessary aggressive treatment Trichodysplasia spinulosa is driven by active replication of a specific human polyomavirus that is probably acquired asymptomatically and remains latent in the skin of most people. When cell-mediated immunity is suppressed, as after organ transplantation, the virus reactivates and productively infects the inner root sheath cells of hair follicles. Uncontrolled viral replication drives abnormal proliferation and differentiation of these cells, with excessive accumulation of trichohyaline and formation of keratinous spines that protrude from distended, dystrophic follicles. The follicular architecture is disrupted, producing the spiny papules, facial thickening, and loss of hair characteristic of the condition. Because the disease depends on the failure of immune control, restoring immune function or reducing immunosuppression typically allows the follicular changes to regress. The condition is disfiguring but not life-threatening, and it commonly improves or regresses when immunosuppression is reduced or immune function recovers; without such change it tends to persist and progress.

Trichoepithelioma — trichoepithelioma, multiple familial trichoepithelioma, epithelioma adenoides cysticum Basal cell carcinoma (especially the keratotic and infiltrative types) Cylindroma Trichoblastoma Desmoplastic trichoepithelioma versus microcystic adnexal carcinoma Syringoma Angiofibromas (as in tuberous sclerosis) for facial papules Skin examination noting central-facial symmetry and multiplicity Skin biopsy with histopathology showing horn cysts and papillary mesenchymal bodies Immunohistochemistry (for example CD10 and other markers) to distinguish from basal cell carcinoma Family history and examination for cylindromas and spiradenomas CYLD genetic testing when multiple familial trichoepithelioma or Brooke-Spiegler syndrome is suspected A benign tumour of follicular (hair-germ) differentiation, presenting as skin-coloured firm papules or nodules The multiple familial form clusters symmetrically on the central face, especially the nasolabial folds, nose, and forehead, appearing around puberty Multiple familial trichoepithelioma is linked to CYLD mutations and overlaps with Brooke-Spiegler syndrome and familial cylindromatosis The chief diagnostic challenge is distinguishing it histologically from basal cell carcinoma, which it closely mimics Helpful discriminators favouring trichoepithelioma include papillary mesenchymal bodies, a fibrocytic stroma, absence of a peritumoural cleft, and stromal amyloid Immunohistochemistry, for example CD10 stromal versus tumoural patterns and other markers, can aid the distinction from basal cell carcinoma in difficult cases Solitary lesions are usually excised, while multiple facial lesions are managed for cosmetic reasons and tend to recur A solitary lesion enlarging, ulcerating, or behaving aggressively, raising concern for basal cell carcinoma New infiltrative or destructive change in a previously stable lesion Family clustering of adnexal tumours indicating a hereditary CYLD syndrome Overdiagnosing basal cell carcinoma on a superficial or partial biopsy and pursuing unnecessary aggressive treatment Conversely, dismissing a genuine basal cell carcinoma as a trichoepithelioma Missing the hereditary CYLD context in patients with multiple facial lesions Confusing desmoplastic trichoepithelioma with microcystic adnexal carcinoma on limited tissue Trichoepithelioma is a benign adnexal neoplasm derived from hair-germ (follicular) epithelium. It is composed of basaloid cells arranged in nests and cords with follicular differentiation, characteristically forming keratin-filled horn cysts and papillary mesenchymal bodies within a cellular fibrocytic stroma. The multiple familial variant arises from germline loss-of-function mutations in the CYLD tumour-suppressor gene, the same gene underlying cylindromas and spiradenomas, so it forms part of the CYLD-related spectrum with Brooke-Spiegler syndrome; loss of CYLD deregulates nuclear factor-kappa B signalling and promotes follicular tumour formation. Although architecturally and cytologically it resembles basal cell carcinoma, it lacks the aggressive infiltrative and destructive behaviour of that malignancy. Trichoepitheliomas are benign with an excellent prognosis; solitary lesions are cured by excision, whereas multiple familial lesions persist and recur and cause cosmetic morbidity. Malignant transformation is rare.

Trichomoniasis — trich, Trichomonas vaginalis infection, trichomonal vaginitis Bacterial vaginosis Vulvovaginal candidiasis Gonococcal or chlamydial cervicitis Atrophic vaginitis Non-specific urethritis in men Bacterial vaginosis with malodorous discharge Candida vulvovaginitis causing itch and discharge Chlamydial or gonococcal cervicitis or urethritis Mycoplasma genitalium urethritis Saline wet-mount microscopy for motile trophozoites and increased polymorphs Nucleic acid amplification testing of vaginal or urethral specimens as the most sensitive method Vaginal pH and whiff testing to help distinguish from bacterial vaginosis Concurrent screening for HIV, syphilis, gonorrhoea and chlamydia Culture in selective medium where molecular testing is unavailable Caused by the flagellated protozoan Trichomonas vaginalis and spread almost exclusively through sexual contact, so it should prompt screening for other sexually transmitted infections Women often present with a malodorous, frothy yellow-green discharge, vulvovaginal itching and dysuria, though a large proportion are asymptomatic The classic 'strawberry cervix' (punctate cervical haemorrhages) is highly suggestive but seen in only a minority of cases Most infected men are asymptomatic carriers but may develop urethritis, making partner treatment essential to prevent reinfection Diagnosis is traditionally by observing motile trophozoites on saline wet mount, but nucleic acid amplification testing is far more sensitive and is now preferred where available Treatment is with an oral nitroimidazole (metronidazole or tinidazole); partners should be treated simultaneously and intercourse avoided until both complete therapy Infection in pregnancy is associated with preterm birth and low birth weight, and it increases susceptibility to HIV acquisition and transmission Infection during pregnancy given the association with preterm delivery and low birth weight Persistent symptoms after treatment suggesting reinfection or nitroimidazole resistance Coexisting HIV infection or features suggesting other serious sexually transmitted disease Signs of pelvic inflammatory disease indicating an alternative or additional pathogen Relying on wet-mount microscopy alone, which misses many infections because of its limited sensitivity Treating the index patient without treating sexual partners, leading to reinfection Overlooking asymptomatic infection, particularly in men, who sustain transmission Failing to screen for coexisting sexually transmitted infections and HIV Trichomonas vaginalis is an anaerobic, flagellated protozoan that adheres to and damages squamous epithelium of the urogenital tract. Cytoadherence and release of proteinases and other virulence factors trigger a local inflammatory response with neutrophil infiltration, producing the characteristic discharge and mucosal microhaemorrhages. The resulting disruption of the epithelial barrier and mucosal inflammation facilitates acquisition and shedding of HIV and other pathogens. The organism cannot survive long outside a moist environment, which underlies its predominantly sexual mode of transmission. With appropriate nitroimidazole therapy and simultaneous partner treatment the cure rate is high; recurrence usually reflects reinfection or non-adherence rather than true drug resistance, which is uncommon but increasingly recognised.

Trichorhinophalangeal syndrome — TRPS, Langer-Giedion syndrome (TRPS type II), trichorhinophalangeal syndrome types I-III, TRPS1 Acrodysostosis and other acromelic dysplasias Ectodermal dysplasias with sparse hair Multiple hereditary exostoses (isolated EXT1/EXT2) Brachydactyly syndromes Cartilage-hair hypoplasia Peripheral dysostosis of other causes Hand and skeletal radiographs demonstrating cone-shaped epiphyses TRPS1 molecular genetic testing Chromosomal microarray or deletion analysis for suspected Langer-Giedion syndrome Hip imaging for degenerative or Perthes-like change Developmental assessment where type II is suspected Dermatological and hair assessment The name captures the triad of hair (tricho-), nose (rhino-), and digit (phalangeal) abnormalities Characteristic features are sparse, slow-growing scalp hair, a bulbous pear-shaped nose, and a long flat philtrum The hallmark radiographic finding is cone-shaped epiphyses of the phalanges, leading to shortened fingers and deviation of the digits Type I is caused by TRPS1 variants; type III is a more severe TRPS1 phenotype with pronounced brachydactyly and short stature Type II (Langer-Giedion syndrome) results from a contiguous deletion involving TRPS1 and the adjacent EXT1 gene, adding multiple cartilaginous exostoses and intellectual disability Premature degenerative joint disease of the hands and hips can develop Hip abnormalities resembling Perthes disease may occur Diagnosis is clinical and radiographic, confirmed by TRPS1 testing or deletion analysis; management is supportive and orthopaedic Nerve or spinal-cord compression from exostoses in Langer-Giedion syndrome Malignant transformation of an exostosis (rare) with new pain or growth Progressive disabling hip or hand arthropathy Significant developmental delay prompting evaluation for type II Overlooking the diagnostic cone-shaped epiphyses on hand radiographs Failing to distinguish type II (contiguous deletion with exostoses) from types I and III Attributing the sparse hair to an isolated ectodermal disorder Not arranging surveillance of exostoses in Langer-Giedion syndrome Trichorhinophalangeal syndrome is caused by loss of function of TRPS1, a zinc-finger transcription factor that regulates chondrocyte and perichondrial development and other aspects of skeletal and ectodermal patterning. Reduced TRPS1 activity disturbs growth-plate function, producing the characteristic cone-shaped epiphyses, brachydactyly, short stature, and hip abnormalities, and also affects hair follicle development, giving the sparse fine hair. Type I arises from intragenic TRPS1 variants, while type III reflects variants with a more severe skeletal effect. Type II (Langer-Giedion syndrome) is a contiguous gene deletion that removes both TRPS1 and the neighbouring EXT1 gene, so the exostoses and cognitive impairment reflect loss of EXT1 in addition to the TRPS1 phenotype. Life expectancy is normal; morbidity arises from short stature, hand deformity, and early degenerative joint disease, with additional risks from exostoses and cognitive impairment in the Langer-Giedion form.

Trichorrhexis nodosa — TN, hair-shaft nodal defect Pili torti, with twisting but no nodes Monilethrix, with regular beading Trichoschisis and trichothiodystrophy Weathering of the hair tip Other causes of hair fragility and breakage Light microscopy of the shaft showing paired brush-like fracture ends at the nodes Trichoscopy demonstrating nodes and transverse fractures Detailed hair-care and cosmetic-processing history Metabolic screening, for example for argininosuccinic aciduria, where a congenital cause is suspected Assessment for associated hair-shaft syndromes or systemic disease A
