accompany metabolic disorders such as argininosuccinic aciduria and other hair-shaft syndromes Trichoscopy shows the nodes and transverse fractures with brush-like broken ends Proximal trichorrhexis nodosa is more common in afro-textured hair and with certain metabolic conditions Management focuses on eliminating traumatic hair practices and treating any underlying disorder, and hair usually recovers once trauma stops in acquired cases Widespread congenital fragility suggesting an underlying metabolic or genetic disorder Associated developmental or neurological features Failure to improve despite stopping trauma, prompting a search for an inherent shaft defect Attributing breakage to hair loss rather than a shaft defect and so missing the true cause Overlooking an underlying metabolic disorder in congenital cases Not taking a full cosmetic and grooming history in acquired disease Failing to examine the shaft microscopically to confirm the diagnosis Trichorrhexis nodosa arises when the protective cuticle is disrupted, exposing the cortex, whose fibres then splay apart to form the characteristic nodes and fracture transversely. It may reflect an inherent weakness of the shaft, as in inherited metabolic disorders affecting keratin sulphur content or amino-acid metabolism, or, more often, cumulative physical and chemical trauma from grooming, heat and cosmetic processing acting on normal or vulnerable hair. The result is localised structural failure and breakage. Acquired distal trichorrhexis nodosa usually recovers once traumatic practices cease, whereas congenital or metabolic-associated forms depend on the underlying disorder and may be more persistent.

Trichostrongyliasis — Trichostrongylus infection, trichostrongylosis, pseudohookworm infection Hookworm infection (Ancylostoma or Necator), given similar eggs Strongyloidiasis and other intestinal nematode infection Giardiasis and other protozoal enteritis Irritable bowel syndrome or functional dyspepsia Other causes of eosinophilia with gastrointestinal symptoms Coeliac disease or another cause of mild malabsorption Stool microscopy for ova and parasites, with concentration methods Careful egg morphometry to distinguish from hookworm eggs Full blood count for eosinophilia and anaemia Larval culture of stool to confirm the species where required Repeat stool sampling in light infection Dietary and occupational history of exposure to livestock and raw vegetables Caused by Trichostrongylus species, small nematodes chiefly of herbivores, with human infection common in rural farming communities of Asia, the Middle East and elsewhere Acquired by ingesting infective larvae on contaminated vegetables and greens, in contrast to the skin-penetrating route of true hookworms Most infections are light and asymptomatic; heavier burdens cause abdominal pain, diarrhoea, nausea and, occasionally, mild anaemia Peripheral eosinophilia is common and may be the clue that prompts stool examination The eggs resemble hookworm eggs but are larger with more pointed ends, and can be mistaken for them on routine microscopy Treatment is with a benzimidazole anthelmintic such as albendazole, which is highly effective Prevention relies on adequate sanitation, avoiding use of animal manure on food crops and washing or cooking vegetables Significant anaemia in heavy or chronic infection Persistent diarrhoea with weight loss Symptoms unresponsive to appropriate anthelmintic therapy Coexisting malnutrition, particularly in children Misidentifying the eggs as hookworm and misdirecting management Missing light infections on a single stool sample Attributing eosinophilia to allergy rather than looking for intestinal helminths Overlooking the animal reservoir and manure exposure when advising on prevention Trichostrongylus species are small nematodes that normally parasitise the intestines of sheep, goats, cattle and other herbivores. Eggs passed in the faeces of these animals develop in soil into infective larvae that contaminate low-growing vegetables and herbage. Humans acquire infection by ingesting these larvae rather than through skin penetration. In the small intestine the larvae mature into adult worms that attach superficially to the mucosa, where light infections cause little harm. Heavier worm burdens produce localised mucosal irritation and inflammation with abdominal symptoms and diarrhoea, and chronic infection can contribute to mild blood and protein loss and anaemia. Eggs shed in the faeces return to the soil to continue the cycle, sustained by both animal reservoirs and human contamination. Prognosis is excellent, as infection is usually mild and clears readily with anthelmintic treatment; heavy chronic infection resolves once the worm burden is eradicated.

Trichothiodystrophy — TTD, sulphur-deficient brittle hair syndrome, Tay syndrome, ERCC2, ERCC3, GTF2H5 Xeroderma pigmentosum Cockayne syndrome Netherton syndrome Menkes disease and other hair-shaft dysplasias Congenital ichthyoses Other syndromic causes of brittle hair with developmental delay Polarised light microscopy of the hair shaft for the tiger-tail banding pattern Biochemical analysis of hair cysteine and sulphur content Molecular genetic testing including ERCC2, ERCC3 and GTF2H5 Functional DNA-repair assay in photosensitive forms MRI brain for dysmyelination Developmental, immunological and growth assessment Autosomal recessive multisystem disorder defined by sulphur-deficient brittle hair, frequently caused by variants in nucleotide excision repair genes such as ERCC2 (XPD), ERCC3 (XPB) or GTF2H5 Hair shows a diagnostic alternating light and dark banding (tiger-tail pattern) under polarised light microscopy The clinical spectrum is captured by the mnemonic PIBIDS: photosensitivity, ichthyosis, brittle hair, intellectual impairment, decreased fertility and short stature Photosensitivity occurs in a subset but, unlike xeroderma pigmentosum, is not associated with a raised skin-cancer risk Neurological features include developmental delay, ataxia and dysmyelination on neuroimaging Recurrent infections and a tendency to febrile illness are recognised, and some patients have features overlapping immunodeficiency Analysis of hair amino acid content demonstrates a low cysteine and sulphur level, supporting the diagnosis Diagnosis integrates the hair microscopy pattern, biochemical hair analysis, DNA-repair testing and molecular confirmation Recurrent or severe infections suggesting associated immune compromise Failure to thrive or feeding difficulty in infancy Progressive neurological decline Severe ichthyosis with skin barrier failure in the neonate Overlooking the diagnosis without polarised light hair microscopy Assuming photosensitivity implies xeroderma pigmentosum and a high cancer risk Missing associated immune deficiency and infection risk Attributing the brittle hair to an acquired or nutritional cause Trichothiodystrophy most commonly results from variants affecting components of the transcription factor TFIIH, which functions in both nucleotide excision repair and basal transcription. Impaired TFIIH activity reduces synthesis of cysteine-rich structural proteins of the hair shaft, producing the sulphur deficiency and brittleness, while defective repair and transcription in other tissues account for the neuroectodermal, cutaneous and developmental manifestations. Non-photosensitive forms arise from variants in genes affecting hair-specific structural or regulatory proteins. Outcome varies widely with severity, from early death in severe neonatal ichthyosiform presentations to survival into adulthood with milder disease. Recurrent infection contributes significantly to morbidity and mortality, and care is supportive.

Trichotillomania — hair-pulling disorder, trichotillosis, traumatic hair-pulling alopecia Alopecia areata, with smooth patches, exclamation-mark hairs and a positive pull test at margins Tinea capitis, with scaling, broken hairs and positive mycology Traction alopecia, which is marginal and tension-related Early scarring alopecia Congenital triangular (temporal) alopecia Trichoscopy to identify broken hairs of varying length, flame hairs and V-signs Mycological examination to exclude tinea capitis Scalp biopsy in equivocal cases showing pigment casts, trichomalacia and empty follicles without significant inflammation Psychological or psychiatric assessment for comorbid anxiety or obsessive-compulsive disorder Abdominal imaging if trichophagia with a bezoar is suspected A compulsive hair-pulling disorder producing irregular, often bizarre patches of incomplete hair loss with hairs broken at varying lengths within the same area Classically affects easily reachable rarely form a gastric trichobezoar, described in Rapunzel syndrome Trichoscopy shows broken hairs of differing lengths, coiled hairs, flame hairs, V-signs and hair powder, with preserved follicular pulling stops, though very prolonged traction may eventually scar Abdominal pain, a palpable mass or obstruction suggesting a trichobezoar (Rapunzel syndrome) Signs of significant underlying psychiatric distress or self-harm Loss of follicular ostia indicating secondary scarring from very prolonged pulling Mistaking the bizarre incomplete patches for alopecia areata and missing the behavioural cause Overlooking trichophagia and the risk of a gastric bezoar Confronting the patient or family unsympathetically, undermining engagement with behavioural therapy Attributing failure of regrowth to the diagnosis rather than considering secondary scarring Trichotillomania is a body-focused repetitive behaviour in which recurrent pulling, twisting or plucking of hair produces mechanical breakage of shafts and traumatic disruption of follicles. It is classified among the obsessive-compulsive and related disorders and often serves to relieve tension or anxiety. Because the follicles are mechanically injured rather than inflamed or destroyed, the ostia are preserved and regrowth occurs once the behaviour ceases, although very prolonged or forceful pulling can occasionally cause permanent follicular damage and secondary scarring. In young children the behaviour is frequently transient and resolves with reassurance and simple behavioural measures; in adolescents and adults it tends to be more chronic and relapsing, but the alopecia is reversible unless prolonged trauma has caused scarring.

with heavy burden Severe or persistent dysenteric symptoms despite treatment Expecting reliable cure from single-dose therapy, to which whipworm responds relatively poorly Overlooking whipworm as a cause of paediatric rectal prolapse Missing coexisting soil-transmitted helminths Attributing chronic colitis to inflammatory bowel disease without stool parasitology in endemic settings Trichuris trichiura eggs passed in faeces embryonate in warm, moist soil and become infective over several weeks; once ingested they hatch in the small intestine and the larvae mature as they move to the large bowel. The adult worm embeds its narrow anterior portion within a syncytial tunnel in the colonic epithelium while its posterior lies free in the lumen. Heavy worm burdens cause a chronic inflammatory colitis with mucosal oedema, friability and bleeding; the resulting colorectal inflammation, chronic blood loss and, in intense infection, mechanical and inflammatory effects on the rectum contribute to dysentery, rectal prolapse, anaemia and, in children, impaired growth and development. Light infections are benign; heavy infections respond to treatment with reversal of dysentery, anaemia and growth effects, although eradication may require repeated courses and reinfection is common without sanitation.

Tricuspid atresia — absent tricuspid valve Other single-ventricle lesions Pulmonary atresia with intact septum Ebstein anomaly Transposition with restricted pulmonary flow Other cyanotic congenital heart disease Echocardiography defining the atretic valve and associated defects Assessment of pulmonary blood flow and ductal dependence Electrocardiogram (left-axis deviation) Pre-operative anatomical imaging Single-ventricle pathway evaluation Congenital absence of the tricuspid valve with no direct connection between the right atrium and right ventricle It is a cyanotic lesion and a form of functionally single ventricle An obligatory atrial communication allows systemic venous blood to reach the left heart, and a ventricular septal defect or duct supplies pulmonary flow Degree of cyanosis depends on the amount of pulmonary blood flow, which may be duct-dependent The electrocardiogram often shows left-axis deviation with left ventricular dominance, unusual for a cyanotic newborn Management follows the single-ventricle palliation pathway culminating in a Fontan circulation Severe cyanosis from inadequate pulmonary blood flow (duct closing) Restrictive atrial septum impeding systemic venous egress Excessive pulmonary flow causing heart failure Failing Fontan circulation later in life Not maintaining ductal patency when pulmonary flow is duct-dependent Overlooking a restrictive atrial communication Misreading the unusual left-axis electrocardiogram Underestimating long-term Fontan complications In tricuspid atresia the absent tricuspid connection forces all systemic venous return to cross the atrial septum into the left atrium, where it mixes with pulmonary venous blood, producing cyanosis. The right ventricle is hypoplastic, and pulmonary blood flow depends on a ventricular septal defect, the arterial duct or associated lesions. Because a single functional (left) ventricle supports both circulations, the physiology and surgical approach follow the single-ventricle pathway, ultimately routing systemic venous blood directly to the lungs (Fontan). Staged single-ventricle palliation allows survival into adulthood for many, but the Fontan circulation carries long-term risks including arrhythmia, protein-losing enteropathy and circulatory failure.

Tricuspid regurgitation — tricuspid insufficiency Right heart failure of other cause Constrictive pericarditis Pulmonary hypertension Mitral valve disease with secondary effects Hepatic disease causing oedema and ascites Echocardiography grading severity and assessing the right ventricle and annulus Assessment of pulmonary artery pressure Evaluation for left-sided valve or myocardial disease Assessment for primary causes (endocarditis, carcinoid, leads) Right heart and hepatic assessment in chronic disease Backflow across the tricuspid valve, most commonly functional (secondary) from right ventricular or annular dilatation rather than primary valve disease Primary causes include endocarditis, rheumatic disease, Ebstein anomaly, carcinoid and device leads Signs include a raised jugular venous pressure with a prominent v wave, a pansystolic murmur that increases on inspiration, pulsatile hepatomegaly and peripheral oedema It is frequently associated with left-sided heart disease and pulmonary hypertension Severe chronic regurgitation leads to right heart failure and hepatic congestion Management addresses the underlying cause and pulmonary hypertension, with valve repair or replacement in selected severe cases Progressive right heart failure with congestion and ascites Severe pulmonary hypertension Endocarditis as a cause (fever, vegetations) Rapidly worsening functional status Overlooking treatable left-sided or pulmonary causes of functional regurgitation Attributing congestion and ascites to liver disease alone Delaying intervention until right ventricular function is severely impaired Missing endocarditis or carcinoid as a primary cause Tricuspid regurgitation most often arises secondarily when right ventricular pressure or volume overload, commonly from left heart disease or pulmonary hypertension, dilates the right ventricle and tricuspid annulus so the leaflets fail to coapt. Primary (structural) regurgitation results from direct valve damage. The regurgitant volume overloads the right atrium and ventricle, raising systemic venous pressure to cause hepatic congestion, ascites and peripheral oedema, and chronic overload progressively impairs right ventricular function. Prognosis depends heavily on the underlying cause and right ventricular function; significant secondary regurgitation is associated with worse outcomes, and intervention decisions are individualised.

Tricuspid Valve Disease — Tricuspid stenosis, Tricuspid regurgitation, TS, TR Mitral stenosis (frequently coexists and dominates the picture) Mitral regurgitation (murmur can be confused with TR without attention to respiratory variation) Constrictive pericarditis / restrictive cardiomyopathy as a cause of right-sided venous congestion Other causes of right heart failure with hepatic congestion and ascites Infective endocarditis of the tricuspid valve causing primary regurgitation Transthoracic echocardiography (Doppler) - assesses leaflet thickening/doming, transvalvular gradient, RA and IVC size, associated TR severity, mitral and LV/RV function, and PA pressure Continuous-wave Doppler of the TR jet velocity to estimate PA systolic pressure (may be blunted when TR is very severe) ECG for right atrial enlargement, RVH, prior inferior/RV MI pattern, atrial fibrillation, or preexcitation in Ebstein's anomaly Chest x-ray - RA and superior vena cava prominence with azygos engorgement in combined TS/MS; RA/RV enlargement in TR Real-time three-dimensional echocardiography and cardiac MR for difficult assessment of TR severity, PA pressures, and RV size/function Exercise testing to assess functional capacity in asymptomatic severe TR Cardiac catheterization - not routinely needed for TS assessment Carcinoid heart disease causing tricuspid leaflet retraction and regurgitation Ebstein's malformation and other congenital tricuspid deformities Myxomatous tricuspid valve prolapse Radiation-induced valve disease Endomyocardial fibrosis Tricuspid stenosis is far less common than mitral stenosis in North America and Western Europe, is usually rheumatic in origin, occurs more often in women, and essentially never appears as an isolated lesion (it is typically combined with mitral stenosis) (Harrison 22e p.2059). Hemodynamically significant tricuspid stenosis is seen in roughly 5-10% of patients with severe mitral stenosis, and rheumatic tricuspid stenosis is commonly accompanied by some tricuspid regurgitation; nonrheumatic causes of stenosis are rare (Harrison 22e p.2059). More than 85% of tricuspid regurgitation encountered clinically is secondary (functional), arising from tricuspid annular dilation and leaflet tethering in the setting of RV remodeling from pressure/volume overload, MI, or trauma rather than from intrinsic valve disease (Harrison 22e p.2060). New-onset atrial fibrillation, especially in older patients, can produce 'atrial functional' tricuspid regurgitation through atrial and annular remodeling (Harrison 22e p.2060-2061). Patients with severe tricuspid stenosis characteristically complain of relatively little dyspnea given the marked hepatomegaly, ascites, and edema present, because the right-sided obstruction limits pulmonary congestion (Harrison 22e p.2059). Tricuspid regurgitation is more often detected by inspecting the neck veins (prominent c-v waves with rapid y descent) than by cardiac auscultation (Harrison 22e p.2061). Carvallo's sign - inspiratory accentuation of the holosystolic murmur at the lower left sternal border - helps distinguish the murmur of tricuspid regurgitation from that of mitral regurgitation; it diminishes on expiration or during the Valsalva strain phase (Harrison 22e p.2061). The murmur of tricuspid stenosis resembles that of mitral stenosis but is best heard at the lower left sternal border/xiphoid, is most prominent in presystole during sinus rhythm, and increases with inspiration while decreasing during expiration and Valsalva strain (Harrison 22e p.2060). In tricuspid stenosis with sinus rhythm, the right atrial a wave can be enormous (approaching RV systolic pressure) and the y descent is prolonged; presystolic pulsations of an enlarged liver may also be palpable (Harrison 22e p.2059). On ECG, absence of right ventricular hypertrophy in a patient with right-sided heart failure who is presumed to have mitral stenosis should raise suspicion for coexisting tricuspid valve disease; right atrial enlargement gives tall peaked P waves in lead II and prominent upright P waves in V1 (Harrison 22e p.2060). A distinct category of tricuspid regurgitation is caused by cardiac implantable electronic device (CIED) leads crossing the valve, producing leaflet entrapment or perforation; right ventricular apical pacing can additionally cause dyssynchronous contraction and functional TR (Harrison 22e p.2060-2061). Coexisting tricuspid stenosis can mask the hemodynamic and clinical features of associated mitral stenosis by lowering cardiac output and keeping left atrial, pulmonary artery, and RV systolic pressures only normal or mildly elevated (Harrison 22e p.2059). Severe hepatic congestion progressing to cirrhosis, jaundice, serious malnutrition, anasarca, and ascites in severe tricuspid valve disease Persistent right-sided failure after an adequate mitral commissurotomy, suggesting unrecognized tricuspid stenosis Progressive RV dilation and declining systolic function in severe TR Marked reduction in cardiac output with prominent c-v wave and rapid y descent and loss of the x descent in severe TR Tricuspid stenosis is easily overlooked because it almost always occurs alongside obvious mitral disease and its diastolic murmur resembles that of mitral stenosis - the diagnosis must be deliberately considered (Harrison 22e p.2059-2060). The TR murmur may be mistaken for mitral regurgitation unless its inspiratory accentuation and the degree of RV enlargement are appreciated (Harrison 22e p.2061). Accurate echocardiographic quantification of TR severity, PA pressure, and RV size/function is genuinely difficult in many patients (Harrison 22e p.2062). Continuous-wave Doppler estimation of PA systolic pressure can be falsely low when TR is very severe because the jet velocity is blunted by rapidly rising RA pressure (Harrison 22e p.2062). Tricuspid stenosis is defined by a diastolic pressure gradient between the right atrium and right ventricle that increases with inspiration (greater transvalvular flow) and falls with expiration. A mean diastolic gradient of about 4 mmHg is usually enough to raise mean right atrial pressure to levels causing systemic venous congestion - hepatomegaly, ascites, and edema. Resting cardiac output is typically depressed and fails to rise with exercise. In tricuspid regurgitation, the incompetent valve allows backward flow from RV to RA, with the regurgitant volume governed by RV systolic driving pressure and the size of the regurgitant orifice; severity is modulated by pulmonary artery systolic pressure, annular dimensions, respiratory changes in RV preload, and RA compliance. Significant TR enlarges the right atrium, raises RA and jugular venous pressures with prominent c-v waves, can 'ventricularize' the RA waveform, and leads to RV volume overload, dilation, and eventual systolic dysfunction - accelerated by any added pressure load from pulmonary hypertension or prior myocardial fibrosis (Harrison 22e p.2059-2061). Mild-to-moderate tricuspid regurgitation is generally well tolerated when there is no other hemodynamic disturbance. Because TR commonly coexists with left-sided valve lesions, LV dysfunction, or pulmonary hypertension, those conditions often dominate the clinical course. As isolated severe TR progresses, reduced forward cardiac output causes fatigue and exertional dyspnea, and declining RV function leads to cervical pulsations, abdominal fullness, anorexia, muscle wasting, weight gain, and painful lower-extremity swelling. Severe TR is associated with markedly reduced cardiac output and elevated mean RA and RV end-diastolic pressures (Harrison 22e p.2061-2062). Severe tricuspid stenosis is defined echocardiographically by a tricuspid valve area of 1 cm2 or less, or a pressure half-time of 190 ms or more; a mean diastolic gradient around 4 mmHg is hemodynamically significant. For tricuspid regurgitation, severity is staged (progressive Stage B, asymptomatic severe Stage C, symptomatic severe Stage D); annular dilation is defined as >40 mm (>21 mm/m2) on transthoracic echocardiography or >70 mm on direct intraoperative measurement, and severe TR is accompanied by hepatic vein systolic flow reversal (Harrison 22e p.2060-2062).

Tricyclic antidepressant overdose — TCA overdose, tricyclic poisoning, amitriptyline overdose, tricyclic antidepressant toxicity Other sodium-channel-blocking drug toxicity (some antiarrhythmics, carbamazepine) Anticholinergic poisoning from other agents Sympathomimetic toxicity Other causes of wide-complex tachycardia Hyperkalaemia causing QRS widening Serial 12-lead ECG focusing on QRS width and the aVR terminal R wave Continuous cardiac monitoring Arterial blood gas and serum electrolytes including potassium Capillary glucose and paracetamol/salicylate co-ingestant screen Creatine kinase if prolonged seizures or immobility raise concern for rhabdomyolysis Toxicity combines an anticholinergic toxidrome (dry flushed skin, dilated pupils, urinary retention, agitation, delirium) with the far more dangerous cardiovascular and neurological effects Sodium-channel blockade widens the QRS complex; a broad QRS is the key marker of cardiotoxicity and predicts arrhythmia and seizures A prominent terminal R wave in lead aVR is a supportive ECG sign of sodium-channel blockade Life-threatening features include ventricular arrhythmias, hypotension from myocardial depression and vasodilatation, seizures, and rapid deterioration in conscious level Intravenous sodium bicarbonate is the cornerstone treatment for a widening QRS, ventricular arrhythmia, or hypotension, working by sodium loading and alkalinisation Deterioration can be abrupt; a patient who looks well early can rapidly progress to coma, seizures, and cardiac arrest, so early cardiac monitoring is essential Class Ia and Ic antiarrhythmics are contraindicated as they aggravate sodium-channel blockade; refractory arrhythmia may be treated with additional bicarbonate and supportive measures Intravenous lipid emulsion may be considered as a rescue therapy in refractory cardiovascular collapse QRS widening on the ECG indicating significant cardiotoxicity Ventricular arrhythmia or haemodynamic instability Seizures or rapidly declining conscious level Refractory hypotension unresponsive to fluids Rapid clinical deterioration in a patient who initially appeared stable Being reassured by an initially well-appearing patient and delaying continuous cardiac monitoring Using class Ia or Ic antiarrhythmics, which worsen sodium-channel blockade Failing to give sodium bicarbonate promptly for a widening QRS or arrhythmia Allowing acidosis from seizures or hypoventilation to persist and aggravate cardiotoxicity Tricyclic antidepressants exert several toxic actions. Blockade of fast cardiac sodium channels slows myocardial depolarisation, widening the QRS and predisposing to ventricular arrhythmia and myocardial depression; this effect is worsened by acidosis. Anticholinergic (antimuscarinic) activity produces the classic peripheral and central anticholinergic features. Antagonism of peripheral alpha-adrenergic receptors causes vasodilatation and hypotension, and central effects plus GABA and other receptor actions lower the seizure threshold. Seizures worsen acidosis, which in turn intensifies sodium-channel blockade in a dangerous positive-feedback loop. Most deaths occur early from arrhythmia, refractory hypotension, or seizures, often before or soon after arrival; patients who reach hospital and receive prompt bicarbonate and supportive care and survive the first day generally recover well.

Trigeminal autonomic cephalalgias — TACs, trigeminal autonomic cephalalgia Trigeminal neuralgia, especially in relation to SUNCT and SUNA Migraine, which may have some autonomic features but a different phenotype Symptomatic trigeminal autonomic cephalalgia from a pituitary tumour, cavernous sinus or posterior fossa lesion or carotid dissection Primary stabbing headache Acute angle-closure glaucoma or other ocular and orbital pathology Sinusitis or dental pathology as non-neurological causes of facial pain MRI brain with dedicated pituitary and cavernous sinus views to exclude a symptomatic cause MR or CT angiography if arterial dissection or a vascular lesion is suspected Detailed headache diary documenting attack duration, frequency, timing and autonomic features A trial of indometacin where paroxysmal hemicrania or hemicrania continua is suspected Pituitary function tests if a sellar lesion is found or suspected Ophthalmological or ENT assessment to exclude a local cause of a red, watering eye A group of primary headaches characterised by strictly unilateral pain in the trigeminal distribution, usually the ophthalmic division, with prominent ipsilateral cranial autonomic features The group comprises cluster headache, paroxysmal hemicrania, short-lasting unilateral neuralgiform headache attacks (SUNCT and SUNA) and hemicrania continua Ipsilateral autonomic signs include conjunctival injection, lacrimation, nasal congestion or rhinorrhoea, eyelid oedema, forehead and facial sweating, miosis and ptosis, while restlessness and agitation are typical of cluster headache The subtypes are distinguished mainly by attack duration and frequency: cluster is the longest with circadian and circannual clustering, paroxysmal hemicrania has many shorter attacks per day, SUNCT and SUNA are very brief but very frequent, and hemicrania continua is continuous with exacerbations Treatment response is a defining clue, as paroxysmal hemicrania and hemicrania continua show an absolute response to indometacin, while cluster headache responds to high-flow oxygen and triptans with preventives such as verapamil SUNCT and SUNA can be triggered by cutaneous stimuli and may mimic trigeminal neuralgia, but the conjunctival injection and tearing help differentiate them A symptomatic (secondary) trigeminal autonomic cephalalgia, especially from a pituitary or posterior fossa lesion, must be excluded, so MRI including dedicated pituitary views is recommended, particularly with atypical features Accurate classification is essential because management differs markedly between the subtypes A new or atypical presentation, or a change in an established pattern, suggesting a secondary cause Persistent focal neurological deficit, visual field loss or a fixed Horner syndrome Features of raised intracranial pressure or a posterior fossa or sellar mass An unusual age of onset or accompanying systemic symptoms A painful red eye requiring exclusion of acute glaucoma Misdiagnosing cluster headache as migraine or sinusitis and delaying effective treatment Not performing an indometacin trial and missing an eminently treatable paroxysmal hemicrania or hemicrania continua Failing to image, including the pituitary, and overlooking a symptomatic trigeminal autonomic cephalalgia Confusing SUNCT or SUNA with trigeminal neuralgia and managing it incorrectly Overusing acute medications and precipitating medication-overuse headache The trigeminal autonomic cephalalgias arise from activation of the trigeminovascular system, referring pain to the ophthalmic trigeminal territory, together with activation of the trigeminal-autonomic (parasympathetic) reflex that produces the ipsilateral cranial autonomic features. Functional imaging implicates the posterior hypothalamus as a generator or permissive region, which underlies the striking circadian and circannual rhythmicity of cluster headache. Parasympathetic outflow via the sphenopalatine ganglion mediates the lacrimation and nasal symptoms, while associated sympathetic dysfunction produces the partial Horner features of ptosis and miosis. The trigeminal autonomic cephalalgias are typically chronic or relapsing conditions; with correct classification most respond well to targeted therapy, although some patients develop chronic or refractory disease requiring specialist or neuromodulation approaches.

Trigeminal Neuralgia, Bell’s Palsy, and Other Cranial Nerve Disorders — Tic douloureux, Idiopathic facial paralysis, Cranial neuropathy, Glossopharyngeal neuralgia, Cavernous sinus syndrome, Tolosa-Hunt syndrome Migraine and cluster headache (deep, steady pain rather than superficial stabbing; similar enhancement can occur in Lyme disease, sarcoidosis, and perineural malignant spread Electromyography for prognosis in Bell’s palsy (denervation evident after 10 days indicates axonal degeneration and a longer, possibly incomplete recovery) In atypical/uncertain facial palsy: testing for diabetes mellitus, Lyme serology, HIV serology, ACE level with chest imaging for sarcoidosis, and lumbar puncture if Guillain-Barré is suspected Lumbar puncture/CSF examination (mild CSF lymphocytosis may occur in Bell’s palsy; useful for meningeal/inflammatory causes) Laryngoscopy and chest/mediastinal imaging for vocal cord palsy to evaluate intrathoracic causes of recurrent laryngeal nerve injury Biopsy when granulomatous/infiltrative cavernous sinus or orbital apex disease (e.g., Tolosa-Hunt mimics, IgG4-related disease) is suspected Sarcoidosis (often bilateral facial palsy; cause of multiple cranial neuropathy) Tolosa-Hunt syndrome and other idiopathic granulomatous orbital/cavernous inflammation IgG4-related disease, granulomatosis with polyangiitis, and other vasculitides Lymphoma and metastatic/locally infiltrating tumors (nasopharyngeal carcinoma, neurofibroma, meningioma, chordoma, cholesteatoma) Melkersson-Rosenthal syndrome (recurrent facial palsy, recurrent facial/labial edema, fissured tongue) Diabetes mellitus, amyloidosis, and connective-tissue/collagen-vascular disease (e.g., Sjögren’s, SLE, scleroderma, MCTD) Skull-base and posterior-fossa structural lesions (acoustic neuroma, platybasia, basilar invagination, Paget’s disease, Chiari malformation) Carotid-cavernous fistula or carotid aneurysm Temporal bone fracture or blunt head injury Iatrogenic/traumatic injury (neck surgery, jugular vein cannulation, carotid endarterectomy/dissection, post-intubation Tapia syndrome) Trigeminal neuralgia produces brief (seconds to a minute or two) paroxysms of excruciating, superficial, stabbing pain usually in the lips, gums, cheek, or chin (V2/V3); ophthalmic-division (V1) involvement is rare. Attacks may be triggered by light tactile stimuli at facial, lip, or tongue trigger zones (washing, brushing teeth, a draft of air) and by speaking, chewing, or smiling. An essential diagnostic feature of classic trigeminal neuralgia is the ABSENCE of demonstrable objective sensory loss on examination; demonstrable trigeminal sensory or motor deficit instead points to a structural trigeminal neuropathy or secondary cause. Trigeminal neuralgia is relatively common (incidence ~4–8 per 100,000/year), affects mainly middle-aged and elderly persons, and roughly 60% of cases occur in women; bouts persist for weeks to months and tend to remit then recur. When trigeminal neuralgia occurs in a young adult or is bilateral, suspect multiple sclerosis (demyelinating plaque near the trigeminal root entry zone in the pons), especially if subtle facial sensory loss is present. Bell’s palsy is the most common form of facial paralysis (annual incidence ~25 per 100,000; lifetime risk ~1 in 60); onset is abrupt with maximal weakness by 48 h, often preceded by retroauricular pain for a day or two, and may include loss of taste and hyperacusis. A peripheral (lower motor neuron) facial palsy weakens the whole hemiface including the forehead and eyelid closure, whereas a supranuclear (central) lesion relatively spares the forehead and orbicularis oculi because upper-face muscles receive bilateral corticobulbar innervation. Localizing the seventh-nerve lesion: loss of taste over the anterior two-thirds of the tongue points to a middle-ear-segment lesion; hyperacusis indicates involvement of the nerve to stapedius; accompanying deafness, tinnitus, or vertigo suggests an internal auditory meatus lesion affecting the eighth nerve. Glossopharyngeal neuralgia resembles trigeminal neuralgia but is much less common; pain is paroxysmal and intense, arises in the tonsillar fossa/throat, may radiate to the ear, and is provoked by swallowing or coughing; rarely it triggers bradycardia/asystole, hypotension, and syncope. Anatomic clustering of cranial nerves yields recognizable syndromes: jugular foramen (IX, X, XI), cavernous sinus (III, IV, V1, VI), pontocerebellar angle (V, VI, VII, VIII), and retroparotid space (IX, X, XI, XII plus Horner’s). Cavernous sinus syndrome is frequently life-threatening: orbital/facial pain, orbital swelling, chemosis, fever, ophthalmoplegia (III, IV, VI), and V1 (±V2) trigeminal involvement—cavernous sinus thrombosis from facial/orbital/sinus infection (including mucormycosis in diabetics) is the most common cause and demands early diagnosis. Tolosa-Hunt syndrome (idiopathic granulomatous cavernous-sinus/orbital inflammation) causes painful ophthalmoparesis with V1/V2 numbness and shows a dramatic response to glucocorticoids, but its picture can be mimicked by sarcoid, vasculitis, IgG4-related disease, lymphoma, and fungal infection—so confirm before attributing to it. An eleventh-nerve (spinal accessory) palsy causes little overt neck weakness because other muscles assist head turning; detection relies on palpating absent sternocleidomastoid contraction during head turning and on noting a lower shoulder, scapular winging, and inability to abduct the arm beyond 90 degrees. Overlooking multiple sclerosis as the cause of trigeminal neuralgia in a young adult or when symptoms are bilateral. Mistaking a central (supranuclear) forehead-sparing facial weakness for peripheral Bell’s palsy and missing a stroke or hemispheric lesion. Failing to examine the eighth and other cranial nerves in a patient with facial palsy—the eighth nerve runs close to the facial nerve at the pontomedullary junction and in the temporal bone. Attributing an insidious, progressive facial weakness to Bell’s palsy when it actually reflects a temporal bone or pontine tumor. Missing Ramsay Hunt syndrome by not inspecting the external auditory canal and palate for zoster vesicles. Misdiagnosing vagal/laryngeal or pharyngeal muscle disease (polymyositis, dermatomyositis, myotonic dystrophy) as a primary vagus nerve lesion in dysphagia/dysphonia. Searching intracranially for an isolated vocal cord palsy when intrathoracic disease (aortic aneurysm, enlarged left atrium, mediastinal/bronchial tumor) is the far more common cause. Delaying recognition and treatment of cavernous sinus thrombosis, an early-diagnosis emergency. The cranial nerves are 12 paired nerves with mixed motor, sensory, and autonomic functions linked by their close brainstem relationships; nine connect directly to brainstem nuclei, while CN I and II are effectively brain fiber tracts and CN XI arises largely from upper cervical cord. In trigeminal neuralgia, symptoms arise from ectopic action-potential generation in pain-sensitive afferents of the fifth-nerve root just proximal to its entry at the lateral pons; demyelination of large myelinated (non-nociceptive) fibers renders them hyperexcitable and electrically coupled to adjacent small unmyelinated/poorly myelinated pain fibers, so tactile input can ignite paroxysms of pain. Compression of the root by a blood vessel—most often the superior cerebellar artery (or a tortuous vein)—is implicated in most cases; age-related brain sagging and increased vascular tortuosity may explain its predilection for later life. The trigeminal nerve carries oligodendrocyte-derived (central-type) myelin for up to ~7 mm beyond the brainstem, which may underlie trigeminal neuralgia in MS. In Bell’s palsy there is inflammation of the facial nerve with mononuclear cell infiltration suggesting an infectious/immune mechanism; reactivation of herpes simplex virus type 1 in the geniculate ganglion is thought to cause most cases, with varicella-zoster reactivation implicated in up to one-third (Ramsay Hunt syndrome). The vagus and other lower cranial nerves can be injured along their medullary, meningeal, foraminal, or extracranial courses; the recurrent laryngeal nerve (especially the left) is most often damaged by intrathoracic disease. Trigeminal neuralgia characteristically remits spontaneously after bouts lasting weeks to months, and remissions can be long-lasting, though the disorder ultimately recurs in most patients. In Bell’s palsy, about 80% of patients recover within a few weeks to months; incomplete paralysis during the first week is the most favorable prognostic sign, whereas EMG evidence of denervation after 10 days predicts axonal degeneration with delayed (typically ~3 months) and possibly incomplete recovery, and recurrences occur in roughly 7% of cases. Idiopathic trigeminal neuropathy usually recovers gradually. Most patients with isolated spinal accessory neuropathy recover. Post-intubation Tapia syndrome (vagal plus hypoglossal palsy) usually resolves within a few months. No formal grading scale is presented in this chapter. In Bell’s palsy, clinical severity is gauged by completeness of paralysis, with incomplete paralysis in the first week being the most favorable prognostic indicator and electromyographic denervation after 10 days indicating axonal degeneration and a worse, more prolonged recovery. The diagnosis of Bell’s palsy is supported clinically by a typical presentation, absence of other risk factors/symptoms, no zoster lesions in the ear canal, and a normal neurologic examination apart from the facial nerve.

Trigeminal trophic syndrome — TTS, trigeminal trophic ulceration, trophic ulceration of the nasal ala Basal cell or squamous cell carcinoma of the nose Cutaneous infection (including mucormycosis and atypical mycobacteria) Granulomatosis with polyangiitis and other vasculitides Pyoderma gangrenosum Factitious dermatitis (dermatitis artefacta) elsewhere Leprosy or other neuropathic ulceration Cutaneous leishmaniasis Skin biopsy of the ulcer edge to exclude malignancy and specific infection Microbiological cultures including fungal and mycobacterial studies MRI or CT of the brain and skull base to identify the underlying trigeminal lesion Vasculitis screen including ANCA where relevant Detailed sensory examination of the trigeminal territory Review of prior trigeminal procedures, zoster, or stroke history Characterised by a triad of trigeminal sensory loss, facial paraesthesia (often a crawling or itching dysaesthesia), and a self-induced ulcer, classically of the nasal ala The crescentic ulcer typically spares the nasal tip because the tip is supplied by a different sensory branch, an important diagnostic clue It follows damage to the trigeminal nerve or its ganglion, commonly after trigeminal ablative procedures for neuralgia, stroke, herpes zoster, or tumour The ulceration is caused by repetitive self-manipulation (rubbing, picking, scratching) of anaesthetic and paraesthetic skin rather than by primary tissue breakdown There may be a long latency, from months to years, between the nerve injury and the appearance of the ulcer Diagnosis is clinical but requires biopsy and investigation to exclude malignancy, infection, and vasculitis, which can mimic it Treatment centres on protecting the area and interrupting the itch-scratch cycle (barriers, behavioural measures, and neuropathic agents such as carbamazepine); surgical repair fails unless self-manipulation is stopped An indurated or non-healing ulcer suggesting malignancy requiring biopsy Rapidly progressive necrosis raising concern for invasive fungal infection Systemic features suggesting vasculitis A new intracranial lesion accounting for the trigeminal injury Mistaking the ulcer for a skin malignancy or infection, or vice versa, without biopsy Attempting surgical reconstruction without first controlling the self-manipulation Failing to recognise nasal tip sparing as a diagnostic clue Overlooking the often long latency between nerve injury and ulceration Not addressing the underlying trigeminal lesion or the paraesthesia driving the behaviour Trigeminal trophic syndrome develops after injury to the trigeminal nerve, ganglion, or its central connections, producing sensory loss and abnormal paraesthetic sensations in the affected dermatome. The disordered sensation drives compulsive rubbing, picking, and scratching of the numb skin, and this repetitive self-inflicted trauma to tissue that lacks protective sensation produces a chronic, painless ulcer, most often on the ala of the nose. Impaired trophic and sensory function of the denervated skin contributes to poor healing, but the primary driver is mechanical self-manipulation rather than an intrinsic ischaemic or infective process. Characteristic sparing of the nasal tip reflects its innervation by a separate nerve branch. The ulcer is chronic and notoriously difficult to heal because it depends on stopping self-manipulation of insensate skin; with effective protection and behavioural interruption of the itch-scratch cycle healing can occur, but recurrence is common and reconstructive surgery fails if manipulation continues.

bundle or digital nerve during release Trigger finger is a stenosing tenosynovitis at the first annular (A1) pulley. Thickening and fibrocartilaginous change of the pulley and of the flexor tendon or its sheath create a mismatch in size, so the tendon catches as it passes through. A nodule on the tendon may become trapped proximal to the pulley, producing the characteristic triggering, locking, and pain, with a mechanical block rather than a simple inflammatory process. Many cases resolve with splinting or a single corticosteroid injection, though recurrence can occur; response is poorer in diabetic patients and longstanding disease, and surgical release is highly effective when needed.

Trigger thumb — stenosing tenosynovitis of the thumb, pollex flexus Thumb metacarpophalangeal or interphalangeal joint osteoarthritis Flexor pollicis longus tendon rupture or partial laceration De Quervain tenosynovitis Sesamoid pathology at the thumb MCP joint Dupuytren nodule of the thumb ray Retained foreign body or infective flexor tenosynovitis Congenital clasped thumb in the paediatric setting Diagnosis is clinical from history and examination of triggering and the Notta node Ultrasound to confirm pulley thickening, tenosynovitis or a discrete nodule in equivocal cases Screening for diabetes mellitus in recurrent or multi-digit disease Thyroid function assessment where clinically suggested Plain radiographs if concomitant joint arthritis or bony pathology is suspected Inflammatory markers and rheumatoid screen when an inflammatory arthropathy is considered Documentation of triggering grade and interphalangeal joint range of motion Stenosing tenosynovitis of flexor pollicis longus at the first annular (A1) pulley, causing catching, locking or triggering of the thumb interphalangeal joint on flexion and extension. A tender palpable nodule (Notta node) is often felt over the A1 pulley at the metacarpophalangeal flexion crease of the thumb. Adult disease is most common in middle-aged women and is associated with diabetes mellitus, rheumatoid arthritis, hypothyroidism and repetitive gripping; diabetic triggering responds less well to conservative measures. Paediatric (congenital) trigger thumb typically presents as a fixed flexion deformity of the interphalangeal joint rather than true triggering, and a proportion resolve spontaneously in early childhood. Grading progresses from painful triggering, to demonstrable catching that self-corrects, to locking requiring passive release, and finally to a fixed contracture. First-line management in adults is activity modification, splinting and corticosteroid injection into the flexor sheath; injection is highly effective though less so in diabetics. Surgical A1 pulley release (open or percutaneous) is definitive for refractory or recurrent cases; the radial digital nerve to the thumb lies close to the sheath and is at risk. Persistent triggering after apparently adequate release should raise suspicion of an incompletely divided pulley or an unrecognised trigger at a more distal site. Fixed interphalangeal flexion contracture that will not passively extend Signs of infective flexor tenosynovitis (fusiform swelling, pain on passive extension, disproportionate tenderness) Loss of active interphalangeal flexion suggesting tendon rupture rather than triggering Sensory disturbance in the thumb suggesting digital nerve involvement Injecting or releasing without recognising an associated fixed contracture that requires additional therapy or splinting Injuring the radial digital nerve, which crosses obliquely near the thumb A1 pulley, during percutaneous release Dividing the oblique pulley in error, which can cause flexor pollicis longus bowstringing and loss of interphalangeal flexion power Attributing a locked thumb to triggering when the underlying problem is joint arthritis or tendon rupture Assuming poor injection response in diabetics reflects wrong diagnosis rather than expected reduced efficacy Trigger thumb arises from a size mismatch between flexor pollicis longus and the mouth of the fibro-osseous A1 pulley. Repetitive loading and shear at the pulley provoke fibrocartilaginous metaplasia and thickening of the pulley together with tenosynovial hyperplasia of the tendon, producing a localised nodule. As the thickened tendon segment is forced through the constricted pulley it catches, generating the characteristic triggering; progressive stenosis leads to locking and, ultimately, a fixed flexion contracture. Systemic conditions such as diabetes mellitus promote glycation and matrix changes that predispose to and perpetuate the stenosis. Generally excellent; most adults respond to corticosteroid injection and the majority of the remainder are cured by A1 pulley release, while a substantial proportion of congenital cases resolve spontaneously or after release. Diabetic patients have higher recurrence and lower injection success.

the usual presentation is a thumb held flexed at the interphalangeal joint, sometimes discovered when the child cannot straighten it It is often bilateral, so both thumbs should be examined; the differential includes a congenital clasped thumb and a thumb-in-palm deformity Many cases resolve spontaneously, particularly in the youngest children, so a period of observation with or without stretching and splinting is reasonable Persistent fixed deformity is treated by surgical release of the A1 pulley, which is highly effective and durable A thumb that cannot be passively extended, suggesting a fixed contracture rather than simple triggering Atypical features suggesting a neurological or syndromic cause Multiple-digit involvement raising suspicion of a metabolic storage disorder (such as a mucopolysaccharidosis) Assuming the condition is present from birth and labelling it congenital, when it usually appears later Confusing it with a congenital clasped thumb, which is an extensor problem Operating too early, before allowing a reasonable chance of spontaneous resolution Injuring the digital nerves, which lie close to the A1 pulley, during release The condition arises from a mismatch between the flexor pollicis longus tendon and the mouth of the A1 pulley at the base of the thumb. Thickening of the tendon, forming the palpable Notta's node, together with relative narrowing of the pulley, impedes smooth gliding so that the thumb catches or becomes locked in flexion at the interphalangeal joint. Because the deformity is commonly absent at birth and only appears later in infancy or early childhood, it is regarded as a developmental or acquired stenosing tenosynovitis rather than a truly congenital anomaly. A substantial proportion resolve spontaneously, especially when identified in infancy; for thumbs that remain fixed, release of the A1 pulley gives reliable and lasting correction with a low complication rate.

treatment Dismissing the complaint as poor hygiene or a psychiatric symptom without objective testing Failing to standardise precursor intake before measuring the trimethylamine/TMAO ratio Overlooking metabolised by gut bacteria to trimethylamine, a volatile compound with a strong fishy smell. The hepatic enzyme flavin-containing monooxygenase 3 normally oxidises absorbed trimethylamine to the non-odorous trimethylamine N-oxide, which is excreted. When FMO3 activity is deficient, unoxidised trimethylamine accumulates and is excreted in sweat, urine, and breath, producing the characteristic odour. The condition is a metabolic capacity defect rather than a toxic disorder, so it causes social and emotional morbidity rather than organ damage. The disorder is medically benign with a normal lifespan, but the persistent odour can cause considerable psychosocial distress. Symptoms are often controllable with dietary and hygiene measures, though not fully curable.

Triosephosphate isomerase deficiency — TPI deficiency, triose phosphate isomerase deficiency, TPI1 gene Pyruvate kinase deficiency Glucose phosphate isomerase deficiency with neuromuscular features Congenital neurodegenerative and mitochondrial disorders Autoimmune haemolytic anaemia Other severe glycolytic enzymopathies Hereditary spastic paraplegia and motor neurone disorders of infancy Red-cell triosephosphate isomerase enzyme assay Measurement of red-cell dihydroxyacetone phosphate accumulation Full blood count, reticulocytes and blood film Haemolysis screen with bilirubin, lactate dehydrogenase and haptoglobin Neurological assessment with neurophysiology and imaging Molecular testing of the TPI1 gene The most severe of the glycolytic enzymopathies, combining chronic non-spherocytic haemolytic anaemia with progressive neuromuscular disease Inherited as an autosomal recessive trait, frequently with consanguinity, and most patients present in infancy A progressive neurological syndrome with spasticity, dystonia, tremor and motor neurone-type weakness typically emerges after the first months of life Recurrent infections and increased susceptibility to bacterial illness are characteristic and contribute to early mortality Cardiac involvement and sudden death may occur, adding to the poor prognosis The metabolic hallmark is a marked accumulation of dihydroxyacetone phosphate in red cells, with reduced enzyme activity on assay and a confirmatory TPI1 mutation Management is supportive with transfusion, folate and vigilant treatment of infections; no disease-modifying therapy exists and splenectomy offers limited benefit Progressive neuromuscular deterioration with respiratory compromise Recurrent or severe bacterial infections Cardiac involvement predisposing to sudden death Severe neonatal jaundice requiring exchange transfusion Aplastic crisis after parvovirus B19 infection Focusing on the anaemia while missing the emerging neuromuscular syndrome Underestimating infection risk and delaying antimicrobial treatment Expecting splenectomy to substantially alter the systemic disease Failing to offer genetic counselling given the recessive inheritance and severe phenotype Triosephosphate isomerase interconverts dihydroxyacetone phosphate and glyceraldehyde-3-phosphate, ensuring both triose phosphates feed into the ATP-yielding steps of glycolysis. Deficiency causes accumulation of dihydroxyacetone phosphate and a fall in glycolytic energy production; in the red cell this shortens survival to produce a chronic non-spherocytic haemolytic anaemia, while in neural and muscle tissue the same energy failure, together with toxic effects of the accumulated substrate, drives a progressive and often fatal neuromuscular disorder with heightened susceptibility to infection. The classic infantile form carries a poor prognosis, with progressive neurological decline, susceptibility to infection and frequent death in early childhood; rare milder variants with residual enzyme activity have a better course.

tripe palms — acanthosis palmaris, pachydermatoglyphy Hereditary or acquired palmoplantar keratoderma Malignant acanthosis nigricans (frequently coexists) Pachydermoperiostosis Hyperkeratotic hand eczema or palmar psoriasis Occupational or frictional keratoderma Keratoderma climactericum CT of the chest to identify lung carcinoma, especially with isolated disease Upper gastrointestinal endoscopy with biopsy for gastric carcinoma when acanthosis nigricans coexists CT of abdomen and pelvis for other primaries Skin biopsy showing hyperkeratosis, papillomatosis and acanthosis Sputum cytology or bronchoscopy where a lung primary is suspected Tumour markers directed by the suspected primary Characterised by thickened, velvety palms with exaggerated dermatoglyphics giving a ridged, honeycomb appearance resembling the surface of bovine foregut (tripe). Strongly paraneoplastic, with the great majority of reported cases occurring in association with an underlying malignancy. The tumour association depends on coexisting acanthosis nigricans: tripe palms with acanthosis nigricans most often signals gastric carcinoma, whereas isolated tripe palms more often signals pulmonary carcinoma. May be accompanied by the sign of Leser-Trelat and florid cutaneous papillomatosis as part of the same paraneoplastic spectrum. Yellowish keratotic thickening of the palm with accentuated ridges over the finger pulps is typical. Onset may precede diagnosis of the tumour and should trigger investigation for gastric and pulmonary primaries. Skin changes may regress with treatment of the underlying malignancy and recur with relapse. New tripe palms in an adult, particularly a smoker Coexistent acanthosis nigricans or the sign of Leser-Trelat Associated weight loss or systemic symptoms Rapidly progressive palmar thickening Mistaking tripe palms for chronic eczema or occupational keratoderma Not tailoring the tumour search to whether acanthosis nigricans coexists (gastric versus lung) Missing an occult lung primary in a patient with isolated tripe palms Failing to recognise recurrence as a sign of tumour relapse Tripe palms share the growth-factor-driven mechanism of malignant acanthosis nigricans, with which they frequently coexist. Tumour secretion of transforming growth factor alpha, acting through the epidermal growth factor receptor, together with fibroblast growth factor and insulin-like growth factor 1, stimulates keratinocyte and dermal fibroblast proliferation. The result is marked palmar epidermal hyperplasia with accentuation of the normal dermatoglyphic ridges, producing the characteristic rugose, velvety surface. Tripe palms indicate an underlying, frequently advanced gastric or pulmonary malignancy; prognosis is that of the associated tumour and is often poor.

Phenotypic severity broadly increases with the number of extra X chromosomes, and mosaicism can attenuate the picture. Generally good; most individuals live independent lives with a normal lifespan, though learning and emotional support is often beneficial, and outcomes are better with earlier recognition and support.

Intellect is normal and the condition is non-progressive Management is supportive with physiotherapy, stretching and occasional surgical release of tendons or the temporomandibular apparatus Anticipated difficult intubation from restricted mouth opening Impaired dental hygiene and access leading to dental disease Feeding difficulty in infancy Progressive limitation of hand or jaw function Mistaking pseudocamptodactyly for a fixed joint contracture and misdirecting treatment Proceeding to anaesthesia without planning for the restricted mouth opening Overlooking the autosomal dominant inheritance in counselling Neglecting dental access problems caused by trismus Trismus-pseudocamptodactyly syndrome is caused by autosomal dominant variants in MYH8, which encodes perinatal myosin heavy chain expressed in developing and neonatal skeletal muscle. Abnormal myosin function alters muscle length and tone during development, leaving the long finger flexors and the muscles of mastication functionally short. The short flexor-digitorum tendons produce the characteristic wrist-dependent finger flexion (pseudocamptodactyly), while shortening around the temporomandibular apparatus limits mouth opening (trismus). Unlike true camptodactyly there is no fixed interphalangeal joint contracture, and the condition remains static after birth. The prognosis is good, with normal intellect and lifespan; symptoms are static and functional limitations from trismus and finger tightness can be improved with stretching, physiotherapy and, in selected cases, surgery.

normal blood karyotype without testing fibroblasts Missing the fall in blood mosaicism that occurs with age Overlooking the recognised association with haematological disease Underrecognising the diagnostic value of deep plantar furrows Trisomy 8 mosaicism reflects two cell lines, one with a normal chromosome complement and one carrying an extra chromosome 8, usually arising from post-zygotic mitotic non-disjunction. Because complete trisomy 8 is incompatible with survival, the viable phenotype depends on the proportion and tissue distribution of trisomic cells, which are highly variable and explain the wide clinical spectrum. The trisomic fraction detectable in blood often falls with age, so skin fibroblast analysis may be needed, and the tissue-limited nature accounts for the frequently milder-than-expected outcome. Fourth nerve palsy — trochlear palsy, superior oblique palsy Skew deviation Myasthenia gravis Thyroid eye disease affecting the inferior rectus Partial third nerve palsy Orbital floor fracture with inferior rectus restriction Ocular tilt reaction Orthoptic assessment with the three-step test and measurement of torsion Comparison with old photographs for a long-standing head tilt MRI of the brain and orbits when the palsy is not clearly traumatic or vasculopathic Vasculopathic risk-factor evaluation Acetylcholine-receptor antibody testing if myasthenia is possible Weakness of the superior oblique produces vertical and torsional diplopia that is worse on looking down and in, as when reading or descending stairs Patients typically adopt a compensatory head tilt away from the affected side to control the diplopia The Parks-Bielschowsky three-step test localises the palsy and shows worsening hypertropia on head tilt toward the affected side It is the commonest cause of vertical diplopia and, because the nerve is thin with a long course, is frequently caused by head trauma Congenital fourth nerve palsy is common and may decompensate in adulthood; old photographs showing a long-standing head tilt support this Bilateral palsies, often traumatic, cause alternating hypertropia and prominent torsion Additional neurological signs or other cranial neuropathies Bilateral palsy without a clear traumatic explanation Progressive deviation or associated headache Features suggesting skew deviation from posterior fossa disease Confusing a decompensated congenital palsy with a new acquired lesion Overlooking skew deviation as a mimic of vertical diplopia Missing subtle torsion that helps localise the palsy Attributing bilateral palsy to a unilateral cause The trochlear nerve supplies the superior oblique, which intorts, depresses and abducts the eye; its palsy leaves the eye relatively elevated and extorted with impaired depression in adduction. The nerve is uniquely long, thin and the only cranial nerve to exit dorsally after decussating, crossing the tentorial edge, which makes it especially susceptible to closed head injury. Microvascular ischaemia is another common cause, while congenital laxity or absence of the tendon can present later when fusional reserves that had compensated finally fail. Microvascular and many traumatic palsies improve over weeks to months; decompensated congenital and persistent palsies are well managed with prisms or superior oblique strengthening or other strabismus surgery.

excised valve tissue in a way that prevents molecular testing Using too short a course of antibiotics, risking relapse and neurological disease Tropheryma whipplei is a slow-growing, environmentally acquired actinobacterium that cannot be recovered on routine blood-culture media, which is why the endocarditis it causes is culture-negative. The organism is taken up by macrophages, in which it persists, and a subtle defect in host immune handling is thought to allow chronic infection. In cardiac disease the bacterium colonises heart valves, driving a low-grade inflammatory process that produces valvular vegetations and progressive tissue destruction, frequently on valves that were previously structurally normal. The characteristic histological finding is an accumulation of foamy macrophages containing periodic acid-Schiff-positive material within the valve tissue. Because the illness is indolent and often lacks fever or the gastrointestinal features of classic Whipple disease, it commonly presents late with valvular regurgitation and heart failure. With valve surgery where indicated and prolonged appropriate antibiotics the prognosis is generally favourable, but delayed diagnosis, extensive valvular destruction, or central nervous system involvement worsen the outlook, and relapse can occur if therapy is insufficient.

Microfilariae released into the circulation are rapidly cleared from the blood by an exuberant immune response and become trapped in the pulmonary vasculature and interstitium. There they trigger intense eosinophil recruitment and release of eosinophil granule proteins and inflammatory mediators, driven by a strong immunoglobulin E and antifilarial antibody response. This causes bronchospasm, alveolar and interstitial inflammation, and, if untreated, progressive interstitial fibrosis. With prompt antifilarial treatment most patients recover fully, but diagnostic delay or recurrent untreated episodes can result in chronic interstitial lung disease and irreversible pulmonary fibrosis.

infection before making the diagnosis Overlooking a remote history of tropical residence Neglecting to replace both folate and vitamin B12 alongside antibiotics Tropical sprue is an acquired malabsorptive disorder of the small intestine occurring in tropical regions, believed to follow an enteric infection that leads to persistent colonisation of the upper small bowel by abnormal coliform bacteria. This chronic overgrowth, together with resulting mucosal injury and impaired motility, damages the villi throughout the small intestine and impairs absorption of nutrients including folate and vitamin B12. Deficiency of these vitamins further impairs enterocyte turnover, perpetuating villous atrophy in a self-sustaining cycle until the abnormal flora and deficiencies are corrected. With appropriate antibiotic therapy and vitamin replacement the prognosis is generally excellent and relapse is uncommon once the patient has left the endemic area, though untreated disease can cause severe nutritional depletion.

SPART encodes spartin, a protein implicated in endosomal trafficking, epidermal growth factor receptor turnover, mitochondrial function, and lipid droplet regulation. Loss of spartin disrupts these processes within neurones, and the extensive functions of the protein are thought to underlie the additional developmental, cognitive, and somatic features that make this a complicated rather than pure form of HSP. Troyer syndrome progresses slowly; many affected individuals remain ambulant into adulthood, though gait, speech, and cognition decline gradually and disability increases with age.

from the common trunk Early surgical repair separates the pulmonary arteries from the trunk, closes the ventricular septal defect and interposes a valved conduit to the pulmonary circulation Early severe heart failure from unrestricted pulmonary overcirculation Signs of advancing pulmonary vascular obstructive disease Significant truncal valve regurgitation or stenosis with ventricular dysfunction Hypocalcaemia, immune deficiency or coexisting interrupted aortic arch in the DiGeorge spectrum Delaying repair and allowing fixed pulmonary vascular disease to develop Overlooking truncal valve dysfunction as a driver of ventricular failure Missing associated 22q11.2 deletion with its hypocalcaemia and immune risks, including the need for irradiated blood products Failing to detect a coexisting interrupted aortic arch Truncus arteriosus results from failure of the embryonic truncus to septate into separate aorta and pulmonary artery, leaving a single great vessel overriding a ventricular septal defect and receiving output from both ventricles. Complete mixing of systemic and pulmonary venous blood occurs at the trunk, so arterial saturation reflects the ratio of pulmonary to systemic flow. As neonatal pulmonary vascular resistance falls, blood floods the pulmonary arteries, causing marked pulmonary overcirculation, torrential left-to-right shunting and congestive heart failure with only mild cyanosis. The frequently abnormal truncal valve may be regurgitant or stenotic, adding to ventricular loading. Persistent high pulmonary flow accelerates pulmonary vascular obstructive disease, which becomes irreversible if repair is delayed. The lesion is strongly linked to 22q11.2 microdeletion. Without surgery the outlook is poor because of early heart failure and irreversible pulmonary vascular disease; with early repair survival is good, though conduit replacement and truncal valve problems commonly require reintervention.

Thrombotic microangiopathy (TTP/HUS) — Blood film (schistocytes) LDH, haptoglobin, bilirubin ADAMTS13 Haematological emergency — urgent plasma exchange Disseminated intravascular coagulation (DIC) — also gives thrombocytopenia and microangiopathy, but a consumptive coagulopathy predominates with prolonged PT and often prolonged aPTT (Harrison 22e p.967) Atypical/complement-mediated HUS (aHUS) as a distinct entity from TTP (Harrison 22e pp.800-801) Antiphospholipid antibody syndrome (Harrison 22e p.450) Heparin-induced thrombocytopenia and thrombosis (HIT) (Harrison 22e p.450) Monoclonal cryoglobulinaemia with intravascular thrombi (Harrison 22e p.450) Malignant hypertension affecting the renal microvasculature (Harrison 22e — listed among renal-microvascular causes of MAHA) Shiga-toxin-producing E. coli O157:H7 gastroenteritis (and other enterohaemorrhagic strains) preceding diarrhoea-associated HUS (Harrison 22e p.968) HIV infection, which is associated with a higher incidence of TTP (Harrison 22e p.968) ADAMTS13 activity level AND anti-ADAMTS13 inhibitor/antibody assay (activity <10% diagnostic of TTP) (Harrison 22e p.968) PT and aPTT — characteristically NORMAL in TTP/HUS; abnormal results point toward DIC (Harrison 22e p.967) Direct antiglobulin (Coombs) test — negative in MAHA (Harrison 22e p.638) Full blood count with platelet count and peripheral smear for schistocytes (Harrison 22e p.968) Reticulocyte count (reticulocytosis supports haemolysis) (Harrison 22e p.638) Renal function / serum creatinine and urinalysis (haematuria, proteinuria, granular or hyaline casts in HUS) (Harrison 22e p.638) Complement-regulatory gene testing (C3, CFB, CFH, CD46, CFI, THBD) and anti-factor-H antibody for suspected atypical HUS — though assigning pathogenicity to variants is difficult and no functional diagnostic assay is established (Harrison 22e pp.968, 800-801) Disseminated intravascular coagulation (distinguished by abnormal PT/aPTT and clotting-factor/fibrinogen consumption) (Harrison 22e p.967) Drug-induced microangiopathy — immune-mediated (ticlopidine, possibly clopidogrel, quinine) or by direct endothelial toxicity (cyclosporine, tacrolimus, gemcitabine, mitomycin C) (Harrison 22e p.968) Chemotherapy-/cancer-associated HUS (mitomycin and gemcitabine most often; also cisplatin, bleomycin, proteasome and VEGF inhibitors) (Harrison 22e p.638) Malignancy-induced HUS from microvascular metastases or extensive marrow invasion (Harrison 22e p.638) Bone-marrow / haematopoietic stem cell transplant-associated microangiopathy (Harrison 22e pp.638, 967) Pregnancy/postpartum-associated thrombotic microangiopathy (including HELLP in the obstetric context) (Harrison 22e pp.967-968) Systemic vasculitis (Harrison 22e p.967) The thrombotic microangiopathies are unified by microangiopathic haemolytic anaemia (MAHA): thrombocytopenia plus fragmented red cells (schistocytes) on the smear, biochemical haemolysis (high LDH, high unconjugated bilirubin, low haptoglobin) and microvascular thrombosis (Harrison 22e p.967). TTP was classically described as a pentad of MAHA, thrombocytopenia, renal failure, neurologic changes and fever; the full pentad is now seen less often because earlier diagnosis and treatment intervene before it evolves (Harrison 22e pp.967-968). ADAMTS13 activity below 10% is diagnostic of TTP; the assay (activity level plus anti-ADAMTS13 antibody) is central to working up any MAHA (Harrison 22e p.968). ADAMTS13 levels are generally normal in HUS, although they have occasionally been reported as decreased — so a normal ADAMTS13 does not exclude a thrombotic microangiopathy other than TTP (Harrison 22e p.968). Schistocytes are red-cell fragments produced by physical disruption against intravascular platelet/fibrin strands or external forces, and are the morphologic hallmark of MAHA (Harrison 22e p.~640). The Coombs (direct antiglobulin) test is negative in microangiopathic haemolysis, helping separate it from autoimmune haemolytic anaemia (Harrison 22e p.638). TTP is more common in women than men, and is over-represented in HIV infection and in pregnancy; congenital ADAMTS13 deficiency (Upshaw-Schulman) may first declare itself during a first pregnancy (Harrison 22e p.968). In a classic HUS presentation, a preceding episode of diarrhoea (often bloody) in a child points to Shiga-toxin-producing E. coli O157:H7 as the commonest, though not the only, cause (Harrison 22e p.968). Atypical HUS is essentially a complement-alternative-pathway disease — driven by mutations in complement components/regulators (C3, CFB, CFH, CD46/MCP, CFI, THBD) or anti-factor-H antibodies — and clinical disease usually requires a trigger such as infection, so penetrance is incomplete (Harrison 22e pp.800-801). New unexplained thrombocytopenia with MAHA is a haematologic emergency — TTP is devastating if not recognised and treated promptly (Harrison 22e p.968) Plasma exchange should be initiated urgently on clinical suspicion without waiting for confirmatory ADAMTS13 results, and likewise re-initiated promptly on suspected relapse (Harrison 22e p.968) Fluctuating neurologic abnormalities (especially headache and confusion) in the setting of MAHA suggest TTP (Harrison 22e p.450) Persistently low ADAMTS13 carries a greater risk of ongoing sequelae including stroke (Harrison 22e p.968) In cancer-/transfusion-associated HUS, severe hypertension, pulmonary oedema and rapid worsening of haemolysis and renal function can follow a blood or blood-product transfusion (Harrison 22e p.638) Do not reflexively transfuse platelets in TTP — platelet transfusion may fuel further microvascular thrombosis and is reserved for life-threatening bleeding (principle, Harrison 22e Chap. 120). Do not assume normal coagulation excludes a thrombotic microangiopathy: PT and aPTT are characteristically normal in TTP/HUS, whereas they are abnormal in DIC — use them to discriminate, not to exclude (Harrison 22e p.967). A normal ADAMTS13 does not point to TTP; ADAMTS13 is usually normal in HUS, so the diagnosis there rests on the clinical picture and complement work-up (Harrison 22e p.968). Atypical HUS is a diagnosis of exclusion; patients may be started on plasma exchange until ADAMTS13 returns and the diagnosis clarifies, even though plasma exchange has not been shown to change clinical outcomes in aHUS (Harrison 22e p.968). Plasma infusion/exchange does not alter the course of typical HUS or aHUS except in the subgroup with anti-factor-H antibodies (Harrison 22e p.968). Drug-induced microangiopathy may improve simply on withdrawing or reducing the offending endothelial-toxic agent, so reflexive long-term plasma exchange may be unnecessary (Harrison 22e p.968). Cancer-associated HUS can present without an evident malignancy — in one series 35% had no apparent cancer when the syndrome appeared, and it may surface weeks to months after the last chemotherapy dose (Harrison 22e p.638). TTP arises from deficient or antibody-inhibited ADAMTS13, the metalloprotease that cleaves von Willebrand factor (VWF). VWF is secreted by endothelium as ultra-large multimers; when these are not cleaved they persist and drive pathological platelet adhesion and aggregation, producing microvascular thrombi. ADAMTS13 deficiency alone is not sufficient — congenitally ADAMTS13-deficient individuals develop TTP only episodically, implying a second trigger. In HUS the dominant lesion is endothelial injury with deposition of fibrin in capillary/arteriolar walls, predominantly in the kidney; typical (diarrhoea-associated) HUS is driven by Shiga toxin from E. coli O157:H7, while atypical HUS results from dysregulated activation of the complement alternative pathway with consequent endothelial damage. The shared downstream picture is microvascular platelet/fibrin thrombi causing red-cell fragmentation (MAHA), consumption thrombocytopenia and end-organ ischaemia (Harrison 22e pp.967-968, 800-801). Plasma exchange transformed TTP outcomes, reducing mortality from roughly 85-100% to about 10-30%. Relapse is common: 25-45% of plasma-exchange-treated patients relapse within 30 days of apparent remission and 12-40% relapse late, with relapse more frequent in those with severe ADAMTS13 deficiency at presentation. In diarrhoea-associated HUS roughly 40% of children need some dialysis but overall mortality is <5%; non-diarrhoeal HUS carries higher mortality (~26%). Untreated atypical HUS had acute-phase mortality up to ~15% with up to 50% progressing to end-stage renal disease, though spontaneous remission occurs and relapse is likely with re-exposure to a trigger. Cancer-/chemotherapy-associated HUS has a high case-fatality rate, with most patients dying within months (Harrison 22e pp.968, 800-801, 638). Harrison does not give a formal TTP/HUS severity score in this material. Functional stratification used: ADAMTS13 activity <10% is diagnostic of TTP and severe deficiency at presentation predicts relapse and worse sequelae. HUS is grouped clinically into diarrhoea-associated (typical, Shiga-toxin) HUS versus non-diarrhoea-associated/atypical (complement-mediated) HUS, which carries higher mortality. (No PLASMIC score is described in the source and none is asserted here.) (Harrison 22e pp.968, 800-801).
