at the other are milder or isolated hypomyelination and the dominant dystonia syndrome DYT4 (whispering dysphonia with generalised dystonia and ataxia) Milder cases may show hypomyelination on MRI with little or no striatal atrophy, so imaging appearances range from pure hypomyelination to the full H-ABC pattern of a shrinking putamen and caudate Clinical features commonly include a movement disorder (dystonia, spasticity, chorea), cerebellar ataxia, dysarthria and variable developmental involvement Most disease-causing variants arise de novo and are dominant, though inherited variants (including the DYT4 variant) occur, so family history may be positive or negative Diagnosis is guided by recognition of a hypomyelinating pattern with or without basal ganglia and cerebellar atrophy, confirmed by TUBB4A sequencing There is no specific therapy; management is supportive and multidisciplinary, targeting dystonia and spasticity, communication, nutrition and physiotherapy Status dystonicus with severe dystonia, pain and metabolic disturbance Progressive dysphagia with aspiration and faltering growth Rapid neurological regression suggesting intercurrent illness or an alternative cause Respiratory compromise from bulbar and truncal involvement Not appreciating the breadth of the TUBB4A spectrum and expecting only the severe H-ABC picture Overlooking basal ganglia atrophy or, conversely, excluding the diagnosis when striatal atrophy is absent in milder cases Assuming autosomal recessive inheritance when most variants are de novo dominant Missing the DYT4 dystonia phenotype as part of the same gene's spectrum Failing to counsel families about recurrence risk, including germline mosaicism TUBB4A-related disease is caused by dominant variants in TUBB4A, which encodes a beta-tubulin isotype highly expressed in the brain. Tubulin heterodimers assemble into microtubules that are essential for cell shape, intracellular transport and division. Variant tubulin perturbs microtubule dynamics in oligodendrocytes and neurons; disrupted oligodendrocyte function impairs myelin formation to produce hypomyelination, while neuronal microtubule dysfunction contributes to degeneration of the striatum and cerebellum in more severe cases. The particular variant strongly influences where on the spectrum a patient falls, from isolated hypomyelination to full H-ABC. Prognosis varies markedly across the TUBB4A spectrum: severe early-onset (H-ABC) disease is progressive with substantial motor and cognitive disability and reduced life expectancy, whereas milder hypomyelination and the DYT4 dystonia phenotype can follow a more indolent course. The specific variant is the main determinant of severity and rate of progression.

Tuberculous meningitis usually develops when a subependymal or subpial focus (a Rich focus), seeded during earlier haematogenous dissemination, ruptures into the subarachnoid space. The released mycobacterial antigens provoke an intense inflammatory exudate that is most marked at the base of the brain. This basal exudate entraps cranial nerves, obstructs cerebrospinal fluid flow to cause hydrocephalus, and induces a vasculitis of perforating arteries leading to ischaemic infarction. The combination of inflammation, raised intracranial pressure and vascular compromise underlies the cranial neuropathies, strokes and depressed consciousness that characterise severe disease. Outcome depends heavily on the neurological stage at which treatment begins; early treatment offers good recovery, whereas presentation with coma, deficits or advanced stage carries high mortality and frequent long-term sequelae such as cognitive impairment, hydrocephalus and paresis.

spectrum and its impact on quality of life Tuberous sclerosis complex is caused by inactivating mutations in either TSC1, encoding hamartin, or TSC2, encoding tuberin. Together these proteins form a complex that inhibits the mechanistic target of rapamycin (mTOR) signalling pathway, which controls cell growth and proliferation. Loss of function releases this inhibition, leading to constitutive mTOR activation and the growth of benign hamartomatous lesions across multiple organs. Inheritance is autosomal dominant, though many cases are de novo, and lesion formation is consistent with a second somatic hit inactivating the remaining allele. The mechanistic understanding underpins the therapeutic use of mTOR inhibitors. Outcome is highly variable; many individuals live full lives, but epilepsy severity, cognitive impairment, and organ complications such as giant cell astrocytomas and renal or pulmonary disease determine morbidity and mortality.

tuberous sclerosis skin — cutaneous manifestations of tuberous sclerosis complex, tuberous sclerosis dermatological features Acne vulgaris or rosacea (mimicking facial angiofibromas) Isolated hypopigmentation such as naevus depigmentosus or vitiligo Birt-Hogg-Dubé syndrome (fibrofolliculomas) Multiple endocrine neoplasia type 1 with cutaneous collagenomas Neurofibromatosis type 1 with café-au-lait macules Idiopathic periungual fibromas from trauma Wood's lamp examination to highlight hypomelanotic macules Genetic testing for TSC1 and TSC2 mutations Brain MRI for cortical tubers, subependymal nodules and giant cell astrocytoma Renal imaging for angiomyolipomas and cysts Echocardiography for cardiac rhabdomyomas, especially in infancy Ophthalmological review for retinal hamartomas Cutaneous signs are among the earliest and most useful diagnostic clues to tuberous sclerosis complex and feature prominently in the diagnostic criteria. Hypomelanotic (ash-leaf) macules are frequently present from infancy and are best demonstrated under Wood's lamp examination. Facial angiofibromas develop over the nasolabial folds, cheeks and chin in childhood and are commonly mistaken for acne. A shagreen patch is a connective-tissue naevus, typically a raised plaque over the lumbosacral region with an orange-peel texture. Peri- and subungual fibromas (Koenen tumours) tend to appear later, around puberty and adulthood. A fibrous cephalic (forehead) plaque is a specific skin marker and may precede other features. The disorder arises from loss-of-function mutations in TSC1 or TSC2 with consequent overactivation of the mTOR pathway. Topical or systemic mTOR inhibitors can reduce facial angiofibromas and address systemic manifestations under specialist supervision. New focal neurological deficit or rising intracranial pressure suggesting subependymal giant cell astrocytoma Flank pain or haematuria indicating angiomyolipoma haemorrhage Respiratory symptoms in women suggesting lymphangioleiomyomatosis Refractory seizures or developmental regression requiring urgent neurological input Treating facial angiofibromas as acne and thereby missing the underlying diagnosis. Overlooking subtle hypomelanotic macules without Wood's lamp examination. Assessing skin in isolation and failing to arrange systemic screening once the diagnosis is suspected. Attributing a solitary skin finding to tuberous sclerosis without applying the full diagnostic criteria. Neglecting genetic counselling given the autosomal dominant inheritance and variable expressivity. Tuberous sclerosis complex is an autosomal dominant disorder caused by inactivating mutations in TSC1 (encoding hamartin) or TSC2 (encoding tuberin). The hamartin-tuberin complex normally inhibits the mechanistic target of rapamycin (mTOR) signalling pathway; its loss releases constitutive mTOR activation, driving unchecked cell growth and the formation of hamartomas across multiple organs. In the skin this dysregulated growth produces the characteristic lesions: hypomelanotic macules reflecting reduced melanogenesis, angiofibromas composed of fibrovascular proliferation, connective-tissue naevi (shagreen patches), and periungual fibromas. The same pathway underlies the systemic hamartomas of brain, kidney, heart and lung, which is why recognition of the skin signs prompts wider evaluation. Cutaneous lesions themselves are benign but can cause considerable cosmetic and psychological burden; overall prognosis is determined by systemic involvement, particularly neurological disease, renal angiomyolipomas and pulmonary lymphangioleiomyomatosis, and has improved with mTOR-inhibitor therapy and multidisciplinary surveillance.

Tubular aggregate myopathy (STIM1/ORAI1) — TAM, STIM1-related tubular aggregate myopathy, ORAI1-related myopathy, Stormorken syndrome spectrum, store-operated calcium entry myopathy Metabolic myopathies with exercise intolerance and cramps Limb-girdle muscular dystrophy Periodic paralysis and other channelopathies Congenital myasthenic syndrome Inflammatory myopathy Other causes of tubular aggregates such as periodic paralysis or drug/toxin exposure Serum creatine kinase Nerve conduction studies and electromyography Muscle biopsy with oxidative enzyme and Gomori trichrome staining and electron microscopy to demonstrate tubular aggregates Full blood count and bleeding assessment to detect thrombocytopenia in the Stormorken spectrum Muscle MRI to characterise involvement Genetic testing of STIM1 and ORAI1 and a broader myopathy panel Caused most often by gain-of-function variants in STIM1 or ORAI1, the key components of store-operated calcium entry; inheritance is usually autosomal dominant Presents with slowly progressive proximal limb weakness, muscle cramps, myalgia, and exercise intolerance, often from childhood or early adulthood STIM1 gain-of-function variants can cause Stormorken syndrome, a multisystem disorder combining myopathy with thrombocytopenia, bleeding tendency, miosis, and other features Creatine kinase is often mildly to moderately elevated and electromyography shows a myopathic pattern The defining biopsy feature is tubular aggregates, densely packed arrays of tubules derived from the sarcoplasmic reticulum, typically in type 2 fibres and best seen with oxidative and Gomori trichrome stains and electron microscopy Tubular aggregates are a non-specific reaction pattern that also occurs in other conditions, so genetic and clinical correlation is needed Assessment should include a platelet count and bleeding history given the Stormorken-syndrome association with STIM1 variants Diagnosis combines the myopathic phenotype, tubular aggregates on biopsy, and STIM1 or ORAI1 genetic testing Bleeding tendency or thrombocytopenia suggesting Stormorken syndrome Multisystem features such as miosis, asplenia, or ichthyosis in the STIM1 spectrum Rapidly progressive weakness atypical for the usual slow course Respiratory or cardiac involvement warranting evaluation Regarding tubular aggregates as diagnostic of a single disease when they are a non-specific reaction pattern Missing the associated thrombocytopenia and bleeding risk of Stormorken syndrome in STIM1 disease Overlooking a treatable alternative such as a metabolic myopathy or channelopathy Failing to confirm the diagnosis genetically after finding tubular aggregates on biopsy Tubular aggregate myopathy arises from dysregulated store-operated calcium entry, the process by which depletion of sarcoplasmic reticulum calcium is sensed by STIM1 and triggers calcium influx through the ORAI1 channel. Gain-of-function variants in STIM1 or ORAI1 cause constitutive or excessive calcium entry, leading to calcium overload and abnormal proliferation and packing of sarcoplasmic reticulum membranes that form the characteristic tubular aggregates. Disturbed calcium homeostasis impairs muscle function, producing weakness, cramps, and exercise intolerance, and the same pathway abnormality accounts for the platelet and other systemic features of Stormorken syndrome. Muscle weakness typically progresses slowly and most patients remain ambulant, giving a generally favourable neuromuscular prognosis; in the Stormorken-syndrome end of the STIM1 spectrum, the bleeding tendency and multisystem involvement add to morbidity and require additional management.

neither sensitive nor specific for AIN (Harrison 22e p.2438) Serum creatinine and BUN to assess azotemia (Harrison 22e p.2437) Anti-Ro (SS-A) and anti-La (SS-B) antibodies when Sjogren's syndrome suspected (Harrison 22e p.2438) Serum and urine protein electrophoresis and immunofixation, plus serum/urine free light chains, when light chain cast nephropathy suspected (Harrison 22e p.2440) Renal ultrasonography - 'medical renal disease' changes (increased echogenicity, loss of corticomedullary differentiation); asymmetric scarred kidneys in reflux nephropathy (Harrison 22e p.2437, p.2441) Kidney biopsy - not usually required for AIN diagnosis but shows interstitial/tubular leukocyte infiltration including eosinophils; required (with other criteria) for aristolochic acid nephropathy (Harrison 22e p.2438, p.2442) Acute tubular necrosis and other causes of unexplained AKI (biopsy-proven AIN accounts for no more than ~15% of unexplained AKI, likely an underestimate) (Harrison 22e p.2437) Primary glomerulonephritis causing secondary tubulointerstitial damage; in advanced disease the initial cause is often difficult to discern on biopsy (Harrison 22e p.2442) Behcet's disease and sarcoidosis as alternative causes of uveitis when considering TINU (Harrison 22e p.2439) Tubulointerstitial diseases primarily affect the tubules and interstitium with relative sparing of the glomeruli and renal vessels, and are divided into acute and chronic tubulointerstitial nephritis (TIN) (Harrison 22e p.2437). Classic allergic acute interstitial nephritis (AIN) presents with fever, rash, peripheral eosinophilia, and oliguric acute kidney injury occurring after 7-10 days of a beta-lactam (e.g., methicillin) - but this classic tetrad is the exception rather than the rule; patients are more often found incidentally to have a rising creatinine (Harrison 22e p.2438). Acute TIN most often presents as acute kidney injury; today AIN is far more often an allergic reaction to a drug than a postinfectious phenomenon (Harrison 22e p.2437). Urinalysis in allergic AIN shows pyuria with white blood cell casts and hematuria; white blood cell (leukocyte) casts are a characteristic finding of interstitial nephritis (Harrison 22e p.2438, p.2456). The mainstay of treatment for drug-induced AIN is discontinuation of the offending agent, which often leads to reversal of kidney injury; glucocorticoids may accelerate recovery but are NOT required in most cases and are reserved for severe injury (Harrison 22e p.2438). Chronic TIN is more indolent and manifests with disorders of tubular function: polyuria from impaired concentrating ability (nephrogenic diabetes insipidus), Fanconi's syndrome from defective proximal reabsorption (glycosuria, phosphaturia, aminoaciduria, hypokalemia, and type II/proximal RTA from bicarbonaturia), or non-anion-gap metabolic acidosis with hyperkalemia (type IV RTA) from impaired ammoniagenesis (Harrison 22e p.2437). Proteinuria in chronic TIN is usually modest (rarely >2 g/d) from decreased tubular reabsorption of filtered proteins, but nephrotic-range albuminuria may occur when secondary focal segmental glomerulosclerosis (FSGS) develops (Harrison 22e p.2437). Tubulointerstitial nephritis with uveitis (TINU) accounts for <5% of AIN, affects females 3x more than males, with median onset age 15 years; hallmark is painful anterior uveitis plus lymphocyte-predominant interstitial nephritis, with sterile pyuria, mild proteinuria, features of Fanconi's syndrome, and elevated ESR (Harrison 22e p.2439). Sterile pyuria with elevated creatinine and features of Fanconi's syndrome should raise suspicion for TINU; ocular symptoms precede or accompany kidney disease in only one-third of cases (Harrison 22e p.2439). Papillary necrosis is a key feature of analgesic nephropathy; a sloughed necrotic papilla can cause gross hematuria and ureteric colic from ureteral obstruction (Harrison 22e p.2442). Renal ultrasound in reflux nephropathy characteristically shows asymmetric small kidneys with irregular outlines, thinned cortices, and regions of compensatory hypertrophy (Harrison 22e p.2441). Classic allergic AIN tetrad: fever, rash, peripheral eosinophilia, and oliguric AKI after a drug (Harrison 22e p.2438) Particularly severe and rapid-onset AIN upon reintroduction of rifampin after a drug-free period (Harrison 22e p.2438) Painful anterior uveitis (often bilateral, with blurred vision and photophobia) with sterile pyuria and AKI - suggests TINU (Harrison 22e p.2439) Gross hematuria with ureteric colic from a sloughed necrotic papilla in analgesic or sickle cell nephropathy (Harrison 22e p.2442) Triad of saturnine gout, hypertension, and impaired kidney function suggesting lead nephropathy (Harrison 22e p.2443) Anemia disproportionately severe relative to kidney dysfunction in aristolochic acid nephropathy (with very high risk of upper urinary tract urothelial cancer) (Harrison 22e p.2442) The classic AIN tetrad (fever, rash, eosinophilia, oliguric AKI) is the exception rather than the rule; relying on it misses most cases (Harrison 22e p.2438). NSAID-induced AIN often lacks fever, rash, and eosinophilia but presents with AKI and heavy proteinuria (Harrison 22e p.2438). Urinary eosinophil testing is neither sensitive nor specific for AIN and is not recommended (Harrison 22e p.2438). Absence of peripheral eosinophilia does not exclude AIN, as it is present in only a minority of patients (Harrison 22e p.2438). A negative urine dipstick for protein with elevated total spot urine protein is highly suggestive of Bence-Jones protein (light chains), which dipsticks do not detect - missing myeloma kidney (Harrison 22e p.2440). Reflux nephropathy may go unnoticed until adulthood and can be mistaken for 'chronic pyelonephritis'; a single affected kidney may be silent except for hypertension (Harrison 22e p.2441). Because chronic TIN histopathology is nonspecific, biopsy rarely gives a specific diagnosis; over-reliance on biopsy without history/exposure analysis is a pitfall (Harrison 22e p.2437). A group of disorders that primarily affect the renal tubules and interstitium with relative sparing of the glomeruli and vessels, divided into acute and chronic tubulointerstitial nephritis (TIN) (Harrison 22e p.2437). Acute TIN causes AKI either via aggressive inflammatory infiltrates producing tissue edema, tubular cell injury, and compromised tubular flow, or via frank tubular obstruction by casts, cellular debris, or crystals; flank pain may arise from renal capsule distention (Harrison 22e p.2437). Acute interstitial nephritis (AIN) is most commonly an allergic, immune-mediated drug reaction (antibiotics such as beta-lactams/sulfonamides/quinolones/vancomycin/rifampin, NSAIDs/COX-2 inhibitors, proton pump inhibitors, diuretics, anticonvulsants, allopurinol, immune checkpoint inhibitors), but may also be immune-mediated within autoimmune syndromes (Sjogren's, SLE, TINU, granulomatous/sarcoid, IgG4-related disease) or infection-associated (Harrison 22e p.2437-2438). Chronic TIN produces interstitial fibrosis with patchy mononuclear cell infiltration, widespread tubular atrophy, luminal dilation, and thickened tubular basement membranes, manifesting as tubular dysfunction (nephrogenic DI, Fanconi's syndrome, RTA) and progressive azotemia (Harrison 22e p.2437). Because the chronic histopathology is nonspecific, biopsy rarely yields a specific diagnosis, so diagnosis relies on history, drug/toxin exposure, associated symptoms, and imaging (Harrison 22e p.2437). In allergic/drug-induced AIN, discontinuation of the offending agent often reverses the kidney injury, though recovery may be incomplete depending on duration of exposure and degree of tubular atrophy and interstitial fibrosis (Harrison 22e p.2438). Granulomatous, idiopathic, TINU, and Sjogren's-related interstitial nephritis generally respond to glucocorticoids, especially when treated early before significant fibrosis, but may relapse and require maintenance immunosuppression (Harrison 22e p.2438-2439). Chronic TIN damage that has already occurred is impossible to reverse, but further deterioration may be slowed by treating glomerular hypertension (Harrison 22e p.2440). Reflux nephropathy affecting both kidneys often progresses inexorably to ESRD over years even without ongoing infection or reflux (Harrison 22e p.2441). Lithium-associated CKD is often irreversible and slowly progresses to ESRD even after lithium is stopped (Harrison 22e p.2443). AKI from acute hypercalcemia may be fully reversible, whereas chronic hypercalcemic kidney dysfunction may not improve even after correcting the calcium disorder (Harrison 22e p.2443). Harrison classifies tubulointerstitial diseases into Acute Tubulointerstitial Disorders - acute interstitial nephritis (therapeutic agents/drugs, infection, autoimmune including TINU, Sjogren's, SLE, granulomatous, IgG4-related) and acute obstructive disorders (light chain cast nephropathy, acute phosphate nephropathy, acute urate nephropathy) - versus Chronic Tubulointerstitial Disorders (reflux nephropathy, sickle cell disease, chronic toxin/drug exposure such as analgesics, lithium, heavy metals, aristolochic acid, calcineurin inhibitors), metabolic disturbances (hypercalcemia/nephrocalcinosis, hyperuricemia, hypokalemia, hyperoxaluria, cystinosis), cystic/hereditary disorders, and miscellaneous causes (aging, chronic glomerulonephritis, obstruction, ischemia, radiation) (Harrison 22e p.2437).

tubulointerstitial nephritis uveitis — TINU syndrome, tubulointerstitial nephritis and uveitis syndrome sarcoidosis with renal and ocular involvement drug-induced acute interstitial nephritis with separate uveitis systemic lupus erythematosus Sjögren syndrome granulomatosis with polyangiitis and other ANCA-associated vasculitis ocular tuberculosis or syphilis with renal disease Behçet disease serum creatinine and estimated glomerular filtration rate urinary beta-2 microglobulin and urinalysis for sterile pyuria, glycosuria and proteinuria renal biopsy showing acute tubulointerstitial nephritis when the diagnosis is uncertain serum angiotensin-converting enzyme and chest imaging to exclude sarcoidosis autoimmune serology including antinuclear and ANCA antibodies syphilis serology and interferon-gamma release assay dilated fundus examination and optical coherence tomography for macular oedema A distinct oculorenal syndrome combining acute tubulointerstitial nephritis with uveitis, most often in adolescent girls and young women. The uveitis is typically bilateral, non-granulomatous and anterior, though intermediate and posterior involvement can occur. Ocular inflammation may precede, coincide with or, most commonly, follow the renal disease, so uveitis can be the presenting feature of occult nephritis. Systemic prodrome of fever, weight loss, fatigue, anorexia and myalgia is common and helps flag the diagnosis. Urinary beta-2 microglobulin is a sensitive marker of tubular injury and is characteristically elevated. Renal features include a raised creatinine, sterile pyuria, low-grade proteinuria, glycosuria and features of tubular dysfunction. It is a diagnosis of exclusion; sarcoidosis, tuberculosis, syphilis, Sjögren syndrome and other systemic causes of oculorenal disease must be ruled out. The nephritis is usually managed with systemic corticosteroids and often recovers, whereas the uveitis tends to be chronic or relapsing and may need prolonged topical and steroid-sparing therapy. acute kidney injury with a rising creatinine requiring urgent nephrology input bilateral uveitis with systemic constitutional symptoms in an adolescent features suggesting systemic vasculitis such as haematuria and pulmonary involvement sight-threatening posterior involvement or persistent macular oedema Treating the uveitis in isolation and missing coexisting or subsequent renal disease. Failing to measure renal function and urinary beta-2 microglobulin in a young patient with bilateral anterior uveitis. Attributing the syndrome to a drug reaction without excluding sarcoidosis and other systemic causes. Assuming the uveitis will resolve with the nephritis, when it commonly relapses and outlasts the renal disease. Overlooking posterior segment involvement and chronic macular oedema as causes of persistent visual loss. Tubulointerstitial nephritis and uveitis syndrome is believed to be an immune-mediated, likely T-cell driven, hypersensitivity disorder in which a shared autoantigen or cross-reactive immune response targets both the renal tubulointerstitium and the uveal tract. The kidney shows an acute interstitial infiltrate of lymphocytes, plasma cells and eosinophils with tubular injury, sometimes with non-caseating granulomata, producing tubular dysfunction and a rise in creatinine. A parallel immune response in the eye generates non-granulomatous uveitis. Cell-mediated immunity, circulating autoantibodies against a modified C-reactive protein found in both renal tubular cells and uveal tissue, and genetic susceptibility through certain HLA associations have all been implicated. Preceding drug exposure or infection may act as a trigger in susceptible individuals. The renal component usually responds well to corticosteroids and often recovers fully, though a minority develop chronic renal impairment; the uveitis frequently follows a chronic or relapsing course and requires longer treatment than the nephritis.

Tufted angioma — Angioblastoma of Nakagawa, Acquired tufted angioma Kaposiform haemangioendothelioma Infantile haemangioma Kaposi sarcoma Capillary or venous malformation Fibrous hamartoma of infancy Plaque-type infantile myofibromatosis Skin biopsy showing cannonball tufts with podoplanin positivity Full blood count and coagulation studies (fibrinogen, D-dimer) to detect the Kasabach-Merritt phenomenon MRI to define depth and soft-tissue extent Doppler ultrasound Serial platelet monitoring in at-risk lesions Regarded as part of a continuum with kaposiform haemangioendothelioma, sharing histological and clinical features. Characterised by discrete capillary tufts scattered through the dermis in a cannonball pattern on histology. Usually presents in infancy or early childhood as a slowly enlarging dull-red to violaceous plaque, sometimes with overlying hypertrichosis and hyperhidrosis. Can trigger the Kasabach-Merritt phenomenon with profound thrombocytopenia and consumptive coagulopathy, though less often than kaposiform haemangioendothelioma. GLUT1-negative; positivity for the lymphatic marker podoplanin (D2-40) supports the diagnosis. Tenderness and induration may accompany platelet trapping. Spontaneous regression can occur, particularly in congenital cases, but many lesions persist. mTOR inhibition with sirolimus is increasingly used for complicated or coagulopathic lesions. Rapid enlargement with a tense, purpuric and painful lesion Falling platelet count with hypofibrinogenaemia (Kasabach-Merritt phenomenon) Spontaneous bleeding or extensive bruising Functional impairment from a large or periarticular lesion Failing to check the platelet count and coagulation in a growing violaceous plaque. Confusing the lesion with a simple bruise or an infantile haemangioma. Not recognising the continuum with kaposiform haemangioendothelioma. Giving platelet transfusion in the Kasabach-Merritt phenomenon except during active bleeding or surgery, since it fuels further trapping. Tufted angioma is a benign but occasionally locally aggressive vascular tumour characterised by discrete lobules or tufts of tightly packed capillaries dispersed through the dermis in a cannonball pattern, often bulging into dilated lymphatic-like channels. It expresses lymphatic endothelial markers such as podoplanin (D2-40), is GLUT1-negative, and shares pathological and behavioural overlap with kaposiform haemangioendothelioma, including the capacity to sequester and consume platelets, producing the Kasabach-Merritt phenomenon. Somatic GNA14 mutations have been implicated in a subset of lesions. The prognosis is generally favourable, with some lesions regressing spontaneously, but persistent pain, disfigurement and the risk of the Kasabach-Merritt phenomenon may complicate the course and require systemic therapy.

parenteral nutrition such as line sepsis or cholestasis Confusing the histology with coeliac disease or other villus-atrophy enteropathies without recognising the diagnostic tufts Relying on light Loss-of-function variants in EPCAM disrupt the epithelial cell adhesion molecule, impairing cell-cell contacts and the normal architecture of the intestinal epithelium. Enterocytes crowd and pile into focal tufts at the villus surface, with associated villus atrophy and crypt changes, so the absorptive surface is compromised. The syndromic SPINT2-associated form involves a serine protease inhibitor and additional developmental anomalies. The net effect is failure of fluid and nutrient absorption producing chronic diarrhoea from early infancy. Most patients require prolonged or indefinite parenteral nutrition; some achieve partial enteral tolerance while severe refractory disease may progress to intestinal transplantation. Outcome is influenced by nutritional complications and any associated anomalies.

Tularemia — Francisella tularensis infection Lung cancer (pulmonary nodules or dense consolidation can mimic malignancy, prompting CT/PET and biopsy before tularemia is suspected) (Harrison 22e p.1337, 1339) Head and neck cancer (Harrison 22e p.1337) Lymphoma (Harrison 22e p.1337) Tuberculosis (Harrison 22e p.1337) Unspecified viral infection / 'a severe virus' (Harrison 22e p.1337) Common skin and soft tissue infection (Harrison 22e p.1337) Community-acquired pneumonia (Harrison 22e p.1337) Undifferentiated fever or sepsis (Harrison 22e p.1337) Tuberculosis (Harrison 22e p.1337) Community-acquired pneumonia (Harrison 22e p.1337) Common skin and soft tissue infection (Harrison 22e p.1337) Unspecified viral infection (Harrison 22e p.1337) Laboratory confirmation by recovery of an F. tularensis isolate, detection of F. tularensis-specific antigens or nucleic acids, or detection of specific antibodies by serology (Harrison 22e p.1338-1339) Direct detection by PCR/nucleic acid testing of clinical specimens is rapid and reliable; for ulcer specimens it is comparable to culture in sensitivity and specificity (Harrison 22e p.1339) Appropriate specimens for direct detection or culture: ulcer specimens (sampled from the wound edge), lower respiratory tract specimens (sputum, tracheal washing, bronchoalveolar lavage), lymph node biopsies or aspirates, and blood cultures (Harrison 22e p.1339) Blood culture: F. tularensis is slow-growing and a 10-day incubation is recommended for optimal sensitivity; MALDI-TOF identification from blood cultures is an increasingly common, sometimes unexpected, finding (Harrison 22e p.1339) Serology (ELISA or microagglutination) is the mainstay in many laboratories and is especially useful when tularemia is suspected at a later stage; antibodies are generally detectable 10-20 days post-infection (Harrison 22e p.1339) Chest imaging in respiratory tularemia: single or multifocal consolidation, pleural effusion, and hilar/mediastinal lymphadenopathy; CT may show rounded subpleural consolidations and necrotic lymph nodes; pathology resolution on imaging can be slow and take months (Harrison 22e p.1339) Lung cancer (Harrison 22e p.1337, 1339) Head and neck cancer (Harrison 22e p.1337) Lymphoma (Harrison 22e p.1337) Suspected tumor with lymphoid tissue engagement (Harrison 22e p.1337) Zoonosis caused by Francisella tularensis, a small facultatively intracellular aerobic gram-negative coccobacillus; humans are infected via arthropod bites (ticks, tabanid/deer flies, mosquitoes), inhalation of infectious aerosols, handling infected animals, or ingestion of contaminated water/food (Harrison 22e p.1335-1336). Take a deliberate exposure history: wild animal contact (rodents, rabbits, hares), inhalation of dust contaminated with their urine or feces, recent tick/fly/mosquito bites, brush-cutting or grass-trimming, handling wood or hay, and walking or hunting in wildlife habitats; cluster cases sharing the same exposure are a clue (Harrison 22e p.1337). The most common initial manifestation is an influenza-like illness with high fever (acute onset, myalgia, headache, constitutional symptoms); fever may be persistent or intermittent. Incubation is usually 3-5 days but may range from 1 to 21 days (Harrison 22e p.1337). Inflamed, swollen, tender regional lymph nodes are typical; the initial infection route determines which lymphoid tissue is engaged (skin or pharyngeal entry gives regional nodes; inhalation gives mediastinal/hilar nodes) (Harrison 22e p.1337). Ulceroglandular form (most common, ~47% of US cases): skin inoculation by a blood-feeding arthropod or direct contact with an infected animal/contaminated material produces a primary ulcer plus tender regional lymphadenopathy; the primary ulcer is often a small skin break with limited inflammation that requires careful examination to detect (Harrison 22e p.1337-1338). Glandular form (~18% of US cases): regional lymphadenopathy without a detectable primary skin ulcer (Harrison 22e p.1338). Oculoglandular form (~2% of US cases): conjunctivitis with pronounced local inflammation plus regional (e.g., preauricular) lymphadenopathy, acquired by touching the eye with contaminated fingers or by contaminated aerosol (Harrison 22e p.1338). Oropharyngeal form (~2% of US cases): acute pharyngitis with pronounced local inflammation following ingestion of contaminated water or food, with cervical/tonsillar lymphadenopathy (Harrison 22e p.1338). Respiratory/pneumonic form (~17% of US cases): acquired by inhaling contaminated aerosol; more often bacteremic and more likely to progress to severe disease requiring inpatient care, particularly in patients aged 65 and over and those with comorbidities. Onset of a dry cough may occur more than 7 days after the influenza-like illness; engaged lymphoid tissue is in the mediastinum or lung hila (Harrison 22e p.1338). Typhoidal form (~14% of US cases): an older term for a typhoid-like syndrome with prolonged high fever, fatigue, headache, and nausea; Harrison recommends avoiding the term because most historic typhoidal cases were in fact respiratory/pneumonic tularemia acquired by inhalation (Harrison 22e p.1338). Routine blood biochemistry is generally unhelpful; findings are nonspecific and may or may not show elevated liver enzymes or hematuria. In a Swedish type B outpatient series, white-cell counts stayed within normal limits in 70% of patients and CRP was only moderately elevated (Harrison 22e p.1338). When tularemia is clinically suspected, communicate the suspicion to the microbiology laboratory in advance so that cultures are handled safely, because F. tularensis causes laboratory-acquired infection and culture requires BSL-3 containment; it is also a US HHS Tier 1 Select Agent (Harrison 22e p.1335, 1339). For ulcer sampling, swab the edge of the wound (remove any scab first) and rub firmly so the specimen is slightly blood-tinged to maximize yield (Harrison 22e p.1339). Respiratory/pneumonic form, which is more often bacteremic and may progress to severe disease requiring inpatient care, particularly in patients aged 65 and over and those with comorbidities (Harrison 22e p.1338) Multiorgan involvement or hemodynamic instability, indicating need for inpatient care (Harrison 22e p.1337) Host factors increasing risk of severe infection: geriatric frailty, immunosuppression, severe lung and/or heart impairment, and other significant comorbidities (Harrison 22e p.1337) Lymph node abscess formation, which occurs in about one-third of patients and is associated with antibiotic treatment delay of more than 2-3 weeks after disease onset (Harrison 22e p.1340) Severe complications reported: adult respiratory distress syndrome, myocarditis, pericarditis, endocarditis, meningitis, osteomyelitis, hepatitis, and renal failure (Harrison 22e p.1340) Clinical recognition is challenging, especially if the patient does not spontaneously report fever; tularemia may not be suspected until after extensive and costly investigations, and even in high-endemic areas patients are often initially mistreated for other conditions. A high index of suspicion is critical (Harrison 22e p.1337). If care is sought several weeks after symptom onset, the acute fever onset may not be reported spontaneously and must be actively elicited (Harrison 22e p.1337). The primary ulcer can be a small, minimally inflamed skin break that is easily missed or may be undetectable, in which case the disease is classified as glandular rather than ulceroglandular (Harrison 22e p.1338). Failure to alert the microbiology laboratory to suspected tularemia risks laboratory-acquired infection, as F. tularensis is highly virulent and requires BSL-3 culture conditions (Harrison 22e p.1335, 1339). Acute-phase serology can be misleading because F. tularensis antibodies persist (single titers can remain above the diagnostic cutoff for at least 1 year), so reliable acute diagnosis should rely on a significant rise between paired sera taken 2-4 weeks apart (Harrison 22e p.1339). Culture specimens taken from an established lymph node abscess are typically F. tularensis negative (Harrison 22e p.1340). Tularemia patients do not require isolation because there is no human-to-human transmission (Harrison 22e p.1340). Natural transmission is usually through the skin or by inhalation of aerosols, but ingestion of contaminated food/water can also infect. An extremely low dose of about 10-50 organisms inoculated through skin microtrauma or inhaled suffices to cause disease, whereas roughly 10^6-10^8 organisms are required by the oral route. Tissue-resident macrophages (alveolar macrophages in lung, Langerhans cells in skin) transport the organism via blood and lymphatics to lymph nodes, spleen, and bone marrow; in skin, neutrophils phagocytose F. tularensis early. After uptake, the bacterium escapes the phagosome into the cytosol, replicates, exits the cell, and disseminates. F. tularensis is a 'stealth pathogen' that manipulates host-cell signaling, delaying the immune response and permitting rapid systemic spread. Characteristic tissue reactions are granuloma formation and necrotic foci surrounded by macrophages, lymphocytes, and giant cells in lymph nodes, lung, spleen, kidney, and liver; pulmonary autopsy findings show necrotizing pneumonia with fibrin, cellular debris, and neutrophils. Effective protective immunity requires both B and T cells, and antigen-specific recall T-cell responses can persist 25-30 years after infection or vaccination (Harrison 22e p.1337, 1339). Before antibiotics, US case-fatality rates were typically 5-15% and could reach as high as 60% in respiratory/pneumonic tularemia. Recent US surveillance (2006-2021) showed 27 of 903 patients (3.0%) with available outcome data died; treatment with at least one high-efficacy antimicrobial class was independently associated with greatly increased odds of survival. Type A is generally more lethal than type B, though there is heterogeneity among type A genetic varieties. Overall type B fatality is estimated at less than 1% in Sweden, where severe respiratory type B tularemia carried about 1.5% fatality. Recovery (and resolution of imaging abnormalities) may be slow, and some patients report postinfectious persisting fatigue and disability of uncertain cause (Harrison 22e p.1339-1340). Harrison does not provide a formal severity score. Clinically, management level is decided by physical examination of the anatomic site and extent of inflammation (pneumonitis, lymph node inflammation, skin ulcers/pustules, pharyngitis), the rate of progression, and host risk factors: localized symptoms are generally suitable for outpatient care, whereas multiorgan involvement or hemodynamic instability suggests inpatient care. The recognized clinical forms (ulceroglandular, glandular, oropharyngeal, oculoglandular, respiratory/pneumonic, typhoidal) are classified by F. tularensis infection route rather than by severity (Harrison 22e p.1337-1338).

hepatocellular carcinoma (HCC) makes up about 85% of primary liver cancers, intrahepatic cholangiocarcinoma about 10%, with rarer entities including fibrolamellar HCC, mixed HCC-iCCA, epithelioid hemangioendothelioma, and pediatric hepatoblastoma (Harrison 22e p.659). Cirrhosis of any cause is the dominant risk factor for HCC; about one-third of cirrhotic patients develop HCC over their lifetime, with an annual risk of roughly 3-8% in HBV- or HCV-related cirrhosis and a lower 1-2% per year in cirrhosis from alcohol, metabolic dysfunction-associated steatohepatitis (MASH), alpha-1-antitrypsin deficiency, autoimmune hepatitis, Wilson's disease, and cholestatic disorders (Harrison 22e p.659-660). HBV accounts for roughly 50% of HCC cases globally (about 60% in Asia and Africa, about 20% in the West) and can cause tumors via insertional mutagenesis; importantly, 25-30% of MASH-associated HCCs arise in the absence of cirrhosis (Harrison 22e p.660). HCC has a strong male preponderance (male-to-female ratio about 2.5:1) and incidence peaks at 65-70 years, though it presents earlier (40-50 years) in populations with vertical HBV transmission (Harrison 22e p.659). The radiologic hallmark of HCC on four-phase CT or dynamic contrast-enhanced MRI is arterial-phase contrast uptake with washout in the portal venous or delayed phase, a pattern with about 95-100% specificity that can make biopsy unnecessary in cirrhotic patients (Harrison 22e p.661). The Barcelona Clinic Liver Cancer (BCLC) system is the most accepted staging scheme; the TNM staging system is NOT used in HCC because it does not capture liver function and performance status, the key prognostic variables (Harrison 22e p.662-664). Cholangiocarcinoma is the second most common primary liver cancer and is classified by location into intrahepatic (iCCA, ~20-30%), perihilar (pCCA, ~50-60%), and distal (dCCA, ~20-30%); perihilar and distal forms together are termed extrahepatic cholangiocarcinoma (Harrison 22e p.667). FGFR2 fusions and IDH1/2 mutations occur mostly in iCCA, whereas ERBB2/3 amplifications and SMAD4 aberrations characterize extrahepatic cholangiocarcinoma; up to about 40% of iCCAs carry a targetable mutation (Harrison 22e p.667). Acute painless jaundice occurs in about 90% of perihilar cholangiocarcinoma patients, while roughly 10% present with cholangitis; distal cholangiocarcinoma can be hard to distinguish from early pancreatic cancer (Harrison 22e p.668-669). Gallbladder cancer is the most common biliary tract malignancy worldwide, has a female-to-male ratio of about 3:1, and cholelithiasis is the major risk factor though fewer than 1% of patients with gallstones develop it; gallbladder polyps 10 mm or larger carry transformation risk (Harrison 22e p.669-670). Fibrolamellar HCC typically affects children and young adults (10-30 years) without underlying liver disease, carries the PRKACA-DNAJB1 fusion oncogene in 80-100% of cases, and has a better prognosis than conventional HCC (Harrison 22e p.670). Hepatic (hepatocellular) adenomas occur predominantly in women aged 35-40 (female-to-male ratio ~10:1), are linked to oral contraceptive use in women and anabolic androgenic steroid use in male bodybuilders, and carry risk of hemorrhage and malignant transformation, particularly when larger than 5 cm (Harrison 22e p.670). Symptomatic HCC (malaise, weight loss, anorexia, abdominal discomfort, or signs of liver dysfunction) indicates advanced disease with median survival under 1 year Macrovascular (portal, hepatic, or branch vein) invasion, lymph node involvement, or extrahepatic spread denotes advanced BCLC C disease Child-Pugh class C / severe liver dysfunction (BCLC D) Rising or markedly elevated AFP (>=20 ng/mL prompting imaging; >=400 ng/dL highly suspicious but not diagnostic) Painless jaundice or cholangitis suggesting biliary tract malignancy Hepatic adenoma larger than 5 cm (hemorrhage and malignant transformation risk); active adenoma bleeding A negative liver biopsy does NOT exclude HCC; sensitivity falls below 50% for tumors 1-2 cm, and a second biopsy is advised if findings are inconclusive or the lesion grows/changes enhancement Nodules under 1 cm are unlikely to be HCC and are difficult to diagnose; short-interval ultrasound follow-up (every 3-4 months) is recommended rather than immediate biopsy PET and contrast-enhanced ultrasound perform poorly for early HCC diagnosis and are not recommended as primary diagnostic tools An AFP of >=400 ng/dL is highly suspicious but NOT diagnostic of HCC by guidelines TNM staging should NOT be applied to HCC because it omits liver function and performance status About 25-30% of MASH-related HCCs occur without cirrhosis, so absence of cirrhosis does not exclude HCC in this group Surveillance is generally NOT recommended in advanced (Child-Pugh C) cirrhosis since curative therapy is precluded, except for liver transplant waiting-list patients Liver biopsy carries a ~2-3% risk of complications including tumor seeding and bleeding HCC develops through a multistep process beginning with precancerous low-grade dysplastic nodules that progress to high-grade dysplastic nodules and then early HCC; adult hepatocytes are the principal cell of origin, either transforming directly or de-differentiating into precursor cells, with progenitor cells contributing in a subset. It is a prototypical inflammation-associated cancer in which oxidative stress and the immune microenvironment of chronically damaged liver drive mutation. Tumors accumulate roughly 40-60 somatic alterations, of which 4-8 are driver genes; the leading drivers are TERT promoter mutations (~56%), TP53 (~27%), and CTNNB1 (~26%), all currently non-actionable. Aflatoxin B1 produces a characteristic TP53 R249S hotspot mutation. Only about 20-25% of HCCs carry an actionable mutation. Two molecular subclasses exist: a proliferative class (poor outcome, HBV-related, AFP overexpression, Ras/mTOR/IGF activation) and a nonproliferative class (often CTNNB1-mutated, better outcome). Intrahepatic cholangiocarcinoma arises from adult cholangiocytes, transdifferentiated hepatocytes, or progenitor-cholangiocyte precursors, whereas extrahepatic cholangiocarcinoma arises from biliary epithelium and peribiliary glands. Hepatic adenomas are clonal proliferations from single-gene driver mutations (e.g., CTNNB1, HNF1A inactivation, inflammatory or Hedgehog pathway activation), and focal nodular hyperplasia is a polyclonal hepatocellular proliferation secondary to an arterial malformation (Harrison 22e p.660-670). Prognosis depends on stage, tumor burden, liver function, and performance status. About 40% of HCC patients are diagnosed at BCLC stage 0 or A and are eligible for potentially curative resection, transplantation, or ablation, with median overall survival beyond 5 years (up to ~10 years after transplantation). Optimal surgical resection candidates have 5-year survival of 60-70% (35-55% in suboptimal candidates); RFA achieves ~60% 5-year survival; liver transplantation within Milan criteria yields 70-80% 5-year survival with ~10-15% recurrence at 5 years. Intermediate-stage (BCLC B) untreated natural history is about 16 months, improved to ~25-30 months with TACE. Symptomatic/advanced disease has median survival under 1 year; end-stage (BCLC D) survival is about 3-6 months. Cholangiocarcinoma overall carries a 5-year survival of about 10%; resectable iCCA single tumors have median survival ~40-50 months. Gallbladder cancer 5-year survival ranges 60-90% in resected localized disease but only ~10-12 months median in advanced disease. Fibrolamellar HCC has better prognosis (median ~70 months after resection). Hepatoblastoma overall 5-year survival is ~70% (50-90% by PRETEXT stage); notably, low AFP (<100 ng/mL) indicates poor prognosis in hepatoblastoma, opposite to HCC. Hepatocellular carcinoma is staged by the Barcelona Clinic Liver Cancer (BCLC) system into five stages: very early (BCLC 0, single nodule <=2 cm, Child-Pugh A, ECOG 0), early (BCLC A, single or up to three nodules <=3 cm, Child-Pugh A-B, ECOG 0), intermediate (BCLC B, multinodular, Child-Pugh A-B, ECOG 0), advanced (BCLC C, portal/macrovascular invasion, N1 or M1, or ECOG 1-2), and terminal (BCLC D, Child-Pugh C or ECOG >2). Liver function is graded by the Child-Pugh score (classes A-C) and performance by ECOG. Milan criteria (single tumor <=5 cm, or up to three nodules each <=3 cm, no macrovascular invasion or extrahepatic spread) define transplant eligibility. Cholangiocarcinoma is classified anatomically into intrahepatic, perihilar, and distal subtypes; hepatoblastoma uses the PRETEXT (Pretreatment Extent of Tumor) classification (Harrison 22e p.661-669).

tumour induced osteomalacia — oncogenic osteomalacia, TIO, phosphaturic mesenchymal tumour syndrome X-linked or other hereditary hypophosphataemia presenting late autosomal dominant hypophosphataemic rickets Fanconi syndrome nutritional osteomalacia drug-induced phosphate wasting (intravenous iron, tenofovir) fibrous dysplasia or McCune-Albright syndrome multiple myeloma serum phosphate, calcium, alkaline phosphatase and PTH 25-hydroxy and 1,25-dihydroxyvitamin D renal tubular phosphate reabsorption (TmP/GFR) intact FGF23 68-gallium DOTATATE PET/CT for tumour localisation whole-body MRI and selective venous sampling for FGF23 if required histology of the resected tumour Tumour-induced osteomalacia is a rare acquired paraneoplastic syndrome caused by FGF23, and other phosphatonins, secreted by usually small benign phosphaturic mesenchymal tumours of the mixed connective tissue variant. Excess FGF23 produces renal phosphate wasting, hypophosphataemia and low 1,25-dihydroxyvitamin D, with normal calcium and PTH. Adults present insidiously with bone pain, muscle weakness, fatigue, height loss and fragility or insufficiency fractures, and are frequently misdiagnosed for years. The biochemistry mirrors X-linked hypophosphataemia but is acquired in adulthood with no family history; a raised or inappropriately normal intact FGF23 supports the diagnosis. Tumours are often tiny and hidden in the extremities, craniofacial bones or sinonasal tract, so localisation depends on functional imaging; 68-gallium DOTATATE PET/CT is the most sensitive, supplemented by MRI. Complete surgical resection is curative, with rapid normalisation of phosphate; incomplete localisation is the main obstacle to cure. When the tumour cannot be found or resected, medical therapy with oral phosphate and active vitamin D, or burosumab, controls the biochemistry. Consider this diagnosis in any adult-onset hypophosphataemic osteomalacia without a hereditary or nutritional explanation. recurrent insufficiency fractures severe refractory hypophosphataemia profound proximal myopathy causing immobility failure to localise a strongly suspected tumour rare malignant phosphaturic mesenchymal tumour with metastases prolonged diagnostic delay from attributing symptoms to osteoporosis or fibromyalgia not measuring phosphate and FGF23 in unexplained bone pain relying on anatomical imaging alone and missing small tumours assuming a drug cause is excluded once the agent is stopped without rechecking phosphate incomplete resection leading to biochemical recurrence Phosphaturic mesenchymal tumours secrete fibroblast growth factor 23 (and less commonly other phosphatonins such as sFRP4 and MEPE). Circulating FGF23 downregulates the proximal tubular sodium-phosphate cotransporters, causing renal phosphate wasting and hypophosphataemia, and suppresses renal 1-alpha-hydroxylase so that 1,25-dihydroxyvitamin D is inappropriately low. The resulting chronic hypophosphataemia impairs mineralisation of osteoid, producing osteomalacia. Because the tumours are typically small, slow-growing and anatomically obscure, the phosphaturic state persists and drives progressive skeletal disease until the lesion is identified and removed. The condition is curable with complete tumour resection, after which symptoms and biochemistry resolve, although localisation may take years and rare malignant variants carry a worse outlook.

tumour lysis syndrome — TLS, acute tumour lysis syndrome Acute kidney injury from sepsis, nephrotoxins or contrast Rhabdomyolysis with hyperkalaemia and hyperphosphataemia Pre-existing chronic kidney disease with electrolyte derangement Lactic acidosis of malignancy Obstructive uropathy from retroperitoneal disease Pseudohyperkalaemia from sample haemolysis or extreme leucocytosis Primary hyperphosphataemia from exogenous phosphate administration Serial urea, electrolytes and creatinine with urate, phosphate, calcium and magnesium Lactate dehydrogenase and uric acid to gauge tumour burden and risk Twelve-lead ECG for hyperkalaemic changes and QT prolongation from hypocalcaemia Venous or arterial blood gas for acid-base status Strict fluid balance and hourly urine output monitoring G6PD assay before rasburicase where clinically feasible Full blood count and coagulation screen to detect concurrent DIC or leukostasis Defined by the Cairo-Bishop criteria as laboratory TLS (two or more of hyperuricaemia, hyperkalaemia, hyperphosphataemia and hypocalcaemia within a defined window) progressing to clinical TLS when renal impairment, arrhythmia, seizure or death supervene. Highest risk with bulky, rapidly proliferating and chemosensitive malignancies: Burkitt and other high-grade non-Hodgkin lymphomas, acute lymphoblastic leukaemia, and acute leukaemias with high white-cell counts or high LDH. Spontaneous TLS may occur before any cytotoxic therapy (classically Burkitt lymphoma) and characteristically shows hyperuricaemia without the hyperphosphataemia typical of treatment-induced TLS, because released phosphate is reincorporated into new tumour cells. Secondary hypocalcaemia results from calcium-phosphate precipitation; give calcium only for symptomatic hypocalcaemia because supplementation risks metastatic calcification and worsening acute kidney injury. Rasburicase (recombinant urate oxidase) rapidly degrades existing urate and is preferred for high-risk or established TLS; it is contraindicated in G6PD deficiency owing to the risk of haemolysis and methaemoglobinaemia. Allopurinol or febuxostat prevents new urate formation but does not lower an existing urate load, so it is a prophylactic (not rescue) agent in lower-risk patients. Aggressive isotonic intravenous fluid to maintain a high urine output is the cornerstone; routine urinary alkalinisation is no longer recommended because it promotes calcium-phosphate deposition in the kidney. Early nephrology involvement and low threshold for renal replacement therapy are warranted for refractory hyperkalaemia, symptomatic hypocalcaemia with hyperphosphataemia, volume overload or oligoanuric acute kidney injury. ECG changes or arrhythmia from severe hyperkalaemia Tetany, carpopedal spasm or seizures from acute hypocalcaemia Oliguria or anuria signalling established acute kidney injury Rapidly rising potassium or phosphate despite fluids Reduced consciousness or cardiovascular collapse Administering intravenous calcium for asymptomatic hypocalcaemia, precipitating calcium-phosphate deposition Relying on allopurinol to treat an already elevated urate load instead of using rasburicase Giving rasburicase without excluding G6PD deficiency Continuing urinary alkalinisation, which worsens calcium-phosphate precipitation Misinterpreting spurious hyperkalaemia from a haemolysed or delayed sample and either over- or under-treating Rapid lysis of a large, proliferative tumour burden—either spontaneously or precipitated by cytotoxic therapy, corticosteroids or radiotherapy—releases intracellular potassium, phosphate and nucleic acids into the circulation faster than renal excretion can clear them. Purine catabolism generates uric acid that precipitates in the distal tubules and collecting ducts, while hyperphosphataemia drives calcium-phosphate crystal deposition; both cause intrarenal obstruction, vasoconstriction and inflammation leading to acute kidney injury, which in turn compounds the metabolic derangement. The resulting hyperkalaemia and hypocalcaemia produce the cardiac and neuromuscular complications that define clinical TLS. With pre-emptive risk stratification, hydration and urate-lowering therapy most cases are preventable or reversible, but established clinical TLS with acute kidney injury carries significant morbidity and mortality. Outcome depends on early recognition, control of the underlying malignancy and timely renal support.

Tungiasis — Tunga penetrans, jigger flea infestation, sand flea disease, chigoe flea, pique Plantar wart (verruca) Foreign body granuloma or splinter reaction Myiasis (furuncular) Paronychia or bacterial abscess Scabies or other pruritic dermatoses of the feet Melanoma or pigmented lesion (when the black dot is prominent) Clinical and epidemiological assessment (travel/residence, barefoot exposure) Dermoscopy to visualise the embedded flea and its pore Examination for multiple lesions and secondary infection Assessment of tetanus immunisation status Swab and culture if secondary bacterial infection is suspected Caused by penetration of the skin by the gravid female sand flea Tunga penetrans, endemic in sub-Saharan Africa, Latin America and the Caribbean Affects impoverished communities where people walk barefoot on sandy or dusty soil; lesions concentrate on the feet, especially the toes, periungual folds and soles The classic lesion is a white papule with a central black dot (the flea's posterior/exsanguination pore) that enlarges into a painful, itchy nodule as eggs develop Lesions can be staged (Fortaleza classification) from penetration through to involution and residual skin changes Diagnosis is clinical, based on typical lesions in an epidemiological context; dermoscopy can confirm the embedded flea Secondary bacterial infection is common and can lead to abscess, ulceration, lymphangitis, and in neglected cases tetanus or gangrene Treatment is careful surgical extraction of the flea under sterile conditions, wound care, and ensuring tetanus immunisation; occlusive topical agents may kill the embedded flea Spreading cellulitis, lymphangitis or abscess formation Signs suggestive of tetanus in an unimmunised patient Gangrene or deep tissue destruction from heavy or neglected infestation Widespread multiple lesions causing difficulty walking and disability Incomplete extraction leaving flea parts that provoke persistent inflammation and infection Performing non-sterile 'home' extraction, introducing secondary infection or tetanus risk Overlooking tetanus prophylaxis Mistaking a solitary lesion for a wart and applying inappropriate destructive treatment Failing to advise on footwear and environmental measures, allowing reinfestation The impregnated female flea burrows head-first into the epidermis, usually of the foot, leaving its posterior end at the skin surface for respiration, defecation and egg expulsion. Over one to two weeks the flea's abdomen swells enormously as eggs mature, producing the characteristic expanding nodule with a central pore. Local inflammation, pain and pruritus result from the parasite and its by-products. Once eggs are shed the flea dies and the lesion involutes, but the breach in the skin and retained flea remnants predispose to secondary bacterial infection. Isolated lesions resolve well after extraction and wound care, but heavy or repeated infestation in endemic settings causes chronic morbidity, deformity and disability, and secondary infection can be limb- or life-threatening if neglected.

severe cases can involve sesamoid fracture, diastasis or dislocation Presents with pain, swelling and bruising at the first MTP joint and painful, limited toe extension Graded by severity, with assessment of sesamoid position and joint stability Radiographs assess sesamoid position and fracture, and MRI best characterises plantar plate and sesamoid injury Management is graded, with relative rest, protection using stiff-soled footwear or taping to limit dorsiflexion, and progressive rehabilitation; higher grades and structural injury such as sesamoid disruption or plate rupture may need surgery Inadequately managed injuries can lead to persistent pain, stiffness and hallux deformity Gross instability or dislocation of the first MTP joint Sesamoid diastasis, retraction or fracture suggesting complete plantar plate rupture Inability to push off or bear weight Failure to improve, risking chronic instability and deformity Underestimating a high-grade injury and returning to play too soon Missing a sesamoid fracture, diastasis or plantar plate rupture Inadequate protection allowing recurrent hyperextension Overlooking progression to hallux rigidus or deformity Turf toe is an injury to the plantar capsuloligamentous complex of the first metatarsophalangeal joint, caused by forced hyperextension (dorsiflexion) of the hallux while the forefoot is fixed on the ground, as in push-off on a hard surface. The plantar plate, the sesamoid apparatus and flexor mechanism, and the collateral ligaments may be stretched or torn; in severe injury there can be sesamoid fracture, retraction or diastasis and joint instability or dislocation. The sesamoids, embedded within the flexor hallucis brevis mechanism, are integral to the injured complex, so their position and integrity guide grading and management. Low-grade sprains generally recover with protected rehabilitation over weeks, whereas high-grade injuries with plantar plate rupture or sesamoid disruption may need surgery and can cause prolonged loss of play and long-term stiffness or deformity.

Haploinsufficiency of X-linked genes that escape inactivation, notably SHOX, contributes to short stature and skeletal features, while accelerated loss of oocytes leads to varying degrees of ovarian insufficiency. Because the phenotype reflects the tissue distribution and proportion of the 45,X line, presentations range from near-normal to features resembling classic Turner syndrome. The absence of any Y-bearing cell line means the streak-gonad tumour risk associated with Y material is not a concern in this karyotype. The prognosis is generally more favourable than in non-mosaic Turner syndrome, with a proportion achieving spontaneous puberty and occasionally fertility, though ovarian insufficiency and short stature are frequent. Long-term outcome depends on cardiovascular surveillance and management of associated endocrine and metabolic conditions.

Turner Syndrome — 45,X, monosomy X, Ullrich-Turner syndrome, gonadal dysgenesis (45,X) Noonan syndrome (overlapping webbed neck and short stature, normal karyotype) Other causes of short stature (growth hormone deficiency, constitutional delay) Other causes of primary ovarian insufficiency or delayed puberty Mixed gonadal dysgenesis Skeletal dysplasias Karyotype to confirm monosomy X or mosaicism (with additional cells if mosaicism suspected) Echocardiography and cardiac MRI to assess aortic valve, arch, and aortic dimensions Renal ultrasound for structural anomalies Gonadotrophins (FSH, LH) and thyroid function testing Audiological assessment Bone age and growth monitoring; screening for coeliac disease A chromosomal disorder affecting females caused by complete or partial absence of one X chromosome, most commonly a 45,X karyotype, with mosaic forms also occurring. The two most consistent features are short stature and gonadal dysgenesis leading to ovarian failure. Newborns may show puffiness of the hands and feet (lymphoedema) and redundant nuchal skin; a fetal cystic hygroma may be detected antenatally. Characteristic features can include a webbed neck, low posterior hairline, widely spaced nipples on a broad chest, and a wide carrying angle at the elbows. Congenital cardiovascular anomalies, particularly bicuspid aortic valve and coarctation of the aorta, carry a risk of aortic dilatation and dissection and require ongoing surveillance. Renal anomalies such as a horseshoe kidney are common, as are recurrent otitis media and hearing loss. Most girls have normal intelligence but may have specific difficulties with visuospatial and mathematical tasks. Growth hormone therapy is used to improve final height, and oestrogen replacement is used to induce puberty and maintain bone and uterine health. Diagnosis is confirmed by karyotype, and lifelong multidisciplinary follow-up addresses cardiac, endocrine, and reproductive needs. Aortic dilatation or symptoms suggesting aortic dissection Severe coarctation or critical cardiac lesions in infancy Progressive hearing loss Features suggesting Y-chromosome material, which raises gonadoblastoma risk Signs of untreated hypothyroidism or coeliac disease Not considering the diagnosis in a girl with unexplained short stature or delayed puberty Missing mosaicism when only a limited number of cells are analysed Overlooking the need for lifelong aortic surveillance Failing to screen for associated hypothyroidism, coeliac disease, and hearing loss Loss of all or part of the second sex chromosome causes haploinsufficiency of genes that normally escape X-inactivation and are needed in two copies. Deficiency of the SHOX gene contributes to short stature and skeletal features, while accelerated loss of ovarian follicles leads to gonadal dysgenesis and oestrogen deficiency. Abnormal fetal lymphatic development produces the lymphoedema, nuchal changes, and associated features such as the webbed neck, and disrupted development contributes to the cardiovascular and renal malformations. With appropriate hormone therapy and surveillance most girls achieve improved height, undergo induced puberty, and have a good quality of life; long-term outlook is influenced chiefly by cardiovascular complications, and fertility is usually impaired though assisted reproduction may be possible.

for significant disease Amnioreduction and, in selected cases, selective reduction are alternative or adjunctive options depending on stage and gestation Rapidly worsening polyhydramnios causing maternal discomfort or threatened preterm labour Abnormal Doppler waveforms or absent bladder filling indicating advancing stage Signs of foetal hydrops in the recipient Sudden demise of one twin threatening the co-twin Failing to establish chorionicity early and missing the at-risk monochorionic pregnancy Attributing amniotic fluid discordance to growth restriction alone and delaying referral Not referring promptly to a fetal medicine centre capable of laser therapy Overlooking the co-twin's risk after single intrauterine death In monochorionic twins a single shared placenta contains vascular anastomoses connecting the two foetal circulations. When net flow through unbalanced arteriovenous connections favours one twin, blood is chronically shunted from a donor to a recipient. The donor responds to relative hypovolaemia with reduced urine output and oligohydramnios and becomes growth-restricted, while the recipient develops volume overload, polyuria, and polyhydramnios, with activation of vasoactive and natriuretic pathways that can lead to cardiac hypertrophy, dysfunction, and hydrops. Without treatment the haemodynamic imbalance progresses and threatens both twins. Untreated advanced TTTS carries a high risk of loss of one or both twins. Fetoscopic laser therapy substantially improves survival and reduces neurological morbidity, though outcomes depend on stage at treatment and gestational age, and long-term neurodevelopmental follow-up is advised.

Perforation following head trauma with cerebrospinal fluid otorrhoea or associated fracture Persistent bloody discharge or granulations raising concern for neoplasm Failing to distinguish a dangerous marginal or attic perforation from a safe central one Allowing water to enter the ear and precipitate recurrent infection Assuming all perforations need surgery when many heal with conservative care produces a perforation, or when external forces (direct trauma, sudden pressure change, or a foreign body) tear it mechanically. Loss of an intact vibrating surface and of the round window sound-shielding effect reduces the efficiency of sound transfer to the cochlea, producing conductive hearing loss proportional to the area lost and its position. Small tears usually re-epithelialise and heal, but persistent perforation, ongoing infection, or ingrowth of squamous epithelium through a marginal or attic defect can prevent closure and predispose to cholesteatoma and chronic disease. Small, uncomplicated and traumatic perforations often heal spontaneously with good recovery of hearing, and surgical repair of dry persistent defects has a high success rate; outcomes are worse when there is ongoing infection, ossicular damage or an underlying cholesteatoma.

Type 1 Diabetes Mellitus (Child) — T1DM, type 1 diabetes, insulin-dependent diabetes, juvenile diabetes, paediatric type 1 diabetes Type 2 diabetes mellitus Monogenic diabetes (MODY) and neonatal diabetes Secondary diabetes (e.g. cystic fibrosis-related, steroid-induced) Diabetes insipidus (for polyuria and polydipsia) Transient stress hyperglycaemia during acute illness Urinary tract infection (for enuresis or dysuria) Blood glucose and HbA1c Blood and/or urine ketones Venous blood gas and electrolytes to assess for ketoacidosis Pancreatic autoantibodies (e.g. GAD, IA-2, ZnT8, islet cell) Thyroid function and coeliac screening at diagnosis and during follow-up C-peptide where the diabetes type is uncertain The most common form of diabetes in children, caused by autoimmune destruction of pancreatic beta cells leading to absolute insulin deficiency. Classic presenting features are polyuria, polydipsia, weight loss, and fatigue, often over a few weeks; new secondary enuresis in a previously dry child is a useful clue. A substantial proportion of children present in diabetic ketoacidosis, which can be the first manifestation of the disease. Lifelong insulin replacement is essential; unlike type 2 diabetes, it cannot be managed by lifestyle measures or oral agents alone. A 'honeymoon' period of partial remission with reduced insulin needs may follow initial stabilisation but is temporary. Management is multidisciplinary, combining insulin, carbohydrate awareness, glucose monitoring, and structured education for the child and family. Careful attention to preventing and recognising hypoglycaemia is central to safe day-to-day care. Long-term care includes screening for associated autoimmune conditions (such as thyroid disease and coeliac disease) and for microvascular complications over time. New-onset type 1 diabetes presenting in diabetic ketoacidosis (vomiting, abdominal pain, deep sighing breathing, dehydration, drowsiness) is a medical emergency Reduced consciousness or focal neurological signs suggesting cerebral oedema during DKA management Severe hypoglycaemia with seizures or loss of consciousness Signs of significant dehydration or shock Persistent vomiting in a known diabetic child, which may signal evolving ketoacidosis Mistaking early symptoms for a urinary tract infection or behavioural enuresis and delaying diagnosis Failing to check ketones and acid-base status in a hyperglycaemic, unwell child Correcting fluids and glucose too aggressively in DKA and precipitating cerebral oedema Assuming the honeymoon phase means resolution and reducing vigilance Overlooking associated autoimmune conditions during follow-up Type 1 diabetes results from T-cell mediated autoimmune destruction of insulin-producing pancreatic beta cells in genetically predisposed children, often triggered by environmental factors. Progressive beta-cell loss produces absolute insulin deficiency, so glucose cannot enter cells and hyperglycaemia develops. Without insulin the body shifts to lipolysis and ketogenesis; unrestrained ketone production causes metabolic acidosis, while osmotic diuresis from glycosuria leads to dehydration and electrolyte loss, culminating in diabetic ketoacidosis if untreated. With modern insulin regimens, glucose monitoring, and multidisciplinary support most children live full lives; long-term outcome depends heavily on sustained glycaemic control, which reduces the risk of microvascular and macrovascular complications. Acute risks include ketoacidosis and severe hypoglycaemia.
