leptin has a limited role when leptin is not deficient It sits at the mild end of the INSR spectrum, far less severe than Rabson-Mendenhall or Donohue syndromes Diagnosis rests on the lean hyperandrogenic phenotype with disproportionate hyperinsulinaemia and INSR genetics Progression to overt, difficult-to-control insulin-resistant diabetes Rapidly worsening virilisation suggesting an alternative androgen source Features suggesting type B (autoimmune) insulin resistance Severe metabolic derangement disproportionate to body habitus Labelling the presentation as ordinary polycystic ovary syndrome and missing the disproportionate insulin resistance Overlooking a lean body habitus as a clue against obesity-driven resistance Failing to separate genetic type A from autoimmune type B insulin resistance Assuming leptin replacement will help when leptin is not deficient Not confirming the diagnosis with INSR genetic testing Type A insulin resistance syndrome is a genetic insulin-signalling defect, usually from heterozygous mutations in the insulin receptor gene (INSR), that impairs insulin action without the obesity, autoimmunity, or lipodystrophy that cause other insulin-resistant states. Reduced receptor function forces compensatory hyperinsulinaemia; the excess insulin acts on ovarian theca cells to stimulate androgen production, generating hirsutism, menstrual disturbance, and polycystic ovaries, while impaired insulin action on skin promotes acanthosis nigricans. Because affected individuals are typically lean, the severity of insulin resistance is out of proportion to body weight, and overt insulin-resistant diabetes may emerge over time as compensation fails. The prognosis is more favourable than the severe childhood INSR disorders; many patients are managed for years with insulin sensitisers, though progression to overt diabetes and the burden of hyperandrogenism require ongoing care.

tyrosinaemia — hereditary tyrosinaemia type 1, hepatorenal tyrosinaemia, fumarylacetoacetate hydrolase deficiency acute intermittent porphyria (crises are clinically similar) Guillain-Barre syndrome (during neurological crisis with weakness) other causes of infantile hepatic failure and cirrhosis (galactosaemia, hereditary fructose intolerance, neonatal haemochromatosis) Wilson disease and other inherited causes of hepatocellular carcinoma predisposition distal or proximal renal tubular acidosis and other causes of hypophosphataemic rickets transient tyrosinaemia of the newborn and hypertyrosinaemia secondary to hepatic failure tyrosinaemia type 2 and type 3 (as differentials of hypertyrosinaemia) quantitative urine and blood succinylacetone (diagnostic marker) plasma amino acids showing raised tyrosine, methionine and phenylalanine urine organic acids and delta-aminolaevulinic acid serum alpha-fetoprotein and liver synthetic function including coagulation FAH gene sequencing and, where relevant, erythrocyte FAH enzyme assay liver ultrasound and MRI for nodules and hepatocellular carcinoma surveillance renal tubular profile (phosphate, bicarbonate, glucose, generalised aminoaciduria) and bone imaging for rickets Hereditary tyrosinaemia type 1 (HT1) results from deficiency of fumarylacetoacetate hydrolase, the terminal enzyme of tyrosine catabolism; accumulated fumarylacetoacetate and succinylacetone are the toxic culprits, so the plasma tyrosine level does not itself reflect disease severity. Succinylacetone in urine or blood is the pathognomonic and most sensitive diagnostic marker; it is the analyte used in expanded newborn screening and should be requested specifically, as a raised tyrosine alone is non-specific and seen in many other states. Nitisinone (NTBC), which blocks the pathway upstream at 4-hydroxyphenylpyruvate dioxygenase, has transformed prognosis and is combined with a tyrosine- and phenylalanine-restricted diet; it must not be given without dietary control or iatrogenic tyrosine crystal keratopathy and skin lesions ensue. Succinylacetone inhibits porphobilinogen synthase (delta-aminolaevulinate dehydratase), producing acute porphyria-like neurological crises with abdominal pain, autonomic instability, hypertension and painful peripheral neuropathy that can mimic Guillain-Barre syndrome or acute intermittent porphyria. Untreated HT1 carries a very high lifetime risk of hepatocellular carcinoma, which may arise even in childhood; alpha-fetoprotein trends and cross-sectional imaging surveillance are central to long-term follow-up, and adults surviving on treatment remain under cancer surveillance. Renal involvement is a proximal (Fanconi-type) tubulopathy causing hypophosphataemic rickets, glycosuria, aminoaciduria and renal tubular acidosis; growth failure and bone disease may be presenting features in the milder chronic form. Tyrosinaemia type 2 (Richner-Hanhart, tyrosine aminotransferase deficiency) is a distinct disorder causing painful palmoplantar hyperkeratosis, dendritic (pseudoherpetic) keratitis and variable intellectual disability, treated by diet alone without hepatorenal or malignancy risk. Transient tyrosinaemia of the newborn and acquired hypertyrosinaemia from advanced liver disease are far commoner than the inherited enzymopathies and must be distinguished, as they lack succinylacetone. acute neurological crisis with severe abdominal pain, hypertension, autonomic instability and progressive weakness suggesting respiratory compromise rapidly deteriorating synthetic liver function with coagulopathy unresponsive to vitamin K rising or newly elevated alpha-fetoprotein or a new hepatic nodule indicating possible hepatocellular carcinoma corneal pain, photophobia and dendritic keratitis suggesting tyrosine keratopathy (type 2 or nitisinone overexposure without diet) hypophosphataemic rickets with fractures and marked growth failure Relying on plasma tyrosine to diagnose or exclude HT1; succinylacetone is the definitive marker and tyrosine may be only modestly raised. Attributing an acute painful neuropathy or abdominal crisis to porphyria or Guillain-Barre syndrome without considering underlying tyrosinaemia. Starting or continuing nitisinone without strict tyrosine restriction, risking tyrosine crystal keratopathy and hyperkeratotic skin lesions. Discontinuing malignancy surveillance in stable treated adults, in whom hepatocellular carcinoma can still arise. Confusing the benign transient tyrosinaemia of the newborn or hepatic-failure-related hypertyrosinaemia with inherited disease. Tyrosine is degraded through a five-enzyme hepatic and renal pathway. In hereditary tyrosinaemia type 1, biallelic loss-of-function variants in FAH abolish fumarylacetoacetate hydrolase, the final step, causing accumulation of the reactive electrophilic intermediates fumarylacetoacetate and maleylacetoacetate and their derivative succinylacetone. These compounds deplete glutathione, form adducts with cellular macromolecules and are mutagenic, injuring hepatocytes and proximal renal tubular cells and predisposing to malignant transformation. Succinylacetone additionally inhibits porphobilinogen synthase, causing accumulation of the neurotoxic haem precursor delta-aminolaevulinic acid that drives porphyria-like neurological crises, and it impairs renal tubular function producing a Fanconi syndrome. Tyrosinaemia type 2 reflects cytosolic tyrosine aminotransferase deficiency with tyrosine crystal deposition in skin and cornea, while type 3 (4-hydroxyphenylpyruvate dioxygenase deficiency) is milder and chiefly neurological; none of the toxic distal intermediates accumulate in these forms. With early nitisinone and dietary therapy, survival and freedom from liver failure and neurological crises are excellent and the risk of hepatocellular carcinoma is greatly reduced, particularly when treatment begins in the neonatal period. Late-treated or untreated disease carries high mortality from hepatic failure, malignancy or neurological crisis, and lifelong biochemical, hepatic imaging and malignancy surveillance remains necessary.

L-dopa, the precursor of dopamine and, in turn, noradrenaline and adrenaline. Biallelic TH mutations reduce enzyme activity, causing a central deficiency of catecholaminergic neurotransmission. Dopaminergic hypofunction produces the extrapyramidal features (dystonia, parkinsonism, hypokinesia, oculogyric crises), while reduced noradrenergic and adrenergic signalling contributes to ptosis, autonomic instability, and, in severe cases, encephalopathy. Because the pterin cofactor pathway is unaffected, phenylalanine handling and pterin concentrations remain normal, and the CSF shows selectively low dopamine metabolites. The milder dopa-responsive phenotype often improves markedly and durably with levodopa and BH4-independent dopaminergic therapy, whereas the severe encephalopathic form responds less completely and may leave residual disability. Early recognition and treatment improve motor and developmental outcomes.

FAH molecular testing Type 1 (hepatorenal) is the most severe form and stems from deficiency of fumarylacetoacetate hydrolase in the tyrosine degradation pathway Acute infantile presentation features liver failure, coagulopathy, ascites and a cabbage-like or boiled-cabbage odour Chronic disease produces cirrhosis, renal tubular dysfunction with hypophosphataemic rickets (renal Fanconi syndrome), and a very high risk of hepatocellular carcinoma Painful neurological crises resembling acute porphyria can occur due to accumulated succinylacetone inhibiting porphyrin synthesis Succinylacetone in blood or urine is the key diagnostic marker and is now used in newborn screening Type 2 causes eye and skin lesions with keratitis, and type 3 is a rare neurological form Management is centred on nitisinone (NTBC), which blocks tyrosine degradation upstream, combined with dietary restriction of phenylalanine and tyrosine Nitisinone therapy has transformed outcomes and reduced the need for liver transplantation, though HCC surveillance is still required Acute liver failure with coagulopathy in an infant is a metabolic emergency Porphyria-like neurological crises with pain, weakness and possible respiratory compromise Rising or persistently elevated alpha-fetoprotein or hepatic nodules suggesting hepatocellular carcinoma Severe electrolyte and phosphate loss from renal tubulopathy Relying on plasma tyrosine alone, which is non-specific, rather than measuring succinylacetone Attributing infantile liver failure to infection or sepsis and missing the treatable metabolic cause Assuming nitisinone eliminates hepatocellular carcinoma risk and stopping surveillance Neglecting phenylalanine and tyrosine dietary control while on nitisinone, risking corneal and skin complications Hereditary tyrosinemia type 1 is an autosomal recessive defect of fumarylacetoacetate hydrolase, the final enzyme of tyrosine catabolism. Its deficiency causes accumulation of the upstream intermediates maleylacetoacetate and fumarylacetoacetate, which are converted to the toxic metabolites succinylacetone and succinylacetoacetate. These compounds are highly reactive and injure hepatocytes and renal tubular cells, driving hepatic failure, cirrhosis, malignant transformation and renal Fanconi syndrome. Succinylacetone also inhibits delta-aminolaevulinic acid dehydratase, causing porphyrin precursor accumulation and porphyria-like neurological crises. Nitisinone works by inhibiting 4-hydroxyphenylpyruvate dioxygenase upstream, preventing formation of the toxic distal metabolites. Untreated type 1 disease historically carried a poor prognosis with death from liver failure in infancy or later hepatocellular carcinoma, but early newborn detection with nitisinone and dietary therapy markedly improves survival and reduces cancer risk; lifelong monitoring remains essential.

titinopathy Cardiac symptoms, since some TTN variants are associated with cardiomyopathy Respiratory muscle weakness with declining vital capacity Rapid progression atypical for the classic heterozygous phenotype Mistaking the foot drop for a peroneal nerve palsy or radiculopathy Failing to consider a severe recessive titinopathy in relatives when counselling families Assuming normal creatine kinase excludes myopathy Overlooking possible cardiac involvement associated with certain titin variants Udd myopathy results from dominant variants affecting the C-terminal M-line region of titin, the giant sarcomeric protein that spans from the Z-disc to the M-line and provides passive elasticity and a scaffold for sarcomere assembly and signalling. considered in end-stage disease Progressive right heart failure in infancy or childhood Ventricular arrhythmia or syncope Signs suggesting risk of sudden cardiac death Severe right ventricular dilatation with haemodynamic compromise Confusing it with arrhythmogenic right ventricular cardiomyopathy, which has different genetics and management Overlooking the arrhythmic and sudden-death risk while focusing on heart failure Misattributing right heart failure to pulmonary or valvular causes Underestimating disease severity from a preserved left ventricle early in the course Uhl anomaly is a congenital cardiomyopathy in which the right ventricular myocardium is almost entirely absent, so the free wall consists of directly apposed endocardium and epicardium with little or no intervening muscle. This is thought to arise from an excessive developmental loss of right ventricular myocytes, in contrast to the progressive fibrofatty myocardial replacement of arrhythmogenic right ventricular cardiomyopathy. The outlook is generally poor, with many patients developing progressive right heart failure and arrhythmia; survival varies with severity, and advanced disease may ultimately require cardiac transplantation.

walking Rapidly progressive scoliosis compromising respiratory function Feeding difficulty and failure to thrive in infancy Loss of ambulation requiring orthopaedic and rehabilitation planning Delaying respiratory surveillance because motor function seems relatively preserved Overlooking the diagnostic combination of proximal contractures with distal hyperlaxity in a hypotonic infant family history Ullrich congenital muscular dystrophy is caused by mutations in the collagen VI genes COL6A1, COL6A2 and COL6A3, which more severely disrupt the assembly or function of the collagen VI microfibrillar network than the milder variants causing Bethlem myopathy. Collagen VI links the muscle-fibre basement membrane to the surrounding interstitial matrix, and its severe deficiency impairs the structural and signalling relationship between fibres and their environment, with dysregulated mitochondrial function and increased apoptosis contributing to early and profound muscle degeneration. Because collagen VI is widespread in connective tissue, the disorder also produces the characteristic joint contractures and hyperlaxity, skeletal deformity and skin abnormalities, and the early respiratory failure that dominates its natural history. Ullrich congenital muscular dystrophy is more severe than Bethlem myopathy, with many affected children losing ambulation in the first or second decade and developing progressive respiratory insufficiency that determines survival, although proactive respiratory and orthopaedic care can substantially prolong and improve life.

(overt prolapse); a cord lying beside the presenting part is occult prolapse, and a cord below the presenting part with intact membranes is a cord presentation It is an acute obstetric emergency because cord compression, together with vasospasm from cooling and handling, interrupts fetal oxygenation and produces rapid fetal hypoxia and bradycardia Risk factors reflect a poorly applied presenting part: malpresentation such as breech or transverse lie, prematurity, polyhydramnios, a high or unengaged presenting part, multiparity, multiple pregnancy, and a long cord Iatrogenic cases vagina or at the introitus, or by an abrupt fetal heart rate abnormality such as variable decelerations or bradycardia soon after membrane rupture Immediate measures relieve cord compression: elevate the presenting part manually or by filling the bladder, position the woman knee-chest or head-down in the left lateral posture, minimise handling of the cord, and consider tocolysis Definitive management is expedited delivery, most often by emergency caesarean section, unless vaginal birth is imminent and would be quicker Outcome depends chiefly on the interval from diagnosis to delivery, so regular drills, early recognition, and rapid transfer are central to safe management Fetal bradycardia or deep variable decelerations following rupture of the membranes Visible or palpable cord at or beyond the introitus Loss of cord pulsation A prolonged diagnosis-to-delivery interval Cord prolapse occurring remote from theatre or skilled help Performing artificial rupture of membranes with a high or ill-applied presenting part, precipitating prolapse Attempting to replace or excessively handle the cord, which aggravates vasospasm Failing to maintain continuous elevation of the presenting part until delivery Delaying delivery to complete investigations or transfer without maintaining decompression measures Overlooking a cord presentation on examination in a woman with risk factors before the membranes rupture The umbilical cord supplies the fetus with oxygenated blood, and vessel patency depends on the cord not being compressed. A presenting part that does not fill the pelvic inlet, as in malpresentation, prematurity, an unengaged head, or polyhydramnios with sudden decompression at membrane rupture, leaves a space through which the cord can slip below or beside the fetus. Once the cord lies below the presenting part with ruptured membranes, descent of the fetus and uterine contractions compress the cord against the bony pelvis and occlude the umbilical vessels. In addition, exposure of the cord to the cooler vaginal environment and physical handling provoke reflex vasospasm. The combination of mechanical occlusion and vasospasm reduces or abolishes umbilical blood flow, causing fetal hypoxaemia, bradycardia, and, if unrelieved, hypoxic-ischaemic injury or death. When recognised promptly and followed by rapid delivery, most babies do well. Delay in relieving cord compression is associated with hypoxic-ischaemic injury and perinatal death, and outcomes are worse when prolapse occurs outside hospital.

hernia Systemic sepsis or peritonism suggesting strangulated bowel Assuming an adult paraumbilical hernia will behave like a self-resolving infantile hernia Underestimating strangulation risk because of the narrow neck Overlooking uncontrolled ascites, which increases recurrence and complicates repair Missing a Sister Mary Joseph nodule by attributing all umbilical lumps to hernia Umbilical and paraumbilical hernias arise from a defect at or adjacent to the umbilical cicatrix. In infants the umbilical ring fails to close fully after cord separation. In adults, weakening and separation of the linea alba fibres around the umbilicus, combined with sustained raised intra-abdominal pressure from obesity, pregnancy, or ascites, allows protrusion of preperitoneal fat, omentum, or bowel through a paraumbilical defect. The characteristically narrow, fibrous neck restricts reduction and readily compromises the vascular supply of trapped contents, predisposing to incarceration and strangulation. Most infantile umbilical hernias close spontaneously. Adult paraumbilical hernias do not resolve and carry a meaningful risk of incarceration and strangulation; elective mesh repair gives good results, whereas emergency surgery, especially in obese or comorbid patients, is associated with higher complication rates.

rarely arises in chronic chromoblastomycosis) Necrotic/embolic skin lesions of other causes (mimicked by painful necrotic lesions of fusariosis) This group spans endemic dimorphic fungi (paracoccidioidomycosis, talaromycosis, emergomycosis, adiaspiromycosis), hyaline and dematiaceous molds (fusariosis, scedosporiosis/lomentosporiosis, phaeohyphomycoses), and the yeast-like Trichosporon; the more common invasive mycoses (histoplasmosis, coccidioidomycosis, blastomycosis, sporotrichosis, candidiasis, cryptococcosis, aspergillosis, mucormycosis) are covered separately (Harrison 22e p.1725). Dimorphic fungi exist as conidia-producing molds in the environment (the infectious form) and convert to yeast (or spherules/adiaspores) at temperatures above about 35 degrees C in tissue; infection generally begins with inhalation of conidia (Harrison 22e p.1725). Paracoccidioidomycosis (Paracoccidioides brasiliensis complex, P. lutzii) is acquired by inhalation in humid Central/South American forests, with highest incidence in Brazil; chronic disease shows a striking male predominance (reported male-to-female ratios from 14:1 up to ~70:1) (Harrison 22e p.1726). The acute/juvenile form of paracoccidioidomycosis is uncommon, occurs typically in those under 30, primarily disseminates through the reticuloendothelial system, and often shows peripheral eosinophilia; the chronic/adult form accounts for ~90% of cases (Harrison 22e p.1726). On tissue, Paracoccidioides yeast classically appears as a central yeast ringed by narrow-necked daughter buds (the 'mariner's wheel'); some commercial serologic tests may fail to detect P. lutzii (Harrison 22e p.1726). Talaromycosis (Talaromyces marneffei, formerly Penicillium marneffei) is endemic in Vietnam, Thailand, and other Southeast Asian countries, is epidemiologically linked to bamboo rats, and occurs mostly in advanced AIDS; its presentation mimics disseminated histoplasmosis with umbilicated molluscum-like skin papules (Harrison 22e p.1727). In culture T. marneffei produces a distinctive diffusible red pigment, and tissue/blood smears show yeast-like organisms reproducing by bipolar fission (two ellipses with a central septum) (Harrison 22e p.1727). Emergomycosis (Emergomyces, several formerly Emmonsia) is an emerging dimorphic-fungus infection of patients with impaired cellular immunity; cutaneous involvement (disseminated ulcers, papules, nodules) accompanies pulmonary disease in most patients, while CNS spread is rare (Harrison 22e p.1727). Fusariosis is angioinvasive and mimics aspergillosis, but is distinguished by very common, often painful, nodular or necrotic skin lesions appearing around the onset of fever and by frequently positive blood cultures (~50%); banana-shaped macroconidia are characteristic on culture (Harrison 22e p.1728). Phaeohyphomycoses are caused by melanin-producing (dematiaceous/brown-black) molds; melanin is a virulence factor, certain species (Cladophialophora bantiana, Rhinocladiella mackenziei) are neurotropic, and golden-brown hyphae are highlighted by the Fontana-Masson melanin stain (Harrison 22e p.1728). Trichosporonosis (most often Trichosporon asahii) resembles invasive candidiasis with fungemia, but the presence of arthroconidia helps distinguish it from candidemia, and the serum cryptococcal antigen latex agglutination test can be falsely positive because T. asahii shares polysaccharide antigens with Cryptococcus neoformans (Harrison 22e p.1729). Scedosporiosis (Scedosporium apiospermum complex) and lomentosporiosis (Lomentospora prolificans) mimic aspergillosis radiographically and histologically; L. prolificans can grow in blood cultures whereas S. apiospermum usually does not (Harrison 22e p.1729). isolate as disease without evidence of tissue invasion, since Scedosporium/Lomentospora may merely colonize the airway (e.g., in bronchiectasis) In vitro susceptibility of dematiaceous molds may not reflect response because muriform/tissue forms can behave differently from hyphal forms Overlooking Fusarium onychomycosis as a portal for later disseminated disease in patients heading into neutropenia or transplantation Missing the diagnosis in 'immunocompetent' patients with disseminated/brain phaeohyphomycosis who may carry CLEC7A/CARD9 pathway defects Most of these fungi enter through inhalation of environmental conidia, with a smaller number introduced by traumatic skin or corneal inoculation or by injection of contaminated material. Dimorphic fungi (Paracoccidioides, Talaromyces, Emergomyces, Emmonsia crescens) convert from mold to invasive yeast/adiaspore form under thermal pressure in the lungs and then disseminate hematogenously to the reticuloendothelial system and other organs; granulomatous inflammation is typical. Disease frequently reflects host immune deficits: inborn errors affecting the IL-12/IFN-gamma axis predispose to severe paracoccidioidomycosis and talaromycosis, and IFN-gamma-primed monocytes/macrophages and neutrophils control Talaromyces. Molds such as Fusarium, Scedosporium, and Lomentospora are angioinvasive, and protection against Fusarium and Trichosporon depends heavily on neutrophils and their oxidative burst, explaining the strong link with profound prolonged neutropenia and with chronic granulomatous disease (defective NADPH oxidase). Dematiaceous molds use melanin as a virulence factor; defense against disseminated phaeohyphomycosis involves Dectin-1 (CLEC7A) and the adaptor CARD9, and deficiencies in this pathway predispose to disseminated and brain infection even in otherwise immunocompetent hosts. In adiaspiromycosis, inhaled E. crescens conidia enlarge into nonreplicating thick-walled adiaspores (up to ~500 micrometers) that drive a granulomatous inflammatory response. Outcomes vary widely by organism and host immune status. Paracoccidioidomycosis generally responds well, though pulmonary fibrosis can progress in chronic disease. Untreated disseminated talaromycosis is usually fatal, but treated mortality is about 10%. Disseminated fusariosis carries high mortality (historically up to ~85%, now around 50% with better therapy) and approaches 100% if neutropenia persists; survival hinges on neutrophil recovery. Invasive S. apiospermum infection has roughly 50% mortality, whereas L. prolificans remains about 85-100% lethal. Disseminated trichosporonosis mortality has been as high as 70% and remains very high with persistent neutropenia. Disseminated and visceral phaeohyphomycoses, particularly with CNS involvement, have high mortality. No single formal staging applies across this heterogeneous group. Practically, infections are stratified by extent and host status: localized cutaneous/keratitis/onychomycosis or pulmonary-limited disease versus disseminated/angioinvasive infection; presence of CNS involvement marks the most severe end (associated with the highest mortality). For dimorphic fungi (e.g., paracoccidioidomycosis, talaromycosis, emergomycosis), disease is broadly described as mild/moderate versus severe, and as acute (juvenile) versus chronic (adult) forms for paracoccidioidomycosis.

comprehensive pathological assessment. It is genomically complex, marked by extensive chromosomal instability, copy-number aberrations, and frequent alterations in tumour-suppressor pathways such as TP53 and RB1, without the single recurrent translocation that characterises many other sarcomas. bone cyst is a benign, likely non-neoplastic, fluid-filled cavity of bone lined by a thin fibrous membrane. Its origin is debated but is thought to involve a local disturbance of interstitial fluid drainage and venous outflow within the metaphysis, producing raised intracystic pressure that promotes bone resorption and cavity expansion. Active lesions abut the physis and tend to enlarge, whereas latent lesions migrate away from the growth plate with maturity and often ossify. unicuspid aortic valve — unicommissural aortic valve, UAV Bicuspid aortic valve Rheumatic aortic stenosis Calcific degenerative tricuspid aortic stenosis Quadricuspid aortic valve Subvalvar (subaortic membrane) or supravalvar aortic stenosis Hypertrophic cardiomyopathy with left ventricular outflow tract obstruction Transthoracic echocardiography with careful short-axis leaflet imaging Transoesophageal echocardiography to define commissural morphology Three-dimensional echocardiography Cardiac CT angiography for valve morphology, calcification and aortic dimensions Cardiac MRI for regurgitant fraction and aortic assessment Electrocardiography for left ventricular hypertrophy Exercise testing in apparently asymptomatic severe stenosis Unicuspid aortic valve is far rarer than bicuspid disease and typically presents with severe stenosis at a younger age, often in the third to fourth decade. Two morphological subtypes exist: acommissural (dome-shaped orifice with no commissural attachment to the aortic wall) and unicommissural (a single eccentric commissure producing a teardrop or keyhole orifice); the unicommissural type is more common. On parasternal short-axis echocardiography the orifice looks eccentric and slit-like, and the classic teardrop shape may be evident only in systole, so image carefully at the leaflet tips. The valve is frequently misdiagnosed as bicuspid; transoesophageal or 3D echocardiography and cardiac CT or MRI improve accurate counting of commissures. Associated aortopathy with ascending aortic dilatation occurs independently of haemodynamic severity, so serial aortic imaging is warranted. Coexisting coarctation of the aorta and other left-heart obstructive lesions should be actively excluded. Infective endocarditis risk is increased on the structurally abnormal valve. Young patients frequently require surgery, including the Ross procedure, valve repair or replacement, often combined with aortic root or ascending aortic replacement. Exertional syncope, angina or heart failure symptoms indicating severe stenosis Rapidly progressive ascending aortic dilatation Fever, new regurgitant murmur or embolic phenomena suggesting infective endocarditis Severe aortic regurgitation with left ventricular dilatation or dysfunction Mislabelling a unicommissural valve as bicuspid because a fused commissure mimics a raphe Assessing morphology only in diastole and missing the systolic teardrop orifice Overlooking associated aortopathy and coarctation Underestimating stenosis severity when the eccentric orifice lies off-axis to the Doppler beam The anomaly arises from failure of separation of the valve cushions during embryogenesis, producing fusion of one or both commissures so that the valve opens through a single eccentric orifice with one functional commissure (unicommissural) or none (acommissural, dome-shaped). The eccentric restrictive orifice generates turbulent transvalvar flow that accelerates leaflet fibrosis and calcification, leading to progressive stenosis, regurgitation, or a mixed lesion. The same developmental disturbance is associated with an intrinsically abnormal aortic wall showing medial degeneration, which predisposes to ascending aortic dilatation and aneurysm irrespective of valve haemodynamics. Without intervention severe obstruction or regurgitation develops earlier than in bicuspid disease and often requires surgery in young adulthood. Long-term outcome after valve or root surgery is good, but lifelong surveillance for aortopathy and prosthesis-related complications is required.

Assuming a normal chromosome number excludes an imprinting disorder Uniparental disomy of chromosome 14 occurs when both copies of the chromosome are inherited from one parent. Because 14q32 carries a differentially methylated, imprinted gene cluster, the parental origin determines the outcome: two maternal copies, with loss of the paternally expressed genes, cause Temple syndrome, whereas two paternal copies, with over-expression of paternally expressed genes and loss of maternally expressed ones, cause Kagami-Ogata syndrome. Identical phenotypes can follow imprinting-centre microdeletions or primary epimutations at the same locus, so these disorders are best understood as disturbances of 14q32 imprinting rather than of chromosome number alone. Outlook varies by parental origin: Temple syndrome generally has a fair outcome with growth and developmental support, whereas Kagami-Ogata syndrome carries higher neonatal mortality from respiratory difficulty; both require multidisciplinary follow-up.

serial tracings are important High-sensitivity troponin measured serially is required to separate unstable angina from NSTEMI, since myocardial necrosis defines the latter Early risk stratification using validated scores guides the timing of an invasive versus a conservative strategy Initial management centres on antiplatelet and anticoagulant therapy, anti-ischaemic measures, and admission for monitoring Because it reflects an unstable coronary plaque, it can progress rapidly to infarction and warrants urgent evaluation rather than outpatient workup MEDICAL EMERGENCY: presentation is an acute coronary syndrome requiring urgent assessment and monitoring because of the risk of progression to myocardial infarction Ongoing or recurrent rest pain despite initial therapy indicating refractory ischaemia Haemodynamic instability, new heart failure, or malignant arrhythmia Dynamic ST-segment shifts or a rising troponin signalling evolving infarction Discharging a patient with rest or crescendo chest pain because a single troponin or ECG is normal Failing to obtain serial ECGs and biomarkers to capture dynamic change Underestimating risk in atypical presentations, particularly in women, older adults, and those with diabetes Delaying antithrombotic therapy or admission while awaiting definitive imaging Unstable angina is usually precipitated by rupture or erosion of an atherosclerotic plaque with superimposed non-occlusive or intermittent thrombus formation, causing an acute reduction in coronary blood flow. Dynamic vasoconstriction and platelet aggregation further limit supply. Unlike infarction, the ischaemia is severe but does not persist long enough or completely enough to produce detectable myocardial necrosis, so cardiac biomarkers remain normal. The same unstable plaque can progress to complete occlusion, linking unstable angina pathophysiologically to NSTEMI and STEMI. With prompt recognition, antithrombotic therapy, and appropriate risk-based revascularisation most patients stabilise, but delayed treatment or high-risk features carry a substantial early risk of infarction, arrhythmia, and death.

urgent review Emergence of prominent ataxia limiting mobility and safety Using phenytoin or other sodium-channel-blocking agents, which markedly worsen myoclonus and cerebellar signs Confusing EPM1 with juvenile myoclonic epilepsy and missing the progressive component Assuming a uniformly poor prognosis and not distinguishing it from Lafora disease Underestimating the functional impact of action myoclonus on daily activities Unverricht-Lundborg disease is caused by deficiency of cystatin B, an inhibitor of cysteine proteases (cathepsins). The commonest mutation is an unstable expansion of a dodecamer repeat in the CSTB promoter that reduces gene expression. Loss of cystatin B is thought to lead to unopposed cathepsin activity, increased oxidative stress, and enhanced neuronal apoptosis, particularly affecting cerebellar and cortical neurones. Unlike Lafora disease there is no storage material; the pathology is one of neuronal loss and gliosis, which correlates with the predominance of myoclonus and ataxia over dementia. With appropriate anti-myoclonic treatment and avoidance of aggravating drugs, many patients have a near-normal lifespan; disability relates mainly to action myoclonus and ataxia rather than dementia, and the course is much better than in Lafora disease.

benign tumors (lipoma, leiomyoma, neurofibroma, lymphoid nodular hyperplasia) Two biologically distinct esophageal cancers arise in the same organ: squamous cell carcinoma (SCC), favoring the upper and mid esophagus, and adenocarcinoma, almost always in the lower esophagus and at the gastroesophageal junction (GEJ); globally SCC predominates while adenocarcinoma now accounts for over 75% of incident U.S./Western European cases. Because dysphagia and odynophagia are typically not noticed until the lumen is substantially obstructed, most esophageal cancers are locally advanced or metastatic at diagnosis; any patient with these symptoms warrants upper endoscopy with biopsy. Helicobacter pylori is a major chronic-inflammation driver of gastric cancer, but cancer develops in only a small subset of the roughly half of humans infected; eradication has been shown in prospective trials to lower subsequent gastric cancer risk, supporting treatment of asymptomatic H. pylori in those with a first-degree relative with gastric cancer or a prior early-stage gastric cancer. Physical findings suggesting advanced/metastatic gastric cancer include left supraclavicular adenopathy (Virchow's node), a periumbilical nodule (Sister Mary Joseph nodule), a palpable rectal-shelf mass (Blumer's shelf), ascites, and an ovarian mass (Krukenberg tumor); more commonly the exam is unrevealing. Diffuse (signet-cell) gastric cancer may not form a discrete mass or ulcer, instead producing thickened gastric rugae and tracking beneath an intact mucosal surface, so initial superficial biopsies can be falsely negative and EUS-guided deeper biopsy may be required. Germline CDH1 (e-cadherin) mutation markedly increases risk of the diffuse/signet-cell gastric cancer subtype and also raises lobular breast cancer risk; prophylactic gastrectomy is an option in CDH1 carriers. Molecular profiling is therapeutically decisive: roughly 20-25% of esophageal/GEJ and about 20% of gastric adenocarcinomas overexpress or amplify HER2/ERBB2, and MSI-high/mismatch-repair-deficient and PD-L1-high (high combined positive score) tumors identify candidates for immune-modulating therapy; NGS plus PD-L1 IHC should be routine in metastatic disease. Gastric lymphomas (about 3% of gastric malignancies) are extranodal non-Hodgkin lymphomas; the GI tract is the most common extranodal NHL site and the stomach is the most common GI site, with MALT (~40%) and diffuse large B-cell lymphoma (~55%) being the dominant subtypes. MALT lymphoma of the stomach is strongly H. pylori-associated, and the stomach accounts for about 35% of all MALT lymphomas; the t(11;18) translocation marks tumors less likely to respond to H. pylori eradication. GISTs arise from the interstitial cells of Cajal and are driven by activating cKIT (~majority) or PDGFRA mutations; the stomach is the most frequent primary site (~60%), followed by small bowel (~25%); spindle-cell histology predominates (~70%) and KIT expression is found in ~95%. Small-bowel neoplasms account for only about 3% of GI tumors; in the U.S., neuroendocrine (carcinoid) tumors (40-45%) slightly outnumber adenocarcinomas (30-40%), and the duodenum is the most common site (~50%). EBV is associated with a distinct gastric cancer subtype (identified in roughly 8-10% of gastric cancer patients) and is described as a driver in some esophageal/GEJ adenocarcinomas; current EBV positivity does not by itself change therapeutic options. New or progressive dysphagia or odynophagia, especially with weight loss Hematemesis or melena, or unexplained iron-deficiency anemia from occult GI bleeding Anorexia, early satiety, and unexplained weight loss Left supraclavicular (Virchow's) node, Sister Mary Joseph periumbilical nodule, Blumer's shelf, ascites, or Krukenberg ovarian mass indicating advanced disease Dysphagia, odynophagia, or upper abdominal discomfort in a patient under 50, given the rising incidence of early-onset upper GI cancers (symptoms must not be dismissed as benign) Small-bowel obstruction, perforation, or intussusception as a presentation of small-bowel neoplasm Falsely reassuring superficial endoscopic biopsies in diffuse-type gastric cancer or gastric lymphoma, which track below the mucosa; adequate deep tissue or EUS-guided sampling is required. Relying on FDG-PET to exclude disease in diffuse-type gastric cancer, which is often not FDG-avid (PET may be non-informative). Using tumor markers (CEA, CA19-9) for diagnosis; they are nonspecific and elevated in many cancers, and are better for monitoring response/progression. Attributing alarm symptoms in patients under 50 to benign illness and delaying diagnostic workup, given rising early-onset upper GI cancer incidence. Missing tracheobronchial invasion in mid/upper esophageal tumors, which precludes curative surgery, by omitting bronchoscopy. Treating gastric lymphoma like adenocarcinoma; surgical resection has no role in primary gastric lymphoma and MALT may respond to H. pylori eradication alone, so accurate subtyping is critical. Assuming a t(11;18)-positive MALT lymphoma will respond to H. pylori eradication; this subgroup is less likely to respond. Forgetting HBV testing before initiating lymphoma therapy (risk of reactivation). Esophageal SCC is linked to mucosal injury from alcohol and tobacco (synergistic), ingestion of very hot beverages, areca/betel-nut chewing, chronic achalasia, prior radiation, lye-induced strictures, and Plummer-Vinson (Patterson-Kelly) syndrome; genomically it resembles SCCs of other sites (e.g., head and neck) more than esophageal adenocarcinoma, and HPV is not implicated. Esophageal/GEJ adenocarcinoma arises in the setting of chronic gastroesophageal reflux producing inflammation and Barrett's metaplasia (glandular gastric-type mucosa extending into the esophagus); progression through dysplasia accumulates TP53 mutations and aneuploidy, with annual risk of progression of Barrett's to cancer about 0.4-0.5%. Gastric adenocarcinoma is predominantly an inflammation-driven malignancy: H. pylori (and the broader gastric microbiome) and ingestion of nitrate-rich smoked/salted/dried foods generate carcinogenic nitrites; the intestinal Lauren subtype associates with H. pylori and atrophic gastritis, while the diffuse subtype (~20%) associates with germline or somatic CDH1 loss. TCGA defines four molecular subtypes (EBV-positive, microsatellite-unstable/hypermutated, genomically stable [diffuse], and chromosomally unstable). The proximal esophagus-GEJ-gastric cardia adenocarcinomas share a similar genomic profile suggesting common driving factors. Gastric MALT lymphoma is driven by chronic antigenic stimulation from H. pylori, with the t(11;18) API1-MALT1 fusion activating NF-kB signaling. GISTs originate from Cajal cells via gain-of-function KIT or PDGFRA mutations. Esophageal cancer prognosis remains poor overall but is slowly improving; by clinical (pretreatment) AJCC staging, 5-year survival ranges from about 75-82% for stage 0-I down to roughly 5-18% for metastatic (stage IVB) disease, and most U.S. patients present with locally advanced or metastatic disease. For gastric cancer, surgery alone yields about 25% overall 5-year survival, with stage-dependent rates falling from about 90% (stage 0) to roughly 3% for stage IV; multimodality therapy (perioperative chemotherapy plus surgery) improves 5-year survival by about 10-15% over surgery alone (e.g., MAGIC trial 36% vs 23%). Even with modern systemic and immune-modulating therapy, overall survival for stage IV gastric cancer is still only about 12-15 months. Gastric MSI-high tumors had the best outcomes and genomically stable (diffuse)/mesenchymal subtypes the worst in genomic series. Lynch-syndrome-associated small-bowel cancers probably have a better prognosis. For nonmetastatic gastric GIST, resected tumors 2 cm or smaller with a mitotic index of 5% or less carry near-zero progression risk, whereas tumors 10 cm or larger with mitotic index above 5% are moderate-to-high risk. Esophageal and gastric cancers are staged with the AJCC TNM system (eighth edition; ninth edition expected 2024), with separate clinical (cTNM, pretreatment), pathologic (pTNM, for patients undergoing initial surgery), and post-neoadjuvant (ypTNM) classifications. The esophageal T stage reflects depth of penetration through the wall (which over most of its course lacks serosa); regional nodal disease is still potentially curable while metastatic disease is generally treated palliatively. Gastric staging similarly progresses from Tis (mucosa-confined, stage 0) through wall penetration and increasing nodal involvement to distant metastasis (stage IV). Gastric lymphomas are NOT staged by TNM; the Lugano system (an Ann Arbor modification) is used: stage I confined to the gastric wall, stage II regional nodal or local-structure involvement, stage III nodes on both sides of the diaphragm, stage IV more extensive nodal or distant/extranodal (including marrow) disease. GIST recurrence risk is stratified by primary tumor size, mitotic index, and GI location. Neuroendocrine tumors are graded 1-3 by Ki-67 positivity, distinct from fully malignant small-/large-cell neuroendocrine carcinomas.

uraemic pericarditis — uremic pericarditis, renal pericarditis, dialysis-associated pericarditis viral or idiopathic acute pericarditis bacterial (purulent) pericarditis tuberculous pericarditis myocardial infarction or acute coronary syndrome systemic lupus erythematosus or other connective tissue disease serositis hypothyroidism-related pericardial effusion malignant pericardial effusion transthoracic echocardiography (effusion size, tamponade physiology) 12-lead ECG (typically lacks diffuse ST/PR changes; assess for ischaemia) serum urea, creatinine and electrolytes with assessment of dialysis adequacy full blood count and inflammatory markers pericardial fluid analysis if drained (haemorrhagic exudate; exclude infection and malignancy) troponin (to help distinguish concurrent myocardial injury) chest radiography (cardiomegaly, pulmonary congestion) A useful distinction is drawn between true uraemic pericarditis, occurring in advanced untreated or under-dialysed renal failure before dialysis initiation, and dialysis-associated pericarditis, arising in established dialysis patients often due to inadequate dialysis or intercurrent illness. Uraemic pericarditis correlates broadly with the degree of azotaemia, though no single threshold of urea or creatinine reliably predicts it. A characteristic feature is that the friction rub and clinical picture often persist despite the absence of the typical diffuse ECG changes of acute pericarditis, because the inflammation spares the underlying epicardial myocardium. The friction rub may be loud and persistent, and effusions are frequently large and haemorrhagic owing to uraemic platelet dysfunction. Because ECG changes are typically absent, new widespread ST elevation in a uraemic patient should prompt consideration of an alternative or additional diagnosis such as myocardial injury. The mainstay of treatment for true uraemic pericarditis is initiation or intensification of dialysis, which resolves most cases; heparin-free or minimal-heparin dialysis is preferred to reduce haemorrhagic effusion risk. Persistent or recurrent effusion despite intensive dialysis, or the development of tamponade, may require pericardiocentesis or a pericardial window; anti-inflammatory agents have a more limited and adjunctive role. Progression to cardiac tamponade is an important and potentially fatal complication requiring urgent recognition and drainage. hypotension, raised jugular venous pressure and pulsus paradoxus indicating tamponade large or rapidly enlarging haemorrhagic effusion widespread ST elevation suggesting concomitant myocardial injury rather than isolated uraemic pericarditis haemodynamic deterioration during or shortly after heparinised dialysis fever and features suggesting superimposed purulent pericarditis Expecting the diffuse ECG changes of typical acute pericarditis, whose absence may lead to the diagnosis being missed. Continuing standard heparinised haemodialysis and thereby worsening a haemorrhagic effusion or precipitating tamponade. Attributing all chest pain in a uraemic patient to pericarditis and overlooking concurrent myocardial ischaemia. Relying on non-steroidal anti-inflammatory drugs, which are often ineffective and nephrotoxic, instead of optimising dialysis. Under-recognising tamponade because hypotension is ascribed to intradialytic fluid shifts. The pericardial inflammation of renal failure is driven by the retention of uraemic toxins and metabolic derangements accompanying severely reduced glomerular filtration, although the precise causative solutes are not fully defined. The visceral and parietal pericardial surfaces develop a fibrinous, sometimes haemorrhagic, exudative reaction. A distinctive feature is that the inflammatory process typically remains confined to the pericardium and does not extend into the subepicardial myocardium, which explains the frequent absence of the diffuse ST-segment and PR-segment changes seen in other forms of acute pericarditis. Uraemia-associated platelet dysfunction and the anticoagulation used during haemodialysis predispose to haemorrhagic effusions, which may accumulate to produce tamponade. In dialysis-associated disease, inadequate solute clearance, volume overload, intercurrent infection or inflammation are contributory. With timely initiation or intensification of dialysis most cases of true uraemic pericarditis resolve, and the outlook is generally favourable; however, large haemorrhagic effusions, tamponade and progression to constriction are recognised complications, and dialysis-associated pericarditis that responds poorly to intensified dialysis carries a worse prognosis.

Urea cycle disorder — urea cycle defect, UCD, hyperammonaemia from urea cycle enzyme deficiency, inherited hyperammonaemia Organic acidaemias (which cause hyperammonaemia with metabolic acidosis) Fatty acid oxidation disorders Transient hyperammonaemia of the newborn Neonatal sepsis and meningitis Liver failure of other cause Hyperinsulinism-hyperammonaemia syndrome Plasma ammonia (urgent) and arterial blood gas showing respiratory alkalosis Plasma amino acids (citrulline, arginine, argininosuccinate) and urine orotic acid to localise the defect Plasma glucose, lactate, and acid-base status to distinguish from organic acidaemias Newborn screening (citrulline and arginine markers) Enzyme assays and molecular genetic testing for the specific defect Neuroimaging to assess cerebral oedema in severe hyperammonaemia A group of inherited defects in enzymes or transporters of the urea cycle that impair conversion of ammonia to urea, causing hyperammonaemia Severe neonatal presentation is typically a well baby who develops poor feeding, lethargy, vomiting, tachypnoea and encephalopathy in the first days of life The hallmark biochemical finding is hyperammonaemia usually with a respiratory alkalosis and, in most defects, a normal anion gap (distinguishing from organic acidaemias) Plasma citrulline and urine orotic acid help localise the enzymatic block within the cycle Later-onset and partial defects can present in older children or adults with episodic encephalopathy, psychiatric symptoms, or protein aversion, often triggered by catabolic stress Acute management principles are to stop protein intake, reverse catabolism with high calorie (glucose and lipid) support, and lower ammonia with nitrogen-scavenging agents and, when severe, haemodialysis Arginine (or citrulline) supplementation is used to replenish urea cycle intermediates in most defects except arginase deficiency Many urea cycle disorders are included in newborn screening panels, though the most severe neonatal cases may present before results return Severe hyperammonaemia with encephalopathy is a medical emergency requiring immediate ammonia-lowering and often dialysis Rapidly declining level of consciousness, seizures, or signs of raised intracranial pressure from cerebral oedema Neonate deteriorating after an initially normal period, mistaken for sepsis Recurrent unexplained encephalopathy or coma triggered by high protein intake, infection, or surgery in older patients Failing to measure ammonia in an encephalopathic neonate or child and attributing symptoms to sepsis Allowing sample delay or poor technique to give falsely elevated or unreliable ammonia results Continuing protein intake or under-treating catabolism during acute decompensation Not recognising milder late-onset presentations, especially in females with ornithine transcarbamylase deficiency The urea cycle detoxifies waste nitrogen by converting ammonia derived from amino acid metabolism into urea for renal excretion. Deficiency of any of its enzymes (carbamoyl phosphate synthetase 1, ornithine transcarbamylase, argininosuccinate synthetase, argininosuccinate lyase, arginase) or of the N-acetylglutamate synthase activator or transporters interrupts this flux, causing ammonia to accumulate. Ammonia is neurotoxic, producing astrocyte swelling, cerebral oedema and glutamine accumulation, leading to encephalopathy and, if untreated, irreversible brain injury or death. The pattern of accumulated intermediates (citrulline, argininosuccinate) and urine orotic acid reflects the position of the block. Outcome correlates strongly with the peak and duration of hyperammonaemia; prolonged severe neonatal hyperammonaemia carries a high risk of death or permanent neurodevelopmental impairment, whereas early recognition, prompt ammonia control and liver transplantation in selected cases improve survival and reduce disability.

Ureaplasma urealyticum infection — Ureaplasma urealyticum, Ureaplasma, U. urealyticum, ureaplasma Chlamydia trachomatis infection Neisseria gonorrhoeae infection Mycoplasma genitalium infection Trichomonas vaginalis infection Bacterial vaginosis Urinary tract infection Non-infective urethritis Nucleic acid amplification testing or specialised culture of genital or urine specimens, with species differentiation where available Concurrent nucleic acid amplification testing for chlamydia and gonorrhoea to exclude established pathogens Microscopy of genital smears to document urethritis or cervicitis Testing for Mycoplasma genitalium and Trichomonas vaginalis in persistent urethritis In relevant pregnancy or neonatal settings, placental histology or neonatal respiratory sampling as clinically indicated Screening for other sexually transmitted infections when a sexually acquired cause is suspected Ureaplasma urealyticum is a cell-wall-deficient mollicute that colonises the lower genital tract of many sexually active adults, so its detection often reflects commensal carriage rather than disease Its pathogenic role is debated; unlike Mycoplasma genitalium it is not consistently proven to cause urethritis, and routine testing or treatment of asymptomatic carriers is generally not advised Ureaplasma urealyticum (as distinct from the usually commensal Ureaplasma parvum) has been implicated in some cases of non-chlamydial non-gonococcal urethritis In pregnancy, ureaplasmas are associated with chorioamnionitis, preterm birth, and low birth weight, and they can be transmitted vertically to the neonate In preterm and very-low-birth-weight infants, respiratory tract colonisation has been linked to neonatal pneumonia and to the development of bronchopulmonary dysplasia Because it lacks a cell wall, it is invisible on Gram stain and inherently resistant to beta-lactams; diagnosis uses culture on specialised media or nucleic acid amplification testing When treatment is genuinely indicated, macrolides such as azithromycin or a tetracycline such as doxycycline are typically used, though tetracycline resistance occurs Interpreting a positive result requires clinical correlation, since a detection alone does not establish causation Preterm labour, prelabour rupture of membranes, or clinical chorioamnionitis in pregnancy Respiratory deterioration in a colonised preterm neonate suggesting pneumonia or evolving chronic lung disease Persistent symptomatic urethritis despite treatment for established pathogens Systemic or invasive infection in an immunocompromised host Treating an asymptomatic positive result and mistaking commensal colonisation for disease Failing to exclude established pathogens such as chlamydia, gonorrhoea, and Mycoplasma genitalium before attributing symptoms to ureaplasma Prescribing a beta-lactam, which is ineffective against a cell-wall-deficient organism Overlooking the perinatal implications of ureaplasma in pregnant and preterm-neonatal populations Ureaplasma species are among the smallest free-living bacteria and, like other mollicutes, lack a cell wall; they are named for their capacity to hydrolyse urea as an energy source. They frequently colonise the urogenital mucosa as commensals, and the balance between harmless carriage and disease appears to depend on host factors, bacterial load, species and serovar, and the presence of co-pathogens. When pathogenic, urease-driven ammonia production and a local inflammatory response are thought to contribute to mucosal injury, and the same mechanisms are implicated in intra-amniotic infection when the organism ascends in pregnancy, provoking chorioamnionitis and inflammation that may precipitate preterm labour and injure the developing fetal lung. Neonatal colonisation, particularly in preterm infants, can be followed by respiratory disease and chronic lung injury. In most immunocompetent adults ureaplasma carriage is benign and needs no treatment; when genuine infection is treated the outlook is generally good, whereas perinatal infection carries a less favourable outlook because of its associations with preterm birth and neonatal respiratory morbidity.

ureterocele Prolapse of an ectopic ureterocele through the urethra in a girl Febrile urinary tract infection or urosepsis with obstruction Deteriorating function of the affected or contralateral renal unit Forgetting the Weigert-Meyer rule and misidentifying which moiety the ureterocele drains Endoscopic incision creating iatrogenic reflux into the decompressed moiety Overlooking obstruction of the contralateral ureter or bladder outlet by a large ureterocele Assuming a poorly functioning upper pole must be removed without confirming function A ureterocele is thought to result from a In duplex systems the upper-pole ureter drains more caudally and medially and is the segment that typically forms an obstructing ureterocele, following the Weigert-Meyer rule. The dilated terminal sac can obstruct urine drainage from its own moiety and, when large or ectopic, may distort the bladder base and outlet, causing wider urinary tract dysfunction and predisposing to infection and upper-tract deterioration. Outcome depends on the function of the affected moiety and on associated reflux and obstruction; simple orthotopic ureteroceles often do well with endoscopic or conservative management, while complex ectopic duplex ureteroceles may require staged reconstruction but generally preserve overall renal function with appropriate treatment.

Ureteropelvic junction obstruction — pelviureteric junction obstruction, PUJ obstruction, UPJ obstruction Vesicoureteric reflux causing pelvicalyceal dilatation Primary obstructive megaureter (obstruction at the vesicoureteric junction) Multicystic dysplastic kidney (non-communicating cysts, no function) Extrarenal pelvis without true obstruction Calyceal or parapelvic cysts Ureteric obstruction from stone or stricture in older patients Renal ultrasound to grade pelvicalyceal dilatation and assess parenchymal thickness MAG3 diuretic renogram to assess drainage and differential function Micturating cystourethrogram (MCUG) to exclude coexisting reflux CT or MR urography to define anatomy and detect a crossing vessel, especially in adults Serial ultrasound for surveillance of antenatally detected hydronephrosis Urinalysis and culture if infection is suspected The commonest cause of congenital hydronephrosis, producing dilatation of the renal pelvis and calyces with a non-dilated ureter below the obstruction Frequently detected on antenatal ultrasound as unilateral hydronephrosis, though it may present later with loin pain, a palpable mass, infection, or haematuria Intrinsic causes include an aperistaltic segment or intrinsic stenosis; extrinsic causes include a crossing lower-pole vessel, more relevant in older children and adults The diuretic renogram (MAG3) is key: an obstructed pattern shows continued tracer accumulation with a rising or non-washout drainage curve after diuretic, whereas a prompt washout suggests no significant obstruction Differential renal function on renography guides the decision to intervene or observe Many mild antenatally detected cases stabilise or resolve, so serial imaging and expectant management are often appropriate Surgical treatment is dismembered pyeloplasty when there is significant or deteriorating obstruction, symptoms, or falling function Declining differential renal function on serial renography Increasing hydronephrosis or thinning renal parenchyma Febrile urinary tract infection or pyonephrosis in an obstructed system Severe or recurrent loin pain, or obstruction in a solitary kidney Interpreting a diuretic renogram without accounting for a full bladder, dehydration, or an immature neonatal kidney, which can mimic obstruction Rushing to surgery for mild stable hydronephrosis that would resolve spontaneously Missing a crossing lower-pole vessel that alters the surgical approach Overlooking coexisting vesicoureteric reflux before attributing all dilatation to junction obstruction Ureteropelvic junction obstruction is a functional or anatomical impedance to urine flow from the renal pelvis into the proximal ureter. Intrinsic obstruction usually results from a congenitally abnormal, aperistaltic or narrowed segment where disorganised smooth muscle and excess collagen prevent effective peristalsis, so a bolus of urine is not propagated across the junction. Extrinsic obstruction may be caused by an aberrant or accessory lower-pole renal artery crossing and kinking the junction. The resulting rise in intrapelvic pressure and stasis produces progressive pelvicalyceal dilatation and, if severe and prolonged, loss of renal parenchyma and function. Many mild antenatally detected cases resolve or remain stable with observation, and pyeloplasty for significant obstruction has a high success rate with preservation or improvement of function; severe long-standing obstruction, however, may leave irreversible parenchymal loss.

Urethral caruncle — caruncle of the urethra, urethral meatus caruncle, distal urethral polyp Urethral carcinoma Urethral mucosal prolapse Urethral diverticulum Periurethral cyst or abscess Condyloma or other meatal lesion Prolapsed ureterocele (rare) Careful clinical examination of the meatus Biopsy or excision histology when features are atypical Urinalysis and urine culture Cystourethroscopy if intraluminal pathology is suspected MRI or examination under anaesthesia for suspicious lesions A benign, fleshy, reddish polypoid lesion at the posterior (dorsal) edge of the external urethral meatus Overwhelmingly a condition of postmenopausal women, linked to oestrogen deficiency and atrophy of the urethral and vaginal tissues Often asymptomatic and found incidentally, but may cause spotting or bleeding, dysuria, local discomfort, or pain on contact Usually small and soft, and the diagnosis is clinical on inspection of the meatus The main concern is distinguishing it from urethral carcinoma or prolapsed urethral mucosa, especially if the lesion is firm, irregular, ulcerated, or enlarging Topical oestrogen and conservative measures suffice for most; surgical excision is reserved for large, symptomatic, or diagnostically uncertain lesions, with biopsy if malignancy is suspected Recurrence can occur, and any atypical lesion should undergo histological examination A firm, irregular, indurated, or ulcerated lesion Rapid growth Persistent bleeding Associated inguinal lymphadenopathy Failure to respond to topical oestrogen Assuming any meatal lesion is a benign caruncle and missing a urethral carcinoma Excising without histology when the features are atypical Overlooking a treatable underlying oestrogen deficiency amenable to topical therapy Confusing it with circumferential urethral mucosal prolapse, which is managed differently Urethral caruncles are thought to arise from oestrogen withdrawal after the menopause, which renders the distal urethral and periurethral mucosa atrophic and prone to eversion or prolapse at the meatus. The exposed tissue becomes chronically inflamed and vascular, forming a soft polypoid nodule composed of loose connective tissue, inflammatory cells, and a rich vascular network covered by transitional or squamous epithelium. The lesion is benign, but because it can bleed, ulcerate, and mimic malignancy, atypical examples warrant biopsy. Benign with an excellent prognosis; symptoms usually settle with conservative or topical oestrogen treatment, though caruncles may recur, and rare atypical lesions require exclusion of malignancy.

Urethral diverticulum — UD, female urethral diverticulum, periurethral diverticulum Recurrent urinary tract infection or cystitis Urethral caruncle Skene's gland cyst or abscess Vaginal wall (Gartner's duct) cyst Urethral or vaginal carcinoma Cystocele Ectopic ureterocele MRI of the urethra and pelvis Voiding cystourethrography Transvaginal or transperineal ultrasound Urethroscopy and cystoscopy Urinalysis and urine culture Double-balloon positive-pressure urethrography where MRI is unavailable An epithelium-lined outpouching arising from the urethra, most commonly in women along the mid or distal posterior urethra The classic triad (the 'three Ds') is dysuria, dyspareunia, and post-void dribbling, though presentations vary widely A tender anterior vaginal wall mass that may express pus or urine from the meatus on compression is characteristic Symptoms are often chronic and non-specific, so diagnosis is frequently delayed and the condition is mistaken for recurrent cystitis or vaginitis MRI of the pelvis and urethra is the most sensitive imaging test and best defines the anatomy; voiding cystourethrography, ultrasound, and urethroscopy also contribute Management is surgical excision (diverticulectomy) with urethral reconstruction for symptomatic cases, while small asymptomatic diverticula may be observed Complications include recurrent infection, stone formation within the diverticulum, and, rarely, malignancy arising in the diverticular lining A firm or fixed mass or a solid component suggesting malignancy within the diverticulum Haematuria Rapid enlargement A stone within the diverticulum with severe pain Recurrent sepsis Repeatedly treating 'recurrent cystitis' without considering a diverticulum as the underlying cause Relying on examination alone and not obtaining dedicated MRI to define the anatomy Missing a malignancy or a stone arising within the diverticulum Incomplete excision leaving a residual sac and causing recurrence or fistula Most acquired female urethral diverticula are thought to arise from the periurethral (paraurethral or Skene's) glands. Repeated infection and obstruction of these glands lead to abscess formation, which then ruptures into the urethral lumen and leaves an epithelium-lined cavity communicating with the urethra through a neck. Urine and debris collect in this sac and drain intermittently, producing post-void dribbling and recurrent infection, while stasis predisposes to stone formation and, rarely, malignant change. The size and location of the sac and its ostium determine the clinical picture and the surgical approach. Good after complete surgical excision, with most patients gaining symptom relief; recurrence, urethrovaginal fistula, or stress incontinence can complicate surgery, and rare diverticular malignancy worsens the outlook.

Urethral Prolapse — urethral prolapse, urethral prolapsus, prolapsed urethra, urethral mucosal prolapse Urethral caruncle Prolapsing ureterocele Periurethral cyst or abscess (e.g. Skene gland) Urethral or periurethral malignancy Vaginal wall prolapse or cystocele Condyloma or other periurethral lesion Genital trauma (a key consideration in children) Careful clinical examination confirming circumferential eversion around the meatus Confirmation that the mass surrounds the urethral opening, often by passing or visualising a catheter through the central lumen Urinalysis and culture if infection or dysuria is present Biopsy or excision histology where malignancy is suspected, particularly in older women Examination under anaesthesia in children if the diagnosis is unclear or examination is difficult Urethral prolapse is circumferential eversion of the distal urethral mucosa through the external meatus, forming a doughnut-shaped ring of tissue around the urethral opening It has a characteristic bimodal distribution, occurring in prepubertal girls and in postmenopausal women, both low-oestrogen states Typical presentations are painless vaginal or vulval bleeding or spotting, a visible periurethral mass, and sometimes dysuria or voiding difficulty In young girls it is an important and benign cause of genital bleeding that can be mistaken for trauma or abuse, so recognition prevents misdirected concern The key clinical feature is that the prolapsed mucosa surrounds the meatus symmetrically, distinguishing it from an eccentric caruncle or other periurethral lesion It must be differentiated from a urethral caruncle, prolapsing ureterocele, periurethral cyst, and, importantly, urethral or other malignancy in older women Uncomplicated cases are often managed conservatively with topical oestrogen, sitz baths, and treatment of any constipation or straining Surgical excision of the prolapsed mucosa is reserved for strangulated, thrombosed, necrotic, or non-resolving cases, or when the diagnosis is uncertain and tissue is needed A strangulated, thrombosed, or necrotic prolapse causing pain or urinary retention warrants prompt urological assessment Strangulated, thrombosed, or necrotic prolapsed mucosa Acute urinary retention from the prolapse Suspicion of malignancy in a postmenopausal woman with an atypical or firm periurethral lesion Uncertain diagnosis where abuse or trauma is being wrongly considered in a child, or genuine trauma is missed Heavy or persistent bleeding Mistaking benign prolapse in a child for signs of trauma or abuse, or vice versa Confusing it with a urethral caruncle or, in older women, with malignancy Overlooking a strangulated or necrotic prolapse needing surgical intervention Failing to address straining and constipation, allowing recurrence Not obtaining histology when the lesion is atypical in a postmenopausal woman Urethral prolapse results from eversion of the distal urethral mucosa through the meatus. A relative deficiency of oestrogen, as in prepubertal girls and postmenopausal women, weakens the periurethral supporting tissues and the attachments between the inner longitudinal and outer circular smooth muscle layers of the urethra. Poor cohesion between these layers, combined with raised intra-abdominal pressure from straining, coughing, or constipation, allows the redundant mucosa to protrude and evert around the meatus. The exposed mucosa becomes congested, oedematous, and friable, and if venous drainage is compromised it may thrombose, strangulate, or necrose. Urethral prolapse is benign and generally responds well to conservative measures, particularly topical oestrogen, with a good prognosis and low recurrence when precipitating factors such as straining are addressed. Surgical excision is curative for complicated or refractory cases. Prompt recognition in children avoids unnecessary distress and investigation, while vigilance in older women ensures malignancy is not overlooked.

Urethral stricture — urethral stenosis, urethral narrowing, stricture urethra Benign prostatic hyperplasia / bladder outlet obstruction Bladder neck stenosis or contracture Prostate cancer Meatal stenosis Neurogenic bladder Urethral or periurethral tumour Detrusor underactivity Uroflowmetry demonstrating a low, plateau-shaped flow pattern Retrograde urethrography with voiding
