ultrasound to assess retention and upper tracts Assessment for lichen sclerosus in distal or meatal strictures A urethral stricture is a fibrotic narrowing of the urethral lumen, largely a condition of the male anterior urethra, presenting with obstructive voiding symptoms such as a weak, splayed, or spraying stream, straining, and incomplete emptying Common causes include prior instrumentation or catheterisation, straddle and pelvic trauma, infection (historically gonococcal urethritis), and lichen sclerosus affecting the meatus and distal urethra Symptoms overlap with prostatic obstruction, but a young man or a history of trauma, catheterisation, or urethritis should raise suspicion of stricture Uroflowmetry classically shows a prolonged, low, plateau-shaped flow curve, and retrograde urethrography with voiding studies defines the site, length, and number of strictures Complications include recurrent urinary infection, bladder stones, diverticula, and, in longstanding severe disease, back-pressure effects on the upper tracts and acute retention Management principles depend on stricture length and location: dilatation or internal urethrotomy for short strictures, and urethroplasty for longer, recurrent, or complex disease, which offers the most durable cure Repeated dilatation or urethrotomy for recurrent strictures tends to fail and may worsen fibrosis, so early referral for reconstructive urethroplasty is preferred in appropriate cases Meatal or distal strictures should prompt evaluation for lichen sclerosus Acute urinary retention from a tight stricture, a urological emergency requiring urgent drainage Obstructive uropathy with upper tract dilatation and renal impairment Recurrent urinary infection, periurethral abscess, or urethral fistula Failure of a difficult catheterisation, which should prompt suprapubic drainage rather than forceful attempts Suspicion of urethral malignancy in an atypical or non-healing stricture Attributing obstructive symptoms to the prostate in a younger man and missing a stricture Repeated dilatation or urethrotomy for recurrent strictures, worsening scarring and delaying definitive repair Forcing a urethral catheter through a stricture, risking false passage and injury Overlooking lichen sclerosus in distal strictures Failing to assess the upper tracts and renal function in longstanding obstruction A urethral stricture is the result of scarring within the corpus spongiosum (spongiofibrosis) and urethral epithelium following injury or inflammation. Trauma, infection, instrumentation, or inflammatory disease such as lichen sclerosus provokes healing by fibrosis, which contracts and narrows the lumen. The narrowed segment increases outflow resistance, causing high-pressure voiding, turbulent flow, and incomplete emptying. Persistent obstruction leads to proximal urethral dilatation, bladder wall changes, stasis with infection and stone formation, and in severe cases upper tract dilatation and retention. Short strictures may respond to dilatation or urethrotomy but recurrence is common; urethroplasty provides high long-term success for suitable strictures, whereas complex, recurrent, or lichen sclerosus-associated disease can require staged or repeated reconstruction.

Urethritis — urethral inflammation, gonococcal urethritis, non-gonococcal urethritis, NGU Cystitis or lower urinary tract infection Prostatitis Epididymo-orchitis Balanitis Reactive arthritis-associated urethritis Non-infective (traumatic or chemical) urethritis Foreign body or instrumentation-related irritation First-void urine or urethral swab nucleic acid amplification testing for gonorrhoea and chlamydia Urethral Gram-stain smear for leucocytes and Gram-negative intracellular diplococci Culture and antimicrobial sensitivities for Neisseria gonorrhoeae given resistance concerns Testing for Mycoplasma genitalium and Trichomonas where indicated Full sexually transmitted infection screen including HIV and syphilis serology Urinalysis to help exclude urinary tract infection Urethritis is inflammation of the urethra presenting with urethral discharge, dysuria, and urethral itch or discomfort, most often sexually transmitted It is broadly divided into gonococcal urethritis (Neisseria gonorrhoeae) and non-gonococcal urethritis, of which Chlamydia trachomatis is the leading cause, along with Mycoplasma genitalium and others Gonococcal urethritis classically produces a profuse purulent discharge, whereas non-gonococcal urethritis tends to cause a scantier, more mucoid discharge, though overlap is common and co-infection frequent Diagnosis rests on demonstrating urethral inflammation (urethral smear with leucocytes or a positive leucocyte esterase on first-void urine) together with nucleic acid amplification testing for the causative organisms Management principles include empirical antibiotic therapy covering both gonococcal and chlamydial infection, guided by local resistance patterns, plus abstinence until treatment is complete Partner notification, treatment of sexual contacts, and a full sexually transmitted infection screen (including HIV and syphilis) are essential components of care Persistent or recurrent urethritis after treatment may reflect reinfection, non-adherence, or organisms such as Mycoplasma genitalium with antimicrobial resistance Reactive arthritis (urethritis, conjunctivitis, arthritis) may follow chlamydial urethritis, particularly in HLA-B27-positive individuals Features of disseminated gonococcal infection (fever, skin lesions, arthritis) Ascending infection causing epididymo-orchitis or prostatitis Persistent or recurrent urethritis suggesting resistant organism or reinfection Systemic sexually transmitted co-infection such as HIV requiring identification Reactive arthritis with ocular or joint involvement Treating for chlamydia alone and missing co-existing gonococcal infection (or vice versa) Neglecting partner notification and treatment, leading to reinfection Failing to perform a full STI screen including HIV and syphilis Overlooking Mycoplasma genitalium in persistent non-gonococcal urethritis Not counselling on abstinence until treatment and partner therapy are complete Urethritis is inflammation of the urethral mucosa, usually caused by sexually transmitted organisms ascending the urethra. Neisseria gonorrhoeae and Chlamydia trachomatis are the principal pathogens, with Mycoplasma genitalium, Trichomonas vaginalis, and other organisms also implicated. Infection provokes a neutrophilic inflammatory response in the urethral epithelium, producing discharge and dysuria. Non-infective urethritis can follow trauma or instrumentation. Untreated infection may ascend or spread, causing epididymo-orchitis, prostatitis, disseminated gonococcal infection, or, historically, inflammatory urethral stricture, and in women pelvic inflammatory disease. Uncomplicated urethritis usually resolves rapidly with appropriate antibiotics and partner treatment; outcomes are worsened by reinfection, non-adherence, resistant organisms, and complications such as epididymo-orchitis or reactive arthritis.

Uric acid nephrolithiasis — uric acid stones, uric acid kidney stones, urate stones, uric acid urolithiasis Calcium oxalate stones Xanthine or 2,8-dihydroxyadenine stones, which are also radiolucent Radiolucent matrix stones A sloughed papilla mimicking a filling defect Urothelial tumour producing a radiolucent filling defect Blood clot within the collecting system Non-contrast CT, noting the characteristically low density of a uric acid stone Repeated fresh urine pH measurement, which is typically persistently acidic 24-hour urine for volume, uric acid, pH and citrate Serum urate and a metabolic screen for diabetes and insulin resistance Analysis of any retrieved stone Full blood count and urate where myeloproliferative disease or tumour lysis is suspected Radiolucent stones that are invisible on plain radiographs but are readily seen on non-contrast CT, where they are of low density The single most important factor is a persistently acidic urine, which favours the insoluble undissociated uric acid over soluble urate Strongly associated with gout, the metabolic syndrome, insulin resistance, type 2 diabetes and obesity Other contributors include a high purine intake, chronic diarrhoea with volume depletion, and states of rapid cell turnover such as tumour lysis or myeloproliferative disease Urine microscopy may show rhomboid or rosette-shaped urate crystals in a characteristically acidic urine Unlike most stones, established uric acid stones can often be dissolved medically rather than removed surgically Management centres on urinary alkalinisation with potassium citrate to raise the urine pH toward neutral, a generous fluid intake, and allopurinol where hyperuricosuria persists Reducing dietary purine and treating the underlying metabolic syndrome are important adjuncts Obstruction with superimposed infection and sepsis Acute kidney injury from massive urate crystal deposition, as in tumour lysis syndrome A rapidly enlarging stone burden in the context of a myeloproliferative disorder Assuming a normal plain radiograph excludes a stone, since uric acid stones are radiolucent Over-alkalinising the urine, which risks precipitating calcium phosphate stones Failing to recognise and treat the underlying metabolic syndrome and insulin resistance Introducing allopurinol during an acute gout flare without appropriate cover Uric acid, the end product of purine metabolism, exists as a soluble ionised urate form and a relatively insoluble undissociated uric acid form, and the balance between them is governed chiefly by urine pH. Below a pH of about 5.5 the poorly soluble undissociated form predominates and precipitates. Patients with uric acid stones characteristically have an unduly acidic urine, frequently because insulin resistance impairs renal ammonium excretion, together with a low urine volume and, in some, hyperuricosuria from gout, high purine intake or rapid cell turnover. The combination of low pH, concentrated urine and increased urate delivery drives crystallisation. Uric acid stones respond well to urinary alkalinisation and can often be dissolved without surgery; long-term recurrence is low provided the urine pH and volume are maintained and the underlying metabolic disorder is addressed.

Urinary incontinence — UI, involuntary urine leakage, loss of bladder control Stress urinary incontinence Urgency incontinence / overactive bladder Mixed incontinence Overflow incontinence from obstruction or detrusor underactivity Neurogenic bladder Urinary tract infection Vesicovaginal or other urinary fistula (continuous leakage) Urinalysis to exclude infection and haematuria Bladder (frequency-volume) diary Post-void residual volume measurement Cough stress test and pelvic examination (assessing prolapse and pelvic floor) Urodynamic studies in complex, mixed, or pre-surgical cases Cystoscopy or imaging when fistula, malignancy, or structural abnormality is suspected Urinary incontinence is any involuntary leakage of urine, and classifying the type guides management: stress, urgency, mixed, overflow, and functional (continuous) incontinence Stress incontinence is leakage with raised intra-abdominal pressure (coughing, laughing, exertion) due to sphincter or pelvic floor weakness, common after childbirth and in men after prostatectomy Urgency incontinence is leakage accompanied by a sudden compelling desire to void, usually from detrusor overactivity, and is part of the overactive bladder syndrome Overflow incontinence is dribbling from a chronically distended, poorly emptying bladder, often due to outlet obstruction or an underactive detrusor, and must not be missed A focused history, examination (including pelvic and neurological), a bladder (frequency-volume) diary, and post-void residual measurement usually clarify the type First-line management of stress incontinence is pelvic floor muscle training, while urgency incontinence is treated with bladder training and antimuscarinic or beta-3 agonist therapy Reversible contributors summarised by the DIAPPERS concept (delirium, infection, atrophic changes, pharmaceuticals, psychological, excess output, restricted mobility, stool impaction) should be sought and corrected Surgical options such as mid-urethral slings or colposuspension are considered for stress incontinence, and intravesical botulinum toxin or neuromodulation for refractory urgency incontinence Associated haematuria requiring exclusion of urinary tract malignancy New incontinence with neurological signs suggesting cord compression or cauda equina syndrome Overflow incontinence from unrecognised chronic retention with risk of renal impairment Continuous leakage suggesting a urinary fistula Recurrent urinary infection or significant post-void residual Mislabelling overflow incontinence as urgency and prescribing antimuscarinics that worsen retention Failing to measure post-void residual before treating Overlooking reversible causes such as infection, medications, or stool impaction Missing haematuria or a neurological cause behind new incontinence Recommending surgery without adequate assessment of the incontinence type Continence requires coordinated bladder storage at low pressure with a competent, closed outlet, governed by autonomic and somatic innervation. Stress incontinence arises from a weakened pelvic floor and urethral sphincter (from childbirth, ageing, or prostatic surgery) so that raised abdominal pressure overcomes closure. Urgency incontinence results from involuntary detrusor contractions (detrusor overactivity), which may be idiopathic or neurogenic. Overflow incontinence occurs when a chronically overdistended bladder leaks around an obstruction or fails to contract effectively, as in outlet obstruction or an underactive/neurogenic detrusor. Mixed incontinence combines these mechanisms. Many patients improve substantially with conservative measures and correction of reversible factors; stress and urgency incontinence respond well to targeted therapy, and surgery offers durable benefit for refractory stress incontinence, though outcomes vary with cause and comorbidity.

Urinary Tract Infections: Cystitis, Prostatitis, and Pyelonephritis — UTI, Acute cystitis, Acute bacterial prostatitis (ABP), Chronic bacterial prostatitis (CBP), Pyelonephritis, Catheter-associated UTI (CAUTI) Asymptomatic bacteriuria (positive culture without localizing symptoms) Sexually transmitted infections - urethritis/cervicitis from Chlamydia trachomatis, Neisseria gonorrhoeae, Mycoplasma genitalium Vaginitis (Candida albicans, Trichomonas vaginalis) Herpetic urethritis Interstitial cystitis Chronic pelvic pain syndrome (in men) Noninfectious vulvar/vaginal irritation Cervicitis due to Chlamydia trachomatis or Neisseria gonorrhoeae Vaginitis (Trichomonas vaginalis, Candida albicans) Herpetic urethritis Urethritis from Mycoplasma genitalium Urine dipstick for nitrite and leukocyte esterase (best used to help rule out UTI; only Enterobacterales convert nitrate to nitrite, so non-Enterobacterales and dilute frequently-voided urine can be falsely negative) Microscopic urinalysis for pyuria and hematuria Urine culture with susceptibilities - warranted in pregnancy, suspected resistant organisms, recurrent or complicated UTI, and all male UTI; ASB screening in pregnancy must use culture because dipstick is not sufficiently sensitive Blood cultures when fever or systemic signs suggest infection beyond the bladder Imaging (CT or ultrasound) in men with febrile UTI (even first episode) to evaluate for obstruction or anatomic abnormality; suspect intraparenchymal abscess with persistent fever/bacteremia despite therapy Urologic consultation for unclear diagnosis or recurrent UTI in men Interstitial cystitis / bladder pain syndrome Chronic pelvic pain syndrome (noninfectious prostatic pain without bacteriuria) Noninfectious vaginal or vulvar irritation Delirium from non-urinary causes mislabeled as UTI in older adults with incidental ASB UTI denotes symptomatic infection somewhere along the urinary tract; bacteria in urine WITHOUT related symptoms is asymptomatic bacteriuria (ASB), not UTI, and generally should NOT be treated (Harrison 22e p.1086). Treatment of ASB is discouraged except in two settings: pregnancy (untreated ASB is linked to pyelonephritis, preterm delivery, and low birth weight) and before urologic procedures causing mucosal injury such as lithotripsy or transurethral prostate resection (Harrison 22e p.1086). Cystitis presents with dysuria, frequency, and urgency, often with suprapubic discomfort, new nocturia, hesitancy, or gross hematuria; fever, rigors, and unilateral flank/back pain are INCONSISTENT with uncomplicated cystitis and point to infection beyond the bladder (Harrison 22e p.1088). Fever is a key feature distinguishing cystitis from pyelonephritis; mild pyelonephritis may show only low-grade fever with or without costovertebral angle pain, while severe disease brings high fever, rigors, nausea, vomiting, and flank pain (Harrison 22e p.1089). E. coli is the predominant uropathogen across UTI syndromes, accounting for roughly 75-90% of acute cystitis isolates; Staphylococcus saprophyticus causes about 5-15% (more in younger women) (Harrison 22e p.1087). Isolation of S. aureus or Salmonella from urine should raise suspicion of concomitant bacteremia, since hematogenous seeding (<2% of UTIs) typically involves these more virulent organisms (Harrison 22e p.1088). Acute bacterial prostatitis (ABP) is a typically severe illness with dysuria, frequency, and prostatic/pelvic/perineal pain, sometimes with fever, rigors, or bladder outlet obstruction; chronic bacterial prostatitis (CBP) presents insidiously as recurrent cystitis episodes, often without systemic signs (Harrison 22e p.1088). Chronic pelvic pain syndrome (formerly chronic prostatitis) is far more common than bacterial prostatitis, is NOT associated with bacteriuria, and does NOT improve with antibiotics; obtaining urine cultures in male UTI helps distinguish these entities (Harrison 22e p.1088). Diagnostic stewardship - not culturing urine in patients lacking UTI signs/symptoms (except pregnancy or pre-urologic-procedure screening) - is the key intervention to reduce misdiagnosis and overtreatment of ASB (Harrison 22e p.1088). In catheterized patients bacteriuria and pyuria are essentially inevitable, so an abnormal urinalysis alone cannot diagnose CAUTI; localizing or systemic symptoms must be present and other causes excluded (Harrison 22e p.1090). Recurrent UTI is not automatically 'complicated' - individual episodes can be uncomplicated; early recurrence (within 2 weeks) is usually relapse rather than reinfection and should prompt a search for a sequestered focus (Harrison 22e pp.1086-1087). Fever, rigors, or unilateral flank/back pain in a patient with urinary symptoms (suggests pyelonephritis, prostatitis, or bloodstream involvement) Severe pyelonephritis with high fever, rigors, nausea, vomiting, and flank pain Emphysematous pyelonephritis (gas in renal/perinephric tissue), occurring almost exclusively in poorly controlled diabetes Acute papillary necrosis causing obstructive uropathy; bilateral papillary necrosis may present with rapidly rising serum creatinine Continued fever and/or bacteremia despite antibiotics (suggests intraparenchymal renal abscess) Signs of sepsis in an older patient with altered mentation S. aureus or Salmonella in urine (consider concomitant bacteremia and metastatic prostatic focus) Bladder outlet obstruction with acute bacterial prostatitis Diagnosing UTI from pyuria/bacteriuria alone without requiring symptoms - this conflates ASB with true UTI; degree of pyuria in an asymptomatic patient should not drive the diagnosis (very high pyuria is common with urinary stasis, ESRD, or obstructed catheters). Treating ASB outside pregnancy or pre-urologic-procedure settings - it does not reduce future UTIs and may even increase infection risk (e.g., in renal transplant recipients). Premature diagnostic closure: attributing an older patient's isolated altered mentation to 'UTI' without excluding sepsis and other time-sensitive causes of delirium; a reported history of recurrent UTIs may actually reflect persistent ASB. Relying on a negative dipstick to rule out UTI - false negatives occur with non-Enterobacterales organisms, dilute frequently-voided urine, and it is insufficiently sensitive to exclude bacteriuria in pregnancy. Mistaking an STI (especially C. trachomatis) for UTI, or treating dysuria due to vaginitis/cervicitis as UTI; vaginal discharge should prompt STI evaluation. Assuming all male UTI is 'complicated' or that complicated-UTI guidelines apply to prostatitis; not all men with UTI have urinary tract abnormalities, especially those 45 years or younger. Misinterpreting a mixed-flora culture as infection - usually contamination except in long-term catheterization, chronic retention, or urinary-enteric/genital fistula. The urinary tract behaves as a continuous column of urine from kidney to urethra. Most UTIs arise by ascending infection: periurethral and vaginal-introital colonization by intestinal flora (usually E. coli) is the critical first step, followed by ascent up the urethra to the bladder and, in renal infection, up the ureter to the kidney. Hematogenous seeding accounts for less than 2% of UTIs and usually involves virulent organisms (e.g., S. aureus, Salmonella). Outcome depends on the interplay of host, pathogen, and environmental factors. The flushing action of normal voiding clears bacteria; urinary stasis, obstruction, foreign bodies (stones, catheters), and biofilm formation favor infection. Uropathogenic E. coli express virulence factors: type 1 pili bind mannose on bladder uroepithelium to initiate cystitis, while P fimbriae bind the P blood-group antigen on renal epithelium and are important in pyelonephritis and bloodstream invasion; toxins, iron-acquisition systems, biofilms, and capsules also contribute. Host susceptibility has a hereditary component (familial/maternal history; non-secretor blood-group phenotypes increasing E. coli adherence; Toll-like receptor and IL-8 receptor gene variants). Disruption of vaginal lactobacilli (spermicide/nonoxynol-9, menopausal atrophy) promotes E. coli colonization (Harrison 22e pp.1087-1088). UTI is common and patients typically respond favorably and rapidly to appropriately chosen modern antimicrobials. Uncomplicated cystitis in low-risk women carries a low risk of serious complications and can often be managed remotely. About 20-30% of women with one UTI develop recurrences (average ~2.6 reinfections/year; rate 0.3-7.6 per patient-year), with likelihood of recurrence decreasing as time since the last infection lengthens. Up to 80% of women have at least one UTI in their lifetime; lifetime prevalence in U.S. men is about 14%. Untreated ASB in pregnancy carries risk of pyelonephritis, preterm delivery, and low birth weight. Xanthogranulomatous pyelonephritis causes suppurative destruction of renal tissue and its mass effect can mimic renal malignancy (Harrison 22e pp.1086-1089). Clinical syndrome-based: asymptomatic bacteriuria (ASB) vs symptomatic UTI. Uncomplicated UTI = infection confined to the bladder (cystitis) in a woman or man without a urinary catheter. Complicated UTI = infection extending beyond the bladder (prostatitis, pyelonephritis, bacteremia) or in the setting of catheterization (CAUTI). Pyelonephritis is graded clinically from mild (low-grade fever +/- back/CVA pain) to severe (high fever, rigors, nausea, vomiting, flank pain). Severe/special forms: emphysematous pyelonephritis and xanthogranulomatous pyelonephritis. Lab/diagnostic thresholds: pyuria conventionally >10 WBCs/HPF (poor specificity ~36%; a cutoff nearer 250 WBCs/HPF correlates better with symptoms in older women); for women with cystitis symptoms a colony count >10^2 bacteria/mL is more sensitive (95%) than the classic 10^5/mL; CAUTI bacteriuria threshold is >=10^3 CFU/mL (Harrison 22e pp.1086-1092).

Urinary Tract Obstruction — obstructive uropathy, hydronephrosis Benign prostatic hyperplasia (bladder outlet obstruction) Carcinoma of prostate, bladder, cervix, colon, or rectum Retroperitoneal fibrosis Lymphoma (particularly follicular) with retroperitoneal involvement Calculi (ureteric, bladder, urethral) Urethral stricture Ureteropelvic junction (UPJ) narrowing/obstruction Vesicoureteral reflux Posterior urethral valves (boys) Neurogenic bladder / functional obstruction (diabetic neuropathy, spinal cord disease, cauda equina syndrome) Pregnant uterus / uterine leiomyomata Accidental surgical ligation or injury of the ureter during pelvic or colonic surgery Aortic aneurysm (extrinsic ureteric compression) Drug-related urinary retention (anticholinergics, alpha-adrenergic agonists, opiates) Pyelonephritis (urinary stasis from obstruction encourages organism growth; UTO must always be considered with UTIs) Generalized sepsis from an infected obstructed system Bladder catheter insertion and postvoid residual measurement Bedside bladder ultrasound to assess bladder volume Abdominal ultrasonography (~90% sensitive and specific for hydronephrosis) Noncontrast multidetector CT (test of choice for acute flank pain; visualizes retroperitoneum and intrinsic/extrinsic sites of obstruction; characterizes stones by Hounsfield units) Duplex Doppler ultrasonography (increased resistive index) Retrograde or antegrade urography (no contrast-induced AKI risk in renal insufficiency) Voiding cystourethrography (vesicoureteral reflux, bladder neck and urethral obstruction; postvoid residual urine) Cystourethroscopy and urodynamic studies (cystometry, pressure-flow analysis) Radionuclide (renal) scan for differential renal function and to predict reversibility after prolonged decompression Abdominal scout film/KUB (insensitive; may show nephrocalcinosis or radiopaque stone) Furosemide-augmented imaging to distinguish functional from anatomic obstruction Prerenal azotemia (acute partial bilateral obstruction may mimic it with high BUN-to-creatinine ratio, concentrated urine, and sodium retention) Renal cystic disease (congenital UPJ obstruction may be mistaken for it; extrarenal pelvis is a normal variant causing false-positive hydronephrosis) Other causes of polyuria/nocturia and concentrating defects ADPKD and other ciliopathies (cystic compression of normal nephrons leading to fibrosis) Urinary tract obstruction (UTO) is a common and potentially reversible cause of both acute and chronic kidney disease (obstructive nephropathy); early recognition and prompt relief can prevent or reverse devastating effects on kidney structure and function (p.2453). Any patient with otherwise unexplained renal failure, or with a history of nephrolithiasis, hematuria, diabetes mellitus, prostatic enlargement, pelvic surgery, trauma, or tumor should be evaluated for UTO (p.2455-2456). When suspected, a bladder catheter should be inserted and abdominal ultrasonography performed to assess renal/bladder size and pyelocalyceal contour; bladder volume can be readily assessed at the bedside by ultrasound (p.2454-2455). Flank pain is the most common presenting symptom and is due to distention of the collecting system or renal capsule; its severity is influenced more by the rate at which distention develops than by the degree of distention (p.2454). Complete bilateral obstruction should be suspected when acute renal failure is accompanied by anuria (p.2455). Wide fluctuations in urine output in an azotemic patient should always raise the possibility of intermittent or partial UTO (p.2455). Azotemia with hyperkalemia and metabolic acidosis (acquired distal renal tubular acidosis pattern) should prompt consideration of UTO (p.2455). Flank pain that occurs only with micturition is pathognomonic of vesicoureteral reflux (p.2455). Lower obstruction above the bladder causes unilateral hydroureter and hydronephrosis, whereas lesions at or below the bladder cause bilateral involvement (p.2454). Posterior urethral valves are the most common cause of bilateral hydronephrosis in boys; in adults UTO is usually due to acquired defects, with pelvic tumors, calculi, and urethral stricture predominating (p.2454). As many as 50% of men aged >40 years may have lower urinary tract symptoms associated with benign prostatic hypertrophy, but these symptoms may occur without bladder outlet obstruction (p.2454). Noncontrast CT is the imaging test of choice for acute flank pain and improves visualization of the urinary tract in renal impairment; retrograde/antegrade urography carry no risk of contrast-induced AKI in patients with renal insufficiency (p.2455-2456). UTO complicated by infection (infected obstructed system) requires immediate relief of obstruction to prevent generalized sepsis and progressive renal damage; sepsis necessitates prompt urologic intervention with drainage (nephrostomy, ureterostomy, or catheterization) Acute renal failure with anuria suggesting complete bilateral obstruction Overflow incontinence with sudden-onset fecal incontinence, severe lower back pain, and saddle anesthesia requires emergency evaluation for cauda equina syndrome Complete obstruction with infection can lead to total destruction of the kidney within days Fetal LUTO with maternal oligohydramnios or anhydramnios (risk of pulmonary hypoplasia and infant death if untreated) UTO is a reversible cause of AKI that must be actively excluded in any unexplained AKI (insert bladder catheter and perform bladder scan/ultrasound) - the urine sediment is often normal even with marked azotemia and extensive structural damage. Hydronephrosis may be ABSENT on ultrasound when obstruction is <48 h in duration, or associated with volume contraction, staghorn calculi, retroperitoneal fibrosis, or infiltrative renal disease - a negative ultrasound does not exclude obstruction when suspicion remains high. False-positive hydronephrosis can occur with diuresis, renal cysts, or a normal extrarenal pelvis. Insidious obstruction (e.g., chronic UPJ narrowing) may cause little or no pain yet result in total destruction of the affected kidney; unilateral ureteric injury during surgery may remain undetected. After relief, anticipate postobstructive diuresis (see below) - iatrogenic over-replacement of fluids can sustain the diuresis, while under-recognition can lead to profound dehydration and vascular collapse. NSAIDs for renal colic must account for potential renal harm, and opiates in patients with decreased renal function may be dangerous and used with caution. Alpha-adrenergic blockers for BPH carry a risk of intraoperative floppy iris syndrome during cataract surgery. Obstruction to urine flow produces stasis and a rise in hydrostatic pressure proximal to the blockade; this pressure is transmitted to the glomerular urinary space, decreasing or stopping filtration. Acutely, bilateral obstruction increases renal blood flow with rising ureteral/tubule pressures (mediated by vasodilator prostaglandins and nitric oxide), then renal blood flow and GFR fall with chronicity as vasoconstrictor prostaglandins and renin-angiotensin production increase. Tubular dysfunction develops: loss of medullary hypertonicity and concentrating ability (AVP-insensitive polyuria, a form of acquired nephrogenic diabetes insipidus from dysregulation of aquaporin-2 water channels), natriuresis from downregulation of proximal salt reabsorption and transporters (Na+/K+-ATPase, NKCC2, ENaC), and partial bilateral UTO causing acquired distal RTA with hyperkalemia and renal salt wasting (disrupted H+-ATPase trafficking in alpha-intercalated cells, reduced ENaC-driven Na+ reabsorption and K+ secretion, impaired ammonium excretion). The renal interstitium becomes edematous with mononuclear infiltrate early; later interstitial fibrosis and atrophy of papillae and medulla precede cortical involvement. Increased angiotensin II drives inflammation and fibroblast accumulation via profibrotic cytokines, progressing to chronic kidney damage and permanent loss of renal mass (renal atrophy). Obstruction can be mechanical (intrinsic or extrinsic) at any level from the renal tubules to the urethral meatus, or functional from abnormal pontine/sacral micturition control (e.g., neurogenic bladder). Genetic/fetal causes (CAKUT, LUTO) reflect reduced nephron number, as there is no nephrogenesis after birth (p.2453-2456). With relief of obstruction, return of renal function depends largely on whether irreversible renal damage has occurred. If obstruction is not relieved, course depends on whether it is complete or incomplete, bilateral or unilateral, and whether infection coexists. Complete obstruction with infection can destroy the kidney within days. Partial return of GFR may follow relief of complete obstruction of 1-2 weeks' duration, but after 8 weeks of obstruction recovery is unlikely. In the absence of definitive evidence of irreversibility, every effort should be made to decompress; a renal radionuclide scan after a prolonged period of decompression may predict reversibility. Chronic fibrotic progression to a failing kidney has no demonstrated reversal of scarring to date (p.2453, 2456-2457). No formal severity grade; characterized along clinically meaningful axes per Tables 331-1 and 331-2: by level (upper tract/ureter vs bladder outlet vs urethra), laterality (unilateral hydroureter/hydronephrosis vs bilateral involvement at/below the bladder), completeness (complete vs partial/incomplete), acuity (acute vs chronic vs release/postobstructive phase), and presence of superimposed infection. Postobstructive diuresis follows relief of bilateral, but not unilateral, complete obstruction.

Urticaria, Angioedema & Allergic Rhinitis — hives, urticaria, hereditary angioedema, allergic rhinitis Acute vs chronic urticaria/angioedema (cutoff 6 weeks duration) Inducible (physical) urticarias: dermatographism, cholinergic, cold, solar, pressure, vibratory, heat, aquagenic, contact Urticarial vasculitis (immune-complex disease; small-vessel leukocytoclastic vasculitis) Mastocytosis (cutaneous or systemic; urticaria pigmentosa) Hereditary angioedema (C1INH type 1/2; type 3 with normal C1INH e.g. factor XII mutation) Acquired C1INH deficiency (lymphoproliferative or autoimmune disease) ACE inhibitor-induced (bradykinin-mediated) angioedema CIAS1/NLRP3-associated periodic fever syndromes (familial cold autoinflammatory syndrome, Muckle-Wells syndrome) Schnitzler's syndrome, Gleich's syndrome, hypereosinophilic syndrome Serum sickness and hypocomplementemic urticarial vasculitis Allergic rhinitis: nonallergic rhinitis with eosinophilia (NARES), vasomotor/perennial nonallergic rhinitis, rhinitis medicamentosa, gustatory rhinitis, hormonal (pregnancy) rhinitis, drug-induced rhinitis, hypothyroidism, anatomic/structural nasal defects, nasal foreign body Viral infection-associated acute urticaria (a common trigger of new-onset acute urticaria) Bacterial or parasitic infection-associated urticaria (travel history should prompt parasite evaluation) Hepatitis B or C and SARS-CoV-2 infection associated with urticaria/urticarial vasculitis Upper respiratory tract infection mimicking rhinitis; secondary bacterial sinusitis/otitis from mucosal swelling History-directed skin testing (puncture/prick) or serum allergen-specific IgE for suspected allergen triggers Provocation/threshold testing for inducible urticaria (e.g. ice-cube test for cold urticaria; stroking for dermatographism) Limited labs in unrevealing chronic urticaria: CBC with eosinophil assessment, ESR or CRP (most chronic urticaria has no lab abnormality) Skin biopsy for lesions lasting >36 h, scarring, or painful/non-pruritic - to assess for urticarial vasculitis (cellular infiltrate, nuclear debris, fibrinoid venular necrosis) For isolated angioedema: basic chemistries with liver function tests and complement levels C1INH antigen level and functional (catalytic inhibition) assay, with C4 and C2 levels, for suspected HAE; C1q and C1 function additionally reduced in acquired C1INH deficiency Evaluation for paraproteinemia/lymphoproliferative disease where presentation suggests acquired C1INH deficiency Autologous serum skin test and basophil activation markers (CD63/CD203) for autoimmune chronic urticaria; antithyroid antibodies Nasal secretion eosinophils and serum/skin specific IgE for allergic rhinitis (skin test more sensitive; serum specific IgE less sensitive but highly specific) Urticarial vasculitis (lesions >24 h, painful/burning rather than pruritic, residual petechiae/bruising) Mastocytosis presenting with flushing and hyperpigmented papules that urticate on stroking (Darier's sign) Thyroid disease (hypo-/hyperthyroidism) and autoimmune thyroiditis Serum sickness / serum sickness-like reactions Vasomotor (nonallergic) rhinitis and NARES mimicking allergic rhinitis Urticaria (hives) are well-circumscribed wheals (dilation of superficial dermal vessels) that are intensely pruritic, often migrate, individually last <24 h, and resolve without bruising or scarring; angioedema arises from deeper dermis/subcutaneous tissue with more pain than pruritus and minimal erythema, taking hours to days to resolve (p.2807). Urticaria and angioedema reflect similar pathophysiology at different skin levels and often co-occur, with roughly 40% of patients reporting both; together they affect >20% of the population at some point in life (p.2807). Acute urticaria/angioedema are episodes lasting <6 weeks (usually food, environmental, or drug allergen, or viral infection); attacks persisting >6 weeks are termed chronic and are often spontaneous/idiopathic with no identifiable cause. More than two-thirds of new-onset cases are ultimately diagnosed as acute (p.2807). Inducible (physical) urticarias are identified by the precipitating stimulus: dermatographism (linear wheal after brisk stroke, affects 2-5%), cholinergic urticaria (small 1-2 mm pruritic wheals with large surrounding erythema triggered by a rise in core body temperature such as fever, hot bath, or exercise), cold, solar, pressure, vibratory, heat, aquagenic, and contact urticaria; most inducible-urticaria lesions individually last <2 h (p.2807-2808). Hereditary angioedema (HAE) is a fully penetrant autosomal dominant disorder from SERPING1 mutation causing C1 inhibitor (C1INH) deficiency (type 1, ~85%) or dysfunctional protein (type 2); presentation in childhood/adolescence and a family history of angioedema are distinguishing features (p.2808). HAE diagnosis is suggested by family history, early age of onset, lack of pruritus and urticarial lesions, recurrent gastrointestinal colic, episodes of laryngeal edema, and failure to respond to H1 antihistamines; laboratory confirmation shows low C1INH antigen (type 1) or nonfunctional protein (type 2), with chronically depleted C4 and C2 that fall further during attacks (p.2808-2809). Cold urticaria can be confirmed by ice-cube placement on the volar forearm provoking a wheal within minutes; cryoglobulins or cold agglutinins are present in up to 5% of these patients, and immersion in cold water (swimming) can progress to vascular collapse (p.2807-2808). Up to 45% of chronic urticaria has an autoimmune basis, including autoantibodies to IgE or to the alpha chain of FcepsilonRI, and may be associated with antithyroid antibodies (antimicrosomal peroxidase/thyroglobulin) in both Hashimoto's thyroiditis and a euthyroid state (p.2808). Allergic rhinitis is characterized by sneezing, rhinorrhea, nasal obstruction, lacrimation, and itching of the conjunctiva/nasal mucosa/oropharynx; the nasal mucosa is classically pale and boggy. It requires a temporal relationship to allergen exposure plus documented IgE sensitization (p.2808-2809). Allergic rhinitis usually occurs in atopic individuals and overlaps strongly with other atopic disease: up to 50% of allergic rhinitis patients have asthma, while 70-80% of asthmatics and 80% of those with chronic bilateral sinusitis have allergic rhinitis (p.2809). Seasonal allergic rhinitis is elicited by wind-pollinated tree, grass, and weed pollens (in temperate North America: trees Mar-May, grasses Jun-early Jul, weeds mid-Aug-early Oct); perennial rhinitis is driven by year-round allergens such as dust mites (Dermatophagoides), animal dander, cockroach proteins, and mold spores (p.2809). Pollen-associated (oral allergy) food syndrome causes oropharyngeal pruritus and/or mild swelling after ingesting plant foods cross-reactive with the offending tree, grass, or weed pollen (p.2809). Angioedema of the upper respiratory tract / larynx may be life-threatening due to transient laryngeal obstruction - airway emergency Gastrointestinal angioedema with abdominal colic can mimic an acute abdomen and lead to unnecessary surgical intervention Cold urticaria with cold-water immersion may progress to vascular collapse Progression of urticaria/angioedema to anaphylaxis with vascular collapse (e.g. exercise-induced anaphylaxis, food/drug triggers) Urticarial lesions lasting >24-36 h with bruising/petechiae, scarring, or burning/pain rather than pruritus suggest urticarial vasculitis and warrant biopsy Failing to distinguish histaminergic from bradykinin-mediated angioedema: bradykinin-mediated angioedema (hereditary angioedema from C1INH deficiency, and ACE inhibitor-induced) is conspicuously WITHOUT concomitant urticaria or pruritus, frequently involves the GI tract, lasts >24 h, and characteristically does NOT respond to H1 antihistamines (nor to adrenaline) - treat with C1INH replacement, bradykinin B2-receptor antagonist (icatibant), or kallikrein inhibitor rather than antihistamines. Mistaking urticarial vasculitis for simple urticaria: individual lesions persist >24 h, may leave bruising/petechiae and scarring, and cause burning rather than pruritus - biopsy shows leukocytoclastic vasculitis and may signal underlying SLE, Sjogren's, or complement deficiency. Overlooking laryngeal angioedema as an airway emergency, or mistaking GI angioedema for a surgical abdomen. Topical glucocorticoids are of no value in urticaria, and systemic glucocorticoids are generally avoided in idiopathic, allergen-induced, or inducible urticaria due to long-term toxicity. Prolonged use of topical alpha-adrenergic nasal decongestants (7-14 days) causes rebound rhinitis medicamentosa. Concomitant beta-adrenergic blocker therapy increases the risk of severe/refractory anaphylaxis during allergen immunotherapy; immunotherapy is contraindicated in significant cardiovascular disease or unstable asthma. Atopy is a tendency to manifest asthma, rhinitis, urticaria, food allergy, and atopic dermatitis in association with allergen-specific IgE, though urticaria and anaphylaxis can also occur in non-atopic individuals. Mast cells are the key effector cells: IgE binds the high-affinity receptor FcepsilonRI (sensitization), and antigen-driven receptor aggregation triggers Lyn/Syk/Fyn tyrosine-kinase signaling, calcium influx, and degranulation. This releases preformed granule mediators (histamine, tryptase, chymase, carboxypeptidase A, proteoglycans), newly generated lipid mediators (PGD2 via cyclooxygenase; LTB4 and cysteinyl leukotrienes LTC4/D4/E4 via 5-lipoxygenase/FLAP; PAF), and cytokines/chemokines (TNF-alpha, IL-4, IL-5, IL-13, GM-CSF). Mast cells can also be activated IgE-independently via C5a/C3a anaphylatoxin receptors, TLRs, alarmin (TSLP, IL-33) receptors, and MRGPRX2 (a target of small-molecule drugs such as ciprofloxacin and rocuronium and of neuropeptides). Histamine and lipid mediators increase venular permeability producing dermal edema (urticaria) or deeper subcutaneous/dermal edema (angioedema). Cold urticaria provides the best evidence for IgE/mast-cell involvement, with documented mast cell degranulation and elevated lesional histamine. In contrast, bradykinin-mediated angioedema (HAE from C1INH deficiency, or ACE inhibitor-induced) results from excess bradykinin: C1INH normally inhibits activated factor XII, kallikrein, and C1r/C1s, and its deficiency leads to bradykinin accumulation with falling C4/C2. Allergic rhinitis arises from sensitized intraepithelial and perivenular nasal mast cells that, on allergen exposure, release histamine, PGD2, and leukotrienes, producing submucosal edema and eosinophilic infiltration. More than two-thirds of new-onset urticaria cases are ultimately acute and self-limited. Chronic spontaneous urticaria is most common in the third to fifth decades and the vast majority shows no laboratory abnormality. Dermatographism generally has a duration of <5 years. Allergic rhinitis prevalence in North America is 10-30% (peak >30% in the fifth decade). Allergen immunotherapy (SCIT/SLIT) for allergic rhinitis provides durable symptom benefit and can reduce asthma symptoms; guidelines recommend 3-5 years of SCIT with discontinuation after minimal symptoms over two consecutive allergen seasons. Urticaria/angioedema classified by duration: acute = episodes lasting <6 weeks; chronic = attacks persisting >6 weeks (Table 363-1 further classifies by precipitating factor into acute vs chronic categories, including drug, food, infection, physical/inducible, autoimmune, vasculitic, mastocytosis, and hereditary forms). Hereditary angioedema typed as: type 1 (low C1INH antigen, ~85%), type 2 (dysfunctional C1INH protein), and type 3 (normal C1INH/complement, often identifiable gene mutation e.g. factor XII). Allergic rhinitis classified as seasonal vs perennial, and managed by severity (mild vs moderate-to-severe).

Urticaria pigmentosa — maculopapular cutaneous mastocytosis Other forms of cutaneous or systemic mastocytosis Chronic urticaria Secondary syphilis or other papular eruptions Histiocytoses Post-inflammatory hyperpigmentation Clinical diagnosis with Darier sign Skin biopsy showing increased dermal mast cells if needed Serum baseline tryptase Assessment for systemic symptoms and, in adults, systemic mastocytosis Trigger history for mediator symptoms The commonest form of cutaneous mastocytosis, presenting as multiple red-brown macules and papules Lesions urticate on rubbing (Darier sign) and may blister in young children It can begin in infancy or in adulthood, with different implications for each Childhood-onset disease often regresses spontaneously, while adult-onset disease is frequently associated with systemic mastocytosis Mediator release can cause flushing, itch and, uncommonly, systemic reactions Baseline serum tryptase and clinical assessment guide the need for systemic evaluation Adult onset suggesting systemic mastocytosis Systemic mediator symptoms or anaphylaxis Extensive disease with blistering in infants A high baseline tryptase Failing to evaluate adults for systemic mastocytosis Overlooking the Darier sign Provoking mediator release by vigorously rubbing lesions Confusing it with chronic urticaria Urticaria pigmentosa is a maculopapular pattern of cutaneous mastocytosis in which increased numbers of clonal mast cells accumulate in the dermis, commonly linked to KIT mutations. Mechanical or chemical stimulation degranulates these mast cells, releasing histamine and other mediators to produce the localised weal-and-flare of the Darier sign and the pigmented appearance from associated increased melanin. As with other cutaneous mastocytosis, childhood disease tends to involute, whereas adult disease often reflects an underlying systemic process. Childhood urticaria pigmentosa commonly improves or clears by adolescence, whereas adult disease tends to persist and may be a marker of systemic mastocytosis.

features pointing to underlying lupus or malignancy Mistaking it for ordinary urticaria and treating with antihistamines alone Failing to biopsy atypical or persistent wheals Not checking complement, thereby missing the hypocomplementaemic systemic subtype Overlooking an underlying connective tissue disease, infection, or drug trigger Urticarial vasculitis is an immune complex-mediated small-vessel vasculitis affecting the postcapillary venules of the dermis. Deposition of immune complexes activates complement and recruits neutrophils, producing leucocytoclastic inflammation with vessel wall damage, fibrin deposition, and extravasation of red cells that accounts for the residual bruising. The persistent inflammatory infiltrate explains why the wheals last longer than in ordinary urticaria. The normocomplementaemic form is usually skin-limited, whereas complement consumption signals a greater likelihood of systemic disease. Normocomplementaemic, skin-limited urticarial vasculitis usually follows a self-limiting or relapsing but benign course. Cases with low complement or systemic involvement carry greater morbidity and require closer monitoring and more intensive therapy.

interactome'), including MYO7A, USH2A and CDH23 Type 1 features profound congenital deafness with absent vestibular function and delayed motor milestones from balance impairment Type 2 features any child with congenital sensorineural hearing loss, and arrange ophthalmology and electroretinography follow-up to detect retinal disease early Congenital deafness with delayed independent walking, suggesting vestibular involvement and type 1 disease Progressive night blindness or narrowing visual field in a deaf child Family history of combined hearing and visual loss Deterioration in mobility and orientation from combined sensory decline Attributing congenital hearing loss to an isolated cause and not screening for retinal disease Mislabelling early balance and motor delay as global developmental delay rather than vestibular loss Assuming normal vision excludes Usher, as retinopathy often manifests later Failing to arrange genetic counselling for an autosomal recessive condition with recurrence risk Usher syndrome is a group of autosomal recessive disorders caused by mutations in genes whose protein products are needed for the structure and function of stereocilia in cochlear hair cells and of the connecting cilium in retinal photoreceptors. Loss of these shared proteins impairs mechanotransduction in the inner ear and progressive degeneration of rod and cone photoreceptors, giving the characteristic combination of sensorineural hearing loss and retinitis pigmentosa. In some subtypes vestibular hair cells are also affected, producing balance disturbance. The clinical subtype reflects which gene is involved and the severity of the resulting protein defect. Hearing loss is generally stable or slowly progressive depending on subtype, while retinitis pigmentosa is progressive and can lead to severe visual impairment in adulthood; early cochlear implantation and low-vision support substantially improve communication and independence.

Uterine atony — atonic uterus, atonic postpartum haemorrhage Genital tract trauma such as cervical, vaginal, or perineal lacerations or a haematoma Retained placental tissue or membranes Coagulopathy, inherited or acquired, including disseminated intravascular coagulation Uterine inversion Uterine rupture Placenta accreta spectrum Assessment of uterine tone by palpation and the response to massage Estimation and ongoing measurement of blood loss with serial maternal observations Full blood count, coagulation screen with fibrinogen, and group-and-save or crossmatch Inspection of the placenta for completeness and examination of the genital tract for trauma Bedside ultrasound to detect retained tissue if bleeding persists Near-patient viscoelastic testing where available to guide blood-product replacement Uterine atony is failure of the myometrium to contract and retract adequately after delivery, and it is the single commonest cause of primary postpartum haemorrhage Effective haemostasis after birth depends on myometrial contraction compressing the spiral arteries of the placental bed (the 'living ligatures'); when the uterus stays relaxed these vessels bleed freely Within the 'four Ts' framework of postpartum haemorrhage (Tone, Trauma, Tissue, Thrombin), atony is the 'Tone' cause and should be excluded first, though causes may coexist Risk factors include overdistension from multiple pregnancy, polyhydramnios, or macrosomia, prolonged or augmented labour, precipitate labour, grand multiparity, chorioamnionitis, retained placental tissue, tocolytic use, and general anaesthesia with volatile agents The classic finding is a soft, poorly contracted, often high uterus with ongoing vaginal bleeding despite a delivered and apparently complete placenta First-line management is uterine massage and bimanual compression, ensuring the bladder is empty, and uterotonic drugs such as oxytocin, ergometrine, prostaglandins, and misoprostol, alongside resuscitation If pharmacological measures fail, mechanical and surgical options include intrauterine balloon tamponade, compression sutures such as the B-Lynch, stepwise uterine and internal iliac artery ligation, uterine artery embolisation, and ultimately hysterectomy Prophylactic active management of the third stage with a uterotonic markedly reduces the incidence of atonic postpartum haemorrhage Continuing heavy bleeding with a soft, poorly contracted uterus Signs of hypovolaemic shock such as tachycardia, hypotension, or altered consciousness Failure to respond to first-line uterotonics Developing coagulopathy or a need for massive transfusion Bleeding out of keeping with the visible loss, suggesting concealed or intra-abdominal haemorrhage Failing to give a prophylactic uterotonic in the third stage Not emptying the bladder, which impairs uterine contraction Attributing ongoing bleeding to atony without excluding trauma, retained tissue, and coagulopathy Underestimating blood loss and escalating too slowly Neglecting to keep the patient warm and correct coagulopathy during resuscitation After the placenta separates, the large uteroplacental blood flow must be arrested rapidly. This is achieved mechanically by contraction and retraction of the interlacing myometrial fibres, which constrict the spiral arteries traversing them, with clotting a secondary contributor. Uterine atony occurs when the myometrium fails to maintain this tonic contraction. Overdistension stretches and fatigues the fibres; prolonged or augmented labour and chorioamnionitis impair contractility; retained tissue mechanically prevents full retraction; and certain drugs, such as tocolytics and volatile anaesthetics, relax smooth muscle. With the vessels left open and uncompressed, blood loss is brisk and can rapidly become life-threatening given the high uterine blood flow at term. With early recognition and a structured escalation of uterotonic, mechanical, and surgical measures, most women recover fully; however, atonic postpartum haemorrhage remains a leading cause of maternal death worldwide, and delayed treatment risks shock, coagulopathy, organ injury, and loss of fertility from hysterectomy.

Uterine fibroid — Uterine leiomyoma, Fibromyoma, Myoma Adenomyosis Endometrial polyp Ovarian or adnexal mass Leiomyosarcoma Endometrial hyperplasia or carcinoma Intrauterine pregnancy causing an enlarged uterus Uterine adenomyoma Full blood count to assess for anaemia Transvaginal with or without transabdominal ultrasound as first-line imaging Saline infusion sonohysterography to delineate submucosal lesions Diagnostic and operative hysteroscopy for submucosal fibroids Pelvic MRI for mapping, distinguishing adenomyosis and planning embolisation or surgery Ferritin and iron studies Endometrial biopsy when abnormal bleeding is accompanied by risk factors for hyperplasia Fibroids are benign monoclonal smooth-muscle tumours and the commonest pelvic tumour of reproductive-age women; the majority are asymptomatic and discovered incidentally. Growth is oestrogen- and progesterone-dependent, so lesions tend to enlarge during pregnancy and typically regress after the menopause. The FIGO leiomyoma classification (types 0 to 8) localises lesions from submucosal through intramural to subserosal; submucosal fibroids most affect menstrual bleeding and fertility. Heavy menstrual bleeding is the dominant symptom and may lead to iron-deficiency anaemia, whereas subserosal and pedunculated lesions rarely cause bleeding. Bulk-related symptoms such as pelvic pressure, urinary frequency and constipation reflect large or subserosal lesions rather than the bleeding pattern. Red (carneous) degeneration classically causes acute pain in mid-pregnancy; other degenerative changes include hyaline, cystic and calcific. Rapid enlargement, or any growth after the menopause, should raise concern for leiomyosarcoma even though malignant transformation is very rare. Management is individualised across expectant, medical (antifibrinolytics, hormonal therapy, gonadotrophin-releasing hormone analogues, selective progesterone receptor modulators), uterine artery embolisation and surgery (myomectomy or hysterectomy), guided by symptoms and fertility wishes. Rapidly enlarging mass, or any growth after the menopause, suggesting leiomyosarcoma Severe symptomatic anaemia from heavy bleeding, potentially requiring transfusion Acute severe pelvic pain from torsion of a pedunculated fibroid or red degeneration Urinary retention or hydronephrosis from mass effect Postmenopausal bleeding requiring exclusion of endometrial pathology Attributing all abnormal uterine bleeding to fibroids and missing coexistent endometrial hyperplasia or carcinoma. Failing to consider leiomyosarcoma before morcellation, particularly in postmenopausal or rapidly growing masses. Overlooking coexisting adenomyosis, which frequently mimics and accompanies fibroids. Neglecting to correct iron-deficiency anaemia before intervention. Assuming subserosal or pedunculated fibroids are the cause of heavy menstrual bleeding. A fibroid arises from a single transformed myometrial smooth-muscle cell that proliferates as a monoclonal nodule of smooth muscle within an abundant extracellular matrix of collagen, fibronectin and proteoglycan, giving the characteristic whorled cut surface and a surrounding pseudocapsule of compressed myometrium. Growth is driven by oestrogen and progesterone, with overexpression of their receptors and of local growth factors, and somatic MED12 mutations are frequently implicated. Heavy menstrual bleeding results from distortion and enlargement of the endometrial surface, dysregulation of vasoactive and angiogenic factors, and impaired local haemostasis, while enlarging lesions produce pressure effects on adjacent pelvic viscera. The prognosis is excellent as fibroids are benign, with most remaining asymptomatic and stable and symptomatic lesions responding well to treatment and regressing after the menopause. Recurrence can follow myomectomy, and malignant transformation is exceptionally rare.
