heavy menstrual bleeding Acute severe pain from fibroid degeneration or torsion of a pedunculated fibroid Hydronephrosis from ureteric compression by a large mass Acute urinary retention from a large or cervical fibroid Assuming all abnormal bleeding in a woman with fibroids is due to the fibroids and missing coexisting endometrial pathology Overlooking submucosal fibroids as a cause of infertility or recurrent bleeding when only transabdominal imaging is used Attributing a rapidly growing mass to a benign fibroid without considering sarcoma Neglecting to treat iron-deficiency anaemia Failing to consider fibroid degeneration as a cause of acute pain in pregnancy Fibroids arise from a single transformed myometrial smooth muscle cell that proliferates under the influence of ovarian sex steroids to form a well-circumscribed, pseudo-encapsulated mass of smooth muscle and extracellular matrix. Oestrogen and progesterone, along with local growth factors, drive their growth, which is why they enlarge in the reproductive years and shrink after menopause. Heavy bleeding results from an increased and distorted endometrial surface, altered local vasculature and prostaglandins, and impaired uterine contraction. As fibroids outgrow their blood supply they can undergo hyaline, cystic, calcific, or red degeneration. Fibroids are benign and most women have a good outcome; malignant transformation is very rare. Symptoms often stabilise or regress after the menopause. Recurrence after uterine-conserving treatments such as myomectomy is possible, whereas hysterectomy is definitive but ends fertility.

Uterine inversion — inverted uterus, puerperal uterine inversion, acute uterine inversion Uterine atony with postpartum haemorrhage Retained placenta Large prolapsing uterine or submucosal fibroid Genital tract trauma with haematoma Amniotic fluid embolism causing collapse Other causes of postpartum collapse such as major haemorrhage or sepsis Clinical examination confirming absence of the fundus abdominally and a vaginal or introital mass Full blood count and coagulation studies Group and crossmatch with activation of major haemorrhage support Continuous monitoring of vital signs and urine output Ultrasound if the diagnosis is uncertain and time permits Assessment for retained placenta once the uterus is replaced Uterine inversion is the turning inside-out of the uterine fundus through the cervix, most often as an acute complication of the third stage of labour It classically presents with sudden severe lower abdominal pain, haemorrhage, and shock that appears disproportionate to visible blood loss A key contributor is excessive cord traction or fundal pressure before placental separation, particularly with a relaxed uterus On examination the fundus may be absent from the abdomen and a mass may be palpable or visible at the introitus or in the vagina Profound, partly neurogenic (vagally mediated) shock is characteristic and may be out of proportion to bleeding Immediate management is resuscitation and prompt manual replacement of the uterus, ideally before a constriction ring forms Uterine relaxation with a tocolytic or anaesthetic agent can facilitate replacement, after which uterotonics are given to restore tone If manual replacement fails, hydrostatic techniques or surgical repositioning are required Postpartum collapse with shock disproportionate to visible blood loss A fundal mass at the introitus or in the vagina with an absent abdominal fundus Failed manual replacement or formation of a tight constriction ring Ongoing haemorrhage after repositioning suggesting atony or retained placenta Applying cord traction or fundal pressure before placental separation, precipitating inversion Attributing profound shock solely to blood loss and missing the neurogenic component Delaying replacement so that a constriction ring forms and prevents manual reduction Removing an adherent placenta before replacing the uterus, worsening haemorrhage Uterine inversion occurs when the fundus descends and passes through the dilated cervix, typically when an atonic or partially relaxed uterus is subjected to traction on the cord or pressure on the fundus while the placenta remains adherent, especially with a fundal placental site. The inverted uterus and its attachments produce intense stimulation of pelvic autonomic nerves, causing a vagally mediated component to the shock alongside haemorrhage from the placental bed. A constriction ring may form at the cervix, trapping the inverted fundus and making replacement progressively harder, which is why speed of recognition and relaxation of the uterus are central to management. With immediate recognition, resuscitation, and prompt replacement, most women recover fully. Delay increases the risk of severe haemorrhage, prolonged shock, need for surgery, and, rarely, hysterectomy or maternal death.

Uterine Prolapse — pelvic organ prolapse, uterovaginal prolapse, descent of the uterus, genital prolapse Cystocele or rectocele without significant uterine descent Vaginal vault prolapse after hysterectomy Enterocele Large vaginal or cervical cyst or fibroid Chronic uterine inversion Urethral diverticulum or other vaginal mass Pelvic examination in different positions and with straining to define the compartments and stage Assessment of pelvic floor muscle strength Urinary assessment including post-void residual and urodynamics where incontinence complicates management Consideration of imaging for large or atypical masses Evaluation and treatment of contributing factors such as constipation, chronic cough, and atrophy Uterine prolapse is descent of the uterus and cervix into or beyond the vagina due to weakening of the pelvic floor supports, and it often coexists with prolapse of the vaginal walls, bladder, and rectum Typical symptoms include a sensation of vaginal bulge or something coming down, pelvic heaviness or dragging, and symptoms that worsen through the day and with standing or straining Associated urinary, bowel, and sexual dysfunction are common and should be assessed directly, as women may not volunteer them Major risk factors include vaginal childbirth, increasing age and menopause, chronically raised intra-abdominal pressure from obesity, chronic cough or constipation, and connective tissue laxity Severity is graded by how far the leading part of the prolapse descends relative to the hymen, using a standardised staging system Conservative management with pelvic floor muscle training and vaginal pessaries is appropriate for many women, particularly if surgery is undesirable or unsafe Surgical options range from uterine-preserving procedures to hysterectomy with vault support, and the choice depends on symptoms, fertility wishes, and fitness Vaginal oestrogen can improve atrophic tissue and support pessary use in postmenopausal women Ulceration, bleeding, or infection of exposed prolapsed tissue Urinary retention or obstructed voiding from advanced prolapse Hydronephrosis or renal impairment from ureteric kinking in severe procidentia New abnormal bleeding requiring exclusion of malignancy Complete procidentia that cannot be reduced, needing prompt specialist assessment Failing to ask about associated urinary, bowel, and sexual symptoms Overlooking coexisting prolapse in other vaginal compartments Missing occult stress incontinence unmasked after prolapse correction Neglecting to exclude malignancy in a woman with abnormal bleeding Not treating vaginal atrophy or constipation that undermines pessary use and surgical outcomes The uterus and vagina are held in position by the levator ani muscles and the endopelvic fascia and ligaments, including the uterosacral and cardinal ligaments. Damage to these supports, most often from stretching and denervation during vaginal delivery, together with age-related and oestrogen-deficiency-related weakening of connective tissue and muscle, allows the pelvic organs to descend. Sustained increases in intra-abdominal pressure accelerate this process. As support fails, the uterus and cervix prolapse downward, frequently dragging the vaginal walls and adjacent bladder and rectum with them. Uterine prolapse is a benign but often progressive quality-of-life condition; conservative measures relieve symptoms in many women, and surgery provides good results though prolapse can recur in other compartments over time. Prognosis is favourable overall, and attention to modifiable risk factors such as weight, constipation, and chronic cough helps limit progression and recurrence.

Uterine rupture — ruptured uterus, uterine scar rupture Placental abruption Placenta praevia or other antepartum haemorrhage Scar dehiscence with incomplete separation Other causes of an acute abdomen in pregnancy such as appendicitis or a ruptured viscus Amniotic fluid embolism causing sudden collapse and fetal compromise Concealed haemorrhage from another source presenting with hypovolaemic shock Continuous cardiotocography, since an abnormal fetal heart rate is often the first clue Urgent clinical abdominal assessment for tenderness, palpable fetal parts, and loss of station Full blood count, coagulation screen, fibrinogen, and group-and-save or crossmatch Ultrasound, if time permits, for free intraperitoneal fluid, fetal position, and viability Urinalysis or catheter specimen for haematuria suggesting bladder involvement or lower-segment extension Blood gas and lactate to gauge maternal and fetal compromise Definitive confirmation at emergency laparotomy Uterine rupture is a full-thickness disruption of the uterine wall involving the myometrium and overlying serosa, often with the membranes, which may extrude the fetus or placenta into the peritoneal cavity; it is distinguished from dehiscence, a partial scar separation with intact serosa The commonest setting is labour in a uterus scarred by previous caesarean section, particularly attempted vaginal birth after a previous classical or inverted-T incision Other risk factors include previous myomectomy or uterine surgery, injudicious use of oxytocin or prostaglandins, obstructed or prolonged labour, grand multiparity, uterine anomaly, trauma, and difficult instrumental delivery The most consistent and often earliest sign is an abnormal fetal heart rate pattern, particularly a prolonged deceleration or bradycardia Maternal features include acute scar or abdominal pain that may break through effective regional analgesia, vaginal bleeding, cessation of contractions, loss of the presenting part with a rising station, palpable fetal parts abdominally, haematuria, and signs of hypovolaemic shock Management is immediate resuscitation and emergency laparotomy with delivery of the fetus, followed by repair of the defect or, when repair is not feasible, hysterectomy Massive obstetric haemorrhage should be anticipated, so major-haemorrhage protocols, blood products, and senior obstetric and anaesthetic support are essential The recurrence risk in a subsequent pregnancy influences counselling about mode of delivery, and induction or augmentation of a scarred uterus must be undertaken with caution Prolonged fetal bradycardia or a sudden severe fetal heart rate abnormality in a labouring woman with a scar Breakthrough scar or abdominal pain despite regional analgesia Maternal haemodynamic instability or signs of hypovolaemic shock Cessation of uterine contractions with recession of the presenting part Palpable fetal parts through the abdominal wall or new haematuria Attributing early fetal heart rate changes to benign causes in a woman attempting vaginal birth after caesarean Aggressive augmentation of a scarred or obstructed uterus with uterotonics Misreading breakthrough pain under epidural as merely inadequate analgesia Underestimating blood loss and activating major-haemorrhage support too late Failing to counsel about recurrence risk and delivery planning in subsequent pregnancies The pregnant uterine wall is subjected to rising intrauterine pressure during contractions. A previous full-thickness scar, or an area weakened by surgery, adenomyosis, or a congenital anomaly, is less elastic and less vascular than surrounding myometrium and can separate under repeated stretching and contraction. When augmentation with oxytocin or prostaglandins produces excessive uterine activity, or when labour is obstructed and the lower segment thins progressively, the wall can give way. Rupture opens uterine vessels, causing haemorrhage into the peritoneum or vagina, and loss of wall integrity abolishes effective contractions and can expel the fetus and placenta from the cavity, abruptly cutting off uteroplacental perfusion. The result is rapid fetal hypoxia and maternal haemorrhagic shock. Prompt recognition and immediate operative delivery are associated with maternal survival and, if the fetus is delivered quickly, a reasonable neonatal outcome. Delay leads to fetal hypoxic injury or death and maternal exsanguination, and future pregnancies carry a raised risk of recurrence.

Prostatic utricle cyst — prostatic utricle cyst, utricular cyst, enlarged prostatic utricle Mullerian duct cyst, which has no urethral communication Ejaculatory duct cyst Seminal vesicle cyst, which is laterally placed Bladder diverticulum Posterior urethral pathology Cystic prostatic mass Voiding cystourethrography to demonstrate communication with the urethra Pelvic MRI for midline anatomy and associated anomalies Retrograde urethrography or urethroscopy to view the utricular opening Cyst fluid analysis for spermatozoa Renal tract imaging for associated anomalies Assessment for disorders of sex development where indicated A midline cyst arising from dilatation of the prostatic utricle, which opens into the prostatic urethra at the verumontanum Strongly associated with genitourinary anomalies such as hypospadias, cryptorchidism, unilateral renal agenesis and disorders of sex development It usually presents in childhood or adolescence, in contrast to mullerian duct cysts, which present later Because it communicates with the urethra it may contain spermatozoa, unlike a mullerian duct cyst It can cause recurrent urinary tract infection, post-void dribbling, epididymitis, stone formation within the cyst, or infertility Voiding cystourethrography may show the cyst filling from the urethra, while MRI defines the surrounding anatomy Small asymptomatic cysts are observed, whereas symptomatic ones may need transurethral or surgical treatment Recurrent infection, abscess or stone formation within the cyst Association with disorders of sex development requiring endocrine and genetic evaluation Obstructive symptoms or upper urinary tract compromise Rare malignant change in long-standing cysts Confusing a utricle cyst, which communicates with the urethra and may contain sperm, with a mullerian duct cyst Missing associated hypospadias, cryptorchidism, renal agenesis or a disorder of sex development Damaging the ejaculatory ducts or continence mechanism during intervention Overlooking the cyst as a cause of recurrent urinary tract infection or epididymitis in a boy The prostatic utricle is a small midline mullerian remnant that opens into the prostatic urethra at the verumontanum. Incomplete regression, often linked with under-virilisation, allows it to dilate into a cyst. Because it communicates with the urethra, urine can reflux into it, predisposing to stasis, infection and stone formation, and when spermatozoa enter it the cyst may contain sperm. Generally good; small cysts are asymptomatic and stable, while symptomatic utricle cysts respond to endoscopic or surgical treatment, although proximity to the ejaculatory ducts and continence structures requires care.

Uveitic glaucoma — inflammatory glaucoma, glaucoma secondary to uveitis, uveitic ocular hypertension, inflammatory ocular hypertension Primary open-angle glaucoma with coincidental uveitis Steroid-induced (corticosteroid-responder) glaucoma Posner-Schlossman syndrome (glaucomatocyclitic crisis) Neovascular glaucoma Primary or secondary angle-closure glaucoma from other causes Herpetic or Fuchs heterochromic uveitis with raised pressure Slit-lamp examination to grade inflammation, keratic precipitates, and synechiae Gonioscopy to identify open-angle, synechial, or pupillary-block mechanisms Applanation tonometry with monitoring during and after inflammatory episodes and steroid treatment OCT of the optic nerve and macula to assess glaucomatous damage and cystoid oedema Automated perimetry to monitor field loss Targeted workup for the underlying uveitis, including infective and systemic causes when indicated A secondary glaucoma arising in eyes with intraocular inflammation, with pressure elevation resulting from several coexisting mechanisms rather than a single cause Open-angle mechanisms include trabecular obstruction by inflammatory cells and debris, trabeculitis, and a steroid-induced pressure response from treatment Angle-closure mechanisms include pupillary block from extensive posterior synechiae with iris bombe, and peripheral anterior synechiae from chronic angle inflammation Pressure may paradoxically be low during active inflammation from ciliary hyposecretion, then surge as inflammation settles or steroids are used Careful gonioscopy is essential to distinguish open-angle from synechial or pupillary-block mechanisms because treatment differs Management balances vigorous control of inflammation with pressure-lowering therapy, while recognising that corticosteroids can both reduce inflammatory outflow obstruction and independently raise pressure Fuchs heterochromic uveitis and herpetic anterior uveitis are characteristically associated with raised pressure Prostaglandin analogues are used with caution as they may theoretically aggravate inflammation and cystoid macular oedema Iris bombe from a completely bound-down pupil producing acute pupillary-block angle closure A marked steroid-induced pressure rise during treatment of the inflammation Very high pressure with corneal oedema during an inflammatory crisis Progressive optic-nerve damage masked by intermittently low pressure during active uveitis Attributing all pressure elevation to steroid response and undertreating the inflammation, or vice versa Missing pupillary block and iris bombe requiring urgent iridotomy rather than only medical therapy Being reassured by low pressure during active inflammation and overlooking later surges Using prostaglandin analogues uncritically where they may worsen inflammation or macular oedema Failing to investigate and treat the underlying cause of the uveitis In uveitic glaucoma intraocular inflammation raises pressure through multiple overlapping pathways. Inflammatory cells, fibrin, and protein clog the trabecular meshwork, and direct inflammation of the meshwork (trabeculitis) reduces outflow facility; scarring can permanently damage the drainage tissue. Chronic inflammation promotes peripheral anterior synechiae that close the angle, while dense posterior synechiae binding the pupil margin to the lens can produce pupillary block with forward bowing of the iris (iris bombe) and secondary angle closure. Corticosteroids used to treat the uveitis may themselves reduce outflow and cause a steroid-induced pressure rise. Active inflammation can transiently lower pressure by suppressing aqueous production, masking a tendency to later elevation. Prognosis depends on controlling the underlying inflammation and the mechanism of pressure rise; open-angle inflammatory hypertension often resolves as the uveitis settles, whereas extensive synechial closure and repeated crises lead to chronic glaucoma that may need drainage surgery and carries a guarded outlook.

VACTERL association — VATER association, VACTERL/VATER spectrum, vertebral-anal-cardiac-tracheoesophageal-renal-limb association Fanconi anaemia (radial defects with marrow failure) CHARGE syndrome Currarino syndrome (sacral, anorectal, presacral mass) 22q11.2 deletion syndrome Feingold syndrome Townes-Brocks syndrome Baller-Gerold syndrome Spinal and skeletal radiographs to identify vertebral segmentation and rib anomalies Echocardiography to characterise congenital heart disease Contrast or endoscopic evaluation and attempts to pass a nasogastric tube for tracheo-oesophageal fistula Renal and abdominal ultrasound to detect urinary tract malformation Limb radiographs to define radial ray defects Chromosome breakage studies to exclude Fanconi anaemia and targeted genetic testing A non-random co-occurrence of congenital defects; the acronym denotes Vertebral anomalies, Anal atresia, Cardiac defects, Tracheo-oesophageal fistula, Renal anomalies, and Limb (usually radial) defects Diagnosis is clinical and conventionally requires at least three of the component features in the absence of an alternative unifying syndrome It is an association rather than a syndrome, meaning the components occur together more often than by chance but without a single known cause Tracheo-oesophageal fistula with oesophageal atresia often presents in the newborn with choking, drooling, and an inability to pass a feeding tube Anorectal malformation may be evident at birth as an absent or abnormally placed anus Limb involvement is typically preaxial or radial, such as a hypoplastic or absent thumb or radius Intellect is usually normal, and its presence should prompt reconsideration of a specific syndromic diagnosis Neonatal respiratory distress and aspiration from tracheo-oesophageal fistula requiring urgent surgery High or complex anorectal malformation needing early surgical management Ductal-dependent or complex cardiac lesion presenting with collapse Bilateral renal anomalies threatening kidney function Features suggesting Fanconi anaemia, which carries marrow failure and malignancy risk Accepting the label without excluding Fanconi anaemia and other definable syndromes Missing a tracheo-oesophageal fistula in a newborn who chokes with feeds Failing to complete systematic screening of all component systems once one defect is found Assuming intellectual disability, which is not typical of the association Overlooking occult vertebral or renal anomalies that alter management VACTERL association is understood as a pattern of defects affecting structures that develop during a shared early embryonic window, particularly disturbances of blastogenesis and midline mesodermal patterning. The components involve organs derived from or dependent on interactions between mesoderm and endoderm, and disruption of common developmental signalling pathways, including those governing left-right and cranio-caudal patterning, is thought to underlie the clustering. No single genetic cause explains most cases, and it remains a diagnosis of exclusion; recognisable single-gene disorders such as Fanconi anaemia and mitochondrial or ciliary conditions can produce an overlapping phenotype and must be considered before accepting the label. Prognosis reflects the number and severity of component defects; with modern neonatal surgery and multidisciplinary care many children survive with good function and normal cognition, though cardiac and renal severity are the main determinants of outcome.

Vaginismus — genito-pelvic pain/penetration disorder, vaginal muscle spasm, penetration disorder Dyspareunia from other causes Vulvodynia or provoked vestibulodynia Vaginal atrophy from oestrogen deficiency Pelvic infection or inflammation Congenital anatomical abnormality such as a vaginal septum Endometriosis or other pelvic pathology Sensitive sexual and psychological history including any trauma or triggering event Gentle, patient-controlled genital and pelvic examination as tolerated Exclusion of infection, atrophy, or dermatological vulval conditions Assessment of pelvic floor muscle tone, often with physiotherapy input Evaluation for structural anomalies when penetration has never been possible Vaginismus is characterised by involuntary contraction of the pelvic floor and perivaginal muscles that makes vaginal penetration painful, difficult, or impossible It is now grouped with dyspareunia under the umbrella of genito-pelvic pain/penetration disorder, reflecting their frequent overlap It may be primary, present from the first attempts at penetration, or secondary, developing after a period of pain-free intercourse Fear and anticipatory anxiety about pain are central, producing a self-reinforcing cycle of muscle guarding, avoidance, and further distress The muscle spasm is involuntary and not under conscious control, a point patients need reassured of to reduce shame and self-blame Examination should be gentle and patient-led, and marked distress or guarding on attempted examination itself supports the diagnosis Organic causes of pain such as infection, atrophy, or structural abnormality should be excluded, since untreated dyspareunia can trigger secondary vaginismus Treatment combines education, pelvic floor physiotherapy, graded desensitisation often using vaginal trainers, and psychological or psychosexual therapy addressing anxiety History of sexual trauma or abuse requiring sensitive, specialised care Findings suggesting an organic structural or gynaecological cause of pain Signs of infection or inflammation needing directed treatment Severe psychological distress or relationship breakdown Attempting a forceful examination, which worsens pain, fear, and guarding Treating it as purely psychological and neglecting pelvic floor physiotherapy Missing an organic cause of dyspareunia that precipitated secondary vaginismus Failing to involve the partner and address relationship and anxiety factors Vaginismus reflects a conditioned, involuntary reflex contraction of the pelvic floor musculature in anticipation of, or response to, attempted vaginal penetration. A trigger, which may be an initial painful experience, infection, trauma, negative sexual conditioning, or fear, leads to protective muscle tightening; the resulting pain reinforces the expectation of pain, so anxiety and guarding become self-perpetuating. Over time the response can be provoked by anticipation alone, independent of any ongoing organic cause. Because the mechanism is largely a learned protective reflex intertwined with anxiety, both the physical muscle response and the psychological component must be addressed for resolution. Vaginismus generally has a good prognosis, with high success rates when treated by a combined approach of education, pelvic floor physiotherapy, graded desensitisation, and psychological support tailored to the individual.

Valsalva retinopathy — Valsalva haemorrhagic retinopathy, Valsalva maculopathy Posterior vitreous detachment with haemorrhage Retinal arterial macroaneurysm Proliferative diabetic retinopathy Retinal tear or detachment Terson syndrome Haemorrhage from neovascular age-related macular degeneration Bleeding related to a blood dyscrasia Dilated fundus examination to identify the dome-shaped pre-retinal haemorrhage Optical coherence tomography to confirm the sub-internal limiting membrane or sub-hyaloid location A clear history of a precipitating Valsalva manoeuvre Full blood count and clotting studies if the event is spontaneous or recurrent B-scan ultrasound when the haemorrhage obscures the fundus view Blood pressure measurement Presents with sudden, painless unilateral loss of vision, a central scotoma or floaters immediately after a Valsalva-type effort such as heavy lifting, coughing, vomiting, straining or childbirth The characteristic finding is a well-circumscribed, dome-shaped pre-retinal haemorrhage at the macula lying beneath the internal limiting membrane or posterior hyaloid The blood may develop a horizontal fluid level as it settles Vision depends on whether the fovea is obscured by the haemorrhage The affected eye is otherwise usually healthy, without retinal vascular disease Optical coherence tomography helps localise the blood to the sub-internal limiting membrane or sub-hyaloid space Most cases are managed by observation as the haemorrhage clears spontaneously, with Nd:YAG hyaloidotomy or vitrectomy reserved for dense or persistent bleeding Bilateral or spontaneous haemorrhage without a clear Valsalva trigger, prompting investigation for a bleeding disorder Associated systemic bleeding or bruising Dense vitreous haemorrhage obscuring underlying pathology Features suggesting an underlying retinal vascular disease Causing unnecessary alarm or over-investigating a self-limiting condition Missing an underlying bleeding disorder in atypical or recurrent cases Assuming every pre-retinal haemorrhage is due to Valsalva Intervening prematurely when observation would allow spontaneous clearance A sudden rise in intrathoracic or intra-abdominal pressure against a closed glottis is transmitted to the ocular venous system, producing an abrupt spike in retinal venous and capillary pressure. This ruptures fragile superficial perifoveal capillaries, and blood collects in the potential space beneath the internal limiting membrane or the posterior hyaloid face, typically pooling at the macula. The outlook is generally excellent, with most haemorrhages clearing spontaneously over weeks to months and full recovery of vision.

Van Buchem disease (SOST regulatory) — hyperostosis corticalis generalisata, endosteal hyperostosis, Van Buchem type, SOST enhancer deletion disorder Sclerosteosis Camurati-Engelmann disease Osteopetrosis Craniometaphyseal dysplasia Pycnodysostosis Paget disease of the skull Plain radiographs showing endosteal cortical thickening and dense skull and mandible Serum alkaline phosphatase and bone turnover markers Serum calcium and phosphate to confirm normal mineral homeostasis Genetic testing for the SOST regulatory-region deletion Skull-base imaging for foraminal narrowing and nerve compression Audiology and visual assessment with monitoring for raised intracranial pressure An autosomal recessive sclerosing dysplasia caused by a deletion of a downstream regulatory (enhancer) element that controls SOST expression, reducing sclerostin production Closely related to sclerosteosis but generally milder, and importantly it lacks the syndactyly and overgrowth of stature seen in sclerosteosis Reduced sclerostin releases the brake on Wnt-mediated bone formation, producing generalised osteosclerosis with prominent mandibular enlargement Cranial and skull-base thickening entraps cranial nerves, causing facial palsy, hearing loss, and sometimes optic compromise Patients typically have raised alkaline phosphatase reflecting increased bone formation, with normal calcium and phosphate Radiographs show endosteal cortical thickening of long bones and dense sclerotic skull and jaw Care centres on surgical decompression of entrapped nerves and surveillance for raised intracranial pressure rather than pharmacological bone reduction Progressive facial-nerve weakness or deteriorating hearing or vision Signs of raised intracranial pressure Brainstem compression from posterior skull-base overgrowth Acute neurological decline requiring urgent surgical decompression Assuming a coding SOST mutation when the underlying lesion is a regulatory-region deletion Confusing it with sclerosteosis and expecting syndactyly or gigantism, which are absent here Overlooking treatable cranial nerve entrapment presenting as isolated facial palsy or deafness Failing to monitor for raised intracranial pressure over time Van Buchem disease is caused by homozygous deletion of a conserved regulatory region located downstream of the SOST gene. This element normally drives SOST transcription in bone, so its loss markedly reduces sclerostin expression while leaving the coding sequence intact. Diminished sclerostin fails to inhibit the Wnt/beta-catenin pathway, resulting in increased osteoblastic bone formation and progressive generalised hyperostosis. Because sclerostin is reduced rather than completely absent as in coding-mutation sclerosteosis, the phenotype is usually less severe, but skull and jaw overgrowth still narrows cranial foramina and can compress cranial nerves. Generally milder and more indolent than sclerosteosis, with a normal lifespan in most patients, but progressive cranial nerve entrapment can cause facial palsy and sensory loss that may require surgical relief.

Van Neck disease — ischiopubic osteochondrosis, van Neck-Odelberg disease Osteomyelitis of the pelvis Ewing sarcoma or other bone tumour Pelvic (ischiopubic) stress or avulsion fracture Other osteochondroses Septic arthritis of the hip Radiographs, ideally with comparison of both sides and follow-up MRI where infection or tumour must be excluded Inflammatory markers to help exclude infection Clinical correlation and observation over time Avoidance of biopsy once the diagnosis is recognised A benign osteochondrosis of the ischiopubic synchondrosis in children It represents exuberant or asymmetric ossification at the junction of the ischium and pubis during normal development It may be asymptomatic or cause groin, buttock or hip pain and a limp The key issue is that its radiographic appearance can mimic osteomyelitis, Ewing sarcoma or a healing fracture MRI can show marrow oedema that adds to the confusion with more serious pathology Recognition of this normal variant avoids unnecessary biopsy and treatment Systemic features or raised inflammatory markers suggesting infection Aggressive imaging features or a soft-tissue mass suggesting tumour Progressive rather than resolving changes Severe or worsening pain Mistaking the normal variant for osteomyelitis or Ewing sarcoma and performing biopsy Over-investigating an asymptomatic incidental finding Failing to compare with the contralateral side Not correlating imaging with the benign clinical picture Van Neck disease reflects a normal but sometimes asymmetric or prominent stage in the ossification and fusion of the ischiopubic synchondrosis, the cartilaginous junction between the ischium and pubis that normally fuses in later childhood. The expanded, sometimes fragmented, appearance and associated marrow oedema are part of physiological development, but they can radiographically resemble infection or tumour. It is essentially a self-resolving developmental variant rather than a disease. The condition is benign and resolves as the synchondrosis fuses, with an excellent prognosis once more serious mimics are excluded.

Adult-onset vanishing white matter disease (EIF2B) — VWM, EIF2B-related leukoencephalopathy, leukoencephalopathy with vanishing white matter, childhood ataxia with central hypomyelination (CACH), ovarioleukodystrophy Multiple sclerosis and other inflammatory demyelination Other adult-onset genetic leukoencephalopathies (including LBSL and adult Alexander disease) Mitochondrial leukoencephalopathy Toxic or post-infectious leukoencephalopathy CADASIL and other hereditary small-vessel diseases Premature ovarian insufficiency with an unrelated incidental white matter change Brain MRI to demonstrate diffuse white matter rarefaction with cystic change and a CSF-like signal, and any radiating stripe pattern EIF2B1 to EIF2B5 sequencing or gene panel to confirm the diagnosis Endocrine assessment of ovarian function in affected women Neuropsychological evaluation to characterise cognitive involvement Exclusion of inflammatory and infective causes (CSF, oligoclonal bands) where multiple sclerosis is considered Serial imaging to document the evolving white matter rarefaction An autosomal recessive leukoencephalopathy caused by variants in any of the five subunits of eukaryotic translation initiation factor 2B (EIF2B1 to EIF2B5) The defining clinical feature is episodic, stepwise deterioration provoked by stressors such as febrile illness, minor head trauma or acute fright, sometimes with disproportionate decline or coma followed by partial recovery The adult-onset form is generally milder and more slowly progressive than the infantile disease, with spasticity, cerebellar ataxia and cognitive or behavioural change predominating Affected women may have primary or secondary ovarian failure, giving the ovarioleukodystrophy phenotype, which is an important clue in females The MRI hallmark is diffuse white matter rarefaction and cystic degeneration, so that over time the abnormal white matter takes on a signal close to cerebrospinal fluid on all sequences, sometimes with a radiating stripe pattern within it Diagnosis rests on the characteristic imaging together with the stress-sensitive clinical course, confirmed by EIF2B gene testing There is no specific therapy; management is supportive and includes avoiding and promptly treating triggers such as fever and head injury Rapid deterioration or coma following fever, head trauma or acute fright New encephalopathy in a patient with known disease requiring assessment for a treatable trigger Progressive cognitive decline with loss of independence Dysphagia and aspiration risk as the disease advances Not recognising the stress-provoked, stepwise course as a specific clue to the diagnosis Misinterpreting the CSF-like white matter as atrophy or old ischaemia rather than rarefaction Overlooking ovarian failure in women, which points towards the diagnosis Mislabelling the disorder as multiple sclerosis and giving inappropriate immunotherapy Failing to advise patients and families about avoiding and promptly managing fever and head injury Vanishing white matter disease is caused by biallelic variants in genes encoding subunits of eukaryotic translation initiation factor 2B (eIF2B), a guanine nucleotide exchange factor central to the initiation of protein synthesis and to the integrated stress response. Impaired eIF2B activity dysregulates the cellular response to stress, rendering glial cells, particularly astrocytes and oligodendrocytes, abnormally vulnerable. Physiological stressors such as fever, trauma or fright overwhelm this defective stress response, precipitating white matter injury. Progressive loss and cystic breakdown of the white matter produce the characteristic rarefaction in which affected tissue comes to resemble cerebrospinal fluid on imaging. Adult-onset vanishing white matter disease is usually slower and milder than childhood forms, but remains progressive and is punctuated by stress-related episodes of decline that may not fully reverse; the overall course varies widely with genotype and age at onset. Careful avoidance of triggers can reduce episodic deterioration, though cumulative disability tends to accrue over time.

Vanishing white matter disease — VWM, childhood ataxia with central hypomyelination, CACH, leukoencephalopathy with vanishing white matter, EIF2B1, EIF2B2, EIF2B3, EIF2B4, EIF2B5 Metachromatic leukodystrophy and other lysosomal leukodystrophies Megalencephalic leukoencephalopathy with subcortical cysts Mitochondrial leukoencephalopathies Acute disseminated encephalomyelitis or post-infectious demyelination Alexander disease Cerebral folate deficiency and other treatable metabolic leukoencephalopathies Brain MRI with FLAIR and T2 sequences to demonstrate diffuse white-matter rarefaction with progressive CSF-like signal Molecular genetic testing of EIF2B1-5 to confirm the diagnosis Metabolic screen to exclude other leukodystrophies (arylsulfatase A, very-long-chain fatty recessive leukodystrophy caused by biallelic variants in any of the five genes encoding subunits of eukaryotic translation initiation factor 2B (EIF2B1-5) Hallmark clinical feature is episodic, through to adult-onset and an ovarioleukodystrophy variant with premature ovarian failure in females MRI shows diffuse, symmetrical white-matter abnormality that progressively rarefies and takes on on avoiding known triggers Families should be counselled to seek early care and antipyresis during infections and to minimise head injury, as these precipitate crises Rapid decline into stupor or coma following a febrile illness or minor head injury Acute loss of previously acquired motor milestones after a trigger event Status epilepticus or intractable seizures during an episode of deterioration Signs of raised intracranial pressure or brainstem dysfunction during a crisis Attributing a post-febrile collapse to encephalitis or sepsis alone and missing the underlying leukodystrophy Misreading early MRI as ordinary demyelination and failing to recognise the FLAIR suppression that signals white-matter liquefaction Overlooking premature ovarian failure as a clue in adolescent or adult females Failing to counsel families about trigger avoidance, prompt antipyresis, and head-injury prevention Vanishing white matter disease results from loss-of-function variants in the genes encoding the five subunits of eukaryotic translation initiation factor 2B (eIF2B), a guanine-nucleotide exchange factor central to the regulation of protein synthesis, particularly under cellular stress. Impaired eIF2B activity deranges the integrated stress response, leaving glial cells (especially astrocytes and oligodendrocytes) unable to adapt to metabolic stresses such as fever, inflammation, or trauma. The result is progressive cerebral white-matter breakdown with abnormal, immature astrocytes and dysmyelination, so that the white matter gradually rarefies and cavitates into a fluid-like state while grey matter is comparatively preserved. The disorder is progressive and currently incurable; the classic childhood form typically causes stepwise decline with death within a few years of onset, whereas later-onset forms progress more slowly. Prognosis is strongly influenced by age at onset, with the earliest-onset presentations carrying the worst outlook.

Variceal bleeding — Urgent upper GI endoscopy Crossmatch, coagulation Vasoactive (terlipressin) + antibiotic prophylaxis Major haemorrhage — resuscitate; antibiotics reduce mortality in cirrhotic GI bleed Peptic ulcer disease — the most common cause of upper GI bleeding (~50% of UGIB hospitalisations) (p.360) Mallory-Weiss tear — ~2-10% of UGIB, classically preceded by vomiting/retching/coughing, usually on the gastric side of the gastro-oesophageal junction; stops spontaneously in ~80-90% (p.360) Bleeding gastric varices, intestinal varices, and portal hypertensive gastropathy/enterocolopathy — other portal-hypertension-related sources distinct from oesophageal varices (p.361, p.2714) Erosive disease — erosive oesophagitis, gastritis, duodenitis (up to ~30% of UGIB), commonly NSAID-related (p.361) Stress-related gastric mucosal injury in the critically ill (p.361) Less common: neoplasm, vascular ectasias (including hereditary haemorrhagic telangiectasia, gastric antral vascular ectasia), Dieulafoy's lesion, aortoenteric fistula, haemobilia/haemosuccus pancreaticus (p.361) Upper endoscopy within 24 h is first-line both to diagnose the bleeding source and to treat acutely; more urgent endoscopy (6-12 h) does not improve outcomes and may worsen them in high-risk patients (p.362, p.2714) Endoscopic surveillance for varices: recommended at diagnosis of compensated cirrhosis, then every 2 years (active liver disease) or every 3 years (inactive); also at the time of hepatic decompensation (p.2714) Liver stiffness by transient elastography — if <20 kPa and no thrombocytopenia, high-risk varices are rare and screening endoscopy may be deferred (p.2714) HVPG measurement by interventional radiology (hepatic vein cannulation) in selected cases to confirm/quantify portal hypertension (p.371, p.2714) Complete blood count (thrombocytopenia from hypersplenism is often the first marker of portal hypertension), liver biochemistry, albumin, and prothrombin time/INR to assess hepatic function and severity (p.371, p.2714) Endoscopic stigmata predicting bleeding risk: red wale signs, hematocystic spots, diffuse erythema, bluish colour, cherry-red spots, white-nipple spots; larger varices and worse Child-Pugh/MELD also predict bleeding (p.2713) Portal hypertensive gastropathy — snakeskin-like mosaic mucosal pattern on endoscopy; can cause acute or chronic (iron-deficiency) GI bleeding and mimics variceal bleeding as a cause of haematemesis/melaena in the same cirrhotic patient (p.2714) Gastric varices — also driven by portal hypertension but managed differently from oesophageal varices (p.361, p.2714) Portal hypertension is defined as a hepatic venous pressure gradient (HVPG) >5 mmHg; compensated cirrhosis typically has an HVPG of 5-10 mmHg, while clinically significant portal hypertension (CSPH), defined as HVPG ≥10 mmHg, carries substantial risk of decompensation (variceal bleeding, ascites, encephalopathy). Patients with a gradient >12 mmHg are at risk for variceal haemorrhage (p.2713-2714). Each episode of variceal haemorrhage carries a 20-30% mortality rate, making it an immediate life-threatening complication of portal hypertension (p.2713). In cirrhotic patients presenting with upper GI bleeding, prophylactic antibiotics (typically ceftriaxone) started before endoscopy reduce bacterial infections, recurrent bleeding AND mortality — this is a mortality-altering intervention, not merely supportive (p.362, p.2714). A vasoactive/vasoconstricting agent (somatostatin, octreotide, terlipressin, vapreotide) improves initial bleeding control, reduces transfusion needs and reduces all-cause mortality; combined endoscopic plus pharmacologic therapy is superior to either alone (p.360, p.2714). A restrictive transfusion strategy (transfuse when haemoglobin <7 g/dL, target 7-9 g/dL) reduced early rebleeding and mortality compared with a liberal threshold in randomised trial; haemoglobin may be normal at initial presentation because plasma and red-cell volumes fall proportionately ("people bleed whole blood") and may take up to 72 h to fall (p.362, p.2714). Roughly one-third of patients with histologically confirmed cirrhosis have varices; about 5-15% of cirrhotics develop varices per year, and roughly one-third of patients with varices will bleed (p.2713). IV erythromycin given shortly before endoscopy is suggested as a promotility agent to improve endoscopic visualisation in UGI bleeding, reducing the need for repeat endoscopy (p.362, p.2713). Routine correction of an elevated prothrombin time with fresh frozen plasma is NOT recommended in acute variceal bleeding unless there is evidence of coagulopathy such as bleeding at other sites (e.g. IV-line sites) (p.2714). Bleeding gastric varices, especially when entirely within the stomach or extending into the proximal stomach, are often not amenable to band ligation; tissue-adhesive injection (e.g. cyanoacrylate), TIPS, or balloon-occluded retrograde transvenous obliteration (BRTO) are alternative principles (p.361, p.2714). Variceal haemorrhage is immediately life-threatening with 20-30% mortality per bleeding episode — treat as a major haemorrhage with airway/haemodynamic priority (p.2713) Hemodynamic compromise (tachycardia, hypotension), increasing age and comorbidities predict rebleeding and death (p.362) Increased frequency of spontaneous bacterial peritonitis (SBP) in patients with variceal haemorrhage — SBP prophylaxis is recommended at presentation with upper GI bleeding (p.2715) Persistent or recurrent bleeding despite endoscopic and medical therapy, and advanced liver disease (Child-Pugh B score 8-9 with active bleeding, or Child-Pugh C score 10-13), mark patients who benefit from early/salvage TIPS (p.360-361) Assuming a normal initial haemoglobin excludes severe bleeding — haemoglobin may be normal or only minimally reduced at presentation and can take up to 72 h to fall as extravascular fluid re-equilibrates (p.362) Reflexively correcting a prolonged prothrombin time with FFP — not recommended in variceal bleeding without evidence of true coagulopathy, and FFP can raise portal pressure and cause volume overload (p.2714) Over-liberal transfusion — a liberal threshold (Hb 9 g/dL) increased early rebleeding and mortality versus a restrictive (<7 g/dL) threshold (p.362, p.2714) Omitting antibiotics in a cirrhotic UGI bleed — prophylactic antibiotics reduce infection, rebleeding and mortality and are a core, not optional, intervention (p.362, p.2714) Attempting band ligation on gastric or proximal-stomach varices, where it is often unsuccessful — consider tissue adhesive, TIPS or BRTO (p.2714) Forgetting that TIPS causes new or worsened hepatic encephalopathy in as many as 20% of patients, especially the elderly and those with pre-existing encephalopathy (p.2714) Oesophageal varices are a consequence of portal hypertension, defined as an HVPG >5 mmHg. Portal hypertension arises from two simultaneous haemodynamic processes: (1) increased intrahepatic resistance to portal blood flow (from cirrhosis, regenerative nodules and microthrombi) and (2) increased splanchnic blood flow secondary to splanchnic vasodilation. Cirrhosis is associated with decreased intrahepatic endothelial nitric oxide synthase and nitric oxide, causing intrahepatic vasoconstriction, while systemically nitric oxide, VEGF and TNF rise, driving splanchnic vasodilation. In advanced stages, neurohumoral and vasoconstrictor activation causes sodium/water retention, increased blood volume and a hyperdynamic circulation that further raises portal pressure. Intrahepatic causes (mainly cirrhosis) account for >95% of portal hypertension; pre-hepatic (portal/splenic vein thrombosis) and post-hepatic (Budd-Chiari, right-heart congestion) causes also occur. Elevated portal pressure decompresses into portosystemic collaterals, producing gastro-oesophageal varices that can rupture and bleed. (p.2713-2714) Variceal haemorrhage carries a 20-30% mortality rate with each bleeding episode and patients with variceal haemorrhage have poorer outcomes than those with other UGIB sources. Control of acute bleeding is achievable in the vast majority of cases, but bleeding recurs in the majority of patients unless definitive endoscopic therapy is instituted; oesophageal varices reflect clinically significant portal hypertension (HVPG ≥10 mmHg), and once cirrhosis decompensates the median survival is <2 years. Prophylactic antibiotics, vasoactive drugs and a restrictive transfusion strategy each independently reduce mortality. (p.360, p.2713-2714) Bleeding/decompensation risk is stratified by Child-Pugh class and MELD score, by HVPG/wedged-hepatic-vein pressure (CSPH ≥10 mmHg; variceal bleeding risk at >12 mmHg), by varix size and location, and by endoscopic high-risk stigmata (red wale signs, cherry-red spots, etc.). For triage of UGIB generally, the Glasgow-Blatchford score (0-23) identifies very-low-risk patients (score 0-1) suitable for outpatient management. Advanced-disease thresholds favouring early TIPS: Child-Pugh B 8-9 with active bleeding at endoscopy, or Child-Pugh C 10-13. (p.362, p.2713-2714)

Varicella-Zoster Virus Infection — chickenpox, shingles, VZV, herpes zoster For chickenpox: disseminated HSV infection in patients with atopic dermatitis; disseminated vesiculopapular lesions of coxsackievirus or echovirus infection; atypical measles (these rashes are more often morbilliform/hemorrhagic than vesicular) (p.1506) Rickettsialpox - distinguished by the 'herald spot' (eschar) at the mite-bite site and a more pronounced headache; serology helps differentiate it from varicella (p.1506) Mpox - consider in travelers from endemic areas and in HIV-infected individuals (p.1506) Smallpox - bioterrorism concern; smallpox lesions are larger than chickenpox lesions and all at the same stage of evolution at any given time (p.1506) For herpes zoster: both HSV and coxsackievirus infections can cause dermatomal vesicular lesions (p.1506) Disseminated HSV infection (notably in atopic dermatitis) (p.1506) Coxsackievirus infection (p.1506) Echovirus infection (p.1506) Atypical measles (p.1506) Rickettsialpox (p.1506) Mpox (p.1506) Smallpox (p.1506) HSV and coxsackievirus causing dermatomal vesicular lesions (mimicking zoster) (p.1506) PCR for VZV DNA in vesicular fluid - diagnostic method of choice; also performed on lesions, blood, and saliva (p.1507) Tzanck smear (scraping of lesion base for multinucleated giant cells) - rapid but low sensitivity (~60%) (p.1507) Viral isolation in susceptible tissue-culture cell lines (unequivocal confirmation) (p.1507) Direct immunofluorescent staining of cells from the lesion base or immunoperoxidase detection of viral antigens (p.1507) Serology: seroconversion or fourfold rise in antibody titer between acute- and convalescent-phase sera; FAMA (fluorescent antibody to membrane antigen) test and ELISA are the most sensitive serologic tools (p.1507) VZV causes two distinct clinical syndromes: primary infection (varicella/chickenpox), usually a benign childhood exanthematous vesicular illness, and reactivation of latent virus (herpes zoster/shingles), a dermatomal vesicular rash usually associated with severe pain (p.1504). In chickenpox, skin lesions appear in successive crops over a 2-4 day period and are present in various stages of evolution simultaneously (maculopapules, vesicles, and scabs) on a given body region - the classic small vesicle on an erythematous base ('dewdrop on a rose petal') (p.1505). Chickenpox is highly contagious (attack rate >=90% in seronegatives); patients are infectious ~48 h before the rash appears, throughout vesicle formation, and until all vesicles are crusted. Incubation is usually 14-17 days (range 10-21) (p.1505). Herpes zoster results from reactivation of latent VZV in dorsal root ganglia; most patients have no recent exposure to others with VZV. Incidence is highest in the sixth decade of life and beyond; recurrent zoster is exceedingly rare except in immunocompromised hosts, especially those with AIDS (p.1505). Zoster pain (dermatomal) may precede visible lesions by 48-72 h; in the prodromal stage before the rash appears, the diagnosis can be exceedingly difficult (p.1505-1506). Dermatomes T3 to L3 are most frequently involved in herpes zoster (p.1505). PCR detection of VZV DNA in vesicular fluid is the diagnostic method of choice; specimens for PCR include lesions, blood, and saliva. The Tzanck smear gives a rapid impression but has low sensitivity (~60%) (p.1507). Patients with herpes zoster can transmit infection to seronegative individuals, resulting in chickenpox (not zoster) in the contact (p.1506). Zoster ophthalmicus - involvement of the ophthalmic branch of the trigeminal nerve; a debilitating condition that can result in blindness in the absence of antiviral therapy. Lesions on the tip of the nose (Hutchinson sign) signal likely ocular involvement; refer immediately to an ophthalmologist (p.1505-1507) Ramsay Hunt syndrome - geniculate ganglion (sensory branch of facial nerve) involvement causing pain and vesicles in the external auditory canal, loss of taste in the anterior two-thirds of the tongue, and ipsilateral facial palsy (p.1506) Disseminated/progressive herpes zoster in immunocompromised hosts - patients with Hodgkin and non-Hodgkin lymphoma are at greatest risk; cutaneous dissemination occurs in ~40% untreated, raising the risk of pneumonitis, meningoencephalitis, and hepatitis by 5-10% (p.1506) Varicella pneumonia - the most serious complication of chickenpox; more common in adults (up to 20%) than children and particularly severe in pregnant women; typically requires ventilatory support (p.1505, 1507) Visceral dissemination in immunocompromised patients - occurs in 30-50% of cases and is fatal 15% of the time without antiviral therapy (p.1505) Perinatal varicella - mortality as high as 30% when maternal disease begins within 5 days before to 48 h after delivery (p.1505) CNS involvement: encephalitis (0.1-0.2% of children with chickenpox), aseptic meningitis, transverse myelitis, Guillain-Barre syndrome; in zoster, symptomatic meningoencephalitis and rare granulomatous angiitis with contralateral hemiplegia (p.1505-1506) Aspirin should never be given to children with chickenpox because of its association with Reye syndrome; aspirin is no longer used for this reason (p.1505, 1507) Zoster sine herpetica: dermatomal pain with serologic evidence of zoster can occur in the absence of any skin lesions - shingles without a rash has been reported, making diagnosis difficult (p.1506) In the prodromal stage of herpes zoster (before lesions appear), diagnosis may be possible only after lesions emerge or by retrospective serology (p.1506) Glucocorticoids for zoster should not be used without concomitant antiviral therapy, and steroid use is appropriate only for relatively healthy elderly patients with moderate/severe pain; patients with osteoporosis, diabetes mellitus, glycosuria, or hypertension may not be appropriate candidates (p.1507) VZIG is NOT indicated for a newborn if the mother has zoster (as opposed to varicella); it is indicated when maternal varicella onsets within 5 days before to 48 h after delivery (p.1507-1508) VZV is a member of the Herpesviridae with double-stranded DNA (~125,000 bp), a lipid envelope, and an icosahedral nucleocapsid (~180-200 nm). Primary transmission is by the respiratory route, with localized replication (presumably nasopharynx) seeding the lymphatic/reticuloendothelial system and producing viremia, which manifests as diffuse, scattered skin lesions. Vesicles involve the corium/dermis with ballooning degeneration, multinucleated giant cells, and eosinophilic intranuclear inclusions; localized skin blood-vessel involvement can cause necrosis and epidermal hemorrhage. During chickenpox the virus infects dorsal root ganglia and remains latent (in sensory dorsal, cranial, and enteric ganglia) until an unknown trigger causes reactivation, producing herpes zoster; active zoster ganglia show hemorrhage, edema, and lymphocytic infiltration. Pulmonary involvement shows interstitial pneumonitis with giant cells, intranuclear inclusions, and hemorrhage; CNS infection produces perivascular cuffing similar to other viral encephalitides, while focal hemorrhagic necrosis (characteristic of HSV encephalitis) develops infrequently in VZV infection (p.1504). In the immunocompetent host chickenpox is usually benign and self-limited (total duration ~7-10 days; skin may take 2-4 weeks to fully normalize). Childhood acute cerebellar ataxia is generally benign and does not require hospitalization. Postherpetic neuralgia is the most debilitating complication of zoster: uncommon in the young but affects at least 50% of patients over age 50, who report dermatomal pain for months after cutaneous healing. Even in immunocompromised patients, disseminated zoster is rarely fatal. Hematopoietic stem cell transplant recipients are at particularly high risk, with a mortality rate of ~10% for posttransplantation VZV infection. The Shingrix subunit vaccine showed 97.2% efficacy in adults >=50 years, although vaccine immunity wanes over time (p.1505-1507).

Varicocele — varicocoele, scrotal varicocele, pampiniform plexus varicosity Spermatocele or epididymal cyst Hydrocele Inguinal hernia (indirect) Testicular tumour Epididymo-orchitis Retroperitoneal or renal mass obstructing venous drainage (secondary varicocele) Scrotal examination in both standing and supine positions with Valsalva Scrotal colour Doppler ultrasound to confirm venous reflux and grade the varicocele Measurement of testicular volume to detect growth arrest, especially in adolescents Semen analysis in men presenting with subfertility Abdominal/renal imaging when a right-sided, isolated, or non-reducing varicocele suggests a retroperitoneal cause A varicocele is an abnormal dilatation of the pampiniform venous plexus, classically described as feeling like a bag of worms on scrotal palpation The great majority occur on the left side, attributed to the left testicular vein draining at a right angle into the left renal vein and having a longer course It is more prominent on standing and with Valsalva and typically decompresses on lying down; a varicocele that does not empty when supine should raise concern for a retroperitoneal or renal mass A sudden new right-sided or non-reducing varicocele in an older patient warrants imaging to exclude a renal tumour obstructing venous drainage Clinical grading ranges from subclinical (detectable only on imaging) to visible through the scrotal skin, with intermediate grades palpable with or without Valsalva Varicoceles are a common and potentially reversible factor in male subfertility, associated with impaired sperm count, motility, and morphology, and sometimes with testicular growth arrest in adolescents Most are asymptomatic or cause a dull dragging ache; treatment (surgical varicocelectomy or radiological embolisation) is considered for pain, infertility with abnormal semen analysis, or testicular growth failure in adolescents Semen analysis and assessment of testicular volume guide management decisions in the fertility and adolescent contexts New-onset right-sided or non-decompressing varicocele suggesting a renal or retroperitoneal tumour Progressive ipsilateral testicular atrophy or growth arrest in an adolescent Acute painful scrotal swelling raising alternative diagnoses that require exclusion Significant deterioration in semen parameters in a man seeking fertility Failing to examine the patient standing and with Valsalva, missing a lower-grade varicocele Overlooking a secondary varicocele from a renal tumour in an isolated right-sided or non-reducible case Recommending repair for asymptomatic subclinical varicoceles without a clear indication Neglecting testicular volume assessment in adolescents Attributing subfertility solely to the varicocele without full evaluation of both partners A varicocele results from incompetent or absent valves in the internal spermatic (testicular) veins, leading to retrograde flow and dilatation of the pampiniform plexus. The predominance on the left relates to the anatomy of left testicular venous drainage into the left renal vein at a right angle with a longer, higher-pressure course. The resulting venous stasis is thought to impair testicular function through elevated scrotal temperature, venous hypertension, hypoxia, and reflux of adrenal or renal metabolites, contributing to defective spermatogenesis and, in some cases, testicular atrophy. Many varicoceles are asymptomatic and require no intervention; when treated for pain, subfertility, or adolescent growth arrest, repair often improves semen parameters and testicular growth, though not all men achieve improved fertility.

identify incompetent junctions and perforators Ankle-brachial pressure index before compression therapy to exclude significant arterial disease Assessment for prior deep vein thrombosis and deep venous patency Photographs or clinical grading (e.g. CEAP classification) to document severity Present as dilated, tortuous, superficial leg veins, often with aching, heaviness, itching, or swelling that worsens with prolonged standing and eases on elevation Most arise from primary valvular incompetence in the great or small saphenous systems, allowing reflux and venous hypertension Assessment includes standing inspection and duplex ultrasound to map the sites of reflux and incompetent junctions, which has largely replaced the older tourniquet tests Chronic venous hypertension produces skin changes: haemosiderin pigmentation, venous eczema, lipodermatosclerosis, atrophie blanche, and ultimately venous ulceration around the gaiter area Conservative measures include graduated compression stockings, weight loss, exercise, and leg elevation Interventional options include endovenous thermal ablation (laser or radiofrequency), foam sclerotherapy, and conventional surgery (ligation and stripping) Secondary varicose veins may follow deep vein thrombosis or pelvic outflow obstruction, so a history of DVT and signs of deep venous disease should be sought Sudden bleeding from a ruptured varicosity is controlled by elevation and direct compression, not by a tourniquet Torrential haemorrhage from a ruptured surface varicosity requiring elevation and direct pressure Non-healing venous ulcer, especially with atypical features suggesting malignant change (Marjolin's ulcer) Signs of deep vein thrombosis or coexisting significant arterial disease before compression Rapidly progressive skin changes or superficial thrombophlebitis extending toward the saphenofemoral junction Applying compression without first excluding significant arterial disease Overlooking underlying deep venous disease or previous DVT causing secondary varicosities Attempting to control variceal bleeding with a tourniquet rather than elevation and compression Missing malignant change in a chronic non-healing venous ulcer Varicose veins develop when incompetent valves in the superficial venous system, or at the saphenofemoral or saphenopopliteal junctions, permit reflux of blood back down the leg. The resulting venous hypertension dilates and elongates the superficial veins, making them tortuous. Sustained ambulatory venous hypertension is transmitted to the skin microcirculation, causing capillary leakage, fibrin deposition, inflammation, and progressive skin changes that culminate in venous ulceration. Contributing factors include heredity, prolonged standing, pregnancy, obesity, and previous deep vein thrombosis, the last causing secondary varicosities through deep venous obstruction or valvular damage. Symptoms and skin changes usually improve with compression and, where appropriate, ablation or surgery, and venous ulcers can heal with effective compression, but recurrence of varicosities and ulcers is common, particularly with deep venous disease or poor compliance.

Variegate porphyria — VP, protoporphyrinogen oxidase deficiency, PPOX deficiency, porphyria variegata, South African genetic porphyria Porphyria cutanea tarda (identical skin picture but no acute attacks) Hereditary coproporphyria (the other mixed acute porphyria) Acute intermittent porphyria during a neurovisceral attack Pseudoporphyria from drugs or renal dialysis Epidermolysis bullosa acquisita and other subepidermal blistering disorders Surgical acute abdomen during an attack Plasma fluorescence scanning showing the characteristic emission peak diagnostic of variegate porphyria Faecal porphyrin profile (protoporphyrin and coproporphyrin) Urinary ALA and PBG during symptomatic attacks Molecular genetic testing of the PPOX gene for confirmation and family screening Skin biopsy in atypical cases to confirm subepidermal bullae and exclude mimics Serum sodium and renal function during acute attacks Autosomal dominant deficiency of protoporphyrinogen oxidase, the penultimate enzyme of haem biosynthesis, notably prevalent in the Afrikaner population owing to a founder mutation A mixed porphyria that can cause both acute neurovisceral attacks (as in acute intermittent porphyria) and chronic photocutaneous skin fragility Skin lesions comprise blistering, erosions, milia and fragility on sun-exposed areas, clinically indistinguishable from porphyria cutanea tarda During acute attacks urinary ALA and PBG rise, but the discriminating feature is a characteristic plasma fluorescence emission peak around the high 620s nanometre range Faecal porphyrin analysis typically shows raised protoporphyrin and coproporphyrin, helping distinguish it from other acute porphyrias Acute attacks share the same drug, fasting and hormonal triggers as acute intermittent porphyria and are managed similarly with trigger removal, glucose loading and intravenous haem Cutaneous disease is managed largely by sun protection and avoidance of skin trauma rather than by the measures effective in porphyria cutanea tarda Progressive motor neuropathy or respiratory compromise during an acute attack Seizures with hyponatraemia during an attack Severe photocutaneous ulceration with secondary infection Exposure to a known porphyrinogenic drug in a symptomatic patient Mistaking the skin disease for porphyria cutanea tarda and applying inappropriate therapy Prescribing porphyrinogenic drugs that precipitate acute attacks Relying on urinary studies alone and missing the diagnosis between attacks when they may be near normal Failing to protect skin from sunlight and trauma Not screening at-risk relatives, particularly in founder populations Variegate porphyria arises from reduced activity of protoporphyrinogen oxidase, the seventh enzyme of the haem pathway, which oxidises protoporphyrinogen to protoporphyrin. Deficiency causes accumulation of protoporphyrinogen and back-up of upstream intermediates. The photoreactive porphyrins deposited in the skin generate reactive oxygen species on light exposure, causing the blistering photodermatosis, while induction of hepatic ALA synthase during metabolic stress raises the neurotoxic precursors ALA and PBG that drive acute neurovisceral attacks. The dual accumulation explains the mixed acute and cutaneous phenotype. Cutaneous manifestations tend to persist while acute attacks are usually preventable with trigger avoidance; most patients maintain a good quality of life, though severe attacks carry the same neurological risks as other acute porphyrias.

Vasa praevia — vasa previa, unprotected fetal vessels over the cervical os Placenta praevia Placental abruption Bloody show of labour Marginal placental bleeding Local maternal genital tract bleeding from a cervical or vaginal lesion A maternal rather than fetal source of intrapartum bleeding Transvaginal ultrasound with colour Doppler to identify vessels crossing or lying near the internal os Pulsed-wave Doppler to confirm a fetal heart rate waveform within the aberrant vessels Assessment of cord insertion site and placental morphology, including a bilobed or succenturiate lobe, at the routine anomaly scan Cardiotocography to detect fetal compromise such as a sinusoidal pattern or bradycardia Bedside testing to distinguish fetal from maternal blood, such as an alkali-denaturation (Apt) or Kleihauer test, though delivery should not await results Maternal full blood count and group-and-save or crossmatch Vasa praevia describes fetal blood vessels coursing through the membranes across or in close proximity to the internal cervical os, unsupported by placental tissue or the umbilical cord Two principal types are recognised: type 1, associated with a velamentous cord insertion, and type 2, in which vessels run between the lobes of a bilobed or succenturiate-lobed placenta The danger is rupture of these unprotected vessels when the membranes rupture, causing rapid fetal exsanguination; because the blood lost is fetal, even a modest volume is life-threatening to the baby The classic intrapartum presentation is painless vaginal bleeding at the time of membrane rupture accompanied by acute fetal heart rate abnormalities such as a sinusoidal trace or bradycardia Antenatal diagnosis by transvaginal ultrasound with colour and pulsed-wave Doppler, demonstrating fetal-origin vessels over the os, transforms the prognosis by allowing planned delivery before labour Risk factors include velamentous cord insertion, a bilobed or succenturiate-lobed placenta, a low-lying placenta or resolved praevia, multiple pregnancy, and conception by assisted reproduction Management of confirmed vasa praevia is planned hospital admission in the third trimester, corticosteroids for lung maturity, and elective caesarean section before the onset of labour and before the membranes rupture When vasa praevia is unrecognised and a vessel ruptures, the priority is immediate delivery and neonatal resuscitation with volume replacement, as the newborn may require urgent transfusion Vaginal bleeding coinciding with rupture of the membranes Sinusoidal or profoundly abnormal fetal heart rate pattern Acute fetal bradycardia after spontaneous or artificial rupture of the membranes Known velamentous cord insertion or succenturiate lobe presenting undiagnosed in labour Rapidly deteriorating fetal condition with only a modest volume of fresh vaginal blood Attributing intrapartum bleeding to a maternal cause and delaying delivery while fetal blood is being lost Rupturing membranes without first palpating for pulsating vessels when vasa praevia is possible Failing to identify a velamentous cord insertion or a succenturiate lobe on antenatal scanning Not re-imaging a low-lying placenta or resolved praevia for associated vasa praevia Under-preparing for immediate neonatal resuscitation and transfusion at delivery Normally the umbilical vessels insert centrally into the placental mass and are cushioned by Wharton's jelly, while the fetal chorionic vessels are protected by surrounding placenta. In vasa praevia this protection is lost: either the cord inserts into the membranes (velamentous insertion) with vessels traversing the membranes before reaching the placenta, or vessels bridge between separate placental lobes. When these membranous vessels overlie the internal os they lie below the presenting part and across the path of delivery, without protective Wharton's jelly, and are vulnerable both to compression by the presenting part and, critically, to laceration when the overlying membranes rupture spontaneously or artificially. Rupture opens the low-volume fetal circulation directly, so brisk fetal haemorrhage and exsanguination can occur within minutes. With antenatal diagnosis and elective caesarean before labour, perinatal survival is excellent. When the diagnosis is first made after vessel rupture, perinatal mortality is high owing to the speed of fetal exsanguination.
