resuscitation and transfusion capability In vasa praevia foetal umbilical vessels traverse the free membranes over or near the internal os without the protection of Wharton's jelly or placental tissue, typically because the cord inserts into the membranes (velamentous insertion) or bridges accessory placental lobes. These exposed vessels are vulnerable to compression by the presenting part and, critically, to laceration when the membranes rupture spontaneously or artificially. Because the circulating blood is foetal and the foetal blood volume is small, even modest bleeding can cause rapid foetal hypovolaemia, exsanguination, and death within minutes. With antenatal diagnosis, planned admission, and elective caesarean before labour, foetal survival is very high. Undiagnosed vasa praevia presenting with membrane rupture and foetal haemorrhage carries a high risk of rapid foetal death despite emergency intervention.

Vascular Dementia — vascular cognitive impairment, multi-infarct dementia Alzheimer's disease (most common dementia; mixed AD-vascular pathology very common) Dementia with Lewy bodies / PDD spectrum Frontotemporal dementia Limbic-predominant age-related TDP-43 encephalopathy (LATE) Normal pressure hydrocephalus Delirium Brain MRI is the mainstay for detection and subtyping of cerebrovascular disease; should include FLAIR, diffusion-weighted, and T2*-weighted sequences to detect large and small chronic infarcts, acute microinfarcts, microbleeds, and white matter hyperintensities (p.3491) Diffusion tensor MRI (e.g., peak width of skeletonized mean diffusivity, PSMD) detects white matter disconnection (largely research use) (p.3490) Vessel imaging (CT or MR angiography) is not required for initial cognitive evaluation but may help determine the cause of identified macroscopic infarcts (p.3491) Screening for atrial fibrillation in individuals with asymptomatic infarcts; prolonged cardiac monitoring for embolic-appearing infarcts (p.3491) Genetic testing for hereditary VCID (CADASIL, hereditary cerebral amyloid angiopathy) when young onset, positive family history, or suggestive imaging—otherwise unnecessary (p.3491) Alzheimer's disease (frequently coexists as mixed dementia—a key pitfall) Normal pressure hydrocephalus (shares gait disturbance) Delirium (prominent attention/executive deficits) Traditionally defined as dementia due primarily to one or more symptomatic strokes; ranked the second most frequent cause of dementia after Alzheimer's disease, and especially common where vascular risk factors are undertreated (p.3489). The concept has been broadened to vascular contributions to cognitive impairment and dementia (VCID), reflecting that cerebrovascular pathology is highly prevalent in the elderly and contributes to cognitive impairment, whether in isolation or—more commonly—combined with neurodegenerative processes (p.3489). Clinical evaluation focuses on identifying vascular risk factors (hypertension, diabetes mellitus, dyslipidemia, tobacco use, atrial fibrillation, coronary artery disease, peripheral vascular disease), prior stroke/TIA, and family history of early stroke or vascular disease (p.3491). Although stepwise progression and deficits such as loss of executive function are particularly suggestive, most individuals with VCID follow the more typical pattern of gradual progression of impaired episodic memory (p.3491). Patients often show a mixture of executive and visuospatial deficits with prominent psychomotor slowing, and may present with psychiatric symptoms such as depression, anxiety, delusions, disinhibition, or apathy (p.196). Gait disturbance is common in vascular dementia (as well as PD/DLB and NPH) (p.195). Strategic single infarcts in locations such as thalamus, medial temporal cortex, anterior corpus callosum, or dominant-side angular gyrus can sufficiently impair episodic memory and function to meet memory-based dementia criteria (p.3489). At least some cognitive impairment is present in approximately half of stroke survivors and increases with longer follow-up; even patients with good cognitive recovery show accelerated poststroke cognitive decline (p.3489). One late-onset community autopsy cohort attributed 25% of dementia risk to cerebrovascular disease (vs 39% Alzheimer's, 17% LATE, 12% Lewy body), and most late-onset dementia involves multiple coexisting pathologies (p.195). Young onset, positive family history, or suggestive neuroimaging—consider hereditary forms such as CADASIL or hereditary cerebral amyloid angiopathy (p.3491) Lobar intracerebral hemorrhage or convexity subarachnoid blood, suggesting cerebral amyloid angiopathy (p.3490) Rapid progression with motor rigidity and myoclonus suggests CJD rather than vascular dementia (p.195) Mixed dementia is the rule rather than the exception—cerebrovascular disease commonly co-occurs with Alzheimer's and other neurodegenerative pathologies, so attributing cognitive impairment to a single etiology is often incorrect (p.3489). Most individuals with VCID do not show classic stepwise decline but instead a gradual progression of impaired episodic memory resembling Alzheimer's (p.3491). White matter hyperintensities are an almost ubiquitous, nonspecific feature of aging (gliosis, demyelination, or increased water content) and should not be over-interpreted (p.3490). Many chronic lacunar infarcts and microinfarcts cannot be readily identified on routine imaging, so absence of visible lesions does not exclude small-vessel disease (p.3490). Vascular dementia results from the cumulative impact of cerebrovascular disease on age-related cognitive decline. Symptomatic strokes (ischemic or hemorrhagic) produce irreversible injury whose cognitive effect depends on size and location. Cerebral small-vessel disease—principally arteriolosclerosis (thickening of arterioles from plasma-protein infiltration; risk factors age, hypertension, diabetes; centered on deep penetrating territories such as thalamus, basal ganglia, brainstem) and cerebral amyloid angiopathy (beta-amyloid deposition in walls of small cortical arteries/arterioles/capillaries; main risk factor advancing age; favoring lobar cortex and subcortical white matter)—is often clinically asymptomatic and produces lacunar infarcts, microinfarcts, cerebral microbleeds, and white matter hyperintensities. These small distributed injuries disconnect nodes within distributed brain networks. Mixed pathology is the rule: cerebrovascular lesions frequently co-occur with neurodegenerative disease (most commonly Alzheimer's), producing greater impairment than either mechanism alone, possibly via loss of blood-brain barrier integrity and impaired perivascular clearance of beta-amyloid (p.3489-3491). Stroke survivors show accelerated poststroke cognitive decline even after good initial recovery; in one longitudinal study trajectory shifted from a prestroke cognitive gain to poststroke loss. Multiple strokes and larger infarcted volumes raise the likelihood of poststroke cognitive dysfunction. Epidemiologic data show declining age-adjusted dementia incidence paralleling improved hypertension control and stroke prevention, and the SPRINT-MIND trial showed intensive systolic blood pressure lowering reduced rates of mild cognitive impairment and combined MCI/probable dementia, underscoring VCID as a target for prevention (p.3489).

Overlooking oesophageal compression as a cause of feeding difficulty Failing to recognise an associated pulmonary artery sling and complete tracheal rings Assuming surgery immediately resolves all symptoms when tracheomalacia persists Vascular rings arise from abnormal regression or persistence of the paired embryonic aortic arches, producing vascular structures that completely or partially encircle the trachea and oesophagus. A double aortic arch forms a complete ring as both arches persist, while a right aortic arch with an aberrant left subclavian artery and a left arterial ligament completes a ring posteriorly. These structures exert extrinsic pressure on the airway and oesophagus, causing airflow obstruction, secondary tracheomalacia and impaired swallowing. A pulmonary artery sling, though strictly a partial ring, compresses the trachea as the anomalous left pulmonary artery courses between trachea and oesophagus and is frequently accompanied by complete cartilaginous tracheal rings that intrinsically narrow the airway. Surgical division of a symptomatic ring generally relieves compression with excellent long-term results, though residual tracheomalacia can cause persistent symptoms; associated complete tracheal rings carry higher risk.

The first step in suspected vasculitis is to exclude conditions that mimic it - especially infections - particularly before starting empirical immunosuppression in a deteriorating patient (Harrison 22e p.2937). Definitive diagnosis usually rests on biopsy of clinically involved tissue; 'blind' biopsy of organs with no clinical evidence of involvement has very low yield and should be avoided. Arteriography is used when PAN, Takayasu, or primary CNS vasculitis is suspected (Harrison 22e p.2937-2938). ANCA-associated vasculitides (GPA, MPA, EGPA) share small-vessel involvement and ANCA positivity but have distinct clinical phenotypes and should be regarded as separate entities (Harrison 22e p.2937). cANCA targets proteinase-3 (PR3) - present in >90% of active GPA; pANCA targets myeloperoxidase (MPO) - only anti-MPO antibodies are convincingly linked to vasculitis (MPA, EGPA, GPA, isolated necrotizing crescentic GN) (Harrison 22e p.2937). A pANCA pattern NOT due to anti-MPO can occur in nonvasculitic conditions: rheumatic/nonrheumatic autoimmune disease, inflammatory bowel disease, certain drugs, and infections including endocarditis and bacterial airway infection in cystic fibrosis (Harrison 22e p.2937). ANCA titres do not reliably track disease activity - GPA can be active despite negative ANCA, titres correlate poorly with activity, and patients in remission may keep high ANCA for years (Harrison 22e p.2937, p.2941). Predictive value of a positive ANCA in GPA is ~90% with active glomerulonephritis but falls to 30-60% in sinus/lung disease without renal involvement; tissue biopsy is then needed to exclude infection or malignancy that may give a false-positive ANCA (Harrison 22e p.2941). In GPA the renal lesion is a pauci-immune (no immune-complex deposition) focal segmental glomerulitis that can evolve into rapidly progressive crescentic glomerulonephritis (Harrison 22e p.2939-2940). Saddle-nose deformity (from nasal septal perforation) and subglottic stenosis (~16% of GPA, may cause severe airway obstruction) are characteristic upper-airway sequelae of GPA (Harrison 22e p.2940). Mononeuritis multiplex is a recurring vasculitic clue - common in EGPA (up to ~72%) and PAN (~51%), and also seen in GPA and MPA (Harrison 22e p.2940, p.2943, p.2944). EGPA (Churg-Strauss) requires asthma, peripheral blood eosinophilia (>1000 cells/uL in >80%), and clinical features of vasculitis; eosinophilic tissue infiltration and extravascular granulomas are characteristic (Harrison 22e p.2943-2944). Cardiac involvement (myocarditis, pericarditis, coronary vasculitis) is the leading cause of death in EGPA, accounting for ~39% of mortality; echocardiography is advised in all newly diagnosed patients (Harrison 22e p.2943-2944). PAN does NOT involve pulmonary arteries and does NOT cause glomerulonephritis, granuloma, or significant eosinophilia; venule involvement points away from PAN and toward microscopic polyangiitis (Harrison 22e p.2944). PAN classically causes microaneurysms of small- and medium-sized renal, hepatic, and visceral arteries; catheter-directed dye arteriography (MR/CT lack resolution) can be diagnostic when accessible tissue is unavailable (Harrison 22e p.2944-2945). Giant cell arteritis occurs almost exclusively in those over 50; jaw/tongue claudication, scalp tenderness, and headache precede the dreaded complication of ischemic optic neuropathy with sudden blindness - therapy should not be delayed for diagnostic testing (Harrison 22e p.2945). GCA and polymyalgia rheumatica are considered spectrums of one disease - PMR occurs in 40-50% of GCA, and 10-20% of isolated PMR later develop GCA (Harrison 22e p.2945). Takayasu arteritis should be strongly suspected in a young woman with diminished/absent peripheral pulses, an inter-arm blood pressure discrepancy, or arterial bruits (Harrison 22e p.2946-2947). Hemoptysis may be the first sign of alveolar haemorrhage in MPA (~12%); upper-airway disease and pulmonary nodules are atypical for MPA and instead suggest GPA (Harrison 22e p.2942). GPA carries an increased risk of venous thrombotic events (DVT/PE); maintain a heightened awareness even though routine anticoagulation is not recommended (Harrison 22e p.2940). Active glomerulonephritis is always classed as severe disease even with normal renal function (Harrison 22e p.2941) Alveolar/pulmonary haemorrhage - severe manifestation of GPA/MPA; hemoptysis may be the first symptom of alveolar haemorrhage in MPA (Harrison 22e p.2941, p.2942) Visual symptoms in a patient over 50 with headache - ischemic optic neuropathy in GCA can cause sudden, irreversible blindness; do not delay treatment for diagnostic workup (Harrison 22e p.2945, p.2946) Rapidly progressive glomerulonephritis with rising creatinine in ANCA-associated vasculitis (Harrison 22e p.2939-2940, p.2942) Jaw/tongue claudication, scalp tenderness, or a tender/nodular temporal artery - cranial ischaemic features of GCA (Harrison 22e p.2945) Inter-arm blood pressure discrepancy, absent pulses, or bruits in a young woman - suggests Takayasu large-vessel involvement (Harrison 22e p.2947) Bowel infarction/perforation and GI bleeding in PAN - leading causes of death (Harrison 22e p.2944-2945) Cardiac involvement in EGPA - the chief cause of death (Harrison 22e p.2944) Signs of deep-vein thrombosis or pulmonary embolism in GPA given the increased venous thrombotic risk (Harrison 22e p.2940) Treating a rise in ANCA titre as a relapse - only ~43% relapse within 1 year of an ANCA increase, so a rising ANCA alone should not prompt reinstitution or escalation of immunosuppression (Harrison 22e p.2941). Relying on ANCA to diagnose vasculitis in sinus/lung disease without renal involvement, where positive predictive value is only 30-60% and biopsy is needed to exclude infection/malignancy with false-positive ANCA (Harrison 22e p.2941). Performing 'blind' biopsies of clinically uninvolved organs - yield is very low (Harrison 22e p.2937). Starting immunosuppression before excluding infectious mimics, especially in a rapidly deteriorating patient (Harrison 22e p.2937). Irradiating upper-airway lesions assuming GPA when the diagnosis is actually NK/T-cell lymphoma - GPA airway lesions should never be irradiated (Harrison 22e p.2941). Overlooking cocaine/levamisole-induced midline destruction, which can produce vasculitis-mimicking serology (anti-elastase ANCA) and granulocytopenia (Harrison 22e p.2941). Using CRP/ESR to monitor disease activity or assess infection in GCA patients on IL-6 inhibitors, which suppress these acute-phase reactants (Harrison 22e p.2946). Attributing every minor ESR/CRP rise during a GCA prednisone taper to a flare - small increases may not reflect arteritis, and can also be caused by infection (Harrison 22e p.2946). Mislabelling a necrotizing vasculitis with venule involvement as PAN - venule involvement indicates microscopic polyangiitis, not PAN (Harrison 22e p.2944). Missing DADA2 (adenosine deaminase 2 deficiency) in early-onset PAN-like vasculitis, which responds to TNF inhibitors rather than standard PAN therapy (Harrison 22e p.2944). Vasculitis is inflammation of and damage to blood vessel walls, usually compromising the lumen and causing ischaemia of supplied tissues; any size, type, or location of vessel may be affected, and disease may be primary/single-organ or secondary to another illness. Most syndromes are at least partly immune-mediated through three broad mechanisms (Harrison 22e p.2936): (1) Immune-complex formation/deposition (e.g., IgA vasculitis, lupus vasculitis, serum sickness, hepatitis-B-associated vasculitis, hepatitis-C cryoglobulinaemic vasculitis) - resembling serum sickness, complexes deposit in vessel walls, activate complement (notably C5a, chemotactic for neutrophils), and neutrophils infiltrate and release enzymes that damage the wall. (2) ANCA production (GPA, MPA, EGPA) - when neutrophils/monocytes are primed by TNF-alpha, IL-1, or alternative-complement activation, PR3 and MPO translocate to the cell membrane where ANCA can engage them, triggering degranulation, reactive oxygen species, endothelial injury, and release of IL-1/IL-8. (3) Pathogenic T-lymphocyte responses and granuloma formation (GCA, Takayasu, GPA, EGPA) - cytokine (IFN-gamma) activated endothelium expresses HLA class II and interacts with CD4+ T cells, with IL-1/TNF-alpha inducing adhesion molecules (ELAM-1, VCAM-1). The 1992/2012 Chapel Hill Consensus nomenclature underpins the classification of these syndromes by predominant vessel size (Harrison 22e p.2936, p.2942). Untreated GPA was historically fatal within months; with cyclophosphamide-based therapy >90% improve, ~75% achieve complete remission, and 5-year survival exceeds 80%, but 50-70% of remissions later relapse and many accrue irreversible damage (renal insufficiency, hearing loss, subglottic stenosis, saddle-nose deformity, chronic sinus dysfunction) (Harrison 22e p.2941). Treated MPA has a ~74% 5-year survival, with deaths from alveolar haemorrhage or GI/cardiac/renal disease, and relapse in at least ~34% (Harrison 22e p.2942). Untreated EGPA has a ~25% 5-year survival; treated, prognosis is favourable (~72% at 78 months), but myocardial involvement causes ~39% of deaths (Harrison 22e p.2944). Untreated PAN has a poor 5-year survival of 10-20% (deaths from GI and cardiovascular causes); prednisone plus cyclophosphamide markedly improves survival, with relapse in ~10-20% (Harrison 22e p.2944-2945). In GCA acute death is uncommon, but patients face late mortality from aortic aneurysm rupture/dissection (18x more likely to develop thoracic aortic aneurysm than the general population) (Harrison 22e p.2946). Takayasu outcomes vary widely (overall survival >=94% in some North American series; 5-year mortality 0-35% elsewhere), and the disease is usually chronic and relapsing (Harrison 22e p.2947). IgA vasculitis has an excellent prognosis with rare mortality and only 1-5% of children progressing to end-stage renal disease (Harrison 22e p.2948). Vasculitides are classified by predominant vessel size per the Chapel Hill Consensus nomenclature (Harrison 22e p.2936, p.2942): LARGE-VESSEL (giant cell/temporal arteritis, Takayasu arteritis); MEDIUM-VESSEL (polyarteritis nodosa, Kawasaki disease); SMALL-VESSEL, which splits into ANCA-associated (GPA, MPA, EGPA) and immune-complex (IgA vasculitis/Henoch-Schonlein, cryoglobulinaemic vasculitis). The chapter also separates PRIMARY syndromes from SECONDARY vasculitis (associated with probable etiology e.g. drug-induced, hepatitis-B/C-related, cancer-associated; or with systemic disease e.g. lupus, rheumatoid, sarcoid vasculitis), and single-organ vasculitis (cutaneous leukocytoclastic angiitis, cutaneous arteritis, primary CNS vasculitis, isolated aortitis) (Harrison 22e p.2936). For management stratification, ANCA-associated vasculitis is divided into SEVERE (life- or organ-threatening; e.g., alveolar haemorrhage, and active glomerulonephritis is severe even with normal renal function) versus NONSEVERE/limited disease - severity depends on both extent and the specific organ involved (e.g., nodular pulmonary disease without respiratory compromise is nonsevere, whereas alveolar haemorrhage is severe) (Harrison 22e p.2941).

Vasovagal / orthostatic syncope — Lying/standing BP ECG (exclude arrhythmia) Exertional or cardiac syncope needs cardiac workup Generalized and partial/partial-complex seizures (with secondary generalization, usually preceded by an aura such as an unpleasant smell, fear, anxiety, or abdominal/visceral sensation). Autonomic seizures (autonomic epilepsy), whose cardiovascular, GI, pulmonary, urogenital, pupillary, and cutaneous manifestations mimic syncopal prodrome; accompanying non-autonomic auras help distinguish them. Hypoglycemia, typically in insulin-treated type 1 or type 2 diabetes (tremor, palpitations, anxiety, diaphoresis, hunger, paresthesias; hunger is not a typical syncope prodrome). Cataplexy (abrupt loss of muscle tone triggered by strong emotion such as laughter or anger; consciousness is preserved, lasts 30 s to 2 min, no prodrome; occurs in 60-75% of narcolepsy). Vertebrobasilar ischemia and hypoxemia as other causes of transient loss of consciousness. Falls due to vestibular dysfunction, cerebellar disease, extrapyramidal/gait disorders, and falls with head trauma (especially difficult in patients with dementia and repeated falls). Psychogenic apparent loss of consciousness from psychiatric disorders (generalized anxiety, panic disorder, major depression, somatization), suggested by frequent fainting without prodrome and rare injury despite numerous falls, with no significant hemodynamic change. 12-lead ECG when arrhythmia or underlying cardiac disease is suspected; look for brady-/tachyarrhythmias, AV block, acute or old myocardial ischemia/infarction, long QT, and bundle branch block. Supine and standing (3 min) blood pressure and heart rate to detect orthostatic hypotension. Tilt-table testing (autonomic testing) to distinguish autonomic-failure orthostatic hypotension from the hypotensive-bradycardic response of neurally mediated syncope, and to identify immediate or delayed orthostatic hypotension; may also reproduce psychogenic syncope when symptoms occur without hemodynamic change. Autonomic function testing in specialized centers: heart rate variability to deep breathing and Valsalva (parasympathetic), thermoregulatory sweat test and quantitative sudomotor axon reflex test (sympathetic cholinergic), and BP response to Valsalva/tilt (sympathetic adrenergic). Carotid sinus massage (under continuous ECG and BP monitoring) for suspected carotid sinus syncope and in patients >40 years with recurrent unexplained syncope; avoid with carotid bruits, plaque, or stenosis. Inpatient ECG monitoring for high arrhythmia risk; ambulatory Holter monitoring for frequent (near-daily) episodes; external or implantable loop recorders for less frequent episodes (monitor for at least twice the interspell interval). Echocardiography for patients with cardiac history or abnormal exam/ECG (may reveal aortic stenosis, hypertrophic cardiomyopathy, cardiac tumors, aortic dissection, pericardial tamponade; also stratifies sudden-death risk by ejection fraction). Treadmill exercise testing with ECG and BP monitoring for syncope during or shortly after exercise. Invasive electrophysiologic studies (low sensitivity/specificity, rarely used) only when pretest probability is high in structural heart disease with ECG abnormalities. Baseline blood tests are rarely helpful and should be reserved for suspected specific disorders (e.g., myocardial infarction, anemia, secondary autonomic failure); psychiatric screening for recurrent unexplained syncope. Syncope is a transient, self-limited loss of consciousness from acute global cerebral hypoperfusion, with rapid onset, brief duration, and spontaneous complete recovery; reorientation is almost immediate after a syncopal event. Causes fall into three categories: neurally mediated (reflex/vasovagal) syncope, orthostatic hypotension, and cardiac syncope; clinical features, mechanisms, and prognosis differ markedly among them. Neurally mediated syncope is the most common cause overall in population-based studies and accounts for the vast majority of syncope in the young (peak incidence ~age 15); incidence is higher in women, and a first-degree family history is common in young patients. Vasovagal syncope (the common faint) is provoked by intense emotion, pain, the sight of blood, venipuncture, and/or orthostatic stress; situational reflex syncopes have specific localized triggers (cough, micturition, swallow, defecation, carotid sinus pressure). Premonitory (prodromal) features of autonomic activation in neurally mediated syncope include diaphoresis, pallor, palpitations, nausea, lightheadedness, hyperventilation, and yawning. A functioning autonomic nervous system is required to develop neurally mediated syncope, in contrast to syncope from autonomic failure (orthostatic hypotension). Neurally mediated syncope can be subdivided by efferent pathway: vasodepressor (sympathetic vasoconstrictor failure), cardioinhibitory (bradycardia/asystole from vagal outflow), or mixed. Orthostatic hypotension is defined as a fall in systolic BP of at least 20 mmHg or diastolic BP of at least 10 mmHg within 3 min of standing or head-up tilt; supine and standing BP/HR at 3 min should be measured in every initial evaluation. Initial clinical assessment plus ECG identifies a cause in about 50% of patients and stratifies cardiac mortality risk. A clinically meaningful syncope usually corresponds to a fall in systolic BP to roughly 50 mmHg or lower; cessation of cerebral blood flow for 6-8 s produces loss of consciousness. Syncope during exertion, or while seated or supine. Sudden onset of palpitations immediately followed by syncope, or palpitations at the time of syncope. Chest pain suggesting coronary ischemia, or features of congestive heart failure. Moderate or severe valvular or structural cardiac disease, or known severe coronary artery disease. ECG features: ischemia, history of ventricular arrhythmias, prolonged QT (>500 ms), repetitive SA block or sinus pauses, persistent sinus bradycardia, bi-/trifascicular block or QRS >=120 ms, atrial fibrillation, nonsustained VT, preexcitation, or a Brugada pattern. Family history of sudden death. New chest discomfort, abdominal pain, shortness of breath, or headache associated with the episode. Exam: unexplained systolic BP <90 mmHg, signs of GI hemorrhage, persistent bradycardia <40 beats/min, or an undiagnosed systolic murmur. Convulsive syncope mimics seizure: myoclonic and other movements occur in up to ~90% of syncopal episodes, but syncope-related jerks are typically arrhythmic, multifocal/generalized, and brief (<30 s), with mild flexor/extensor posturing; EEG seizure discharges are absent during syncope. Distinguishing features from seizure: seizure loss of consciousness usually lasts >5 min with prolonged postictal drowsiness/disorientation, whereas reorientation after syncope is almost immediate; muscle aches are longer and more severe after seizures; seizures are rarely provoked by emotion or pain. Urinary incontinence can occur in both syncope and seizure and does not distinguish them; fecal incontinence is very rare in syncope and postictal confusion is rare after syncope. During neurally mediated syncope the eyes typically remain open and deviate upward with dilated pupils, and grunting/moaning/stertorous breathing may occur, which can be mistaken for a seizure. Orthostatic hypotension syncope is usually preceded by warning symptoms but may occur suddenly, mimicking a seizure or cardiac cause. Supine hypertension is common (>50%) in autonomic-failure orthostatic hypotension; treating one condition can unmask or worsen the other. Initial orthostatic hypotension (BP fall within 15 s, resolving by 45 s) and delayed orthostatic hypotension (beyond 3 min) can be missed by a single 3-min standing measurement; initial orthostatic hypotension does not represent autonomic failure. Standing pools 500-1000 mL of blood in the lower extremities, buttocks, and splanchnic circulation, reducing venous return, ventricular filling, cardiac output, and blood pressure. Normally baroreceptors in the carotid sinus and aortic arch trigger a compensatory reflex that raises sympathetic outflow and lowers vagal activity, increasing peripheral resistance, venous return, and cardiac output. In neurally mediated (reflex/vasovagal) syncope this reflex transiently fails: there is a paroxysmal shift in autonomic efferent activity with increased parasympathetic outflow plus sympathoinhibition, producing bradycardia, vasodilation/loss of vasoconstrictor tone (vasodepressor response), and reduced cardiac output. The resulting fall in systemic blood pressure drops cerebral blood flow below the limits of autoregulation, causing transient global cerebral hypoperfusion and loss of consciousness. Multiple afferent triggers (orthostatic stress, carotid sinus, gastrointestinal tract, bladder) converge on the central autonomic network in the medulla. Hyperventilation-induced hypocarbia (cerebral vasoconstriction) and raised intrathoracic pressure (impaired venous return) contribute to many situational reflex syncopes. By contrast, orthostatic hypotension reflects chronic impairment of these homeostatic reflexes (autonomic failure), and cardiac syncope results from arrhythmias or structural disease reducing cardiac output. Syncope of noncardiac and unexplained origin in younger individuals carries an excellent prognosis with unaffected life expectancy. In contrast, cardiac syncope (structural heart disease or primary arrhythmia) is associated with an increased risk of sudden cardiac death and overall mortality, and mortality is also increased with orthostatic hypotension related to age and comorbidities. Hospitalization and mortality risk are higher in older adults. Harrison categorizes syncope by mechanism rather than a graded severity score: (1) neurally mediated (reflex/vasovagal) syncope, (2) orthostatic hypotension, and (3) cardiac syncope. For risk stratification, Table 23-1 lists high-risk features indicating hospitalization or intensive evaluation (e.g., ischemic chest pain, heart failure, significant valvular/structural disease, ECG ischemia, ventricular arrhythmia history, QT >500 ms, SA block/sinus pauses, persistent sinus bradycardia, bi-/trifascicular block or QRS >=120 ms, atrial fibrillation, nonsustained VT, family history of sudden death, preexcitation, Brugada pattern, palpitations at syncope, syncope at rest or during exercise). Neurally mediated efferent subtypes are vasodepressor, cardioinhibitory, and mixed.

vein of galen malformation — vein of Galen aneurysmal malformation, VGAM structural congenital heart disease causing neonatal heart failure other cerebral or hepatic arteriovenous malformations persistent pulmonary hypertension of the newborn neonatal sepsis with cardiovascular collapse congenital hydrocephalus of other cause dural sinus malformation transfontanelle cranial ultrasound with Doppler brain MRI and MR angiography/venography catheter cerebral angiography to define feeding arteries and drainage echocardiography for shunt burden and pulmonary pressure B-type natriuretic peptide and cardiac biomarkers renal and hepatic function panels for multi-organ effect The vein of Galen aneurysmal malformation is a congenital arteriovenous fistula between choroidal or quadrigeminal arteries and the persistent embryonic median prosencephalic vein of Markowski, not a true aneurysm of the mature vein of Galen. The neonatal form presents with high-output cardiac failure that is disproportionate to any structural cardiac lesion, driven by the massive intracranial left-to-right shunt. A loud cranial bruit audible over the fontanelle or orbits in a neonate with heart failure is a valuable clue. Because so much combined ventricular output is diverted to the low-resistance shunt, there may be retrograde diastolic flow in the aorta and compromised systemic and coronary perfusion. Later infantile presentation is dominated by macrocephaly, hydrocephalus and developmental delay rather than cardiac failure. The melting brain phenomenon reflects chronic cerebral venous hypertension and hypoperfusion causing progressive parenchymal loss. Staged endovascular embolisation, timed to balance cardiac stability against neurological maturation, is the mainstay of treatment. A validated neonatal scoring system incorporating cardiac, cerebral, respiratory, hepatic and renal function guides whether to intervene urgently or defer. neonatal high-output cardiac failure refractory to medical therapy cranial bruit with rapidly increasing head circumference signs of raised intracranial pressure or seizures multi-organ dysfunction indicating systemic steal Attributing neonatal heart failure solely to a cardiac cause and omitting cranial imaging. Emergency embolisation of a neonate with irreversible brain injury when comfort care is more appropriate. Placing a ventriculoperitoneal shunt for hydrocephalus before addressing venous hypertension, which can worsen haemorrhage. Underestimating pulmonary hypertension and its impact on peri-procedural stability. Missing the diagnosis in an older infant presenting only with macrocephaly and delay. The malformation arises early in gestation from a persistent arteriovenous shunt draining into the median prosencephalic vein, the embryonic precursor that normally regresses as the internal cerebral veins form. Persistent high-flow shunting dilates this venous sac and diverts a large fraction of cardiac output through a low-resistance circuit. In the neonate this imposes a huge volume load, producing high-output biventricular failure, pulmonary hypertension and a diastolic steal that impairs systemic organ perfusion. Within the brain, impaired venous drainage raises cerebral venous pressure, causing hydrocephalus, impaired cerebrospinal fluid resorption, and chronic ischaemic injury with calcification and atrophy. Outcome depends on the severity of cardiac failure and the degree of established brain injury at presentation; neonates with intractable heart failure or extensive parenchymal loss fare poorly, whereas selected infants treated by staged embolisation can achieve good neurodevelopmental outcomes.

Venezuelan equine encephalitis — VEE, Venezuelan equine encephalitis virus infection, VEEV infection Dengue and other arboviral febrile illnesses Other equine encephalitides (eastern and western equine encephalitis) Influenza and nonspecific viral febrile illness Bacterial or viral meningoencephalitis Malaria in co-endemic regions Leptospirosis RT-PCR on blood for viral RNA during the acute viraemic phase Serum and cerebrospinal fluid IgM serology Full blood count often showing leucopenia Cerebrospinal fluid analysis when encephalitis is suspected Neuroimaging in patients with neurological features Testing to exclude co-endemic febrile illnesses such as dengue and malaria A mosquito-borne alphavirus of Central and South America and occasionally the southern United States, with rodents as enzootic reservoirs and epizootic strains amplified in horses In contrast to eastern equine encephalitis, most human infections cause a self-limiting acute febrile illness with headache, myalgia, and prostration rather than encephalitis A minority, particularly children, develop neuroinvasive disease with seizures and encephalitis; overall mortality is much lower than for eastern equine encephalitis Large epizootics in horses, which suffer high mortality and amplify the virus, typically precede and predict human outbreaks The virus is highly infectious as an aerosol, making it a recognised laboratory-acquired infection hazard requiring enhanced biosafety Management is supportive with no licensed specific antiviral; equine vaccination and mosquito control are central to outbreak prevention Diagnosis uses RT-PCR early and serology (IgM) thereafter, interpreted with the mosquito-exposure and equine-outbreak history Seizures or declining consciousness signalling neuroinvasive disease, especially in children Focal neurological deficits Signs of raised intracranial pressure Rapid clinical deterioration during an active equine epizootic Laboratory exposure raising concern for aerosol-acquired infection Assuming encephalitis is the usual presentation when most cases are a self-limiting febrile illness Neglecting aerosol biosafety precautions in the laboratory Overlooking the predictive value of concurrent equine outbreaks Failing to distinguish it from dengue and other co-endemic arboviral fevers Underestimating neuroinvasive risk in paediatric patients Venezuelan equine encephalitis virus circulates in enzootic cycles between rodents and mosquitoes, while epizootic variants replicate to high titres in horses that serve as amplifying hosts and drive outbreaks. Following a mosquito bite the virus replicates in lymphoid tissue and produces viraemia, giving rise to a systemic febrile illness. Neuroinvasion occurs in a subset of patients, with the virus infecting neurons and provoking inflammation, but central nervous system involvement is less frequent and generally less devastating than in eastern equine encephalitis. Its efficient aerosol infectivity accounts for the laboratory-acquired infection risk. Most patients recover fully from the febrile illness; neuroinvasive disease is uncommon and carries a lower fatality than eastern equine encephalitis, though children with encephalitis may have neurological sequelae.

aneurysm as the source in unexplained or recurrent pulmonary embolism Attempting to distinguish a venous from an arterial aneurysm on clinical grounds alone Venous aneurysms arise from a focal The cause is frequently congenital or idiopathic, although trauma, chronic inflammation, degenerative change and localised elevations in venous pressure are implicated. The dilated segment behaves as a low-flow reservoir in which turbulence and stasis promote the formation of mural thrombus; within a deep vein such as the popliteal, this thrombus can detach and embolise to the pulmonary circulation. A saccular morphology tends to carry a greater thrombogenic and embolic risk than a fusiform dilatation. Superficial and small venous aneurysms are generally benign and can be observed. Popliteal and other deep venous aneurysms carry a genuine risk of potentially fatal pulmonary embolism, but surgical repair has good long-term outcomes with a low rate of recurrence.

Venous malformation — VM, Cavernous haemangioma (obsolete term) Lymphatic malformation Infantile or congenital haemangioma Arteriovenous malformation Glomuvenous malformation Kaposiform haemangioendothelioma Soft-tissue tumour such as a haemangiopericytoma Doppler ultrasound showing compressible channels with monophasic slow or absent flow Contrast-enhanced MRI (T2-hyperintense lobulated lesion with phleboliths) Plain radiograph demonstrating phleboliths Coagulation screen including D-dimer and fibrinogen Direct phlebography at the time of sclerotherapy Genetic testing (TEK, PIK3CA) in selected or familial cases Slow-flow malformation of dysplastic venous channels present at birth, though sometimes only apparent later; grows proportionately and does not involute. Soft, compressible, blue-purple lesion that swells with dependency, Valsalva or crying and empties on compression or elevation. Phleboliths (calcified thrombi) are pathognomonic and a common cause of localised pain. Sporadic lesions commonly harbour somatic TIE2 (TEK) mutations; PIK3CA mutations also occur, and familial mucocutaneous forms are TEK-related. Localised intravascular coagulopathy with raised D-dimer and low fibrinogen is common and can worsen with intervention or in extensive lesions. Sclerotherapy is first-line for most symptomatic lesions; surgery is reserved for well-localised disease. Glomuvenous malformations (glomulin gene) are firmer, more nodular and painful on compression, forming a distinct subtype. MRI best characterises extent, while ultrasound shows compressible channels with slow or absent flow. Rapid painful swelling suggesting acute thrombosis Airway, orbital or visceral involvement Extensive lesions with severe localised intravascular coagulopathy risking haemorrhage Functional impairment or neurological compression Using the obsolete term cavernous haemangioma and implying that the lesion will involute. Neglecting to assess and correct localised intravascular coagulopathy before intervention. Mistaking phlebolith pain for another cause. Assuming surgery alone will cure a diffuse lesion. Venous malformation is a congenital slow-flow vascular malformation composed of ectatic, thin-walled venous channels lined by flat, quiescent endothelium with a deficient and irregular smooth-muscle layer, which impairs contraction and causes progressive dilatation and stasis. Most sporadic lesions arise from somatic activating mutations in the endothelial receptor TIE2 (TEK) or in PIK3CA, driving PI3K/AKT/mTOR signalling. Venous stasis within the malformation activates coagulation locally, producing a chronic localised intravascular coagulopathy with thrombosis, phlebolith formation and pain. Venous malformations are chronic and tend to enlarge slowly over life, particularly around puberty. Symptoms are often controllable with sclerotherapy and compression, but complete cure is uncommon in extensive lesions.

Ventricular Septal Defect — VSD, ventricular septal defects Atrioventricular septal defect Patent ductus arteriosus Atrial septal defect Tetralogy of Fallot with a dominant VSD murmur Innocent (functional) murmur Aortic or pulmonary stenosis Echocardiography to localise the defect and quantify shunt and chamber size Chest radiograph for cardiomegaly and pulmonary plethora in large shunts Electrocardiogram for left or biventricular hypertrophy Assessment of growth and feeding as markers of shunt significance Cardiac catheterisation to measure pulmonary vascular resistance when pulmonary hypertension is suspected The most common congenital heart malformation, an opening in the interventricular septum that permits shunting between the ventricles; most are membranous or muscular in location. The direction and size of the shunt depend on the defect size and the relative resistances of the pulmonary and systemic circulations, so many defects become clinically apparent only as pulmonary resistance falls in the first weeks of life. Small defects produce a loud, often harsh holosystolic murmur at the lower left sternal border but little haemodynamic burden, and many close spontaneously. Large defects cause a significant left-to-right shunt with excessive pulmonary blood flow, leading to heart failure signs such as tachypnoea, poor feeding, sweating, and failure to thrive in infancy. A large shunt may generate a mid-diastolic rumble at the apex from increased flow across the mitral valve. Untreated large defects risk progressive pulmonary vascular disease that can eventually reverse the shunt (Eisenmenger physiology), a late and largely irreversible complication. Echocardiography defines the defect location and size, estimates shunt magnitude, and assesses chamber enlargement and pulmonary pressures. Management of a haemodynamically significant defect focuses on treating heart failure and supporting growth, with surgical or catheter closure for defects that do not shrink or that cause failure or pulmonary hypertension. Many small muscular and membranous defects close on their own during early childhood. Signs of congestive heart failure in infancy: tachypnoea, feeding difficulty, sweating, and failure to thrive Development of pulmonary hypertension or a shrinking left-to-right shunt suggesting rising pulmonary resistance New cyanosis or a diminishing murmur indicating shunt reversal (Eisenmenger physiology) Poor weight gain despite medical therapy Signs of infective endocarditis in a child with a known defect Assuming a loud murmur means a large, dangerous defect when small defects are often the loudest Missing a large defect in the newborn period before pulmonary resistance falls and the murmur becomes apparent Overlooking progression to pulmonary vascular disease by delaying closure of a significant shunt Attributing poor growth to feeding problems rather than an underlying significant shunt Failing to recognise shunt reversal when cyanosis appears in a previously acyanotic child A communication in the ventricular septum allows blood to shunt according to the pressure and resistance gradient between the ventricles. After birth, as pulmonary vascular resistance declines, left-to-right shunting increases, raising pulmonary blood flow and volume-loading the left atrium and left ventricle. A large, sustained shunt increases pulmonary artery pressure and flow, and over time medial hypertrophy and intimal changes in the pulmonary vasculature raise resistance irreversibly; when pulmonary resistance exceeds systemic, the shunt reverses and produces cyanosis (Eisenmenger syndrome). Small defects have an excellent outlook and often close spontaneously. Large defects, if repaired before irreversible pulmonary vascular disease develops, generally have a good outcome; delayed closure risks fixed pulmonary hypertension and a markedly worse prognosis.

blocking drugs Delaying cardioversion in an unstable patient in favour of drug therapy Missing a reversible cause such as ischaemia, hyperkalaemia, hypomagnesaemia, or QT-prolonging drugs Overlooking Prognosis is strongly tied to the underlying substrate and left ventricular function; VT in structurally normal hearts is often benign, whereas sustained VT with impaired ventricular function or scar carries a high risk of sudden death that is mitigated by defibrillator therapy and substrate-targeted treatment.

Vernal keratoconjunctivitis is a chronic allergic inflammation of the ocular surface involving both IgE-mediated (type I) and cell-mediated (type IV) hypersensitivity, with a prominent role for eosinophils, mast cells, and T lymphocytes. Repeated allergen exposure and chronic inflammation drive proliferation of the tarsal conjunctiva into giant cobblestone papillae and produce gelatinous limbal papillae with Horner-Trantas dots. Eosinophil-derived toxic mediators, together with mechanical rubbing by giant papillae, damage the corneal epithelium and can produce a sterile shield ulcer in the superior cornea. Chronic severe disease may injure the limbal stem cells and cause scarring, and eye rubbing contributes to associated keratoconus. The disease is usually self-limiting and tends to resolve after adolescence, but severe or poorly controlled cases can cause shield ulcers, corneal scarring, limbal stem cell damage, and keratoconus with lasting visual consequences.

Somatic activating variants in MAP3K3 drive the lesion and separate it molecularly from common venous malformations. Because the malformed vessels frequently extend deeper than the visible verrucous surface, superficial or incomplete treatment tends to be followed by recurrence and progressive enlargement. Verrucous venous malformation is benign but persistent and does not involute; it commonly enlarges with the patient and is prone to recurrence after incomplete treatment, so wide complete excision offers the best chance of durable control while symptoms otherwise guide conservative management.

Infection then spreads across the relatively avascular intervertebral disc to involve the adjacent vertebra, producing the characteristic pattern of spondylodiscitis. Progressive infection can form paravertebral or epidural abscesses, erode bone leading to vertebral collapse and deformity, and compress neural structures. Less commonly infection reaches the spine by contiguous spread or direct inoculation from surgery or trauma. With early diagnosis and appropriate prolonged antibiotics most patients recover, but delayed treatment or epidural abscess with cord compression can leave permanent neurological deficits; relapse is more likely with inadequate therapy duration or unaddressed source.

imaging Hypertension or proteinuria indicating reflux nephropathy Bilateral high-grade reflux with declining renal function Attributing all renal damage to reflux when congenital dysplasia may account for much of it Ignoring underlying bladder and bowel dysfunction, which undermines both medical and surgical treatment Over-investigating or over-treating low-grade reflux likely to resolve spontaneously Failing to monitor blood pressure and renal function in children with established scarring The normal ureterovesical junction acts as a one-way flap valve because the intravesical ureter runs obliquely through the bladder wall and is compressed during filling and voiding. In primary reflux this valve is incompetent, usually because of a short intramural ureteric tunnel or a laterally placed ureteric orifice. Secondary reflux develops when abnormally high bladder pressures, as in outlet obstruction or neurogenic or dysfunctional bladders, overwhelm a marginally competent junction. Reflux of infected urine, and possibly of sterile urine at high pressure, delivers pathogens and pressure to the renal papillae, producing pyelonephritic inflammation and scarring known as reflux nephropathy. Low-grade reflux commonly resolves spontaneously with an excellent prognosis, whereas high-grade bilateral reflux, especially with recurrent pyelonephritis and pre-existing dysplasia, carries a meaningful risk of scarring, hypertension, and chronic kidney disease requiring long-term monitoring.

reflux Overlooking bladder and bowel dysfunction, which perpetuates reflux and infection Missing secondary reflux from obstruction such as posterior urethral valves Neglecting long-term monitoring of blood pressure and renal function in children with scarring Delaying treatment of a febrile infection in an obstructed, refluxing system Vesicoureteric reflux occurs when the valve-like mechanism of the vesicoureteric junction fails, allowing urine to reflux from the bladder into the ureter and renal pelvis. Normally an adequate length of submucosal ureter within the bladder wall is compressed during bladder filling and voiding, preventing reflux; in primary VUR this tunnel is congenitally short or laterally placed. Reflux of infected urine and elevated pressures transmitted to the kidney cause pyelonephritis and scarring (reflux nephropathy), which underlies later hypertension and renal impairment. Many children with low-grade primary reflux resolve spontaneously as they grow and do well with infection prevention; high-grade reflux, recurrent pyelonephritis, and established scarring carry a greater risk of hypertension and chronic kidney disease, making surveillance important.

vestibular migraine — migrainous vertigo, migraine-associated vertigo, migraine-associated dizziness Menière's disease benign paroxysmal positional vertigo vestibular paroxysmia episodic ataxia type 2 posterior circulation transient ischaemic attack or stroke persistent postural-perceptual dizziness panic disorder with vestibular symptoms pure-tone audiometry to exclude the fluctuating low-frequency loss of Menière's disease video head impulse testing and caloric testing (typically normal or non-lateralising interictally) cervical and ocular vestibular evoked myogenic potentials MRI of the brain and internal auditory meati to exclude structural or central pathology orthostatic blood pressure measurement to exclude an orthostatic contribution structured headache and vertigo diary to demonstrate the temporal relationship of migrainous features The commonest cause of recurrent spontaneous vertigo and a frequently under-recognised diagnosis; it should be considered in any patient with episodic vestibular symptoms and a migraine history. Vertigo need not be temporally linked to headache — episodes may occur with, before, after, or entirely without cephalgia, which is a common reason the diagnosis is missed. Attack phenomenology is highly variable: spontaneous or positional vertigo, head-motion intolerance, or internal/external illusory movement, lasting anywhere from a few minutes to as long as a few days. Diagnosis requires a current or past history of migraine plus migrainous features (migraine-type headache, photophobia, phonophobia, or visual aura) during at least half of the vestibular episodes. Interictal examination is usually normal, although subtle central oculomotor signs such as gaze-evoked or positional nystagmus of central type may be present. It overlaps and may coexist with Menière's disease and benign paroxysmal positional vertigo, and can evolve into persistent postural-perceptual dizziness. Osmophobia, visual aura, and a family history of migraine strengthen the diagnosis; triggers mirror those of migraine (sleep disturbance, stress, hormonal fluctuation, dietary and sensory stimuli). Management combines trigger avoidance and lifestyle measures with migraine prophylaxis (beta-blockers, tricyclic antidepressants, anticonvulsants, or calcium-channel blockers) rather than long-term vestibular sedatives. acute severe vertigo accompanied by brainstem signs (dysarthria, diplopia, limb ataxia, sensory loss) suggesting posterior circulation stroke progressive unilateral sensorineural hearing loss or persistent unilateral tinnitus suggesting retrocochlear pathology or Menière's disease first presentation of vestibular symptoms in an older patient with vascular risk factors new persistent headache with focal neurological deficit or papilloedema sudden thunderclap headache with vertigo attributing all episodic vertigo to migraine without excluding Menière's disease or benign paroxysmal positional vertigo expecting headache to accompany every attack and therefore rejecting the diagnosis when vertigo occurs in isolation over-relying on normal interictal vestibular tests, which do not exclude the diagnosis missing a coexisting benign paroxysmal positional vertigo that is independently treatable long-term use of vestibular suppressants, which impair central compensation and may perpetuate symptoms The mechanism is incompletely understood but is thought to arise from the same trigeminovascular and central sensory-processing dysfunction that underlies migraine, applied to vestibular pathways. Reciprocal anatomical connections link trigeminal nociceptive neurones with central vestibular nuclei, and neuropeptides such as calcitonin gene-related peptide modulate vestibular processing. Cortical spreading depression, thalamocortical dysrhythmia, and transient dysfunction of central multisensory integration are all implicated, producing episodic mismatch between vestibular, visual, and proprioceptive signals. A strong genetic predisposition exists, and channelopathy genes (notably CACNA1A, shared with familial hemiplegic migraine and episodic ataxia type 2) illustrate the mechanistic overlap between migraine and paroxysmal vestibular disorders. Vestibular migraine typically follows a chronic relapsing-remitting course that fluctuates over years and often improves with prophylaxis and lifestyle modification. A proportion of patients develop chronic dizziness or secondary persistent postural-perceptual dizziness if untreated.

vestibular neuritis by relying on imaging that can be falsely reassuring early Prescribing prolonged vestibular suppressants, which impair central compensation Assuming any acute vertigo is peripheral without performing the HINTS examination Overlooking associated hearing loss that changes the differential Delaying vestibular rehabilitation and prolonging disability Vestibular neuritis is attributed to inflammation of the vestibular nerve, possibly from reactivation of latent herpes simplex virus in the vestibular ganglion, causing acute unilateral loss of peripheral vestibular input. The superior vestibular division is most often affected. The sudden asymmetry between the two vestibular systems generates a strong sense of rotational vertigo and spontaneous nystagmus. Over subsequent days to weeks, central adaptive mechanisms recalibrate the vestibular imbalance (central compensation), which underlies clinical recovery even if peripheral function does not fully return. Most patients recover over days to weeks as central compensation develops, though some have persistent unsteadiness or motion sensitivity; early vestibular rehabilitation improves recovery and reduces chronic dizziness.

vestibular paroxysmia — neurovascular cross-compression of the eighth nerve, disabling positional vertigo, microvascular compression syndrome of cranial nerve VIII benign paroxysmal positional vertigo vestibular migraine Menière's disease episodic ataxia type 2 posterior circulation transient ischaemic attack superior semicircular canal dehiscence or perilymph fistula panic attacks with vestibular symptoms high-resolution heavily T2-weighted MRI (CISS/FIESTA) with MR angiography of the cerebellopontine angle pure-tone audiometry to detect an associated cochlear deficit or exclude other causes video head impulse testing, caloric testing, and vestibular evoked myogenic potentials bedside hyperventilation testing for provoked nystagmus positional testing to exclude benign paroxysmal positional vertigo a monitored therapeutic trial of a sodium-channel-blocking anticonvulsant The hallmark is short, recurrent, stereotyped spells of spinning or non-spinning vertigo lasting seconds to under a minute, which may occur many times a day. It is attributed to pulsatile neurovascular cross-compression of the vestibulocochlear nerve, mechanistically analogous to trigeminal neuralgia and hemifacial spasm. Attacks may arise spontaneously or be provoked by particular head positions or by hyperventilation, and may be accompanied by transient unilateral tinnitus or a change in hearing. A clear response to low doses of a sodium-channel-blocking anticonvulsant (such as carbamazepine or oxcarbazepine) supports the diagnosis and is one of the formal diagnostic criteria. High-resolution heavily T2-weighted MRI (CISS or FIESTA) may show a vessel, most often the anterior inferior cerebellar artery, looping onto the nerve, but such contact is frequent in asymptomatic people, so imaging is supportive rather than diagnostic. Between attacks the examination is usually normal, although some patients develop a mild progressive vestibular or cochlear deficit over time. Hyperventilation-induced nystagmus may be demonstrable and is a useful bedside clue. The condition must be distinguished from benign paroxysmal positional vertigo, vestibular migraine, Menière's disease, and panic attacks before treatment is committed. progressive unilateral sensorineural hearing loss suggesting a vestibular schwannoma or other cerebellopontine angle tumour facial weakness, facial numbness, or additional cranial neuropathies signs of brainstem ischaemia such as dysarthria, diplopia, or limb ataxia papilloedema or other features of raised intracranial pressure failure to respond to an adequate trial of a sodium-channel-blocking drug, prompting reconsideration of the diagnosis over-diagnosing the condition on the basis of incidental neurovascular contact seen on MRI in an asymptomatic person confusing brief positional attacks with benign paroxysmal positional vertigo or with vestibular migraine treating a therapeutic response as definitive proof, since other paroxysmal disorders may also respond neglecting to exclude a cerebellopontine angle tumour before attributing symptoms to vascular compression escalating medication without re-examining the diagnosis when attacks fail to remit Vestibular paroxysmia is caused by pulsatile compression of the vestibulocochlear nerve by an adjacent artery — most often the anterior inferior cerebellar artery — at or near the root entry zone, where central oligodendrocyte myelin transitions to peripheral Schwann-cell myelin and the nerve is especially vulnerable. Chronic mechanical irritation produces focal demyelination, which permits ephaptic (cross-talk) transmission between axons and generates paroxysmal ectopic and self-sustaining discharges. These brief bursts of abnormal afferent activity are perceived as short, stereotyped attacks of vertigo, exactly analogous to the paroxysms of trigeminal neuralgia and hemifacial spasm arising from compression of neighbouring cranial nerves. Membrane-stabilising, sodium-channel-blocking drugs suppress this ectopic firing, which accounts for their characteristic therapeutic effect. The disorder usually responds well to sodium-channel-blocking anticonvulsants, often at low doses, with a marked reduction in attack frequency; medically refractory cases may be considered for microvascular decompression, though some patients show slow progression of vestibulocochlear deficit.

enhancing tumour may expand into the cerebellopontine angle Facial nerve function is typically preserved until tumours are large, whereas early facial weakness should raise suspicion of an alternative pathology such as a facial nerve schwannoma Large tumours can cause trigeminal sensory loss, cerebellar signs, brainstem compression and hydrocephalus Management options include surveillance imaging, microsurgical resection, or stereotactic radiosurgery, chosen by tumour size, growth, hearing and patient factors Rapidly progressive symptoms, severe headache or reduced consciousness suggesting brainstem compression or hydrocephalus Cerebellar signs such as ataxia, dysmetria or nystagmus indicating a large cerebellopontine angle mass Trigeminal sensory loss or facial weakness signalling significant tumour extension Bilateral tumours or a family history indicating neurofibromatosis type 2 Attributing asymmetric hearing loss or unilateral tinnitus to presbycusis or noise exposure without imaging Assuming vertigo excludes the diagnosis, since imbalance is often subtle owing to gradual compensation Failing to consider neurofibromatosis type 2 in young or bilateral cases Confusing a facial nerve schwannoma with a vestibular schwannoma when facial weakness appears early Vestibular schwannomas are slow-growing benign neoplasms of Schwann cells, usually originating at the transition zone of the vestibular nerve near the internal auditory meatus. Growth within the confined meatus compresses adjacent auditory and vestibular fibres and their blood supply, producing progressive sensorineural hearing loss and vestibular symptoms. As the tumour enlarges it extends medially into the cerebellopontine angle, where it may compress the trigeminal and facial nerves, the cerebellum and eventually the brainstem, and obstruct cerebrospinal fluid flow. Most are sporadic and unilateral; biallelic inactivation of the NF2 tumour-suppressor gene underlies both sporadic tumours and the bilateral tumours of neurofibromatosis type 2. As benign tumours, vestibular schwannomas carry an excellent survival prognosis, and many small tumours remain stable under surveillance. Hearing preservation depends on tumour size and treatment, and both microsurgery and radiosurgery carry a risk to hearing and facial nerve function that rises with larger tumours; large untreated lesions can be life-threatening through brainstem compression.

alone and missing the underlying UBA1 clone Overlooking macrocytosis and early cytopenias as clues to a marrow-based process Failing to send UBA1 sequencing because the phenotype mimics a well-known rheumatological disease Under-recognising the high thrombotic risk and not considering prophylaxis Escalating immunosuppression without haematology involvement despite marrow dysplasia VEXAS syndrome arises from an acquired somatic mutation in the UBA1 gene within haematopoietic stem cells. UBA1 encodes the principal E1 enzyme that initiates cellular ubiquitylation. The mutation, usually at the p.Met41 site, impairs production of the cytoplasmic UBA1 isoform, disrupting ubiquitin-dependent protein turnover and triggering unchecked activation of innate immune and inflammatory pathways. Many patients remain corticosteroid-dependent; allogeneic haematopoietic stem cell transplantation is the only potentially curative option, while hypomethylating agents such as azacitidine and JAK inhibition are used to control disease.

iron-overload state in a patient with a marine exposure and systemic illness Clinical or imaging evidence of necrotising fasciitis requiring emergency surgery Attributing early leg pain and fever to simple cellulitis and delaying surgical assessment Failing to elicit the marine or shellfish exposure history in a septic patient Overlooking underlying cirrhosis or haemochromatosis that dramatically raises risk Delaying combination antibiotics while awaiting microbiological confirmation Vibrio vulnificus is a salt-requiring marine bacterium that causes disease when ingested in contaminated shellfish or when it enters through a break in the skin exposed to seawater. It expresses a polysaccharide capsule that resists phagocytosis and complement, together with cytolysins, proteases and other exotoxins that damage tissue and increase vascular permeability. The resulting endotoxaemia and toxin release produce septic shock, and local toxin activity generates the characteristic haemorrhagic bullae and necrotising soft-tissue destruction. Wound infections treated early with appropriate antibiotics and debridement often recover, but primary septicaemia carries very high mortality, particularly in those with liver disease, and outcome depends heavily on rapid antibiotic and surgical intervention.

at-risk families Vici syndrome is caused by loss-of-function variants in EPG5, which encodes a key regulator of the late steps of autophagy, particularly the maturation of autophagosomes and their fusion with lysosomes. Defective autophagic clearance leads to accumulation of dysfunctional proteins and organelles within cells that are highly dependent on autophagy, including neurons, cardiomyocytes, skeletal myocytes, immune cells, and melanocytes. This explains the multisystem phenotype: impaired neurodevelopment with callosal agenesis, cardiomyopathy, a vacuolar myopathy, combined immunodeficiency, and defective melanin handling producing hypopigmentation. The disorder illustrates how disruption of a fundamental cellular degradation pathway produces widespread, progressive tissue dysfunction. The prognosis is poor, with most affected children dying in early childhood from cardiac failure or infection; survival beyond a few years is uncommon.

(achlorhydria or hypochlorhydria) and may cause flushing and hypercalcaemia Diagnosis relies on demonstrating a markedly elevated fasting plasma VIP level in the setting of secretory diarrhoea Most
