somatostatin analogues to control secretion and surgery for resectable disease Severe dehydration and haemodynamic instability from massive fluid loss Life-threatening hypokalaemia with cardiac dysrhythmia Metastatic disease, most commonly hepatic, at presentation Refractory diarrhoea unresponsive to initial supportive measures Attributing chronic watery diarrhoea to common causes and delaying measurement of VIP Failing to recognise the secretory nature of the diarrhoea because it persists with fasting Under-resuscitating profound fluid and potassium losses Overlooking a possible MEN1 association and associated tumours A VIPoma is a functioning neuroendocrine tumour, usually arising in the pancreatic islets, that secretes excessive vasoactive intestinal peptide. VIP stimulates intestinal secretion of water and electrolytes while inhibiting absorption, producing a high-volume secretory diarrhoea that continues despite fasting. The consequent losses of potassium and bicarbonate in stool lead to hypokalaemia and metabolic acidosis, and VIP's inhibition of gastric acid secretion causes achlorhydria. VIP can also promote vasodilation and flushing and, through its effects on bone and calcium handling, contribute to hypercalcaemia. A significant proportion of these tumours are malignant and may have metastasised, most often to the liver, by the time of diagnosis. Symptom control with rehydration and somatostatin analogues is usually achievable, and complete surgical resection of localised disease can be curative; however, many tumours are malignant with metastases at diagnosis, and prognosis then depends on tumour burden and response to systemic therapy.

Viral Exanthems of Childhood — viral rashes in children, childhood exanthems, exanthematous viral illness Meningococcaemia or other bacterial sepsis with petechiae or purpura Scarlet fever Kawasaki disease Drug eruption or hypersensitivity reaction Enteroviral exanthems Other congenital or systemic infections with rash Clinical diagnosis based on rash pattern and associated features in most cases Serology or PCR for specific viruses when confirmation is needed (e.g., measles, parvovirus) Full blood count and inflammatory markers if a bacterial or inflammatory cause is considered Public health notification and testing for notifiable infections such as measles Investigations to exclude serious mimics when the child is unwell or the rash is atypical Viral exanthems are widespread skin eruptions accompanying systemic viral infections and are among the most common causes of rash with fever in children. The classic childhood exanthems include measles, rubella, erythema infectiosum (parvovirus B19), roseola (human herpesvirus 6/7), and varicella, each with fairly characteristic patterns. Diagnosis is often clinical, based on the morphology and distribution of the rash, its timing relative to fever, and associated features such as enanthems and prodromal symptoms. Measles is distinguished by high fever with cough, coryza, and conjunctivitis, Koplik spots on the buccal mucosa, and a rash spreading from the head downward. Roseola typically causes several days of high fever in a well-appearing infant, followed by a rash that appears as the fever resolves. Erythema infectiosum produces the characteristic slapped-cheek facial appearance followed by a lacy, reticular rash on the limbs. Most viral exanthems are self-limiting and managed supportively, but measles carries a notable risk of complications and remains vaccine-preventable. Recognising non-viral mimics, especially meningococcaemia, scarlet fever, Kawasaki disease, and drug reactions, is essential because some require urgent specific treatment. Petechial or purpuric, non-blanching rash Toxic or septic appearance Signs suggesting Kawasaki disease (prolonged fever with mucocutaneous features) Mucosal involvement, blistering, or skin sloughing suggesting a severe drug reaction Features of measles complications such as pneumonia or encephalitis Mislabelling a serious non-blanching or purpuric rash as a benign viral exanthem Failing to consider Kawasaki disease in a child with prolonged fever and rash Overlooking measles and its public health and complication implications Attributing a drug hypersensitivity eruption to a viral cause In many viral exanthems the rash reflects the systemic phase of infection when virus disseminates through the bloodstream and, together with the host immune response, involves the skin. Some eruptions result from direct viral infection of skin cells (as in varicella, where the virus produces vesicular lesions), while others are largely immune-mediated, appearing as the immune response develops and sometimes coinciding with defervescence, as in roseola. The specific morphology, distribution, and timing are determined by the particular virus, its tropism, and the character of the immune reaction, which is why individual exanthems have recognisable patterns. The great majority of viral exanthems are benign and self-limiting with full recovery, though certain infections, notably measles and varicella in vulnerable hosts, and parvovirus in specific settings, can cause significant complications.

Viral Gastroenteritis — Acute viral gastroenteritis, Norovirus gastroenteritis, Norwalk virus infection, Rotavirus gastroenteritis, Stomach flu Bacterial gastroenteritis (e.g., Salmonella, Shigella, Campylobacter, Vibrio cholerae, enterotoxigenic E. coli) - distinguished by inflammatory/bloody diarrhea, fecal leukocytes, and epidemiologic features Preformed bacterial toxin food poisoning (Staphylococcus aureus, Bacillus cereus) - very short incubation of hours Clostridioides difficile colitis Protozoal/parasitic diarrhea (e.g., Giardia, Cryptosporidium) Bacterial enteritis (Salmonella, Shigella, Campylobacter jejuni, Vibrio, E. coli) Staphylococcus aureus and Bacillus cereus preformed-toxin food poisoning Clostridioides difficile colitis Gastrointestinal symptoms of systemic respiratory viral infections (SARS-CoV, influenza A/H5N1, pandemic influenza A/H1N1) Commercial enzyme immunoassays (EIA) for rotavirus and enteric adenovirus in stool RT-PCR / multiplex molecular panels for norovirus and other enteric pathogens (increasingly used clinically) Electron microscopy and polyacrylamide gel electrophoresis (PAGE) for viral RNA - largely research/public-health tools Fecal examination for leukocytes and blood to help separate viral (typically negative) from inflammatory bacterial causes Stool culture on special media when bacterial pathogens are suspected Osmotic or secretory diarrhea from other causes Carbohydrate malabsorption states Other causes of acute vomiting without true gastroenteritis Most viral gastroenteritis is caused by RNA viruses, but DNA enteric adenoviruses (types 40 and 41) are also recognized causes; the principal pathogens are rotavirus, norovirus, sapovirus, astrovirus, and enteric adenovirus. Illness presents with acute onset of vomiting and/or diarrhea, often with fever, nausea, abdominal cramps, anorexia, and malaise; the diarrhea is characteristically watery and nonbloody, without mucus or fecal leukocytes. Norovirus has become the leading cause of medically attended gastroenteritis in young children in the United States and other developed countries following the decline in severe rotavirus disease after routine rotavirus vaccination, and it affects all age groups. Norovirus is responsible for roughly half of all reported gastroenteritis outbreaks in the United States and is the major cause of gastroenteritis epidemics worldwide; it also causes traveler's diarrhea and outbreaks among deployed military personnel. The infectious dose for most viral agents is very low (about 10-100 viral particles), in contrast to the higher inoculum typically required for many bacterial pathogens; norovirus can spread by fecal-oral route, aerosolization of vomitus, contaminated fomites, and person-to-person contact. Nearly all children worldwide are infected with rotavirus by 3-5 years of age; first symptomatic infection usually occurs after 3 months of age, disease incidence peaks at 4-23 months, and severity decreases with each repeat infection. Protection against rotavirus correlates with virus-specific secretory IgA in the intestine (and to some degree serum); because intestinal IgA is short-lived, full protection is temporary, but successive reinfections build progressively greater immunity. Susceptibility to norovirus is influenced by host genetics: histo-blood group antigen (HBGA) phenotype and secretor status affect attachment, and functional antibodies that block norovirus binding to HBGAs correlate with protective immunity. Rotavirus antigenemia and viremia are common in acutely infected children, although serum antigen and RNA levels are far lower than stool levels; rotavirus is shed in very large quantities in stool (10^7-10^12 per gram). In temperate climates viral gastroenteritis shows winter seasonality, whereas in tropical/year-round settings seasonal peaks are less pronounced; before vaccination, US rotavirus season began in the Southwest in autumn/early winter and migrated to peak in the Northeast in late winter/spring. Fever is common with both rotavirus and norovirus but uncommon with the other viral agents; up to one-third of rotavirus patients may have a temperature above 39 degrees C. Death is a rare outcome and usually results from severe dehydration in vulnerable hosts such as debilitated elderly patients and young children; acute gastroenteritis is a leading cause of childhood death in developing countries (roughly 0.5 million deaths annually) and a major cause of pediatric hospitalization (6-8%) in industrialized nations. Signs of severe dehydration (especially in young children and debilitated elderly) Inability to tolerate oral intake due to frequent vomiting Bloody diarrhea or fecal leukocytes - should prompt evaluation for a bacterial/inflammatory cause rather than viral gastroenteritis Protracted diarrhea with prolonged viral excretion or systemic dissemination in severely immunocompromised hosts (e.g., post-bone-marrow transplant rotavirus disease) Distinguishing viral from bacterial gastroenteritis on clinical and epidemiologic grounds alone is often unreliable; laboratory testing may be needed, and viral gastroenteritis is frequently a diagnosis of exclusion in practice. Antibiotics and antimotility agents are inappropriate for viral gastroenteritis and are contraindicated. Commercial stool EIA kits for norovirus have limited sensitivity and are most useful in outbreak investigation (many specimens tested) rather than for diagnosing individual patients. Higher preexisting antibody to Norwalk virus does not guarantee protection - early studies paradoxically found higher antibody levels associated with greater susceptibility, later explained by host HBGA genetics rather than simple antibody titer. Rotavirus has been associated with diverse conditions (SIDS, necrotizing enterocolitis, intussusception, Kawasaki disease, type 1 diabetes) and with respiratory/neurologic features, but no causal relationship has been confirmed for any of these. Asymptomatically infected and pre-symptomatic persons can shed norovirus, and shedding can persist for weeks after recovery (prolonged in immunocompromised hosts), so a single negative or positive result must be interpreted with care. Enteric viruses injure the small-intestinal mucosa to produce predominantly watery diarrhea. With human caliciviruses (Norwalk/norovirus), carbohydrates resembling human histo-blood group antigens on the gastroduodenal epithelium of secretor-phenotype individuals appear to serve as attachment ligands; infection causes reversible lesions of the upper jejunum with broadening and blunting of villi, microvillar shortening, epithelial vacuolization, crypt hyperplasia, and lamina propria infiltration by neutrophils and lymphocytes. These changes persist for at least 4 days after symptom resolution and produce malabsorption of carbohydrates and fats with reduced brush-border enzymes; adenylate cyclase activity is unchanged. No histopathologic change occurs in stomach or colon, but delayed gastric motor function is thought to drive the characteristic nausea and vomiting. Rotavirus infects and destroys mature enterocytes of the proximal small-intestinal villous epithelium; loss of absorptive cells plus proliferation of secretory crypt cells yields secretory diarrhea, while reduced brush-border enzymes leave unmetabolized disaccharides that cause osmotic diarrhea. The nonstructural rotavirus protein NSP4 acts as an enterotoxin altering epithelial permeability and function, and rotavirus may also stimulate fluid secretion via activation of the enteric nervous system. Viral gastroenteritis is generally self-limited. Human calicivirus illness has a sudden onset after a mean incubation of about 24 hours (range 12-72 h) and typically lasts 12-60 h; norovirus and sapovirus illness usually resolves in 1-3 days. Rotavirus illness begins abruptly after a 1-3 day incubation, with vomiting often preceding diarrhea, and gastrointestinal symptoms generally resolve in 3-7 days. Among healthy young adults the illness is rarely fatal but causes substantial morbidity and lost work time. The main serious complication is dehydration; death is uncommon and concentrated in the very young, the elderly, and those with debilitating conditions. Severely immunodeficient children may develop protracted rotavirus diarrhea with prolonged shedding and, rarely, systemic dissemination. Harrison does not provide a formal grading scale; clinical severity is described per agent and ranges from subclinical/mild infection to severe gastroenteritis with life-threatening dehydration. Relative clinical severity by virus: group A rotavirus is the most severe (predominantly children under 5), norovirus is moderate (all ages), and sapovirus, astrovirus, and enteric adenovirus are generally milder (mainly children under 5).

Viral Hemorrhagic Fever — Ebola, Marburg, VHF Falciparum malaria (a most important mimic and a treatable, potentially fatal alternative) Typhoid fever Other treatable travel-associated febrile illnesses: shigellosis, leptospirosis, relapsing fever, rickettsial diseases Other VHFs/high-consequence viral infections, in particular Lassa fever and yellow fever Dengue and other viral hemorrhagic fevers in the bleeding/febrile traveler Falciparum malaria Typhoid fever Enterohemorrhagic E. coli enteritis Gram-negative septicemia (including shigellosis) Meningococcal septicemia Rickettsial infections Fulminant viral hepatitis Leptospirosis Measles Other high-consequence viral infections (Lassa fever, yellow fever) RT-PCR targeting one or more filovirid genes is the diagnostic assay of choice; in-field PCR platforms (e.g., Cepheid GeneXpert) are deployed during outbreaks Acute-phase blood/serum is the preferred specimen as it usually contains high virion titers Antigen-capture ELISA / immunochromatographic rapid diagnostic tests (currently limited; EBOV antigen RDT sensitivity restricts use largely to postmortem samples) IgM- and IgG-capture ELISAs (including multiplex) for antibodies in later disease and in survivors Virus isolation/plaque assays and electron microscopy require maximum-containment laboratories; in-field genome sequencing supports outbreak epidemiology Supportive labs typically show leukopenia (then leukocytosis), thrombocytopenia, raised aminotransferases (AST > ALT) and GGT, raised creatinine/urea with proteinuria, electrolyte derangement, hypoglycemia, hypoalbuminemia, prolonged PT/PTT, elevated CPK, and markedly elevated CRP in severe illness Hemoconcentration from vascular leakage is usually evident (most marked in HFRS and severe dengue) Venomous snakebite Warfarin (anticoagulant) intoxication Acquired or inherited coagulopathies in the bleeding patient VHF is an acute viral syndrome of severe disease and multisystem organ dysfunction sharing a common disruption of vascular function, stability, and integrity; overt hemorrhage is often NOT the most prominent or severe feature, so absence of bleeding does not exclude VHF (p.1674). Travel to an endemic or active-outbreak area within the incubation period is a major diagnostic clue; rural exposures more often suggest VHF except for urban-host/vector agents (Seoul virus, dengue, yellow fever) (p.1675). For filovirid (Ebola/Marburg) disease, the incubation period is 2-25 days (most commonly 7-10 days), beginning with a nonspecific influenza-like illness (sudden fever/chills, headache, myalgia, pharyngitis, arthralgia, maculopapular rash) before a second phase (~5-7 days on) with GI, respiratory, cardiovascular, and CNS involvement (p.1685). Common filovirid hemorrhagic signs are subconjunctival injection, petechial rash, gingival bleeding, and bleeding at injection sites; frank epistaxis, hematemesis, hematuria, and melena occur but are LESS common, and severe blood loss is rare (except during/after childbirth) (pp.1684-1685). Ebola/Marburg present with very similar clinical phenotypes that cannot be distinguished at the bedside and, for practical purposes, may be managed as the same disease (p.1685). Early recognition is crucial: prompt isolation and hospitalization are indicated even in the absence of clinical signs, with rapid triage and ongoing vital-sign monitoring (p.1675). Filovirids are highly infectious but not exceptionally contagious; human-to-human spread occurs by direct contact with an infected person or their body fluids/tissues, with NO evidence of aerosol or respiratory droplet transmission in natural outbreak settings (p.1679). Persistence of filovirids in immune-privileged sites (most commonly semen of male survivors; rarely CNS, eye, placenta) can cause recrudescent disease and rare reignition of outbreaks; sexual abstinence or condom use is advised for male survivors until semen is shown to be filovirid-RNA free (pp.1686-1687). Strict barrier nursing and infection-control isolation with appropriate PPE are mandatory for suspected VHF (except dengue, orthohantavirus, RVFV, or yellow fever); isolate and hospitalize even before clinical signs appear Immediately notify infectious disease specialists and public health authorities if filovirid disease is suspected on epidemiologic or clinical grounds Progressive multiorgan dysfunction: shock, acute kidney injury, CNS injury (encephalopathy, coma, seizures), respiratory failure, and severe hemorrhage signal critical illness Exposure history raising suspicion: caves/mines, direct contact with bats, nonhuman primates, or bushmeat, contact with severely ill local residents, or patient-to-patient/healthcare-worker clusters in rural hospitals Hemodynamic instability/hypotension and capillary leak with effusions and edema Pregnancy and labor are associated with severe complications and poor outcomes (clotting-factor consumption, fetal loss, severe peripartum hemorrhage) Filovirid/VHF disease cannot be diagnosed on clinical presentation alone; numerous more common febrile illnesses (especially malaria and typhoid) closely mimic it and are far more likely in non-outbreak settings, so do not anchor on VHF without epidemiologic context and laboratory confirmation. Absence of overt hemorrhage does not exclude VHF, since hemorrhagic manifestations are often neither the most prominent nor the most severe feature. Treat DIC only with clear laboratory evidence and feasible monitoring; there is no proven benefit otherwise. Fluid management is a balancing act: VHF patients are commonly hypovolemic from insensible and GI losses, yet may also have decreased cardiac output, capillary leak, and oliguria requiring judicious fluids and inotropic/vasopressor support. Do not assume respiratory/aerosol spread for filovirids in natural settings and do not reuse medical equipment (gloves, syringes) used for an infected patient. Across VHFs, direct or indirect microvascular damage increases vascular permeability and (when platelet function is reduced) causes disruption and local hemorrhage, most evident in skin and mucous membranes; hypotension and shock reflect generalized circulatory dysfunction rather than life-threatening blood loss. Pathogenesis is incompletely understood and varies by virus, with direct vascular/parenchymal damage in some and soluble mediators dominating in others. For filovirids specifically, virions enter via skin lesions, mucosal surfaces, or parenteral inoculation; GP1,2 spikes engage cell-surface molecules and the intracellular receptor NPC1. First targets are macrophages, monocytes, and dendritic cells, and viral proteins (VP35, VP40, VP24) suppress innate immunity (e.g., type I interferon pathways), enabling high viral titers and widespread tissue dissemination. Hallmarks include profound immune dysregulation, massive lymphoid depletion with severe lymphopenia, coagulopathy (thrombocytopenia, elevated tissue factor, consumption of clotting factors, raised D-dimers, falling protein C; possible DIC, though controversial), hepatocyte necrosis with synthetic dysfunction contributing to coagulopathy, and endothelial dysfunction with increased vascular permeability leading to fluid redistribution, interstitial edema, and hypovolemic or septic shock (pp.1674-1675, 1683-1685). FVD is among the most severe acute human viral diseases and generally carries a poor prognosis, though with far more heterogeneity than historically assumed (the long-cited 70-90% case-fatality rate for EVD has required revision). Outcome likely depends on the specific filovirid, host factors (age, immune status, coinfections, host genetics), exposure route and dose, viral load, presence and severity of organ dysfunction, and critically the availability of filovirid-specific countermeasures and supportive/critical care. Even with effective EBOV-specific therapeutics, outcomes in severe EVD with high viral loads and complex organ dysfunction remain suboptimal. For other VHFs prognosis varies widely by agent (e.g., Argentinian/Bolivian hemorrhagic fevers can have case-fatality rates exceeding 50% in individual outbreaks) (pp.1675, 1685-1687). No formal numeric severity score is provided; clinically, the illness progresses from an incubation period through a nonspecific febrile prodrome (early phase) to a peak phase, with severity marked by progressive multiorgan dysfunction (shock, acute kidney injury, respiratory failure, CNS injury, severe hemorrhage). Filovirid disease course is depicted across incubation, early, peak, and recovery phases. Severity and case-fatality vary by causative virus and the availability of specific countermeasures and supportive care (pp.1675, 1683-1686).

Viral Warts — verruca, verruca vulgaris, common wart, plantar wart, verruca plantaris, HPV wart Corn or callus (skin lines preserved, no capillary dots) Molluscum contagiosum Seborrhoeic keratosis Actinic keratosis or squamous cell carcinoma in a persistent lesion on sun-damaged skin Acral or amelanotic melanoma masquerading as a plantar wart Knuckle pads or other keratotic papules Diagnosis is usually clinical, aided by paring the lesion and by dermoscopy Skin biopsy for atypical, persistent, or rapidly changing lesions to exclude malignancy Assessment for immunosuppression when warts are extensive or recalcitrant Sexual health screening for anogenital warts Common warts are firm, hyperkeratotic papules with a rough surface, often studded with tiny black dots representing thrombosed capillaries Paring the surface of a plantar wart reveals these capillary dots and interrupts the skin lines, helping to distinguish it from a corn or callus Morphological variants include flat (plane) warts, filiform warts around the face, and mosaic plantar warts Transmission is by direct contact and via contaminated moist surfaces such as swimming-pool floors, with autoinoculation and the Koebner phenomenon spreading lesions Most warts in healthy people resolve spontaneously as immunity develops, so a period of watchful waiting is reasonable First-line treatments such as topical keratolytics and cryotherapy work by physical destruction and stimulating an immune response, and typically require repeated, persistent application Widespread, recalcitrant, or unusual warts should prompt consideration of immunosuppression Genital warts require assessment for sexually transmitted infection, and their prevention links to HPV vaccination A verrucous or ulcerated lesion that is enlarging, bleeding, or failing to respond, raising concern for squamous cell carcinoma A pigmented or irregular acral lesion that could be melanoma rather than a wart Numerous or atypical warts suggesting underlying immunosuppression, including epidermodysplasia verruciformis Anogenital warts in a child prompting safeguarding consideration Misdiagnosing an amelanotic melanoma or squamous cell carcinoma as a resistant wart and delaying biopsy Confusing a plantar wart with a simple corn or callus Persisting with destructive treatments that cause more scarring and pain than the wart itself, particularly in children Failing to consider immunosuppression in widespread or treatment-resistant disease Viral warts result from infection of keratinocytes by human papillomavirus, which enters through microabrasions and drives epidermal proliferation and hyperkeratosis. Different HPV genotypes show tropism for particular sites and clinical morphologies. The virus establishes infection in the basal layer and completes its life cycle as keratinocytes differentiate towards the surface, producing the koilocytic changes seen histologically. Clearance depends on an effective cell-mediated immune response, which explains both spontaneous resolution over time and the persistence or proliferation of warts in immunocompromised patients. Certain high-risk genital genotypes carry oncogenic potential. The outlook is generally excellent, with most warts in immunocompetent people clearing spontaneously within one to two years; some are stubborn and require repeated treatment, and clearance is slower and relapse more likely where immunity is impaired.

Visceral artery aneurysm — Splanchnic artery aneurysm, VAA Other causes of acute abdomen or gastrointestinal haemorrhage Abdominal aortic aneurysm Pancreatic pseudocyst or cystic neoplasm as an imaging mimic Retroperitoneal haematoma from another cause Arteriovenous malformation or hypervascular tumour Median arcuate ligament syndrome Splenic or hepatic mass CT angiography of the abdomen for diagnosis, size and anatomical relationships Digital subtraction catheter angiography, usually with intent to treat Duplex ultrasound for splenic and hepatic lesions and for surveillance MR angiography where iodinated contrast or radiation is to be avoided Assessment of the coeliac axis for stenosis or median arcuate ligament compression Liver function tests and evaluation for portal hypertension Cross-sectional surveillance imaging for small asymptomatic aneurysms Encompasses true aneurysms and pseudoaneurysms of the coeliac, superior and inferior mesenteric arteries and their branches; the splenic artery is the commonest site (about 60%), followed by the hepatic artery. Splenic artery aneurysms are more frequent in women, particularly with multiparity, portal hypertension and prior liver transplantation. Pseudoaneurysms, often hepatic, pancreaticoduodenal or gastroduodenal, are usually secondary to pancreatitis, trauma, infection or iatrogenic injury and carry a high rupture risk irrespective of size. Most true aneurysms are asymptomatic and discovered incidentally on cross-sectional imaging. Rupture is catastrophic, into the peritoneum, retroperitoneum or gastrointestinal tract, and splenic aneurysms may show the classic 'double rupture' first into the lesser sac then the free peritoneum. Pancreaticoduodenal and gastroduodenal aneurysms are frequently associated with coeliac axis stenosis or occlusion, often from median arcuate ligament compression. CT angiography is the mainstay of diagnosis and planning; endovascular embolisation or stent-grafting is now first-line for most lesions. Rupture risk is markedly increased in pregnancy for splenic aneurysms, with high maternal and foetal mortality. Sudden severe abdominal or flank pain with haemodynamic instability, indicating rupture. Gastrointestinal bleeding, haematemesis or melaena with a known or suspected pseudoaneurysm (haemosuccus pancreaticus, haemobilia). Pregnancy with a known splenic artery aneurysm. Rapid aneurysm enlargement or any symptomatic aneurysm. Features of sepsis suggesting a mycotic aneurysm. Applying a single size threshold to pseudoaneurysms, which should generally be treated regardless of diameter. Missing coeliac axis compression when treating pancreaticoduodenal arcade aneurysms, risking recurrence if inflow is not addressed. Overlooking a splenic artery aneurysm in a pregnant or portal-hypertensive patient. Dismissing curvilinear 'signet ring' calcification of a splenic aneurysm as a benign finding. Failing to consider bowel or splenic ischaemia after aggressive embolisation without assessing collateral supply. True visceral artery aneurysms arise from medial degeneration with loss of elastic and smooth-muscle elements, driven by atherosclerosis, fibromuscular dysplasia, connective-tissue disorders, altered splanchnic haemodynamics (as in portal hypertension or pregnancy) and high-flow states. Pseudoaneurysms result from full-thickness arterial wall disruption contained by surrounding tissue, typically from enzymatic autodigestion in pancreatitis, penetrating or blunt trauma, infection (mycotic) or iatrogenic injury; their wall is fibrous rather than arterial and prone to expansion and rupture. Coeliac axis occlusion diverts flow through the pancreaticoduodenal arcades, and the resulting increased flow and shear predispose to arcade aneurysm formation. Elective endovascular or surgical treatment has low mortality and good outcomes, whereas rupture, especially of pseudoaneurysms or during pregnancy, carries high mortality. Pseudoaneurysms warrant treatment irrespective of size given their unpredictable rupture risk.

Visceral larva migrans — toxocariasis, Toxocara canis infection, Toxocara cati infection, VLM Hypereosinophilic syndrome Other tissue-migrating helminth infections (ascariasis, strongyloidiasis, hookworm) Acute schistosomiasis (Katayama syndrome) Hepatic abscess or other focal liver lesions Retinoblastoma (in the ocular form) Eosinophilic leukaemia or lymphoma Allergic or asthmatic pulmonary disease Full blood count and blood film for eosinophilia Toxocara-specific serology (antibody testing) Serum total immunoglobulin E Liver ultrasound or cross-sectional imaging for hepatic and pulmonary lesions Ophthalmological examination when ocular disease is suspected Exclusion of other tissue-invasive helminths and haematological causes of eosinophilia A tissue-invasive infection caused by migrating larvae of the dog and cat roundworms Toxocara canis and Toxocara cati Humans, especially young children who ingest soil contaminated with embryonated eggs, are accidental hosts in which larvae cannot mature The classic visceral form presents with fever, hepatomegaly, wheeze or cough, and marked eosinophilia A separate ocular form causes unilateral visual loss, often mistaken for retinoblastoma, and typically lacks prominent eosinophilia Diagnosis relies on serology (Toxocara-specific antibodies), as larvae are rarely recovered and stool examination is unhelpful because worms do not reach the gut in humans A history of pica, geophagia, or close contact with puppies or contaminated environments supports the diagnosis Most visceral disease is self-limiting; anthelmintics such as albendazole with corticosteroids for the inflammatory reaction are used in significant or organ-threatening infection Prevention centres on deworming pets, hand hygiene and reducing environmental soil contamination Neurological features suggesting central nervous system involvement Unilateral visual loss or leukocoria requiring urgent ophthalmological review Myocardial or severe pulmonary involvement Persistent very high eosinophilia with systemic upset Examining stool for ova, which is futile because the parasite does not mature in humans Overlooking the diagnosis in a child with eosinophilia and pica or puppy contact Confusing ocular toxocariasis with retinoblastoma Relying on a single serology result without clinical correlation Neglecting anti-inflammatory cover when treating heavy infection with anthelmintics Visceral larva migrans occurs when a human ingests embryonated Toxocara eggs from soil, faeces or contaminated food. The eggs hatch in the intestine and release larvae that penetrate the gut wall and migrate through the bloodstream to organs such as the liver, lungs, muscle, eye and brain. Because humans are not the natural host, the larvae cannot complete their life cycle or mature into adult worms; instead they persist and wander through tissues, provoking eosinophil-rich granulomatous inflammation and a strong immunoglobulin E response. The organ-specific symptoms and the intense eosinophilia reflect this larval migration and the host inflammatory reaction to it. The visceral form is usually self-limiting with a good outcome, but heavy or organ-threatening infection, and particularly ocular or central nervous system disease, can cause lasting damage such as permanent visual impairment.

Vitamin A Deficiency — hypovitaminosis A, xerophthalmia, retinol deficiency Other causes of night blindness (retinitis pigmentosa) Fat malabsorption syndromes (cystic fibrosis, cholestatic liver disease, coeliac disease) Protein-energy malnutrition with multiple deficiencies Infective keratoconjunctivitis Zinc deficiency Dry eye from other causes Serum retinol level Clinical ocular examination for Bitot spots, xerosis, and corneal changes Assessment of nutritional status and dietary intake Investigation for fat malabsorption where suspected Screening for coexisting micronutrient deficiencies A major cause of preventable childhood blindness and increased infection-related mortality in low- and middle-income countries. The earliest and most sensitive symptom is night blindness, reflecting impaired rod photoreceptor function. Progressive ocular signs (xerophthalmia) include conjunctival dryness, Bitot spots, corneal xerosis, and ultimately corneal ulceration and keratomalacia that can rapidly destroy the eye. Deficiency also impairs epithelial integrity and immune function, increasing severity of infections such as measles and diarrhoeal disease. It commonly coexists with protein-energy malnutrition and other micronutrient deficiencies. Measles can precipitate acute deficiency and corneal damage, so supplementation is recommended during measles infection in at-risk children. Diagnosis is largely clinical, supported by a low serum retinol level and dietary history. High-dose vitamin A supplementation reverses early ocular signs and reduces mortality, and periodic supplementation programmes are a key public health measure. Excessive vitamin A intake is toxic, so dosing schedules must be followed carefully. Corneal ulceration or keratomalacia threatening irreversible blindness Rapidly progressing ocular signs, particularly during measles Severe concurrent infection in a malnourished child Signs of advanced protein-energy malnutrition Bilateral corneal involvement Overlooking night blindness as an early, treatable warning sign Failing to supplement vitamin A during measles in at-risk children Missing underlying fat malabsorption in a child with deficiency and adequate intake Causing toxicity by exceeding recommended supplementation doses Vitamin A (retinol) is essential for the visual cycle, where its aldehyde form retinal combines with opsin to form rhodopsin in rod cells; deficiency reduces rhodopsin regeneration and causes night blindness. Retinoic acid also regulates differentiation and maintenance of epithelial tissues and mucosal barriers, so deficiency leads to squamous metaplasia and keratinisation of conjunctival and corneal epithelium (xerophthalmia) and of other epithelia. Impaired epithelial barriers and immune regulation increase susceptibility to and severity of infection. Early ocular changes are fully reversible with prompt supplementation, but corneal ulceration and keratomalacia can cause permanent blindness; adequate vitamin A status also lowers infection-related mortality.

Vitamin and Trace Mineral Deficiency and Excess — Micronutrient deficiency, Hidden hunger, Vitamin deficiency, Trace mineral deficiency, Hypovitaminosis, Vitamin toxicity Protein-energy malnutrition Malabsorption syndromes (celiac disease, Crohn's disease, short-bowel syndrome) Chronic alcohol use disorder Post-bariatric-surgery nutrient deficiency Inborn errors of metabolism affecting micronutrient handling (Hartnup disease, biotinidase deficiency, abetalipoproteinemia, Menkes/Wilson disease) Erythrocyte transketolase activity with thiamine pyrophosphate stimulation (>25% / activity coefficient >1.25 abnormal); serum/blood thiamine by HPLC Erythrocyte glutathione reductase activity for riboflavin; urinary 2-pyridone/2-methylnicotinamide for niacin Plasma pyridoxal 5'-phosphate (deficiency <20 nmol/L) for vitamin B6; plasma/leukocyte ascorbate for vitamin C Serum retinol (normal 1.05-3.50 micromol/L; deficient <0.70 micromol/L [20 microg/dL]) interpreted alongside C-reactive protein and alpha1-acid glycoprotein Serum 25-hydroxyvitamin D (>20 ng/mL adequate for bone health); plasma alpha-tocopherol (deficient <5 microg/mL) for vitamin E Prothrombin time and PIVKA-II (undercarboxylated prothrombin) plus serum phylloquinone (<0.15 microg/L) for vitamin K Serum zinc (<12 micromol/L / <70 microg/dL), serum copper (<65 microg/dL) with ceruloplasmin (<20 mg/dL), interpreted with albumin and acute-phase status Peripheral neuropathy from diabetes or heavy-metal toxicity (mimics thiamine, B6, B12, or vitamin E deficiency) Dermatitis/seborrhea of other cause (mimics niacin, riboflavin, biotin, or zinc deficiency) Megaloblastic anemia from drugs or marrow disease (mimics folate/B12 deficiency) Pseudotumor cerebri or hypercalcemia of other etiology (mimics chronic vitamin A or D toxicity) Coagulopathy of hepatic disease (mimics vitamin K deficiency - distinguished by failure of prothrombin time to correct with vitamin K) Overt single-nutrient deficiencies are uncommon in Western settings, but subclinical 'hidden hunger' is frequent in the elderly and the socioeconomically deprived; multiple deficiencies cluster in the chronically ill, those with alcohol use disorder, the impoverished, and post-bariatric-surgery patients. Body stores differ enormously: vitamin B12 and vitamin A reserves are large (deficiency may take a year or more to appear), whereas folate and thiamine can be depleted within weeks of an inadequate diet. Thiamine should be replenished before or during refeeding of malnourished or alcoholic patients, because giving carbohydrate (especially IV glucose) without thiamine can precipitate acute deficiency with lactic acidosis and Wernicke encephalopathy. Wernicke encephalopathy is the classic triad of ophthalmoplegia/nystagmus, cerebellar ataxia, and confusion; addition of memory loss and confabulation defines Wernicke-Korsakoff syndrome, which is underdiagnosed despite a typical history. Pellagra (niacin deficiency) is remembered as the 'four Ds' - dermatitis (notably the photosensitive Casal's necklace), diarrhea, dementia, and death; it arises with corn-based diets, alcoholism, Hartnup disease, carcinoid syndrome, and isoniazid use. Pyridoxine (B6) should be co-administered with isoniazid to prevent neuropathy; paradoxically, chronic high-dose B6 (above ~100 mg/d) itself causes a reversible severe sensory neuropathy, so long-term supplementation should be discouraged. Vitamin A deficiency is the leading cause of preventable childhood blindness worldwide (xerophthalmia, Bitot's spots, keratomalacia) and impairs immune defenses, increasing mortality from diarrhea, measles, malaria, and respiratory infection. Fat-soluble vitamin deficiencies (A, D, E, K) characteristically accompany fat-malabsorptive states such as celiac disease, cholestatic liver disease, cystic fibrosis, short-bowel syndrome, and bariatric surgery. Zinc deficiency presents with growth retardation/dwarfism, hypogonadism, hypogeusia, alopecia, immune dysfunction, and a periorificial/acral rash; the inherited form is acrodermatitis enteropathica, and penicillamine or chronic zinc itself (via copper depletion) can be culprits. Copper deficiency causes an anemia refractory to iron plus neutropenia and can be precipitated by chronic high-dose zinc; inherited disorders include Menkes kinky-hair syndrome (ATP7A) and aceruloplasminemia. Selenium deficiency causes Keshan cardiomyopathy in low-soil regions; combined iodine and selenium deficiency can aggravate cretinism, while selenium excess causes selenosis (hair/nail loss, garlic breath, neuropathy). Biotin and choline deficiencies occur mainly with inborn errors or parenteral nutrition; high-dose biotin supplements can spuriously skew streptavidin-biotin immunoassays (e.g., falsely high free T4, falsely low TSH or troponin). Confusion, ophthalmoplegia, or ataxia in an alcoholic or malnourished patient before/during refeeding - possible Wernicke encephalopathy requiring immediate thiamine High-output cardiac failure with edema (wet beriberi) or Keshan-type cardiomyopathy (selenium) Night blindness, corneal xerosis, or keratomalacia signaling sight-threatening vitamin A deficiency Bleeding/hemorrhage with prolonged prothrombin time, especially neonatal intracranial or GI bleeding (vitamin K deficiency) Increased intracranial pressure, bulging fontanels, hypercalcemia, or papilledema suggesting vitamin A or D intoxication Iron-refractory anemia with neutropenia (copper deficiency, often from chronic high-dose zinc) Interpreting micronutrient blood levels during inflammation/acute illness without accounting for acute-phase redistribution (e.g., copper rises with ceruloplasmin, zinc and retinol fall), leading to over- or under-diagnosis Refeeding a malnourished or alcoholic patient with carbohydrate before giving thiamine, precipitating acute deficiency and lactic acidosis Attributing a prolonged prothrombin time solely to vitamin K deficiency in liver disease - if it fails to correct with vitamin K, the cause is hepatocellular Overlooking drug-induced deficiencies (isoniazid-B6, warfarin/orlistat-vitamin K, metformin-B12, chronic zinc-copper, penicillamine-zinc) and chronic high-dose B6 causing neuropathy Missing biotin supplement interference with streptavidin-biotin immunoassays (spurious thyroid, troponin, or hCG results) Assuming carotenemia (yellow palms/soles, spared sclerae) indicates jaundice; and giving high-dose beta-carotene to smokers, which raises lung cancer risk Vitamins are organic micronutrients that the body cannot synthesize in adequate amounts and that act largely as coenzymes or prosthetic groups (e.g., thiamine pyrophosphate in alpha-ketoacid decarboxylation; FAD/FMN flavoenzymes; NAD/NADP in redox reactions; pyridoxal phosphate in amino-acid metabolism). Fat-soluble vitamins (A, D, E, K) require intact fat absorption and act in vision, gene transcription, calcium homeostasis, antioxidant defense, and gamma-carboxylation of clotting factors. Trace minerals function within metalloenzymes (zinc in numerous metalloenzymes and transcription factors; copper in ceruloplasmin/ferroxidase, cytochrome c oxidase, superoxide dismutase; selenium in glutathione peroxidase and deiodinases). Deficiency arises from inadequate intake, malabsorption, increased losses (hemodialysis, diuretics, increased urinary excretion), drug interference (isoniazid-B6, warfarin-vitamin K, metformin-B12/thiamine, penicillamine-zinc), or genetic transport/enzyme defects. Conversely, supplements, fortification, and occupational exposures can cause clinically important toxicities; in the inflammatory/acute-phase state, micronutrients redistribute and standard laboratory levels become unreliable. Most deficiency syndromes respond well and reversibly to timely repletion: thiamine produces cardiovascular and ophthalmoplegic improvement within ~24 hours and scurvy improves within days, although Wernicke-Korsakoff psychosis may be permanent and vitamin E or B12 neurologic deficits may only partially recover if advanced. Vitamin A deficiency carries substantial mortality - keratomalacia blinds an estimated quarter-million children yearly with case-fatality of 4-25%, and supplementation in deficient populations reduces childhood mortality by roughly 23-34%. Untreated severe thiamine, niacin (death is the fourth 'D'), or selenium (Keshan) deficiency can be fatal, as can acute vitamin A or D intoxication. Deficiency severity is graded from subclinical/biochemical (laboratory abnormality without symptoms - 'hidden hunger') through overt clinical deficiency syndromes (beriberi, pellagra, scurvy, xerophthalmia, rickets) to life-threatening complications (Wernicke-Korsakoff, keratomalacia/blindness, hemorrhage, cardiomyopathy). Thiamine deficiency is classically dichotomized into wet (cardiovascular) and dry (neuropathic) beriberi with considerable overlap, and vitamin A xerophthalmia is staged from night blindness and conjunctival xerosis/Bitot's spots to corneal ulceration and keratomalacia.

Vitamin B12 deficiency — cobalamin deficiency, pernicious anaemia, hypocobalaminaemia Folate deficiency (other cause of megaloblastic anaemia) Myelodysplastic syndrome Hypothyroidism causing macrocytosis Alcohol-related macrocytosis and marrow suppression Other causes of peripheral neuropathy such as diabetes Copper deficiency myeloneuropathy Full blood count and blood film for macrocytosis and hypersegmented neutrophils Serum cobalamin, with methylmalonic acid and homocysteine when the level is equivocal Anti-intrinsic factor and anti-parietal cell antibodies for pernicious anaemia Reticulocyte count and haemolysis markers as ineffective erythropoiesis can raise LDH and bilirubin Assessment for malabsorption and coexisting iron or folate deficiency Classically causes a macrocytic megaloblastic anaemia, but neurological features can appear before anaemia and even with normal blood counts Subacute combined degeneration of the cord produces symmetrical distal paraesthesiae, loss of proprioception and vibration sense, and an unsteady gait Autoimmune loss of gastric intrinsic factor (pernicious anaemia) and prior gastric or terminal ileal surgery are common mechanisms of malabsorption Strict vegetarian and vegan diets, common in parts of India, are an important dietary cause because the vitamin is almost exclusively of animal origin A blood film may show oval macrocytes and hypersegmented neutrophils; marrow is megaloblastic Serum cobalamin can be borderline, so raised methylmalonic acid and homocysteine are useful confirmatory markers Replacement reverses the anaemia reliably, but longstanding neurological damage may only partially recover, making early treatment important Correcting B12 with folate alone can precipitate or worsen neurological deterioration, so B12 status must be assessed before treating a megaloblastic anaemia Progressive myelopathy or gait disturbance indicating subacute combined degeneration needing urgent treatment Severe anaemia with cardiorespiratory compromise Cognitive decline or psychiatric change attributable to deficiency Pancytopenia from profound megaloblastic marrow failure Treating megaloblastic anaemia with folate alone and masking or worsening B12-related neurological disease Attributing neurological symptoms to another cause because the blood count is normal Relying solely on a borderline serum cobalamin without functional markers Failing to identify and monitor pernicious anaemia and its association with other autoimmune disease and gastric cancer Cobalamin is a cofactor for methionine synthase and methylmalonyl-CoA mutase. Deficiency impairs conversion of homocysteine to methionine and of methylmalonyl-CoA to succinyl-CoA, disrupting DNA synthesis and myelin maintenance. Impaired DNA synthesis in haematopoietic precursors yields megaloblastic, ineffective erythropoiesis, while disordered myelin metabolism underlies the neuropathy and cord degeneration. Absorption depends on intrinsic factor from gastric parietal cells and an intact terminal ileum, so autoimmune gastritis, atrophic gastritis, gastric or ileal resection, and malabsorptive states all reduce uptake; dietary lack occurs when animal products are excluded. Haematological recovery is usually complete with replacement, but neurological recovery depends on how long deficiency was present; early treatment gives the best outcome while advanced cord degeneration may leave residual deficits.

Vitamin D deficiency — hypovitaminosis D, rickets, osteomalacia, calciferol deficiency Primary hyperparathyroidism Renal osteodystrophy in chronic kidney disease Hypophosphataemic rickets and other inherited defects Osteoporosis Malignancy or other cause of bone pain Inflammatory myopathy for the muscle weakness Serum 25-hydroxyvitamin D as the primary measure of status Calcium, phosphate, alkaline phosphatase, and parathyroid hormone Renal and liver function, given their role in vitamin D activation Radiographs showing looser zones (pseudofractures) or rachitic growth-plate changes Assessment for malabsorption when deficiency is severe or refractory In children deficiency causes rickets with bowing of the legs, widened wrists, a rachitic rosary, and delayed growth; in adults it causes osteomalacia with bone pain and proximal myopathy It is highly prevalent across India despite abundant sunshine, owing to skin pigmentation, covering clothing, indoor lifestyles, air pollution, and low dietary intake Serum 25-hydroxyvitamin D is the best marker of body stores; 1,25-dihydroxyvitamin D is not a reliable indicator of deficiency Biochemistry classically shows low or low-normal calcium and phosphate with a raised alkaline phosphatase and secondary hyperparathyroidism Risk groups include exclusively breastfed infants without supplementation, older housebound adults, and people with malabsorption or chronic kidney or liver disease Proximal muscle weakness and increased fall and fracture risk are important, sometimes overlooked, consequences Correction of deficiency together with adequate calcium intake improves bone mineralisation and muscle function Symptomatic hypocalcaemia with tetany, laryngospasm, or seizures Fragility or insufficiency fractures Severe deficiency in an infant with hypocalcaemic seizures or cardiomyopathy Refractory deficiency suggesting malabsorption or renal or hepatic disease Measuring 1,25-dihydroxyvitamin D instead of 25-hydroxyvitamin D to assess status Treating vitamin D without ensuring adequate calcium intake Overlooking deficiency as a cause of proximal myopathy and falls in older adults Missing severe hypocalcaemia before starting treatment Vitamin D is synthesised in skin under ultraviolet B exposure and obtained in smaller amounts from diet, then hydroxylated in the liver to 25-hydroxyvitamin D and in the kidney to the active 1,25-dihydroxyvitamin D. Its main role is to maintain calcium and phosphate homeostasis by enhancing intestinal absorption and supporting bone mineralisation. Deficiency reduces calcium and phosphate absorption, provoking secondary hyperparathyroidism that mobilises calcium from bone and increases phosphate loss. The resulting failure to mineralise osteoid produces soft bone: rickets at the growth plates of children and osteomalacia in adults. With adequate replacement and calcium intake, bone mineralisation and muscle strength recover and childhood rickets heals, though severe or prolonged rickets may leave residual skeletal deformity.

Vitamin D-dependent rickets type 1A (CYP27B1) — VDDR1A, pseudovitamin D deficiency rickets, 1-alpha-hydroxylase deficiency, vitamin D-dependent rickets type I Nutritional vitamin D deficiency rickets Vitamin D-dependent rickets type 2 (VDR resistance) Hypophosphataemic (FGF23-mediated) rickets Hypophosphatasia Renal osteodystrophy / chronic kidney disease mineral bone disorder Primary hypoparathyroidism causing hypocalcaemia Serum calcium, phosphate, and alkaline phosphatase Parathyroid hormone, typically elevated as a secondary response 25-hydroxyvitamin D (normal or high) with 1,25-dihydroxyvitamin D (characteristically low) Radiographs of wrists and knees showing rachitic metaphyseal changes Urinary calcium monitoring during treatment to avoid hypercalciuria CYP27B1 gene sequencing to confirm the diagnosis An autosomal recessive disorder caused by loss-of-function mutations in CYP27B1, the gene encoding renal 1-alpha-hydroxylase The enzyme defect prevents conversion of 25-hydroxyvitamin D to active 1,25-dihydroxyvitamin D, so activation rather than intake is the problem Presents in the first year or two of life with rickets, hypotonia, growth failure, tetany or seizures from hypocalcaemia, and skeletal deformity Biochemistry shows hypocalcaemia, hypophosphataemia, raised alkaline phosphatase, and secondary hyperparathyroidism The hallmark is a normal or high 25-hydroxyvitamin D with a characteristically low 1,25-dihydroxyvitamin D, distinguishing it from nutritional deficiency Unlike vitamin D-dependent rickets type 2, there is no alopecia because the receptor pathway is intact Treatment is lifelong physiological replacement with the active hormone calcitriol, which bypasses the enzymatic block, with calcium supplementation as needed Hypocalcaemic seizures or tetany in an infant Failure to thrive with progressive skeletal deformity Cardiac dysfunction from severe hypocalcaemia Hypercalcaemia or hypercalciuria from over-replacement with active vitamin D Misdiagnosing as ordinary nutritional deficiency and giving only parent vitamin D, which cannot bypass the enzyme block Not measuring 1,25-dihydroxyvitamin D, missing the diagnostic low-active/normal-substrate pattern Confusing it with type 2 disease, where high-dose therapy and receptor resistance apply Failing to monitor urinary calcium, allowing hypercalciuria and nephrocalcinosis on active vitamin D CYP27B1 encodes the renal mitochondrial enzyme 1-alpha-hydroxylase, which converts 25-hydroxyvitamin D into the biologically active 1,25-dihydroxyvitamin D. Biallelic loss-of-function mutations abolish this final activation step, so despite adequate substrate the active hormone cannot be produced. Deficient 1,25-dihydroxyvitamin D reduces intestinal calcium and phosphate absorption, producing hypocalcaemia and hypophosphataemia, which impair mineralisation of growth-plate cartilage and osteoid, causing rickets and osteomalacia. Hypocalcaemia drives secondary hyperparathyroidism, further increasing renal phosphate loss and bone resorption. Because the enzyme, not the receptor, is defective, providing calcitriol directly restores signalling and corrects the disorder. Prognosis is excellent with lifelong physiological calcitriol replacement, which normalises calcium and heals the rickets; growth and bone health are usually restored, provided treatment is maintained and monitored to avoid toxicity.

Vitamin D-dependent rickets type 2 (VDR, hereditary vitamin D resistance) — VDDR2, hereditary vitamin D-resistant rickets, HVDRR, vitamin D receptor defect rickets Vitamin D-dependent rickets type 1A (CYP27B1) Nutritional vitamin D deficiency rickets Hypophosphataemic (FGF23-mediated) rickets Hypophosphatasia Ectodermal dysplasia or other causes of congenital alopecia Primary hypoparathyroidism Serum calcium, phosphate, and alkaline phosphatase Parathyroid hormone, usually elevated 25-hydroxyvitamin D (normal) with markedly elevated 1,25-dihydroxyvitamin D Radiographs demonstrating rachitic changes Clinical assessment for alopecia and its extent as a prognostic marker VDR gene sequencing to confirm the receptor defect An autosomal recessive disorder caused by loss-of-function mutations in the vitamin D receptor (VDR), producing end-organ resistance to 1,25-dihydroxyvitamin D Unlike type 1A, the active hormone is made in abundance but cannot signal, so 1,25-dihydroxyvitamin D is markedly elevated Presents in infancy with rickets, hypocalcaemia, hypophosphataemia, raised alkaline phosphatase, and secondary hyperparathyroidism A characteristic and often distinguishing feature is total-body alopecia, reflecting the VDR role in the hair follicle, which does not occur in type 1A The degree of receptor dysfunction determines severity, and alopecia generally signals more severe, treatment-resistant disease Diagnosis rests on the combination of rickets with very high 1,25-dihydroxyvitamin D and normal 25-hydroxyvitamin D, confirmed by VDR sequencing Management uses high-dose active vitamin D (calcitriol) with high-dose calcium; unresponsive cases may need long-term intravenous or intensive enteral calcium to bypass defective intestinal absorption Hypocalcaemic seizures or tetany in infancy Total alopecia signalling severe, potentially calcitriol-resistant disease Progressive deformity and growth failure despite therapy Hypercalcaemia or nephrocalcinosis from aggressive calcium and active vitamin D regimens Confusing it with type 1A, where standard-dose calcitriol suffices and there is no alopecia Interpreting the very high 1,25-dihydroxyvitamin D as adequacy rather than resistance Underdosing calcium in resistant cases where enteral or intravenous calcium is the key therapy Overtreating and causing hypercalcaemia and nephrocalcinosis without urinary calcium monitoring The vitamin D receptor mediates the genomic actions of 1,25-dihydroxyvitamin D. Loss-of-function mutations, affecting hormone binding or DNA binding, render target tissues resistant to the active hormone despite high circulating levels. Intestinal calcium and phosphate absorption fail, causing hypocalcaemia, hypophosphataemia, and impaired mineralisation with rickets and osteomalacia. Hypocalcaemia stimulates secondary hyperparathyroidism, and the unopposed feedback loop drives 1-alpha-hydroxylase, elevating 1,25-dihydroxyvitamin D further. Because the receptor is also essential for postnatal hair follicle cycling, many mutations cause alopecia, which tends to accompany the more severe, calcitriol-resistant phenotypes. Overcoming resistance therapeutically requires supraphysiological active vitamin D and calcium, sometimes delivered parenterally. Outcome depends on the residual receptor function: milder defects may respond to high-dose active vitamin D and calcium, whereas severe receptor-null disease, often with alopecia, may require prolonged intensive or intravenous calcium, and some patients improve spontaneously after childhood.

Vitamin E deficiency — tocopherol deficiency Friedreich ataxia Subacute combined degeneration (vitamin B12 deficiency) Other spinocerebellar ataxias Copper deficiency myeloneuropathy Abetalipoproteinaemia Serum vitamin E interpreted relative to serum lipids Assessment for fat malabsorption and its cause Lipid profile and lipoprotein studies (for abetalipoproteinaemia) Neurological examination and, where needed, nerve conduction studies Genetic testing for ataxia with vitamin E deficiency in suggestive cases A fat-soluble vitamin deficiency that chiefly causes a progressive neurological syndrome Features resemble Friedreich ataxia: spinocerebellar ataxia, loss of proprioception and vibration sense, and areflexia A pigmentary retinopathy and, in infants, haemolysis can occur Dietary deficiency is rare; most cases result from fat malabsorption (for example cholestasis, cystic fibrosis, short bowel) or from the inherited disorder ataxia with vitamin E deficiency Abetalipoproteinaemia is an important cause in which vitamin E cannot be transported Serum vitamin E is measured relative to lipids, and treatment is supplementation with correction of malabsorption Progressive ataxia and sensory loss Visual decline from retinopathy Underlying severe malabsorptive disease Infantile haemolysis Interpreting vitamin E levels without correcting for lipids Missing the treatable genetic cause (ataxia with vitamin E deficiency) mimicking Friedreich ataxia Overlooking underlying fat malabsorption Delaying replacement until deficits are irreversible Vitamin E (alpha-tocopherol) is a lipid-soluble antioxidant that protects cell membranes, particularly of neurons, from oxidative damage. Deficiency, usually from fat malabsorption or defective tocopherol transport, leads to oxidative injury of the large myelinated sensory neurons and spinocerebellar and posterior column pathways, producing a sensory ataxic neuropathy. Because absorption depends on normal fat digestion and lipoprotein handling, disorders of these processes, or the genetic ataxia with vitamin E deficiency, are the usual causes. Early supplementation can halt and partially reverse neurological features, but established deficits may be permanent if treatment is delayed.

Vitamin K deficiency — hypovitaminosis K, vitamin K deficiency bleeding, haemorrhagic disease of the newborn Liver disease causing impaired synthesis of clotting factors Disseminated intravascular coagulation Inherited coagulation factor deficiencies Warfarin or other anticoagulant effect Other bleeding disorders such as thrombocytopenia or platelet dysfunction Prothrombin time and activated partial thromboplastin time Assessment of liver function to distinguish hepatic synthetic failure Response of coagulation parameters to vitamin K repletion Evaluation for fat malabsorption and biliary obstruction in adults Consideration of coexisting fat-soluble vitamin deficiencies Deficiency causes a bleeding tendency with a prolonged prothrombin time, and in more severe cases a prolonged activated partial thromboplastin time Newborns are especially vulnerable because of low placental transfer, immature gut flora, and low vitamin K content of breast milk, causing vitamin K deficiency bleeding Routine neonatal vitamin K prophylaxis prevents haemorrhagic disease of the newborn, including its dangerous late intracranial form In adults it results from fat malabsorption, biliary obstruction, prolonged antibiotic use, or poor intake, since much vitamin K also comes from gut bacteria Warfarin acts by antagonising vitamin K, and its effect can be reversed by vitamin K when correction is needed The coagulopathy corrects with vitamin K repletion, and rapid correction confirms the diagnosis Because it is fat soluble, deficiency clusters with deficiencies of vitamins A, D, and E in malabsorptive states Active or severe bleeding, including gastrointestinal haemorrhage Intracranial haemorrhage, especially late vitamin K deficiency bleeding in an infant Coagulopathy in a patient requiring urgent surgery or intervention Bleeding in the context of significant liver disease requiring broader management Assuming a prolonged prothrombin time reflects liver disease when it is correctable vitamin K deficiency, or vice versa Overlooking fat malabsorption or biliary obstruction as the underlying cause Failing to ensure neonatal vitamin K prophylaxis Not recognising coexisting deficiency of other fat-soluble vitamins Vitamin K is a cofactor for the gamma-carboxylation of glutamate residues on clotting factors II, VII, IX, and X and on the anticoagulant proteins C and S, a modification required for their activity. Deficiency leaves these factors undercarboxylated and functionally inactive, impairing coagulation and producing bleeding. The vitamin is fat soluble and derives from dietary green vegetables and from synthesis by intestinal bacteria, so inadequate intake, fat malabsorption, absence of bile, and suppression of gut flora all reduce availability. Neonates start with low stores and sterile guts, explaining their particular susceptibility. Deficiency-related coagulopathy corrects reliably and rapidly with vitamin K when there is no severe liver disease; neonatal prophylaxis largely prevents the life-threatening bleeding of infancy.

Combined vitamin K-dependent clotting factor deficiency (GGCX/VKORC1) — VKCFD, combined deficiency of vitamin K-dependent clotting factors, GGCX deficiency, VKORC1 deficiency, gamma-glutamyl carboxylase deficiency Acquired vitamin K deficiency (malabsorption, poor intake, biliary obstruction) Warfarin or other vitamin K antagonist effect, including inadvertent ingestion Haemorrhagic disease of the newborn from vitamin K deficiency Liver disease with impaired factor synthesis Isolated inherited deficiency of a single vitamin K-dependent factor Disseminated intravascular coagulation Prothrombin time and activated partial thromboplastin time, both prolonged Individual assays of factors II, VII, IX and X, and of proteins C and S Response of clotting times to vitamin K administration Measurement of undercarboxylated (des-gamma-carboxy) proteins where available GGCX and VKORC1 gene analysis to confirm the diagnosis Evaluation for skeletal or connective-tissue features in suspected GGCX defects A rare autosomal recessive disorder causing concurrent deficiency of the vitamin K-dependent clotting factors II, VII, IX and X, and of proteins C and S Bleeding varies from mild to severe and may present in the neonatal period with intracranial or umbilical bleeding, mimicking severe haemorrhagic disease of the newborn Both the prothrombin time and the activated partial thromboplastin time are prolonged, reflecting the multiple factor deficiencies GGCX variants can also cause skeletal and connective-tissue features, such as a pseudoxanthoma-elasticum-like phenotype, alongside the coagulopathy Affected individuals show marked sensitivity to warfarin because the same vitamin K cycle enzymes are involved Some patients respond, at least partially, to vitamin K because it drives residual carboxylase or reductase activity Management uses vitamin K and, for acute or severe bleeding, replacement of the vitamin K-dependent factors Neonatal intracranial haemorrhage Severe mucosal, gastrointestinal, or intra-abdominal bleeding Marked bleeding provoked by a standard warfarin dose Umbilical or postpartum bleeding suggesting a severe congenital coagulopathy Attributing the coagulopathy solely to dietary vitamin K deficiency or occult warfarin exposure Not recognising warfarin hypersensitivity, leading to over-anticoagulation Overlooking associated skeletal or connective-tissue features in GGCX defects Failing to check the response to vitamin K, which can guide management The vitamin K-dependent clotting factors require gamma-carboxylation of glutamate residues to become functional, a reaction catalysed by gamma-glutamyl carboxylase (GGCX) that consumes reduced vitamin K. Vitamin K epoxide reductase (VKORC1) regenerates the reduced vitamin needed for this cycle. Loss-of-function variants in GGCX or VKORC1 impair carboxylation, so factors II, VII, IX and X, and the anticoagulant proteins C and S, are secreted as poorly functional undercarboxylated proteins. The dominant clinical effect is bleeding, and because the same enzymes are the target of coumarin anticoagulants, affected patients are hypersensitive to warfarin. With vitamin K supplementation and factor replacement for acute bleeding, most patients achieve satisfactory haemostasis and a good long-term outlook. Severity depends on the residual enzyme activity, and neonatal presentations carry higher risk if not promptly recognised.

Vitiligo — leucoderma, acquired depigmentation Pityriasis versicolor (hypopigmented type) Post-inflammatory hypopigmentation Pityriasis alba Tuberculoid leprosy (hypopigmented anaesthetic patch) Naevus depigmentosus or naevus anaemicus Chemical or occupational leucoderma Clinical diagnosis aided by Wood's lamp examination Thyroid function tests and thyroid autoantibodies given autoimmune associations Screening for other autoimmune disease when clinically indicated Skin biopsy only in atypical cases to confirm melanocyte loss Assessment of disease activity and extent to guide and monitor therapy Presents as well-demarcated, chalk-white macules and patches with complete loss of pigment, typically symmetrical in the common non-segmental form Favoured sites include periorificial areas (around the eyes and mouth), the hands, and other acral and extensor surfaces Wood's lamp examination accentuates the depigmented patches and helps detect early or subtle lesions, especially in lighter skin New patches may appear at sites of trauma or friction (Koebner phenomenon) As an autoimmune condition, it is associated with other autoimmune diseases, particularly thyroid disease, so consider screening for these Management options include topical corticosteroids and calcineurin inhibitors, phototherapy for more extensive disease, and rigorous photoprotection of depigmented skin The psychosocial impact can be substantial, particularly in darker skin and in visible areas, and should be addressed directly Set realistic expectations: repigmentation is slow and variable, and hair-bearing and facial areas respond better than acral sites Rapidly spreading depigmentation indicating active, unstable disease A solitary hypopigmented patch with reduced sensation, which should prompt exclusion of leprosy where endemic Symptoms suggesting associated autoimmune disease, such as thyroid dysfunction Significant psychological distress warranting mental health support Confusing it with pityriasis versicolor or post-inflammatory hypopigmentation Failing to protect depigmented skin from sunburn and photodamage Overlooking associated autoimmune thyroid disease Underestimating the psychological burden and promising unrealistic repigmentation Vitiligo is an acquired disorder characterised by immune-mediated destruction of epidermal melanocytes, leading to loss of pigment. Current understanding emphasises an interplay of genetic susceptibility, intrinsic melanocyte vulnerability with oxidative stress, and an autoimmune response in which CD8 cytotoxic T cells and interferon-gamma signalling target and destroy melanocytes. The absence of functioning melanocytes leaves affected skin devoid of melanin, producing the characteristic depigmented macules. Non-segmental vitiligo tends to be symmetrical and progressive with autoimmune associations, whereas segmental vitiligo is localised to a dermatomal-like distribution and often stabilises after an early active phase. Vitiligo follows an unpredictable course; spontaneous repigmentation is uncommon and treatment results are variable, with facial and truncal lesions generally more responsive than acral and hair-bearing sites. It is not physically dangerous but can be psychologically distressing and often chronic.

Vitreomacular traction syndrome — VMT, vitreomacular traction, vitreomacular traction syndrome, symptomatic vitreomacular adhesion Full-thickness or lamellar macular hole Epiretinal membrane (macular pucker) Cystoid macular oedema Diabetic macular oedema with vitreomacular interface disease Central serous chorioretinopathy Choroidal neovascular membrane Myopic traction maculopathy Optical coherence tomography to confirm vitreomacular adhesion and traction and to grade its extent Amsler grid testing to detect and monitor metamorphopsia Best-corrected visual acuity measurement to follow functional change Fundus examination to assess the vitreoretinal interface and exclude coexisting pathology B-scan ultrasonography where media opacity limits OCT assessment of the vitreous Serial imaging to detect progression to a macular hole or spontaneous resolution Arises when an incomplete posterior vitreous detachment leaves the vitreous abnormally adherent to the macula and exerting anteroposterior and tangential traction More common with increasing age and in conditions with abnormal vitreoretinal adhesion, and it forms part of a spectrum with macular hole and epiretinal membrane Symptoms include metamorphopsia, blurred central vision, micropsia and sometimes photopsia Optical coherence tomography is the definitive investigation, showing persistent vitreomacular adhesion with distortion of the foveal contour, intraretinal cysts and elevation Traction is often classified by the breadth of adhesion (focal versus broad) and by whether concurrent macular pathology such as an epiretinal membrane is present, which influences management The Amsler grid is useful for detecting and monitoring distortion between reviews Some cases resolve spontaneously when the vitreous fully separates, so observation is reasonable for mild, stable disease Management of persistent or progressive symptomatic traction includes pars plana vitrectomy to relieve traction, with pharmacologic vitreolysis or observation considered in selected cases Progressive distortion or acuity loss indicating worsening traction Development of a full-thickness macular hole Associated retinal detachment or a peripheral retinal tear Rapid change suggesting a coexisting exudative or vascular macular process Relying on fundus examination alone without OCT to confirm and characterise the traction Intervening early in mild cases that might resolve spontaneously with completion of vitreous separation Missing an evolving or established macular hole beneath the traction Overlooking a coexisting epiretinal membrane that alters the surgical plan and prognosis Attributing visual symptoms solely to traction while missing a concurrent macular disease With ageing, the vitreous gel liquefies and begins to separate from the retina, but abnormally strong adhesion at the fovea can cause the separation to be incomplete. The persistently attached posterior hyaloid then exerts anteroposterior and tangential traction on the macula. This mechanical traction distorts the foveal architecture, produces intraretinal cystic spaces and can elevate or detach the fovea, causing metamorphopsia and reduced acuity. If traction is unrelieved it may progress to a lamellar or full-thickness macular hole or contribute to macular oedema; conversely, spontaneous completion of the posterior vitreous detachment can release the traction and resolve the syndrome. Outcomes vary with the severity and duration of traction: mild cases may resolve spontaneously with good vision, while persistent traction can cause lasting distortion or progress to a macular hole; surgical relief of traction generally improves symptoms, though visual recovery may be partial and gradual.

haemorrhage warrants a search for an underlying vascular or neovascular cause An underlying retinal tear or detachment requiring urgent treatment to preserve vision Sudden profound visual loss with an obscured fundus needing prompt ultrasound assessment Neovascularisation from proliferative diabetic retinopathy or ischaemic vein occlusion requiring timely treatment Vitreous haemorrhage in a child raising concern for non-accidental injury Bilateral haemorrhage or associated neurological symptoms suggesting Terson syndrome Failing to perform B-scan ultrasound and missing an underlying retinal detachment behind dense blood Attributing the bleed to an obvious cause without examining for a retinal tear Overlooking non-accidental injury in a child with vitreous haemorrhage Delaying treatment of proliferative retinopathy while awaiting spontaneous clearance Vitreous haemorrhage is extravasation of blood into or around the vitreous cavity. It occurs when abnormal new vessels (as in proliferative diabetic retinopathy or ischaemic vein occlusion) bleed, when normal retinal vessels are torn during posterior vitreous detachment or a retinal tear, or when trauma ruptures vessels. Blood disperses through the vitreous gel, scattering light and obscuring vision. Clearance is slow because the avascular vitreous reabsorbs blood inefficiently, and long-standing blood can lead to fibrosis and tractional complications. Prognosis depends on the cause; haemorrhage from a posterior vitreous detachment often clears well, whereas bleeding from proliferative retinopathy or an associated retinal detachment carries a higher risk of recurrence and permanent visual loss without treatment.

Vocal cord dysfunction — paradoxical vocal fold motion, inducible laryngeal obstruction Asthma Exercise-induced bronchoconstriction Fixed laryngeal or tracheal obstruction Anaphylaxis with laryngeal oedema Bilateral vocal cord palsy Anxiety or panic attacks Flexible laryngoscopy, ideally during symptoms or after provocation Spirometry with attention to truncation of the inspiratory flow-volume loop Assessment for reflux, rhinosinusitis and asthma as triggers or comorbidities Exercise or irritant challenge where episodes are provoked Psychological assessment where relevant Inappropriate adduction of the vocal folds during inspiration causes episodic breathlessness and stridor that mimic asthma Symptoms characteristically feature difficulty getting air in, throat tightness and inspiratory noise localised to the neck Attacks are often sudden in onset and offset and may be triggered by exercise, irritants, strong smells or stress It is frequently misdiagnosed as refractory asthma, leading to escalating and ineffective inhaled therapy Direct laryngoscopy during an episode, showing paradoxical adduction, is the diagnostic gold standard Speech and language therapy with breathing retraining is the cornerstone of management Stridor with hypoxia or signs of significant airway compromise Suspected anaphylaxis Features suggesting a fixed structural airway lesion Progressive or persistent (non-episodic) obstruction Misdiagnosing it as refractory asthma and escalating inhaled or oral steroids Failing to capture the larynx during an episode Overlooking coexisting asthma, reflux or rhinosinusitis Not involving speech and language therapy early Vocal cord dysfunction, also termed inducible laryngeal obstruction, involves paradoxical closure of the vocal folds during inspiration, transiently narrowing the glottic airway. Laryngeal hyperresponsiveness to triggers such as reflux, postnasal drip, exercise, airborne irritants and psychological stress is thought to drive the abnormal reflex adduction. Because the obstruction is at the larynx rather than the lower airways, it produces predominantly inspiratory symptoms and does not respond to bronchodilators, distinguishing it from asthma even though the two can coexist. The condition is not life-threatening in most cases and responds well to breathing retraining and treatment of triggers, though it can be recurrent and disabling if unrecognised.
