vocal fold (contact or vocal process) granuloma is an inflammatory reparative response rather than a true tumour. Mechanical trauma to the thin mucosa overlying the arytenoid vocal process, from forceful vocal contact, chronic cough or throat clearing, or an endotracheal tube, denudes the epithelium and exposes perichondrium. Acid and pepsin refluxing to the posterior larynx impair healing and perpetuate mucosal injury, so exuberant granulation tissue forms. Because the insult is ongoing, granulomas frequently recur unless the underlying reflux and phonotraumatic behaviours are corrected. Many granulomas resolve slowly with medical and behavioural treatment, though this can take months; recurrence is frequent if reflux and phonotrauma are not controlled, whereas long-term outcomes are good once the underlying causes are addressed.

Vocal cord nodules — vocal fold nodules, singer's nodules, screamer's nodules Vocal cord polyp (usually unilateral) Reinke oedema Vocal cord cyst Contact granuloma of the vocal process Laryngeal papilloma Early laryngeal carcinoma or leukoplakia Functional (muscle tension) dysphonia Laryngoscopy (flexible or rigid) to visualise the folds Videostroboscopy to assess the mucosal wave and glottic closure Voice assessment and acoustic analysis by a speech and language therapist Biopsy of any atypical or suspicious lesion to exclude malignancy Assessment for contributing factors such as reflux, allergy and vocal habits Vocal cord nodules are small, usually bilateral swellings on the vocal folds caused by chronic voice misuse or overuse They typically sit at the junction of the anterior third and posterior two-thirds of the fold, the point of maximal contact during phonation They are common in professional voice users, teachers, singers and habitually loud children The main symptom is progressive hoarseness, often with vocal fatigue and a breathy quality, worse with use On laryngoscopy early lesions look soft and reddish while long-standing nodules become firm, white and fibrotic The mainstay of treatment is voice rest and speech therapy to correct the underlying vocal behaviour, which resolves most early nodules Surgical excision (microlaryngoscopy) is reserved for mature fibrotic nodules that fail conservative treatment, and must be followed by voice therapy to prevent recurrence Any hoarseness persisting beyond a few weeks, particularly in adults with risk factors, needs laryngeal examination to exclude malignancy Persistent hoarseness beyond a few weeks in an adult, especially with smoking or alcohol use, requiring exclusion of malignancy A unilateral, irregular or ulcerated lesion suggesting neoplasia rather than a nodule Associated stridor, airway compromise or difficulty swallowing Neck mass or referred otalgia accompanying the voice change Unexplained weight loss or haemoptysis Proceeding to surgery before an adequate trial of voice therapy Mistaking a unilateral polyp, cyst or malignancy for benign nodules Failing to arrange voice therapy after surgery, leading to recurrence Ignoring persistent adult hoarseness that warrants cancer exclusion Overlooking contributing factors such as reflux and ongoing vocal abuse Vocal cord nodules form in response to repeated mechanical trauma from vocal abuse. Forceful or excessive vocal fold collision, especially at the midpoint of the membranous cord where impact stress is greatest, causes localised oedema and microhaemorrhage in the superficial lamina propria. With continued strain this reactive change organises into fibrosis and thickening of the overlying epithelium, producing symmetrical nodules on the medial edges of both folds. These masses prevent complete glottic closure and add mass to the vibrating edge, disrupting the mucosal wave and generating hoarseness and a breathy voice. Because both folds strike each other, lesions are characteristically bilateral and roughly symmetrical. Early, soft nodules usually resolve completely with voice rest and speech therapy, and the outlook is excellent when vocal behaviour is corrected; mature fibrotic nodules may need surgery and, without behavioural change, nodules commonly recur.

intrinsic laryngeal muscles, and may be unilateral or bilateral Unilateral palsy typically causes a breathy, weak voice and sometimes aspiration, as the healthy cord may compensate over time Bilateral palsy is more dangerous: the cords may sit near the midline, threatening the airway and causing stridor The left recurrent laryngeal nerve has a longer intrathoracic course, making it more vulnerable to chest pathology such as mediastinal or lung disease Common causes include surgical injury (notably thyroid surgery), malignancy along the nerve's course, and neurological or idiopathic causes A thorough search for the cause is essential, examining the neck, thyroid, chest and skull base along the nerve pathway Management principles include voice therapy, treating the underlying cause, and procedures such as injection or medialisation to improve glottic closure In bilateral palsy with airway compromise, securing the airway takes priority, sometimes requiring tracheostomy Bilateral palsy with stridor or respiratory distress requiring urgent airway management Progressive symptoms with a neck mass, weight loss or haemoptysis suggesting malignancy Aspiration with recurrent chest infections from poor glottic closure Associated cranial nerve deficits pointing to a skull base or brainstem lesion Labelling a palsy idiopathic without imaging the entire nerve pathway to exclude a tumour Underestimating airway risk in bilateral palsy Missing silent aspiration in patients with poor glottic closure Confusing cricoarytenoid joint fixation or cancer with a neurogenic palsy Vocal cord palsy arises from interruption anywhere along the motor pathway to the larynx, from the brainstem nucleus through the vagus and recurrent laryngeal nerves to the intrinsic laryngeal muscles. Loss of innervation impairs abduction and adduction of the affected fold, so it rests in a position determined by the residual muscle tone and any compensatory changes. The recurrent laryngeal nerve's long course, especially on the left where it loops under the aortic arch, exposes it to compression or invasion by neck and chest disease and to iatrogenic injury during surgery. The functional consequence depends on the resting position of the cords and whether one or both are affected. Prognosis depends on the cause and whether the palsy is unilateral or bilateral; some idiopathic or postviral unilateral palsies recover, others compensate with voice therapy, while bilateral palsy often needs airway intervention and malignant causes carry the outlook of the underlying disease.

tracheostomy for the airway, with later procedures to enlarge the glottis balanced against voice Bilateral paralysis with stridor or dyspnoea, an airway emergency A new paralysis without an obvious surgical cause, mandating a search for malignancy along the nerve Significant aspiration with recurrent chest infection or weight loss Accompanying cranial nerve deficits pointing to a skull base or brainstem lesion Labelling a paralysis idiopathic before adequately imaging the entire course of the vagus and recurrent laryngeal nerve Mistaking cricoarytenoid joint fixation for neurogenic paralysis without electromyography Performing a permanent static medialisation too early, before spontaneous recovery has been given time Underestimating the airway risk of bilateral paralysis and delaying airway protection Vocal fold paralysis arises from interruption of the motor supply to the intrinsic laryngeal muscles anywhere along the vagus nerve and its recurrent laryngeal branch, from the brainstem nucleus to the muscle. Because the recurrent laryngeal nerve loops into the thorax, particularly on the left around the aortic arch, lesions in the neck, chest, or skull base can all be responsible; common mechanisms include surgical trauma, malignant infiltration, and neuropathy, with a proportion remaining idiopathic. Loss of adductor and abductor tone leaves the fold in a paramedian or intermediate position. In unilateral loss the mobile fold cannot fully compensate, giving incomplete closure with a breathy voice and aspiration; in bilateral loss both folds sit near the midline, so the voice may be preserved but the airway is critically narrowed. Idiopathic and some postsurgical unilateral palsies may recover over many months, and most patients achieve a functional voice with therapy or medialisation; bilateral paralysis has a more guarded outlook because improving the airway usually comes at the expense of voice quality.

electromyography shows myopathic changes that may coexist with features suggesting neurogenic involvement Diagnosis relies on the characteristic distal-plus-bulbar phenotype confirmed by MATR3 genetic testing Progressive dysphagia with aspiration risk or weight loss Declining respiratory function or nocturnal hypoventilation Features of motor neuron disease such as fasciculations, brisk reflexes, or bulbar wasting Rapid deterioration atypical for a slowly progressive distal myopathy Stridor or airway compromise from vocal cord dysfunction Mistaking the bulbar features for oculopharyngeal muscular dystrophy or myasthenia gravis Overlooking respiratory muscle weakness and aspiration risk Missing an overlapping motor neuron disease phenotype linked to MATR3 Attributing dysphonia solely to a laryngeal cause without recognising the underlying myopathy The disorder is caused by dominant variants in MATR3, encoding matrin-3, an RNA- and DNA-binding protein of the nuclear matrix involved in RNA processing, stability, and transport. Disease-associated variants alter matrin-3 handling of RNA and its protein interactions, leading to abnormal protein accumulation and dysfunction in muscle and, in some individuals, motor neurons. This shared molecular biology explains the overlap with motor neuron disease. In muscle the process causes a distal myopathy with particular vulnerability of laryngeal and pharyngeal muscles, producing the characteristic vocal cord and swallowing involvement. Limb weakness usually progresses slowly, but bulbar and respiratory involvement can significantly affect quality of life and survival; prognosis is worse if the phenotype overlaps with motor neuron disease, making swallowing and respiratory surveillance essential.

form) Clinical and photographic monitoring of digital constriction bands Radiographs of digits where bony involvement or impending autoamputation is suspected Assessment for associated ichthyosis in the variant form A mutilating palmoplantar keratoderma characterised by a distinctive honeycomb (honeycomb-patterned) hyperkeratosis of the palms and soles Starfish-shaped (stellate) keratoses over the knuckles and dorsa of the digits are a highly suggestive sign Constricting fibrous bands (pseudo-ainhum) form around digits and can progress to autoamputation The classic form is associated with sensorineural deafness and results from dominant GJB2 (connexin 26) mutations A variant form (Camisa) has associated ichthyosis and is caused by loronin mutations in the LOR gene Onset is usually in infancy or early childhood with progression of the keratoderma over time Management is supportive with emollients/keratolytics and oral retinoids, with surgical release of constricting bands to prevent digital loss Progressive pseudo-ainhum threatening digital viability or autoamputation Secondary infection or ulceration of fissured keratotic skin New or worsening hearing loss requiring audiological input Functional impairment of the hands limiting activity Failing to recognise and release pseudo-ainhum bands early, allowing digital autoamputation Not distinguishing the deafness-associated (GJB2) form from the ichthyosis (loricrin) variant, which affects counselling Overlooking the honeycomb pattern and stellate knuckle keratoses that distinguish it from other keratodermas Reliance on keratolytics alone when retinoids and surgery may be needed Vohwinkel syndrome exists in two genetically distinct forms. The classic form with deafness is caused by dominant mutations in GJB2 encoding connexin 26, a gap-junction protein; abnormal gap-junction channels disturb epidermal cell-to-cell communication and cochlear function. The variant form associated with ichthyosis arises from mutations in LOR encoding loricrin, a major component of the cornified cell envelope, leading to defective envelope assembly and abnormal terminal differentiation of keratinocytes. In both, disordered keratinisation produces the honeycomb keratoderma and stellate keratoses, and progressive fibrous constriction (pseudo-ainhum) around digits can strangulate them, causing autoamputation. The keratoderma is chronic and progressive, and the principal threat is loss of digits from constricting bands. With emollient/keratolytic care, oral retinoids and timely surgical band release, digital function can often be preserved, though the condition is not curable.

Von Gierke disease (glycogen storage disease type I) — glycogen storage disease type I, GSD I, glucose-6-phosphatase deficiency, G6PC deficiency, SLC37A4 deficiency, GSD Ia, GSD Ib Other hepatic glycogen storage diseases (types III, VI, IX) Fructose-1,6-bisphosphatase deficiency and other gluconeogenesis defects Hereditary fructose intolerance and galactosaemia Fatty acid oxidation disorders causing fasting hypoglycaemia Hyperinsulinism Organic acidaemias with lactic acidosis Blood glucose, lactate, uric acid, and lipid profile during controlled fasting Liver ultrasonography and surveillance imaging for hepatic adenomas Renal function tests and urinalysis for proteinuria and microalbuminuria Full blood count for neutropenia in suspected type Ib Molecular genetic testing of G6PC and SLC37A4 Bone densitometry for osteopenia in longstanding disease Autosomal recessive disorder of the terminal step of gluconeogenesis and glycogenolysis; type Ia results from glucose-6-phosphatase deficiency (G6PC) and type Ib from a defect in the glucose-6-phosphate transporter (SLC37A4) Presents in infancy with severe fasting hypoglycaemia, marked hepatomegaly, and a doll-like facies with truncal adiposity The biochemical hallmark is fasting hypoglycaemia accompanied by lactic acidosis, hyperuricaemia, and hyperlipidaemia (raised triglycerides and cholesterol) Type Ib additionally causes neutropenia and impaired neutrophil function, predisposing to recurrent infections and inflammatory bowel-like disease Long-term complications include hepatic adenomas (with malignant potential), nephropathy with proteinuria, gout, growth retardation, and osteopenia Cornerstone of management is maintaining euglycaemia with frequent feeds and uncooked cornstarch therapy while restricting galactose and fructose Lactate can serve as an alternative cerebral fuel, which may partly protect the brain during hypoglycaemic episodes Severe symptomatic hypoglycaemia with seizures or reduced consciousness Severe lactic acidosis during metabolic decompensation Rapidly enlarging or bleeding hepatic adenoma or features suggesting malignant transformation Serious infection or gut inflammation in neutropenic type Ib patients Failing to prevent nocturnal hypoglycaemia by omitting overnight feeding or cornstarch Overlooking neutropenia and its complications in type Ib Missing surveillance for hepatic adenoma and renal disease during long-term follow-up Giving galactose- or fructose-containing feeds that worsen the metabolic derangement Glycogen storage disease type I is caused by deficiency of the glucose-6-phosphatase system, which catalyses the final common step releasing free glucose from glucose-6-phosphate in both glycogenolysis and gluconeogenesis. In type Ia the catalytic enzyme glucose-6-phosphatase is deficient, whereas in type Ib the microsomal transporter that moves glucose-6-phosphate into the endoplasmic reticulum is defective. As a result the liver, kidney, and intestine cannot release glucose during fasting, causing profound hypoglycaemia. Accumulating glucose-6-phosphate is diverted into glycolysis and the pentose phosphate and lipogenic pathways, generating excess lactate, uric acid, and triglycerides, while glycogen and fat accumulate in the liver and kidney. In type Ib, impaired glucose-6-phosphate transport also disturbs neutrophil function, producing neutropenia. With meticulous dietary control to maintain euglycaemia, most patients survive into adulthood with good outcomes; long-term risks of hepatic adenoma with malignant potential, progressive nephropathy, and, in type Ib, infective complications remain the major determinants of prognosis.

Von Hippel-Lindau disease — VHL, VHL syndrome, familial cerebelloretinal angiomatosis, VHL gene Sporadic haemangioblastoma or isolated renal cell carcinoma Hereditary phaeochromocytoma-paraganglioma syndromes (SDHx, MAX, TMEM127) Multiple endocrine neoplasia type 2 Neurofibromatosis type 1 Tuberous sclerosis complex with renal angiomyolipomas and cysts Birt-Hogg-Dube syndrome with renal tumours Germline molecular genetic testing of the VHL gene, including deletion/duplication analysis Dilated retinal examination for retinal haemangioblastomas Contrast-enhanced MRI of brain and spine for haemangioblastomas Cross-sectional abdominal imaging (MRI or ultrasound) for renal, pancreatic and adrenal lesions Plasma or urinary fractionated metanephrines to detect catecholamine-secreting tumours Audiology and dedicated internal auditory meatus imaging if endolymphatic sac tumour suspected Autosomal dominant tumour-predisposition syndrome caused by germline loss-of-function variants in the VHL tumour-suppressor gene on chromosome 3p, with tumours arising after a somatic second hit Hallmark lesions are retinal and central nervous system haemangioblastomas, especially of the cerebellum, brainstem and spinal cord Clear-cell renal cell carcinoma and renal cysts are a major cause of morbidity and mortality and are frequently bilateral and multifocal Phaeochromocytomas and paragangliomas may be the presenting feature and can be catecholamine-secreting, so screening before any surgery is essential Endolymphatic sac tumours can cause hearing loss and tinnitus, and pancreatic serous cystadenomas and neuroendocrine tumours also occur The VHL protein regulates degradation of hypoxia-inducible factors, so loss drives a pseudohypoxic, pro-angiogenic state that explains the vascular tumour spectrum Lifelong multisystem surveillance from childhood with ophthalmoscopy, abdominal imaging, catecholamine testing and periodic neuroaxis MRI underpins management Unrecognised catecholamine-secreting phaeochromocytoma precipitating hypertensive crisis during surgery or pregnancy Rapidly enlarging or symptomatic central nervous system haemangioblastoma causing raised intracranial pressure or cord compression New or growing solid renal lesion suggesting renal cell carcinoma requiring intervention Progressive visual loss from retinal haemangioblastoma Operating on a renal or other tumour without first excluding an occult phaeochromocytoma Attributing an isolated haemangioblastoma or renal cell carcinoma to sporadic disease and missing the underlying syndrome Failing to offer predictive genetic testing and surveillance to at-risk relatives Overlooking endolymphatic sac tumours as a treatable cause of hearing loss Von Hippel-Lindau disease results from inactivating germline variants in the VHL tumour-suppressor gene, inherited in an autosomal dominant pattern with tumour formation following a somatic second hit in susceptible tissues (Knudson two-hit model). The VHL protein forms part of an E3 ubiquitin ligase complex that targets the alpha subunits of hypoxia-inducible factor for oxygen-dependent degradation. When VHL function is lost, hypoxia-inducible factor accumulates even under normoxia, driving transcription of pro-angiogenic and growth factors such as vascular endothelial growth factor and erythropoietin. This pseudohypoxic drive underlies the characteristic highly vascular tumours, including haemangioblastomas and clear-cell renal cell carcinoma. With structured lifelong surveillance and timely intervention, many complications can be treated before they become life-threatening, though renal cell carcinoma and central nervous system haemangioblastomas remain the principal causes of reduced life expectancy. Outcomes have improved substantially with early detection programmes.

Von Willebrand disease — VWD, von Willebrand disease, vWD, von Willebrand factor deficiency Haemophilia A (factor VIII deficiency) Platelet function disorders (e.g. Glanzmann thrombasthenia, storage pool disease) Immune thrombocytopenia and other causes of thrombocytopenia Acquired von Willebrand syndrome Vascular/connective tissue causes of mucocutaneous bleeding Vitamin K deficiency or liver disease affecting coagulation Full blood count and blood film to assess platelet number and morphology Coagulation screen including activated partial thromboplastin time Von Willebrand factor antigen level and functional (ristocetin cofactor/collagen-binding) activity Factor VIII coagulant activity Von Willebrand factor multimer analysis and ristocetin-induced platelet aggregation to define subtype Repeat testing when results are borderline, accounting for stress, pregnancy, and hormonal influences The most common inherited bleeding disorder, caused by a quantitative or qualitative defect in von Willebrand factor, which mediates platelet adhesion and carries and stabilises factor VIII The bleeding pattern is that of primary haemostatic failure: mucocutaneous bleeding with easy bruising, epistaxis, menorrhagia, and prolonged bleeding after dental or surgical procedures Type 1 is a partial quantitative deficiency (most common and usually mild), type 2 comprises qualitative variants, and type 3 is a severe near-complete deficiency with the heaviest bleeding Because von Willebrand factor protects factor VIII, low levels can produce a modestly prolonged activated partial thromboplastin time alongside normal platelet count Diagnosis relies on measuring von Willebrand factor antigen, its functional (ristocetin cofactor or equivalent) activity, and factor VIII, with multimer analysis to subtype Factor levels fluctuate with stress, pregnancy, oestrogens, and inflammation, so borderline results may need repeat testing Desmopressin releases stored von Willebrand factor and is useful in type 1 and many type 2 cases but is ineffective or inappropriate in type 3 and certain subtypes When desmopressin is unsuitable, von Willebrand factor-containing concentrates and antifibrinolytic agents are the mainstays for bleeding or procedures; an acquired form can occur with other disorders Severe or life-threatening haemorrhage, including gastrointestinal or intracranial bleeding, particularly in type 3 disease Uncontrolled menorrhagia causing haemodynamic compromise or severe anaemia Major unplanned surgery or trauma in a patient with a significant factor deficiency New or worsening bleeding suggesting acquired von Willebrand syndrome linked to another disease Excluding VWD on the basis of a normal activated partial thromboplastin time or normal platelet count Missing the diagnosis because factor levels are transiently normalised by stress, pregnancy, or oestrogen use Giving desmopressin in type 2B (which can worsen thrombocytopenia) or in type 3 (where it is ineffective) Overlooking acquired von Willebrand syndrome in older patients or those with lymphoproliferative, myeloproliferative, or cardiac conditions Failing to plan replacement or antifibrinolytic cover before invasive procedures Von Willebrand factor is a large multimeric glycoprotein synthesised by endothelial cells and megakaryocytes. It bridges platelets to exposed subendothelial collagen at sites of vascular injury (particularly under high shear) and serves as the carrier that protects circulating factor VIII from degradation. In VWD, reduced quantity (types 1 and 3) or impaired function (type 2 variants) of this factor impairs platelet adhesion and aggregation, and the loss of factor VIII protection lowers its level, adding a secondary coagulation defect. The result is defective primary haemostasis with a mucocutaneous bleeding phenotype. Acquired von Willebrand syndrome can arise from adsorption onto abnormal cells, high shear (e.g. aortic stenosis), or autoantibodies. Most patients, especially those with type 1 disease, have a mild course and a normal life expectancy with appropriate peri-procedural planning; type 3 and severe type 2 disease carry a higher lifelong bleeding burden but are manageable with modern replacement and adjunctive therapy.

Vulvar cancer — vulval cancer, vulvar carcinoma, vulvar squamous cell carcinoma, cancer of the vulva Vulvar intraepithelial neoplasia (pre-invasive disease) Lichen sclerosus or lichen planus Vulvar dermatitis or eczema Genital warts (condylomata acuminata) Bartholin gland cyst or abscess Vulvar melanoma, Paget disease, or basal cell carcinoma Biopsy of the vulvar lesion for histological diagnosis and depth of invasion Examination of the inguinal regions and vulva under adequate visualisation, with colposcopy where indicated Pelvic MRI to assess local extent and nodal involvement CT or PET-CT for regional and distant staging Sentinel lymph node evaluation in appropriately selected early-stage tumours Most are squamous cell carcinomas and arise through two main routes: an HPV-associated pathway seen in younger women and an HPV-independent pathway linked to lichen sclerosus and chronic inflammation in older women It commonly presents as persistent vulvar itching, a lump, ulcer, or plaque, sometimes with bleeding, pain, or discharge, and diagnosis is often delayed by patient reluctance and repeated empirical treatment Any persistent or atypical vulvar lesion should undergo biopsy rather than prolonged treatment for presumed dermatitis or infection Spread occurs predominantly to inguinofemoral lymph nodes, so accurate groin node assessment is critical to staging and prognosis Sentinel lymph node biopsy is used in selected early tumours to reduce the morbidity of full inguinofemoral lymphadenectomy Surgery is the mainstay for localised disease, with wide local excision or vulvectomy and appropriate groin node management guided by tumour depth and size Radiotherapy, often combined with chemotherapy, is used for advanced disease, positive nodes, or to preserve function and reduce the extent of surgery Precursor vulvar intraepithelial neoplasia and lichen sclerosus warrant surveillance because of their malignant potential A persistent vulvar lump, ulcer, or plaque that does not resolve with treatment Chronic vulvar itching or bleeding in an older woman with lichen sclerosus Palpable or fixed inguinal lymph nodes Rapidly enlarging or ulcerating vulvar lesion Repeatedly treating a persistent vulvar lesion as dermatitis or thrush without biopsy Failing to assess and manage inguinal lymph nodes appropriately Neglecting surveillance of lichen sclerosus and vulvar intraepithelial neoplasia Underestimating the psychosexual and functional impact when planning surgery Vulvar squamous cell carcinoma develops from the vulvar epithelium by two principal mechanisms. In younger women, persistent high-risk human papillomavirus infection drives usual-type vulvar intraepithelial neoplasia that can progress to invasive cancer. In older women, chronic dermatological conditions such as lichen sclerosus produce differentiated vulvar intraepithelial neoplasia and HPV-independent carcinoma. Invasive tumour infiltrates local structures and spreads first to superficial and deep inguinofemoral nodes and subsequently to pelvic nodes, with distant metastasis occurring late. Prognosis is largely determined by inguinofemoral nodal status and tumour stage; node-negative localised disease has good survival after surgery, whereas nodal involvement or advanced local spread substantially reduces outcomes.

Vulvar intraepithelial neoplasia — VIN, usual-type VIN, differentiated VIN, vulvar high-grade squamous intraepithelial lesion, vulval HSIL Lichen sclerosus Lichen planus of the vulva Invasive vulval squamous cell carcinoma Vulval Paget disease Condylomata acuminata (genital warts) Vulval melanocytic lesions or melanoma Chronic vulval dermatoses and candidal or contact dermatitis Vulval biopsy for histological confirmation and grading Vulvoscopy with acetic acid to delineate lesion extent and guide directed biopsies p16 and HPV testing to distinguish usual-type from differentiated disease Colposcopic assessment of the cervix, vagina, and anus given multicentric potential Assessment of the perianal region and mapping biopsies where multifocal disease is suspected Screening for immunosuppression, including HIV testing where clinically appropriate Usual-type VIN (vulval high-grade squamous intraepithelial lesion) is driven by high-risk human papillomavirus, expresses p16, and typically affects younger women, often with multifocal or multicentric disease involving cervix or anus Differentiated VIN is HPV-independent, usually arises on a background of lichen sclerosus or lichen planus in older women, and carries a disproportionately high and rapid risk of progression to invasive squamous carcinoma Symptoms are non-specific and include persistent itch, soreness, or a visible lesion, but a proportion are asymptomatic and found incidentally Lesions are clinically variable, ranging from white, red, or pigmented plaques to raised or eroded areas, so appearance alone cannot exclude malignancy Diagnosis rests on adequate biopsy, and any suspicious or non-healing vulval lesion should be sampled rather than treated empirically Vulvoscopy after application of acetic acid, with directed biopsies, helps map the extent of disease and identify occult invasion Management is individualised and may include local surgical excision, ablative treatment, or topical immune-modulating therapy for usual-type disease, whereas differentiated VIN generally warrants excision because of its cancer risk Long-term surveillance is essential because recurrence and new lesions are common, particularly in immunosuppressed women and those with persistent HPV Ulceration, induration, bleeding, or a nodular lesion suggesting occult invasion Rapidly enlarging or non-healing lesion, particularly on a background of lichen sclerosus Differentiated VIN histology, which mandates prompt excision because of high malignant potential Recurrent or persistent disease in an immunosuppressed woman New pigmented lesion raising concern for melanoma Treating a suspicious vulval lesion empirically without biopsy and missing invasive carcinoma Overlooking differentiated VIN because its histological changes are subtle and the lesion may look like benign lichen sclerosus Failing to examine the cervix, vagina, and anus in usual-type disease with multicentric potential Discharging women prematurely when recurrence and metachronous lesions are common Attributing persistent vulval itch to candidiasis or dermatitis and delaying diagnosis Vulvar intraepithelial neoplasia describes dysplastic change confined to the vulval squamous epithelium above the basement membrane. Two distinct pathways are recognised. Usual-type disease follows persistent infection with high-risk human papillomavirus, which through its oncoproteins disrupts cell-cycle control and produces the surrogate marker of diffuse p16 positivity; it tends to occur in younger women and is frequently multifocal. Differentiated VIN is unrelated to HPV and instead develops within chronically inflamed skin, classically lichen sclerosus, where cumulative genetic damage in the basal keratinocytes drives neoplasia; despite often subtle histology it progresses to invasive squamous carcinoma more readily and more quickly than the usual type. Usual-type VIN may occasionally regress but frequently persists or recurs and can progress to invasive carcinoma, whereas differentiated VIN carries a substantially higher and faster risk of malignant transformation; with adequate treatment and lifelong surveillance most women avoid invasive cancer, though recurrence is common.

Vulvodynia — vulval pain syndrome, provoked vestibulodynia, localised vulvodynia, generalised vulvodynia, vestibulodynia Recurrent vulvovaginal candidiasis or other infection Lichen sclerosus, lichen planus, or contact dermatitis Vulvar intraepithelial neoplasia or malignancy Pudendal neuralgia or other neuropathy Atrophic vulvovaginitis from oestrogen deficiency Pelvic floor myofascial dysfunction Herpes simplex or postherpetic neuralgia Cotton-swab (Q-tip) test to localise and grade vestibular tenderness Vaginal swabs and microscopy to exclude infection Vulval examination for dermatoses, with biopsy of any abnormal area Assessment of pelvic floor tone and tenderness Oestrogen status assessment in peri- or postmenopausal women Screening for anxiety, depression, and comorbid chronic pain to guide holistic care Vulvodynia is chronic vulval pain, usually burning, stinging, or rawness, present for at least several months with no identifiable clinical or laboratory cause, making it a diagnosis of exclusion It is subclassified by site into localised (most often provoked vestibulodynia at the vestibule) and generalised forms, and by whether pain is provoked, spontaneous, or mixed Provoked vestibulodynia typically causes entry dyspareunia and pain on tampon insertion or tight clothing, with tenderness reproduced by light touch of the vestibule Generalised vulvodynia produces more diffuse, often spontaneous neuropathic pain that may be unprovoked and less clearly localised Examination is frequently normal apart from focal tenderness, and the cotton-swab (Q-tip) test helps map painful points at the vestibule Associated features often include pelvic floor muscle overactivity, anxiety, and other chronic pain conditions, reflecting a component of central sensitisation Management is multimodal and generic, combining vulval care advice, pelvic floor physiotherapy, psychological and pain-focused therapies, topical or systemic neuromodulating treatment, and occasionally surgery for refractory localised disease The diagnosis should only be made after infective, dermatological, neurological, and neoplastic causes of vulval pain have been excluded Visible ulcer, mass, or persistent abnormal lesion requiring biopsy to exclude malignancy Neurological deficit or dermatomal pain suggesting a specific neuropathy Features of active infection or a dermatosis that would reclassify the pain as having an identifiable cause Rapidly worsening pain or systemic symptoms Repeatedly treating presumed thrush without confirming infection and overlooking a pain syndrome Labelling the pain as purely psychological and failing to address peripheral and pelvic floor contributions Making the diagnosis without first excluding dermatoses, infection, and neoplasia Neglecting pelvic floor assessment, which is frequently abnormal and treatable Offering surgery before adequate conservative and medical management in localised disease Vulvodynia is understood as a chronic pain condition rather than a structural disease. In localised provoked vestibulodynia, increased density and sensitisation of nociceptive nerve fibres in the vestibular mucosa, together with local inflammatory and hormonal influences, lower the threshold for pain so that normally innocuous touch is felt as burning. Peripheral sensitisation is compounded by amplification within the spinal cord and brain (central sensitisation) and by reflex overactivity and guarding of the pelvic floor musculature. Generalised vulvodynia is thought to reflect a more neuropathic, spontaneous pain process. Psychological factors and comorbid pain syndromes modulate the experience but are not the primary cause. Vulvodynia is a chronic relapsing condition, but many women improve substantially with a combined, individualised approach; provoked vestibulodynia in particular can respond well to physiotherapy and neuromodulation, though complete and permanent resolution is not guaranteed.

Vulvovaginal Candidiasis — vaginal thrush, candidal vaginitis, yeast infection, monilial vaginitis Bacterial vaginosis Trichomonas vaginalis infection Contact or irritant vulvar dermatitis Lichen sclerosus or lichen planus Genital herpes Physiological discharge Vaginal pH measurement, typically normal in candidiasis Saline and potassium hydroxide wet-mount microscopy for yeasts and pseudohyphae Fungal culture in recurrent, severe, or treatment-resistant cases to speciate Blood glucose or HbA1c testing where recurrent infection suggests diabetes Consideration of HIV or immunosuppression assessment in refractory disease Most infections are caused by Candida albicans, a commensal yeast that becomes symptomatic when the vaginal environment or host defences change Typical features are intense vulval itching, soreness, and a thick, white, non-malodorous discharge often likened to cottage cheese, with vulval erythema and sometimes fissuring The vaginal pH usually remains normal and acidic, which helps distinguish it from bacterial vaginosis and trichomoniasis Predisposing factors include recent antibiotic use, pregnancy, diabetes, immunosuppression, and high oestrogen states Diagnosis is clinical, supported by microscopy showing budding yeasts and pseudohyphae, and culture is useful in recurrent or treatment-resistant cases to identify non-albicans species Uncomplicated disease responds well to topical or oral antifungal therapy, whereas recurrent disease often needs a longer induction and maintenance approach Recurrent or resistant infection should prompt evaluation for diabetes, immunosuppression, and non-albicans species such as Candida glabrata, which are less responsive to standard azoles It is not classed as a sexually transmitted infection, and routine treatment of asymptomatic male partners is not indicated Recurrent or refractory infection suggesting undiagnosed diabetes or immunosuppression Severe vulval swelling, fissuring, or ulceration prompting reconsideration of the diagnosis Systemic candidiasis in significantly immunocompromised patients Failure to respond to standard azole therapy suggesting a non-albicans species Coexisting symptoms pointing to another sexually transmitted infection Diagnosing thrush on symptoms alone and missing bacterial vaginosis or dermatoses Repeatedly treating recurrent infection without investigating for diabetes or immunosuppression Assuming all cases are Candida albicans and overlooking azole-resistant species Unnecessarily treating asymptomatic partners Attributing chronic vulval symptoms to candidiasis when a dermatological condition is responsible Candida species colonise the vagina asymptomatically in many women, kept in check by the resident lactobacillus-dominant flora and local immunity. Disturbance of this balance, for example by antibiotics, or increased glycogen availability from high oestrogen states and hyperglycaemia, allows the yeast to proliferate and transform into an invasive hyphal form. Adherence to and penetration of the vaginal epithelium triggers a brisk inflammatory response, producing the pruritus, erythema, and discharge characteristic of symptomatic infection. Uncomplicated vulvovaginal candidiasis responds rapidly to antifungal treatment with an excellent outlook. A minority of women develop recurrent disease that is troublesome and requires prolonged maintenance therapy, and outcomes in these cases improve when underlying predisposing factors and non-albicans species are identified and addressed.

Waardenburg syndrome — PAX3, MITF, SOX10, auditory-pigmentary syndrome, WS Other syndromic sensorineural hearing loss such as Pendred or branchio-oto-renal syndrome Piebaldism (KIT mutation) with depigmentation but without hearing loss Vitiligo and other acquired pigmentary disorders Tietz syndrome with generalised hypopigmentation and deafness Isolated congenital sensorineural hearing loss Hirschsprung disease from non-syndromic causes in type 4 presentations Audiometry with age-appropriate testing to characterise hearing loss Detailed dermatological and ophthalmic examination for pigmentary features and iris colour Measurement of inner canthal and interpupillary distances to assess dystopia canthorum Assessment for constipation or bowel obstruction and Hirschsprung disease in suspected type 4 Molecular genetic testing (PAX3, MITF, SOX10 and related genes) to confirm subtype An auditory-pigmentary syndrome combining sensorineural hearing loss with pigmentary anomalies of the eyes, hair and skin Characteristic features include heterochromia or brilliant blue irides, a white forelock, patchy skin depigmentation, and early greying Dystopia canthorum (lateral displacement of the inner canthi) distinguishes type 1 from type 2, in which it is absent Most commonly autosomal dominant with variable expressivity; PAX3 underlies types 1 and 3, and MITF and SOX10 are associated with type 2 Type 3 (Klein-Waardenburg) adds musculoskeletal limb abnormalities, and type 4 (Waardenburg-Shah) is associated with Hirschsprung disease via SOX10, EDN3 or EDNRB Hearing loss is congenital, non-progressive and may be unilateral or bilateral, reflecting absence of melanocytes in the stria vascularis Family examination frequently reveals affected relatives with subtle pigmentary signs Neonatal bowel obstruction or severe constipation suggesting associated Hirschsprung disease Bilateral profound hearing loss affecting speech development in an infant Progressive rather than static hearing loss, prompting reconsideration of the diagnosis Family history of combined pigmentary and hearing anomalies indicating dominant inheritance Overlooking subtle pigmentary signs when hearing loss is the presenting problem Confusing dystopia canthorum with true hypertelorism and misclassifying the subtype Assuming normal hearing in one ear excludes the syndrome, as loss may be unilateral Failing to consider Hirschsprung disease in a neonate with pigmentary features Waardenburg syndrome arises from mutations affecting the development, migration or survival of neural-crest-derived melanocytes. Melanocytes contribute pigment to the skin, hair and iris and are also essential within the stria vascularis of the cochlea for maintaining the endolymphatic environment needed for normal hearing. Genes such as PAX3, MITF and SOX10 encode transcription factors within this developmental pathway, so their disruption produces both the pigmentary abnormalities and the sensorineural hearing loss. In type 4 the same neural-crest defect also affects enteric ganglion cells, causing aganglionic megacolon (Hirschsprung disease). Hearing loss is congenital and generally non-progressive, and prognosis is favourable with hearing aids or cochlear implantation and early language support; the pigmentary features are cosmetic, though associated Hirschsprung disease in type 4 requires surgical management.

and choroidal thinning develop over time (the erosive vitreoretinopathy phenotype) Patients may have myopia, early cataract, ectopic or dragged fovea and reduced night vision Risk of retinal detachment is increased, though generally lower than in Stickler syndrome Electroretinography may show progressive reduction in rod and cone responses as chorioretinal degeneration advances Management is refractive correction, cataract surgery when indicated, lifelong monitoring for retinal detachment, and genetic counselling New floaters, flashes or field loss suggesting retinal detachment and needing urgent review Progressive night blindness and field constriction from advancing chorioretinal atrophy Early or rapidly progressive cataract affecting vision Affected relatives requiring examination given dominant inheritance Failing to distinguish Wagner syndrome from Stickler syndrome, which has systemic features and a higher detachment risk Overlooking the increased retinal detachment risk during routine follow-up Attributing the vitreous changes to simple myopic degeneration Not offering genetic counselling for a dominantly inherited condition Wagner syndrome is caused by dominant mutations in VCAN, which encodes versican, a large proteoglycan of the vitreous extracellular matrix. Abnormal splicing and altered versican disrupt the normal collagen-hyaluronan gel structure of the vitreous, producing liquefaction and the characteristic optically empty cavity with residual avascular membranes. Over time there is progressive chorioretinal and retinal pigment epithelial atrophy, giving the erosive vitreoretinopathy picture, together with an increased predisposition to retinal detachment. Vision is often reasonable in early life but can decline with progressive chorioretinal atrophy, cataract and the risk of retinal detachment; long-term outcome varies and lifelong surveillance is warranted.

may include BTK inhibition or rituximab-based therapy Symptomatic hyperviscosity with neurological or visual compromise requiring urgent plasmapheresis Severe anaemia or cytopenias from marrow infiltration Progressive peripheral neuropathy Transformation to a high-grade lymphoma with rapid clinical deterioration Attributing symptoms to anaemia alone and missing hyperviscosity that needs urgent plasmapheresis Spurious laboratory results, including pseudohyponatraemia and interference, from a high IgM level Failing to distinguish it from IgM myeloma or marginal zone lymphoma Overlooking MYD88 testing that clarifies the diagnosis and predicts therapy response Waldenstrom macroglobulinaemia is a clonal B-cell disorder in which lymphoplasmacytic cells, spanning small lymphocytes to plasma cells, infiltrate the bone marrow and sometimes lymphoid organs and secrete a monoclonal immunoglobulin M. The recurrent MYD88 L265P mutation activates downstream NF-kappaB signalling through the Bruton tyrosine kinase pathway, promoting tumour survival, and CXCR4 mutations modify disease behaviour and treatment response. The large pentameric IgM molecule raises serum viscosity and can behave as a cryoglobulin, cold agglutinin or autoantibody, so many clinical features stem from the physical and immunological properties of the paraprotein rather than tumour bulk alone. Waldenstrom macroglobulinaemia is generally an indolent, treatable but incurable disorder with prolonged survival for many patients; outcome is influenced by age, cytopenias, paraprotein level and molecular features, and hyperviscosity is usually reversible with plasmapheresis.

Confusing cobblestone (type II) lissencephaly with classic (type I) lissencephaly, which has different genetics and no primary muscle or eye disease Overlooking the raised creatine kinase and muscle involvement when focused on the brain malformation Missing treatable ocular complications such as retinal detachment Failing to place the child on the dystroglycanopathy spectrum, affecting prognosis and counselling Walker-Warburg syndrome is a dystroglycanopathy caused by biallelic variants in genes required for O-linked glycosylation of alpha-dystroglycan. Defective glycosylation prevents alpha-dystroglycan from binding extracellular matrix ligands such as laminin, disrupting the integrity of basement membranes. In the developing brain, breaches of the pial-glial limiting membrane allow neurons to over-migrate beyond the cortex, producing cobblestone lissencephaly, brainstem and cerebellar malformation, and hydrocephalus. The same defect impairs the muscle basement membrane, causing congenital muscular dystrophy, and disrupts ocular development, causing the retinal and anterior segment anomalies. Walker-Warburg syndrome carries the worst prognosis of the dystroglycanopathies, with most affected children dying within the first years of life from neurological, respiratory, and feeding complications. Care is largely supportive alongside genetic counselling.

Walled-off pancreatic necrosis — WON, walled-off necrosis, organised pancreatic necrosis, mature necrotic collection Pancreatic pseudocyst Acute necrotic collection (before maturation of the wall) Pancreatic abscess Cystic pancreatic neoplasm with debris Duodenal or gastric outlet obstruction from other causes Infected peripancreatic haematoma Contrast-enhanced CT to define the extent, wall maturity, and solid content of the collection MRI or endoscopic ultrasound to better characterise solid debris and guide drainage Inflammatory markers and blood cultures if infection is suspected Image-guided aspiration for culture when infected necrosis is in question Assessment of pancreatic duct integrity (for example MRCP) to detect disconnected duct syndrome Monitoring of nutritional status and glycaemic control A mature, encapsulated collection of necrotic pancreatic and peripancreatic tissue that develops typically about four weeks after an episode of necrotising pancreatitis Distinguished from a pseudocyst by its heterogeneous content, which includes solid debris rather than pure fluid, under the revised Atlanta classification May be sterile or become infected; infected necrosis is suggested by clinical deterioration, sepsis, or gas within the collection on imaging Contrast-enhanced CT shows an encapsulated collection with variable solid and liquid components in or around the pancreas Asymptomatic sterile collections can be managed conservatively, as many resolve or remain stable without intervention When drainage is needed, a step-up approach is favoured, beginning with percutaneous or endoscopic drainage before escalating to minimally invasive necrosectomy Endoscopic transmural drainage with lumen-apposing metal stents and, where required, direct endoscopic necrosectomy has become a mainstay of management Clinical deterioration, persistent fever, or sepsis suggesting infected necrosis Gas within the collection on imaging Gastric outlet or biliary obstruction from mass effect Haemorrhage into the collection or a pseudoaneurysm of a splanchnic vessel Rapid enlargement of the collection Intervening too early before the wall has matured, which increases complications Mistaking walled-off necrosis for a simple pseudocyst and attempting drainage of solid debris through inadequate routes Overlooking a disconnected pancreatic duct, which predisposes to persistent or recurrent collections Failing to recognise vascular complications such as pseudoaneurysm before drainage Delaying antibiotics and source control once infection is established Walled-off pancreatic necrosis is a late local complication of necrotising pancreatitis. During the acute illness, ischaemic and enzymatic injury produces necrosis of pancreatic parenchyma and surrounding fat, generating an acute necrotic collection containing both liquefied and solid material. Over the following weeks a fibrous and granulation-tissue wall matures around this collection, converting it into an organised, encapsulated cavity that still contains devitalised solid debris. The retained necrotic tissue can become secondarily infected by gut-derived organisms, and the collection may erode adjacent structures, obstruct the stomach or duodenum, compress the bile duct, or communicate with the pancreatic duct, producing persistent leakage. Sterile, asymptomatic collections often resolve or stabilise without intervention and carry a good outlook; infected necrosis substantially increases morbidity and mortality, though outcomes have improved with a minimally invasive step-up strategy and delayed intervention where possible.

wandering spleen — ectopic spleen, splenoptosis, floating spleen Ovarian or other adnexal mass or torsion Mesenteric or omental cyst Retroperitoneal or gastrointestinal tumour Ectopic or ptotic kidney Acute appendicitis when the spleen lies in the right or lower abdomen Intra-abdominal lymphadenopathy or lymphoma Contrast-enhanced CT of the abdomen and pelvis, assessing the splenic fossa and the vascular pedicle Doppler ultrasound of the ectopic spleen to assess perfusion and the twisted pedicle Technetium sulphur-colloid or heat-damaged red cell scintigraphy to confirm splenic tissue and viability MRI, favoured in children to limit ionising radiation Full blood count to detect cytopenias from hypersplenism Assessment for associated gastric volvulus or malrotation when clinically suspected Arises from absence or laxity of the splenic suspensory ligaments (gastrosplenic, splenorenal and phrenocolic), allowing the spleen to migrate on a long, mobile vascular pedicle May be congenital, from failure of the dorsal mesogastrium to fuse, or acquired through multiparity, hormonally mediated ligamentous laxity or splenomegaly Typically presents in children and women of reproductive age as a mobile palpable abdominal or pelvic mass, intermittent pain, or an acute abdomen when the pedicle twists Torsion of the pedicle is the feared complication, producing venous congestion followed by arterial infarction of the spleen Cross-sectional imaging shows an empty splenic fossa with an ectopically sited spleen; a whirl sign of the twisted pedicle with absent Doppler flow indicates torsion Splenopexy to fix a viable spleen is preferred, especially in children, to preserve immune function, with splenectomy reserved for a non-viable infarcted organ May coexist with gastric volvulus, intestinal malrotation and diaphragmatic or abdominal wall defects, reflecting shared abnormal visceral fixation A palpable notched mass that can be manually returned towards the left upper quadrant is a helpful clinical clue Acute severe abdominal pain with a tender mobile mass, indicating pedicle torsion Signs of infarction with peritonism and systemic upset Haemodynamic instability suggesting infarction with haemorrhage Retching with inability to pass a nasogastric tube, suggesting associated gastric volvulus Mistaking the ectopic spleen for a tumour and proceeding to biopsy or inappropriate resection Delayed recognition of torsion, converting a salvageable spleen into a non-viable one Performing splenectomy when splenopexy would have preserved function, particularly in children Omitting post-splenectomy immunisation and antibiotic prophylaxis when the spleen must be removed The spleen is normally anchored in the left upper quadrant by peritoneal ligaments derived from the dorsal mesogastrium. When these ligaments fail to develop or become lax, the spleen loses its fixation and hangs from an elongated pedicle carrying the splenic vessels, so that it can migrate freely into the abdomen or pelvis. The mobile, narrow pedicle is prone to rotation; torsion first obstructs the thin-walled splenic vein, producing congestion and enlargement, and if it progresses occludes the arterial supply, causing ischaemia and infarction. Chronic partial torsion may instead produce venous congestion with hypersplenism, while the elongated vessels can also compromise the pancreatic tail and predispose to associated gastric volvulus. When recognised and treated before infarction, splenopexy carries an excellent outcome and preserves splenic immune function. Delayed diagnosis of torsion leads to infarction and loss of the spleen, with the attendant lifelong risks of hyposplenism.

The red cells aggregate with Tamm-Horsfall protein to form obstructing red-cell casts in the tubules, causing tubular obstruction, direct epithelial injury and reduced glomerular filtration. Underlying glomerular disease or endothelial and basement-membrane fragility, as in diabetes or hypertension, predisposes to this glomerular haemorrhage, explaining why it occurs largely in patients with pre-existing renal impairment. Anticoagulant-related nephropathy is associated with incomplete renal recovery, accelerated progression of underlying chronic kidney disease and increased mortality, particularly in those with pre-existing renal impairment. Prompt correction of over-anticoagulation and attention to comorbidities improve the chance of stabilising function, but a proportion sustain a permanent decline.

Warfarin inhibits the vitamin K-dependent gamma-carboxylation of clotting factors II, VII, IX and X and of the natural anticoagulants protein C and protein S. Because protein C has a short half-life, similar to that of factor VII, its anticoagulant activity falls rapidly in the first days of treatment, before the procoagulant factors with longer half-lives are fully depleted. This creates a transient net hypercoagulable state, which is exaggerated in patients with pre-existing protein C (or protein S) deficiency and by large initial doses. The resulting thrombosis of dermal and subcutaneous small vessels causes ischaemia, haemorrhagic infarction and full-thickness skin necrosis in areas rich in subcutaneous fat. Concurrent parenteral anticoagulation during initiation bridges this vulnerable period. Early recognition and treatment can limit tissue loss, but established necrosis may require debridement or reconstructive surgery and can cause significant morbidity. Prompt correction of the coagulopathy and appropriate anticoagulation improve outcomes.

Antibody-coated cells are recognised by splenic macrophages through Fc receptors and are partially or wholly phagocytosed, producing spherocytes and predominantly extravascular haemolysis. The bone marrow compensates with brisk reticulocytosis. Secondary forms arise when an underlying lymphoproliferative or autoimmune disorder, or a drug, disturbs immune tolerance and drives autoantibody production. Many patients respond to corticosteroids, but relapse is common and refractory disease requires escalation; prognosis in secondary forms depends on the underlying disorder.

marrow suppression Features of an underlying lymphoma or connective tissue disease Difficulty obtaining compatible blood when urgent transfusion is required Withholding necessary transfusion for fear of incompatibility when the anaemia is life-threatening Failing to search for an underlying lymphoproliferative or autoimmune disorder Overlooking a masked alloantibody during compatibility testing red-cell membrane antigens most avidly at core body temperature. Antibody-coated red cells are recognised by Fc receptors on splenic macrophages, which remove portions of the membrane, generating spherocytes that are less deformable and are ultimately trapped and destroyed in the spleen. This predominantly extravascular haemolysis raises unconjugated bilirubin, lactate dehydrogenase and reticulocytes while consuming haptoglobin. When complement is also fixed, some intravascular haemolysis and hepatic clearance occur. The autoantibody may be idiopathic or arise secondary to lymphoproliferative disease, connective tissue disorders or drugs, and its broad specificity complicates compatibility testing. Many patients respond to corticosteroids, but relapse is common and some require second-line therapy; the course and outlook are strongly influenced by any underlying secondary cause.

Warthin tumour — Papillary cystadenoma lymphomatosum, Adenolymphoma Pleomorphic adenoma Oncocytoma Intraparotid or reactive lymph node Lymphoepithelial cyst Mucoepidermoid carcinoma (cystic, low-grade) Acinic cell carcinoma Metastatic cystic squamous carcinoma Fine-needle aspiration cytology of the mass Ultrasound demonstrating a well-defined, often cystic, hypoechoic lesion in the parotid tail Technetium pertechnetate scintigraphy showing focal uptake (historically supportive) MRI to characterise multifocal or bilateral disease Documentation of smoking history Histological examination of the excised specimen The second commonest benign parotid tumour, arising almost exclusively in the parotid, characteristically in the tail of the gland. Strongly associated with cigarette smoking, and notable for being bilateral or multifocal in a substantial minority of patients. Histology is distinctive: a bilayered oncocytic (mitochondria-rich) epithelium lining papillary cystic spaces, supported by a dense lymphoid stroma with germinal centres. Thought to arise from salivary ductal inclusions trapped within intraparotid or periparotid lymph nodes during development. Technetium pertechnetate scintigraphy shows avid uptake because of the abundant mitochondria in oncocytes, a feature shared with oncocytoma. Malignant transformation is exceedingly rare, so observation is a reasonable option in elderly or comorbid patients once the diagnosis is secure. Aspirated cyst fluid is often mucoid and cellular; oncocytes with a lymphoid background can be mistaken for a cystic or mucoepidermoid lesion. The tumour may undergo infarction after fine-needle aspiration, producing squamous and reactive change that can mimic malignancy. Rapid enlargement or new pain in a previously stable parotid mass Facial nerve weakness, which is atypical and suggests an alternative diagnosis Fixation to surrounding structures Constitutional symptoms or diffuse nodal enlargement raising concern for lymphoma in the lymphoid stroma Persistent or bloody cyst content after aspiration Failing to recognise bilateral or multifocal disease Misinterpreting mucoid, oncocyte-rich aspirate as a low-grade mucoepidermoid carcinoma Over-calling post-aspiration infarction as malignancy Overlooking lymphoma arising within the lymphoid stroma Proceeding to unnecessarily radical surgery for a benign lesion Warthin tumour is a benign neoplasm believed to originate from ectopic salivary gland ductal epithelium sequestered within lymphoid tissue in and around the parotid during embryogenesis, an anatomical relationship unique to the parotid. The epithelial component undergoes oncocytic metaplasia, accumulating large numbers of mitochondria that impart the granular eosinophilic cytoplasm and account for technetium avidity. A prominent, immunologically reactive lymphoid stroma with germinal centres accompanies the epithelium, and the striking epidemiological link with tobacco smoke suggests that carcinogen exposure promotes both oncocytic change and the lymphoid reaction. The tumour is frequently multicentric and bilateral, reflecting its origin from multiple ductal inclusions rather than from a single focus. Prognosis is excellent as the tumour is benign, and malignant change is extremely rare. Apparent recurrence usually reflects a separate multifocal or metachronous lesion rather than inadequate excision.

or unusually severe disease Development of skin cancer at a young age Extensive disease in a patient with unexplained recurrent infection Dismissing persistent flat warts and versicolor-like macules as ordinary warts or tinea Failing to institute lifelong photoprotection and skin-cancer surveillance Missing an underlying T-cell immunodeficiency in the syndromic form Assuming systemic immune treatment will clear the lesions in the classic keratinocyte-intrinsic form Under-recognising the malignancy risk and delaying biopsy of changing lesions In the classic form, loss-of-function mutations in EVER1/TMC6 or EVER2/TMC8, or in their partner CIB1, disrupt a keratinocyte protein complex that normally restricts the replication of beta-genus human papillomaviruses within skin cells, in part by regulating intracellular zinc handling. Without this intrinsic keratinocyte defence, these otherwise poorly pathogenic beta-papillomaviruses replicate unchecked in the epidermis, producing the persistent flat warts and versicolor-like macules. Because the defect is largely confined to keratinocyte control of these particular viruses rather than a global immune failure, susceptibility is narrowly restricted to beta-papillomaviruses. Chronic viral infection combined with ultraviolet exposure drives keratinocyte genomic damage over years, explaining the marked risk of squamous cell carcinoma on sun-exposed skin. In the syndromic form, an underlying T-cell immunodeficiency, rather than a keratinocyte-intrinsic defect, permits the same beta-papillomavirus disease alongside wider infection. Life expectancy in the classic form is largely determined by the risk of cutaneous squamous cell carcinoma, which is high on sun-exposed skin from early adulthood; with strict photoprotection and vigilant surveillance many cancers are caught early, whereas the syndromic form carries the additional prognosis of the underlying immunodeficiency.

dislocation of the lens into the anterior chamber Progressive visual loss from uncontrolled intraocular pressure Rapidly rising intraocular pressure requiring urgent ophthalmic intervention Dilating the pupil without recognising that it can precipitate pupillary block in microspherophakia Confusing it with Marfan syndrome despite the opposite stature and direction of lens dislocation Missing homocystinuria as an alternative cause of ectopia lentis Underestimating the glaucoma risk and deferring intraocular pressure monitoring Weill-Marchesani syndrome is a disorder of the fibrillin microfibril system that supports the ocular zonule and connective tissue. Variants in ADAMTS10, LTBP2 or FBN1 disrupt assembly or regulation of microfibrils, weakening the zonular apparatus so that the lens becomes small, spherical and poorly suspended, predisposing to dislocation and angle-closure glaucoma. The same microfibrillar disturbance and associated dysregulated TGF-beta signalling in the skeleton produce the short stature, brachydactyly and joint stiffness that characterise the acromelic phenotype. General health and life expectancy are usually good, but vision is at significant risk from lens dislocation and secondary glaucoma, so the ophthalmic outcome depends heavily on early detection and careful long-term eye care.

muscle disease Overlooking the characteristic founder-population family history Welander distal myopathy is caused by a dominant founder variant in TIA1, which encodes an RNA-binding protein that The mutation is thought to alter stress-granule dynamics and RNA handling, promoting accumulation of misfolded and aggregated proteins within muscle fibres. This produces the rimmed vacuoles and protein deposits seen on biopsy and places the disorder within the broader family of rimmed-vacuolar myopathies, with the earliest and most severe involvement in the distal upper-limb muscles. The disorder progresses slowly over years to decades and heterozygous patients usually retain functional independence with a normal or near-normal lifespan; the rare homozygous form is considerably more severe with earlier and more widespread weakness.

characteristically young age of cataract onset Failing to maintain vigilant malignancy surveillance, particularly for sarcomas Underestimating premature cardiovascular and diabetic complications in a relatively young patient Werner syndrome arises from biallelic loss-of-function variants in WRN, which encodes a member of the RecQ family of DNA helicases with additional exonuclease activity. The protein participates in DNA replication, repair, recombination and telomere maintenance. Its loss produces genomic instability, accelerated telomere attrition and premature cellular senescence, which underlie the segmental (partial) acceleration of ageing phenotypes and the predisposition to cancer seen in affected individuals. Life expectancy is shortened, with most affected individuals dying in the fifth to sixth decade, predominantly from malignancy or atherosclerotic cardiovascular disease. Careful metabolic control, cardiovascular risk reduction and cancer surveillance may improve outcomes.

Wernicke encephalopathy — Clinical triad (confusion, ataxia, ophthalmoplegia) Give IV thiamine BEFORE glucose Reversible — treat empirically with thiamine, do not delay Supranuclear gaze disorder mimicking combined abducens and oculomotor nerve palsy (Wernicke can itself cause this pattern) Other metabolic encephalopathies (hepatic, hypercarbic, hyper-/hyponatremic, hyper-/hypoglycemic) Sepsis-associated encephalopathy Osmotic demyelination syndrome (central pontine myelinolysis) Marchiafava-Bignami disease (corpus callosum degeneration in chronic alcoholism) Alcoholic cerebellar degeneration Encephalitis (including herpes simplex encephalitis as a cause of an amnestic state) Whipple's disease (cause of supranuclear gaze palsy) MRI may show changes including abnormal enhancement of the mammillary bodies (coronal T1 postcontrast), typical of acute Wernicke Erythrocyte transketolase activity assay measured before and after adding thiamine pyrophosphate; >25% stimulation (activity coefficient >=1.25) is abnormal Serum/blood thiamine or its phosphorylated esters by high-performance liquid chromatography Serum magnesium (required cofactor for thiamine activation) Autoimmune limbic encephalitis (e.g., AMPAR, LGI1 antibodies) causing amnesia Paraneoplastic encephalitis (e.g., Ma antibodies) Thalamic, medial temporal, or posterior corpus callosum tumor causing amnesia Anterior/posterior cerebral artery territory infarction causing amnesia Stroke (infarct/hemorrhage), multiple sclerosis, vasculitis, or tumor causing supranuclear gaze palsy The classic triad (ophthalmoplegia, ataxia, global confusion) is present in only about one-third of acute cases, so a complete triad should not be required to make the diagnosis. Most patients are profoundly disoriented, apathetic/indifferent, and inattentive rather than agitated; agitated delirium, when present, is usually from coexisting alcohol withdrawal. Thiamine deficiency causing Wernicke is not confined to alcohol use; non-alcoholic risk groups include hyperemesis, starvation/malnutrition, renal dialysis, cancer, HIV/AIDS, gastric/bariatric surgery, and chronic diuretic therapy (increased urinary thiamine loss). Certain drugs (e.g., metformin, verapamil) can inhibit intestinal thiamine transporters (ThTR-2) and add to deficiency risk. Ocular signs include horizontal nystagmus on lateral gaze, bilateral lateral rectus (abducens) palsy, conjugate gaze palsies, and rarely ptosis; pupils are usually spared but may become miotic in advanced disease. Gait ataxia is multifactorial, arising from a combination of peripheral polyneuropathy, cerebellar involvement, and vestibular paresis. Treat on clinical suspicion as a medical emergency: it is common, preventable, and reversible if thiamine is given early. Korsakoff amnestic state may only become apparent as the acute confusion recedes, characterized by recent-memory/learning impairment, confabulation, and disordered temporal sequencing. The amnestic deficit correlates with lesions of the dorsomedial (dorsal medial) thalamic nuclei. Untreated disease can progress to stupor, coma, and death Giving glucose (parenteral dextrose) before thiamine can precipitate Wernicke in a previously unaffected at-risk patient or rapidly worsen an early form New amnestic state emerging as confusion clears signals evolution to Korsakoff syndrome Waiting for the full classic triad before treating, when only about one-third of patients show all three features. Attributing the quiet, indifferent, inattentive confusional state to depression, sedation, or simple intoxication and missing the diagnosis. Assuming Wernicke occurs only in alcoholics and overlooking it in hyperemesis, malnutrition, dialysis, bariatric surgery, cancer, or HIV patients. Administering glucose-containing fluids before thiamine in an at-risk patient, which can trigger or worsen Wernicke. Thiamine deficiency being overlooked in the setting of head injury (and possibly contributing to motor vehicle accidents). Wernicke disease results from thiamine (vitamin B1) deficiency. Thiamine is a cofactor for several enzymes including transketolase, pyruvate dehydrogenase, and alpha-ketoglutarate dehydrogenase. Deficiency causes a diffuse fall in cerebral glucose utilization and mitochondrial damage; impaired alpha-ketoglutarate dehydrogenase leads to glutamate accumulation, which together with the energy deficit may produce excitotoxic neuronal injury. Lesions are periventricular, surrounding the third ventricle, aqueduct, and fourth ventricle, with predilection for midline structures (dorsomedial thalamus, mammillary bodies, midline cerebellum, periaqueductal gray, and trochlear/abducens nuclei). Acute cases may show petechial hemorrhages; chronic cases show mammillary body atrophy. Outcome depends on early thiamine administration. Ocular palsies improve within hours of thiamine; horizontal nystagmus may persist. Ataxia improves more slowly than ocular signs, and roughly half of patients recover incompletely, left with a slow, wide-based, shuffling gait and inability to tandem walk. Apathy, drowsiness, and confusion resolve gradually. Korsakoff psychosis is frequently persistent, with permanent gaps in memory, confabulation, and disordered temporal sequencing; prolonged untreated deficiency can cause an irreversible profound amnestic syndrome or death. Wernicke-Korsakoff syndrome is underdiagnosed despite a typical history and picture.

humans are incidental dead-end hosts The large majority of infections are asymptomatic, and most symptomatic cases present as a self-limiting febrile illness (West Nile fever) with headache, myalgia, and sometimes a transient rash A small proportion develop neuroinvasive disease: meningitis, encephalitis, or an acute flaccid paralysis resembling poliomyelitis Advancing age and immunosuppression are the strongest risk factors for severe neuroinvasive disease Acute flaccid paralysis from anterior horn cell involvement is an important clue that distinguishes WNV from many other causes of encephalitis Transmission can also occur through blood transfusion and organ transplantation, so donor screening is relevant in endemic areas Management is supportive; there is no specific licensed antiviral therapy, and prevention centres on mosquito control and personal protection Altered consciousness, seizures, or focal neurological signs indicating encephalitis Acute flaccid limb weakness suggesting anterior horn cell involvement Signs of raised intracranial pressure or brainstem dysfunction Severe disease in an elderly or immunocompromised patient with rapid deterioration Assuming a benign viral illness and missing early neuroinvasive features in an older patient Failing to distinguish WNV flaccid paralysis from Guillain-Barre syndrome, which has different management Not considering transfusion- or transplant-associated transmission in a recently exposed patient Delaying empirical treatment for herpes simplex encephalitis while awaiting WNV confirmation West Nile virus is a single-stranded RNA flavivirus circulating between birds and Culex mosquitoes. After a mosquito bite the virus replicates locally and in regional lymph nodes, producing viraemia. In a minority of hosts it crosses into the central nervous system, where it infects neurons, particularly in the brainstem, deep grey matter, and anterior horn cells of the spinal cord, producing encephalitis and flaccid paralysis. Host factors such as age and immune status strongly influence whether infection stays confined to a febrile illness or becomes neuroinvasive. Uncomplicated West Nile fever resolves fully, but neuroinvasive disease carries substantial morbidity and mortality, and survivors of encephalitis or flaccid paralysis may be left with long-lasting neurological and functional deficits, particularly older patients.

West syndrome — Infantile spasms, Infantile epileptic spasms syndrome Benign non-epileptic infantile spasms and benign myoclonus of infancy Sandifer syndrome and gastro-oesophageal reflux Early infantile developmental and epileptic encephalopathy (Ohtahara) Early myoclonic encephalopathy Startle responses and benign sleep myoclonus Tonic seizures of other origin Prolonged or video EEG including sleep to confirm hypsarrhythmia and capture spasms MRI brain to identify a structural cause Metabolic screen including consideration of pyridoxine-dependent and biotinidase disorders Genetic testing (chromosomal microarray, gene panels or exome) Skin examination and imaging for tuberous sclerosis Ophthalmology assessment with fundoscopy Therapeutic trial of pyridoxine where indicated Classic triad of epileptic (infantile) spasms, hypsarrhythmia on EEG, and developmental arrest or regression. Onset is typically between 3 and 12 months, peaking around 4 to 7 months. Spasms occur in clusters, often on awakening, with brief symmetrical flexion or extension of trunk and limbs. Aetiology is diverse: structural (tuberous sclerosis, cortical malformation, hypoxic-ischaemic injury), genetic or metabolic, or unknown. Hypsarrhythmia is a chaotic, high-amplitude, disorganised interictal pattern; modified or fragmented variants occur. First-line treatments are hormonal therapy (adrenocorticotrophic hormone or corticosteroids) and vigabatrin, the latter being especially effective in tuberous sclerosis. Prompt recognition and treatment improve developmental outcome, reflecting a treatment-lag effect. The condition may evolve into Lennox-Gastaut syndrome or other epilepsies. Developmental regression or plateau Clusters of spasms, especially on waking Focal neurological signs suggesting a structural lesion Features of raised intracranial pressure or an underlying metabolic crisis Mistaking spasms for colic, reflux or startle and delaying diagnosis. Not obtaining a sleep EEG and thereby missing hypsarrhythmia. Prolonging the treatment lag by delaying therapy. Overlooking tuberous sclerosis, which changes drug choice. Failing to investigate for treatable metabolic causes. West syndrome reflects age-specific hyperexcitability of the developing brain. Diverse structural, genetic and metabolic insults converge on dysregulated cortical, subcortical and brainstem networks during a critical developmental window; proposed contributors include abnormal corticotrophin-releasing hormone signalling and an imbalance of excitatory and inhibitory neurotransmission. The result is the characteristic clustered spasms and disorganised hypsarrhythmic EEG, with disruption of normal synaptic maturation contributing to developmental regression. Outcome depends heavily on aetiology and treatment lag; cryptogenic cases treated promptly may do well, whereas symptomatic cases often have persistent epilepsy and intellectual disability, and many evolve into other epilepsy syndromes.

detect the antibody deficiency Being reassured by transient rises in neutrophil count during acute illness WHIM syndrome is caused by gain-of-function variants, usually truncations of the C-terminal With immunoglobulin replacement, infection prophylaxis and measures to raise the neutrophil count, many patients survive into adulthood, but the persistent HPV burden carries a significant long-term risk of malignancy and chronic morbidity from bronchiectasis.
