the underlying infection Failing to consider Whipple disease in seronegative arthritis with systemic or gastrointestinal features Relying on histology alone without confirmatory PCR Under-treating by not addressing potential central nervous system involvement Whipple disease is a chronic systemic infection caused by the actinomycete Tropheryma whipplei, and the joints are among the earliest and most frequently affected sites. Although driven by an organism, the articular manifestation behaves as a seronegative inflammatory arthropathy: infiltration of tissues by bacteria-laden macrophages provokes chronic inflammation with a characteristically non-erosive, migratory joint disease. A subtle underlying defect in host macrophage handling of the organism is thought to permit persistent infection. The arthritis often long predates the classic intestinal malabsorptive phase, and immunosuppressive treatment given for a presumed primary inflammatory arthritis can accelerate the systemic disease. Untreated Whipple disease is progressive and can be fatal, but the arthropathy and systemic disease usually respond well to prolonged appropriate antibiotic therapy; central nervous system involvement carries a poorer prognosis and relapse can occur, warranting long-term follow-up.

plasma cell-free DNA next-generation sequencing for endocarditis (p.1369, p.1370) Crohn disease (intestinal phase confusion) (p.1368) Celiac disease (intestinal phase confusion; small-bowel biopsy differential) (p.1368, p.2546) Other rheumatologic disorders during the early arthralgic stage (p.1368) Whipple disease is a rare chronic infection caused by Tropheryma whipplei; because it is uncommon, mimics many other conditions, and needs nonroutine tests, years typically pass between symptom onset and diagnosis (p.1367). "Classic" Whipple disease presents as some combination of migratory arthralgias/seronegative arthritis, weight loss, chronic diarrhea, abdominal pain, and fever, with the duodenum and/or jejunum involved over years (p.1367, p.1368). Migratory oligo- or polyarthralgia (knees, wrists, ankles, MCP joints) typically precedes gastrointestinal symptoms by an average of 6-8 years; joint disease is present in >80% of patients (p.1368, p.2546). CNS disease (detected by CSF PCR for T. whipplei) develops in roughly 50% of patients and many are asymptomatic; manifestations include cognitive decline progressing to dementia, personality/mood change, and hypothalamic involvement, and portend a poor prognosis (p.1368). Oculomasticatory and oculofacial myorhythmia are highly suggestive of Whipple disease; supranuclear gaze palsy (usually vertical) is another neuro-ophthalmologic clue (p.1368). Diagnosis rests on small-bowel (postbulbar duodenal) biopsy showing lamina propria infiltration by foamy macrophages with diastase-resistant PAS-positive inclusions, combined with PCR for T. whipplei; PCR has substantially improved sensitivity and specificity (p.1368, p.1369). It is prudent to collect CSF even without CNS symptoms, because asymptomatic CNS disease is common and the CNS is the most common site of relapse, informing treatment duration (p.1369). Treatment requires prolonged therapy; clinical response is often rapid, but eradication and durable cure are challenged by relapse and host predisposition to reinfection, which can occur years to decades later (p.1369, p.1370). WD should be considered in any chronic multisystemic process, especially the combination of rheumatologic and intestinal disease with weight loss, with or without neurologic and cardiac involvement (p.1368, p.1369). CNS involvement (cognitive decline/dementia, personality change, hypothalamic dysfunction such as polyuria/polydipsia or sleep-cycle disorder, supranuclear gaze palsy, oculomasticatory myorhythmia) portends a poor prognosis with significant mortality risk and neurologic sequelae (p.1368) Endocarditis (often afebrile, Duke criteria rarely met) may be complicated by congestive heart failure (~40%), embolic events, arrhythmias, or mycotic aneurysm (p.1368) Progressive weight loss with chronic diarrhea and malabsorption (p.1367, p.1368) Immune reconstitution inflammatory syndrome (IRIS) after treatment, with recurrent fever, arthritis, skin lesions, pleuritis, uveitis, and periorbital inflammation; some cases have been fatal (p.1369) Serology is of little value: patients with active infection mount a poor IgM/IgG response, and a positive result most likely reflects prior exposure and clearance (p.1369) A normal macroscopic duodenal appearance is common, and a negative test does not exclude WD; pretest probability must be considered (p.1369) Histology/PAS alone is not optimally sensitive and is nonspecific (also positive with mycobacteria and other organisms); anti-TNF-alpha therapy may decrease PAS sensitivity (p.1369) Saliva and fecal PCR are inappropriate as sole diagnostic tools because of low positive predictive value (more often reflecting colonization than disease); a positive result needs confirmation from end-organ tissue or body fluid (p.1370) Treating presumed inflammatory arthritis or uveitis with glucocorticoids or anti-TNF-alpha agents can accelerate disease progression and unmask/precipitate disease; consider screening for WD before immunosuppression (p.1368) Oral tetracycline or TMP-SMX monotherapy has unacceptable relapse rates, particularly for CNS disease; sequence data indicate TMP is not active against T. whipplei (no dihydrofolate reductase) (p.1369, p.1370) Detection of T. whipplei sequence in BALF of asymptomatic individuals does not establish disease; caution is needed before diagnosing isolated pneumonia on sequence alone (p.1368) Culture is not practical for diagnosis as it takes months to turn positive (p.1370) T. whipplei is a weakly staining gram-positive, non-acid-fast bacillus with a small (<1-megabase) genome and incomplete biosynthetic pathways, consistent with an intracellular/nutritionally dependent pathogen; it is one of the slowest-growing human pathogens (doubling time ~18 days). Exposure is far more common than disease, and chronic infection (WD) is a rare outcome (<0.01% of those exposed). Establishing chronic infection involves both an impaired host inflammatory response and pathogen-driven immune modulation: HLA alleles DRB1*13 and DQB1*06 (favoring humoral over cell-mediated responses) raise risk, an impaired TH1 response with increased anti-inflammatory cytokines and regulatory T-cell activity, M2 macrophage polarization with impaired phagosome-lysosome fusion, and blunted T. whipplei-specific T-cell development occur. The organism has tropism for myeloid cells, which it invades and within which it avoids killing; affected tissue is infiltrated by foamy macrophages containing PAS-staining inclusions (ingested bacteria). In the small intestine, villus atrophy, lymphangiectasia, crypt hyperplasia, and surface epithelial apoptosis lead to malabsorptive diarrhea. (p.1367, p.1368) Untreated Whipple disease is often fatal, and delayed diagnosis can lead to irreparable organ damage, particularly in the CNS. With appropriate treatment, clinical response is often rapid and at times remarkable, and timely recognition may yield cure with medical management alone; however, eradication requires prolonged therapy and a durable response is challenged by relapse (especially CNS relapse) and host predisposition to reinfection occurring years to decades later. CNS disease carries a significant mortality risk and may leave neurologic sequelae. (p.1367, p.1368, p.1369, p.1370) Harrison frames the disease by clinical syndrome rather than a graded severity score: asymptomatic colonization/carriage (PCR-detectable T. whipplei in stool, saliva, or duodenal tissue without symptoms); acute infection (e.g., gastroenteritis in children, febrile bacteremia, acute pneumonia); chronic infection comprising "classic" Whipple disease (intestinal involvement with multisystem disease) and "isolated" infection (organ disease such as endocarditis, neurologic, ocular, or pulmonary disease without intestinal symptoms); and reinfection/relapsing disease, including treatment-associated IRIS. (p.1367, p.1368, p.1369)

for hyperphagia and obesity as the child grows Assuming inheritance from a parent when most cases are de novo White-Sutton syndrome results from heterozygous loss-of-function variants in POGZ, which encodes a heterochromatin-associated protein containing zinc-finger domains that participates in chromatin regulation, chromosome segregation, and the control of gene transcription during neurodevelopment. By influencing the expression of genes required for the development and function of neurones, POGZ contributes to normal cognition, behaviour, and sensory processing. Reduced dosage of the protein through haploinsufficiency disrupts these processes, producing the intellectual disability, autism spectrum features, visual problems, and associated findings that characterise the syndrome. Inheritance is autosomal dominant, and most cases occur as de novo events. Lifespan is generally normal, and the long-term picture is defined by intellectual disability and autism spectrum features of variable severity together with any behavioural, visual, and weight-related issues; developmental progress is expected with educational and therapeutic support, and outcome depends chiefly on the degree of neurodevelopmental involvement.

Widow (Latrodectus) spider envenomation — latrodectism, black widow bite, redback spider bite, Latrodectus bite, katipo bite Acute abdomen (appendicitis, perforated viscus, renal colic) Acute coronary syndrome given chest and abdominal pain with autonomic features Tetanus or other cause of muscle rigidity Sympathomimetic toxidrome Recluse spider or other envenomation Hypocalcaemia or other electrolyte-driven cramping Clinical diagnosis based on history and characteristic syndrome Electrocardiography if chest pain or marked hypertension is present Creatine kinase if muscle spasm is severe or prolonged Basic electrolytes and calcium to exclude metabolic causes of cramp Blood pressure and pain monitoring to gauge severity and treatment response Latrodectism is dominated by pain and autonomic features rather than local tissue destruction; the bite site itself is often unremarkable Pain begins locally and radiates to become regional or generalised, with muscle cramping and spasm that may involve the abdomen and mimic an acute abdomen Diaphoresis is characteristic and may be localised or regional, sometimes with a distribution around the bitten limb Associated features include hypertension, tachycardia, nausea, headache, tremor and restlessness Symptoms can be prolonged and wax and wane over days; the bite is rarely life-threatening in otherwise healthy adults Management principles centre on analgesia; antivenom may be considered for severe or refractory systemic symptoms with attention to allergic reaction risk There is no dermonecrosis with widow bites, which helps distinguish latrodectism from recluse (loxoscelism) envenomation Severe uncontrolled hypertension with end-organ symptoms Chest pain suggesting cardiac involvement Symptoms in pregnancy, in young children or in patients with significant comorbidity Progressive or refractory pain and spasm despite analgesia Mistaking abdominal muscle rigidity for a surgical abdomen and proceeding to unnecessary laparotomy Providing inadequate analgesia for what can be very severe, protracted pain Expecting local necrosis and doubting the diagnosis when the bite site looks benign Overlooking heightened risk in pregnancy, children or cardiac patients Widow spider venom contains alpha-latrotoxin, which binds pre-synaptic nerve terminals and forms cation-permeable pores that trigger massive, calcium-independent exocytosis of neurotransmitters. Depletion and unregulated release of acetylcholine and catecholamines at neuromuscular junctions and autonomic synapses produce sustained muscle contraction, cramping and autonomic hyperactivity. The result is severe pain, diaphoresis and cardiovascular stimulation without significant local tissue necrosis, since the venom acts on nerve terminals rather than directly on tissue. Latrodectism is painful and can be debilitating for days, but is very rarely fatal in healthy individuals and generally resolves fully with symptomatic care and, where indicated, antivenom.

of histone H3 at lysine 4, a modification associated with open, transcriptionally active chromatin at gene promoters and enhancers. Loss-of-function variants reduce the enzyme's dose (haploinsufficiency), blunting the deposition of these activating marks and disturbing the precise programmes of gene expression required for growth and neurodevelopment. The consequent dysregulation of developmental gene networks yields the characteristic pattern of intellectual disability, growth restriction, hypertrichosis and craniofacial features, and because the defect produces a reproducible genome-wide methylation signature it can be detected by episignature testing. The disorder is compatible with survival into adulthood; intellectual disability is usually mild to moderate but ranges more widely, and most individuals benefit substantially from early developmental, educational and behavioural support, with growth and feeding issues tending to improve after infancy.

Duane anomaly for a simple sixth nerve palsy Failing to recognise the female predominance and its genetic implications Neglecting early hearing intervention critical to language development Wildervanck syndrome combines features attributable to disturbed development in overlapping embryonic regions. The cervical vertebral fusion results from failed segmentation of cervical somites, as in Klippel-Feil syndrome, while the Duane retraction anomaly arises from maldevelopment of the abducens nucleus and nerve, with aberrant innervation of the lateral rectus by a branch of the oculomotor nerve, causing co-contraction and globe retraction. The sensorineural hearing loss reflects inner ear or eighth nerve maldevelopment. The strong female predominance points to an X-linked dominant mechanism with male lethality or a sex-limited multifactorial cause, though the precise genetic basis remains incompletely defined. The malformations are static and non-progressive; with hearing rehabilitation, ophthalmological management, and attention to cervical stability, affected individuals generally have normal cognition and a good functional outlook.

cause and missing the congenital pattern Not recognising the characteristic mid-airway distribution distal to normal proximal bronchi Failing to exclude cystic fibrosis, ciliary dyskinesia, and immunodeficiency Overlooking the diagnostic value of dynamic imaging showing bronchial ballooning and collapse Williams-Campbell syndrome is characterised by a congenital deficiency or absence of the cartilaginous support in the medium-sized subsegmental bronchi, typically the fourth to sixth generations. Lacking rigid cartilage, these airway segments lose their structural integrity and behave abnormally with respiration, distending on inspiration and collapsing on expiration. This dynamic instability impairs airflow and cough-driven clearance, leading to secretion retention, recurrent infection, and the development of characteristic distal cystic bronchiectasis. Because the proximal airways and the more peripheral airways retain normal or adequate structure, the disease has a distinctive intermediate distribution. The condition is generally considered congenital, and its precise molecular cause is not established. Prognosis depends on the extent of bronchiectasis and frequency of infection; with diligent airway clearance and infection control some patients do well, while extensive disease can lead to progressive respiratory impairment and, in severe cases, respiratory failure.

Wilms Tumour — nephroblastoma, Wilms tumor Neuroblastoma Mesoblastic nephroma (in infants) Renal cell carcinoma (older children) Clear cell sarcoma or rhabdoid tumour of the kidney Multicystic dysplastic kidney or hydronephrosis Hepatoblastoma or other abdominal masses Abdominal ultrasound as the initial imaging test Cross-sectional imaging (CT or MRI) of the abdomen to define the mass and the contralateral kidney Chest imaging to assess pulmonary metastases Full blood count, renal and liver function, urinalysis Blood pressure measurement Assessment for inferior vena cava or renal vein tumour thrombus The most common primary renal malignancy of childhood, typically presenting in preschool children around 2-5 years of age. The usual presentation is an asymptomatic, smooth abdominal mass discovered by a parent or on routine examination, sometimes with abdominal pain, haematuria, or hypertension. The mass characteristically does not cross the midline, in contrast to neuroblastoma. Associated with syndromes and anomalies such as WAGR, Beckwith-Wiedemann, and Denys-Drash, and with hemihypertrophy and aniridia; these children warrant surveillance. Examination should be gentle, avoiding vigorous palpation of the mass because of the risk of tumour rupture. Staging and histology (favourable versus anaplastic) guide a multimodal approach combining surgery, chemotherapy, and sometimes radiotherapy. Bilateral disease occurs in a minority and requires nephron-sparing strategies to preserve renal function. The lungs are the most common site of metastatic spread, so chest imaging is part of staging. Overall survival is high, making Wilms tumour one of the success stories of paediatric oncology. Rapidly enlarging abdominal mass Gross haematuria or significant hypertension Features of tumour rupture (acute abdominal pain, distension, haemodynamic instability) Respiratory symptoms suggesting pulmonary metastases Signs of vascular (caval) extension Aggressive palpation of the abdominal mass, risking rupture Confusing it with neuroblastoma, which typically crosses the midline and has different markers Missing hypertension as an associated finding Failing to screen children with predisposing syndromes Overlooking the contralateral kidney for bilateral disease Wilms tumour arises from embryonal nephrogenic (metanephric) blastema, often showing a classic triphasic pattern of blastemal, epithelial, and stromal elements. It is linked to abnormalities of genes involved in kidney development, including WT1, and to epigenetic changes at chromosome 11p; persistent nephrogenic rests are precursor lesions. Anaplastic histology confers a worse prognosis and greater treatment resistance. With risk-adapted multimodal therapy, most children with favourable-histology disease are cured; prognosis is worse with anaplastic histology, advanced stage, or unfavourable biological features.

Wilson's Disease — hepatolenticular degeneration Viral hepatitis and cirrhosis (often the initial diagnostic considerations in patients who actually have WD) (p.3338) Autoimmune hepatitis / chronic hepatitis (WD in adolescence may present with chronic-hepatitis features long before neurologic signs or Kayser-Fleischer rings appear) (p.3026-area AIH text, ch.355/427) Parkinson disease and other movement disorders (WD may be mistakenly diagnosed as these) (p.3338, p.3518) Substance abuse (a competing consideration in late-teen/early-twenties patients presenting with psychiatric features) (p.3339) Viral hepatitis (a frequent initial misdiagnosis in patients with the hepatic presentation of WD) (p.3338) Serum ceruloplasmin (initial screening test; characteristically low) and serum copper (low) (p.3339) 24-h urinary copper excretion (elevated, >100 ug/24 h; use acid-washed copper-free containers); penicillamine challenge with serial urine copper as a variation (p.3339) Percutaneous needle liver biopsy for quantitative hepatic copper (gold standard; >200 ug/g dry weight characteristic) by ICP-MS or atomic absorption spectrometry; histochemical copper staining is less reliable (p.3339) Slit-lamp or optical coherence tomography ophthalmologic examination for Kayser-Fleischer rings (required to detect early rings) (p.3339) Radiolabeled 64Cu incorporation into ceruloplasmin (highly specific; WD patients incorporate very little) (p.3339) ATP7B molecular/genetic testing (>650 pathogenic variants catalogued; common missense variants H1069Q, M645R, R778L) (p.3339) T2-weighted brain MRI in neurologic disease may show generalized atrophy and signal hypointensity in caudate head, putamen, globus pallidus, substantia nigra, and red nucleus (~50%), though imaging correlates poorly with clinical features (p.3518) Cirrhosis of other cause (p.3338) Autoimmune/chronic hepatitis (p.3338, ch.355/427) Parkinson disease and other movement disorders (p.3338, p.3518) Primary psychiatric illness or substance abuse in adolescents/young adults (p.3339) Autosomal recessive disorder of copper transport caused by loss-of-function variants in ATP7B (a P-type copper-transporting ATPase), which normally mediates copper removal from the liver via biliary excretion and prevents brain copper accumulation (p.3338). Typically affects adolescents and young adults; presenting features include nonspecific liver disease, neurologic abnormalities, psychiatric illness, hemolytic anemia, renal tubular Fanconi syndrome, and skeletal abnormalities (p.3338). Age influences presentation: nearly all individuals presenting with liver disease are <30 years, whereas neurologic or psychiatric presentations may range from the first to the fifth decade; regardless of presentation, some degree of liver disease is invariably present (p.3338). Neurologic presentation reflects basal ganglia (caudate, putamen) involvement: dysarthria, dystonia (including facial grimacing/risus sardonicus), rigidity, tremor (classically 'wing-beating'), choreiform movements, abnormal gait, and uncoordinated handwriting; WD can properly be classified as a movement disorder (p.3338, p.3518). Kayser-Fleischer ring (golden to greenish-brown band in the peripheral cornea, from copper deposition in Descemet's membrane) is pathognomonic; present in ~95% of patients with neurologic signs but only about two-thirds of those with hepatic presentations (p.3339). Supportive biochemistry: low serum copper, low serum ceruloplasmin, increased 24-h urinary copper excretion (>100 ug/24 h), elevated transaminases, aminoaciduria, and hemolytic anemia (p.3339). Hepatic copper >200 ug per gram dry weight (normal 20-50) on percutaneous needle liver biopsy is a gold-standard biochemical diagnostic finding (p.3339). Diagnosis relies on a combination of clinical, biochemical, and molecular features; the Leipzig scoring system (2001), endorsed by EASL, weights and collates these features as a valuable diagnostic guide (p.3339). One of the best-characterized and most effectively managed inborn errors of metabolism; prompt diagnosis in the presymptomatic or early symptomatic phase plus lifelong treatment are needed to prevent premature mortality (p.3338). Hemolytic anemia from sudden, massive release of hepatic copper into the circulation directly toxic to red cell membranes can be sudden and catastrophic (p.3339). Any teenager or young adult with new-onset psychiatric signs should have WD formally excluded (p.3339). WD should always be considered in the differential of a movement disorder, particularly when arising in the first decades of life (p.3518). WD is treatable and progression is preventable, so it is critical to test for it in any young patient with liver disease and/or a movement disorder or new psychiatric illness; missed diagnoses are tragic (p.3338, p.3518). Normal blood copper, ceruloplasmin, or urinary copper levels do NOT exclude the diagnosis (p.3518). WD in adolescence may present with chronic-hepatitis features long before neurologic manifestations or Kayser-Fleischer rings appear (p.427/355). Kayser-Fleischer rings are absent in about one-third of patients with hepatic presentations, so their absence does not rule out WD (p.3339). In patients with neurologic presentations, penicillamine treatment can induce paradoxical worsening of neurologic status (p.3340). Autosomal recessive disease caused by loss-of-function variants in ATP7B, a highly conserved P-type copper-transporting ATPase expressed primarily in liver and kidney. ATP7B normally mediates copper removal from the liver via biliary excretion and prevents brain copper accumulation; its loss leads to pathologic copper accumulation, primarily impacting the liver and brain. Neurologic disease reflects copper toxicity in the basal ganglia (caudate, putamen, striatum) with neurodegeneration and astrogliosis. Copper also deposits in the cornea (Kayser-Fleischer ring) and lens (sunflower cataract), and renal copper toxicity produces tubular (Fanconi) dysfunction. Massive sudden release of hepatic copper into the circulation directly damages red cell membranes, causing hemolytic anemia (p.3338-3339). In the absence of treatment, the course is progressive, leading to severe neurologic dysfunction and early/premature death in most patients, although a small proportion experience a relatively benign course. WD is one of the most effectively managed inborn errors of metabolism: prompt diagnosis in the presymptomatic or early symptomatic phase and lifelong treatment prevent premature mortality. Liver transplantation, generally needed only when delayed diagnosis or poor compliance has caused irreversible hepatic damage, can correct both hepatic failure and crippling neurologic impairment (p.3338, p.3340, p.3518). No single graded severity scale is given in the source; diagnosis is formalized using a combination of clinical, biochemical, and molecular features, collated by the Leipzig scoring system (2001, endorsed by EASL). Disease is broadly staged as presymptomatic/early symptomatic versus advanced; advanced or medically unresponsive hepatic disease is the indication for liver transplantation (p.3339-3340).

Wiskott-Aldrich syndrome — WAS, eczema-thrombocytopenia-immunodeficiency syndrome Immune thrombocytopenic purpura (ITP) Atopic dermatitis with recurrent infection Severe combined immunodeficiency and other combined immunodeficiencies X-linked thrombocytopenia (milder WAS spectrum) Hyper-IgE syndrome Congenital thrombocytopenias with normal platelet size Full blood count and blood film assessing platelet number and platelet size (mean platelet volume) WAS gene sequencing and analysis of WAS protein expression Immunoglobulin levels and specific antibody responses Lymphocyte subsets and functional T-cell testing Autoimmune and haemolysis screens where indicated Surveillance for lymphoma in older patients Wiskott-Aldrich syndrome is an X-linked disorder classically presenting in boys with the triad of eczema, thrombocytopenia with small platelets, and recurrent infections It is caused by mutations in the WAS gene encoding the WAS protein, which regulates the actin cytoskeleton in haematopoietic cells The thrombocytopenia is distinctive for producing microthrombocytes (abnormally small platelets), unlike most other causes of low platelets Bleeding, ranging from petechiae and bruising to serious intracranial haemorrhage, is often the earliest and most dangerous manifestation The infection pattern reflects combined humoral and cellular immunodeficiency, with encapsulated bacteria, opportunistic organisms, and viruses all contributing There is a marked predisposition to autoimmune disease (such as haemolytic anaemia and vasculitis) and to malignancy, particularly lymphoma Milder allelic conditions include X-linked thrombocytopenia, while certain mutations cause X-linked neutropenia Definitive treatment is haematopoietic stem cell transplantation, with gene therapy an emerging option; supportive care includes immunoglobulin replacement, infection prophylaxis, and careful bleeding management Significant bleeding, especially intracranial haemorrhage, as an emergency Recurrent or opportunistic infections requiring urgent immunological workup New lymphadenopathy or systemic symptoms suggesting lymphoma Live vaccines must be avoided because of the combined immunodeficiency Blood products should be irradiated and leucodepleted to prevent transfusion-associated graft-versus-host disease Diagnosing isolated ITP and giving immunosuppression or splenectomy without recognising the underlying syndrome Overlooking the diagnostic clue of small platelet size on the blood film Administering live vaccines or non-irradiated blood products Underestimating the lifelong risks of autoimmunity and malignancy after immune reconstitution Delaying referral for transplantation in a child with classic severe disease Wiskott-Aldrich syndrome results from loss-of-function mutations in the WAS gene on the X chromosome, which encodes a protein that links cell-surface signalling to reorganisation of the actin cytoskeleton in blood cells. Defective cytoskeletal dynamics impair the formation of immune synapses, the motility and function of T cells, dendritic cells, and phagocytes, and the normal production and structure of platelets, yielding small, poorly functioning platelets and combined immunodeficiency. Disturbed regulatory T-cell function and abnormal B-cell responses drive the high rate of autoimmunity, while impaired immune surveillance and chronic immune dysregulation predispose to lymphoid malignancy. Untreated classic disease carries a poor prognosis owing to bleeding, infection, autoimmunity, and malignancy, but successful haematopoietic stem cell transplantation, ideally performed early, can be curative; milder phenotypes such as X-linked thrombocytopenia have a better outlook though still require monitoring.

X-linked thrombocytopenia (Wiskott-Aldrich variant) — X-linked thrombocytopenia, XLT, Attenuated Wiskott-Aldrich syndrome Classic Wiskott-Aldrich syndrome Immune (idiopathic) thrombocytopenic purpura Congenital amegakaryocytic thrombocytopenia MYH9-related disorders (giant platelets, in contrast) X-linked thrombocytopenia with dyserythropoietic anaemia (GATA1 mutation) Bernard-Soulier syndrome Inherited thrombocytopenias with normal platelet size Full blood count with mean platelet volume showing small platelets Peripheral blood film for platelet size and morphology Flow cytometry for WAS protein expression in leucocytes WAS gene sequencing to confirm hypomorphic mutation Immunoglobulin levels and specific antibody responses Lymphocyte subset analysis and regulatory T-cell assessment Direct platelet antibody testing to help exclude immune thrombocytopenia A milder allelic variant of Wiskott-Aldrich syndrome caused by hypomorphic missense mutations in the WAS gene that retain partial WAS protein expression. Cardinal feature is congenital microthrombocytopenia: a low platelet count with characteristically small platelet volume. Bleeding is usually mild, with petechiae, bruising and epistaxis, in contrast to the severe eczema and profound immunodeficiency of classic Wiskott-Aldrich syndrome. Eczema and infections are absent or mild, but immune dysregulation and autoimmunity can still occur over time. Small platelet size distinguishes it from immune thrombocytopenia, where platelets are normal or large, and helps avoid unnecessary immunosuppression or splenectomy. The WAS protein regulates actin cytoskeletal remodelling in haematopoietic cells; the degree of residual function correlates inversely with disease severity. Even in this attenuated form there is a lifelong, if lower, risk of autoimmune complications and lymphoid malignancy requiring surveillance. Splenectomy raises the platelet count but increases sepsis risk and is used cautiously; haematopoietic stem cell transplantation is curative and considered in severe cases. Intracranial or other severe haemorrhage during marked thrombocytopenia Emergence of autoimmune cytopenias or vasculitis Development of lymphoma or other lymphoid malignancy Progressive fall in platelet count or new eczema/infection suggesting phenotype conversion Post-splenectomy overwhelming encapsulated-organism sepsis Misdiagnosing the condition as immune thrombocytopenia and giving repeated immunosuppression or splenectomy. Overlooking the diagnostic clue of small mean platelet volume. Assuming the attenuated phenotype removes the need for surveillance of autoimmunity and malignancy. Performing splenectomy without appreciating the lifelong infection risk in a WAS-related disorder. Failing to test the WAS gene in a boy with congenital microthrombocytopenia and a suggestive family history. X-linked thrombocytopenia is caused by mutations in the WAS gene on the X chromosome that encode Wiskott-Aldrich syndrome protein, a regulator of actin polymerisation in haematopoietic cells acting downstream of Rho-family GTPases. Hypomorphic (usually missense) mutations preserve some residual protein and function, producing the attenuated phenotype rather than the null mutations that cause classic Wiskott-Aldrich syndrome. Defective cytoskeletal remodelling impairs megakaryocyte platelet production and shortens platelet survival, and it disturbs the immunological synapse, cell migration and regulatory T-cell function. The result is microthrombocytopenia with relatively preserved immunity, though residual defects in immune regulation still predispose to autoimmunity and malignancy. Life expectancy is substantially better than in classic Wiskott-Aldrich syndrome, and many patients do well with supportive care, but lifelong risks of severe bleeding, autoimmunity and malignancy persist. Haematopoietic stem cell transplantation can be curative and is weighed against the milder natural history.

MEDICAL EMERGENCY: pre-excited atrial fibrillation with a rapid, irregular, broad-complex response that can degenerate into ventricular fibrillation Haemodynamic instability during any pre-excited tachyarrhythmia requiring urgent synchronised cardioversion Syncope or aborted sudden cardiac death indicating a high-risk pathway Use of AV nodal blocking agents in pre-excited atrial fibrillation, which can precipitate deterioration Administering AV nodal blocking drugs in pre-excited atrial fibrillation Assuming an asymptomatic WPW pattern requires no assessment when risk stratification may be warranted Mistaking pre-excited atrial fibrillation for ventricular tachycardia or ordinary atrial fibrillation Delaying cardioversion in an unstable pre-excited tachyarrhythmia In WPW an accessory atrioventricular pathway bypasses the normal AV nodal delay, allowing early activation of ventricular myocardium and producing the delta wave and short PR interval. This creates the substrate for reentry: in orthodromic AVRT the impulse travels down the AV node and back up the accessory pathway, while in the less common antidromic form the direction is reversed, giving a wide-complex tachycardia. The gravest scenario occurs when atrial fibrillation develops and the accessory pathway, lacking the rate-limiting properties of the AV node, conducts rapid atrial impulses to the ventricles, risking degeneration to ventricular fibrillation and sudden death. Most patients have an excellent prognosis, and catheter ablation is curative in the great majority; the principal risk is sudden death from rapidly conducted atrial fibrillation in the minority with a short-refractory-period pathway, which risk stratification and ablation substantially reduce.

wolff parkinson white syndrome — WPW syndrome, ventricular pre-excitation syndrome atrioventricular nodal reentrant tachycardia concealed accessory pathway atrioventricular reentrant tachycardia bundle branch block mimicking a wide QRS ventricular tachycardia atrial fibrillation without pre-excitation fasciculoventricular and other variant pathways twelve-lead ECG to characterise the delta wave and localise the pathway exercise stress testing to assess abrupt loss of pre-excitation ambulatory monitoring to document tachyarrhythmias transthoracic echocardiography to exclude Ebstein anomaly and cardiomyopathy electrophysiological study with measurement of the shortest pre-excited RR interval in atrial fibrillation procainamide or other pharmacological challenge to gauge pathway refractoriness WPW syndrome is the combination of ventricular pre-excitation on the resting ECG and symptomatic tachyarrhythmia; pre-excitation without symptoms is termed a WPW pattern. The classic triad is a short PR interval, a slurred delta wave and a widened QRS, reflecting fusion of accessory-pathway and nodal ventricular activation. The delta-wave vector and precordial transition allow bedside prediction of pathway location, guiding ablation. Orthodromic AVRT is the commonest tachycardia, but pre-excited atrial fibrillation is the most dangerous because it can conduct rapidly and degenerate to ventricular fibrillation. An irregular, broad, rapid tachycardia with varying QRS morphology should raise immediate suspicion of pre-excited atrial fibrillation. AV-nodal blocking drugs including adenosine, verapamil, diltiazem and digoxin are contraindicated in pre-excited atrial fibrillation as they can accelerate pathway conduction. Abrupt, complete loss of pre-excitation during exercise or with procainamide suggests a pathway with a long refractory period and lower risk. Ebstein anomaly is associated with WPW and frequently with multiple right-sided accessory pathways. pre-excited atrial fibrillation with a very short shortest pre-excited RR interval syncope, particularly during exertion or palpitations resuscitated cardiac arrest or documented ventricular fibrillation family history of sudden death with pre-excitation haemodynamic instability during any wide-complex tachycardia Treating pre-excited atrial fibrillation with AV-nodal blockers and precipitating ventricular fibrillation. Dismissing asymptomatic pre-excitation without considering risk stratification in higher-risk occupations or athletes. Confusing a fusion or pre-excited complex with myocardial infarction because of pseudo-Q waves and repolarisation change. Assuming a single pathway when multiple pathways, especially in Ebstein anomaly, are present. Interpreting intermittent pre-excitation as invariably low-risk without confirming it is abrupt and rate-related. The syndrome results from a congenital accessory atrioventricular pathway that bypasses the physiological delay of the atrioventricular node, allowing early activation of ventricular myocardium (pre-excitation). Because the pathway conducts faster than the node, part of the ventricle depolarises early, shortening the PR interval and inscribing a delta wave, while the remainder is activated normally, producing a fusion QRS. The same pathway provides a limb for macroreentrant tachycardia. When atrial fibrillation develops, an accessory pathway with a short antegrade refractory period can transmit disorganised atrial impulses to the ventricle at extremely high rates, and this rapid irregular ventricular response may deteriorate into ventricular fibrillation and sudden death. Most patients have an excellent prognosis and catheter ablation is curative with a high success rate, but a small subset with rapidly conducting pathways are at risk of sudden cardiac death, which may occasionally be the first manifestation. Risk stratification of asymptomatic pre-excitation is therefore central to management.

Wolfram syndrome — DIDMOAD, WFS1-related Wolfram syndrome, diabetes insipidus, diabetes mellitus, optic atrophy and deafness, wolframin deficiency Type 1 (autoimmune) diabetes mellitus Isolated hereditary optic atrophy (e.g. dominant optic atrophy, Leber hereditary optic neuropathy) Mitochondrial disease with diabetes and deafness (e.g. maternally inherited diabetes and deafness) Other causes of cranial diabetes insipidus Thiamine-responsive megaloblastic anaemia syndrome (SLC19A2) with diabetes and deafness Bardet-Biedl and other syndromic causes of visual and endocrine disturbance WFS1 (and CISD2) gene sequencing to confirm the diagnosis Diabetes work-up including islet autoantibodies (negative) and C-peptide Water deprivation/desmopressin testing and paired plasma/urine osmolality for diabetes insipidus Formal ophthalmological assessment with optical coherence tomography and visual fields for optic atrophy Audiometry for sensorineural hearing loss Brain MRI to assess brainstem, cerebellar, and posterior pituitary changes; urodynamics for neurogenic bladder Usually autosomal recessive neurodegenerative and endocrine disorder caused by WFS1 mutations encoding wolframin, an endoplasmic reticulum membrane protein; a rarer CISD2-related form exists The acronym DIDMOAD summarises the core features: Diabetes Insipidus, Diabetes Mellitus, Optic Atrophy, and Deafness Childhood-onset non-autoimmune, insulin-dependent diabetes mellitus is typically the first feature, followed by progressive bilateral optic atrophy causing visual loss The diabetes mellitus is islet-cell-antibody negative and not HLA-associated, distinguishing it from type 1 diabetes, and coexisting optic atrophy should prompt consideration of Wolfram syndrome Cranial diabetes insipidus, sensorineural deafness, neurodegeneration (brainstem and cerebellar signs, neurogenic bladder), and psychiatric disturbance develop over time Diagnosis is clinical supported by WFS1 sequencing; management is supportive and multidisciplinary, coordinating diabetes, endocrine, ophthalmology, audiology, urology, and neurology care Progressive visual loss from optic atrophy threatening independence Unrecognised cranial diabetes insipidus causing dehydration and electrolyte disturbance Brainstem neurodegeneration with central apnoea or swallowing difficulty Severe psychiatric disturbance or suicidality requiring urgent mental-health support Labelling the childhood diabetes as type 1 and missing the syndromic diagnosis when optic atrophy appears Attributing polyuria solely to poor glycaemic control and overlooking coexisting cranial diabetes insipidus Neglecting audiological, urological, and psychiatric surveillance in a multisystem disorder Failing to offer genetic counselling given the mainly autosomal recessive inheritance Wolfram syndrome is most often caused by biallelic WFS1 mutations encoding wolframin, an endoplasmic reticulum transmembrane protein important for calcium homeostasis and the endoplasmic reticulum stress response. Loss of wolframin function heightens endoplasmic reticulum stress and triggers apoptosis in highly secretory and neuronal cells, notably pancreatic beta cells, retinal ganglion cells and the optic nerve, the hypothalamic-pituitary vasopressin system, the cochlea, and diffuse brain regions. This progressive cellular loss produces non-autoimmune insulin-dependent diabetes mellitus, optic atrophy, cranial diabetes insipidus, sensorineural deafness, and wider neurodegeneration. Wolfram syndrome is progressive with accumulating disability; visual and hearing loss, neurological decline, and endocrine complications develop over years, and premature death, often from brainstem involvement or its complications, is typical. Coordinated multidisciplinary care can preserve function and quality of life.

with rapid clinical deterioration Overlooking the diagnosis in a neonate with failure to thrive and hepatosplenomegaly Missing adrenal calcification on imaging as a diagnostic pointer Failing to recognise the milder cholesteryl ester storage disease as the same enzyme deficiency Delaying enzyme replacement therapy, which is most beneficial when started early Wolman disease is caused by biallelic pathogenic variants in LIPA, encoding lysosomal acid lipase, the enzyme that hydrolyses cholesteryl esters and triglycerides delivered to the lysosome. Deficient activity causes these lipids to accumulate within lysosomes of the liver, spleen, intestine, adrenal glands, and macrophages throughout the body. Massive lipid storage produces hepatosplenomegaly, hepatic dysfunction, adrenal infiltration with calcification, and intestinal involvement causing malabsorption. Disrupted intracellular cholesterol sensing also drives a proatherogenic dyslipidaemia. The severe infantile phenotype reflects near-absent enzyme activity, whereas residual activity underlies the milder cholesteryl ester storage disease. Untreated infantile Wolman disease is rapidly progressive and usually fatal within the first months of life. Enzyme replacement therapy has substantially improved survival in this severe form, and the later-onset cholesteryl ester storage disease has a more chronic course dominated by liver disease and dyslipidaemia with associated cardiovascular risk.

associated hair-shaft defects on microscopy Woolly hair reflects an abnormal, tightly coiled hair shaft with an altered elliptical cross-section and often reduced diameter, present from birth in Hereditary diffuse forms and the localised naevus arise from defects in hair-shaft formation. The clinically critical recessive syndromes, Naxos disease and Carvajal syndrome, result from mutations in desmosomal genes encoding plakoglobin and desmoplakin, which impair cell-to-cell adhesion in the epidermis, hair and myocardium and thereby explain the triad of woolly hair, palmoplantar keratoderma and cardiomyopathy with arrhythmogenic risk. Isolated woolly hair and the woolly hair naevus are benign and tend to improve in later childhood or adult life, but the outlook in Naxos and Carvajal syndromes is dominated by the cardiomyopathy and its arrhythmic risk, making early cardiac diagnosis potentially life-saving.

cause Assuming the dystonia will remain confined to writing Writer's cramp reflects maladaptive sensorimotor plasticity and deficient inhibition within the motor system, in which repetitive, highly practised writing drives abnormal cortical reorganisation and blurring of the cortical representation of the fingers. Some patients manage well with practical adaptations alone.

Writer's cramp — writing dystonia, task-specific focal hand dystonia Musician's and other task-specific dystonias Generalised or segmental dystonia with hand involvement Essential tremor affecting writing Functional (psychogenic) hand movements Overuse or repetitive strain injury Clinical diagnosis from the task-specific pattern Examination to exclude weakness, sensory loss or other neurological signs Assessment of whether the dystonia is simple or has spread to other tasks MRI of the brain only if features suggest a secondary cause Occupational assessment of writing technique and ergonomics A task-specific focal dystonia in which abnormal hand and forearm posturing appears specifically during writing In the simple form the dystonia occurs only with writing, whereas in the dystonic form it spreads to other manual tasks Patients describe excessive gripping, finger extension or flexion and wrist deviation that impair legibility It usually begins in adulthood and is not explained by weakness or sensory loss Sensory tricks and changes in writing implement or grip may give partial relief Botulinum toxin to selected muscles, retraining and adaptive strategies are the main treatments Spread to rest or to many tasks suggesting evolving segmental dystonia Associated weakness, wasting or sensory signs Rapid progression or other neurological features Onset in childhood suggesting a genetic generalised dystonia Dismissing it as anxiety or overuse rather than recognising a focal dystonia Missing spread to other tasks that changes management Overlooking a secondary cause when there are additional signs Neglecting ergonomic and retraining approaches alongside injections Writer's cramp is a task-specific dystonia thought to arise from maladaptive plasticity and impaired sensorimotor integration within basal ganglia and cortical motor networks controlling skilled hand movements. Reduced inhibition and abnormal cortical representation of the hand lead to excessive and poorly focused muscle activation during the highly overlearned task of writing. The task specificity reflects the abnormal motor programme being tied to a particular practised movement. The condition is generally chronic and non-life-threatening; symptoms often stabilise, and botulinum toxin, retraining and adaptive techniques can meaningfully improve function.

neurological deficit New seizures or progressive neurological signs Acute visual loss Symptoms suggesting raised intracranial pressure Treating a retinal arteriovenous malformation as isolated without neuroimaging for intracranial lesions Overlooking a subtle facial vascular naevus that signals deeper malformation Attempting intervention on high-flow lesions without full angiographic assessment mesodermal vascular precursors along a single developmental axis, producing arteriovenous malformations that link the retina, optic pathway and midbrain on one side. These high-flow lesions consist of direct arterial-to-venous connections without an intervening capillary bed, leading to dilated tortuous vessels. In the retina this produces a racemose angioma that may compromise vision, while intracranial arteriovenous malformations carry a risk of haemorrhage, seizures and progressive neurological deficit. Overlying facial cutaneous vascular naevi reflect involvement of the same regional vascular field. Prognosis depends on the extent and location of the arteriovenous malformations; small stable lesions may remain asymptomatic, but large intracranial malformations carry a risk of haemorrhage and neurological morbidity, and extensive retinal involvement can cause permanent visual loss.

adrenal hyperplasia and missing the underlying diagnosis Failing to anticipate later hypogonadotropic hypogonadism and delayed puberty Overlooking associated neuromuscular disease from a contiguous gene deletion Underestimating the ongoing risk of adrenal crisis during intercurrent illness DAX1, the product of NR0B1, is a nuclear receptor essential for the development and function of the adrenal X-linked agammaglobulinaemia — Bruton agammaglobulinaemia, XLA, Bruton tyrosine kinase deficiency Common variable immunodeficiency Autosomal recessive agammaglobulinaemia (mu heavy chain, lambda-5, BLNK or Ig-alpha defects) Transient hypogammaglobulinaemia of infancy Hyper-IgM syndrome Severe combined immunodeficiency Good syndrome (thymoma with immunodeficiency) Protein-losing states causing secondary hypogammaglobulinaemia Serum immunoglobulin levels (IgG, IgA, IgM) showing panhypogammaglobulinaemia Peripheral blood lymphocyte immunophenotyping demonstrating absent CD19+/CD20+ B cells BTK gene sequencing and assessment of BTK protein expression in monocytes Specific antibody responses to protein and polysaccharide vaccines (absent) High-resolution CT of the chest to detect bronchiectasis Sputum and stool cultures for recurrent or atypical pathogens Carrier testing and genetic counselling for female relatives Caused by loss-of-function mutations in the BTK gene, arresting B-cell development at the pre-B stage so that mature B cells and immunoglobulin of all classes are profoundly deficient. Affected boys typically present after 6 months of age once transplacental maternal IgG wanes, with recurrent sinopulmonary infections by encapsulated bacteria such as pneumococcus and Haemophilus. Hallmark examination finding is absent or vestigial tonsils and lymph nodes because germinal centres cannot form without B cells. Enteroviral infection is a feared complication, causing chronic meningoencephalitis and a dermatomyositis-like syndrome; live oral poliovirus vaccine is contraindicated. Diagnosis rests on very low or absent circulating CD19+ B cells (usually under 2 percent) together with markedly reduced IgG, IgA and IgM. Immunoglobulin replacement, given intravenously or subcutaneously, is the mainstay of therapy and dramatically reduces infection frequency. Susceptibility to Giardia, Campylobacter, Mycoplasma and Ureaplasma is characteristic, and Pneumocystis is not typical because T-cell immunity is intact. Bronchiectasis from recurrent or inadequately treated pulmonary infection remains the major cause of long-term morbidity. Enteroviral central nervous system infection presenting with progressive encephalitis Established bronchiectasis with declining pulmonary function Overwhelming sepsis from encapsulated organisms Chronic Giardia or Campylobacter infection with malabsorption and failure to thrive Development of lymphoreticular or gastrointestinal malignancy Attributing recurrent infections in an infant to normal childhood illness and delaying immunological work-up. Measuring immunoglobulins before 6 months when maternal IgG may mask the deficiency. Administering live vaccines, particularly oral polio, which can cause vaccine-associated disease. Under-dosing immunoglobulin replacement so that trough levels remain inadequate to prevent sinopulmonary infection. Overlooking chronic enteroviral or ureaplasmal infection because routine cultures are negative. X-linked agammaglobulinaemia results from mutations in the gene encoding Bruton tyrosine kinase (BTK), a cytoplasmic signalling molecule essential for pre-B-cell receptor signalling. Without functional BTK, developing B lymphocytes cannot progress beyond the pro-B to pre-B transition in the bone marrow, so peripheral mature B cells are virtually absent. The consequent failure to generate plasma cells leaves the patient without effective antibody of any isotype, crippling humoral defence against encapsulated pyogenic bacteria and enteroviruses, while T-cell-mediated immunity is preserved. The X-linked recessive inheritance explains near-exclusive occurrence in males. With early diagnosis and lifelong immunoglobulin replacement most patients reach adulthood with a good quality of life, though chronic lung disease and enteroviral infection can shorten survival. Delayed recognition and consequent bronchiectasis are the principal determinants of poor outcome.

recurrent childhood infections to ordinary illness and delaying immunoglobulin measurement Overlooking the physical clue of absent tonsils and lymph nodes Giving live vaccines, particularly oral poliovirus vaccine Assuming normal viral immunity fully protects, thereby missing enteroviral complications Under-dosing or interrupting immunoglobulin replacement, allowing breakthrough infection and lung damage X-linked agammaglobulinemia results from loss-of-function mutations in BTK, a cytoplasmic tyrosine kinase that transmits signals from the pre-B-cell and B-cell receptors. Without functional BTK, developing B cells arrest at the pre-B stage in the bone marrow and fail to mature, so mature B cells and plasma cells are largely absent from the periphery and lymphoid tissue. As an X-linked disorder, hemizygous males are more severely and consistently affected than heterozygous females. Hearing loss is progressive and mixed, and while stapes surgery is contraindicated, carefully planned cochlear implantation can rehabilitate advanced sensorineural loss despite the gusher risk.

carrier detection and genetic counselling are important Hyperthermia or febrile seizures from impaired heat dissipation, especially in infants Recurrent unexplained high fevers mistaken for infection Failure to thrive with recurrent respiratory or ear infections Heat-related collapse during hot weather or exertion Repeatedly investigating recurrent fevers for infection while overlooking impaired sweating Missing subtle or patchy features in carrier females Underestimating the risk of dangerous overheating in infancy Neglecting early dental planning and psychological support X-linked hypohidrotic ectodermal dysplasia is caused by loss-of-function mutations in the EDA gene, which encodes ectodysplasin A. This ligand signals through its receptor during embryonic development to direct formation of ectodermal appendages, including sweat and other exocrine glands, hair follicles, and tooth germs. Without functional signalling these structures fail to develop normally, producing absent or reduced eccrine sweat glands, sparse hair, and missing or malformed teeth. Loss of sweating removes a key route of heat dissipation, so affected individuals overheat readily and are prone to hyperthermia. Intelligence and lifespan are usually normal with appropriate care; the main morbidity comes from heat intolerance and recurrent infections in early childhood and from the dental and cosmetic effects, which can be substantially improved with multidisciplinary and dental management.

x linked hypophosphataemia — XLH, X-linked hypophosphataemic rickets, familial hypophosphataemic rickets nutritional vitamin D-deficiency rickets autosomal dominant or recessive hypophosphataemic rickets (FGF23, DMP1, ENPP1) hereditary hypophosphataemic rickets with hypercalciuria (HHRH, SLC34A3) tumour-induced osteomalacia Fanconi syndrome and Dent disease McCune-Albright syndrome or fibrous dysplasia renal tubular acidosis serum phosphate, calcium, alkaline phosphatase and PTH 25-hydroxy and 1,25-dihydroxyvitamin D renal tubular phosphate reabsorption (TmP/GFR) intact FGF23 PHEX and related gene testing renal ultrasound for nephrocalcinosis wrist and knee radiographs and DXA X-linked hypophosphataemia is the commonest heritable form of rickets and osteomalacia, inherited as an X-linked dominant trait caused by loss-of-function mutations in PHEX. Loss of PHEX function leads to excess circulating FGF23, which drives renal phosphate wasting and suppresses 1-alpha-hydroxylation, giving an inappropriately normal or low calcitriol. Biochemistry shows low phosphate with high urinary phosphate (low TmP/GFR), normal calcium, normal or low 1,25-hydroxyvitamin D, normal or mildly raised PTH, raised alkaline phosphatase and raised or inappropriately normal FGF23. Unlike nutritional rickets, calcium and 25-hydroxyvitamin D are normal and there is no hypocalcaemia or tetany. Children present with leg bowing, short stature, a waddling gait, delayed walking and spontaneous dental abscesses. Conventional treatment with oral phosphate salts plus active vitamin D (alfacalcidol or calcitriol) risks nephrocalcinosis and secondary or tertiary hyperparathyroidism, and requires careful monitoring. The anti-FGF23 monoclonal antibody burosumab is now preferred for children and selected adults, improving phosphate handling and healing rickets. Adults may have persistent osteomalacia, pseudofractures, enthesopathy, degenerative arthritis, dental sepsis and, from childhood, craniosynostosis. nephrocalcinosis or declining renal function on conventional treatment tertiary hyperparathyroidism developing during phosphate therapy craniosynostosis with raised intracranial pressure spinal canal stenosis or cord compression from enthesopathy and ligament ossification recurrent spontaneous dental abscesses misdiagnosing as nutritional rickets and giving only nutritional vitamin D, which is ineffective failing to monitor for treatment-induced nephrocalcinosis over-treatment provoking secondary or tertiary hyperparathyroidism not screening at-risk family members neglecting regular dental surveillance PHEX encodes an endopeptidase expressed in osteoblasts and osteocytes. Its loss of function leads, through incompletely defined signalling, to overproduction of the phosphaturic hormone FGF23 by bone cells. Elevated FGF23 acts on the proximal renal tubule to downregulate the sodium-phosphate cotransporters NaPi-IIa and NaPi-IIc, causing renal phosphate wasting and hypophosphataemia. FGF23 simultaneously suppresses 1-alpha-hydroxylase and stimulates 24-hydroxylase, so calcitriol is inappropriately low or normal rather than rising in response to hypophosphataemia. Chronic hypophosphataemia impairs mineralisation of the growth plate (rickets) and of osteoid in mature bone (osteomalacia). This is a lifelong condition; with treatment growth and deformity improve, but many adults have residual short stature, enthesopathy, degenerative joint disease and dental problems.

the FGF23-targeted monoclonal antibody burosumab is now used for eligible patients Monitoring for treatment complications, including nephrocalcinosis and hyperparathyroidism, is essential on conventional therapy In adults the disease causes osteomalacia, enthesopathy, pseudofractures and dental problems Progressive limb deformity or fractures despite treatment Nephrocalcinosis or declining renal function on conventional phosphate and vitamin D therapy Development of tertiary hyperparathyroidism during long-term treatment Recurrent dental abscesses or spinal stenosis and cord compression from enthesopathy in adults Treating as ordinary nutritional rickets with vitamin D alone, which does not correct phosphate wasting Failing to recognise that a normal 1,25-vitamin D is inappropriate in the face of hypophosphataemia Overtreating with phosphate and active vitamin D and causing nephrocalcinosis or hyperparathyroidism Missing the diagnosis in adults presenting with osteomalacia, enthesopathy or dental abscesses X-linked hypophosphataemia is caused by inactivating mutations in PHEX, a membrane endopeptidase expressed in bone and teeth. Loss of PHEX function leads, through incompletely defined mechanisms, to excessive circulating fibroblast growth factor 23 (FGF23). FGF23 reduces expression of renal sodium-phosphate cotransporters, causing phosphate to be lost in the urine, and it also suppresses the enzyme that generates active 1,25-dihydroxyvitamin D. The result is chronic hypophosphataemia with an inappropriately low or normal active vitamin D level, impairing mineralisation of the growth plate and osteoid and producing rickets and osteomalacia. With early and sustained treatment, rickets heals and growth and deformity improve, though short stature and dental problems may persist; FGF23-targeted therapy has improved outcomes, but lifelong monitoring for skeletal, renal and dental complications is required.

standard care, prompting reassessment of the diagnosis Confusing it with ichthyosis vulgaris, which spares extremities less consistently and is associated with atopy and keratosis pilaris Overlooking associated cryptorchidism or contiguous gene syndrome features Failing to recognise the enzyme deficiency implication for atypical labour or low maternal oestriol Attributing corneal opacities to unrelated ocular disease X-linked ichthyosis is caused by deficiency of steroid sulfatase, an enzyme that hydrolyses cholesterol sulfate and sulfated steroid precursors. In the epidermis, accumulation of cholesterol sulfate destabilises the intercellular lipid lamellae of the stratum corneum and inhibits proteases responsible for corneodesmosome breakdown, so desquamation is impaired and corneocytes are retained. This produces the characteristic retention hyperkeratosis with large adherent scales. Because the STS gene lies in a region of the X chromosome that partly escapes inactivation and is prone to deletion, larger deletions may remove neighbouring genes and cause a contiguous gene syndrome. It is a benign, lifelong condition confined largely to the skin in the isolated form, with scaling that persists but is manageable with regular emollient and keratolytic care; prognosis depends on any associated features in patients with larger deletions.

X-linked lymphoproliferative disease — XLP, Duncan disease, SH2D1A, SAP deficiency, XIAP, BIRC4, XLP1, XLP2 Familial haemophagocytic lymphohistiocytosis from other genetic causes Other primary EBV-susceptibility disorders (e.g. ITK, CD27, MAGT1 defects) Common variable immunodeficiency presenting with dysgammaglobulinaemia Sporadic EBV-associated lymphoma Very-early-onset inflammatory bowel disease (for the XIAP phenotype) Severe primary infectious mononucleosis without underlying defect Flow cytometry for intracellular SAP and XIAP protein expression Molecular genetic testing of SH2D1A and XIAP/BIRC4 Quantitative immunoglobulins and specific antibody responses Natural killer and cytotoxic T-cell function assays EBV viral load and HLH markers including ferritin and soluble interleukin-2 receptor Enumeration of natural killer T cells (typically reduced or absent in XLP1) An X-linked disorder of boys defined by an extreme and often fatal immune dysregulation triggered by Epstein-Barr virus infection XLP1 results from SH2D1A mutation causing loss of the signalling adaptor SAP; XLP2 results from XIAP (BIRC4) mutation The three classic manifestations of XLP1 are fulminant EBV-driven haemophagocytic lymphohistiocytosis, dysgammaglobulinaemia, and B-cell lymphoma XIAP deficiency more often presents with recurrent haemophagocytic lymphohistiocytosis, splenomegaly and inflammatory-bowel-disease-like colitis, and lymphoma is uncommon SAP is required for normal function of natural killer T cells and for cytotoxic control of EBV-infected B cells, explaining the catastrophic response to primary EBV Any boy with fulminant or fatal infectious mononucleosis, or EBV-associated HLH, should prompt evaluation for XLP Haematopoietic stem cell transplantation is the only curative therapy and is best undertaken before or after control of an HLH episode Fulminant or progressive infectious mononucleosis with cytopenias and organ dysfunction Ferritin and inflammatory markers rising in keeping with evolving HLH Rapidly enlarging lymphadenopathy suggesting lymphoma Recurrent HLH episodes or refractory colitis in a boy (XIAP phenotype) Dismissing severe mononucleosis in a boy as an ordinary viral illness without considering XLP Attributing hypogammaglobulinaemia to common variable immunodeficiency and missing an X-linked cause Failing to test both SAP and XIAP, since their phenotypes overlap but differ in lymphoma risk Delaying definitive transplant planning until after a life-threatening HLH episode X-linked lymphoproliferative disease is a genetic failure to regulate the immune response, classically unmasked by Epstein-Barr virus. In XLP1 the SH2D1A gene encodes the SLAM-associated protein SAP, an intracellular adaptor essential for signalling through the SLAM family of receptors on T cells and natural killer cells; its loss cripples cytotoxic killing of EBV-infected B cells and impairs natural killer T-cell development. In XLP2 the affected gene XIAP encodes an inhibitor-of-apoptosis protein important for inflammasome signalling and lymphocyte survival. In both, uncontrolled activation and expansion of T cells and macrophages during viral challenge drives a hyperinflammatory, cytokine-rich state that produces haemophagocytic lymphohistiocytosis, together with a spectrum of antibody deficiency and, in XLP1, lymphoma. The natural history is severe, with EBV-triggered HLH carrying high mortality, but early recognition, control of hyperinflammation, and haematopoietic stem cell transplantation markedly improve survival, particularly when transplantation is undertaken before the onset of fulminant disease.

a classic sign is a spoke-wheel or cartwheel pattern of foveal cystic change radiating from the centre Optical coherence tomography is diagnostic, showing splitting (schisis) of the inner retinal layers, most characteristically in the fovea, and often in the peripheral retina Peripheral retinoschisis, when present, predisposes to vitreous haemorrhage and to schisis-related retinal detachment The electroretinogram characteristically shows a selective reduction of the b-wave with relative preservation of the a-wave, giving an electronegative configuration Fundus autofluorescence and OCT often reveal the foveal changes even when the spoke-wheel appearance is subtle on ophthalmoscopy Management is supportive with carbonic anhydrase inhibitors sometimes used for the cystic maculopathy, surveillance for and repair of retinal detachment or vitreous haemorrhage, and genetic counselling; gene therapy is under investigation Sudden visual loss from vitreous haemorrhage or retinal detachment requiring urgent assessment New floaters, field loss or a curtain in the vision indicating possible detachment Bilateral macular schisis with declining central acuity Family history along an X-linked pattern prompting screening of relatives Mistaking foveal schisis for cystoid macular oedema and treating inappropriately Failing to examine the peripheral retina for schisis and detachment risk Attributing the electronegative electroretinogram to another disorder without OCT confirmation of schisis Overlooking the X-linked inheritance and neglecting carrier and relative counselling X-linked retinoschisis is caused by mutations in RS1, encoding retinoschisin, a secreted adhesion protein produced by photoreceptors and bipolar cells that maintains the structural integrity and cell-to-cell adhesion of the retinal layers. Deficiency leads to splitting within the inner retina, classically at the fovea and often in the periphery, disrupting synaptic transmission between photoreceptors and bipolar cells. The impaired bipolar signalling accounts for the selectively reduced b-wave and electronegative electroretinogram, while structural schisis explains the cystic maculopathy and the risk of haemorrhage and detachment. Central acuity is often reduced from childhood and may decline slowly with age; visual prognosis worsens if peripheral schisis leads to vitreous haemorrhage or retinal detachment, which can cause severe loss if untreated.

carrier females are usually mild or unaffected but can be symptomatic through skewed lyonisation, sometimes presenting only in later life Produces a microcytic, hypochromic anaemia with a characteristic dimorphic blood film and ring sideroblasts (iron-laden mitochondria encircling the erythroblast nucleus) on marrow iron staining Many cases are pyridoxine (vitamin B6) responsive because the enzyme uses pyridoxal phosphate as a cofactor, so a therapeutic trial is warranted Systemic iron overload is characteristic and occurs independently of transfusion, driven by ineffective erythropoiesis and hepcidin suppression, and may be the dominant clinical problem In contrast with iron deficiency, the anaemia is microcytic but iron stores are high, so iron supplementation is harmful Co-inheritance of an HFE haemochromatosis variant can accentuate iron loading, and the X-linked pattern with a supportive family history aids diagnosis Iron overload with cardiac, hepatic or endocrine dysfunction Inappropriate iron therapy worsening iron loading Severe or transfusion-dependent anaemia Family history of unexplained iron overload or anaemia in males Treating the microcytic anaemia as iron deficiency and giving iron, which aggravates overload Not offering a pyridoxine trial Overlooking symptomatic female carriers because the condition is labelled X-linked Missing iron overload because the patient has never been transfused Attributing ring sideroblasts to myelodysplasia without considering a congenital cause in a younger patient X-linked sideroblastic anaemia results from loss-of-function or hypomorphic mutations in ALAS2 on the X chromosome, encoding the erythroid isoform of delta-aminolaevulinate synthase, which condenses glycine and succinyl-CoA using pyridoxal 5'-phosphate as cofactor in the first and rate-limiting step of haem biosynthesis. Deficient enzyme activity leaves iron that has entered the erythroblast mitochondrion unincorporated into protoporphyrin, so iron accumulates within perinuclear mitochondria to form ring sideroblasts. The impaired haemoglobinisation produces a microcytic hypochromic anaemia with ineffective erythropoiesis, while suppressed hepcidin drives increased dietary iron absorption and progressive systemic iron overload. Pyridoxine-responsive disease often has a good outlook with correction or improvement of the anaemia, but iron overload remains the principal threat and requires lifelong monitoring. Non-responsive or transfusion-dependent cases carry greater morbidity, much of it preventable with chelation and, where appropriate, venesection.

progressive neurodegenerative disorder Failing to distinguish it genetically from ALAS2 and SLC25A38 sideroblastic anaemias ABCB7 encodes a mitochondrial inner-membrane transporter essential for Generally severe, with significant early morbidity and frequently early respiratory compromise; outcome depends on the degree of weakness and respiratory involvement.
