The WAS gene encodes WASP, a cytoskeletal regulator expressed in haematopoietic cells that links signalling to actin polymerisation. Mutations preserving partial WASP function cause the milder X-linked thrombocytopenia phenotype, whereas null mutations produce classic Wiskott-Aldrich syndrome. Impaired cytoskeletal dynamics disturb platelet formation and lead to production of small, structurally abnormal platelets that are also removed prematurely, giving microthrombocytopenia. Residual immune-cell dysfunction predisposes to autoimmunity, and reduced immune surveillance contributes to a smaller malignancy risk. The milder phenotype generally carries a better outlook than classic Wiskott-Aldrich syndrome, but lifelong surveillance is needed because bleeding, autoimmunity, and a smaller malignancy risk persist; allogeneic transplantation is curative and considered in more severe cases.

Xanthelasma — xanthelasma palpebrarum, eyelid xanthoma Necrobiotic xanthogranuloma (often with periorbital induration and paraproteinaemia) Syringoma of the eyelid Sebaceous hyperplasia or sebaceous gland carcinoma Adult-onset asthma and periocular xanthogranulomatous disease (Erdheim-Chester, adult xanthogranuloma) Amyloid deposits of the eyelid Juvenile xanthogranuloma Lipoid proteinosis Fasting serum lipid profile (total cholesterol, LDL, HDL, triglycerides) Fasting glucose or HbA1c to screen for diabetes Thyroid function tests to exclude hypothyroidism Liver function tests to exclude cholestatic liver disease Assessment for familial hypercholesterolaemia including family history and, where indicated, genetic evaluation Overall cardiovascular risk stratification Skin biopsy only if the diagnosis is atypical or xanthogranulomatous disease is suspected Xanthelasma palpebrarum presents as soft, symmetrical, yellowish plaques on the eyelid skin, most often at the medial canthus of the upper lids, and is the commonest cutaneous xanthoma. Roughly half of affected patients have normal serum lipids, so a normolipidaemic result does not exclude the diagnosis, but a fasting lipid profile should still be checked in all cases. When associated with dyslipidaemia it typically reflects raised low-density lipoprotein or a reduced high-density lipoprotein, and may be a clue to familial hypercholesterolaemia, especially with young onset or a family history. Xanthelasma has been linked to increased cardiovascular risk independent of measured lipids, so its presence warrants overall cardiovascular risk assessment, not merely a cosmetic view. The lesions are benign and mainly a cosmetic concern; treatment options include surgical excision, chemical cautery, ablative laser and cryotherapy, all with a notable tendency to recur. Recurrence after treatment is common, particularly in patients with persistent hyperlipidaemia, so lipid control and patient counselling about recurrence are integral to management. Consider secondary causes of hyperlipidaemia such as diabetes, hypothyroidism, cholestatic liver disease and nephrotic syndrome when xanthelasma is florid or of early onset. Eruptive or tuberous xanthomas elsewhere, or extensive early xanthelasma, should prompt evaluation for a primary lipid disorder. Early-onset or florid lesions suggesting familial hypercholesterolaemia Associated periorbital induration, ulceration or systemic features suggesting necrobiotic xanthogranuloma and paraproteinaemia Rapidly enlarging, firm or ulcerated eyelid lesion raising concern for sebaceous carcinoma Features of undiagnosed diabetes, hypothyroidism or cholestasis on systemic enquiry Assuming normal lipids exclude the diagnosis or obviate cardiovascular risk assessment Treating the lesions cosmetically without addressing underlying dyslipidaemia, leading to recurrence Mislabelling necrobiotic xanthogranuloma or sebaceous carcinoma as simple xanthelasma Aggressive excision of medial canthal lesions risking cicatricial ectropion or canthal webbing Neglecting to screen for secondary causes such as hypothyroidism and cholestasis Xanthelasma results from accumulation of lipid-laden macrophages (foam cells) in the superficial dermis of the thin eyelid skin. Circulating lipoproteins, particularly low-density lipoprotein, extravasate through leaky periocular capillaries and are taken up by dermal macrophages, which become engorged with cholesterol and cholesteryl esters to form perivascular and periadnexal foam-cell aggregates. Local capillary permeability, oxidative modification of lipoproteins and macrophage scavenger-receptor activity all contribute, which explains why lesions can develop even in normolipidaemic individuals in whom local rather than systemic factors predominate. Benign with no direct threat to vision; the main significance is as a marker of possible dyslipidaemia and cardiovascular risk. Cosmetic treatment is effective but recurrence is frequent, particularly when hyperlipidaemia is uncontrolled.

Xanthogranulomatous pyelonephritis — XGP, XGPN Renal cell carcinoma Renal tuberculosis Pyonephrosis or renal abscess Malakoplakia Emphysematous pyelonephritis Renal lymphoma Obstructive uropathy with chronic pyelonephritis Contrast CT showing the bear-paw sign, staghorn calculus and a non-functioning kidney Urine microscopy, culture and sensitivities Blood cultures and inflammatory markers Full blood count (anaemia, leucocytosis) and renal function DMSA or MAG3 renography for differential renal function Imaging for fistulae and perinephric extension Histology of the nephrectomy specimen (definitive, showing foam cells) A chronic destructive granulomatous infection of the kidney in which lipid-laden foamy macrophages progressively replace the parenchyma. It is strongly associated with chronic obstruction, typically a staghorn calculus, and recurrent infection. Proteus mirabilis and Escherichia coli are the commonest organisms. It is usually unilateral and presents with flank pain, fever, malaise, weight loss, a palpable mass and recurrent urinary infections. The classic bear-paw sign on CT shows an enlarged non-functioning kidney with dilated calyces around a central calculus. It mimics renal cell carcinoma radiologically and histologically, so the diagnosis is often confirmed only after nephrectomy. It may form fistulae (nephrocutaneous or reno-colic) and involve the perinephric space and psoas muscle. Definitive treatment is usually total nephrectomy, with partial nephrectomy occasionally suitable for focal disease. Sepsis from an obstructed infected kidney (pyonephrosis) Fistula formation (reno-colic or nephrocutaneous) Perinephric or psoas abscess Diagnostic uncertainty with possible renal malignancy Misdiagnosing the condition as renal cell carcinoma, or vice versa Underestimating perinephric extension that complicates surgery Attempting nephron-sparing surgery in diffuse disease Inadequate perioperative treatment of sepsis and obstruction Xanthogranulomatous pyelonephritis is a chronic granulomatous inflammatory response to long-standing renal infection in the setting of obstruction, typically a calculus, and impaired urinary drainage. Persistent bacterial infection with incomplete clearance provokes accumulation of lipid-laden foamy macrophages (xanthoma cells) mixed with other inflammatory cells, which progressively destroy and replace the renal parenchyma. The process may extend beyond the capsule into perinephric fat, the psoas muscle and adjacent organs and can generate fistulae, mimicking malignant infiltration both radiologically and macroscopically. The prognosis is excellent after complete surgical removal of the affected kidney, with low recurrence; morbidity relates chiefly to the extent of local invasion, fistulae and perioperative complications.

Xanthoma disseminatum — Montgomery syndrome, disseminated xanthosiderohistiocytosis Eruptive xanthomas of hyperlipidaemia Generalised eruptive histiocytosis Langerhans cell histiocytosis Multicentric reticulohistiocytosis Erdheim-Chester disease Progressive nodular histiocytosis Sarcoidosis Skin biopsy with histology and immunohistochemistry (CD68, factor XIIIa, CD1a, langerin) Fasting serum lipid profile to confirm normolipaemia Early-morning paired serum and urine osmolality and water-deprivation testing if diabetes insipidus suspected MRI of the hypothalamic-pituitary region when endocrine features are present Laryngoscopy or airway endoscopy if hoarseness, dysphagia or stridor Serum and urine protein electrophoresis with immunofixation to detect monoclonal gammopathy Baseline anterior pituitary hormone profile A rare normolipaemic non-Langerhans cell histiocytosis characterised by hundreds of red-brown to yellow papules and nodules with a striking predilection for flexural and intertriginous skin. Lesions cluster symmetrically in the axillae, groin, antecubital and popliteal fossae and periorbital region, and mucous membrane involvement of the upper aerodigestive tract may occur. Mucosal disease of the oral cavity, pharynx, larynx and trachea can cause hoarseness, dysphagia or airway obstruction and is an important cause of morbidity. Up to a third to a half of patients develop transient central diabetes insipidus from infiltration of the hypothalamic-pituitary region, which is usually mild and may remit. Serum lipids are characteristically normal, distinguishing it from the hyperlipidaemic xanthomas it can mimic clinically. It affects predominantly young adult males and typically follows a persistent, progressive course rather than the spontaneous involution seen in juvenile xanthogranuloma. Histology shows a mixed infiltrate of foamy histiocytes, scattered Touton giant cells and inflammatory cells; cells are CD68 positive and CD1a negative. An association with monoclonal gammopathy and other paraproteinaemias is reported, warranting haematological screening. Hoarseness, dysphagia or stridor indicating laryngeal or tracheal mucosal involvement and potential airway compromise Polyuria and polydipsia suggesting central diabetes insipidus Visual disturbance or ophthalmoplegia from periorbital or orbital infiltration Rapidly progressive or widespread cutaneous and mucosal disease Detection of a monoclonal paraprotein on electrophoresis Misdiagnosing the yellowish papules as eruptive xanthomas and pursuing lipid-lowering treatment despite normal serum lipids. Failing to enquire about polyuria and polydipsia and thereby missing central diabetes insipidus. Overlooking upper airway mucosal disease that can progress to obstruction. Not screening for an associated monoclonal gammopathy. Expecting spontaneous involution as occurs in juvenile xanthogranuloma, leading to under-monitoring. Xanthoma disseminatum is a proliferative disorder of macrophage-derived histiocytes belonging to the non-Langerhans cell histiocytoses. Lesional histiocytes accumulate lipid to form foam cells and Touton giant cells despite normal circulating lipids, indicating that lipid uptake and storage occur locally within a reactive histiocytic infiltrate rather than as a consequence of dyslipidaemia. The cells express macrophage markers such as CD68 and factor XIIIa but not the Langerhans cell markers CD1a and langerin. The disorder is generally regarded as a reactive rather than clearly neoplastic process, although its persistence, mucosal and pituitary infiltration, and reported associations with monoclonal gammopathy suggest a dysregulated histiocytic response. Infiltration of the hypothalamic-pituitary axis interrupts vasopressin delivery to produce central diabetes insipidus, while mucosal deposits in the airway account for the potential for obstructive complications. The cutaneous disease is typically persistent and only rarely regresses, following a chronic course; overall prognosis depends on the extent of mucosal, airway and pituitary involvement, and although diabetes insipidus is often transient, airway disease can be life-threatening.

inherited defects in the nucleotide excision repair pathway, which normally recognises and removes bulky DNA lesions such as the cyclobutane pyrimidine dimers produced by ultraviolet radiation; the XP variant form instead reflects loss of DNA polymerase eta, needed for accurate translesion synthesis. Because damaged DNA cannot be repaired efficiently, ultraviolet-induced mutations accumulate in keratinocytes, melanocytes, and ocular surface cells. This drives premature photoageing, pigmentary change, and early malignant transformation. In certain genotypes, accumulated unrepaired damage in neurons produces progressive neurodegeneration independent of sun exposure. Life expectancy is reduced, largely from early and recurrent skin and ocular malignancies and, in neurological subtypes, from progressive neurodegeneration; with meticulous photoprotection and close cancer surveillance, tumour burden and its consequences can be substantially reduced.

MECP2 encodes a methyl-CpG-binding protein that regulates transcription of many neuronal genes, and both excess and deficiency of the protein disrupt neurodevelopment. Overexpression produces progressive neurological dysfunction, hypotonia evolving to spasticity, and an immune phenotype predisposing to recurrent infection. Because the gene is X-linked, males with a single X are affected, whereas carrier females with favourably skewed X-inactivation are typically spared. The condition is generally severe and progressive, with profound intellectual disability, loss of independent mobility and a significant risk of premature death, frequently from recurrent respiratory infection. Attentive respiratory care, infection prevention, seizure management and nutritional support can improve comfort and reduce complications, but the overall outlook remains guarded.

assessment and replacement of testosterone in adolescence Attributing behavioural difficulties to environment alone 48,XXYY results from the presence of two extra sex chromosomes, one additional X and The greater chromosomal imbalance underlies the more pronounced cognitive, behavioural, and physical features compared with 47,XXY. Lifespan is generally near-normal but influenced by vascular and thrombotic and other complications; most individuals require lifelong endocrine, educational, and behavioural support, and infertility is the rule.

47,XYY syndrome — XYY syndrome, Jacobs syndrome, 47,XYY, YY syndrome Familial or constitutional tall stature Other sex-chromosome aneuploidies such as 47,XXY and 48,XXYY Idiopathic attention-deficit/hyperactivity disorder or autism spectrum disorder Developmental language disorder Marfan syndrome, for tall stature Karyotype, which is diagnostic Chromosomal microarray, which detects the extra Y Developmental, speech and language, and educational assessment Assessment for attention-deficit/hyperactivity disorder or autism spectrum disorder where indicated Growth monitoring Tall stature is the most consistent feature, often with accelerated growth during childhood Physical appearance and fertility are usually normal, and many individuals remain undiagnosed There is an increased risk of speech and language delay and of learning difficulties, especially with reading Higher rates of attention-deficit/hyperactivity, autism spectrum traits, and emotional or behavioural difficulties occur, but the historical link with aggression is outdated and stigmatising Motor coordination difficulties and childhood hypotonia are common Arises from a paternal second-division meiotic error producing a YY sperm, with no maternal-age effect IQ is usually within the normal range but on average slightly lower than that of siblings Significant behavioural or mental-health disturbance needing support Marked developmental delay suggesting an additional diagnosis Emotional distress in the individual or family after diagnosis, needing counselling Perpetuating the discredited and stigmatising link with criminality or aggression Assuming uniform severity when the phenotype is highly variable Overlooking treatable learning and attention difficulties Causing undue alarm after an incidental prenatal diagnosis 47,XYY arises when an error at the second paternal meiotic division produces a sperm carrying two Y chromosomes, giving a male with an extra Y. Additional dosage of Y-linked and pseudoautosomal genes, including growth-related genes in the short-stature homeobox region, is thought to underlie the tall stature, while effects on neurodevelopment produce the associated language, learning, and behavioural profile. Expressivity is very variable and many individuals are only mildly affected. Good, with a normal lifespan and usually normal fertility; most individuals lead independent lives, and neurodevelopmental and educational outcomes improve with early support.

Yao syndrome — NOD2-associated autoinflammatory disease, formerly NOD2-associated autoinflammatory syndrome, NOD2, nucleotide-binding oligomerisation domain 2 disorder Adult-onset Still disease Familial Mediterranean fever and other hereditary periodic fevers Blau syndrome / early-onset sarcoidosis Crohn disease Schnitzler syndrome Chronic urticaria with systemic features NOD2 genotyping for associated variants Acute-phase reactants during and between episodes Autoantibody and infection screens to exclude alternative diagnoses Skin biopsy of the rash where diagnosis is unclear Gastrointestinal evaluation if bowel symptoms predominate Assessment for sicca symptoms and salivary gland involvement An adult-onset periodic fever syndrome associated with specific NOD2 gene variants, distinct from Blau syndrome and Crohn disease Presents with recurrent fevers, a patchy or urticaria-like rash, and episodes lasting several days to a week Common features include arthralgia or arthritis, gastrointestinal symptoms, and sicca-like complaints Attacks are recurrent rather than continuous, with symptom-free intervals between episodes Diagnosis is clinical with supportive NOD2 genotyping and exclusion of infection, autoimmune, and other autoinflammatory diseases It is more frequently reported in adult women of European ancestry Management uses anti-inflammatory and immunomodulatory therapy, with variable response; some patients benefit from interleukin-1 or interleukin-6 directed treatment Persistent rather than episodic inflammation suggesting an alternative diagnosis Features of inflammatory bowel disease requiring separate evaluation Development of amyloidosis from chronic uncontrolled inflammation Systemic features raising concern for malignancy or infection Equating any NOD2 variant with Blau syndrome or Crohn disease Diagnosing on genotype alone without a compatible clinical picture and exclusion of mimics Missing the episodic nature by assessing patients only during quiescent intervals Overlooking treatable alternative causes of periodic fever Yao syndrome is linked to variants in NOD2, an intracellular sensor of bacterial cell-wall components that regulates inflammatory signalling. Unlike the specific NOD2 mutations causing Blau syndrome, the variants in Yao syndrome are thought to dysregulate innate immune signalling and cytokine production, producing periodic systemic inflammation. This drives recurrent fevers, dermatitis, arthralgia, and gastrointestinal symptoms without the granulomatous triad of Blau syndrome. The condition is regarded as a polygenically influenced autoinflammatory disease rather than a simple single-gene disorder, which contributes to its variable presentation and treatment response. Yao syndrome typically follows a relapsing course with good overall life expectancy; symptoms can often be controlled with anti-inflammatory therapy, though responses vary and some patients have persistent troublesome attacks.

Yaws — Treponema pallidum subspecies pertenue, framboesia tropica, pian, bouba Venereal syphilis (serologically identical) Other endemic treponematoses (bejel, pinta) Cutaneous leishmaniasis Impetigo and other pyodermas Tropical ulcer Verrucous fungal infection (e.g. chromoblastomycosis) Warts or condylomata Dark-field microscopy of lesion exudate for spirochaetes Non-treponemal serology (e.g. RPR/VDRL) for activity and treatment response Treponemal serology (e.g. TPPA/TPHA) for confirmation PCR of lesion material where available, which can help distinguish subspecies Radiographs of affected bones for periostitis or destructive change Clinical and epidemiological assessment of contacts in endemic communities Yaws is a chronic non-venereal (endemic) treponematosis caused by Treponema pallidum subspecies pertenue, affecting mainly children in warm, humid rural areas of West Africa, Southeast Asia and the Pacific Transmission is by direct skin-to-skin contact with lesion exudate, not sexually, and is favoured by crowding, poor hygiene and minor skin trauma The primary lesion ('mother yaw' or framboesioma) is a painless papilloma or raspberry-like papillomatous nodule at the inoculation site, often on the leg Secondary yaws follows with multiple similar skin lesions, along with painful hyperkeratotic palmar/plantar lesions ('crab yaws') and osteoperiostitis of long bones and fingers (dactylitis) Late (tertiary) yaws causes destructive gummatous lesions of skin and bone, including gangosa (destruction of nose and palate) and sabre tibia Serological tests are the same non-treponemal and treponemal assays used for venereal syphilis and cannot distinguish the two; dark-field microscopy shows treponemes indistinguishable from T. pallidum Treatment for the endemic treponematoses uses benzathine penicillin, with a macrolide alternative used in mass-treatment eradication campaigns Destructive facial lesions (gangosa) causing disfigurement Extensive bone involvement with deformity or disability Painful crab yaws impairing mobility Uncertainty distinguishing from venereal syphilis where the latter has serious sequelae Treatment failure or reappearance of lesions after therapy Assuming positive treponemal serology indicates venereal syphilis and mislabelling children accordingly Failing to treat close contacts, allowing continued transmission Overlooking early painless primary lesions and missing the diagnosis Confusing yaws with pinta or bejel without regional and clinical context Not recognising that mass treatment strategy differs from individual management Treponema pallidum subspecies pertenue enters through breaks in the skin after contact with an infectious lesion. It multiplies locally to form the primary papillomatous lesion, then disseminates via blood and lymphatics to produce widespread secondary skin and bone lesions after weeks to months. A latent phase follows, during which relapsing secondary lesions may occur. In a minority, years later, destructive tertiary gummatous lesions develop in skin, bone and cartilage. Unlike venereal syphilis, yaws does not cause congenital infection or significant cardiovascular or neurological disease. Early and secondary yaws heal completely with penicillin and carry an excellent prognosis, but untreated late disease can cause permanent, disfiguring destruction of skin, bone and cartilage; the disease is a target for global eradication.

Yellow fever — YF, yellow fever virus infection, yellow jack Other viral haemorrhagic fevers (e.g. Ebola, Lassa, Marburg) Severe malaria Leptospirosis (Weil disease) Viral hepatitis with fulminant course Severe dengue Rickettsial infection Fulminant viral hepatitis of other cause Sepsis with disseminated intravascular coagulation Other flaviviral illnesses Drug-induced or toxic hepatic failure RT-PCR for yellow fever virus in early illness Yellow fever IgM serology with confirmatory testing given flavivirus cross-reactivity Liver function tests and coagulation profile to assess hepatic injury and coagulopathy Renal function and urinalysis to detect kidney involvement Concurrent testing to exclude malaria, leptospirosis and other haemorrhagic fevers A mosquito-borne flaviviral haemorrhagic fever endemic to parts of sub-Saharan Africa and tropical South America, transmitted by Aedes and forest mosquitoes India has no endemic yellow fever, but requires proof of vaccination from travellers arriving from endemic areas because the competent Aedes vector is present, posing an introduction risk Illness is often biphasic: an initial febrile phase with headache and myalgia, sometimes followed after a brief remission by a toxic phase with jaundice, haemorrhage and organ failure The toxic phase is characterised by hepatic and renal injury, coagulopathy and bleeding, and carries high mortality A relative bradycardia despite high fever (Faget sign) is a described clinical clue There is no specific antiviral treatment; care is supportive with management of bleeding, liver and kidney failure A single dose of the live attenuated vaccine confers durable, likely lifelong immunity and is the cornerstone of prevention and international travel requirements Diagnosis uses RT-PCR in early illness and serology (IgM), with care to distinguish from other flaviviruses and viral haemorrhagic fevers Entry into the toxic phase with jaundice, bleeding and organ dysfunction, a life-threatening emergency Haemorrhagic manifestations with coagulopathy and shock Acute kidney injury or fulminant hepatic failure A febrile returning traveller from an endemic region, requiring isolation, notification and exclusion of other viral haemorrhagic fevers Failing to elicit a travel history and consider yellow fever in a febrile traveller from an endemic area Mistaking the early phase for uncomplicated dengue or influenza and missing progression to the toxic phase Overlooking vaccination requirements and prevention counselling for travellers Not instituting appropriate isolation and public-health notification pending exclusion of viral haemorrhagic fever Yellow fever virus, an RNA flavivirus, is inoculated by an infected mosquito and spreads via lymphatics and blood to target organs, with marked hepatotropism. Infection and death of hepatocytes (with characteristic midzonal necrosis and Councilman bodies) impair synthesis of clotting factors and cause jaundice, while direct renal injury produces acute kidney injury. The combination of coagulopathy, thrombocytopenia and vascular injury drives the haemorrhagic manifestations, and a dysregulated inflammatory response contributes to shock and multi-organ failure in the toxic phase. Many infections are mild or self-limiting and recover fully. Once the toxic phase develops, mortality is high, with death typically from hepatic and renal failure, bleeding and shock; survivors of the toxic phase generally recover without chronic sequelae.

diagnostic and monitoring tool Failing to recognise a mixed germ-cell component that alters management Choosing overly radical surgery when fertility-sparing treatment is appropriate Ovarian yolk sac tumour is a malignant germ-cell neoplasm that differentiates towards extra-embryonic yolk sac and allantoic structures, recapitulating the endodermal sinus of the developing embryo. This differentiation explains the production of alpha-fetoprotein, a normal yolk sac product, which serves as a specific serum marker. Histologically the tumour displays diverse patterns, the most recognisable being the Schiller-Duval body, a papillary tuft with a central capillary that resembles a primitive glomerulus, together with intracellular and extracellular hyaline globules. The tumour grows rapidly and disseminates readily within the abdomen, but its germ-cell lineage confers marked sensitivity to chemotherapy, which underpins the possibility of cure even in advanced disease. Historically dismal but now substantially improved by platinum-based chemotherapy; early-stage disease has a high cure rate, and even advanced tumours can be cured, with AFP trends guiding treatment.

of graft-versus-host disease from non-irradiated blood products Complications following live vaccination Severe autoimmune cytopenia Being falsely reassured by a normal total lymphocyte count and not measuring subsets Overlooking the functional CD4 defect because CD4 numbers appear normal Confusing the CD8 lymphopenia with an MHC class I (TAP) defect without protein or genetic testing Giving live vaccines or non-irradiated blood products before diagnosis Delaying referral for transplantation ZAP70 (zeta-chain associated protein kinase of 70 kDa) is a tyrosine kinase that couples the engaged T-cell receptor to downstream signalling and is essential for the positive selection of thymocytes. Its deficiency blocks the selection and export of CD8 single-positive T cells, so peripheral CD8 cells are essentially absent, while CD4 T cells are selected and reach the circulation in normal numbers but cannot signal properly through the receptor and are therefore non-functional. The absent cytotoxic compartment and the functionally paralysed CD4 cells together produce a combined immunodeficiency with impaired cellular immunity and, through defective T-cell help, poor antibody responses. Without treatment the condition is fatal in early childhood from infection, but allogeneic haematopoietic stem cell transplantation, particularly when performed early, is curative and offers an excellent chance of long-term immune reconstitution.

Zellweger syndrome — cerebrohepatorenal syndrome, PEX gene disorder, peroxisome biogenesis disorder, Zellweger spectrum disorder, PBD-ZSD Other neonatal hypotonia and encephalopathy syndromes Single peroxisomal enzyme defects (for example X-linked adrenoleukodystrophy, D-bifunctional protein deficiency) Congenital muscular dystrophies and congenital myopathies Chromosomal and other multiple congenital anomaly syndromes Rhizomelic chondrodysplasia punctata Neonatal metabolic encephalopathies of other causes Plasma very-long-chain fatty acid profile (raised) as the key screening test Erythrocyte plasmalogen levels (reduced) and plasma bile acid intermediates Molecular genetic testing of the PEX genes Neuroimaging assessing neuronal migration defects and white matter change Renal ultrasound for cortical cysts and skeletal imaging for stippled epiphyses Hearing and ophthalmological assessment and liver function tests Autosomal recessive peroxisome biogenesis disorder caused by variants in one of many PEX genes, most often PEX1 It is the most severe end of the Zellweger spectrum, which also includes neonatal adrenoleukodystrophy and infantile Refsum disease Failure of peroxisome assembly impairs multiple peroxisomal functions, including very-long-chain fatty acid beta-oxidation and plasmalogen synthesis The biochemical signature is raised plasma very-long-chain fatty acids, with low plasmalogens and abnormal bile acid intermediates Neonates present with profound hypotonia, poor feeding, seizures, a characteristic dysmorphic facies and a large fontanelle Hepatic dysfunction, renal cortical cysts and chondrodysplasia punctata (stippled epiphyses) are supporting features Sensorineural deafness and retinal and other ocular abnormalities are common There is no curative treatment; management is supportive and the classic form is usually fatal in infancy Profound neonatal hypotonia with seizures and poor feeding Dysmorphic facies with a large fontanelle and hepatic dysfunction Progressive deterioration with apnoea and failure to thrive Coagulopathy or bleeding from hepatic involvement Attributing severe neonatal hypotonia to a neuromuscular disorder without checking peroxisomal biochemistry Missing the diagnosis by not requesting very-long-chain fatty acids Overlooking associated hearing and visual impairment that affect management Failing to recognise milder Zellweger spectrum phenotypes presenting later Peroxisomes are organelles that carry out several essential metabolic reactions, including the beta-oxidation of very-long-chain fatty acids, synthesis of ether phospholipids (plasmalogens) and bile acids, and detoxification of hydrogen peroxide. PEX genes encode peroxins required to assemble the peroxisomal membrane and import matrix enzymes. In Zellweger syndrome, defective peroxins prevent normal peroxisome assembly, so matrix enzymes are not imported and are degraded, leaving functionally empty or absent peroxisomes. The resulting accumulation of very-long-chain fatty acids and deficiency of plasmalogens disrupt membrane and myelin integrity and neuronal migration, producing the severe multisystem, and particularly neurological, phenotype. The classic Zellweger phenotype carries a very poor prognosis, with most affected infants dying within the first year of life. Milder disorders within the Zellweger spectrum have longer survival with progressive neurological, hepatic, visual and hearing impairment.

Zenker diverticulum — pharyngeal pouch, pharyngo-oesophageal diverticulum, hypopharyngeal diverticulum Oesophageal or pharyngeal malignancy Achalasia and other oesophageal motility disorders Peptic or other benign oesophageal stricture Globus sensation Neurological causes of oropharyngeal dysphagia such as stroke or Parkinson disease Barium swallow to demonstrate and size the pouch Careful upper endoscopy where malignancy needs exclusion, with awareness of perforation risk Videofluoroscopic swallow study to assess swallowing mechanics Assessment for aspiration including chest imaging when respiratory symptoms are present Oesophageal manometry in selected cases to characterise sphincter dysfunction Presents in older adults with oropharyngeal dysphagia, regurgitation of undigested food, halitosis, a gurgling neck and sometimes a palpable neck swelling Regurgitation of retained food, especially at night, predisposes to cough and aspiration pneumonia It is a false (pulsion) diverticulum, a mucosal herniation through Killian's dehiscence, a weak area between the two parts of the inferior pharyngeal constrictor Underlying incoordination and impaired relaxation of the upper oesophageal sphincter (cricopharyngeus) drives pouch formation Barium swallow is the preferred diagnostic test and clearly outlines the posterior midline pouch above the sphincter Passing an endoscope or nasogastric tube blindly risks perforating the pouch, so caution is required Symptomatic pouches are treated by dividing the cricopharyngeus with endoscopic stapling or laser, or by open surgical diverticulectomy with myotomy Recurrent aspiration pneumonia Significant weight loss or rapidly progressive dysphagia raising concern for malignancy A new hard neck mass or bleeding, since carcinoma can rarely arise within a long-standing pouch Complete dysphagia or inability to maintain nutrition and hydration Blindly intubating the oesophagus or passing tubes and perforating the pouch Attributing dysphagia to age or reflux without imaging the pharynx Overlooking aspiration as a cause of recurrent chest infection Failing to divide the cricopharyngeus, which risks recurrence after simple pouch removal Zenker diverticulum is an acquired outpouching of pharyngeal mucosa through Killian's dehiscence, a triangular zone of muscular weakness between the oblique and horizontal fibres of the inferior pharyngeal constrictor just above the upper oesophageal sphincter. Impaired relaxation and reduced compliance of the cricopharyngeus muscle raise hypopharyngeal pressure during swallowing, and this repeated pressure forces the mucosa and submucosa through the weak point, creating a false (pulsion) diverticulum. As the pouch enlarges it retains food and secretions, causing regurgitation, halitosis and a risk of aspiration. Small asymptomatic pouches may be observed, while symptomatic pouches respond well to endoscopic or surgical treatment, though recurrence and, rarely, malignant change within a chronic pouch can occur.

Zieve syndrome — Zieve's syndrome, alcoholic hyperlipaemia with haemolysis Autoimmune haemolytic anaemia Alcoholic hepatitis without haemolysis Biliary obstruction or choledocholithiasis Acute pancreatitis with hypertriglyceridaemia Spur-cell haemolytic anaemia of advanced liver disease Haemolysis from another cause such as G6PD deficiency Full blood count and blood film assessing for haemolysis Reticulocyte count, lactate dehydrogenase, haptoglobin and unconjugated bilirubin Direct antiglobulin (Coombs) test, expected to be negative Fasting lipid profile demonstrating transient hyperlipidaemia Liver function tests and abdominal ultrasound to characterise the liver and exclude obstruction Alcohol and dietary history A self-limiting triad of haemolytic anaemia, transient hyperlipidaemia and jaundice occurring after heavy alcohol use, usually on a background of fatty liver or alcoholic hepatitis Should be suspected when jaundice and anaemia in an alcohol-dependent patient are accompanied by an unexpectedly high lipid profile The haemolysis is Coombs-negative, distinguishing it from autoimmune haemolytic anaemia Abdominal pain and tender hepatomegaly are common, mimicking other acute hepatobiliary emergencies Bilirubin is disproportionately elevated relative to the degree of hepatocellular injury because of the haemolytic contribution The hyperlipidaemia and haemolysis typically resolve within weeks of alcohol cessation and supportive care Recognition avoids unnecessary invasive haemolysis and biliary work-up, as the condition remits with abstinence Severe symptomatic anaemia requiring urgent transfusion Features of decompensated alcoholic hepatitis or liver failure Signs of biliary obstruction or cholangitis needing intervention Very high triglycerides with associated pancreatitis Mislabelling the haemolysis as autoimmune and starting inappropriate immunosuppression Attributing all the jaundice to hepatocellular disease and missing the haemolytic contribution Undertaking extensive haemolysis or biliary investigations before considering the diagnosis Overlooking the transient hyperlipidaemia, a key clue to the syndrome Zieve syndrome develops in the setting of alcohol-related liver injury, where transient hyperlipidaemia and abnormal red-cell membrane lipid composition render erythrocytes fragile and prone to haemolysis. Pyruvate-kinase instability and altered red-cell membrane cholesterol and phospholipid content, together with the effects of acute alcohol excess, are thought to shorten red-cell survival. The combination of haemolysis-driven unconjugated hyperbilirubinaemia and coexisting cholestatic liver injury produces marked jaundice, while the associated hyperlipidaemia is characteristically transient and resolves with abstinence. The syndrome is self-limiting and carries a good prognosis with alcohol cessation and supportive care, though the underlying alcohol-related liver disease governs the longer-term outlook.

Zika virus infection — ZIKV, Zika fever, Zika virus disease Dengue fever Chikungunya Measles and rubella Parvovirus B19 infection Leptospirosis Other flaviviral febrile illnesses Drug reaction with rash Acute rheumatological illness with arthralgia and rash Enteroviral exanthem RT-PCR of serum and urine during the acute viraemic phase Zika IgM serology with confirmatory neutralisation testing given flavivirus cross-reactivity Fetal ultrasound surveillance in infected pregnant women Concurrent testing for dengue and chikungunya in co-endemic settings Nerve conduction studies if Guillain-Barre syndrome is suspected A mosquito-borne flavivirus spread chiefly by Aedes aegypti and Aedes albopictus, the same vectors as dengue and chikungunya Most infections are asymptomatic or mild; when symptomatic, features include low-grade fever, maculopapular rash, arthralgia and notably non-purulent conjunctivitis The major clinical concern is congenital infection: maternal Zika in pregnancy can cause microcephaly and a broader congenital Zika syndrome It is also associated with Guillain-Barre syndrome as a post-infectious complication Beyond mosquito bites, sexual and vertical transmission are recognised, which influences counselling and prevention India has reported local outbreaks, so it should be considered alongside dengue and chikungunya in febrile patients with rash Management is supportive; there is no specific antiviral therapy or licensed vaccine Diagnosis uses RT-PCR in blood and urine during acute viraemia, with serology complicated by cross-reactivity among flaviviruses Infection or exposure during pregnancy, given risk of severe congenital malformation Progressive ascending weakness suggesting Guillain-Barre syndrome and possible respiratory failure Features overlapping with dengue warning signs that require exclusion of severe dengue Neurological deterioration warranting urgent evaluation Assuming a dengue-like febrile rash illness cannot be Zika in co-endemic regions Failing to counsel about sexual transmission and pregnancy risk after exposure Over-relying on serology alone given cross-reactivity with other flaviviruses Missing evolving Guillain-Barre syndrome in a recently infected patient Zika virus is an RNA flavivirus that, after inoculation by an Aedes mosquito, replicates in dendritic cells and spreads via lymphatics and blood. It has particular tropism for neural progenitor cells, which underlies its ability to disrupt fetal brain development when it crosses the placenta, producing microcephaly and other structural anomalies. Immune-mediated mechanisms, including molecular mimicry, are implicated in the associated Guillain-Barre syndrome. The virus can persist in immune-privileged sites such as semen, enabling sexual transmission. In non-pregnant adults the illness is usually mild and self-limiting with full recovery. The serious burden lies in adverse pregnancy and neonatal outcomes from congenital infection and in Guillain-Barre syndrome, which can cause prolonged disability or, rarely, death.

Zinc deficiency — hypozincaemia, acrodermatitis enteropathica Other nutritional deficiency dermatoses (for example essential fatty acid or biotin deficiency) Necrolytic migratory erythema of glucagonoma Atopic or seborrhoeic dermatitis Chronic mucocutaneous candidiasis Other causes of growth failure in children Serum zinc, interpreted alongside albumin and inflammatory markers Assessment for malabsorption and chronic gastrointestinal losses Dietary history focusing on cereal-based, high-phytate diets Skin examination and biopsy if the diagnosis is uncertain Evaluation for the inherited disorder in an infant with typical features Characteristic features include a periorificial and acral dermatitis, diarrhoea, alopecia, impaired wound healing, and altered taste In children it causes growth faltering, recurrent infection, and delayed sexual maturation Acquired deficiency arises with malabsorption, high-phytate cereal-based diets, chronic diarrhoea, extensive burns, and prolonged unsupplemented parenteral nutrition The inherited disorder acrodermatitis enteropathica reflects defective intestinal zinc absorption and presents in infancy Zinc supplementation reduces the duration and severity of acute diarrhoea in young children, a key public health measure in India and other low-income settings The rash can closely mimic other nutritional dermatoses and is often initially misdiagnosed Serum zinc is an imperfect marker because it falls with inflammation and hypoalbuminaemia, so results need cautious interpretation Severe dermatitis with secondary infection or extensive skin breakdown Failure to thrive with recurrent serious infection in a child Severe or persistent diarrhoea with dehydration Deficiency in a patient on prolonged parenteral nutrition without trace element supplementation Interpreting a low serum zinc without accounting for inflammation and low albumin Mistaking the dermatitis for eczema or another primary skin disease Forgetting trace element provision during long-term parenteral nutrition Overlooking high dietary phytate as a cause of poor absorption Zinc is a component or regulator of hundreds of enzymes and transcription factors and is essential for cell division, protein synthesis, immune function, and epithelial integrity. Deficiency therefore most affects rapidly dividing and metabolically active tissues, producing dermatitis, impaired wound healing, mucosal disease, immune dysfunction, and, in children, growth and developmental impairment. Dietary phytates in cereals and legumes bind zinc and reduce its absorption, while malabsorptive states, excess gastrointestinal or urinary losses, and increased demand in growth, pregnancy, and tissue repair contribute to negative balance. Both acquired and inherited deficiency respond well to zinc repletion, with rapid resolution of skin and gastrointestinal features; the inherited form requires lifelong supplementation.

Zinner syndrome — Zinner syndrome, seminal vesicle cyst with renal agenesis, mesonephric duct malformation triad Isolated seminal vesicle cyst without a renal anomaly Midline mullerian duct cyst Midline prostatic utricle cyst Ejaculatory duct cyst or obstruction from other causes Bladder or ureteric diverticulum Cystic pelvic mass of another origin Pelvic MRI to define the cyst and ejaculatory duct anatomy and to confirm renal agenesis Abdominal ultrasound or CT to document the absent or dysplastic ipsilateral kidney Transrectal ultrasound to characterise the seminal vesicle cyst Semen analysis where fertility is a concern, which may show low volume or oligo/azoospermia Assessment of renal function given a solitary functioning kidney Cyst aspiration for cytology or culture if infection or diagnostic doubt arises A rare congenital malformation comprising the triad of a seminal vesicle cyst, ipsilateral renal agenesis or dysplasia, and ejaculatory duct obstruction It arises from maldevelopment of the distal mesonephric (Wolffian) duct during embryogenesis, which affects both the ureteric bud and the seminal vesicle on the same side Often silent until early adulthood, when the seminal vesicle cyst enlarges and causes perineal or pelvic pain, painful ejaculation, dysuria, haematospermia, or infertility It is regarded as the male counterpart of Mayer-Rokitansky-Kuster-Hauser syndrome in females Pelvic MRI is the investigation of choice, demonstrating the cyst, the absent ipsilateral kidney, and the associated ductal anatomy It may be discovered incidentally during imaging performed for other reasons or during an infertility evaluation Management ranges from surveillance of small asymptomatic cysts to aspiration or surgical excision, increasingly by a laparoscopic or robotic approach, for symptomatic lesions Infection or abscess formation within the cyst Obstructive uropathy or any compromise of the solitary functioning kidney Rapid enlargement or atypical imaging features raising concern for neoplasm Intractable pain or infertility significantly affecting quality of life Overlooking the associated renal agenesis and its implications for a solitary kidney Mistaking a laterally placed seminal vesicle cyst for a midline mullerian or utricle cyst Attributing symptoms to prostatitis and missing the underlying congenital malformation Failing to consider the diagnosis in a young man with painful ejaculation and infertility During embryogenesis the mesonephric (Wolffian) duct gives rise to the ureteric bud and to the seminal vesicle, vas deferens and ejaculatory duct. An insult to the distal mesonephric duct early in gestation disrupts ureteric bud induction of the metanephros, causing ipsilateral renal agenesis, while the maldeveloped duct produces an obstructed, cystically dilated seminal vesicle. The result is the characteristic ipsilateral triad of cyst, absent kidney and ejaculatory duct obstruction. The outlook is excellent for small asymptomatic cysts managed conservatively, and symptomatic cases generally do well after aspiration or excision, although fertility depends on the degree of ejaculatory duct obstruction and on contralateral function.

Zollinger-Ellison syndrome — ZES, gastrinoma syndrome, gastric acid hypersecretion syndrome Helicobacter pylori-associated peptic ulcer disease NSAID-induced ulceration Idiopathic gastro-oesophageal reflux disease Other causes of hypergastrinaemia (proton pump inhibitor use, atrophic gastritis, renal failure) Other secretory diarrhoeas (VIPoma, carcinoid, coeliac disease) Retained gastric antrum or antral G-cell hyperplasia Chronic pancreatitis or bile acid diarrhoea Fasting serum gastrin off acid suppression where safe Gastric pH or acid output measurement to confirm hypersecretion Secretin stimulation test in equivocal cases Upper gastrointestinal endoscopy documenting ulcers, prominent gastric folds and reflux disease Somatostatin receptor PET/CT and cross-sectional imaging to locate and stage the gastrinoma Serum calcium, PTH and prolactin with MEN1 genetic testing Chromogranin A for monitoring tumour burden Clinical syndrome of gastric acid hypersecretion, severe or refractory peptic ulcer disease and diarrhoea caused by a gastrin-secreting neuroendocrine tumour (gastrinoma) Suspect it with multiple or recurrent ulcers, ulcers in unusual sites (distal duodenum or jejunum), ulcers refractory to therapy or recurring after Helicobacter eradication, and ulcers accompanied by diarrhoea Diarrhoea is common and sometimes dominant, and characteristically improves with acid suppression, which helps distinguish it from other secretory diarrhoeas Diagnosis requires a raised fasting serum gastrin together with demonstrated gastric acid hypersecretion (low gastric pH); a positive secretin stimulation test supports equivocal cases Proton pump inhibition is the cornerstone of symptom control and is often needed at higher-than-standard doses; it must be interrupted carefully before gastrin testing Around one-quarter of cases occur within MEN1, so hypercalcaemia and other endocrine features should be actively sought Gastro-oesophageal reflux and oesophagitis with their complications are common because of the acid load Complications include ulcer haemorrhage, perforation and stricture, and long-standing untreated disease carries substantial morbidity Upper gastrointestinal haemorrhage, perforation or obstruction from ulcer disease Ulcers refractory despite adequate acid suppression and Helicobacter eradication Severe dehydration or electrolyte disturbance from high-volume diarrhoea Evidence of metastatic gastrinoma Hypercalcaemia or other features indicating MEN1 Diagnosing on gastrin alone without confirming acid hypersecretion, since proton pump inhibitors raise gastrin physiologically Under-dosing acid suppression and accepting persistent symptoms Discontinuing acid suppression abruptly for testing without safeguards, risking ulcer complications Missing MEN1 and its implications for surgery and family screening Overlooking that MEN1-related hypercalcaemia can worsen gastrin secretion and acid output In Zollinger-Ellison syndrome, autonomous gastrin secretion from a gastrinoma stimulates enterochromaffin-like and parietal cells, producing sustained hyperchlorhydria. The excess acid overwhelms mucosal defences, causing multiple and refractory peptic ulcers throughout the upper gastrointestinal tract, and inactivates pancreatic lipase while injuring the small bowel mucosa, resulting in maldigestion and secretory diarrhoea. Hypergastrinaemia also drives enterochromaffin-like cell hyperplasia, which in MEN1 may progress to type 2 gastric neuroendocrine tumours. The tumour itself may be sporadic or arise within MEN1. With effective proton pump inhibition the acid-related morbidity of Zollinger-Ellison syndrome is largely controllable, so long-term prognosis is dictated by the behaviour of the underlying gastrinoma, particularly whether hepatic metastases are present.

Zoon balanitis — plasma cell balanitis, balanitis circumscripta plasmacellularis Erythroplasia of Queyrat (penile carcinoma in situ) Lichen planus of the glans Psoriasis Candidal or other infective balanitis Fixed drug eruption Lichen sclerosus Clinical assessment of the characteristic plaque Biopsy to confirm plasma-cell infiltrate and exclude carcinoma in situ Swabs to exclude infective balanitis where relevant Assessment of foreskin and hygiene factors Follow-up to ensure resolution and exclude malignancy A benign chronic inflammatory dermatosis of the glans and prepuce, occurring almost exclusively in uncircumcised men It presents as a well-demarcated, shiny, red-orange plaque, sometimes with pinpoint (cayenne pepper) spots It is a diagnosis often confirmed by biopsy showing a dense plasma-cell infiltrate Chronic irritation under the foreskin, with poor aeration and retained smegma, is thought to drive it The main concern is to exclude erythroplasia of Queyrat (penile carcinoma in situ) and lichen planus It often responds to improved hygiene, topical anti-inflammatory treatment, and definitively to circumcision Features suggesting erythroplasia of Queyrat or invasive carcinoma Failure to respond to conservative treatment Ulceration or induration Progressive or atypical lesion Missing penile carcinoma in situ, which can look similar Treating it as candidal balanitis without response Not biopsying a persistent or atypical lesion Overlooking the role of the foreskin and hygiene Zoon balanitis is a chronic reactive mucosal inflammation of the glans and prepuce characterised histologically by a band-like dermal infiltrate rich in plasma cells. It is thought to result from chronic low-grade irritation, friction, moisture and retained smegma beneath the foreskin, since it occurs in uncircumcised men and typically resolves after circumcision. It is not an infection or a premalignant condition, though its appearance overlaps with penile carcinoma in situ, necessitating exclusion of the latter. The condition is benign and often resolves with conservative measures or circumcision, though it can be chronic and relapsing if predisposing factors persist.
